preface.title: How to Read This Book
preface.p: This book assumes algebra, trigonometry, and single-variable calculus: limits, continuity, derivatives and their product and chain rules, the Mean Value Theorem, definite integrals, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and basic substitution. It does not assume prior multivariable calculus, differential geometry, or exterior algebra. Vectors and the linear algebra used in the book are developed in Chapters 13.

Read sections in the order presented. A worked example may introduce a new idea before its formal definition; the explanation supplies the tools needed for the following checkpoints. Looking-ahead remarks motivate later topics and do not add prerequisites to the current exercises. When a theorem's proof is deferred, its statement may be used under its stated hypotheses, but the forward reference is not a proof already given. The appendices are references, not additional assumed background unless a passage explicitly directs you to the needed explanation.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

introduction.p: Coordinates turn points, displacements, and geometric shapes into objects we can calculate with. Starting from algebra and the Pythagorean theorem, we develop vectors, linear combinations, bases, distance, and equations of lines and planes. These supply the language used by the later calculus.

section.title: Why multivariable calculus begins with geometry
section.p: Single-variable calculus lived on a line. A point was described by one number, and there were only two directions to move: left or right. But many real-life questions do not live on a real line. A storm moves across a map, a satellite moves through space, and the temperature in a room depends on where you stand.

subsection.title: From one input to many inputs
subsection.p: Imagine a small weather station on the coast. A radar image says that the center of a storm cell is 12 \text{ km east}, \qquad 5 \text{ km north} of the station. The location is naturally written as the ordered pair P=(12,5). A helicopter hovering above the same point needs a third number. If it is 0.8 km above the ground, its position is H=(12,5,0.8).

The numbers in these lists do not all have the same meaning. The first two numbers locate a point on a flat map. The third number locates height. But the idea is the same: a position is described by several coordinates.

figure.caption: The storm moves from P to Q, requiring a larger coordinate grid.

subsection.p: This is the first reason multivariable calculus begins with geometry. Before we can differentiate or integrate, we need to know where things are.

subsection.title: Position, displacement, and measured quantities
subsection.p: Now suppose the storm moves. One hour later its center is Q=(15,9). We can subtract the coordinates to find the displacement: Q-P=(15-12,\;9-5)=(3,4). That means the storm moved 3 km east and 4 km north.
If it moved in a straight line, the distance traveled is found from the same Pythagorean theorem used in the plane: \sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5 \text{ km}.

example.title: A storm displacement

statement.p: The point P=(12,5) is a location. The ordered pair (3,4) is a displacement. It tells us how to move from P to Q: (12,5)+(3,4)=(15,9). The same displacement could start somewhere else: (2,1)+(3,4)=(5,5). So a displacement is not tied to one fixed place. It can be applied to any point.

subsection.p: This distinction is small, but it will save us from confusion later.
A point is a location. A vector is a displacement. Coordinates let us write both with ordered lists, but the meanings are different.

statement.p: One drone lifts off from the rooftop R=(2,1); a second drone lifts off from a different rooftop S=(7,3). Both receive the same instruction, the displacement (4,4). Without computing either landing point, decide two things and say why: do the drones end at the same place, and does the pair (4,4) on its own tell you where either drone is? In one sentence, what does a displacement record, and what does it deliberately leave out?

hint.p: Ask what question each ordered pair answers. A point answers where?; a displacement answers which way, and how far? Try applying the same instruction at two different starting points and notice whether the change depends on where you began.

subsection.title: A first story: locating a storm, a satellite, and a temperature reading
subsection.p: The same coordinates can also be used as inputs to a function.

At the point (12,5), a weather sensor might report a temperature of 18^\circC. Then temperature is not itself a point. It is a number assigned to a point: T(12,5)=18. If the temperature is measured over a whole region, we have a function T(x,y). The input is a point on a map, and the output is a number.
A satellite position is different. At time t, the satellite has three coordinates: \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)). Here the input is one number, time, but the output is a point in space.
So several kinds of functions will appear in this book:

table.title: Kinds of functions appearing in this book.

subsection.p: The last example is especially important. A wind field assigns an arrow to every point. At one point the wind may blow east; at another, northeast; at another, not at all. Later, this idea will become a vector field. Vector fields are the natural language of fluids, force, electricity, magnetism, and many of the integral theorems near the end of the book.

statement.p: On the same weather map, the temperature reading T(x,y) and the wind \mathbf F(x,y) are both functions of position. Yet only one of them is called a vector field. Without writing any formulas, explain what the wind output carries at each point that the temperature output does not, and why that difference is exactly what earns the wind the name vector field.

hint.p: Picture standing at one spot and asking, What does this map hand me here? The thermometer hands you a single number; the wind hands you something you could draw as an arrow. Think about what an arrow records that a number alone cannot.

subsection.title: What changes from single-variable calculus, and what stays the same
subsection.p: Single-variable calculus asked questions like these: \text{How fast is } f(x) \text{ changing?} and \text{How much has accumulated from } a \text{ to } b?
Those questions remain. But the geometry changes.

For a function of one variable, the graph is a curve in the plane. At a point, there is one main direction to move along the input line. For a function of two variables, the graph is usually a surface in space. At a point in the input plane, there are infinitely many directions to move.
A hiker standing on a hillside can walk north, south, east, west, or along any slanted path between them. A single slope number no longer tells the whole story.

exercise.title: Why one slope is not enough?

statement.p: On a single-variable graph, asking how steep is it here? has one answer. On a hillside, the same question feels incomplete until you add something. What is the missing piece of information that the hiker must supply before how steep? becomes a sensible question, and why did that piece never come up on the number line?

hint.p: On a line there were only two ways to move, so the answer was forced. On a hill the hiker gets to choose a way to step. Think about what changes between facing uphill and facing along the slope at the same spot.

subsection.p: The old ideas will return in new forms:

table.title: How single-variable ideas reappear in several variables.

row.cell: rates of change in many directions

subsection.p: The last line is the beginning of the long story of the book. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus will not disappear. It will generalize.

For now, the next step is much simpler. The difference between two locations behaves like a reusable instruction: \text{move } 3 \text{ east and } 4 \text{ north}. That instruction is the first object we need to understand carefully. It is called a vector.

section.title: Vectors in the plane and in space
section.p: The storm story in the previous section used two kinds of objects. Points told us where something was. Displacements told us how to move from one point to another. Those displacements are the vectors.

subsection.title: Vectors as arrows, displacements, and ordered lists
subsection.p: A drone starts at P=(1,2,1) where the coordinates are measured in meters: east, north, and up. It receives the instruction \mathbf v=(4,-1,3). This means: 4 \text{ meters east}, \qquad 1 \text{ meter south}, \qquad 3 \text{ meters up}. After carrying out the instruction, the drone is at P+\mathbf v=(1,2,1)+(4,-1,3)=(5,1,4).

example.title: The same vector in different places

statement.p: The vector \mathbf v=(4,-1,3) can be drawn with its tail at the point (1,2,1), but it does not belong only there. If the same drone instruction starts at A=(10,0,2), then the endpoint is A+\mathbf v=(14,-1,5). The arrow has moved, but the displacement is the same.
A vector in the plane is an ordered pair \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2). A vector in space is an ordered triple \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3). The numbers v_1,v_2,v_3 are called the components of the vector.

subsection.p: The zero vector is \mathbf 0=(0,0) in the plane and \mathbf 0=(0,0,0) in space. It means no displacement.

subsection.title: Addition and scalar multiplication
subsection.p: Suppose a kayak moves through still water with displacement \mathbf p=(3,1) during a short time interval. At the same time, the current pushes it by \mathbf c=(1,2). The actual displacement is \mathbf p+\mathbf c=(3,1)+(1,2)=(4,3). Vector addition adds the motions component by component.

statement.p: For vectors in the plane, \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2), their sum is \mathbf u+\mathbf v=(u_1+v_1,\;u_2+v_2). If c is a number, then c\mathbf u=(cu_1,\;cu_2). The same rules hold in space: (u_1,u_2,u_3)+(v_1,v_2,v_3)=(u_1+v_1,\;u_2+v_2,\;u_3+v_3), and c(u_1,u_2,u_3)=(cu_1,\;cu_2,\;cu_3).

subsection.p: Geometrically, \mathbf u+\mathbf v is found by placing the tail of \mathbf v at the head of \mathbf u. The combined displacement goes from the first tail to the last head.

figure.caption: Adding vectors by placing arrows head-to-tail.

subsection.p: Multiplying by c stretches or reverses a vector. For example, if \mathbf u=(3,1), then 2\mathbf u=(6,2), \qquad -\mathbf u=(-3,-1), \qquad \frac12\mathbf u=\left(\frac32,\frac12\right). The vector 2\mathbf u points in the same direction as \mathbf u and is twice as long. The vector -\mathbf u points in the opposite direction.

exercise.title: What does a negative scalar do?

statement.p: You scale a nonzero vector \mathbf u by some number c. For which values of c does c\mathbf u still point the same way as \mathbf u, and for which does it point the opposite way? What single value of c collapses the arrow to no displacement at all?

hint.p: Try a few cases like c=2, c=\tfrac12, and c=-1, and watch only the direction of the arrow, not its length. Where does the dividing line between same way and opposite way sit on the number line?

subsection.title: Linear combinations and spans
subsection.p: A city map gives two basic walking instructions: \mathbf e=(1,0), \qquad \mathbf n=(0,1). Here \mathbf e means one block east, and \mathbf n means one block north. Then 4\mathbf e+3\mathbf n=(4,0)+(0,3)=(4,3). So the instruction walk 4 blocks east and 3 blocks north is built from the two basic directions.

statement.p: A vector of the form a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v is called a linear combination of \mathbf u and \mathbf v. The numbers a and b are called coefficients.

subsection.p: The same idea works with more vectors: a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v+c\mathbf w. A linear combination is just a recipe: take some amount of each vector and add the results.

example.title: Two directions may fill the plane

statement.p: Every vector (x,y) in the plane can be written as (x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1). So the two basic vectors (1,0), \qquad (0,1) can build every displacement in the plane.

The span of vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v is the set of all their linear combinations: \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u,\mathbf v\}=\{a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v : a,b\in\mathbb R\}. For one vector, \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}=\{a\mathbf u : a\in\mathbb R\}.

subsection.p: The word span means all the places these directions can reach if we are allowed to scale them and add them.

exercise.title: Why is the origin always in a span?

statement.p: No matter which vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v you start with, the zero vector \mathbf 0 always belongs to \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u,\mathbf v\}. Why must this be true for every span?

hint.p: A span is the set of all linear combinations a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v. Is there a choice of the coefficients a and b that is always allowed and that always lands you back at \mathbf 0?

subsection.title: Lines through the origin and planes through the origin
subsection.p: Start with one nonzero vector in the plane: \mathbf u=(2,1). Its span is \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}=\{t(2,1):t\in\mathbb R\}. Writing out a few values gives the points in .

table.title: A few points on the span of (2,1).

figure.caption: The span of one nonzero vector is a line through the origin.

subsection.p: In space, one nonzero vector also spans a line through the origin. Two genuinely different directions can span a plane. For example, \mathbf u=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,0). Then a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v=a(1,0,0)+b(0,1,0)=(a,b,0). This is the xy-plane: z=0.

definition.title: Lines and planes through the origin

subsection.p: The condition not multiples of each other matters. If \mathbf u=(1,2,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(2,4,0), then \mathbf v=2\mathbf u. The two vectors look like two directions, but they are really the same direction with different lengths. Their span is still only a line, not a plane.
This is our first encounter with redundancy. Later we will give it a name: linear dependence.

subsection.title: Affine lines and affine planes: translating a span
subsection.p: So far, every line and plane passed through the origin. Most lines and planes do not.

A trail in space starts at the campsite P=(1,2,0) and follows the direction \mathbf u=(2,0,1). A point on the trail has the form P+t\mathbf u=(1,2,0)+t(2,0,1). For example, t=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad (1,2,0), and t=3 \quad \Rightarrow \quad (1,2,0)+3(2,0,1)=(7,2,3).
The expression P+t\mathbf u means: start at the point P, then move by the vector t\mathbf u.

statement.p: Let P be a point.
The affine line through P in the direction \mathbf u\neq \mathbf 0 is P+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}=\{P+t\mathbf u:t\in\mathbb R\}.

If \mathbf u and \mathbf v are not multiples of each other, the affine plane through P in the directions \mathbf u and \mathbf v is P+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u,\mathbf v\}=\{P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v:s,t\in\mathbb R\}.

subsection.p: The word affine means that we have translated a line or plane away from the origin. The direction is still controlled by vectors. The starting location is controlled by the point P.

exercise.title: When is an affine line a line through the origin?

statement.p: An affine line has the form P+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}. Geometrically, how is it different from the plain line \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\} through the origin? Under what condition on the point P do the two lines actually coincide?

hint.p: Think of the affine line as the origin line slid over so that it passes through P instead of through \mathbf 0. What if P already lies on the original line? Use P=t_0\mathbf u to compare the sets of points.

example.title: A translated plane

statement.p: Let P=(0,0,2), \qquad \mathbf u=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,0). Then P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v=(0,0,2)+s(1,0,0)+t(0,1,0)=(s,t,2). This is the horizontal plane z=2. It has the same directions as the xy-plane, but it has been lifted two units upward.

subsection.p: Vectors let us talk about direction without caring where the arrow is drawn. Points let us anchor those directions to actual places. This is enough to describe many lines and planes, but something is still hidden: the coordinates themselves. Writing (3,2) quietly assumes that we have chosen an east direction, a north direction, and a unit of measurement. Change those choices, and the same geometric vector may get different coordinates. The next task is to understand what coordinates are really doing.

section.title: Coordinates and dimension
section.p: The last section ended with a quiet warning. A vector can be drawn as an arrow, but its coordinates depend on the directions and units we choose. Coordinates are not the vector itself; they are the vector written in a particular language.
That language is still powerful. It lets us describe locations, directions, lines, planes, and higher-dimensional data with the same simple algebra.

subsection.title: The spaces \mathbb R^2, \mathbb R^3, and \mathbb R^n
subsection.p: A small warehouse robot moves along three natural directions: east-west, north-south, and up-down. If it starts at the charging station and moves to (7,3,2), we may read this as 7 \text{ meters east}, \qquad 3 \text{ meters north}, \qquad 2 \text{ meters up}. The same list of numbers could describe a point, if we are locating the robot, or a vector, if we are describing a displacement.

Two coordinates give the plane: \mathbb R^2=\{(x,y):x,y\in\mathbb R\}. Three coordinates give ordinary space: \mathbb R^3=\{(x,y,z):x,y,z\in\mathbb R\}. There is no reason to stop at three coordinates. A weather station might record (\text{temperature},\text{pressure},\text{humidity},\text{wind speed}), which is a point in a four-dimensional data space. We cannot draw four perpendicular axes on a page, but the algebra still works.

statement.p: For a positive integer n, the space \mathbb R^n is the set of all ordered lists of n real numbers: \mathbb R^n=\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n):x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R\}. The numbers x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n are called the coordinates of the point, or the components of the vector.

subsection.p: The notation is the same for points and vectors because the same ordered lists are used for both. The meaning comes from the sentence around the notation.
For example, P=(7,3,2) may mean a location in the warehouse. But \mathbf v=(7,3,2) may mean a displacement: move 7 east, 3 north, and 2 up.

This is why we often use letters like P,Q,A,B for points and bold letters like \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w for vectors. The notation helps us remember the difference, even though the coordinates look alike.

subsection.title: Standard basis vectors
subsection.p: On a map, the coordinate pair (3,2) can be built from two basic moves: 3(1,0)+2(0,1)=(3,0)+(0,2)=(3,2). The vector (1,0) means one unit in the first coordinate direction. The vector (0,1) means one unit in the second coordinate direction.
These two vectors are so common that they get special names: \mathbf e_1=(1,0), \qquad \mathbf e_2=(0,1). In space we use \mathbf e_1=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf e_2=(0,1,0), \qquad \mathbf e_3=(0,0,1).

figure.caption: The standard basis vectors build the usual coordinates in the plane.

statement.p: In \mathbb R^n, the standard basis vector \mathbf e_j is the vector whose j-th component is 1 and whose other components are 0: \mathbf e_j=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0).

subsection.p: Every vector in \mathbb R^n is built from the standard basis vectors: (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=x_1\mathbf e_1+x_2\mathbf e_2+\cdots+x_n\mathbf e_n. This formula is more than two different types of notation. It says that coordinates are instructions: x_1 \text{ steps in direction } \mathbf e_1,\quad x_2 \text{ steps in direction } \mathbf e_2,\quad \ldots The standard coordinate system is the grid made from these standard directions.

exercise.title: What does a coordinate tell you to do?

statement.p: We wrote (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=x_1\mathbf e_1+x_2\mathbf e_2+\cdots+x_n\mathbf e_n and called the coordinates instructions. In your own words, what instruction does a single coordinate, say x_2, give, and why does the basis vector \mathbf e_2 make that instruction precise?

hint.p: Think of each \mathbf e_j as a single step in one pure direction. What role does the number x_2 play once you know which direction \mathbf e_2 points?

example.title: A displacement in space

statement.p: A drone displacement is \mathbf v=(4,-1,3). Using the standard basis in \mathbb R^3, \mathbf v=4\mathbf e_1-\mathbf e_2+3\mathbf e_3. So the command says: move 4 units in the first direction, -1 unit in the second direction, and 3 units in the third direction.

subsection.title: Coordinate descriptions of geometric objects
subsection.p: Coordinates let us describe entire geometric objects, not only single points.

A walking path in the plane starts at P=(2,1) and follows the direction \mathbf u=(3,2). The affine line from the previous section is P+t\mathbf u=(2,1)+t(3,2). Writing out the coordinates gives x=2+3t,\qquad y=1+2t. This is a parametric description of the line. The parameter t is a clock for the motion along the line.

We can also remove t. From x=2+3t we get t=\frac{x-2}{3}. Substituting into y=1+2t, y=1+\frac{2(x-2)}{3}. After simplifying, 2x-3y=1. So the same line has two descriptions: \boxed{(x,y)=(2,1)+t(3,2)} and \boxed{2x-3y=1.}
The parametric description tells us how to move along the line. The equation tells us how to test whether a point lies on the line.

exercise.title: Why keep two descriptions of one line?

statement.p: The same line was written both as (x,y)=(2,1)+t(3,2) and as 2x-3y=1. If both describe the very same set of points, why might you reach for one form rather than the other? Give a task that the parametric form handles easily and a task that the equation handles easily.

hint.p: One form is good at producing points on the line; the other is good at checking whether a given point belongs. Which is which?

example.title: A plane from two directions

statement.p: A tilted sheet of metal passes through the point P=(1,0,2) and contains the two directions \mathbf u=(1,2,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,1). Points on the sheet have the form P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v. Writing out the coordinates, (x,y,z)=(1,0,2)+s(1,2,0)+t(0,1,1), so x=1+s,\qquad y=2s+t,\qquad z=2+t. From the first and third equations, s=x-1,\qquad t=z-2. Substitute these into the equation for y: y=2(x-1)+(z-2)=2x+z-4. Thus the same plane can be written as \boxed{(x,y,z)=(1,0,2)+s(1,2,0)+t(0,1,1)} or as \boxed{2x-y+z=4.}

subsection.p: Equations and inequalities describe regions too. For example, 0\leq x\leq 12,\qquad 0\leq y\leq 8,\qquad 0\leq z\leq 3 describes a rectangular room that is 12 units long, 8 units wide, and 3 units high.

The set z=2 is a horizontal plane. The set x=5 is a vertical plane. The set x^2+y^2=1 in \mathbb R^3 is a cylinder of radius 1 around the z-axis. The equation does not mention z, so z is free to take any value.
This is a useful habit: when an equation does not mention one coordinate, the object extends freely in that coordinate direction.

subsection.title: When a picture stops being possible: why \mathbb R^n still works
subsection.p: The plane is easy to draw. Space is harder, but still visible. Four-dimensional space is different. There is no honest picture of four perpendicular coordinate axes in our ordinary three-dimensional world.
But many useful objects are naturally four-dimensional or higher.

A sensor in a greenhouse might record (T,p,h,c), where T=\text{temperature},\quad p=\text{pressure},\quad h=\text{humidity},\quad c=\text{carbon dioxide level}. This point lives in \mathbb R^4. A small change in the sensor reading might be \Delta \mathbf s=(2,-0.1,5,0.03). That means temperature rose by 2, pressure fell by 0.1, humidity rose by 5, and carbon dioxide level rose by 0.03.
We cannot draw this vector as an ordinary arrow. Still, we can add it, scale it, and compare it component by component: (T,p,h,c)+\Delta \mathbf s=(T+2,\;p-0.1,\;h+5,\;c+0.03).
That is why \mathbb R^n is not just a strange abstraction. It is the natural home for any situation described by n numbers.

exercise.title: Computing in \mathbb R^4 with no picture?

statement.p: We cannot draw the greenhouse reading (T,p,h,c) as an arrow in four perpendicular directions, yet we still added \Delta\mathbf s to it and compared components. What is it about the way addition and scaling are defined that lets the algebra keep working even after the picture disappears?

hint.p: Look back at how a sum or a scalar multiple is actually computed. Does any step require you to see the vectors, or does each step only touch the coordinates one at a time?

subsection.p:
The standard basis in \mathbb R^4 is
\mathbf e_1 \amp=(1,0,0,0), \mathbf e_2 \amp=(0,1,0,0), \mathbf e_3 \amp=(0,0,1,0), \mathbf e_4 \amp=(0,0,0,1).
So (T,p,h,c)=T\mathbf e_1+p\mathbf e_2+h\mathbf e_3+c\mathbf e_4. The picture disappears, but the coordinate story remains.

The standard basis works so efficiently that it hides the next question. What if we do not choose the standard directions? A city may have diagonal streets. A crystal may have slanted axes. A surface may carry its own natural grid. Some chosen directions work perfectly as coordinates; others are redundant or incomplete. The test for this is one of the most important ideas in the book: linear independence.

section.title: Linear independence and bases
section.p: The standard basis vectors from the last section did two jobs at once. They gave directions, and they gave coordinates. But not every list of directions can do that.
Some directions can be redundant. Other directions can be incomplete. To build a coordinate system, the directions must be neither redundant nor incomplete.

subsection.title: Redundant and nonredundant directions
subsection.p: Imagine a small robot on a flat floor. It has two movement buttons.

Button A moves the robot by \mathbf u=(2,1). Button B moves it by \mathbf v=(4,2). At first this looks like two directions. But \mathbf v=2\mathbf u. Button B is just a longer version of Button A. No combination of the two buttons can move the robot away from the line spanned by \mathbf u: a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v=a(2,1)+b(4,2)=(a+2b)(2,1). The robot has two buttons, but only one genuine direction.

Now replace Button B with a new button: \mathbf w=(1,3). The two directions \mathbf u=(2,1),\qquad \mathbf w=(1,3) are no longer copies of each other. For example, 3\mathbf u+2\mathbf w=3(2,1)+2(1,3)=(8,9). The robot can combine the two commands to reach many different directions in the plane. In fact, these two directions can build every vector in the plane.

figure.caption: Two arrows may be two copies of one direction, or they may give two genuine directions.

subsection.p: The equation 2\mathbf u-\mathbf v=\mathbf 0 reveals the redundancy in the first pair. It says that a nonzero combination of the vectors cancels out completely. That is the key idea.

statement.p: A list of vectors \mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_k is called linearly independent if the only way to make c_1\mathbf v_1+c_2\mathbf v_2+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k=\mathbf 0 is to use c_1=c_2=\cdots=c_k=0. If there is a nonzero choice of coefficients that gives the zero vector, the vectors are called linearly dependent.

subsection.p: A linear dependence relation is a sign that one direction is unnecessary. For example, 2(2,1)-(4,2)=(0,0) says that (4,2) is already built from (2,1).
A few immediate facts are worth keeping close:

table.title: Quick facts about independence.

row.cell: two vectors where one is a multiple of the other

subsection.p: The zero vector is always redundant because 1\cdot \mathbf 0=\mathbf 0 is a nontrivial zero combination.

exercise.title: Why can the zero vector never join an independent list?

statement.p: Suppose a list of vectors includes the zero vector \mathbf 0. Explain in your own words why such a list can never be linearly independent, no matter what the other vectors are.

hint.p: What happens if you take a nonzero multiple of \mathbf 0 and zero times every other vector? Is that combination forced to be trivial?

subsection.title: Linear independence in \mathbb R^2 and \mathbb R^3
subsection.p: In the plane, the picture is especially simple.

statement.p: Two vectors in \mathbb R^2 are linearly independent exactly when neither vector is a scalar multiple of the other.

proof.title: Why this is true
proof.p: If one vector is a multiple of the other, say \mathbf v=c\mathbf u, then c\mathbf u-\mathbf v=\mathbf 0. That is a nontrivial zero combination, so the vectors are dependent.

Conversely, suppose two vectors are dependent. Then there are numbers a and b, not both zero, such that a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v=\mathbf 0. If b\neq 0, then \mathbf v=-\frac{a}{b}\mathbf u. So \mathbf v is a multiple of \mathbf u. If b=0, then a\neq 0, and the equation gives \mathbf u=\mathbf 0, which is also a multiple of \mathbf v.

example.title: Checking independence in the plane

statement.p: Let \mathbf u=(2,1),\qquad \mathbf w=(1,3). Suppose a\mathbf u+b\mathbf w=\mathbf 0. Then a(2,1)+b(1,3)=(0,0), so (2a+b,\;a+3b)=(0,0). This gives the system 2a+b=0,\qquad a+3b=0. From the first equation, b=-2a. Substitute into the second: a+3(-2a)=0, so -5a=0. Thus a=0, and then b=0. The only zero combination is the trivial one, so \mathbf u and \mathbf w are linearly independent.

subsection.p: In space, the same idea is present, but the geometry has one more possibility. Two nonparallel vectors span a plane through the origin. A third vector may either leave that plane or stay inside it.

example.title: Three directions that look like space but are only a plane

statement.p: Let \mathbf u=(1,0,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,1),\qquad \mathbf w=(1,1,2). These are three vectors in \mathbb R^3. But \mathbf w=\mathbf u+\mathbf v. Therefore \mathbf u+\mathbf v-\mathbf w=\mathbf 0. This is a nontrivial zero combination, so the three vectors are linearly dependent. They do not give three independent directions in space. The third one was already inside the plane spanned by the first two.

subsection.p: The standard vectors \mathbf e_1=(1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf e_2=(0,1,0),\qquad \mathbf e_3=(0,0,1) are independent in \mathbb R^3, because a\mathbf e_1+b\mathbf e_2+c\mathbf e_3=(a,b,c). This is (0,0,0) only when a=b=c=0.

subsection.title: Bases and coordinates relative to a basis
subsection.p: The standard basis is not the only possible coordinate system. On a city map with diagonal streets, it may be more natural to use diagonal directions.
Let \mathbf b_1=(1,1),\qquad \mathbf b_2=(1,-1). These two vectors point along two diagonal directions in the plane.

Suppose a wind displacement is \mathbf v=(5,1) in standard coordinates. We want to describe the same displacement using \mathbf b_1 and \mathbf b_2: \mathbf v=a\mathbf b_1+b\mathbf b_2. That means (5,1)=a(1,1)+b(1,-1). So (5,1)=(a+b,\;a-b). Matching components gives a+b=5,\qquad a-b=1. Adding the equations, 2a=6, so a=3. Then b=2. Thus (5,1)=3(1,1)+2(1,-1).

The vector has standard coordinates (5,1), but relative to the diagonal basis \mathcal B=(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2), its coordinates are [\mathbf v]_{\mathcal B}=(3,2). Those are not a new vector. They are instructions in a different coordinate language.

statement.p: A list of vectors is a basis for a space if it satisfies two conditions:

ol.li: It spans the space: every vector can be built from it.
It is linearly independent: no vector in the list is redundant.

subsection.p: When a basis is used for coordinates, the order matters. The basis (\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2) is an ordered list, not just a set. The first coordinate tells how much of the first basis vector to use; the second coordinate tells how much of the second basis vector to use.

statement.p: Let \mathcal B=(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2,\ldots,\mathbf b_n) be a basis for \mathbb R^n. Then every vector \mathbf v\in\mathbb R^n has one and only one expression of the form \mathbf v=c_1\mathbf b_1+c_2\mathbf b_2+\cdots+c_n\mathbf b_n. The numbers c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_n are called the coordinates of \mathbf v relative to the basis \mathcal B.

proof.title: Why this is true
proof.p: Because the basis spans \mathbb R^n, every vector has at least one expression as a linear combination of the basis vectors.

Now suppose a vector has two such expressions: \mathbf v=c_1\mathbf b_1+\cdots+c_n\mathbf b_n and \mathbf v=d_1\mathbf b_1+\cdots+d_n\mathbf b_n. Subtract the second equation from the first: \mathbf 0=(c_1-d_1)\mathbf b_1+\cdots+(c_n-d_n)\mathbf b_n. Since the basis vectors are linearly independent, the only zero combination is the trivial one. Therefore c_1-d_1=0,\qquad \ldots,\qquad c_n-d_n=0. So c_1=d_1,\qquad \ldots,\qquad c_n=d_n. The coordinates are unique.

subsection.p: Both conditions in the definition of a basis are necessary.

If a list spans but is not independent, coordinates need not be unique. In \mathbb R^2, the three vectors (1,0),\qquad (0,1),\qquad (1,1) span the plane, but they are dependent because (1,0)+(0,1)-(1,1)=\mathbf 0. The vector (1,1) has at least two descriptions: (1,1)=1(1,1) and (1,1)=1(1,0)+1(0,1). So spanning alone gives existence, but not uniqueness.

If a list is independent but does not span, some vectors cannot be described at all. The one-vector list (1,0) is linearly independent in \mathbb R^2, but it does not span the plane. It can build only vectors of the form a(1,0)=(a,0). It cannot build (0,1). So independence alone prevents redundancy, but it does not guarantee enough directions.

exercise.title: What does uniqueness of coordinates really say?

statement.p: A basis gives every vector exactly one coordinate list. In plain language, what would go wrong if a vector had two different coordinate lists relative to the same basis? Why is having a single, unambiguous list the whole point of a coordinate system?

hint.p: Think of coordinates as an address. If one location had two different addresses, could you trust the address to name the location? Connect this to the two conditions in the definition of a basis.

subsection.p: A basis is exactly the balance point: enough directions, but no extra directions.

subsection.title: Dimension as the number of independent directions
subsection.p: A line has one direction. A plane has two. Ordinary space has three. The word dimension makes this counting precise.

Why is this count independent of the chosen basis? Suppose a space is spanned by m vectors and contains an independent list \mathbf v_1,\ldots,\mathbf v_k. Express \mathbf v_1 using the spanning list. Some coefficient is nonzero, so we can solve for that spanning vector and replace it by \mathbf v_1 without changing the span. Next express \mathbf v_2 using the new list. Independence means a coefficient of one of the still-unreplaced vectors is nonzero; replace that vector by \mathbf v_2. Continue. After m replacements there are no vectors left to replace, so independence forces k\le m. Applying this argument to two bases in both orders shows that they have the same number of vectors. In particular, an independent list in \mathbb R^n has at most n members.

statement.p: The dimension of a space is the number of vectors in a basis for that space.

subsection.p: The standard basis of \mathbb R^2 has two vectors: (1,0),\qquad (0,1). So \dim(\mathbb R^2)=2. The standard basis of \mathbb R^3 has three vectors: (1,0,0),\qquad (0,1,0),\qquad (0,0,1). So \dim(\mathbb R^3)=3. In general, the standard basis of \mathbb R^n has n vectors, so \dim(\mathbb R^n)=n.

The dimension counts genuine directions, not the number of vectors written down. The three vectors (1,0,0),\qquad (0,1,0),\qquad (1,1,0) span only the xy-plane, because the third is built from the first two: (1,1,0)=(1,0,0)+(0,1,0). Three vectors are present, but only two independent directions are present.

exercise.title: Why does dimension count directions, not vectors?

statement.p: Someone writes down four vectors in \mathbb R^3 and concludes that they span a four-dimensional space. Without doing any computation, explain why this conclusion must be wrong, and what the number of vectors actually tells you here.

hint.p: Dimension is the number of vectors in a basis, and a basis must be independent. Could four vectors in \mathbb R^3 ever stay independent? What does the standard basis suggest about the most genuine directions available?

subsection.title: A preview of tangent spaces
subsection.p: The language of spans, bases, and dimension will return in a new form when we study curves and surfaces.

A curve has one direction of motion at each point, as long as it is not stopped there. For example, the curve \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2) passes through \mathbf r(1)=(1,1). Its image is the familiar graph y=x^2. Single-variable calculus gives slope 2 at x=1, so (1,2) is a direction vector for the tangent. The tangent line at (1,1) has the form (1,1)+s(1,2). That is an affine line: a point plus the span of one direction.

A surface usually has two independent tangent directions at each point. Those two directions span a tangent plane. Later, when we differentiate parametrized surfaces, this idea will become concrete: \text{tangent plane}=\text{point}+\operatorname{span}\{\text{two tangent directions}\}.

This is the first glimpse of a theme that will follow us through the book. Geometry near a point often becomes linear. A curve becomes a tangent line. A surface becomes a tangent plane. A nonlinear function becomes its best linear approximation.

Linear independence tells us when directions can serve as coordinates. But it does not yet tell us how long a direction is. In standard coordinates the vector (3,4) has length 5, but in a diagonal or slanted basis the coordinate pair (3,4) may represent a very different geometric arrow. To talk about speed, distance, spheres, and unit directions, we need a way to measure length itself.

section.title: Norm, distance, and spheres
section.p: The last section ended with a simple problem. We know how to describe directions with vectors, and we know when directions are redundant. But we still do not know how long a vector is.
That question sounds small. It is not. Length is what turns a displacement into a distance, a velocity vector into a speed, and a direction into a unit direction.

subsection.title: Length of a vector
subsection.p: A drone receives the command \mathbf v=(6,2,3). The command means: 6 \text{ meters east},\qquad 2 \text{ meters north},\qquad 3 \text{ meters up}. How far is the drone from where it started?

First ignore the upward motion. On the floor, the drone moves (6,2), whose length is \sqrt{6^2+2^2}=\sqrt{40}. Now add the upward motion. The floor displacement \sqrt{40} and the height 3 make another right triangle, so the total length is \sqrt{(\sqrt{40})^2+3^2}=\sqrt{40+9}=7. The vector (6,2,3) has length 7.

statement.p: The norm of a vector \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n) in \mathbb R^n is \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+\cdots+v_n^2}. The norm is also called the length or magnitude of the vector.

subsection.p: In the plane, \|(a,b)\|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}. In space, \|(a,b,c)\|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}.

example.title: A familiar length

statement.p: The vector \mathbf v=(3,4) has norm \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5. So the old 3-4-5 right triangle is now a vector length calculation.

example.title: A space displacement

statement.p: The vector \mathbf w=(2,-1,2) has norm \|\mathbf w\|=\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{9}=3. The negative sign does not make the vector shorter or longer. It only says that the motion in that coordinate direction is opposite to the positive direction.

figure.caption: The norm is the distance from the tail of the vector to its head.

subsection.p: The norm of the zero vector is \|\mathbf 0\|=0. Every other vector has positive norm.

subsection.title: Distance between points
subsection.p: A vector has length. Two points have distance between them.

Suppose a ranger station is at P=(2,1) on a map, and a campfire is reported at Q=(8,9). The displacement from P to Q is Q-P=(8-2,\;9-1)=(6,8). Therefore the distance from P to Q is \|Q-P\|=\|(6,8)\|=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10.

statement.p: The distance between points P=(p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n) and Q=(q_1,q_2,\ldots,q_n) in \mathbb R^n is d(P,Q)=\|Q-P\|=\sqrt{(q_1-p_1)^2+(q_2-p_2)^2+\cdots+(q_n-p_n)^2}.

subsection.p: The order of the points does not matter: d(P,Q)=d(Q,P). Indeed, Q-P=-(P-Q), and a vector and its negative have the same length.

example.title: Distance in space

subsection.p: Notice the pattern:

table.title: Length of a vector versus distance between points.

subsection.p: A vector has a length by itself. Two points have a distance because their difference is a vector.

subsection.title: Circles, spheres, and higher-dimensional spheres
subsection.p: A radio transmitter sits at C=(3,2) on a flat map. Its signal reaches every point within 5 km of C. The edge of the coverage region is the set of points (x,y) whose distance from C is 5: d((x,y),C)=5. Using the distance formula, \sqrt{(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2}=5. Squaring both sides gives (x-3)^2+(y-2)^2=25. This is a circle.
The filled-in coverage region is (x-3)^2+(y-2)^2\leq 25. The boundary is a circle; the filled-in region is a disk.

figure.caption: A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a center.

subsection.p: The same idea works in space. A point (x,y,z) is on the sphere of radius 5 centered at C=(3,2,1) when d((x,y,z),C)=5. Thus (x-3)^2+(y-2)^2+(z-1)^2=25.

statement.p: In \mathbb R^n, the sphere of radius r\geq 0 centered at C=(c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_n) is the set of points X=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) satisfying \|X-C\|=r. Equivalently, (x_1-c_1)^2+(x_2-c_2)^2+\cdots+(x_n-c_n)^2=r^2.
The ball of radius r centered at C is the set of points satisfying \|X-C\|\leq r.

subsection.p: In \mathbb R^2, a sphere is what we usually call a circle. In \mathbb R^3, a sphere is the surface of a round ball. In \mathbb R^4 and beyond, we cannot draw the sphere honestly, but the equation still makes perfect sense.
The condition r\geq 0 is not decoration. Distance is never negative. If r<0, then \|X-C\|=r has no solutions. If r=0, the sphere is just the single point C.

statement.p: We just saw that the sphere of radius r=0 centered at C is the single point C. Explain, without computing, why that has to be so. What is the only point X whose distance from C can equal 0?

hint.p: Remember that \|X-C\| is a distance, and a distance is 0 only when there is nothing to travel. When does a vector have length 0?

subsection.title: The triangle inequality and why it matters
subsection.p: A hiker walks from a cabin to a lake, then from the lake to a lookout point. The direct path from the cabin to the lookout cannot be longer than the broken path through the lake. This everyday fact becomes one of the most useful inequalities in calculus.

For example, let \mathbf u=(3,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,2). Then \mathbf u+\mathbf v=(4,3). The lengths are \|\mathbf u\|=\sqrt{10},\qquad \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{5},\qquad \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|=5. The direct vector \mathbf u+\mathbf v is shorter than taking \mathbf u and then \mathbf v: 5 \leq \sqrt{10}+\sqrt{5}.

statement.p: For any vectors \mathbf u,\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^n, \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|\leq \|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\|. Equivalently, for any three points P,Q,R\in\mathbb R^n, d(P,R)\leq d(P,Q)+d(Q,R).

proof.title: Why this is true geometrically
proof.p: Draw \mathbf u first, then draw \mathbf v starting at the head of \mathbf u. The vector \mathbf u+\mathbf v goes directly from the first tail to the last head. These three segments form a triangle, possibly flattened into a line. The direct side of a triangle is never longer than the other two sides together.
The algebraic proof in uses the expression u_1v_1+u_2v_2+\cdots+u_nv_n. This expression is called the dot product.

subsection.p: Equality happens when either vector is zero, or when both nonzero vectors point in the same direction. For example, \mathbf u=(2,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(6,3)=3\mathbf u. Then \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|=\|(8,4)\|=4\sqrt{5}, while \|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt5+3\sqrt5=4\sqrt5. The broken path is not really broken; both pieces lie along the same ray.

exercise.title: When is the detour no detour?

statement.p: The triangle inequality \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|\leq \|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\| becomes an equality exactly when \mathbf u and \mathbf v point the same way. Using the hiker who walks cabin to lake to lookout, describe in words what the three stops look like when the direct path is exactly as long as the broken path.

hint.p: Picture the triangle formed by \mathbf u, \mathbf v, and \mathbf u+\mathbf v. What happens to that triangle when there is no real bend at the lake? Think about a triangle that has been flattened.

subsection.p: The triangle inequality will return often. When we later say that a function is continuous, or that a curve stays close to another curve, the triangle inequality is the tool that lets us control a complicated distance by breaking it into simpler pieces.

subsection.title: Unit vectors and normalization
subsection.p: Sometimes length is not what we care about. We only want direction.

A wind sensor reports the displacement direction \mathbf v=(6,2). Its length is \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{6^2+2^2}=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}. If we divide \mathbf v by its own length, we get \frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}=\frac{(6,2)}{2\sqrt{10}}=\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\right). This new vector points in the same direction as \mathbf v, but has length 1.

statement.p: A vector \mathbf u is a unit vector if \|\mathbf u\|=1. If \mathbf v\neq \mathbf 0, the unit vector in the direction of \mathbf v is \widehat{\mathbf v}=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}. This process is called normalizing the vector.

subsection.p: The condition \mathbf v\neq \mathbf 0 matters. The formula \frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|} would require division by 0 if \mathbf v=\mathbf 0. But the deeper problem is geometric: the zero vector has no direction. There is no unit vector pointing in the same direction as no direction.

statement.p: Suppose a stubborn friend insists on normalizing the zero vector by computing \mathbf 0/\|\mathbf 0\|. Point to two separate things that go wrong: one purely arithmetic, and one about what a unit vector is supposed to mean. Why does the geometric problem run deeper than the arithmetic one?

hint.p: For the arithmetic issue, look at the denominator \|\mathbf 0\|. For the geometric issue, ask yourself: if someone asked you which way \mathbf 0 points, what could you possibly answer?

example.title: Speed and direction

statement.p: A small boat has velocity \mathbf v=(12,5) measured in meters per second. Its speed is \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13. Its direction is the unit vector \widehat{\mathbf v}=\left(\frac{12}{13},\frac{5}{13}\right). So the velocity can be written as \mathbf v=13\left(\frac{12}{13},\frac{5}{13}\right). This separates the motion into \text{speed}\times\text{direction}.

subsection.p: Now that length and distance are available, our earlier descriptions of lines and planes become sharper. A road is not just a set of points of the form P+t\mathbf u; we can ask how far a house is from that road. A wall is not just a flat surface; we can ask for the shortest distance from a sensor to the wall. Those questions lead us back to lines and planes, but now with measurement attached.

section.title: Lines, planes, and hyperplanes
section.p: In , lines and planes appeared as translated spans: P+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}, \qquad P+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u,\mathbf v\}. In , we learned how to measure distance. Put those together, and flat geometry becomes useful: we can describe roads, walls, flight paths, and constraints, and then measure how far away things are from them.

subsection.title: Parametric equations of lines
subsection.p: A trail in space begins at P=(2,-1,3) and follows the direction \mathbf u=(1,4,-2). A point on the trail has the form P+t\mathbf u=(2,-1,3)+t(1,4,-2). Writing the coordinates separately gives x=2+t,\qquad y=-1+4t,\qquad z=3-2t. The parameter t tells how far we have moved in the chosen direction, measured in units of the vector \mathbf u.

statement.p: Let P be a point in \mathbb R^n, and let \mathbf u\neq \mathbf 0 be a vector. The line through P in the direction \mathbf u is L=\{P+t\mathbf u:t\in\mathbb R\}. The equation X=P+t\mathbf u is called a parametric equation of the line.

subsection.p: The condition \mathbf u\neq \mathbf 0 is essential. If \mathbf u=\mathbf 0, then P+t\mathbf 0=P for every t. The formula does not trace a line at all. It stays at one point.

example.title: A line in the plane

statement.p: The line through P=(1,2) in the direction \mathbf u=(3,1) has parametric equation (x,y)=(1,2)+t(3,1). Thus x=1+3t,\qquad y=2+t. When t=0, the point is (1,2). When t=2, the point is (1,2)+2(3,1)=(7,4). When t=-1, the point is (1,2)-(3,1)=(-2,1).

subsection.p: The same geometric line can have many parametric equations. For example, (x,y)=(1,2)+t(3,1) and (x,y)=(7,4)+s(-6,-2) describe the same line. The second one starts at a different point and uses a direction vector pointing the opposite way with twice the length.
A parametrization is a way of moving through the line, not the line itself.

statement.p: The same geometric line can be written as X=P+t\mathbf u in infinitely many ways. Without computing anything, explain what you are free to change about P and \mathbf u while still tracing out exactly the same set of points.

hint.p: Ask yourself two questions: which starting points P already lie on the line, and which directions \mathbf u point along it? Think about what scaling or reversing \mathbf u does to the path versus the set of points it covers.

subsection.title: Parametric equations of planes
subsection.p: A flat sheet in space needs a point and two independent directions.

Suppose a shade sail has one corner at P=(1,0,2) and follows two support directions \mathbf u=(2,1,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,3). Points on the sail have the form P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v. So (x,y,z)=(1,0,2)+s(2,1,0)+t(0,1,3), or x=1+2s,\qquad y=s+t,\qquad z=2+3t.

statement.p: Let P be a point in \mathbb R^3, and let \mathbf u and \mathbf v be two vectors that are not scalar multiples of each other. The plane through P in the directions \mathbf u and \mathbf v is \Pi=\{P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v:s,t\in\mathbb R\}. The equation X=P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v is called a parametric equation of the plane.

subsection.p: The condition on \mathbf u and \mathbf v matters. If \mathbf v=3\mathbf u, then P+s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v=P+s\mathbf u+3t\mathbf u=P+(s+3t)\mathbf u. This is only a line. Two written vectors do not guarantee two genuine directions.

figure.caption: A plane is swept out by two independent directions from a starting point.

subsection.title: Normal equations of planes
subsection.p: Parametric equations describe how to move around inside a plane. There is another way to describe a plane: give a direction straight across it.

Consider the plane 2x-y+3z=0. If we move inside this plane by a small displacement (\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z), then the value of 2x-y+3z should not change. Therefore the displacement must satisfy 2\Delta x-\Delta y+3\Delta z=0. For example, (1,2,0) is allowed because 2(1)-2+3(0)=0. Also (0,3,1) is allowed because 2(0)-3+3(1)=0. These are directions along the plane.

The coefficients (2,-1,3) measure motion across the plane. This vector is called a normal vector to the plane. The next chapter will explain this language using the dot product. For now, the key point is that the plane is made of all points where the linear expression 2x-y+3z has one fixed value.

statement.p: Let \mathbf n=(A,B,C)\neq \mathbf 0 and let P_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0). The plane through P_0 with normal vector \mathbf n has equation A(x-x_0)+B(y-y_0)+C(z-z_0)=0. Equivalently, it can be written Ax+By+Cz=D for some constant D.

subsection.p: The condition (A,B,C)\neq (0,0,0) is necessary. If A=B=C=0, then the equation becomes 0=D. If D=0, every point in space satisfies it. If D\neq0, no point satisfies it. Neither case gives a plane.

example.title: From a normal vector to a plane equation

statement.p: Find the plane through P_0=(1,2,0) with normal vector \mathbf n=(2,-1,3). Using the definition, 2(x-1)-(y-2)+3(z-0)=0. Simplifying, 2x-2-y+2+3z=0, so 2x-y+3z=0.

example.title: From a plane equation to a parametrization

statement.p: The plane 2x-y+3z=0 can be parametrized by choosing two coordinates freely. Let x=s,\qquad z=t. Then the equation gives 2s-y+3t=0, so y=2s+3t. Therefore (x,y,z)=(s,2s+3t,t). Writing this as a point plus directions, (x,y,z)=s(1,2,0)+t(0,3,1). So a parametric equation is (x,y,z)=s(1,2,0)+t(0,3,1).

subsection.p: The two descriptions tell different stories.

exercise.title: What does the normal vector know?

statement.p: A normal vector \mathbf n=(A,B,C) records the coefficients of the plane Ax+By+Cz=D. Explain, in your own words, why directions that lie inside the plane leave the value of Ax+By+Cz unchanged, while moving along \mathbf n changes it. What does this tell you about the relationship between \mathbf n and the plane?

hint.p: Imagine taking a tiny step (\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z) and watching the number Ax+By+Cz. Staying on the plane means that number must not move. You do not need the dot product yet, just the idea of which steps keep the value fixed.

table.title: Two descriptions of a plane.

row.cell: How to move inside the plane
How to test whether a point is on the plane

subsection.p: Both are useful.

subsection.title: Distances to lines and planes
subsection.p: Distance questions turn flat geometry into calculus.
A road in the plane is described by L=(1,2)+t(3,1). A house is located at A=(4,6). How far is the house from the road?

A point on the road is P(t)=(1+3t,\;2+t). The squared distance from A to P(t) is
D(t)^2 \amp= (4-(1+3t))^2+(6-(2+t))^2 \amp= (3-3t)^2+(4-t)^2.
We minimize D(t)^2 instead of D(t), because the square root is not needed to find the closest point.

Expanding, D(t)^2=10t^2-26t+25. This is a single-variable calculus problem. Differentiate: \frac{d}{dt}D(t)^2=20t-26. Set this equal to zero: 20t-26=0, so t=\frac{13}{10}. The nearest point on the road is P\left(\frac{13}{10}\right)=\left(1+3\cdot\frac{13}{10},\;2+\frac{13}{10}\right)=\left(\frac{49}{10},\frac{33}{10}\right). The distance is
d(A,L) \amp= \sqrt{\left(4-\frac{49}{10}\right)^2+\left(6-\frac{33}{10}\right)^2} \amp= \sqrt{\left(-\frac{9}{10}\right)^2+\left(\frac{27}{10}\right)^2} \amp= \frac{9\sqrt{10}}{10}.

example.title: The nearest point formula for a line

statement.p: Let L=P+t\mathbf u be a line in \mathbb R^n, where P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n),\qquad \mathbf u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\neq \mathbf 0. Let A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n) be a point.

The value of t that gives the closest point on the line is t_*=\frac{(a_1-p_1)u_1+\cdots+(a_n-p_n)u_n}{u_1^2+\cdots+u_n^2}. Then the distance from A to the line is d(A,L)=\|A-(P+t_*\mathbf u)\|. The numerator in this formula will soon get a name. It is the dot product hiding in plain sight.

subsection.p: Planes have an especially clean distance formula.

example.title: Distance from a point to a plane

statement.p: Find the distance from A=(3,1,4) to the plane 2x-y+2z=5. The normal direction is \mathbf n=(2,-1,2). A line starting at A and moving straight across the plane is (x,y,z)=(3,1,4)+t(2,-1,2). Substitute this into the plane equation: 2(3+2t)-(1-t)+2(4+2t)=5. Simplify: 13+9t=5. Thus t=-\frac{8}{9}. The distance traveled along the normal line is \left|-\frac{8}{9}\right|\|(2,-1,2)\|=\frac{8}{9}\sqrt{4+1+4}=\frac{8}{3}. So the distance from the point to the plane is \frac83.

theorem.title: Distance from a point to a plane

statement.p: Let \Pi:\quad \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=d be a plane, where (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\neq (0,0,0). The distance from A=(a,b,c) to \Pi is \boxed{d(A,\Pi)=\frac{|\alpha a+\beta b+\gamma c-d|}{\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2}}.}

proof.p: Move from A in the normal direction \mathbf n=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma). The normal line is (x,y,z)=(a,b,c)+t(\alpha,\beta,\gamma). Substitute into the plane equation: \alpha(a+t\alpha)+\beta(b+t\beta)+\gamma(c+t\gamma)=d. This becomes \alpha a+\beta b+\gamma c+t(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)=d. Thus t=\frac{d-(\alpha a+\beta b+\gamma c)}{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2}. Let Q=A+t\mathbf n be this intersection point. To check that it is closest, take any other point X=Q+\mathbf w in the plane. Subtracting the plane equations for X and Q gives \alpha w_1+\beta w_2+\gamma w_3=0. Expanding the three squares, the mixed term vanishes, so \|A-X\|^2=\|-t\mathbf n-\mathbf w\|^2=t^2\|\mathbf n\|^2+\|\mathbf w\|^2\ge t^2\|\mathbf n\|^2=\|A-Q\|^2. Equality holds only when \mathbf w=\mathbf0. Thus Q is the nearest point, using only coordinate algebra. The distance traveled is |t|\|\mathbf n\|=\left|\frac{d-(\alpha a+\beta b+\gamma c)}{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2}\right|\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2}. After simplifying, this gives d(A,\Pi)=\frac{|\alpha a+\beta b+\gamma c-d|}{\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2}}.

subsection.p: The absolute value is important. The expression \alpha a+\beta b+\gamma c-d can be positive or negative depending on which side of the plane the point lies. Distance does not remember the side. It only remembers how far.

subsection.title: Hyperplanes in \mathbb R^n
subsection.p: In \mathbb R^2, an equation like 3x-2y=5 describes a line.
In \mathbb R^3, an equation like 3x-2y+z=5 describes a plane.
In \mathbb R^4, an equation like 3x_1-2x_2+x_3+7x_4=5 describes something we cannot draw honestly. But the pattern is clear: one linear constraint removes one free direction.

statement.p: A hyperplane in \mathbb R^n is a set of points satisfying one linear equation a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n=d, where at least one coefficient a_i is nonzero.

subsection.p: A hyperplane in \mathbb R^2 is a line. A hyperplane in \mathbb R^3 is a plane. A hyperplane in \mathbb R^4 is a three-dimensional flat slice of four-dimensional space.

example.title: A constraint in a data space

statement.p: A greenhouse sensor records four quantities: (T,p,h,c), where T is temperature, p is pressure, h is humidity, and c is carbon dioxide level.

Suppose an alarm triggers when 2T+p-3h+4c=100. The set of all readings that trigger the alarm is a hyperplane in \mathbb R^4. We cannot draw it as a surface in ordinary space, but we can still work with it algebraically.

subsection.p: If a_n\neq0, then the hyperplane equation can be solved for x_n: x_n=\frac{d-a_1x_1-\cdots-a_{n-1}x_{n-1}}{a_n}. The first n-1 coordinates may be chosen freely, and the last one is then determined. That is why a hyperplane in \mathbb R^n has dimension n-1.

statement.p: A single linear equation in \mathbb R^n produces a hyperplane of dimension n-1, not n-2 and not n. Explain why one honest linear constraint removes exactly one free direction. What goes wrong with the counting if all the coefficients a_i were zero?

hint.p: Count the choices: before the equation you may pick all n coordinates freely. The equation lets you solve for one coordinate in terms of the rest. How many remain free? Then ask what the equation even says when no a_i can be used to solve for anything.

subsection.p: Lines, planes, and hyperplanes are the flat objects of multivariable calculus. They are simple enough to compute with, but rich enough to approximate curved objects. Later, a curve will become a tangent line when we zoom in. A surface will become a tangent plane. A nonlinear constraint will become a hyperplane.

But one important piece is still missing. We can add vectors and stretch them. We can measure their length. We still cannot multiply two vectors in a useful way. There is not just one useful multiplication. One product will measure how much two directions agree. Another will measure the signed area they create. Those two ideas begin the next chapter.

introduction.p: Chapter 1 began with locations and displacements. It ended with distances to planes and hyperplanes. The main change was not a new formula; it was a new way to see geometry. Points tell us where. Vectors tell us how to move. Spans tell us what directions can build. Norms and distances tell us how large those motions are.
The problems below are meant to make those ideas usable. Some are short checks. Some are small discoveries. Draw pictures whenever a picture is possible.

exercises.title: Concept check: vectors as objects, not just coordinates

statement.p: What is the difference between a point and a vector, even when both are written with ordered pairs such as (3,4)?
Explain why the displacement from P=(2,-1,5) to Q=(7,3,1) is not the point Q, but the vector Q-P.
The same vector can be drawn with its tail at many different points. Why does moving the drawing of an arrow not change the vector it represents?
What does it mean for a vector to be a linear combination of two other vectors?
Why do the vectors (2,1),\qquad (4,2) not give two genuine directions?
Give an example of two vectors in \mathbb R^2 that are linearly independent. Explain how you know.
Give an example of three vectors in \mathbb R^3 that are linearly dependent even though none of them is the zero vector.
What two conditions must a list of vectors satisfy to be a basis?
Why can the zero vector not be normalized?
What is the difference between the sphere (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=9 and the ball (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2\leq 9?
A plane can be described parametrically or by a normal equation. What does each description make easy to do?
Why is the equation 0x+0y+0z=4 not the equation of a plane?

exercises.title: Skills: vectors, distances, lines, and planes

statement.p: Let \mathbf u=(3,-1,4),\qquad \mathbf v=(-2,5,0). Compute \mathbf u+\mathbf v,\qquad 2\mathbf u-3\mathbf v,\qquad -\mathbf u.
Find the norm of each vector: (5,12),\qquad (2,-1,2),\qquad (1,1,1,1).
Find the distance between P=(1,2,3) and Q=(5,-1,9).
Find the equation of the sphere centered at C=(2,-1,4) with radius 6.
Find the center and radius of the sphere (x-3)^2+y^2+(z+5)^2=49.
Normalize the vector \mathbf v=(4,0,-3).
Write a parametric equation of the line through P=(1,0,2) in the direction \mathbf u=(3,-1,4).
Does the point (7,-2,10) lie on the line (x,y,z)=(1,0,2)+t(3,-1,4)?
Write a parametric equation of the plane through P=(0,1,2) in the directions \mathbf u=(1,0,3),\qquad \mathbf v=(2,1,0).
Find three points on the plane (x,y,z)=(0,1,2)+s(1,0,3)+t(2,1,0).
Find a normal equation for the plane through P_0=(1,2,3) with normal vector \mathbf n=(2,-1,5).
Does the point (3,4,1) lie on the plane 2x-y+5z=9?
Parametrize the plane x+2y-z=4 by choosing y=s and z=t.
Find the distance from A=(1,2,3) to the plane 2x-y+2z=7.
Find the closest point on the line L=(0,0)+t(2,1) to the point A=(3,4). Then find the distance from A to L.

exercises.title: Discovery: why two independent directions make a plane

introduction.p: These problems are meant to be explored slowly. They explain why linear independence is not just a definition, but the hidden rule behind coordinates.

statement.p: Let \mathbf u=(2,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,3). Try to solve s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v=(x,y) for s and t. Your answer should express s and t in terms of x and y. What does this prove about the span of \mathbf u and \mathbf v?
Repeat the previous problem with \mathbf u=(2,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(4,2). Which points (x,y) can be reached? Which cannot?

In \mathbb R^3, let \mathbf u=(1,0,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,1). Points in the span of \mathbf u and \mathbf v have the form s(1,0,1)+t(0,1,1). Write the coordinates of such a point as (x,y,z). Then find one equation involving x,y,z that every such point satisfies.
The previous problem found a plane through the origin. Translate it through the point P=(2,0,1). Write both a parametric equation and a normal equation for the translated plane.
Suppose three vectors in \mathbb R^3 all lie in the same plane through the origin. Explain why they must be linearly dependent.
Suppose three vectors in \mathbb R^3 are linearly independent. Explain why they cannot all lie in one plane through the origin.

A basis in \mathbb R^2 is like a pair of street directions. Use the basis \mathbf b_1=(1,1),\qquad \mathbf b_2=(1,-1) to express each vector below in \mathcal B-coordinates: (4,0),\qquad (0,6),\qquad (5,1).
Draw the grid formed by all points s(1,1)+t(1,-1) where s and t are integers between -3 and 3. How does this grid differ from the usual square coordinate grid?

exercises.title: Hook: the need for a multiplication of vectors

introduction.p: Addition and scaling have carried us far. But many geometric questions do not ask for another vector of the same kind.

statement.p: A force \mathbf F=(10,0) pushes an object through the displacement \mathbf d=(3,0). It seems natural that the work should be 30. What should the work be if \mathbf d=(0,3)? What about \mathbf d=(3,4)? What kind of vector multiplication would answer this?

The vectors \mathbf u=(3,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,2) form a rectangle of area 6. The vectors \mathbf a=(3,1),\qquad \mathbf b=(1,2) form a slanted parallelogram. Estimate its area from a drawing. Then try to find an algebraic rule that gives the signed area from the four components.
Swapping the order of two directions should not change the size of the parallelogram, but it should reverse its orientation. What should this suggest about the sign of an area product?

A multiplication that measures agreement in direction should be symmetric: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u. A multiplication that measures oriented area should change sign when the order is swapped. Why might one product not be enough?

conclusion.p: The next chapter begins with this surprise: vectors have more than one useful kind of multiplication. One product measures how much two directions line up. Another measures the oriented area or volume they create. Those products will eventually lead to the dx\wedge dy that appears in differential forms, where signed area becomes an integrand rather than just a number.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

introduction.p: Dot products measure angles and projections, cross products encode oriented area in space, and determinants measure signed area and volume. We develop their algebra from coordinates, then introduce constant linear and alternating measurements as a first special case of differential forms. The chapter closes with a quaternion rotation project and review.

section.title: Complex numbers as a warm-up
section.p: A vector in the plane can be written as (a,b). A complex number writes the same two pieces of data in a different language: a+bi. At first, the symbol i may look like a trick. But geometrically it is one of the most useful symbols in mathematics. Multiplying by i means rotating a plane vector by 90^\circ counterclockwise.
For example, i(3+2i)=3i+2i^2=-2+3i. So the vector (3,2) has become (-2,3). That is exactly a 90^\circ counterclockwise turn.

figure.caption: Multiplication by i rotates a plane vector by 90^\circ.

section.p: This is the first hint that multiplication can carry geometry.

subsection.title: Complex numbers as points and arrows in the plane
subsection.p: A complex number has the form z=a+bi, where a and b are real numbers and i^2=-1.

statement.p: A complex number is an expression z=a+bi, where a,b\in\mathbb R and i^2=-1.
The number a is the real part of z, and b is the imaginary part of z: \operatorname{Re}(z)=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(z)=b.

subsection.p: We identify a+bi with the point or vector (a,b) in the plane. So 3+2i is the same plane arrow as (3,2).
Addition is exactly the vector addition from Chapter 1: (a+bi)+(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i. For example, (3+2i)+(-1+4i)=2+6i. In vector language, this says (3,2)+(-1,4)=(2,6).
The length of a complex number is the length of the corresponding vector: |a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}. This is the same norm as before, written with complex-number notation.

example.title: A complex number as a vector

statement.p: The complex number z=-2+5i corresponds to the vector (-2,5). Its length is |z|=\sqrt{(-2)^2+5^2}=\sqrt{29}.

subsection.p: So far, complex numbers have only repackaged plane vectors. The real surprise comes from multiplication.

subsection.title: Multiplication as scaling and rotation
subsection.p:
To multiply complex numbers, we use ordinary algebra and the rule i^2=-1:
(a+bi)(c+di) \amp =ac+adi+bci+bdi^2 \amp =(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i.

statement.p: For complex numbers z=a+bi,\qquad w=c+di, their product is zw=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i.

subsection.p: The formula may look artificial. It is not. It is the algebraic shadow of a simple geometric fact: multiplying complex numbers multiplies lengths and adds angles.
Start with the easiest special case: i(a+bi)=ai+bi^2=-b+ai. So a+bi \quad\longmapsto\quad -b+ai. In vector notation, (a,b) \quad\longmapsto\quad (-b,a). That is a 90^\circ counterclockwise rotation.

exercise.title: Why does multiplying by i turn the plane a quarter turn?

statement.p: You just saw that i sends (a,b) to (-b,a). Without computing any example, explain in your own words why this single algebraic rule i^2=-1 forces multiplication by i to be a quarter-turn rotation rather than, say, a stretch or a reflection.

hint.p: Apply multiplication by i twice. Where does 1 land after one step, and after two? A quarter turn done twice should be a half turn — and a half turn is exactly multiplication by -1.

subsection.p: Multiplying by 2i does two things: 2i(a+bi)=-2b+2ai. It rotates by 90^\circ and doubles the length.

example.title: Multiplying by 1+i

statement.p: Let z=3+i. Then (1+i)z=(1+i)(3+i)=3+i+3i+i^2=2+4i. The multiplier 1+i has length |1+i|=\sqrt2 and direction 45^\circ. So multiplying by 1+i rotates by 45^\circ and stretches by a factor of \sqrt2.
Indeed, |3+i|=\sqrt{10}, while |2+4i|=\sqrt{20}=\sqrt2\sqrt{10}. The length has been multiplied by \sqrt2.

subsection.p: To state the rotation rule clearly, it is useful to write a nonzero complex number in polar form. If z\neq0, then z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta), where r=|z| and \theta is the angle from the positive real axis to the vector z.

statement.p: Let z=r(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha), \qquad w=s(\cos\beta+i\sin\beta), where r,s>0. Then zw = rs\bigl(\cos(\alpha+\beta)+i\sin(\alpha+\beta)\bigr). So multiplication by w stretches lengths by |w|=s and rotates angles by \beta.

proof.p:
Multiply:
zw \amp = r(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha)\, s(\cos\beta+i\sin\beta) \amp = rs\Bigl( \cos\alpha\cos\beta -\sin\alpha\sin\beta +i(\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta) \Bigr).
Using the angle-addition formulas, \cos(\alpha+\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta and \sin(\alpha+\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta, we get zw = rs\bigl(\cos(\alpha+\beta)+i\sin(\alpha+\beta)\bigr).

subsection.p: The condition r,s>0 is there for a reason. The zero complex number has length 0, but it has no direction. We cannot assign it a unique angle. Multiplication by zero does not rotate the plane; it collapses every vector to the origin: 0\cdot z=0. So the rotation picture belongs to multiplication by a nonzero complex number.

subsection.title: Why two-dimensional geometry has a natural product
subsection.p: Complex multiplication works because a nonzero plane vector has exactly two pieces of geometric information: \text{length} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \text{angle}.
Lengths multiply naturally. Angles add naturally. That gives a product.

exercise.title: What makes complex multiplication the natural product of the plane?

statement.p: A nonzero plane vector carries exactly two pieces of geometric data: a length and an angle. Why does this fact make multiply the lengths, add the angles the most natural rule for combining two such vectors, rather than something we simply chose to define?

hint.p: Ask what operation on positive numbers is most natural, and what operation on angles stacks one turn on top of another. Multiplication already does both jobs separately — the plane just lets you do them at the same time.

subsection.p: For instance, suppose z=2(\cos 30^\circ+i\sin30^\circ) and w=3(\cos 80^\circ+i\sin80^\circ). Then zw = 6(\cos110^\circ+i\sin110^\circ). The product has length 6 and direction 110^\circ.
This is a remarkable fact. The plane is not only a place where vectors live. It is also a place where vectors can be multiplied, provided we interpret plane vectors as complex numbers.
But this product is not the only useful way to combine two plane vectors.

Let z=a+bi,\qquad w=c+di. The complex conjugate of z is \overline z=a-bi. Now multiply \overline z and w:
\overline z\,w \amp =(a-bi)(c+di) \amp =ac+adi-bci-bdi^2 \amp =(ac+bd)+(ad-bc)i.
The real part is ac+bd. The imaginary part is ad-bc.
Those two expressions are not random. They are two of the most important measurements in geometry.
The number ac+bd measures how much the vectors (a,b) and (c,d) point in the same direction. It will become the dot product.
The number ad-bc measures the signed area of the parallelogram made by the two vectors. It will become the 2\times2 determinant, and later it will reappear as the coefficient of dx\wedge dy.

example.title: Two measurements hidden in one complex product

statement.p: Let z=2+i,\qquad w=4+3i. Then \overline z\,w=(2-i)(4+3i)=8+6i-4i-3i^2=11+2i. The real part is 11=2\cdot4+1\cdot3. The imaginary part is 2=2\cdot3-1\cdot4. So the same product has packaged two different geometric measurements: \text{directional agreement} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{signed area}.

subsection.p: This is the first glimpse of the larger story. Vector multiplication is not one thing. Different products measure different geometry.

subsection.title: The question Hamilton asked: can triples be multiplied?
subsection.p: Complex numbers multiply plane vectors. That raises an irresistible question: \text{Can we multiply vectors in space the same way?}

A point in space has three coordinates: (x,y,z). So it is tempting to invent a number of the form x+yi+zj or perhaps xi+yj+zk, and hope that multiplication will behave as cleanly as it does for complex numbers.

The dream is easy to describe. We would like multiplication to understand three-dimensional length and rotation. Multiplying by a special unit should rotate space in some natural way, just as multiplying by i rotates the plane.

But there is a problem. In the plane, there is only one direction perpendicular to the real axis: the i-direction. In space, there are many perpendicular directions. No single imaginary unit can control all of them.

exercise.title: Why did Hamilton's three-dimensional dream run into trouble?

statement.p: In the plane, one imaginary unit i was enough to capture rotation. Hamilton hoped to multiply triples x+yi+zj in space the same way. What is the conceptual obstacle that makes a single extra imaginary unit not enough in three dimensions?

hint.p: Count the directions perpendicular to a given axis. In the plane there is essentially one; in space there is a whole circle of them. If multiplication must respect all of those perpendicular directions at once, can one unit speak for all of them?

subsection.p: Hamilton's breakthrough was to stop trying to multiply triples. He added one more component and introduced numbers of the form a+bi+cj+dk. These are called quaternions. They are four-dimensional numbers, but hidden inside them is exactly the three-dimensional vector geometry we need.

That may sound like a detour. It is not. The detour will explain why three-dimensional vectors have two famous products instead of one: the dot product and the cross product. Both are already waiting inside quaternion multiplication.
But to see them, we first need to meet the strange multiplication rules for i,\qquad j,\qquad k.

section.title: Pure imaginary quaternions and three-dimensional vectors
section.p: The complex numbers used one imaginary unit: i^2=-1. For space, Hamilton introduced three: i,\qquad j,\qquad k. They do not behave like ordinary numbers. That is the whole point.
If they did behave like ordinary commuting numbers, the geometry would break.

subsection.title: The units i, j, and k
subsection.p: Think of i,j,k as three perpendicular direction symbols. For now, they play the roles of the three standard coordinate directions: i \leftrightarrow (1,0,0),\qquad j \leftrightarrow (0,1,0),\qquad k \leftrightarrow (0,0,1).
A quaternion has the form q=a+bi+cj+dk, where a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R. The number a is the real part. The remaining part bi+cj+dk is the imaginary part.

statement.p: A quaternion is an expression q=a+bi+cj+dk, where a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R, and the symbols i,j,k multiply according to the quaternion rules stated below.

subsection.p: For this chapter, the most important quaternions are the ones with no real part.

statement.p: A quaternion of the form bi+cj+dk is called a pure imaginary quaternion.

subsection.p: Pure imaginary quaternions are the bridge back to ordinary vectors in space: bi+cj+dk \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad (b,c,d). For example, 2i-j+3k \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad (2,-1,3).
Addition and scalar multiplication work exactly as they do for vectors: (2i-j+3k)+(i+4j-k)=3i+3j+2k, and 5(2i-j+3k)=10i-5j+15k.
So far, this is only a new notation for \mathbb R^3. Multiplication is where the new geometry enters.

subsection.title: The rule i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1
subsection.p: The quaternion units satisfy i^2=j^2=k^2=-1 and ijk=-1. These compact rules produce the multiplication table:

table.title: The quaternion multiplication table.

subsection.p: This table says, for example, ij=k, \qquad ji=-k, and jk=i, \qquad kj=-i, and ki=j, \qquad ik=-j.
The positive products follow the cyclic order i\longrightarrow j\longrightarrow k\longrightarrow i. Going backward changes the sign.

statement.p: Hamilton packed everything into the single line i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1. Take the piece ijk=-1 and ask: if you already know i^2=-1, what must the product ij equal? Try to deduce the value of ij from ijk=-1 alone, without peeking at the table.

hint.p: Multiply both sides of ijk=-1 on the right by k, and remember that k^2=-1. One short rearrangement reveals ij.

figure.caption: The cyclic order i\to j\to k\to i controls quaternion signs.

example.title: Basic products

statement.p: Using the table, ij=k, but ji=-k. Also, jk=i, but kj=-i. So multiplication remembers orientation. The ordered pair (i,j) points toward +k, while the ordered pair (j,i) points toward -k.

subsection.p: This sign change is not a minor detail. It is what allows quaternion multiplication to encode three-dimensional orientation.

subsection.title: Noncommutativity: why order matters
subsection.p: Ordinary real numbers commute: ab=ba. Complex numbers also commute: zw=wz. Quaternions do not.
ij=k, \qquad ji=-k. So ij\neq ji.

statement.p: A multiplication rule is called noncommutative if changing the order can change the product: ab\neq ba. Quaternion multiplication is noncommutative.

subsection.p: The noncommutativity may feel strange, but it is forced by the geometry.

statement.p: It is tempting to read ij=-ji as a flaw, as if the algebra simply failed to be tidy. But think about turning a book around two different axes in space, first one order and then the reversed order. Why is it actually desirable that ij\neq ji if these symbols are meant to describe three-dimensional rotation?

hint.p: Ask what would go wrong if order did not matter. If ij equalled ji, could the algebra ever tell two opposite spatial orientations apart?

example.title: A commutative attempt breaks

statement.p: Suppose we tried to make i^2=j^2=k^2=-1, and also tried to keep multiplication commutative. If ij=k and ji=ij, then k^2=(ij)(ij).
