Since multiplication is being assumed commutative in this failed attempt, we could rearrange: (ij)(ij)=i^2j^2=(-1)(-1)=1. So this attempt would force k^2=1. But we wanted k^2=-1. The rules contradict each other.
The lesson is clear: if i,j,k are going to multiply in a way that matches three-dimensional orientation, then order has to matter.

subsection.p: Here is a less abstract way to feel the same thing. In the plane, rotating 90^\circ and then stretching by 2 gives the same final effect as stretching by 2 and then rotating 90^\circ. But in space, rotations around different axes usually do not commute. Turning a book around one axis and then another can leave it in a different orientation than doing the same two turns in the opposite order.
Quaternion multiplication has that spatial behavior built into its algebra.

example.title: A product that changes when order changes

statement.p: Compute (i+j)k and k(i+j). First, (i+j)k=ik+jk. Using the table, ik=-j,\qquad jk=i. So (i+j)k=i-j. But k(i+j)=ki+kj. Using the table again, ki=j,\qquad kj=-i. Thus k(i+j)=j-i. Therefore (i+j)k\neq k(i+j). In fact, k(i+j)=-(i-j).

subsection.p: Order has become geometry.

subsection.title: Pure imaginary quaternions as vectors in \mathbb R^3
subsection.p: Now return to ordinary vectors. The vector \mathbf v=(x,y,z) can be written as the pure imaginary quaternion V=xi+yj+zk. This lets us use quaternion multiplication to discover hidden measurements of vectors.
The first surprise comes from squaring a pure imaginary quaternion.

example.title: The square of a pure imaginary quaternion

statement.p:
Let V=2i-j+3k. Then
V^2 \amp=(2i-j+3k)(2i-j+3k).
If we expanded every term, the square terms are (2i)^2+(-j)^2+(3k)^2 = 4i^2+j^2+9k^2 = -4-1-9 = -14. The cross terms cancel in pairs. For instance, (2i)(-j)+(-j)(2i) = -2ij-2ji = -2k-2(-k) = 0. The same cancellation happens for the i,k terms and the j,k terms. Therefore V^2=-14. But \|(2,-1,3)\|^2=2^2+(-1)^2+3^2=14. So V^2=-\|V\|^2.

subsection.p: This example was not special.

statement.p: Let V=xi+yj+zk. Then V^2=-(x^2+y^2+z^2). Equivalently, V^2=-\|V\|^2.

proof.p:
Expand:
V^2 \amp=(xi+yj+zk)(xi+yj+zk).
The square terms give x^2i^2+y^2j^2+z^2k^2 = -x^2-y^2-z^2. The mixed terms come in opposite pairs: xy(ij+ji)=xy(k-k)=0, xz(ik+ki)=xz(-j+j)=0, and yz(jk+kj)=yz(i-i)=0. Thus V^2=-(x^2+y^2+z^2).

subsection.p: This theorem gives a beautiful reason for the minus sign in i^2=j^2=k^2=-1. A pure imaginary quaternion behaves like a direction whose square is negative length squared.

exercise.title: Why call them vectors at all?

statement.p: We keep writing (x,y,z)\leftrightarrow xi+yj+zk as if a pure imaginary quaternion simply is a vector in \mathbb R^3. What earns that identification? Name a couple of features of pure imaginary quaternions that line up exactly with how vectors in space already behave.

hint.p: Think about addition, scalar multiplication, and especially the quantity V^2. Which familiar measurement of the vector (x,y,z) is hiding inside V^2?

subsection.p: The zero vector still behaves as expected: 0i+0j+0k=0, and 0^2=0. Every nonzero pure imaginary quaternion has a negative real square.

example.title: Unit vectors square to -1

statement.p: The coordinate units satisfy i^2=j^2=k^2=-1. But so does any unit direction.

For example, let U=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(i+j+k). The corresponding vector is \left(\frac1{\sqrt3},\frac1{\sqrt3},\frac1{\sqrt3}\right), which has length 1. By the theorem, U^2=-\|U\|^2=-1. So i,j,k are not the only square roots of -1 inside the quaternions. Every unit direction in space gives one.

subsection.p: This is very different from the complex plane. In the complex numbers, the two square roots of -1 are i \quad\text{and}\quad -i. In the quaternions, every unit vector direction gives a square root of -1. The algebra has become large enough to hold the geometry of space.
But it has also become stranger. When we multiply two pure imaginary quaternions, the answer usually does not stay pure imaginary.
For example, ij=k is pure imaginary. But i^2=-1 is real. A general product mixes both kinds of output.

Try (2i+j)(i+3j). Then
(2i+j)(i+3j) \amp= 2i^2+6ij+ji+3j^2 \amp= 2(-1)+6k+(-k)+3(-1) \amp= -5+5k.
The product has a real part, -5, and an imaginary vector part, 5k.

That split is the doorway to the rest of the chapter. The real part will become one kind of vector product. The imaginary part will become another. One measures how much two vectors point together. The other measures the oriented area they create. The quaternions do not make us choose between them; they show that both were part of one multiplication all along.

section.title: The scalar and vector parts of a quaternion product
section.p: At the end of the last section, something surprising happened. When we multiplied two pure imaginary quaternions, the answer did not usually stay pure imaginary. It split into two pieces: \text{a real part} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \text{a pure imaginary vector part}.

subsection.title: Multiplying two pure imaginary quaternions
subsection.p:
Start with two simple vectors in the plane, but write them as pure imaginary quaternions: U=2i+j, \qquad V=i+3j. Their product is
UV \amp=(2i+j)(i+3j) \amp=2i^2+6ij+ji+3j^2 \amp=-2+6k-k-3 \amp=-5+5k.
The product has two parts: -5 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 5k.
The real part is -5=-(2\cdot 1+1\cdot 3). The vector part is 5k=(2\cdot3-1\cdot1)k.

So quaternion multiplication has found two different measurements at once. The number 2\cdot1+1\cdot3=5 measures how much the two vectors are aligned together in the same direction (it also accounts for their magnitudes). The number 2\cdot3-1\cdot1=5 measures the signed area of the parallelogram they make in the xy-plane.

figure.caption: The vector part 5k records the signed area of the parallelogram.

subsection.p: The direction k matters. The parallelogram lies in the xy-plane, so its oriented area points perpendicular to that plane. The order (2,1) then (1,3) gives the positive k-direction.

If we reverse the order, the real part stays the same, but the vector part changes sign:
VU \amp=(i+3j)(2i+j) \amp=2i^2+ij+6ji+3j^2 \amp=-2+k-6k-3 \amp=-5-5k.
The same two arrows make the same area, but the opposite orientation.
This is exactly the kind of behavior an oriented area should have.

subsection.title: The general product
subsection.p: Now do the same multiplication without choosing numbers.

Let \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3), and write the corresponding pure imaginary quaternions as U=u_1i+u_2j+u_3k, \qquad V=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k. Expanding UV gives
UV \amp=(u_1i+u_2j+u_3k)(v_1i+v_2j+v_3k) \amp=u_1v_1i^2+u_1v_2ij+u_1v_3ik \amp\qquad +u_2v_1ji+u_2v_2j^2+u_2v_3jk \amp\qquad +u_3v_1ki+u_3v_2kj+u_3v_3k^2.
Using i^2=j^2=k^2=-1, and ij=k,\quad jk=i,\quad ki=j, while reversing order changes the sign, we get
\boxed{\begin{aligned} UV \amp=-(u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3)\\ \amp\qquad +(u_2v_3-u_3v_2)i\\ \amp\qquad +(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)j\\ \amp\qquad +(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)k. \end{aligned}}
This formula is long, but it has a simple structure: UV = \text{scalar part} + \text{vector part}.

statement.p: For a quaternion q=a+bi+cj+dk, the scalar part is \operatorname{Scal}(q)=a, and the vector part is \operatorname{Vec}(q)=bi+cj+dk.

subsection.p: For the product of two pure imaginary quaternions, the scalar part is \operatorname{Scal}(UV)=-(u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3), and the vector part is \operatorname{Vec}(UV) = (u_2v_3-u_3v_2)i +(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)j +(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)k.
The two expressions are important enough to receive their own names.

definition.title: Dot product and cross product from quaternions

statement.p: For vectors \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3), the dot product is \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v = u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3. The cross product is \mathbf u\times\mathbf v = (u_2v_3-u_3v_2)i +(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)j +(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)k.

subsection.p: With these names, the quaternion product becomes beautifully short: \boxed{ UV= -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. }

theorem.title: The quaternion product splits into dot and cross

statement.p: Let U=u_1i+u_2j+u_3k, \qquad V=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k be pure imaginary quaternions, corresponding to vectors \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3). Then UV= -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. The scalar part of UV is -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v, and the vector part of UV is \mathbf u\times\mathbf v.

proof.p: This is exactly the expansion above. The real terms are -u_1v_1-u_2v_2-u_3v_3 = -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v. The i, j, and k terms are (u_2v_3-u_3v_2)i, (u_3v_1-u_1v_3)j, and (u_1v_2-u_2v_1)k, which together form \mathbf u\times\mathbf v.

subsection.p: The hypothesis that U and V are pure imaginary matters. If real parts are present, new terms appear.

For example, let q=1+i, \qquad r=j. Then qr=(1+i)j=j+ij=j+k. But if we only used the vector parts i and j, the formula would give -\mathbf i\cdot\mathbf j+\mathbf i\times\mathbf j=k. It misses the extra j, which came from the real part 1 multiplying j. So the clean split UV=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v belongs to products of pure imaginary quaternions.

subsection.title: The scalar part and the dot product
subsection.p: The scalar part is easiest to feel when two vectors point in the same direction.

Let U=3i+4j, \qquad V=6i+8j. These represent \mathbf u=(3,4,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(6,8,0). The second vector is twice the first: \mathbf v=2\mathbf u. Their dot product is \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v = 3\cdot6+4\cdot8+0\cdot0 = 18+32 = 50. The scalar part of UV is therefore -50.
The minus sign is not a mistake. It comes from the fact that i^2=j^2=k^2=-1. When a direction multiplies itself, it contributes a negative real number.
This is why we define \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v as the negative of the scalar part of UV. The dot product is positive when vectors point together.

exercise.title: Why does the scalar part carry the dot product?

statement.p: When you multiply two pure imaginary quaternions, the scalar part of the product turns out to be -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v. Without computing anything, can you explain where that minus sign comes from, and why a quantity built from a product of directions ends up measuring how much the two vectors point the same way?

hint.p: Think about what happens when a single direction multiplies itself. What is i^2, j^2, or k^2? Those self-products are exactly the terms that survive in the scalar part when \mathbf u and \mathbf v line up.

subsection.p: Now compare that with a perpendicular vector: W=-4i+3j. Then \mathbf u=(3,4,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(-4,3,0), and \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf w = 3(-4)+4(3)+0 = -12+12 = 0. So the scalar part of UW is zero.
The dot product measures directional agreement:

table.title: What the sign of the dot product means.

row.cell: the vectors are perpendicular, if both are nonzero
the vectors point somewhat against each other

subsection.title: The vector part and the cross product
subsection.p: The vector part remembers orientation.

The basic quaternion products give ij=k, \qquad ji=-k. So \mathbf i\times\mathbf j=\mathbf k, \qquad \mathbf j\times\mathbf i=-\mathbf k. This is the seed of the right-hand rule. The ordered pair i,j points toward k. Reverse the order, and the direction reverses.

exercise.title: Why does the vector part carry the cross product?

statement.p: The vector part of UV is \mathbf u\times\mathbf v, and swapping the order of the two quaternions flips its sign. Why is it natural that the vector part of a product should reverse direction when you reverse the order, while the scalar part does not? What feature of an oriented area is the quaternion product faithfully recording?

hint.p: Compare ij=k with ji=-k. Picture the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors and ask what should happen to its orientation when you trace its edges in the opposite order.

example.title: A three-dimensional product

statement.p: Let U=2i-j+3k, \qquad V=i+4j+2k. The corresponding vectors are \mathbf u=(2,-1,3), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,4,2). Their dot product is \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v = 2\cdot1+(-1)\cdot4+3\cdot2 = 2-4+6 = 4. So the scalar part of UV is -4.

The cross product is
\mathbf u\times\mathbf v \amp= ((-1)(2)-3(4))i +(3(1)-2(2))j +(2(4)-(-1)(1))k \amp= (-2-12)i+(3-4)j+(8+1)k \amp= -14i-j+9k.
Therefore UV=-4-14i-j+9k.

subsection.p: This product has packed two answers into one line: \text{directional agreement} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{oriented area}. The dot product is the scalar measurement. The cross product is the vector measurement.

subsection.title: Symmetric and antisymmetric parts of multiplication
subsection.p: Quaternion multiplication is not commutative: UV\neq VU in general. But if we add and subtract UV and VU, the two pieces separate cleanly.

For the example U=2i+j, \qquad V=i+3j, we found UV=-5+5k, and VU=-5-5k. Adding gives UV+VU=-10. Subtracting gives UV-VU=10k. So \frac{UV+VU}{2}=-5, and \frac{UV-VU}{2}=5k. The average keeps the scalar part. The half-difference keeps the vector part.
This always happens.

statement.p: Let U and V be pure imaginary quaternions corresponding to vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v. Then \frac{UV+VU}{2} = -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v, and \frac{UV-VU}{2} = \mathbf u\times\mathbf v.

proof.p: From the product formula, UV=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. If we reverse the order, the dot product stays the same: \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u=\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v. But the cross product changes sign: \mathbf v\times\mathbf u=-(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v). Therefore VU=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v-\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. Adding, UV+VU=-2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v. Subtracting, UV-VU=2\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. Dividing by 2 gives the result.

subsection.p: The words symmetric and antisymmetric describe what happens when we swap the two inputs.
The dot product is symmetric: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u. The cross product is antisymmetric: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=-(\mathbf v\times\mathbf u).

This sign change is the same sign change we saw in oriented area: \text{area}(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) = -\text{area}(\mathbf v,\mathbf u). That idea will return later in a more flexible form as the wedge product.

exercise.title: What do the two halves of a product measure?

statement.p: Any product UV can be split into a symmetric piece \tfrac{1}{2}(UV+VU) and an antisymmetric piece \tfrac{1}{2}(UV-VU). In plain words, what does each half measure about the relationship between \mathbf u and \mathbf v, and why does it make sense that the symmetric half ignores order while the antisymmetric half depends on it?

hint.p: One half survives a swap unchanged; the other flips sign. Match each half to a quantity you have already met in this section, and ask which of those quantities cares about which vector comes first.

subsection.title: What this explains better than a memorized determinant
subsection.p: Many calculus books introduce the dot product by a formula and the cross product by a determinant. Those formulas are useful, and we will use them. But by themselves they can feel like two unrelated tricks.
Quaternion multiplication tells a more coherent story.
Multiplying two pure imaginary quaternions gives UV=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. One product splits into two geometric measurements.
The scalar part measures how much the two vectors point in the same direction. The vector part measures the oriented area they create.
That explains why the dot product is symmetric: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u. Pointing together does not depend on order.
It also explains why the cross product is antisymmetric: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=-(\mathbf v\times\mathbf u). Oriented area does depend on order.

The dot product deserves its own closer look. It has no direction, but it controls length, angle, perpendicularity, projection, and work. Before following the vector part into areas and normal directions, we should understand this scalar measurement well.

section.title: The dot product
section.p: The last section pulled the dot product out of the scalar part of quaternion multiplication: \operatorname{Scal}(UV)=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v. Now we study the dot product on its own. It is the simplest way to ask a geometric question: \text{How much does one vector point along another?}

subsection.title: Algebraic definition and first examples
subsection.p: Imagine dragging a sled across flat snow. The sled moves \mathbf d=(3,4) meters: 3 meters east and 4 meters north.

First suppose the pull is purely east: \mathbf F=(10,0). Only the east part of the motion helps the pull do work. The northward motion is sideways to the force. So the useful multiplication is 10\cdot3+0\cdot4=30.
Now suppose the force is \mathbf F=(6,8). Then both components help: 6\cdot3+8\cdot4=18+32=50.
Finally suppose the force is \mathbf F=(-4,3). Then (-4)\cdot3+3\cdot4=-12+12=0. This force is perpendicular to the displacement. It pulls sideways, so it does no work along that motion.
The same component-by-component multiplication is the dot product.

statement.p: For vectors in the plane, \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2),\qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2), the dot product is \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2.
For vectors in space, \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3),\qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3), the dot product is \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3.

subsection.p: In any \mathbb R^n, use the same coordinate rule: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\sum_{j=1}^n u_jv_j. The algebra below, including \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=\|\mathbf u\|^2, follows from this finite sum in every dimension. Angle pictures use the plane or ordinary space; the inequalities will also receive a purely algebraic justification.

example.title: A dot product in space

statement.p:
Let \mathbf u=(2,-1,3),\qquad \mathbf v=(4,5,-2). Then
\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v \amp= 2\cdot4+(-1)\cdot5+3\cdot(-2) \amp= 8-5-6 \amp= -3.
The negative answer tells us that the two vectors point somewhat against each other.

subsection.p: The dot product behaves like multiplication in several useful ways.

theorem.title: Basic algebra of the dot product

statement.p: For vectors \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w and a scalar c, \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u, \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v+\mathbf w)=\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf w, and (c\mathbf u)\cdot\mathbf v=c(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v). Also, \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=\|\mathbf u\|^2.

proof.p:
All four statements follow by writing the components and using ordinary arithmetic. For example, in space,
\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v+\mathbf w) \amp= u_1(v_1+w_1)+u_2(v_2+w_2)+u_3(v_3+w_3) \amp= (u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3)+(u_1w_1+u_2w_2+u_3w_3) \amp= \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf w.
And \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2=\|\mathbf u\|^2.

subsection.p: That last identity is the first sign that the dot product knows about length: \|\mathbf u\|=\sqrt{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}.

subsection.title: Length, angle, and orthogonality
subsection.p: The dot product does more than compute a number. It computes angles.

Take \mathbf u=(3,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(2,2\sqrt3). Then \|\mathbf u\|=3, and \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{2^2+(2\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{4+12}=4. Their dot product is \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=3\cdot2+0\cdot2\sqrt3=6. So \frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|}=\frac{6}{3\cdot4}=\frac12. The angle whose cosine is 1/2 is 60^\circ, or \pi/3 radians. So these vectors meet at a 60^\circ angle.

figure.caption: The dot product finds the angle through \cos\theta.

subsection.p: The pattern is general.

statement.p: Let \mathbf u and \mathbf v be nonzero vectors in the plane or in space. If \theta is the angle between them, with 0\leq \theta\leq \pi, then \boxed{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta.} Equivalently, \cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|}.

proof.p:
Look at the triangle formed by the two vectors \mathbf u, \mathbf v, and \mathbf u-\mathbf v. By algebra,
\|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2 \amp= (\mathbf u-\mathbf v)\cdot(\mathbf u-\mathbf v) \amp= \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u-2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v \amp= \|\mathbf u\|^2+\|\mathbf v\|^2-2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v.
By the Law of Cosines applied to the same triangle, \|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf u\|^2+\|\mathbf v\|^2-2\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta. Comparing the two formulas gives \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta.

subsection.p: We required both vectors to be nonzero. That condition is not cosmetic. The zero vector has length 0, but it has no direction. So there is no well-defined angle between \mathbf 0 and (1,0,0). The formula \cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|} would also divide by 0.
The dot product still makes sense with the zero vector: \mathbf 0\cdot\mathbf v=0. But the angle interpretation needs two nonzero vectors.

statement.p: Two vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v are called orthogonal if \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0. When both vectors are nonzero, this means they are perpendicular.

example.title: A perpendicular pair

statement.p: Let \mathbf u=(3,4),\qquad \mathbf v=(-4,3). Then \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=3(-4)+4(3)=-12+12=0. So the two vectors are perpendicular.

subsection.p: There is a useful trick hiding in that example. In the plane, if \mathbf u=(a,b), then (-b,a) is perpendicular to \mathbf u, because (a,b)\cdot(-b,a)=-ab+ab=0. This is the same 90^\circ rotation we saw when multiplying a complex number by i.

exercise.title: Why does a zero dot product mean perpendicular?

statement.p: The angle formula says \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta. Using this, explain in your own words why \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0 forces two nonzero vectors to be perpendicular. Then say what goes wrong with this reasoning if one of the vectors is \mathbf 0.

hint.p: Both lengths are positive when the vectors are nonzero, so look at which factor in the product is allowed to vanish. What angle in [0,\pi] has that cosine?

subsection.title: Projection onto a line
subsection.p: The dot product tells us how much one vector lies along another.
Suppose a narrow trail runs in the direction \mathbf u=(3,4). A gust of wind pushes a hiker by the displacement \mathbf v=(7,1). Part of this displacement is along the trail. Part is sideways.

The dot product finds the along-trail part: \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u=7\cdot3+1\cdot4=25. Also, \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=3^2+4^2=25. So the coefficient of \mathbf u in the along-trail part is \frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}=\frac{25}{25}=1. Thus the projection of \mathbf v onto the trail direction is 1\cdot \mathbf u=(3,4). The sideways leftover is \mathbf v-\mathbf u=(7,1)-(3,4)=(4,-3). Check that it is perpendicular to the trail: (4,-3)\cdot(3,4)=12-12=0.

figure.caption: A vector splits into an along-line projection and a perpendicular leftover.

statement.p: Let \mathbf u\neq \mathbf 0. The projection of \mathbf v onto the line spanned by \mathbf u is \boxed{\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\,\mathbf u.} The scalar component of \mathbf v in the direction of \mathbf u is \frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\|\mathbf u\|}.

subsection.p: The condition \mathbf u\neq\mathbf 0 is necessary. The zero vector does not determine a line direction, and the formula would divide by \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=0. For example, asking for the projection of (1,2) onto the direction (0,0) has no geometric meaning. There is no direction to project onto.
Projection is not only a formula. It is a closest approximation.

exercise.title: What is the projection, and why subtract it?

statement.p: Describe geometrically what \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v represents: where does it sit relative to \mathbf v and the line through \mathbf u? Then explain why the leftover \mathbf v-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v is exactly the perpendicular part of \mathbf v, rather than just whatever is left.

hint.p: Picture the shadow \mathbf v casts onto the line. Then dot the leftover with \mathbf u: what value would confirm it points straight across the line?

theorem.title: Projection is the closest vector on the line

statement.p: Let \mathbf u\neq\mathbf 0, and let \mathbf p=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v. Then \mathbf p is the vector on the line \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\} closest to \mathbf v.

proof.p:
The vector \mathbf p has the form \mathbf p=c\mathbf u,\qquad c=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}. The leftover \mathbf r=\mathbf v-\mathbf p is perpendicular to \mathbf u, because
\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf u \amp= (\mathbf v-c\mathbf u)\cdot\mathbf u \amp= \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u-c(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u) \amp= \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u-\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u) \amp= 0.
Now take any other vector t\mathbf u on the same line. Then \mathbf v-t\mathbf u=(\mathbf v-\mathbf p)+(\mathbf p-t\mathbf u). The first vector is perpendicular to the line, and the second vector lies on the line. So by the Pythagorean theorem, \|\mathbf v-t\mathbf u\|^2=\|\mathbf v-\mathbf p\|^2+\|\mathbf p-t\mathbf u\|^2. This is smallest when \|\mathbf p-t\mathbf u\|^2=0, which happens only when t\mathbf u=\mathbf p.

subsection.p: This theorem is the first glimpse of a large idea: dot products allow us to turn geometry into approximation. Later, the same idea will become least squares, tangent planes, and orthogonal projections in higher-dimensional spaces.

subsection.title: Work as force times displacement
subsection.p: In single-variable physics, constant work is often introduced as \text{work}=\text{force}\times\text{distance}. That formula assumes the force points in the same direction as the motion.
The dot product gives the correct formula when force and displacement may point in different directions.

example.title: Pushing a crate

statement.p: A crate moves \mathbf d=(4,0) meters across a floor. A force \mathbf F=(12,5) newtons acts on it. The work done is W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=12\cdot4+5\cdot0=48. So the force does 48\ \text{joules} of work.
The vertical component 5 does not contribute to the work across the floor, because the displacement has no vertical component.

subsection.p: Using the angle formula for the dot product, \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=\|\mathbf F\|\,\|\mathbf d\|\cos\theta. So only the component of the force in the direction of motion contributes to the work.
If the force is perpendicular to the displacement, then \theta=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad \cos\theta=0, and the work is zero.
If the force points against the displacement, then \cos\theta<0, and the work is negative. This is what friction does.

subsection.title: Cauchy–Schwarz and the geometry of approximation
subsection.p: A projection cannot be longer than the vector being projected.

For instance, if \widehat{\mathbf u} is a unit vector, then \mathbf v\cdot\widehat{\mathbf u} is the signed length of the shadow of \mathbf v in the direction \widehat{\mathbf u}. A shadow on a line cannot be longer than the object casting it: |\mathbf v\cdot\widehat{\mathbf u}|\leq \|\mathbf v\|. If \mathbf u is not a unit vector, the same idea becomes |\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|\leq \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|.

statement.p: For vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v in \mathbb R^n, \boxed{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|\leq \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|.} If both vectors are nonzero, equality holds exactly when the two vectors lie on the same line through the origin.

proof.p: If \mathbf u=\mathbf0, both sides vanish. Otherwise set t=(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)/\|\mathbf u\|^2. Expanding the nonnegative sum of squares gives 0\le\|\mathbf v-t\mathbf u\|^2=\|\mathbf v\|^2-\frac{(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)^2}{\|\mathbf u\|^2}. Multiply by \|\mathbf u\|^2 and take square roots. Equality holds precisely when \mathbf v=t\mathbf u. For two nonzero vectors, this means they lie on the same line, either in the same or in opposite directions. No angle formula in higher dimensions was needed.

corollary.title: The triangle inequality in every dimension

statement.p: For \mathbf u,\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^n, \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|\le\|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\|.

proof.p: By CauchySchwarz, \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf u\|^2+2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\|\mathbf v\|^2\le(\|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\|)^2. Both sides are nonnegative, so taking square roots proves the claim promised in . Equality holds if one vector is zero or the two nonzero vectors point in the same direction.

subsection.p: The equality condition needs the nonzero assumption. If \mathbf u=\mathbf 0, then |\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|=0=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\| for every \mathbf v. Equality holds, but not because the zero vector has the same or opposite direction as \mathbf v. The zero vector has no direction.
Cauchy–Schwarz says that the dot product cannot be too large. It is the algebraic version of a geometric fact: the shadow of a vector cannot exceed the vector itself.

It also explains why the angle formula is safe: \cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|}. Cauchy–Schwarz guarantees that the right side lies between -1 and 1, exactly where a cosine should live.

exercise.title: What does Cauchy–Schwarz say about the angle?

statement.p: Cauchy–Schwarz says |\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|\leq \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|. Reading this through the angle formula, what does the inequality tell you about \cos\theta? And in geometric terms, what has to be true about \mathbf u and \mathbf v for the inequality to become an equality?

hint.p: Divide both sides by \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\| (for nonzero vectors) and compare with |\cos\theta|. Equality forces |\cos\theta| to its largest possible value, which pins down the angle.

subsection.p: The dot product measures agreement, projection, and work. But the quaternion product had another half. The vector part does not measure agreement; it measures oriented area. It points perpendicular to the plane of two vectors, and its length is the area of their parallelogram. That object is the cross product, and it is stranger than the dot product in one important way: it only works in three-dimensional space.

section.title: The cross product
section.p: The dot product measured agreement: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta. It told us how much one vector points along another. But the quaternion product had another half: UV=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. The vector part is the cross product. It does not measure agreement. It measures oriented area.

subsection.title: A first cross product
subsection.p: Picture a small rectangular metal plate lying flat on a workbench. One edge points 2 units in the x-direction, and the adjacent edge points 3 units in the y-direction: \mathbf u=2\mathbf i,\qquad \mathbf v=3\mathbf j. The area of the rectangle is 2\cdot 3=6. But the rectangle also has an orientation. If we walk first along \mathbf u and then along \mathbf v, the right-hand rule points upward, in the \mathbf k-direction.

The cross product records both pieces: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(2\mathbf i)\times(3\mathbf j)=6\mathbf k. Its length is the area: \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=6. Its direction is perpendicular to the plate.
If we reverse the order, the same plate gets the opposite orientation: \mathbf v\times\mathbf u=(3\mathbf j)\times(2\mathbf i)=-6\mathbf k. The area is still 6, but the sign has flipped.

figure.caption: The cross product points perpendicular to the oriented rectangle. Here \mathbf u=2\mathbf i and \mathbf v=3\mathbf j lie in the xy-plane, and \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=6\mathbf k rises straight up the z-axis, perpendicular to both.

subsection.p: This first example already shows the main idea: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\text{oriented area vector}.

subsection.title: Algebraic definition and the right-hand rule
subsection.p:
The cross product is defined only for vectors in three-dimensional space. If \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3),\qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3), then
\mathbf u\times\mathbf v \amp= (u_2v_3-u_3v_2)\mathbf i \amp\quad +(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)\mathbf j \amp\quad +(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)\mathbf k.
This is exactly the vector part of the quaternion product from .

The basic products are \mathbf i\times\mathbf j=\mathbf k,\qquad \mathbf j\times\mathbf k=\mathbf i,\qquad \mathbf k\times\mathbf i=\mathbf j. These follow the cyclic order \mathbf i\to \mathbf j\to \mathbf k\to \mathbf i. Reversing the order changes the sign: \mathbf j\times\mathbf i=-\mathbf k,\qquad \mathbf k\times\mathbf j=-\mathbf i,\qquad \mathbf i\times\mathbf k=-\mathbf j.

figure.caption: The right-hand rule is the orientation rule for the cross product.

subsection.p: Here is a full computation.

example.title: A cross product in space

statement.p:
Let \mathbf u=(2,-1,3),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,4,2). Then
\mathbf u\times\mathbf v \amp= ((-1)(2)-3(4))\mathbf i \amp\quad +(3(1)-2(2))\mathbf j \amp\quad +(2(4)-(-1)(1))\mathbf k \amp= (-2-12)\mathbf i+(3-4)\mathbf j+(8+1)\mathbf k \amp= -14\mathbf i-\mathbf j+9\mathbf k.
So (2,-1,3)\times(1,4,2)=(-14,-1,9).

subsection.p: The formula is not beautiful by itself. The geometry makes it worth remembering.

subsection.title: The cross product is perpendicular to both inputs
subsection.p:
Take \mathbf u=(2,-1,3),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,4,2), from the previous example. We found \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(-14,-1,9). Now dot this result with \mathbf u:
\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v) \amp= (2,-1,3)\cdot(-14,-1,9) \amp= 2(-14)+(-1)(-1)+3(9) \amp= -28+1+27 \amp= 0.
So \mathbf u\times\mathbf v is perpendicular to \mathbf u.

Dot it with \mathbf v:
\mathbf v\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v) \amp= (1,4,2)\cdot(-14,-1,9) \amp= -14-4+18 \amp= 0.
So it is also perpendicular to \mathbf v.

theorem.title: Basic algebra of the cross product

statement.p: For vectors \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^3 and a scalar c, \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=-(\mathbf v\times\mathbf u), \mathbf u\times(\mathbf v+\mathbf w)=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v+\mathbf u\times\mathbf w, (c\mathbf u)\times\mathbf v=c(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v), and \mathbf u\times\mathbf u=\mathbf 0. Also, \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)=0,\qquad \mathbf v\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)=0. Thus \mathbf u\times\mathbf v is perpendicular to both \mathbf u and \mathbf v.

proof.p: The first four identities follow by substituting components into the formula for the cross product and simplifying.

For perpendicularity, write \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1). Then
\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v) \amp= u_1(u_2v_3-u_3v_2)+u_2(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)+u_3(u_1v_2-u_2v_1) \amp= u_1u_2v_3-u_1u_3v_2+u_2u_3v_1-u_1u_2v_3+u_1u_3v_2-u_2u_3v_1 \amp= 0.
The proof that \mathbf v\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)=0 is the same cancellation with the roles arranged differently.

subsection.p: The identity \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=-(\mathbf v\times\mathbf u) is worth pausing over. The cross product is not commutative. This is not a defect. It is exactly what oriented area demands.
For example, \mathbf i\times\mathbf j=\mathbf k, but \mathbf j\times\mathbf i=-\mathbf k. The two ordered pairs make the same parallelogram, but with opposite orientation.

statement.p: We checked by computation that \mathbf u\times\mathbf v is perpendicular to both \mathbf u and \mathbf v. Thinking of \mathbf u\times\mathbf v as the oriented area vector of the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf u and \mathbf v, explain in words why it has to point perpendicular to both, rather than slanting off in some other direction.

hint.p: The parallelogram lives flat inside one plane. If a single vector is going to stand in for that flat sheet, which direction is the only one that does not favor \mathbf u over \mathbf v or lean back into the sheet?

subsection.title: Cross product as oriented area
subsection.p: A tilted parallelogram has area \text{base}\times\text{height}. If two vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v meet at angle \theta, then the base is \|\mathbf u\|, and the height is \|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta. So the area is \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta.
The cross product has exactly this length.

example.title: Area of a slanted parallelogram

statement.p:
Let \mathbf u=(3,0,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,2,0). These vectors lie in the xy-plane. Their cross product is
\mathbf u\times\mathbf v \amp= (3\mathbf i)\times(\mathbf i+2\mathbf j) \amp= 3(\mathbf i\times\mathbf i)+6(\mathbf i\times\mathbf j) \amp= 0+6\mathbf k \amp= 6\mathbf k.
The parallelogram has base 3 and height 2, so its area is 6. The cross product says the same thing: \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=6. The positive \mathbf k-direction records that the ordered pair \mathbf u,\mathbf v turns counterclockwise in the xy-plane.

Let \mathbf u and \mathbf v be nonzero vectors in \mathbb R^3, and let \theta be the angle between them, with 0\leq \theta\leq \pi. Then \boxed{\|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta.} Therefore \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\| is the area of the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf u and \mathbf v.

proof.p:
A direct component calculation gives the identity \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf u\|^2\|\mathbf v\|^2-(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)^2. Using the dot product formula \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta, we get
\|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|^2 \amp= \|\mathbf u\|^2\|\mathbf v\|^2-\|\mathbf u\|^2\|\mathbf v\|^2\cos^2\theta \amp= \|\mathbf u\|^2\|\mathbf v\|^2(1-\cos^2\theta) \amp= \|\mathbf u\|^2\|\mathbf v\|^2\sin^2\theta.
Since 0\leq \theta\leq \pi, we have \sin\theta\geq0. Taking square roots gives \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta.

subsection.p: The nonzero condition is needed for the angle \theta. The zero vector has no direction, so there is no well-defined angle between \mathbf 0 and (1,0,0). The cross product itself still makes sense: \mathbf 0\times(1,0,0)=\mathbf 0. The area of the collapsed parallelogram is 0. But the angle formula should not be used with a zero vector.

There is another warning. The cross product gives a direction only when the parallelogram has positive area. If \mathbf u=(1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(2,0,0), then the two vectors are parallel, and \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\mathbf 0. The parallelogram has collapsed to a line segment. It has no preferred normal direction. So the zero cross product is not pointing in some mysterious direction. It is telling us that there is no oriented area vector to point anywhere.

exercise.title: What do length and direction each measure?

statement.p: The vector \mathbf u\times\mathbf v carries two pieces of information at once: its length and its direction. In your own words, what does the length \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\| measure, and what does its direction encode? What changes about each piece if you swap the order to \mathbf v\times\mathbf u?

hint.p: One piece is a size that cannot be negative; the other is an orientation that the right-hand rule decides. Swapping the order leaves the parallelogram unchanged but reverses how you walk around it.

subsection.title: Normal vectors to planes
subsection.p: A plane can be described by directions lying inside it, or by a vector perpendicular to it. The cross product turns the first description into the second.

Suppose a wooden sign is supported by a flat metal plate. The plate passes through the point P=(1,0,2) and contains the two direction vectors \mathbf a=(2,1,0),\qquad \mathbf b=(0,1,3). A vector perpendicular to the plate is
\mathbf n \amp= \mathbf a\times\mathbf b \amp= (2,1,0)\times(0,1,3) \amp= (1\cdot3-0\cdot1)\mathbf i+(0\cdot0-2\cdot3)\mathbf j+(2\cdot1-1\cdot0)\mathbf k \amp= 3\mathbf i-6\mathbf j+2\mathbf k.
So \mathbf n=(3,-6,2) is normal to the plate.

Any point (x,y,z) on the plane has displacement from P (x,y,z)-(1,0,2)=(x-1,y,z-2). This displacement lies in the plane, so it is perpendicular to \mathbf n: (3,-6,2)\cdot(x-1,y,z-2)=0. Thus 3(x-1)-6y+2(z-2)=0. Simplifying, \boxed{3x-6y+2z=7.}

theorem.title: Cross product normal to a plane

statement.p: If \mathbf a and \mathbf b are nonparallel direction vectors in a plane, then \mathbf a\times\mathbf b is a nonzero normal vector to that plane.

proof.p: The cross product \mathbf a\times\mathbf b is perpendicular to \mathbf a and to \mathbf b. Since \mathbf a and \mathbf b are nonparallel, they span the directions in the plane. A vector perpendicular to both spanning directions is perpendicular to every direction in the plane.

subsection.p: The nonparallel condition matters. If \mathbf a=(1,2,3),\qquad \mathbf b=(2,4,6), then \mathbf b=2\mathbf a. These are not two genuine plane directions. Their cross product is \mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\mathbf 0. The zero vector is not a useful normal vector. A single line direction lies in many different planes, so it cannot determine one plane normal.

subsection.title: Torque: when a force turns something
subsection.p: A force can push. It can also turn.

A wrench is attached to a bolt. The vector \mathbf r points from the bolt to the place where the force is applied. The force is \mathbf F. The turning effect is called torque: \boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F.

For example, suppose a wrench extends 0.30 meters in the positive x-direction: \mathbf r=(0.30,0,0). A force of 20 newtons is applied in the positive y-direction: \mathbf F=(0,20,0). Then
\boldsymbol\tau \amp= (0.30,0,0)\times(0,20,0) \amp= (0,0,6).
The torque has magnitude 6\ \text{newton-meters}, and it points in the positive z-direction.

If the force is applied along the wrench instead, say \mathbf F=(20,0,0), then \mathbf r\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0. The force may be large, but it produces no turning around the bolt. It is trying to pull or push along the wrench, not rotate it.
This is exactly what the formula \|\mathbf r\times\mathbf F\|=\|\mathbf r\|\,\|\mathbf F\|\sin\theta says. Only the perpendicular part of the force contributes to torque.

subsection.title: Angular velocity
subsection.p: The cross product also describes rigid rotation.
Suppose a disk rotates around the z-axis with angular velocity \boldsymbol\omega=4\mathbf k. This means 4 radians per second around the vertical axis.

A point on the disk is located at \mathbf r=2\mathbf i. Its velocity is \mathbf v=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r. Compute:
\mathbf v \amp= (4\mathbf k)\times(2\mathbf i) \amp= 8(\mathbf k\times\mathbf i) \amp= 8\mathbf j.
So the point at 2\mathbf i moves in the positive y-direction with speed 8.
The direction is not an arbitrary convention. It is the same right-hand rule that tells us \mathbf k\times\mathbf i=\mathbf j.

subsection.title: Why the cross product is special to three dimensions
subsection.p: The cross product turns an oriented area into a vector perpendicular to that area. This is possible in three dimensions because a plane has one perpendicular direction line.

In the plane, two vectors already fill the whole space. There is no perpendicular direction inside the plane. The best we can do is assign a signed area number: u_1v_2-u_2v_1. That number says whether the ordered pair turns counterclockwise or clockwise.
In four-dimensional space, the opposite problem appears. A two-dimensional plane has too many perpendicular directions.

For example, in \mathbb R^4, the plane spanned by \mathbf e_1=(1,0,0,0),\qquad \mathbf e_2=(0,1,0,0) has both \mathbf e_3=(0,0,1,0) and \mathbf e_4=(0,0,0,1) perpendicular to it. There is not one preferred normal direction. So an oriented area cannot be honestly represented by a single normal vector.
Three dimensions sit in the lucky middle. A plane has exactly one perpendicular line, so the area can be encoded as a vector.

statement.p: The dot product \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v makes sense for vectors in any dimension, yet the cross product \mathbf u\times\mathbf v lives only in three. Explain why a plane in \mathbb R^3 can hand its oriented area to a single normal vector, while the same trick fails both in \mathbb R^2 and in \mathbb R^4.

hint.p: Count the directions perpendicular to a plane. In \mathbb R^2 there are none to spare; in \mathbb R^4 there are too many to choose from. Only one dimension leaves exactly one perpendicular line.

subsection.p: But the area itself is the deeper object. The cross product is one three-dimensional way to package it. The next section will strip away the packaging and look directly at the numbers that measure signed area and signed volume. Those numbers are determinants.

section.title: Determinants and signed volume
section.p: The cross product gave us an oriented area vector. But sometimes we do not want the normal vector. We only want the signed amount of area or volume. That number is a determinant.

subsection.title: The 2\times2 determinant as signed area
subsection.p: Start in the plane.

Let \mathbf u=(4,1), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,3). These two vectors form a parallelogram. Embed them in the xy-plane as \widetilde{\mathbf u}=(4,1,0), \qquad \widetilde{\mathbf v}=(1,3,0). Then
\widetilde{\mathbf u}\times\widetilde{\mathbf v} \amp= (4,1,0)\times(1,3,0) \amp= (0,0,4\cdot3-1\cdot1) \amp= (0,0,11).
So the parallelogram has signed area 11. The sign is positive because \mathbf u followed by \mathbf v turns counterclockwise.

figure.caption: The determinant 4\cdot3-1\cdot1=11 is the signed area.

subsection.p: That expression 4\cdot3-1\cdot1 is the determinant of the two vectors.

statement.p:
If \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2), then the 2\times2 determinant with columns \mathbf u and \mathbf v is
\boxed{ \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] = \begin{vmatrix} u_1 & v_1\\ u_2 & v_2 \end{vmatrix} = u_1v_2-u_2v_1. }
For vectors \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2), the determinant \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] = u_1v_2-u_2v_1 is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf u and \mathbf v.

proof.p: Embed the plane in space by adding a zero z-coordinate: \widetilde{\mathbf u}=(u_1,u_2,0), \qquad \widetilde{\mathbf v}=(v_1,v_2,0). Then \widetilde{\mathbf u}\times\widetilde{\mathbf v} = (0,0,u_1v_2-u_2v_1). The cross product is the oriented area vector. Its z-component is therefore the signed area in the xy-plane: u_1v_2-u_2v_1.

subsection.p: The sign contains orientation.

exercise.title: What is the sign telling you?

statement.p: You compute two 2\times2 determinants and get +7 for one pair of vectors and -7 for another. The two parallelograms have exactly the same area. So what difference is the sign actually recording? Describe, in words, what the sign of \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] tells you about how \mathbf u and \mathbf v sit relative to each other.

hint.p: Picture sweeping from \mathbf u toward \mathbf v through the parallelogram. Which way does that turn go? Think about what changes when you read the two vectors in the opposite order.

subsection.p:
If \mathbf u=(4,1), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,3), then \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=11. But if we swap the order,
\det[\mathbf v\ \mathbf u] = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4\\ 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1\cdot1-3\cdot4 = -11.
The parallelogram is the same. The orientation is opposite.

If the two vectors are parallel, the determinant is zero. For example, \mathbf u=(1,2), \qquad \mathbf v=(2,4). Then
\det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 1\cdot4-2\cdot2 = 0.
The parallelogram has collapsed into a line segment. Its area is zero.

subsection.title: A square pushed into a parallelogram
subsection.p: The determinant becomes especially useful when a whole grid is moved.

Suppose a machine sends the basic horizontal step \mathbf e_1=(1,0) to \mathbf u=(2,1), and sends the basic vertical step \mathbf e_2=(0,1) to \mathbf v=(1,3). The unit square becomes a parallelogram with signed area
\det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6-1 = 5.
So this machine multiplies small signed areas by 5.

figure.caption: A linear grid machine scales area by the determinant.

subsection.p: This idea will return in change of variables for double integrals. When a coordinate change bends and stretches a region, the determinant tells us the local area-scaling factor.

subsection.title: The 3\times3 determinant as signed volume
subsection.p: In three dimensions, three vectors form a parallelepiped: a slanted box.

Take the simple case \mathbf u=(2,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(0,3,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(0,0,4). They form a rectangular box with volume 2\cdot3\cdot4=24. The determinant gives the same number:
\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 3 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 24.

Now tilt the box without changing its vertical height: \mathbf u=(2,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,3,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(1,1,4). The volume is still 24. The base parallelogram in the xy-plane has signed area
\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6,
and the height is 4. So the volume is 6\cdot4=24.
The determinant packages this calculation into one number.

statement.p:
If \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3), \qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3), \qquad \mathbf w=(w_1,w_2,w_3), then the 3\times3 determinant with columns \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w is
\boxed{ \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w] = \begin{vmatrix} u_1 & v_1 & w_1\\ u_2 & v_2 & w_2\\ u_3 & v_3 & w_3 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w). }
Expanded out,
\det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w] \amp= u_1(v_2w_3-v_3w_2) \amp\qquad -v_1(u_2w_3-u_3w_2) \amp\qquad +w_1(u_2v_3-u_3v_2).

example.title: A slanted box

statement.p:
Let \mathbf u=(2,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,3,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(1,1,4). Then \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w] = \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w). First compute
\mathbf v\times\mathbf w \amp= (1,3,0)\times(1,1,4) \amp= (3\cdot4-0\cdot1,\;0\cdot1-1\cdot4,\;1\cdot1-3\cdot1) \amp= (12,-4,-2).
Then
\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w) \amp= (2,0,0)\cdot(12,-4,-2) \amp= 24.
So the signed volume is 24.

figure.caption: Three vectors form a parallelepiped. The determinant is its signed volume. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.title: Scalar triple product
subsection.p: The expression \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w) has a name.

The geometry is clean. The vector \mathbf v\times\mathbf w is an oriented area vector for the base parallelogram spanned by \mathbf v and \mathbf w. Dotting with \mathbf u takes the component of \mathbf u in the normal direction and multiplies by that base area. That is base area times signed height.

theorem.title: Scalar triple product as signed volume

proof.p: The vector \mathbf v\times\mathbf w is perpendicular to the base parallelogram spanned by \mathbf v and \mathbf w, and its length is the area of that base.

If \mathbf v\times\mathbf w\neq\mathbf 0, then \widehat{\mathbf n} = \frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf w}{\|\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\|} is a unit normal to the base. The signed height of \mathbf u above the base is \mathbf u\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}. So the signed volume is
\text{base area}\cdot\text{signed height} \amp= \|\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\| \left( \mathbf u\cdot \frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf w}{\|\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\|} \right) \amp= \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w).

If \mathbf v\times\mathbf w=\mathbf 0, then \mathbf v and \mathbf w are parallel, so the base has zero area. The parallelepiped has volume 0, and the formula also gives \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w) = \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf 0 = 0.

subsection.p: The proof divided by \|\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\| only when this number was not zero. That condition matters. If \mathbf v=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(2,0,0), then \mathbf v\times\mathbf w=\mathbf 0, so the unit normal \frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf w}{\|\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\|} is meaningless. But the volume formula survives: \mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf w)=0. The box has collapsed because two of its edges point along the same line.

subsection.title: Orientation of ordered bases
subsection.p: The sign of a determinant tells us orientation.

The standard ordered basis in space is \mathbf i=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf j=(0,1,0), \qquad \mathbf k=(0,0,1). Its determinant is
\det[\mathbf i\ \mathbf j\ \mathbf k] = \begin{vmatrix} 1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1 \end{vmatrix} = 1.
So (\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k) is positively oriented.

If we swap the first two vectors, we get (\mathbf j,\mathbf i,\mathbf k). Its determinant is
\det[\mathbf j\ \mathbf i\ \mathbf k] = \begin{vmatrix} 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&1 \end{vmatrix} = -1.
The volume is still 1, but the orientation has reversed.

exercise.title: Why does one swap flip the sign?

statement.p: Swapping just two vectors in an ordered basis turned \det=+1 into \det=-1, even though the same box was described both times. Why should interchanging two of the vectors reverse the orientation rather than leave it unchanged? Explain why a single swap must flip the sign, and predict what happens to the orientation if you then perform a second swap.

hint.p: A determinant is built so that two identical columns force it to be zero. Imagine slowly sliding one vector until it coincides with another: the signed volume must pass through 0. What does that forced passage through zero say about the sign on the two sides of the swap?

definition.title: Orientation of an ordered basis in \mathbb R^3

statement.p: An ordered triple of vectors (\mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w) is a basis of \mathbb R^3 if the vectors are independent, so that their parallelepiped has nonzero volume.
The basis is positively oriented if \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w]>0. It is negatively oriented if \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w]<0.

subsection.p: The word basis matters. If \mathbf u=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(1,0,0), then the determinant is \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w]=0. These three vectors do not fill space. They lie in the same plane because \mathbf w=\mathbf u. So the triple has no positive or negative orientation as a basis. It is not a basis at all.

The same idea works in the plane. The ordered pair ((1,0),(0,1)) is positively oriented because
\begin{vmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&1 \end{vmatrix} = 1.
The ordered pair ((0,1),(1,0)) is negatively oriented because
\begin{vmatrix} 0&1\\ 1&0 \end{vmatrix} = -1.
Orientation is the mathematical version of choosing clockwise versus counterclockwise in the plane, or right-handed versus left-handed in space.

subsection.title: Determinants as volume-scaling factors
subsection.p: A determinant does not only measure one parallelogram or one parallelepiped. It measures how a linear machine scales area or volume.

Consider the plane machine T(x,y)=x(2,1)+y(1,3). It sends (1,0)\mapsto (2,1), \qquad (0,1)\mapsto (1,3). So it sends the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf u=(2,1), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,3). The determinant is
\det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] = \begin{vmatrix} 2&1\\ 1&3 \end{vmatrix} = 5.
Therefore the machine multiplies signed area by 5.
A tiny rectangle with side lengths \Delta x \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta y has area \Delta x\,\Delta y. After applying T, it becomes a tiny parallelogram with area 5\,\Delta x\,\Delta y.

exercise.title: Why does one number rescale every rectangle?

statement.p: A rectangle has edge vectors (h,0) and (0,k), where h,k>0. Under T(x,y)=x(2,1)+y(1,3), what are the two image edge vectors? Compute their determinant and explain why the ratio of image area to original area is always 5, independent of h and k.

hint.p: The image edges are (2h,h) and (k,3k). Their determinant is (2h)(3k)-hk; the original rectangle has area hk.

subsection.p: In space, if a machine sends the coordinate steps \mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k to \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w, then it sends the unit cube to the parallelepiped spanned by \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w. The signed volume scaling factor is \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w].

example.title: A shear preserves area

statement.p:
Let T(x,y)=(x+2y,y). Then T(1,0)=(1,0), \qquad T(0,1)=(2,1). The area scaling factor is
\begin{vmatrix} 1&2\\ 0&1 \end{vmatrix} = 1.
This machine slants squares into parallelograms, but it preserves area.
A square can be pushed sideways without changing its area. The determinant sees that.

example.title: A coordinate stretch changes volume

statement.p:
Let a space machine stretch x-distances by 2, y-distances by 3, and z-distances by 4: T(x,y,z)=(2x,3y,4z). Then T(\mathbf i)=(2,0,0), \qquad T(\mathbf j)=(0,3,0), \qquad T(\mathbf k)=(0,0,4). The volume scaling factor is
\begin{vmatrix} 2&0&0\\ 0&3&0\\ 0&0&4 \end{vmatrix} = 24.
So every small volume is multiplied by 24.

subsection.p: This is why determinants appear in change of variables. When we later replace (x,y) by better coordinates, the determinant will tell us how much each little area piece has been stretched. In polar coordinates, that mysterious extra factor r in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta will turn out to be a determinant.

But the determinant has revealed something even more basic: area and volume change sign when we swap directions. Ordinary multiplication does not behave that way: ab=ba. Oriented area does: \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=-\det[\mathbf v\ \mathbf u]. That sign flip is not a technicality. It is the beginning of a new product, built for oriented geometry. The next section gives it a name: the wedge product.

section.title: Alternating products: a first glimpse of forms
section.p: The determinant gave us signed area and signed volume. That sign was not decoration. It was the whole point. When we swapped two directions, the parallelogram stayed the same, but its orientation reversed: \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=-\det[\mathbf v\ \mathbf u]. Now we give that sign-changing behavior a name. It is the first step toward differential forms.

subsection.title: Area as a bilinear alternating measurement
subsection.p: A carpenter lays a small slanted tile on the floor. One side of the tile follows the vector \mathbf u=(3,1), and the adjacent side follows \mathbf v=(1,2). The signed area of the parallelogram is \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot2-1\cdot1=5.
The tile has ordinary area 5. It also has positive orientation because the ordered pair \mathbf u,\mathbf v turns counterclockwise.

If we walk around the same tile in the opposite order, the signed area becomes \det[\mathbf v\ \mathbf u]=\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\2&1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot1-2\cdot3=-5. The tile did not shrink. Only the orientation changed.

figure.caption: The same parallelogram has opposite signed area when the order is reversed.

subsection.p:
The determinant also behaves linearly in each input. For example, split \mathbf u=(3,1) into \mathbf u=(3,0)+(0,1). Then
\det[(3,1)\ \mathbf v]\amp=\det[(3,0)\ \mathbf v]+\det[(0,1)\ \mathbf v].
With \mathbf v=(1,2), this says 5=\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{vmatrix}+\begin{vmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{vmatrix}=6+(-1). So signed area is additive in the first vector. It is also additive in the second vector. Stretch one side by a factor of c, and the signed area is stretched by the same factor.
This is the pattern.

exercise.title: Why do repeated vector inputs give zero?

statement.p: The word alternating means that swapping the two inputs reverses the sign: B(\mathbf v,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v). Think about what this says geometrically for a parallelogram's signed area, and then explain why feeding the same vector into both slots of this real-valued measurement must give zero.

hint.p: Put \mathbf u=\mathbf v into the swap rule. You get B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u). What is the only number equal to its own negative? Geometrically, a vector and itself span no area.

statement.p: A function B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) that takes two vectors and returns a number is called bilinear if it is linear in each input separately: B(a\mathbf u+b\mathbf w,\mathbf v)=aB(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)+bB(\mathbf w,\mathbf v), and B(\mathbf u,a\mathbf v+b\mathbf w)=aB(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)+bB(\mathbf u,\mathbf w).
It is called alternating if swapping the two inputs changes the sign: B(\mathbf v,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v). In particular, B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u)=0.

subsection.p: The determinant in the plane is bilinear and alternating: \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=u_1v_2-u_2v_1.

theorem.title: Every planar alternating bilinear measurement is area times a constant

statement.p: Let B be a bilinear alternating function of two vectors in \mathbb R^2. Then there is a constant c such that \boxed{B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=c(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)} for all \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2),\qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2). In other words, every bilinear alternating measurement in the plane is a constant multiple of signed area.

proof.p:
Let \mathbf e_1=(1,0),\qquad \mathbf e_2=(0,1). Write \mathbf u=u_1\mathbf e_1+u_2\mathbf e_2,\qquad \mathbf v=v_1\mathbf e_1+v_2\mathbf e_2. By bilinearity,
B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=B(u_1\mathbf e_1+u_2\mathbf e_2,\, v_1\mathbf e_1+v_2\mathbf e_2) \amp=u_1v_1B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)+u_1v_2B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2) \amp\qquad +u_2v_1B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)+u_2v_2B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_2).
Because B is alternating, B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=0,\qquad B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_2)=0, and B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)=-B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2). Let c=B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2). Then
B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=u_1v_2c-u_2v_1c \amp=c(u_1v_2-u_2v_1).

subsection.p: The two hypotheses are real hypotheses.

First, bilinearity matters. Define B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)^3. Swapping \mathbf u and \mathbf v changes the sign, so this function is alternating. But it is not bilinear. For example, B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=1, while B(2\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=8. A bilinear function would have given 2, not 8. So this is not a constant multiple of signed area.

Second, alternating matters. The dot product D(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v is bilinear, but it is not alternating. Indeed, D(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=1, while an alternating measurement must give B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=0. The dot product measures alignment, not oriented area.

subsection.title: The coordinate measurements dx, dy, and dz
subsection.p: The determinant formula u_1v_2-u_2v_1 has two parts. It uses the x-component of one vector and the y-component of the other, then subtracts the same measurement with the roles reversed.
To name those component measurements, we write dx(a,b)=a,\qquad dy(a,b)=b. So dx reads the x-component of a vector, and dy reads the y-component.
For example, if \mathbf u=(3,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,2), then dx(\mathbf u)=3,\qquad dy(\mathbf u)=1, and dx(\mathbf v)=1,\qquad dy(\mathbf v)=2.

These are the first examples of 1-forms: objects that take one vector and return one number. Later, a 1-form like P\,dx+Q\,dy will be the kind of object we integrate along a curve. For now, dx and dy are simply coordinate-measuring devices.
In space we also have dz(a,b,c)=c.

subsection.title: Why dx\,dy should not mean ordinary multiplication
subsection.p: A parallelogram has two side vectors. So an area measurement must take two vector inputs, not one.

If \mathbf u=(3,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,2), then ordinary multiplication might tempt us to write dx(\mathbf u)\,dy(\mathbf v)=3\cdot2=6. But the signed area is not 6. It is 3\cdot2-1\cdot1=5. The missing piece is the swapped product: dy(\mathbf u)\,dx(\mathbf v)=1\cdot1=1. Signed area is the difference: dx(\mathbf u)\,dy(\mathbf v)-dy(\mathbf u)\,dx(\mathbf v).
This difference is important enough to get its own symbol.

statement.p: More generally, let \alpha and \beta be linear functions from vectors to real numbers. Their wedge is the two-input measurement (\alpha\wedge\beta)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=\alpha(\mathbf u)\beta(\mathbf v)-\alpha(\mathbf v)\beta(\mathbf u). Thus \alpha and \beta each take one vector, while \alpha\wedge\beta takes an ordered pair of vectors and returns a scalar. This definition does not define a wedge of two vectors.

subsection.p: A sum or scalar multiple of measurements is evaluated by adding or scaling their values. Expanding the preceding definition therefore gives (a\alpha+b\beta)\wedge\gamma=a(\alpha\wedge\gamma)+b(\beta\wedge\gamma), and the same distributive rule in the second factor. Interchanging the two scalar products gives \beta\wedge\alpha=-\alpha\wedge\beta. In particular, \alpha\wedge\alpha=0: its value on every ordered pair is the difference of two identical products. These are identities of measurements, meaning that both sides give the same value on every pair of vectors.
So dx\wedge dy is not ordinary multiplication. The wedge symbol \wedge is a warning: \text{measure the ordered area, and subtract the swapped order.}

exercise.title: Why isn't dx\wedge dy ordinary multiplication?

statement.p: Ordinary multiplication is commutative: ab=ba. But the definition gives dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. Using the idea that dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of the parallelogram built from two ordered vectors, explain in your own words why reversing the order of dx and dy should flip the sign rather than leave it unchanged.

hint.p: Evaluate both dx\wedge dy and dy\wedge dx on the same ordered pair (\mathbf u,\mathbf v). Their two scalar products occur with opposite signs. Compare this with the effect of swapping the vector inputs.

subsection.p: This is why the notation dx\,dy is too quiet when orientation matters. In ordinary double integrals, dA often means unsigned little area. But the form dx\wedge dy remembers orientation. Reversing the order reverses the sign.

subsection.title: Coordinate shadows in space
subsection.p: A parallelogram in space casts shadows onto the coordinate planes. Each shadow has a signed area.

Let \mathbf u=(2,1,3),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,4,0). The signed area of the shadow on the xy-plane is
(dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\1&4\end{vmatrix} \amp=2\cdot4-1\cdot1 \amp=7.

The signed area of the shadow on the yz-plane is
(dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}1&4\\3&0\end{vmatrix} \amp=1\cdot0-3\cdot4 \amp=-12.

The signed area of the shadow on the zx-plane is
(dz\wedge dx)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{vmatrix} \amp=3\cdot1-2\cdot0 \amp=3.
This is a beautiful fact. The cross product packages three coordinate area measurements into one vector. But the area measurements themselves are the wedge products.
That is why the wedge product survives in every dimension, while the cross product is special to three dimensions.

subsection.title: Signed volume as dx\wedge dy\wedge dz
subsection.p: The same idea works for volume.
A signed volume measurement takes three vectors. It is linear in each input and changes sign whenever two inputs are swapped.
The basic signed volume measurement in space is dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

definition.title: The volume form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz

statement.p: For vectors \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^3, the form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is defined by \boxed{(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w)=\det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w].} It measures the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the ordered triple \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w.

subsection.p:
For example, let \mathbf u=(1,2,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,3),\qquad \mathbf w=(2,0,1). Then
(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}1&0&2\\2&1&0\\0&3&1\end{vmatrix} \amp=13.
So the ordered triple spans signed volume 13.
If we swap the first two vectors, the sign flips: (dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf v,\mathbf u,\mathbf w)=-13. Again, the box is the same. The orientation is not.

subsection.title: Forms as future integrands
subsection.p: The word form may sound abstract, but at this stage it means something very concrete.
A 1-form measures a vector: dx,\qquad dy,\qquad P\,dx+Q\,dy. Later, 1-forms will be integrated along curves.
A 2-form measures oriented area: dx\wedge dy,\qquad dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx. Later, 2-forms will be integrated over surfaces and regions.
A 3-form measures oriented volume: dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Later, 3-forms will be integrated over solids.

exercise.title: Why does an ordered pair carry a sign?

statement.p: The vectors \mathbf u=(3,1) and \mathbf v=(1,2) span a parallelogram. Evaluate (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) and (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf v,\mathbf u). Explain why reversing the ordered pair changes signed area but leaves ordinary area unchanged.

hint.p: Use u_1v_2-u_2v_1, then interchange \mathbf u and \mathbf v. Ordinary area is the absolute value of the signed result.

subsection.p: This chapter began with Hamilton trying to multiply directions. It ends with a different kind of product, one that does not try to turn area into a vector. It lets area be area. Before these forms become integrals, one more piece of machinery has to arrive. We need rules that move every vector in a grid at once. Those rules are linear maps, and their bookkeeping devices are matrices.

introduction.p: In the complex plane, multiplication can turn an arrow without changing its length. Can quaternion multiplication do the same thing for an arrow in space? There is a small obstacle: a quaternion has four real coordinates, while our arrow has only three. This project uses that extra coordinate to discover how spatial rotations work.

Work through the steps in order. Keep the quaternion multiplication table from nearby, and sketch the two-dimensional planes as they appear. You will need distributivity, the dot and cross products, and the angle-addition identities for sine and cosine. No matrix formulas are needed. Try each checkpoint before opening its hint.

Throughout the project, vectors move while the coordinate axes stay fixed. Positive spatial angles follow the right-hand rule: point your right thumb along the positive axis and curl your fingers in the direction of the turn. We use \phi for the angle in a quaternion exponential and reserve \theta for the eventual angle of rotation in three-dimensional space. Discovering their relationship is part of the work.

subsection.title: Step 1: recall how complex multiplication turns a plane
subsection.p: Use the polar expression from with the notation e^{i\phi}=\cos\phi+i\sin\phi. For the next few steps, abbreviate c=\cos\phi and s=\sin\phi. The complex plane has the ordered basis (1,i): draw 1 to the right and i upward.

li.p: Compute (c+si)1 and (c+si)i. Draw their images when \phi=\pi/6. What angle has each arrow turned?
Use distributivity to find (c+si)(x+yi). Write the resulting coordinates, and check that their squared length is x^2+y^2.
Write x+yi=r(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha). Use the angle-addition identities to show that multiplication replaces \alpha by \alpha+\phi. Why does this establish a rotation for every arrow?

hint.p: The basis images are c+si and -s+ci. In the length calculation, the mixed terms cancel and c^2+s^2=1.

subsection.p: Keep the resulting pattern in view: (x,y)\longmapsto(cx-sy,sx+cy). More generally, in a plane with ordered perpendicular unit directions (A,B), a positive turn through \phi sends A\longmapsto cA+sB,\qquad B\longmapsto-sA+cB. The order matters: a small positive angle turns the first direction toward the second. We will recognize rotations by this pattern, even when the plane sits in four dimensions.

subsection.title: Step 2: find two rotating planes inside four dimensions
subsection.p: Regard the quaternion space \mathbb H as the real coordinate space a_0+a_1i+a_2j+a_3k\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3). Its four perpendicular unit directions are 1,i,j,k. The direction 1 is a genuine coordinate direction here. It is perpendicular to the three-dimensional subspace of pure imaginary quaternions.

Each of i,j,k squares to -1. Thus each gives its own version of Euler's formula:
q_i=e^{i\phi}\amp=c+si, q_j=e^{j\phi}\amp=c+sj, q_k=e^{k\phi}\amp=c+sk.
If you recall the exponential series, this follows by grouping its even and odd powers: for E=i,j,k,
e^{E\phi}\amp=\left(1-\frac{\phi^2}{2!}+\frac{\phi^4}{4!}-\cdots\right) \amp\qquad+E\left(\phi-\frac{\phi^3}{3!}+\frac{\phi^5}{5!}-\cdots\right).
You may use the sine-cosine expressions directly for all the calculations below.

exercise.title: Multiply every basis direction on the left

statement.p: Define L_{q_i}(X)=q_iX, and similarly for q_j,q_k. Here X can be any quaternion. Verify the first row of the table and fill every question mark in the other two rows. Keep the multiplier on the left.

table.title: Images of the four basis directions under left multiplication.

li.p: For L_{q_i}, recognize the rotation pattern in the ordered planes (1,i) and (j,k). Sketch these as two separate ordinary planes. Mark the angle \phi in each.

For L_{q_j}, use the ordered planes (1,j) and (k,i). For L_{q_k}, use (1,k) and (i,j). Check that both planes in each pair turn by +\phi. Why would writing (i,k) in place of (k,i) reverse the reported sign?
Use the two perpendicular planes to explain why each map preserves |X|^2, the sum of the four squared real coordinates.

hint.p: For example, q_jk=ck+s(jk)=ck+si, while q_ji=ci+s(ji)=ci-sk. Read these as images of the ordered pair (k,i). The squared lengths of the two plane components add to the squared length in four dimensions.

exercise.title: Why is one multiplication not yet our spatial rotation?

statement.p: Compute the real part of q_i(xi+yj+zk). Then set \phi=\pi/2 and follow the input i. Does its image still represent a vector in three-dimensional space? Explain why preserving length in four dimensions does not by itself give a rotation of the pure imaginary subspace.

hint.p: The real part is -sx. In particular, ii=-1 points along the real coordinate direction.

subsection.title: Step 3: use right multiplication to control the two turns

statement.p:
For q=a_0+a_1i+a_2j+a_3k, define its quaternion conjugate and its length by
\overline q\amp=a_0-a_1i-a_2j-a_3k, |q|\amp=\sqrt{a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2}.
A unit quaternion has |q|=1.

li.p: Write q=a_0+V, where V=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k, and use V^2=-(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2) to prove q\overline q=\overline q q=|q|^2.
Deduce that q^{-1}=\overline q/|q|^2 for q\ne0. Check that q_i,q_j,q_k are unit quaternions. What is q_i^{-1}?

hint.p: Expand (a_0+V)(a_0-V). Real numbers commute with every quaternion, so the mixed terms cancel. For q_i, the inverse is c-si.

subsection.p: Now try the map R_{q_i^{-1}}(X)=Xq_i^{-1}=X(c-si). Because multiplication does not commute, changing sides may change the geometry.

li.p: Compute 1(c-si), i(c-si), j(c-si), and k(c-si). Compare each with the first row of .
Show that right multiplication by q_i^{-1} turns the ordered plane (1,i) through -\phi, but turns (j,k) through +\phi.
Predict what happens if you first apply L_{q_i} and then R_{q_i^{-1}}. Which plane should stop turning? Which angle should add?

hint.p: The crucial sign is ji=-k, so j(c-si)=cj-sji=cj+sk. On the other hand, i(c-si)=s+ci.

subsection.p: Record your prediction in this table before multiplying the two operations out.

table.title: Two plane rotations combine.

subsection.title: Step 4: discover a spatial rotation and its half-angle
subsection.p: The combined operation is C_{q_i}(X)=q_iXq_i^{-1}. It is called conjugation by q_i. Distinguish this map from taking the quaternion conjugate \overline X: conjugation by a fixed quaternion means multiplying on the left by that quaternion and on the right by its inverse.

exercise.title: Check the prediction on all four directions

li.p: Compute q_i1q_i^{-1} and q_iiq_i^{-1}. Explain why both 1 and i return to their starting positions.

Complete this calculation without moving factors past one another:
q_ijq_i^{-1}\amp=(cj+sk)(c-si) \amp=c^2j-csji+sck-s^2ki.
Collect the j and k terms and use c^2-s^2=\cos(2\phi) and 2cs=\sin(2\phi).
Compute q_ikq_i^{-1} in the same way. Use distributivity to find the image of xi+yj+zk. Does any real part remain?

hint.p: Use ji=-k and ki=j in the displayed expansion. For the final part, C_{q_i}(xi+yj+zk)=xC_{q_i}(i)+yC_{q_i}(j)+zC_{q_i}(k).

subsection.p:
Check your result against the coordinate rule
(x,y,z)\longmapsto \bigl(x,\ y\cos(2\phi)-z\sin(2\phi),\ y\sin(2\phi)+z\cos(2\phi)\bigr).
The x-coordinate stays fixed, and the yz-plane follows the complex rotation pattern. Thus the pure imaginary subspace stays pure imaginary. It rotates about the +i axis, with positive motion from j toward k. The angle is 2\phi: the two four-dimensional turns cancelled in (1,i) and added in (j,k).

exercise.title: Choose the quaternion for a quarter turn

li.p: To obtain a spatial angle \theta, what value of \phi should you use? Write the quaternion for a positive \pi/2 rotation about the x-axis.
Use your quaternion to rotate V=i+2j+3k. Check your result geometrically in the yz-plane and compare the squared lengths.
If someone uses q=i=e^{i\pi/2} in qVq^{-1}, what spatial angle do they actually get? Test the input j.
Why would the analogous complex expression e^{i\phi}ze^{-i\phi} leave every complex number z unchanged?

hint.p: A spatial quarter turn needs q=(1+i)/\sqrt2 and gives i-3j+2k in the second part. Complex numbers commute, so their two multipliers can be brought together and cancelled.

subsection.title: Step 5: rotate about the other coordinate axes
subsection.p: Return to your rows for q_j and q_k in . The same cancellation-and-addition mechanism should work, with the quaternion units in cyclic order.

exercise.title: Use cyclic order to keep the signs straight

li.p: For q_j=c+sj, compute the four images under right multiplication by c-sj. Compare the turns in (1,j) and (k,i) with left multiplication. Then find all four images under X\longmapsto q_jXq_j^{-1}.
Repeat for q_k=c+sk, using (1,k) and (i,j).
Replace 2\phi by \theta. Write coordinate rules for rotating (x,y,z) about the y- and z-axes.
Check positive quarter turns: about +j, k should move to i; about +k, i should move to j. Where do the other two coordinate directions go in each case?

hint.p: For the y-axis, the coordinate rule is (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\cos\theta+z\sin\theta,\ y,\ -x\sin\theta+z\cos\theta). For the z-axis, it is (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta,\ x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta,\ z). In each case the coordinate along the axis stays fixed.

subsection.title: Step 6: build the same two planes around any axis
subsection.p: A rotation axis need not be a coordinate axis. Choose a unit vector \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3) and represent it by U=u_1i+u_2j+u_3k,\qquad u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2=1. The identity in gives U^2=-1. Thus U can play the role of an imaginary unit, and q=e^{U\phi}=\cos\phi+U\sin\phi=c+sU is a unit quaternion with inverse c-sU.

exercise.title: Make a basis suited to the chosen axis

statement.p: Choose any unit vector \mathbf b perpendicular to \mathbf u, write its pure imaginary quaternion as B, and set W=UB.

li.p: Use the scalar-vector product identity UB=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf u\times\mathbf b to explain why W is pure imaginary and corresponds to the unit vector \mathbf u\times\mathbf b. Why are 1,U,B,W four mutually perpendicular unit directions?
Use the same product identity to prove BU=-UB=-W. Then use associativity to show UW=-B,\qquad WU=B. You have recovered the multiplication relations needed for two rotating planes.
Compute the images of 1,U,B,W under left multiplication by c+sU and under right multiplication by c-sU. Identify the angles in the ordered planes (1,U) and (B,W).

Combine the two maps. Show that conjugation fixes 1,U and sends
B\amp\longmapsto\cos(2\phi)B+\sin(2\phi)W, W\amp\longmapsto-\sin(2\phi)B+\cos(2\phi)W.
Why is positive motion from B toward W=UB the right-hand direction about \mathbf u?
