statement.p: Suppose q(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x is positive definite. In plain words, what does that tell you about the shape of the graph z=q(x,y) near the origin, and what does it say about the origin itself?

hint.p: Positive definite means q(\mathbf x)>0 for every \mathbf x\neq\mathbf 0. So the origin is the only place the surface touches its lowest level. Picture which way every direction bends.

statement.p: Let q(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x be a quadratic form.

row.cell: if q(\mathbf x)>0 for every \mathbf x\neq\mathbf 0.
if q(\mathbf x)<0 for every \mathbf x\neq\mathbf 0.
if q takes both positive and negative values.

subsection.p: The pictures are memorable:

table.title: Sign patterns of a quadratic form and the shape of its graph.

subsection.p: There is also a borderline case. The form q(x,y)=(2x+y)^2 is never negative, but it is zero along the whole line 2x+y=0. So it is not positive definite. It has a flat direction.
For 2\times2 symmetric matrices, there is a simple determinant test.

statement.p: Let A=\begin{pmatrix}a\amp b\\b\amp c\end{pmatrix} be symmetric, and let q(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}x\amp y\end{pmatrix}A\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=ax^2+2bxy+cy^2. Let \Delta=\det A=ac-b^2. Then:

row.cell: q is positive definite if and only if a>0 and \Delta>0.
q is negative definite if and only if a<0 and \Delta>0.

proof.p:
Assume first that a\neq0. Complete the square:
q(x,y) \amp= ax^2+2bxy+cy^2\\ \amp= a\left(x+\frac ba y\right)^2+\left(c-\frac{b^2}{a}\right)y^2\\ \amp= a\left(x+\frac ba y\right)^2+\frac{ac-b^2}{a}y^2\\ \amp= a\left(x+\frac ba y\right)^2+\frac{\Delta}{a}y^2.
If a>0 and \Delta>0, then both coefficients are positive. The form is positive except at the origin.
If a<0 and \Delta>0, then both coefficients are negative. The form is negative except at the origin.
If \Delta<0 and a\neq0, then the two square terms have opposite signs. The form takes both positive and negative values, so it is indefinite.
If a=0 and \Delta<0, then \Delta=-b^2<0, so b\neq0. In that case q(x,y)=2bxy+cy^2. Taking y=1, the expression q(x,1)=2bx+c takes both positive and negative values as x varies. So q is indefinite.

Conversely, if q is positive definite, then a=q(1,0)>0, and evaluating the completed square at (-b/a,1) gives \Delta/a>0, so \Delta>0. Applying the same reasoning to -q proves necessity in the negative-definite case.

subsection.p: Each condition matters.

First, \Delta>0 alone does not mean positive definite. The matrix A=\begin{pmatrix}-1\amp 0\\0\amp -1\end{pmatrix} has \det A=1>0, but q(x,y)=-x^2-y^2 is negative definite, not positive definite. We also need the sign of a.

Second, a>0 alone does not mean positive definite. The matrix A=\begin{pmatrix}1\amp 0\\0\amp -1\end{pmatrix} has a=1>0, but q(x,y)=x^2-y^2 takes both signs. The determinant is \det A=-1<0, and the form is indefinite.

Third, when \Delta=0, there is a flat direction. For example, q(x,y)=(2x+y)^2 has matrix A=\begin{pmatrix}4\amp 2\\2\amp 1\end{pmatrix}, and \det A=4\cdot1-2\cdot2=0. The form is not positive definite because q(1,-2)=0 even though (1,-2)\neq(0,0).
The determinant has returned as a collapse detector. For a linear transformation, \det A=0 meant area was collapsed. For a quadratic form, \det A=0 means one curvature direction has flattened.

subsection.title: Preview: the Hessian matrix will classify critical points
subsection.p: Quadratic forms matter in calculus because a curved function often looks quadratic after its linear part disappears.

Suppose a hiker stands at a point on a hill where the tangent plane is horizontal. There is no first-order uphill direction at that exact point. The next question is not Which way is the slope? The slope starts at zero. The next question is: \text{Does the surface bend up, bend down, or bend both ways?} That bending is measured by a quadratic form.

Later, near a point (a,b), a function f(x,y) will have an approximation of the form f(a+h,b+k)\approx f(a,b)+\text{linear part}+\frac12\begin{pmatrix}h\amp k\end{pmatrix}H\begin{pmatrix}h\\k\end{pmatrix}. The matrix H=\begin{pmatrix}f_{xx}\amp f_{xy}\\f_{yx}\amp f_{yy}\end{pmatrix} is called the Hessian matrix.
At a critical point, the linear part is zero. Then the Hessian's quadratic form becomes the first visible shape:

table.title: The Hessian's sign pattern and the local shape at a critical point.

row.cell: the quadratic part is not enough

subsection.p: This is only a preview. We do not yet have the derivative of a multivariable function. But the pattern is now visible: matrices describe the best linear part, and symmetric matrices describe the first curved part. The next step is to make the phrase best linear part precise. That phrase will become the multivariable derivative.

section.title: Linear approximation as a preview of the derivative
section.p: ended with the phrase best linear part. That phrase is the reason Chapter 3 belongs in a calculus book. Matrices are not only a way to solve systems. They are the language of what a curved function looks like when we zoom in close enough.
A curve may bend. A surface may bend in many directions. But at a small enough scale, the first visible piece is often linear.

subsection.title: A curved function looks linear when viewed very close
subsection.p: Suppose a cyclist rides along a mountain road. Let t be distance along the road, measured in kilometers from a marker, and let H(t)=20+6t-\frac12 t^2 be the altitude in meters above some reference level.

At t=4, H(4)=20+24-8=36. Now move a small amount h farther along the road. The new altitude is
H(4+h) \amp= 20+6(4+h)-\frac12(4+h)^2 \amp= 20+24+6h-\frac12(16+8h+h^2) \amp= 36+2h-\frac12h^2.
So the change in altitude is H(4+h)-H(4)=2h-\frac12h^2.
The term 2h is linear in the displacement h. The term -\frac12h^2 is quadratic. If h is small, the quadratic term is much smaller than the linear term.
For example:

table.title: Linear and quadratic parts of the change in altitude.

subsection.p: The closer we zoom to t=4, the more the change looks like H(4+h)-H(4)\approx 2h. Equivalently, H(4+h)\approx 36+2h.

figure.caption: Near t=4, the curved altitude graph is well approximated by a line.

subsection.p: The line 36+2h has two parts: \underbrace{36}_{\text{starting value}} + \underbrace{2h}_{\text{linear change}}. The derivative is the linear-change part: h\longmapsto 2h. In single-variable calculus, we often store this information as the number H'(4)=2. But for the multivariable story, it is better to think of the derivative as the linear function L(h)=2h.

This small shift in viewpoint is important. In one variable, a linear function is just multiplication by a number. In several variables, a linear function or linear transformation may need a whole matrix.

exercise.title: Why does zooming make a curve look straight?

statement.p: When we zoom in on a smooth graph near a point, it looks more and more like a straight line. Using the split H(4+h)-H(4)=2h-\frac12h^2, explain in your own words why the curved-looking piece fades from view faster than the straight piece as h shrinks. What is special about the size of h^2 compared with h when h is tiny?

hint.p: Compare the two terms at h=0.01: one is about 0.02, the other about 0.00005. Think about the ratio \frac{h^2}{h}=h and where it goes as h\to0.

subsection.title: The derivative as the best linear map
subsection.p:
Now imagine a gently curved roof. Near one support beam, choose coordinates so that the beam is at the origin. Suppose the height of the roof is f(x,y)=12+3x-2y+\frac14x^2-\frac12xy+\frac18y^2. At the origin, f(0,0)=12. For a small displacement (h,k), we have
f(h,k) \amp= 12+3h-2k+\frac14h^2-\frac12hk+\frac18k^2 \amp= 12+\underbrace{(3h-2k)}_{\text{linear part}} + \underbrace{\left(\frac14h^2-\frac12hk+\frac18k^2\right)}_{\text{quadratic error}}.
So near the origin, f(h,k)\approx 12+3h-2k. The tangent plane preview is z=12+3x-2y.

But the derivative is not the whole affine expression 12+3h-2k. The derivative is only the linear change: L(h,k)=3h-2k. In the language of Chapter 3, L:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R is a linear function. By , it is a dot product: L(h,k)=(3,-2)\cdot(h,k).

Using the component-reading forms from Chapter 2, we can also write the same linear function as L=3\,dx-2\,dy. This means L(h,k)=3\,dx(h,k)-2\,dy(h,k)=3h-2k. Later, this linear function will be called the differential of f at the origin, and we will write df=3\,dx-2\,dy at that point.
For now, the main idea is this:

p.md: \boxed{\text{A derivative is the best linear rule for predicting small changes.}}

statement.p: Let F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m be a function, and let \mathbf a\in\mathbb R^n. A linear map L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m is the best linear approximation to F at \mathbf a if F(\mathbf a+\mathbf h) = F(\mathbf a)+L(\mathbf h)+\text{error} and the error becomes small compared with \|\mathbf h\| as \mathbf h\to\mathbf 0. In symbols, \frac{\|\text{error}\|}{\|\mathbf h\|}\to0.
When such an L exists, it is called the derivative of F at \mathbf a, and is written DF(\mathbf a).

subsection.p: The phrase small compared with \|\mathbf h\| is the important part. It says the error is not merely small. It is smaller than first-order size.

theorem.title: The best linear part is unique

statement.p: If a function F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m has a best linear approximation at \mathbf a, then that linear approximation is unique.

proof.p: Suppose two linear maps L and M both work. Then F(\mathbf a+\mathbf h) = F(\mathbf a)+L(\mathbf h)+\mathbf r_L(\mathbf h) and F(\mathbf a+\mathbf h) = F(\mathbf a)+M(\mathbf h)+\mathbf r_M(\mathbf h), where both errors are small compared with \|\mathbf h\|.

Subtract the two equations: (L-M)(\mathbf h)=\mathbf r_M(\mathbf h)-\mathbf r_L(\mathbf h). Now choose any unit vector \mathbf u, and set \mathbf h=t\mathbf u. Because L-M is linear, (L-M)(t\mathbf u)=t(L-M)(\mathbf u). Dividing by |t|, the left side has size \|(L-M)(\mathbf u)\|. The right side tends to 0, because both errors are small compared with \|\mathbf h\|=|t|. Therefore (L-M)(\mathbf u)=\mathbf 0. This holds for every unit vector \mathbf u, so L=M.

subsection.p: The condition on the error is necessary. If we only required the error to go to zero, the zero function F(h)=0 would have many linear approximations at the origin. For example, L(h)=0 and M(h)=7h would both give errors that go to zero as h\to0. But M is not a first-order approximation to the zero function, because its error -7h is the same size as h, not smaller.
So the derivative is not just a nearby linear rule. It is the linear rule that captures all first-order change.

statement.p: Many linear maps L can sit near a function and produce an error that goes to zero as \mathbf h\to\mathbf 0. Yet only one of them is called the derivative. What extra demand does best place on the error that ordinary smallness does not, and why does that demand single out a unique linear map?

hint.p: Re-read the phrase small compared with \|\mathbf h\|. For the map M(h)=7h on the zero function, the error has the same size as h, not smaller. Which comparison is the strict one?

example.title: A cone has no best linear part at its tip

statement.p: Consider c(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. This is the height of a cone whose tip is at the origin.
The function is continuous at the origin: c(x,y)\to0 \qquad\text{as}\qquad (x,y)\to(0,0). But it has no best linear approximation there.
To see why, restrict to the x-axis. Along points (h,0), c(h,0)=|h|. If c had a linear approximation L at the origin, then along the x-axis it would look like L(h,0)=ah for some number a.
For h>0, the approximation to |h| would force a=1. For h<0, it would force a=-1. No single number a can do both.
The cone is not failing because it is discontinuous. It is failing because the tip has a corner. When we zoom in, the corner remains a corner; it never becomes a plane.

subsection.p: This is the first warning for multivariable derivatives. A function can be continuous and still fail to have a linear part.

subsection.title: Why matrices appear in multivariable differentiation
subsection.p: Scalar-valued functions produce one linear function as their derivative. Vector-valued functions produce a linear transformation, and therefore a matrix.

Consider the nonlinear transformation F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2 given by F(s,t)= \bigl(2s+t+s^2,\;s-3t+st\bigr). We study it near the point (1,2). Write a nearby input as (s,t)=(1+h,2+k). Then
F(1+h,2+k) \amp= \bigl(2(1+h)+(2+k)+(1+h)^2,\; (1+h)-3(2+k)+(1+h)(2+k)\bigr) \amp= \bigl(5+4h+k+h^2,\;-3+3h-2k+hk\bigr).
So F(1+h,2+k) = (5,-3) + (4h+k,\;3h-2k) + (h^2,hk). The first term is the starting output: F(1,2)=(5,-3). The second term is linear in (h,k): (h,k)\longmapsto (4h+k,\;3h-2k). The last term is quadratic error: (h^2,hk).
The derivative is therefore the linear transformation DF(1,2)(h,k)=(4h+k,\;3h-2k). Its matrix is \boxed{ DF(1,2)= \begin{pmatrix} 4&1\\ 3&-2 \end{pmatrix}. }
This matrix has the same two readings as every matrix from .

The rows are the linear functions that give the output coordinates: 4h+k, \qquad 3h-2k. The columns are the images of the basic small input directions: \begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}.

A tiny square with edge vectors \varepsilon\mathbf e_1 and \varepsilon\mathbf e_2, based at (1,2), has image edges approximately \varepsilon(4,3) and \varepsilon(1,-2). The figure shows the unit directions and their images under the derivative; the small scale factor multiplies both columns.

figure.caption: A derivative matrix tells what a nonlinear map does to tiny displacements, to first order.

subsection.p: The determinant of this derivative matrix is \det \begin{pmatrix} 4&1\\ 3&-2 \end{pmatrix} = 4(-2)-1(3) = -11. This means that, near (1,2), the map reverses orientation and multiplies small areas by about 11. The word about matters because F is nonlinear. Larger regions bend and distort. But smaller and smaller regions behave more and more like the derivative matrix.

exercise.title: Why a matrix, and not a number?

statement.p: For a map F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, the derivative at a point turns out to be a matrix rather than a single number. Thinking about what the derivative must do to a small input displacement (h,k), explain why one number could not carry enough information, and why an m\times n array is exactly the right size.

hint.p: The derivative is a linear map from \mathbb R^n to \mathbb R^m. How many numbers does it take to record where each of the n basic input directions lands in \mathbb R^m?

subsection.p: This is where the determinant from becomes a calculus object. A determinant no longer measures only the area scaling of a fixed linear machine. It will measure the local area scaling of a nonlinear transformation.

subsection.title: Curves are the simplest moving linear approximations
subsection.p: The same idea appears in its simplest form when the input is one-dimensional.

A curve in space is a function \mathbf r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3. The input is time t. The output is a point in space: \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)). Near a time t=a, the best linear approximation has the form \mathbf r(a+h)\approx \mathbf r(a)+h\mathbf v. The vector \mathbf v is the velocity. It is the derivative of the curve at that instant.
So the old single-variable derivative reappears as a linear map h\longmapsto h\mathbf v from \mathbb R to \mathbb R^3. Its matrix is a 3\times1 column: \begin{pmatrix} v_1\\ v_2\\ v_3 \end{pmatrix}.
This is a good place to pause. Chapter 3 has built the linear machines that calculus will use under a microscope:

table.title: The linear ideas that calculus objects need.

row.cell: a determinant for local area or volume scaling
a quadratic form for the first curved part

subsection.p: But before we begin differentiating functions of several variables, we need a better supply of geometric objects to differentiate and integrate over. A curve is a moving point. A surface is a moving curve. A polar grid bends the coordinate lines before calculus even begins. The next chapter builds that geometry first, so that when the derivative finally arrives, it has something real to act on.

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

introduction.p: This chapter uses algebra, trigonometry, and the vector geometry of Chapters 13 to describe curves and surfaces. We will evaluate parametrizations, choose domains, draw coordinate grids, and recognize repetitions before differentiating surfaces.

section.title: Parametric curves
section.p: A graph like y=f(x) describes a curve by using x as the input. That works well for many curves, but it is not how a moving object usually reports its position. A boat, a drone, a planet, and a particle do not usually say, here is my y-coordinate as a function of my x-coordinate. They say where they are at each time.
That is the idea of a parametric curve.

subsection.title: Curves as moving points
subsection.p: Imagine an ant walking around the rim of a circular fountain of radius 3. Put the center of the fountain at the origin. Let t denote the angle in radians, increasing as the ant moves. Suppose the ant is at \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t). A few parameter values give:

table.title: Values of \mathbf r(t) at selected times.

subsection.p: The point moves counterclockwise and returns to where it started.

statement.p: The equation x^2+y^2=9 and the parametrization \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t), 0\le t\le2\pi, describe the same circle. What does the parametrization capture about the ant's journey that the equation alone does not specify?

hint.p: Think about what changes as t increases: where the point begins, which way it heads, and how fast it sweeps around. Could a graph y=f(x) even represent a full circle?

figure.caption: A parametrization of a circle records a moving point, not just a set of points.

subsection.p: The coordinates satisfy x=3\cos t,\qquad y=3\sin t. Using \cos^2t+\sin^2t=1, we get x^2+y^2=9. So the image is the circle of radius 3. But the parametrization gives more information than the equation x^2+y^2=9. It tells us where the ant starts, which direction it walks, and how the point is traced.

statement.p: A parametric curve in \mathbb R^n is a function \mathbf r:I\to\mathbb R^n, where I is an interval of real numbers. The input is called the parameter. Usually we write it as t.
In the plane, \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)). In space, \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)).
The image of the curve is the set of points \{\mathbf r(t):t\in I\}.

subsection.p: The parameter often represents time, but it does not have to. It might represent an angle, a distance along a track, or simply a label that tells us where we are on the curve.
There is one quiet condition we usually want: the coordinate functions should be continuous. A curve should not teleport.

example.title: Why continuity matters

statement.p: So when we speak of a curve as a moving point, we usually mean that the component functions are continuous. Later, when we want velocity, we will ask for differentiability as well.

subsection.title: Plane curves and space curves
subsection.p: A plane curve has two coordinate functions. A space curve has three.

example.title: A line segment as a parametric curve

statement.p: The straight path from P=(1,2) to Q=(5,4) can be written as \mathbf r(t)=P+t(Q-P),\qquad 0\le t\le1. Since Q-P=(4,2), this becomes \mathbf r(t)=(1,2)+t(4,2)=(1+4t,2+2t). At t=0, the curve is at P. At t=1, it is at Q. At t=1/2, it is halfway between them: \mathbf r(1/2)=(3,3).

subsection.p: This formula is the affine line from Chapter 1 with a restricted range of t. If we let t run through all real numbers, we get the whole line. If we keep 0\le t\le1, we get only the segment.

example.title: A helix around a spiral staircase

statement.p:
A point moving around a circular staircase may have position
\mathbf r(t)= \left( 2\cos t,\, 2\sin t,\, \frac{t}{2\pi} \right), \qquad 0\le t\le 6\pi.
The x- and y-coordinates move around a circle of radius 2. The z-coordinate rises steadily. One full turn raises the point by \frac{2\pi}{2\pi}=1. The image is a helix.

figure.caption: A helix can be viewed as circular motion together with steady upward motion.

subsection.p: The helix is not the graph of a single function y=f(x). It can pass over the same x-value many times. Parametric equations are more flexible than ordinary graph equations because each coordinate is allowed to depend on the parameter.

subsection.title: Eliminating the parameter when possible
subsection.p: Sometimes a parametric curve can be rewritten as a familiar Cartesian equation.

example.title: A parabola from a moving point

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2),\qquad -2\le t\le2. Then x=t,\qquad y=t^2. Since x=t, we get y=x^2. So this parametrization traces the part of the parabola y=x^2 with -2\le x\le2.

subsection.p: The parameter was easy to eliminate because one coordinate was just t.

statement.p: Suppose you eliminate the parameter and arrive at a clean Cartesian equation such as y=x^2 or x^2+y^2=9. The equation is tidy, but something about the original moving point has been thrown away. What kind of information disappears when you trade \mathbf r(t) for an equation in x and y alone?

hint.p: An equation in x and y records which points belong to the curve. Does it remember the order in which they are visited, the starting point, the direction, or whether some points are passed more than once?

example.title: A circle from trigonometry

statement.p: For \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t), we have x=3\cos t,\qquad y=3\sin t. Squaring and adding gives x^2+y^2=9\cos^2t+9\sin^2t=9. So the image lies on x^2+y^2=9. If 0\le t\le2\pi, every point on this circle is reached.

subsection.p: Eliminating the parameter can help us recognize the shape. But it can also hide important information.

example.title: Elimination can lose information

statement.p: Consider \mathbf r(t)=(t^2,t^4),\qquad -2\le t\le2. Then x=t^2,\qquad y=t^4. Since y=(t^2)^2, we get y=x^2. But this parametrization does not trace the whole parabola y=x^2. Because x=t^2\ge0, it only traces the right-hand half: y=x^2,\qquad 0\le x\le4. Also, most points are traced twice: once by t and once by -t.

subsection.p: The Cartesian equation tells us the set of points. The parametrization tells us how the set is traveled.

subsection.title: Different parametrizations of the same curve
subsection.p: The same geometric curve may have many different parametrizations.

statement.p: One curve can be described by many different parametrizations. Why is a single geometric shape able to support so many different rules \mathbf r(t), and what is the one thing all parametrizations of that curve must have in common?

hint.p: Two travelers can drive the same road using different speedometers and clocks. What do their trips necessarily agree on, and what are they free to choose differently?

example.title: Same circle, different clocks

statement.p: The two parametrizations \mathbf r_1(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, and \mathbf r_2(s)=(\cos 2s,\sin 2s),\qquad 0\le s\le\pi, trace the same unit circle once in the counterclockwise direction.
The second curve uses a different clock. When s increases by \pi, the angle 2s increases by 2\pi, so the point completes one full turn.

example.title: Same circle, opposite direction

statement.p: The parametrization \mathbf r_3(t)=(\cos t,-\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, also traces the unit circle. But it moves clockwise.
At t=0, \mathbf r_3(0)=(1,0). At t=\pi/2, \mathbf r_3(\pi/2)=(0,-1). So the point goes downward first, not upward.
The direction in which a parametrized curve is traced as the parameter increases is called its orientation.

subsection.p: Orientation records the direction of traversal. Later we will use that choice when measuring work along a path.

statement.p: A parametrized curve \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n is called closed if \mathbf r(a)=\mathbf r(b).
It is called simple if it does not pass through the same point twice, except possibly at the endpoints of a closed curve.

subsection.p: A circle traced once is closed and simple. A figure-eight curve is closed but not simple, because it crosses itself.

example.title: A curve with a self-crossing

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(\sin t,\sin 2t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. At t=0,\quad t=\pi,\quad t=2\pi, the point is (0,0). The curve returns to the origin in the middle of its trip, so it has a self-crossing.

subsection.p: A curve is therefore more than its equation and more than its picture. It is a moving point with a chosen parameter and a chosen direction.

Rectangular coordinates describe many curves well, but they are clumsy for curves that circle around a point. The circle x^2+y^2=9 looks simpler as distance from the origin equals 3. That sentence is not written in x and y. It is written in distance and angle. The next coordinate system is built for exactly that language.

section.title: Polar coordinates
section.p: The circle in kept producing the same pair of functions: x=3\cos t,\qquad y=3\sin t. This was not an accident. Rectangular coordinates describe a point by its shadows on two perpendicular axes. For a point moving around a center, another description is often more natural: \text{How far from the center?}\qquad\text{At what angle?} That is polar coordinates.

subsection.title: The plane described by distance and angle
subsection.p: A radar screen tracks a small boat. The boat is 5 km from the radar station, in a direction 30^\circ counterclockwise from east.

In rectangular coordinates, the position is \left(5\cos 30^\circ,5\sin 30^\circ\right)=\left(\frac{5\sqrt3}{2},\frac52\right). But the radar description itself is shorter: (r,\theta)=\left(5,\frac{\pi}{6}\right). Here r is distance from the origin, and \theta is angle from the positive x-axis.

exercise.title: What do the two numbers measure?

statement.p: In the polar pair (r,\theta), one number reports a length and the other reports a direction. Suppose a friend tells you only the angle \theta=\pi/6 but forgets to mention r. Have they pinned down a single point, or could they mean many different points? What does the missing number r contribute that the angle by itself cannot?

hint.p: Picture every point you could reach by walking outward from the origin along the direction \theta=\pi/6. The angle fixes the line of sight; ask yourself what is still free to change along that line.

figure.caption: Polar coordinates describe a point by distance from the origin and angle from the positive x-axis.

statement.p: The polar coordinates of a point in the plane are written (r,\theta). The number r is the distance from the origin, and \theta is the angle measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.
The positive x-axis is called the polar axis.

subsection.p: The origin is called the pole. When r=0, the angle does not matter. All of these describe the same point: (0,0),\qquad\left(0,\frac{\pi}{3}\right),\qquad(0,100).

subsection.title: Converting between polar and Cartesian coordinates
subsection.p: The conversion formulas come directly from right-triangle trigonometry: \boxed{x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta.} Also, \boxed{r^2=x^2+y^2.} When x\neq0, \tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}, but this last formula must be used carefully because tangent does not determine the quadrant by itself.

example.title: From polar to Cartesian

statement.p: Convert (r,\theta)=\left(4,\frac{\pi}{3}\right) to Cartesian coordinates.
Using x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta, we get x=4\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=4\cdot\frac12=2, and y=4\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=2\sqrt3. So (x,y)=(2,2\sqrt3) in Cartesian coordinates.

example.title: From Cartesian to polar

statement.p: Find polar coordinates for (-3,3). First, r=\sqrt{(-3)^2+3^2}=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2. The point lies in the second quadrant. The reference angle is \pi/4, so one possible angle is \theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}. Thus one polar description is \left(3\sqrt2,\frac{3\pi}{4}\right).

subsection.p: The quadrant matters. The points (1,1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(-1,-1) both satisfy \frac{y}{x}=1. So both have \tan\theta=1. But their angles are different: (1,1) \text{ has angle } \frac{\pi}{4}, while (-1,-1) \text{ has angle } \frac{5\pi}{4}. The tangent ratio alone cannot see the quadrant.

subsection.title: Polar coordinates are not unique
subsection.p: Rectangular coordinates are unique: a point has exactly one pair (x,y). Polar coordinates are different.

In the coordinate identities below, equality means that the descriptions represent the same geometric point, not that their numerical entries are equal. The angle can always be changed by a full turn: (r,\theta)=(r,\theta+2\pi)=(r,\theta-2\pi). For example, \left(5,\frac{\pi}{6}\right) and \left(5,\frac{13\pi}{6}\right) represent the same point.

exercise.title: Why so many names for one point?

statement.p: Rectangular coordinates give each point exactly one address, yet a single point has infinitely many polar addresses. Where does this endless supply of names come from? And think about the pole itself: when r=0, why does every choice of \theta name the very same point?

hint.p: Turning the angle by a full revolution leaves a point unchanged. For the origin, ask what distance you travel once r=0 — does the direction you face still take you anywhere?

subsection.p: There is another source of non-uniqueness. If we allow negative r, then (-r,\theta) means: go distance r in the opposite direction. Equivalently, \boxed{(-r,\theta)=(r,\theta+\pi).} For example, \left(-2,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\left(2,\frac{5\pi}{4}\right).

example.title: Three names for one point

statement.p: The point with polar coordinates \left(3,\frac{\pi}{3}\right) also has coordinates \left(3,\frac{7\pi}{3}\right) because adding 2\pi does not change the direction.
It also has coordinates \left(-3,\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) because a negative radius reverses the direction by \pi.

subsection.p: This non-uniqueness is not a mistake. It is part of what makes polar equations flexible. Some polar curves are much simpler if negative values of r are allowed.

subsection.title: Polar graphs and their symmetries
subsection.p: A polar equation relates r and \theta. The most common kind has the form r=f(\theta). To graph it, choose an angle \theta, compute r, and plot the point (r,\theta).

example.title: The equation r=3

statement.p: The polar equation r=3 means that every point is distance 3 from the origin. The angle is free. Therefore the graph is the circle x^2+y^2=9.

example.title: The equation \theta=\pi/4

statement.p: The polar equation \theta=\frac{\pi}{4} means that the direction is fixed and the distance may vary. The graph is the line through the origin making angle \pi/4 with the positive x-axis.
If we allow negative r, then the same equation gives the whole line. If we require r\ge0, it gives only one ray.

subsection.p: Symmetry can often be read from the equation before drawing the whole curve.

table.title: Polar symmetry tests.

example.title: A symmetric curve

statement.p: The curve r=2+\cos\theta is symmetric across the x-axis because r(-\theta)=2+\cos(-\theta)=2+\cos\theta=r(\theta). So once we know the upper half of the graph, the lower half is its mirror image.

subsection.p: These tests are helpful, but they are not a substitute for understanding the curve. Polar coordinates can describe the same point in more than one way, especially when negative values of r occur. Symmetry tests are guides, not laws to follow blindly.

subsection.title: Circles, spirals, and roses
subsection.p: Polar coordinates are especially good for curves built from distance and angle.

exercise.title: Why are circles and spirals so simple here?

statement.p: A circle centered at the origin is the single equation r=3 in polar form, but becomes x^2+y^2=9 in rectangular form. A spiral is just r=\theta/4 in polar, yet has no tidy Cartesian formula at all. What is it about distance and angle that lets these curves be written so cleanly, when x and y struggle to keep up?

hint.p: Both a circle and a spiral are really statements about how far you are as the angle turns. Notice that polar coordinates measure exactly those two things directly, while x and y have to encode distance and direction together.

example.title: A circle not centered at the origin

statement.p: Consider r=4\cos\theta. Multiply both sides by r: r^2=4r\cos\theta. Using r^2=x^2+y^2,\qquad r\cos\theta=x, we get x^2+y^2=4x. Complete the square: x^2-4x+y^2=0, so (x-2)^2+y^2=4. This is a circle centered at (2,0) with radius 2.

figure.caption: The polar equation r=4\cos\theta is a circle tangent to the origin.

subsection.p: This example shows why polar equations can be surprising. A simple expression in r and \theta may hide a familiar Cartesian curve.

example.title: An Archimedean spiral

statement.p: The polar equation r=\frac{\theta}{4},\qquad 0\le\theta\le6\pi, describes a point whose distance from the origin grows steadily as the angle turns. The result is a spiral.

figure.caption: A spiral appears when the distance from the origin changes with the angle.

example.title: A rose curve

statement.p: The polar equation r=2\cos(3\theta) produces a three-petaled rose.
When \cos(3\theta)>0, the radius is positive. When \cos(3\theta)<0, the radius is negative, so the point is plotted in the opposite direction. This sign change is what helps create petals.

figure.caption: A rose curve uses negative radius values as part of the drawing.

subsection.p: Polar coordinates are not only a way to draw pretty curves. They are a coordinate change: (r,\theta)\longmapsto (r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta). This map bends a rectangular grid in the (r,\theta)-plane into circles and rays in the (x,y)-plane.

figure.caption: The polar coordinate map turns a rectangular coordinate grid into a curved grid.

subsection.p: This curved grid carries a hidden warning. A small change \Delta\theta sweeps a short arc near the origin but a longer arc farther away. So a tiny polar rectangle with side lengths \Delta r and \Delta\theta does not have area \Delta r\,\Delta\theta. The angular side has length about r\,\Delta\theta. The length follows from the circle arc formula: radius times angle in radians. This geometric stretching will explain an area factor in later integration lessons.

Polar coordinates solve circular problems in the plane. But a pipe has height, a sphere has latitude as well as longitude, and a planet is better described by distance and two angles than by x,y,z. The next step is to let polar coordinates grow upward into space: first into cylindrical coordinates, then into spherical coordinates.

section.title: Cylindrical and spherical coordinates
section.p: Polar coordinates gave us a better language for circular motion in the plane: (r,\theta)\longmapsto (r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta). At the end of , we saw that this coordinate map bends a rectangular (r,\theta)-grid into circles and rays. It also brought a warning: angular motion has different physical length depending on how far we are from the origin.
Now we lift that idea into space.

A point in space can be described by its rectangular coordinates (x,y,z). But if the object is a pipe, a silo, a planet, a cone of light, or a sphere, rectangular coordinates often hide the shape. Circular and spherical objects ask for circular and spherical coordinates.

subsection.title: Cylindrical coordinates as polar coordinates with height
subsection.p: Imagine a worker standing inside a round grain silo. To describe her location, it is natural to say: \text{distance from the center axis},\qquad \text{angle around the silo},\qquad \text{height above the floor}.
That is not a new idea. It is just polar coordinates in the floor, together with the old vertical coordinate z.

example.title: A point in a round silo

statement.p: Suppose a point is 4 \text{ meters from the center axis}, at angle \theta=\frac{\pi}{6}, and at height z=7. Then its cylindrical coordinates are \left(4,\frac{\pi}{6},7\right). To convert to rectangular coordinates, use the polar formulas in the xy-plane: x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta. So x=4\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=2\sqrt3, and y=4\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=4\cdot\frac12=2. The height remains z=7. Thus (x,y,z)=(2\sqrt3,2,7) in rectangular coordinates.
The cylindrical coordinates of a point in space are written (r,\theta,z). The first two coordinates (r,\theta) are polar coordinates in the xy-plane, and z is the usual height coordinate.

subsection.p: The repeated symbol z=z in the conversion formula is not a joke. It says that the height coordinate is unchanged. Cylindrical coordinates change how we describe motion around the vertical axis, but they keep the vertical direction as it was.

figure.caption: Cylindrical coordinates use polar coordinates in the horizontal plane and keep the usual height coordinate.

example.title: From rectangular to cylindrical

statement.p: Find cylindrical coordinates for (x,y,z)=(-3,3,5). First, r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{(-3)^2+3^2}=3\sqrt2. The point (-3,3) lies in the second quadrant of the xy-plane, so one possible angle is \theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}. The height is unchanged: z=5. Thus one cylindrical description is \left(3\sqrt2,\frac{3\pi}{4},5\right).

subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates are not unique. As in polar coordinates, the equality below means the descriptions name the same point: (r,\theta,z)=(r,\theta+2\pi,z). Also, if r=0, the angle does not matter. Every point on the z-axis has the form (0,\theta,z), for any angle \theta.

Usually we take r\ge0. Negative radii can be allowed, just as in polar coordinates, but most multivariable calculus problems avoid them in cylindrical coordinates because the standard range r\ge0 already describes space cleanly.

subsection.title: Coordinate surfaces in cylindrical coordinates
subsection.p: A coordinate system gives us a grid. In three dimensions, the grid is made from surfaces, not lines.
In cylindrical coordinates, each coordinate surface comes from holding one coordinate constant.

table.title: Coordinate surfaces in cylindrical coordinates.

example.title: A pipe as a coordinate surface

statement.p: The equation r=3 means every point is distance 3 from the z-axis. In rectangular coordinates, this is x^2+y^2=9. There is no restriction on z, so the graph is an infinite circular cylinder.

example.title: A cone in cylindrical coordinates

statement.p: The equation z=r says that the height equals the distance from the z-axis. In rectangular coordinates, z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Squaring gives z^2=x^2+y^2, with the extra condition z\ge0. So this is the upper half of a circular cone.

subsection.p: The equation z=r is much easier to read in cylindrical coordinates than in rectangular coordinates. It says: as you move one unit away from the central axis, you rise one unit.

figure.caption: Cylindrical coordinates make cylinders and cones simple to describe. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)
cylinder r=a
cone z=r

subsection.title: Spherical coordinates as radius and two angles
subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates are built around an axis. Spherical coordinates are built around a point.

Imagine a small drone flying near a weather balloon. The balloon is the origin. To describe the drone's position, one natural report is: \text{how far from the balloon}, \text{which compass direction around the vertical axis}, \text{how far down from the positive vertical axis}.
That is spherical coordinates.

example.title: A point described by distance and two angles

statement.p: A point is \rho=6 units from the origin. Its horizontal direction is \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}, and its angle down from the positive z-axis is \phi=\frac{\pi}{4}. The point has spherical coordinates \left(6,\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{4}\right), where the coordinates are listed as (\rho,\theta,\phi).

Its rectangular coordinates are x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta, \qquad y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta, \qquad z=\rho\cos\phi. Therefore x=6\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{3\sqrt2}{2}, y=6\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = 6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \frac{3\sqrt6}{2}, and z=6\cos\frac{\pi}{4} = 3\sqrt2.
The spherical coordinates of a point in space are written (\rho,\theta,\phi). Here

table.title: The three spherical coordinates.

row.cell: angle around the z-axis, measured in the xy-plane
angle down from the positive z-axis

statement.p: The conversion formulas are \boxed{ x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\qquad y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\qquad z=\rho\cos\phi. }

subsection.p: The angle \theta is the same angle used in polar and cylindrical coordinates. The new angle is \phi, which measures how far the point has tilted away from the positive z-axis.
A useful way to remember the formulas is this:

First project the point down to the xy-plane. The projected radius is r=\rho\sin\phi. Then use polar coordinates in that plane: x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta. So x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta, \qquad y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta. The vertical coordinate is z=\rho\cos\phi.

figure.caption: Spherical coordinates use one distance \rho and two angles \theta and \phi.

example.title: From rectangular to spherical

statement.p: Find spherical coordinates for (x,y,z)=(1,1,\sqrt2). First, \rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} = \sqrt{1^2+1^2+(\sqrt2)^2} = \sqrt4 = 2. The angle around the z-axis is found from the projection (1,1) in the xy-plane: \theta=\frac{\pi}{4}. Finally, z=\rho\cos\phi. So \sqrt2=2\cos\phi, which gives \cos\phi=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}. Thus \phi=\frac{\pi}{4}. One spherical description is \left(2,\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right).

subsection.title: Coordinate surfaces in spherical coordinates
subsection.p: Spherical coordinates have their own grid surfaces.

table.title: Coordinate surfaces in spherical coordinates.

row.cell: cone for 0\lt\beta\lt\pi, \beta\ne\pi/2; the plane z=0 for \beta=\pi/2

example.title: A sphere

statement.p: The equation \rho=5 means the distance from the origin is 5. In rectangular coordinates, x^2+y^2+z^2=25. So \rho=5 is the sphere of radius 5 centered at the origin.

example.title: A cone

statement.p: The equation \phi=\frac{\pi}{4} means every point makes a 45^\circ angle with the positive z-axis. Since r=\rho\sin\phi \qquad\text{and}\qquad z=\rho\cos\phi, when \phi=\pi/4 we have r=z. So z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. This is the upper cone z^2=x^2+y^2, \qquad z\ge0.

subsection.p: At \phi=0 or \phi=\pi, the image is a ray on the z-axis. At \rho=0, it is only the origin.

Spherical coordinates are not unique. We can always add 2\pi to \theta: (\rho,\theta,\phi) = (\rho,\theta+2\pi,\phi). At the origin, \rho=0, both angles are irrelevant. At the north and south poles, where \phi=0 \quad\text{or}\quad \phi=\pi, the angle \theta is irrelevant because all horizontal directions meet at the same point.

There is also a convention warning. Some books use the letters \theta and \phi in the opposite way. In this book, \theta \text{ goes around the } z\text{-axis}, and \phi \text{ comes down from the positive } z\text{-axis}.

statement.p: In spherical coordinates, holding one coordinate fixed usually traces out a surface. Use \rho\gt0 and 0\lt\phi\lt\pi for the usual cases, and include the special plane at \phi=\pi/2. Without converting to rectangular coordinates, picture each of \rho=\text{const}, \phi=\text{const}, and \theta=\text{const}. What shape is each one, and why does fixing a distance behave so differently from fixing an angle?

hint.p: Read each coordinate's meaning out loud: \rho is distance from the origin, \phi is the angle down from the z-axis, and \theta is the angle around it. Let the words, not the formulas, suggest the surface.

subsection.title: When cylindrical or spherical coordinates are the natural choice
subsection.p: A coordinate system is a language. The best language is the one in which the geometry speaks simply.

table.title: Matching coordinates to geometry.

row.cell: pipes, cylinders, vertical axes, spinning objects
spheres, balls, shells, distance from one center

example.title: A thick pipe

statement.p: A pipe of inner radius 2, outer radius 3, and height 5 around the z-axis is described simply by 2\le r\le3, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le z\le5. In rectangular coordinates, the same solid would require 4\le x^2+y^2\le9, \qquad 0\le z\le5. The rectangular description is not wrong, but it hides the circular structure.

example.title: A spherical shell

statement.p: A shell between two spheres centered at the origin, with radii 1 and 4, is described by 1\le \rho\le4, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. In rectangular coordinates, the condition becomes 1\le x^2+y^2+z^2\le16, which is readable, but the angular structure is hidden.

subsection.p: Not every problem with a circle needs cylindrical coordinates, and not every problem in space needs spherical coordinates. A rectangular box is easier in x,y,z. A plane like 2x-y+z=5 is usually easier in rectangular coordinates. The goal is not to use the fanciest system. The goal is to choose the coordinates that match the shape.

statement.p: A long straight pipe and a solid ball each have round symmetry, yet we usually reach for cylindrical coordinates for the pipe and spherical coordinates for the ball. What is it about the shape of each object that makes one coordinate system speak more simply than the other?

hint.p: Ask what stays constant as you travel along each object. A pipe has a special axis; a ball has a special center. Which coordinate is held fixed by the surface in each case?

subsection.title: The hidden size of coordinate boxes
subsection.p: In rectangular coordinates, a tiny box with side lengths \Delta x,\quad \Delta y,\quad \Delta z has volume exactly \Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z.
Curved coordinates are different.

In cylindrical coordinates, a tiny coordinate box has side lengths approximately \Delta r,\qquad r\,\Delta\theta,\qquad \Delta z. So its volume is approximately r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta\,\Delta z. The angular edge follows from radius times angle in radians.

In spherical coordinates, a tiny coordinate box has side lengths approximately \Delta\rho, \qquad \rho\,\Delta\phi, \qquad \rho\sin\phi\,\Delta\theta. So its volume is approximately \rho^2\sin\phi\,\Delta\rho\,\Delta\phi\,\Delta\theta. Here the latitude circle has radius \rho\sin\phi, which explains the length of its angular edge.

These are geometric approximations for short edges away from the poles and axis, where the coordinate grid collapses. Later integration lessons will turn these local size comparisons into precise formulas.

exercise.title: Why isn't every little box the same?

statement.p: A spherical coordinate box with edges \Delta\rho, \Delta\phi, \Delta\theta uses the same three increments everywhere, yet the physical box it carves out is large in some places and tiny in others. Why does the same triple of increments not enclose the same amount of space everywhere?

hint.p: An angular increment sweeps out more length the farther you are from what you are turning around. Compare a step of \Delta\theta near the z-axis with one far from it, and observe that the radial edge stays \Delta\rho while the angular edges grow with their circle radii.

subsection.p: Coordinates help us describe space. They also help us recognize surfaces: cylinders, cones, spheres, and shells appeared almost automatically. But many surfaces are not coordinate surfaces in a single coordinate system. Some are bowls, some are saddles, some are stretched spheres, and some are stranger than their equations first suggest. To read them, we need one more geometric skill: slicing a surface and studying its cross-sections.

section.title: Quadric surfaces and level surfaces
section.p: A sphere can be written in spherical coordinates as \rho=3. The same sphere can be written in rectangular coordinates as x^2+y^2+z^2=9. One surface, two languages.

The next surfaces are the three-dimensional relatives of conic sections. In the plane, second-degree equations gave circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas. In space, second-degree equations give cylinders, cones, paraboloids, ellipsoids, hyperboloids, and saddles.
The trick is not to memorize a gallery. The trick is to slice.

subsection.title: A first surface from an equation
subsection.p: Start with the equation x^2+y^2=4. In the plane, this is a circle of radius 2. But in space, the equation does not mention z. That means z is free.
If (x,y) lies on the circle, then every point (x,y,z) lies on the surface, no matter how high or low z is. The circle is lifted upward and downward forever.
So x^2+y^2=4 is a circular cylinder in space.

example.title: A missing variable creates a cylinder

statement.p: The equation y=x^2 is a parabola in the xy-plane. In space, if the equation is still y=x^2, then z is free. Every point on the parabola can move up and down parallel to the z-axis.
The result is a parabolic cylinder.

subsection.p: A cylinder does not have to be circular. In multivariable calculus, a cylinder means a surface made by dragging a plane curve along a straight direction.

figure.caption: If an equation in space is missing one variable, a plane curve is dragged along that missing direction.

subsection.title: Cylinders, cones, paraboloids, and ellipsoids
subsection.p: A quadric surface is a surface in space described by a second-degree equation in x,y,z. The simplest examples use squares and no mixed terms.

statement.p: A quadric surface is the graph or level set of a second-degree equation in x,y,z. Typical terms include x^2,\qquad y^2,\qquad z^2,\qquad xy,\qquad xz,\qquad yz, together with possible linear and constant terms.

subsection.p: The word surface is a little generous. Some second-degree equations degenerate.

For example, x^2+y^2+z^2=-1 has no real points at all. The equation x^2+y^2+z^2=0 has only one point, the origin. And x^2-y^2=0 factors as (x-y)(x+y)=0, so it gives two planes: x=y \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=-y. These warning examples remind us that equations must be read, not merely classified.
Now let us look at the main shapes.

example.title: An elliptic paraboloid: a bowl

statement.p: Consider z=\frac{x^2}{4}+y^2. At z=0, the only point is (0,0,0). At z=1, we get \frac{x^2}{4}+y^2=1, an ellipse. At z=4, we get \frac{x^2}{4}+y^2=4, a larger ellipse.
So horizontal slices are ellipses that grow as z increases. The surface is a bowl opening upward. It is called an elliptic paraboloid.

subsection.p: The circular paraboloid z=x^2+y^2 is the special case where the horizontal slices are circles. But most bowls are not perfectly round; their slices may be ellipses.

example.title: An ellipsoid: a stretched sphere

statement.p: The equation \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}+z^2=1 describes a stretched sphere, called an ellipsoid.
To see the stretches, set two variables to zero.
If y=0,\qquad z=0, then \frac{x^2}{9}=1, so x=\pm3. Along the x-axis, the ellipsoid reaches 3 units.
If x=0,\qquad z=0, then \frac{y^2}{4}=1, so y=\pm2. Along the y-axis, it reaches 2 units.
If x=0,\qquad y=0, then z^2=1, so z=\pm1. Along the z-axis, it reaches 1 unit.

subsection.p: So the ellipsoid \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}+\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1 is stretched by a, b, and c along the coordinate axes.

example.title: A double cone

statement.p: The equation z^2=x^2+y^2 describes a double cone.
For z=0, we get x^2+y^2=0, so the slice is only the origin.
For z=2, we get x^2+y^2=4, a circle of radius 2.
For z=-2, we again get x^2+y^2=4. So the surface has one cone opening upward and one cone opening downward, meeting at the origin.

figure.caption: Several common quadric surfaces can be recognized from their slices. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)
elliptic paraboloid z=x^2+y^2
ellipsoid
double cone z^2=x^2+y^2

subsection.title: Hyperboloids and saddle surfaces
subsection.p: The signs in a quadric equation matter. Positive square terms tend to make ellipses. A mixture of positive and negative square terms tends to create hyperbolas.

example.title: A hyperboloid of one sheet

statement.p: Consider x^2+y^2-z^2=1. At z=0, the horizontal slice is x^2+y^2=1, a circle of radius 1.
At z=2, the slice is x^2+y^2-4=1, so x^2+y^2=5, a larger circle.
At z=-2, we get the same circle.
The surface is connected, with a narrow waist at z=0. It is called a hyperboloid of one sheet.

example.title: A hyperboloid of two sheets

statement.p: Now change the signs: z^2-x^2-y^2=1. At z=0, the equation becomes -x^2-y^2=1, which has no real solutions.
At z=2, we get 4-x^2-y^2=1, so x^2+y^2=3. At z=-2, we get the same circle.
The surface has two disconnected pieces: one above and one below. It is called a hyperboloid of two sheets.

subsection.p: The difference between x^2+y^2-z^2=1 and z^2-x^2-y^2=1 is not cosmetic. It changes a connected surface into two separated pieces.

example.title: A saddle surface

statement.p: The equation z=x^2-y^2 describes a hyperbolic paraboloid, often called a saddle.
Look at two vertical slices.
If y=0, then z=x^2. This is an upward-opening parabola.
If x=0, then z=-y^2. This is a downward-opening parabola.
So in one direction the surface bends upward, while in the perpendicular direction it bends downward. That is the saddle shape.

figure.caption: Three surfaces defined by equations with mixed signs. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)
hyperboloid of one sheet x^2+y^2-z^2=1
hyperboloid of two sheets z^2-x^2-y^2=1
saddle z=x^2-y^2
Families of traces for the saddle surface z=x^2-y^2.

subsection.p: A saddle is one of the most important shapes in multivariable calculus. Later, when we study optimization, saddle points will be the places where a surface is level to first order but is neither a maximum nor a minimum.

subsection.title: Traces and cross-sections
subsection.p: A trace is a slice of a surface by a coordinate plane or by a plane parallel to a coordinate plane.
The basic method is simple:

table.title: The trace method.

row.cell: Set one coordinate equal to a constant.
Recognize the curve left in the slice.

example.title: Traces of an ellipsoid

statement.p: Consider \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}+z^2=1. Horizontal traces come from fixing z.
If z=0, then \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1. This is an ellipse.
If z=\frac12, then \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}+\frac14=1, so \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=\frac34. This is a smaller ellipse.
If z=1, then \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=0, so the slice is only the point (0,0,1). If |z|\gt 1, there are no points.
These slices tell us that the ellipsoid is widest at the middle and closes at the top and bottom.

example.title: Identifying a surface from traces

statement.p: Identify the surface z=9-x^2-4y^2. Fix z=c. Then c=9-x^2-4y^2, so x^2+4y^2=9-c. For c\lt 9, this is an ellipse. For c=9, it is a single point. For c\gt 9, there are no points.
So the surface has elliptical horizontal slices, with the largest slices lower down and a top point at (0,0,9). It is an elliptic paraboloid opening downward.

subsection.p: The same surface can often be recognized in several ways. For z=9-x^2-4y^2, fixing y=0 gives z=9-x^2, a downward-opening parabola. Fixing x=0 gives z=9-4y^2, another downward-opening parabola, steeper in the y-direction.
That extra steepness is visible in the coefficient 4.

exercise.title: Why do traces reveal the surface?

statement.p: For the given equation z=9-x^2-4y^2, describe the complete family of horizontal traces z=c. How does that family, together with the equation, identify a downward-opening elliptic paraboloid? Would a few isolated slices determine an arbitrary surface?

subsection.title: A small gallery of standard quadric surfaces
subsection.p: The following table is not meant to replace slicing. It is a quick reference after slicing has shown where the shapes come from.

table.title: A small gallery of standard quadric surfaces.

subsection.p: A coefficient changes the stretching. A sign changes the shape. A missing variable usually means a cylinder. A shifted expression, such as (x-2)^2+y^2+z^2=9, moves the surface away from the origin.

example.title: A shifted sphere

statement.p: The equation (x-2)^2+(y+1)^2+(z-3)^2=16 is a sphere of radius 4, centered at (2,-1,3). The shifted terms tell us the center: x-2,\qquad y+1=y-(-1),\qquad z-3.

subsection.title: Level surfaces as three-dimensional contour maps
subsection.p: A topographic map of a mountain uses level curves: h(x,y)=c. Each curve connects points with the same elevation.
In space, a function F(x,y,z) can have level surfaces: F(x,y,z)=c. Each surface connects points where F has the same value.

statement.p: Let F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R be a scalar-valued function. A level surface of F is a set of the form F(x,y,z)=c, where c is a constant. More generally this is a level set: it need not be a smooth sheet, or even two-dimensional. For example, x^2+y^2+z^2=0 contains only the origin.

example.title: Temperature around a hot source

statement.p: Suppose the temperature near a small heater at the origin is modeled by T(x,y,z)=\frac{100}{1+x^2+y^2+z^2}. The temperature depends only on distance from the origin.
The level surface where T=20 satisfies \frac{100}{1+x^2+y^2+z^2}=20. So 1+x^2+y^2+z^2=5, and therefore x^2+y^2+z^2=4. This is a sphere of radius 2.
So all points at distance 2 from the heater have the same temperature 20.

example.title: Distance from the z-axis

statement.p: Let F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2. Then the level surface F(x,y,z)=9 is x^2+y^2=9. This is a cylinder of radius 3 around the z-axis.
The function F measures squared distance from the z-axis, so its level surfaces are cylinders.

subsection.p: Level surfaces are not just a way to draw shapes. They are a way to understand scalar fields in space: temperature, pressure, density, electric potential, gravitational potential, and many others.

statement.p: A graph z=g(x,y) and a level set f(x,y,z)=c describe sets in space in different ways. In z=g(x,y) one coordinate is singled out and expressed in terms of the other two; in f(x,y,z)=c all three coordinates appear on equal footing. How does this difference show up in the shapes each can describe, and why can a level surface represent something a graph cannot?

hint.p: Ask whether a vertical line can ever cross the surface more than once. A graph z=g(x,y) assigns exactly one height to each (x,y). Could a sphere, written as a level surface, ever be a graph of that kind?

subsection.p: For these examples, the equation F(x,y,z)=c identifies points of equal value. Later we will learn to find slopes and measure surface patches.

subsection.title: Equations describe surfaces, but not how to move on them
subsection.p: An equation like x^2+y^2+z^2=9 tells us which points lie on a sphere. But it does not tell us how to draw a grid on the sphere. It does not tell us how to walk across it using two parameters. It does not tell us, at least not directly, how a tiny patch of the surface should be measured.

statement.p: A curve was described by motion: a single parameter t moves a point along, and you could ask how fast it travels. A surface, by contrast, is described by an equation that simply tests whether a point belongs. Why is it natural that a curve comes with a built-in sense of motion while a surface, given only by an equation like x^2+y^2+z^2=9, does not?

hint.p: Count the dimensions, or the degrees of freedom. A curve is one-dimensional, so one moving number can trace it out. How many independent numbers would you need to roam freely over a surface, and what does that suggest an equation alone is leaving out?

subsection.p: For that, we need another description. Instead of saying which points satisfy an equation, we will build the surface from two moving parameters: \mathbf r(u,v). A curve was a moving point. A surface will be a moving curve, or equivalently, a point that depends on two inputs. We begin by locating points and drawing coordinate grids.

introduction.p: described surfaces by equations: x^2+y^2+z^2=9, \qquad z=x^2-y^2, \qquad F(x,y,z)=c. An equation tells us which points belong to a surface. But it does not tell us how to locate a point using two inputs or draw a coordinate grid on it.
For that, we need parameters.

A curve used one parameter: \mathbf r(t). The surface-coordinate descriptions in this chapter use two: \mathbf r(u,v). One parameter can move a point along a curve. Two parameters can move a point across a sheet.

subsection.title: Two parameters locate a point
subsection.p: Start with a round pipe of radius 2 and height 5. A point on the pipe can be described by two choices: \text{angle around the pipe},\qquad \text{height along the pipe}. Let the angle be \theta and the height be z. Then \mathbf r(\theta,z) = (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), \qquad 0\le \theta\le2\pi,\quad 0\le z\le5.

If we hold z fixed, the point moves around a circle: \theta\mapsto (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). If we hold \theta fixed, the point moves up a vertical line: z\mapsto (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). The surface is made by letting both motions happen.

statement.p: In the cylinder formula above, explain what changes when you vary only the angle, and what changes when you vary only the height. Why are two input numbers useful for specifying a point on this pipe?

hint.p: On the pipe you can change the angle and the height independently, so it takes two numbers to say where you are. How many independent ways can you move along a single curve?

figure.caption: The rectangle of parameter values is wrapped into a cylinder.

subsection.title: Parameter domain and image

statement.p: A parametrization for the sheets considered here is a continuous map \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3, where D is a region in the uv-plane. We write \mathbf r(u,v)=\bigl(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)\bigr). The image of the parametrization is the set of points \{\mathbf r(u,v):(u,v)\in D\}.

subsection.p: The region D is called the parameter domain. It might be a rectangle, a disk, a triangle, or some other region.

We often use the same phrase parametric surface for both the map \mathbf r(u,v) and the geometric surface it traces. When the distinction matters, we will say parametrization for the map and surface for the image.

Here continuity means that small changes of the two inputs produce small changes of the output point; Chapter 6 makes that precise. Continuity alone does not ensure a sheet: \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,0,0) collapses to a line and \mathbf r(u,v)=(0,0,0) to a point. Our present examples describe sheets; later regularity conditions will identify nondegenerate differentiable patches.

example.title: One formula, different domains

statement.p: Keep \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). The domain 0\le\theta\le2\pi, z\in\mathbb R describes the whole infinite cylinder. Restricting to 1\le z\le4 gives a shorter band. Restricting also to 0\le\theta\le\pi gives its half with y\ge0, since \sin\theta\ge0 on that interval.

On the original pipe, direct substitution gives \mathbf r(0,0)=(2,0,0),\quad \mathbf r(\pi/2,3)=(0,2,3),\quad \mathbf r(\pi/3,2)=(1,\sqrt3,2). The input pair is a point in the parameter domain; the output triple is a point in space.

example.title: A discontinuous rule is not a sheet

statement.p: Define \mathbf r(u,v)= \begin{cases} (u,v,0), \amp u\lt 0,\\ (u,v,1), \amp u\ge0, \end{cases} on the square -1\le u\le1,\qquad -1\le v\le1. The left half of the square is sent to the plane z=0, while the right half is sent to the plane z=1. Along u=0, the image jumps upward by one unit.
This is not one continuous surface patch. It is two half-sheets separated by a tear.

subsection.title: Graphs as parametrized surfaces
subsection.p: For a continuous function f, the graph z=f(x,y) has a natural parametrization: \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,f(u,v)). The parameters are just the input coordinates.

example.title: A bowl as a parametrized surface

statement.p: Consider the elliptic bowl z=4-\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}. Using x=u,\qquad y=v, we get \mathbf r(u,v) = \left( u,\, v,\, 4-\frac{u^2}{9}-\frac{v^2}{4} \right). If we use all pairs (u,v), this traces the whole paraboloid. If we restrict the domain, for example to -3\le u\le3,\qquad -2\le v\le2, we get only a rectangular patch of the bowl.

subsection.p: This is one reason parametrizations are useful. The same formula can describe a whole surface or only a chosen piece of it, depending on the parameter domain.

A plane from Chapter 1 is also a parametrized surface: \mathbf r(u,v)=P+u\mathbf a+v\mathbf b. Here \mathbf a and \mathbf b must be linearly independent. The parameters are the scalar multiples of the two plane directions.

example.title: An affine plane as a parametrized surface

statement.p: Let P=(1,0,2),\qquad \mathbf a=(2,1,0),\qquad \mathbf b=(0,1,3). Then \mathbf r(u,v) = (1,0,2)+u(2,1,0)+v(0,1,3). So \mathbf r(u,v)=(1+2u,\;u+v,\;2+3v). This is the plane through P spanned by the directions \mathbf a and \mathbf b.

subsection.p: The formula P+u\mathbf a+v\mathbf b describes the whole plane when both parameters range over all real numbers. For the example above, substituting the coordinate formulas into 3x-6y+2z=7 verifies its plane equation.

subsection.title: Coordinate grids on surfaces
subsection.p: A parametrization does more than trace points. It brings a grid with it.
For a surface \mathbf r(u,v), there are two natural families of curves.

If we hold u=u_0 fixed, we get the curve v\mapsto \mathbf r(u_0,v). If we hold v=v_0 fixed, we get the curve u\mapsto \mathbf r(u,v_0). These are called coordinate curves or grid curves. They are entire curves on the surface, not vectors attached to one point.

definition.title: Grid curves on a parametrized surface

statement.p: For a parametrized surface \mathbf r(u,v), the curves \mathbf r(u_0,v) and \mathbf r(u,v_0) are called the grid curves of the parametrization.

subsection.p: On the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), the grid curves are easy to see.
Holding z fixed gives horizontal circles. Holding \theta fixed gives vertical lines.
On a sphere, the same idea becomes latitude and longitude.

example.title: Latitude and longitude as grid curves

statement.p: The sphere of radius 3 can be parametrized by \mathbf r(\theta,\phi) = (3\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, 3\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, 3\cos\phi), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi. Here \theta goes around the z-axis, and \phi measures angle down from the positive z-axis.
If 0\lt\phi\lt\pi is fixed, then z=3\cos\phi is fixed, and the point moves around a circle of latitude.
If \theta is fixed, then the point moves along a meridian from the north pole to the south pole.

subsection.title: Repeated points, seams, and collapsed edges
subsection.p: The spherical parametrization also shows a small warning. At \phi=0 all values of \theta give the same point: (0,0,3). At \phi=\pi, all values of \theta give (0,0,-3). Also, \theta=0 and \theta=2\pi trace the same meridian. So the parametrization is not one-to-one on the full parameter rectangle.

That is not a mistake. Many useful parametrizations repeat some points. The important thing is to notice when it happens. A collapsed parameter edge does not by itself mean that the geometric surface has a sharp point: the sphere is round even at its poles.

subsection.title: Choosing and checking a parametrization
subsection.p: Start with the shape: use angle and height for a cylinder, two angles for a sphere, and the two input coordinates for a graph. Then check both the formula and its domain. Substitution shows that the output satisfies the desired equation; the parameter ranges tell you which points are reached and which are repeated.

statement.p: For \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), find \mathbf r(\pi/3,2). Give a domain for the part with y\ge0 and height between 1 and 4.

hint.p: Use the signs of sine on [0,\pi].

solution.p: The point is (1,\sqrt3,2); one domain is 0\le\theta\le\pi, 1\le z\le4.

statement.p: Describe the grid curves of \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,uv) with u=c and with v=c.

hint.p: Replace the fixed parameter by the number c before interpreting the formula.

solution.p: They are the straight lines (c,v,cv) and (u,c,cu). A curved surface can contain straight lines.

exercise.title: Check the sphere and its repetitions

statement.p: For the radius-three spherical formula in , verify x^2+y^2+z^2=9. Which two edges describe the same meridian? Which edges collapse to poles?

hint.p: Use \sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1 twice, then substitute the four boundary values.

solution.p: The sum of squares is 9\sin^2\phi(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)+9\cos^2\phi=9. The edges \theta=0,2\pi share a meridian; \phi=0,\pi collapse to (0,0,3) and (0,0,-3).

statement.p: Use the cylinder formula with 0\le z\le5. Compare the angular domains [0,2\pi] and [0,4\pi]. Do they have the same image? How many parameter pairs represent a point away from the seam in each case?

hint.p: Adding 2\pi to the angle leaves sine and cosine unchanged.

solution.p: Both describe the same cylindrical side. Away from the seam, each point occurs once in the first domain and twice in the second.

subsection.p: In , we will differentiate these grid curves one parameter at a time to find their velocities and surface normals. Surface area is developed in .

introduction.p: Chapter 4 began with a moving point \mathbf r(t), then widened the language of coordinates and surfaces. We learned that the same geometric object can have several descriptions: an equation, a coordinate condition, a level surface, or a parametrization.
The skill is not to memorize one favorite description. The skill is to choose the one that makes the geometry speak clearly.

subsection.title: The chapter in one picture

table.title: Descriptions of geometric objects

row.cell: distance and angle in the plane
distance and angles from a center
equal values of a scalar field
a grid drawn on a surface

subsection.p:
A surface like a sphere may appear in many rows of this table: x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2, \rho=a, or
\mathbf r(\theta,\phi) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, a\cos\phi).
Each description sees a different part of the same geometry.

subsection.title: Skills: converting coordinates and recognizing surfaces
subsection.p: By the end of this chapter, the following moves should feel familiar.

paragraphs.title: Coordinate conversions

table.title: Conversions to rectangular coordinates

paragraphs.p: The distance formulas are r^2=x^2+y^2 and \rho^2=x^2+y^2+z^2.

paragraphs.title: Surface recognition
paragraphs.p: A missing variable often means a cylinder. For example, x^2+y^2=9 in space is a cylinder, because z is free.
A squared-distance equation usually points toward a sphere or ellipsoid: x^2+y^2+z^2=25 is a sphere, while \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}+z^2=1 is an ellipsoid.
A variable equal to a sum of squares usually gives a paraboloid: z=x^2+4y^2 opens upward, while z=9-x^2-4y^2 opens downward.
Mixed signs create hyperbolic behavior: x^2+y^2-z^2=1 is a hyperboloid of one sheet, while z^2-x^2-y^2=1 is a hyperboloid of two sheets.
A difference of squares in a graph gives a saddle: z=x^2-y^2.

paragraphs.title: Slicing strategy
paragraphs.p: To understand a surface, slice it.

li.p: Fix z=c for horizontal traces.
Fix x=c or y=c for vertical traces.
Simplify the remaining equation.
Recognize the curve in the slice.

example.title: A review identification

statement.p: Identify 4x^2+y^2+z^2=16. Divide by 16: \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{16}+\frac{z^2}{16}=1. This is an ellipsoid. It reaches x=\pm2,\qquad y=\pm4,\qquad z=\pm4. So it is shorter in the x-direction than in the y- and z-directions.

example.title: A review parametrization

statement.p:
Parametrize the upper cone z=2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Use cylindrical coordinates: x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad z=2r. So
\mathbf r(r,\theta) = (r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,2r), \qquad r\ge0,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.
If we only want the part below z=6, then 2r\le6, so 0\le r\le3.

exercises.title: A. Parametric curves and polar coordinates

statement.p: Sketch the curve \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le\pi. State its orientation.
The curve \mathbf r(t)=(\cos 2t,\sin 2t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, traces the unit circle how many times?
Convert the polar point \left(6,\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) to Cartesian coordinates.
Convert the Cartesian point (2,-2) to polar coordinates with r>0 and 0\le\theta<2\pi.
Identify the polar graph r=5.
Convert r=6\sin\theta to a Cartesian equation and identify the curve.
Convert (r,\theta,z)=\left(4,\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) to rectangular coordinates.
Convert (x,y,z)=(-1,\sqrt3,5) to cylindrical coordinates.
Convert the spherical point \left(\rho,\theta,\phi\right) = \left(3,\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{3}\right) to rectangular coordinates.
Describe the cylindrical surface r=2.
Describe the spherical surface \rho=4.
Describe the spherical surface \phi=\frac{\pi}{6}.
Identify the surface x^2+y^2=16.
Identify the surface z=x^2+3y^2.
Identify the surface \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+\frac{z^2}{25}=1.
Identify the surface x^2+y^2-z^2=4.
Identify the surface z=x^2-y^2.
The temperature in a room is modeled by T(x,y,z)=20+x^2+y^2+z^2. Describe the level surface T=29.
Identify the surface \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,u^2+v^2).
Identify the surface \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(3\cos\theta,3\sin\theta,z).
Find a parametrization of the plane through P=(1,2,3) with direction vectors \mathbf a=(1,0,1), \qquad \mathbf b=(0,2,-1).
Find a parametrization of the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=9.
For \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,uv), describe the two families of grid curves: u=\text{constant} \qquad\text{and}\qquad v=\text{constant}.

For \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), with 0\le\theta\le2\pi and 0\le z\le5, compare the points at \theta=0 and \theta=2\pi for each height. Which edges of the parameter rectangle have the same image? Describe the two families of grid curves.

subsection.title: Project: build a gallery of quadrics
subsection.p: Create a visual gallery of the main quadric surfaces from .
For each surface, include:

li.p: the equation,
three traces or cross-sections,
a hand sketch or computer-generated plot,
one sentence explaining how the signs and coefficients shape it.

subsection.p:
Use at least six of the following:
x^2+y^2=4, z=x^2+y^2, z=x^2-y^2, \dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}+z^2=1, x^2+y^2-z^2=1, z^2-x^2-y^2=1, z^2=x^2+y^2, y=x^2.
For the last equation, y=x^2, remember that this is a surface in space, not just a plane parabola. The missing variable z is free.
A good gallery should not look like a list of formulas. It should show how the formulas turn into shapes.

subsection.title: Project: compare several parametrizations of a sphere
subsection.p: For a>0, the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2 has many parametrizations. Compare the following three.

paragraphs.title: 1. Spherical-coordinate parametrization
paragraphs.p:
\mathbf r_1(\theta,\phi) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, a\cos\phi),
where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi.

paragraphs.title: 2. Upper and lower graph parametrizations
paragraphs.p:
The upper hemisphere is
\mathbf r_2(u,v) = \left(u,v,\sqrt{a^2-u^2-v^2}\right), \qquad u^2+v^2\le a^2.
The lower hemisphere is
\mathbf r_3(u,v) = \left(u,v,-\sqrt{a^2-u^2-v^2}\right), \qquad u^2+v^2\le a^2.

paragraphs.title: 3. Height-angle parametrization
paragraphs.p:
Use height z and angle \theta:
\mathbf r_4(\theta,z) = \left( \sqrt{a^2-z^2}\cos\theta,\, \sqrt{a^2-z^2}\sin\theta,\, z \right),
where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad -a\le z\le a.

subsection.p: For each parametrization, answer:

li.p: What is the parameter domain?
Which parameter curves look like circles?
Which parameter curves run from pole to pole?
Where does the parametrization repeat points?
Where does the parametrization collapse a whole edge or curve to one point?
Which parametrization would you use to draw latitude and longitude?
Which would you use to describe the sphere as two graphs?

subsection.p: This project is not only about spheres. It teaches a larger lesson: a parametrization is a choice of coordinates on a surface, and different choices reveal different geometry.

subsection.title: A final hook: once curves move, velocity returns
subsection.p: A curve can be described as a set of points, but a parametrized curve remembers how the points are traced. The circle x^2+y^2=1 does not know whether a particle moves clockwise or counterclockwise, quickly or slowly, once or many times. The parametrization \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t) does know.

That difference is about to become calculus again. Once the parameter is time, a curve has velocity. Once velocity changes, it has acceleration. The old single-variable idea \text{rate of change} returns, but now the output is a vector and the path may bend through space.
The next chapter begins there: not with a new kind of surface, but with a moving point.

part.title: Curves and Differential Calculus in Several Variables

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

introduction.p: We now apply single-variable calculus to the parametrized curves of Chapter 4. Component derivatives and integrals lead to velocity, arc length, curvature, and the Frenet frame and torsion of space curves. Polar motion then provides a second example of a moving frame, before the chapter review gathers these tools in applications.

section.title: Vector-valued functions
section.p: Chapter 4 used parametric curves to describe shapes. The circle \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t) was a set of points traced by a moving point. Now we read the same notation in a more physical way: at time t, where is the object?
A function like this has one input, but its output is a vector. That is why it is called a vector-valued function.

subsection.title: Position as a function of time
subsection.p: Imagine a firefly circling a porch light while slowly rising. Put the light at the origin of the xy-plane, and measure height by z. Suppose the firefly's position at time t is \mathbf r(t)=\left(2\cos t,\;2\sin t,\;1+\frac{t}{4}\right), \qquad 0\le t\le 4\pi. At a few times,

table.title: Sample positions of the firefly.

subsection.p: The x- and y-coordinates circle around the light. The z-coordinate rises steadily. The path is a helix.

figure.caption: A vector-valued function can record the position of a moving point. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The input t is a number. The output \mathbf r(t) is a vector in \mathbb R^3. So this is not a real-valued function like f(t)=t^2. It is a function whose values are vectors.

statement.p: A vector-valued function is a function whose output is a vector.
A vector-valued function into \mathbb R^n has the form \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),r_2(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr), where each r_i(t) is an ordinary real-valued function.
When \mathbf r(t) describes motion, we call \mathbf r(t) the position vector at time t.

subsection.p: For plane motion, \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)). For space motion, \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)).
The coordinate functions x(t),\qquad y(t),\qquad z(t) are called the component functions. They are ordinary single-variable functions, so the tools of single-variable calculus can act on them.

subsection.title: Component functions
subsection.p: A bird flying through a room might have position \mathbf r(t)=(3+t,\;2+\sin t,\;5-\cos t). This one vector equation is really three equations: x(t)=3+t, y(t)=2+\sin t, and z(t)=5-\cos t. Each coordinate tells a different part of the motion. The x-coordinate increases steadily. The y-coordinate oscillates. The z-coordinate also oscillates, but with a different timing.

example.title: Reading a motion component by component
