statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(4\cos t,\;4\sin t,\;2t), \qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi. Then x(t)=4\cos t,\qquad y(t)=4\sin t,\qquad z(t)=2t. The first two coordinates keep the point on the cylinder x^2+y^2=16. The third coordinate rises from 0 to 4\pi. So the image is one turn of a helix on a cylinder of radius 4.

subsection.p: This way of reading a vector-valued function is simple, but important. Almost every calculus operation in this chapter will happen component by component.

statement.p: Suppose a friend says, “If I understand each of the component functions x(t), y(t), and z(t) separately, then I understand the whole vector-valued function \mathbf r(t).” Why is that a reasonable thing to claim? What is it about how \mathbf r(t) is built that lets us study it one coordinate at a time?

hint.p: Look again at how \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)) is assembled. Knowing where the point is at time t means knowing each coordinate at that time, and nothing more.

subsection.title: Limits of vector-valued functions
subsection.p: A moving object has a limiting position as t approaches a if its whole position settles down to one vector.

For example, consider \mathbf r(t)= \left( \frac{t^2-1}{t-1},\; \sin(\pi t),\; \sqrt{t+3} \right), \qquad t\ne 1. The formula is not defined at t=1, because the first component contains \frac{t^2-1}{t-1}. But for t\ne1, \frac{t^2-1}{t-1} = \frac{(t-1)(t+1)}{t-1} = t+1. So as t\to1, \frac{t^2-1}{t-1}\to2, \sin(\pi t)\to \sin\pi=0, and \sqrt{t+3}\to2. Therefore \lim_{t\to1}\mathbf r(t)=(2,0,2).

statement.p: We write \lim_{t\to a}\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf L if the distance \|\mathbf r(t)-\mathbf L\| approaches 0 as t approaches a.

subsection.p: The definition says exactly what it should say: the vector \mathbf r(t) gets close to \mathbf L if the distance between them gets small.
The previous example suggests the main rule.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),r_2(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr) and \mathbf L=(L_1,L_2,\ldots,L_n). Then \lim_{t\to a}\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf L if and only if \lim_{t\to a}r_i(t)=L_i for every component i=1,2,\ldots,n.

proof.p: The distance from \mathbf r(t) to \mathbf L is \|\mathbf r(t)-\mathbf L\| = \sqrt{ (r_1(t)-L_1)^2+\cdots+(r_n(t)-L_n)^2 }. If this distance goes to 0, then each component difference must go to 0.
Conversely, if every component difference goes to 0, then the sum of their squares goes to 0, so the square root also goes to 0. Thus the whole vector approaches \mathbf L.

subsection.p: We really do need every component to settle down.

example.title: One bad component breaks the limit

statement.p: Define \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\sin\frac{1}{t}\right), \qquad t\ne0. The first component has a limit: t\to0. But the second component \sin\frac{1}{t} oscillates forever as t\to0. It does not approach one number.
So the vector-valued function has no limit at t=0. The first coordinate behaves well, but the whole point does not settle down.

subsection.p: This is the same lesson as in single-variable calculus, but now it can fail in any coordinate.

exercise.title: Why does the limit split apart?

statement.p: The theorem says \lim_{t\to a}\mathbf r(t) is just the vector whose entries are the limits of the components. Give an intuitive reason why this should be true. Why does asking the whole vector \mathbf r(t) to settle down to \mathbf L amount to asking every component to settle down on its own?

hint.p: Think about the distance \|\mathbf r(t)-\mathbf L\|. For that single distance to shrink to 0, what has to happen to each coordinate gap at once?

subsection.title: Continuity
subsection.p: A position function is continuous when the moving point does not jump.

statement.p: A vector-valued function \mathbf r(t) is continuous at a if \lim_{t\to a}\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf r(a). It is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of that interval with the usual one-sided interpretation at endpoints.

subsection.p: By the componentwise limit theorem, continuity is also componentwise.

statement.p: The vector-valued function \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),r_2(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr) is continuous at a if and only if each component function r_i(t) is continuous at a.

example.title: A continuous motion

statement.p: The function \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,t) is continuous for every t, because \cos t, \sin t, and t are continuous. The curve is a helix with no jumps.

subsection.p: Here is why the continuity condition matters.

example.title: A jump is not a curve of steady motion

statement.p: Define \mathbf r(t)= \begin{cases} (t,0), & t<0,\\ (t,1), & t\ge0. \end{cases} For t<0, the point moves along the line y=0. For t\ge0, it moves along the line y=1.
At t=0, \mathbf r(0)=(0,1). But as t\to0^-, \mathbf r(t)\to(0,0). The left-hand limiting position and the actual position at 0 do not agree. The point teleports upward.
So this function is not continuous at t=0.

subsection.p: A curve used to model physical motion is usually continuous. Later, when we want velocity, we will ask for more: differentiability.

subsection.title: Space curves as images of intervals
subsection.p: The image of a vector-valued function \mathbf r:I\to\mathbb R^n is the set of all points reached: \{\mathbf r(t):t\in I\}. This image is the geometric curve. But the function \mathbf r(t) contains more information than the image alone.

example.title: The same image with different clocks

statement.p: The two functions \mathbf r_1(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, and \mathbf r_2(s)=(\cos 2s,\sin 2s), \qquad 0\le s\le\pi, have the same image: the unit circle.
But the clocks are different. In \mathbf r_1, the angle is t. In \mathbf r_2, the angle is 2s. The second parametrization moves around the circle twice as fast with respect to its parameter.

example.title: The same circle traced twice

statement.p: The function \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le4\pi, also has the unit circle as its image. But it traces the circle twice.
The image does not remember how many times the curve is traced. The parametrization does.

subsection.p: This distinction will matter whenever we integrate along a curve. If we walk around a circle twice, an accumulated quantity may be twice as large. If we reverse direction, some accumulated quantities change sign.

statement.p: Two different functions \mathbf r_1(t) and \mathbf r_2(t) can have exactly the same image, yet we still treat them as different objects. In your own words, what does the function \mathbf r(t) know that the curve it traces does not? Give one piece of information carried by \mathbf r(t) that is invisible if you only look at the set of points.

hint.p: A curve is just a set of points sitting in space. The function also records a clock: when you arrive at each point, how fast you pass through, and how many times you return.

subsection.p: In the language of differentials, the components of a curve also tell us how dx, dy, and dz change along the curve. If x=x(t), then later we will write dx=x'(t)\,dt. That is the first hint of how a 1-form like P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz will be pulled back to an ordinary one-variable integral along a path.
For now, a vector-valued function gives us a position record. The next question is the one every motion problem asks first: how fast is the position changing?

section.title: Derivatives and integrals of vector-valued functions

introduction.p: made \mathbf r(t) a position record. A position record becomes useful when we compare nearby times. The difference \mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t) is a displacement. Dividing by h gives average velocity over a short time interval.
Then the old single-variable idea returns: let the time interval shrink.

subsection.title: Velocity from a difference quotient
subsection.p: A small drone flies through a warehouse. Its position, in meters, is \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\;t^2,\;3-\frac{t}{2}\right), where t is measured in seconds.

At t=1, \mathbf r(1)=\left(1,1,\frac52\right). At time 1+h, \mathbf r(1+h)=\left(1+h,\;(1+h)^2,\;3-\frac{1+h}{2}\right). The displacement from t=1 to t=1+h is
\mathbf r(1+h)-\mathbf r(1) \amp= \left(h,\;(1+h)^2-1,\;-\frac{h}{2}\right) \amp= \left(h,\;2h+h^2,\;-\frac{h}{2}\right).
The average velocity over that interval is \frac{\mathbf r(1+h)-\mathbf r(1)}{h}=\left(1,\;2+h,\;-\frac12\right). Letting h\to0, we get the instantaneous velocity at t=1: \left(1,2,-\frac12\right).
This vector points in the direction the drone is moving at that instant.

exercise.title: Why does \mathbf r'(t) point along the path?

statement.p: Suppose \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf0. The derivative is a limit of difference quotients \frac{\mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t)}{h}. Each numerator \mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t) is a displacement vector connecting two nearby points on the curve. As h\to 0^+, what happens to the direction of that displacement vector, and why does this explain that \mathbf r'(t) ends up pointing along the path rather than off in some other direction?

hint.p: Picture the two points \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf r(t+h) sliding toward each other as h shrinks. The chord between them is a secant of the curve; think about what a secant becomes in the limit. Dividing by the positive number h only rescales the vector, it does not turn it.

statement.p: The derivative of \mathbf r(t) at t=a is \boxed{\mathbf r'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathbf r(a+h)-\mathbf r(a)}{h}} when this limit exists.

subsection.p: When \mathbf r(t) is a position vector, the derivative \mathbf v(t)=\mathbf r'(t) is called the velocity. The derivative of velocity, \mathbf a(t)=\mathbf v'(t)=\mathbf r''(t), is called the acceleration.
For the drone, \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\;t^2,\;3-\frac{t}{2}\right), so we expect \mathbf v(t)=\left(1,2t,-\frac12\right), and \mathbf a(t)=(0,2,0). We will justify the component-by-component rule next.

subsection.title: Differentiating component by component
subsection.p: A helix gives a clean example. Let \mathbf r(t)=\left(2\cos t,\;2\sin t,\;\frac{t}{3}\right). The component functions are x(t)=2\cos t,\qquad y(t)=2\sin t,\qquad z(t)=\frac{t}{3}. Differentiating each one gives x'(t)=-2\sin t, y'(t)=2\cos t, and z'(t)=\frac13. So \mathbf r'(t)=\left(-2\sin t,\;2\cos t,\;\frac13\right). At t=0, \mathbf r(0)=(2,0,0), and \mathbf r'(0)=\left(0,2,\frac13\right). The point is at the right side of the circle and is moving in the positive y-direction while also rising.

figure.caption: The derivative vector points tangent to the path. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The rule is exactly what the example showed.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),r_2(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr). Then \mathbf r'(a) exists if and only if each component derivative r_i'(a) exists. In that case, \boxed{\mathbf r'(a)=\bigl(r_1'(a),r_2'(a),\ldots,r_n'(a)\bigr).}

proof.p: Use the definition: \frac{\mathbf r(a+h)-\mathbf r(a)}{h}=\left(\frac{r_1(a+h)-r_1(a)}{h},\ldots,\frac{r_n(a+h)-r_n(a)}{h}\right). A vector limit exists exactly when all component limits exist. Those component limits are the ordinary derivatives r_i'(a).

subsection.p: The hypothesis that the component derivatives exist is real. A continuous curve can still fail to have a velocity.

example.title: A sharp corner has no velocity vector

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(|t|,t). This curve is continuous at t=0, but \frac{\mathbf r(h)-\mathbf r(0)}{h}=\left(\frac{|h|}{h},1\right). If h>0, this quotient is (1,1). If h<0, it is (-1,1). The two one-sided limits do not agree. Therefore \mathbf r'(0) does not exist.
Geometrically, the curve has a corner at the origin. The point arrives from one direction and leaves in another, so there is no single tangent velocity at that instant.

subsection.p: At endpoints of a time interval, we use the same caution as in single-variable calculus. A curve defined only for t\ge0 may have a right-hand velocity at t=0, but not a two-sided derivative there unless the curve is defined on both sides.

subsection.title: Tangent lines to a motion path
subsection.p: If \mathbf r'(a)\ne\mathbf 0, then the tangent line to the curve at time a is the line through \mathbf r(a) in the direction \mathbf r'(a). Thus \boxed{\mathbf L(s)=\mathbf r(a)+s\mathbf r'(a)} is a parametrization of the tangent line.

example.title: A tangent line to a drone path

statement.p: For \mathbf r(t)=\left(t,\;t^2,\;3-\frac{t}{2}\right), we found \mathbf r(1)=\left(1,1,\frac52\right) and \mathbf r'(1)=\left(1,2,-\frac12\right). So the tangent line at t=1 is \mathbf L(s)=\left(1,1,\frac52\right)+s\left(1,2,-\frac12\right). In coordinates, x=1+s,\qquad y=1+2s,\qquad z=\frac52-\frac{s}{2}.

subsection.p: The velocity vector gives the instantaneous direction of motion, not merely the direction of the curve as a set. If the same geometric curve is traced with a different clock, the velocity vector changes.

example.title: Same circle, different speeds

statement.p: Let \mathbf r_1(t)=(\cos t,\sin t) and \mathbf r_2(t)=(\cos 2t,\sin 2t). Both trace the unit circle. But \mathbf r_1'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t), while \mathbf r_2'(t)=(-2\sin 2t,2\cos 2t). The second velocity vector has twice the length. The same circle is being traced twice as fast.

subsection.p: The length of the velocity vector is the speed: \text{speed}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|. Speed will become the key to arc length in .

exercise.title: What does the tangent vector's direction and length tell you?

statement.p: The tangent line at time a uses \mathbf r'(a) as its direction, so \mathbf r'(t) is tangent to the curve. Yet two motions can trace the very same curve while their velocity vectors differ in length, as the unit circle examples above showed. Explain in your own words why the direction of \mathbf r'(t) determines the tangent line to the curve, with its sign recording the chosen direction of travel, while the length \|\mathbf r'(t)\| is instead a feature of how the curve is being traced.

hint.p: Imagine driving along a fixed road. The road decides which way your car is pointing at each spot, but you choose how fast to go. Which of those two things is "direction" and which is "length"? Re-tracing the same circle twice as fast multiplies the velocity by a constant without rotating it.

subsection.title: Differentiation rules
subsection.p: Since derivatives are computed component by component, the familiar single-variable rules return almost unchanged.
Before listing them, here is one example.

example.title: A dot product changing with time

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,0),\qquad \mathbf s(t)=(1,\cos t,\sin t). Then \mathbf r(t)\cdot\mathbf s(t)=t+t^2\cos t. Differentiating directly, \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r(t)\cdot\mathbf s(t)\bigr)=1+2t\cos t-t^2\sin t.

Now compute using a product rule: \mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t,0), \mathbf s'(t)=(0,-\sin t,\cos t). Then
\mathbf r'(t)\cdot\mathbf s(t)+\mathbf r(t)\cdot\mathbf s'(t) \amp= (1,2t,0)\cdot(1,\cos t,\sin t) \amp\quad +(t,t^2,0)\cdot(0,-\sin t,\cos t) \amp= 1+2t\cos t-t^2\sin t.
The ordinary product rule is still there, but now it is written with dot products.

Suppose \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf s(t) are differentiable vector-valued functions, and f(t) is a differentiable real-valued function. Then \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r+\mathbf s\bigr)=\mathbf r'+\mathbf s', \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(f\mathbf r\bigr)=f'\mathbf r+f\mathbf r', and \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s\bigr)=\mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf s+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s'. If \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf s(t) are functions into \mathbb R^3, then \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\mathbf r\times\mathbf s\bigr)=\mathbf r'\times\mathbf s+\mathbf r\times\mathbf s'.

proof.p:
Each rule follows by writing the vectors in components and applying the ordinary single-variable differentiation rules. The dot product rule, for example, is just the product rule applied to each term: \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s=r_1s_1+\cdots+r_ns_n. Then
\frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s) \amp= (r_1's_1+r_1s_1')+\cdots+(r_n's_n+r_ns_n') \amp= \mathbf r'\cdot\mathbf s+\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf s'.
The cross product rule is checked the same way from the component formula for \mathbf r\times\mathbf s.

subsection.p: The differentiability assumptions matter. If a component has a corner, as in |t|, then the corresponding vector function may fail to have a derivative, and the rules above have nothing to apply to at that time.

subsection.title: Integrating vector-valued functions
subsection.p: Differentiation takes us from position to velocity: \mathbf r(t)\longmapsto \mathbf r'(t). Integration goes the other way. It adds many tiny velocity vectors to recover a net displacement.

Suppose a drifting boat has velocity \mathbf v(t)=(2,\cos t,3t^2),\qquad 0\le t\le\pi. The displacement from t=0 to t=\pi is \int_0^\pi \mathbf v(t)\,dt. Compute component by component:
\int_0^\pi (2,\cos t,3t^2)\,dt \amp= \left(\int_0^\pi 2\,dt,\;\int_0^\pi \cos t\,dt,\;\int_0^\pi 3t^2\,dt\right) \amp= \left(2\pi,\;\sin t\bigg|_0^\pi,\;t^3\bigg|_0^\pi\right) \amp= (2\pi,0,\pi^3).
The boat's net displacement is (2\pi,0,\pi^3).

statement.p: If \mathbf v(t)=\bigl(v_1(t),v_2(t),\ldots,v_n(t)\bigr), then \boxed{\int_a^b \mathbf v(t)\,dt=\left(\int_a^b v_1(t)\,dt,\;\int_a^b v_2(t)\,dt,\;\ldots,\;\int_a^b v_n(t)\,dt\right)} whenever the component integrals exist.

subsection.p: For an indefinite integral, \int \mathbf v(t)\,dt means a vector-valued antiderivative: \mathbf R'(t)=\mathbf v(t). The constant of integration is now a constant vector.

exercise.title: What does integrating velocity recover, and why a whole vector \mathbf C?

statement.p: When you integrate a velocity \mathbf v(t), the result is again a vector. In words, what quantity does this integral recover, and how does that meaning explain why the constant of integration must be a whole vector \mathbf C rather than a single number? Think about what kind of information you must supply to pin down the actual motion.

hint.p: Antidifferentiating each component leaves one unknown number per component, and there is a separate one in each coordinate direction. What single object do you get when you collect (C_1,C_2,C_3) together? Geometrically, knowing the velocity tells you the shape of the trip but not where it began.

example.title: A vector antiderivative

statement.p: Let \mathbf v(t)=(6t,\;e^t,\;\cos t). Then \int \mathbf v(t)\,dt=(3t^2,\;e^t,\;\sin t)+\mathbf C, where \mathbf C=(C_1,C_2,C_3) is a constant vector.

subsection.p: The condition that the component integrals exist is not decoration. If even one component fails to have an ordinary definite integral, then the vector integral fails.

example.title: One bad component breaks the vector integral

statement.p: The function \mathbf v(t)=\left(\frac1t,0\right) is not bounded near t=0. The ordinary integral \int_0^1 \frac1t\,dt does not exist as a finite definite integral. Therefore \int_0^1 \left(\frac1t,0\right)\,dt does not exist as an ordinary vector integral.
A vector integral is only as well behaved as its components.

subsection.title: The Fundamental Theorem for vector-valued functions
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus now returns in vector form.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=\bigl(r_1(t),\ldots,r_n(t)\bigr) be differentiable on an interval, and suppose \mathbf r'(t) has continuous components on [a,b]. Then \boxed{\int_a^b \mathbf r'(t)\,dt=\mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a).}

proof.p:
Write \mathbf r'(t)=\bigl(r_1'(t),\ldots,r_n'(t)\bigr). Then
\int_a^b \mathbf r'(t)\,dt \amp= \left(\int_a^b r_1'(t)\,dt,\ldots,\int_a^b r_n'(t)\,dt\right) \amp= \left(r_1(b)-r_1(a),\ldots,r_n(b)-r_n(a)\right) \amp= \mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a).
The middle step is the single-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, applied one component at a time.

subsection.p: The continuity assumption on the components of \mathbf r' is a friendly sufficient condition. It guarantees that the component integrals behave exactly as expected. There are more advanced versions with weaker hypotheses, but this one is the right tool for the curves in this course.

subsection.title: Initial value problems for motion
subsection.p: Often we know velocity or acceleration first, and we want position.

A basketball is thrown across a gym. Let the x-axis point across the court, the y-axis point sideways, and the z-axis point upward. Suppose the ball starts at \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1) meters and has initial velocity \mathbf v(0)=(8,3,10) meters per second. Ignore air resistance. Then acceleration is constant: \mathbf a(t)=(0,0,-9.8).

Since \mathbf v'(t)=\mathbf a(t), we integrate acceleration: \mathbf v(t)=\int (0,0,-9.8)\,dt=(0,0,-9.8t)+\mathbf C. Use \mathbf v(0)=(8,3,10) to get \mathbf C=(8,3,10). Thus \mathbf v(t)=(8,3,10-9.8t).
Now integrate velocity: \mathbf r(t)=\int (8,3,10-9.8t)\,dt=(8t,3t,10t-4.9t^2)+\mathbf D. Use \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1) to get \mathbf D=(0,0,1). Therefore \boxed{\mathbf r(t)=(8t,\;3t,\;1+10t-4.9t^2).}

The three coordinates tell three simpler stories: x(t)=8t, y(t)=3t, z(t)=1+10t-4.9t^2. The horizontal motion is linear. The vertical motion is the familiar falling-object parabola from single-variable calculus.

example.title: Recovering position from velocity

statement.p: A small underwater robot has velocity \mathbf v(t)=(1+t,\;2,\;e^{-t}) and starts at \mathbf r(0)=(3,-1,0). Find \mathbf r(t).

Since \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf v(t), we integrate: \mathbf r(t)=\left(t+\frac{t^2}{2},\;2t,\;-e^{-t}\right)+\mathbf C. Use the initial position: \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,-1)+\mathbf C=(3,-1,0). So \mathbf C=(3,-1,1). Therefore \boxed{\mathbf r(t)=\left(3+t+\frac{t^2}{2},\;-1+2t,\;1-e^{-t}\right).}

subsection.p: This is an initial value problem. The derivative information gives a family of possible motions. The initial condition chooses the one motion that actually starts in the given place.

Differentiation and integration now work for motion in space. But a subtle problem has appeared. The integral of velocity gives displacement, not distance traveled. A runner who completes one lap has \mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a)=\mathbf 0, but she certainly did not run zero meters. To measure distance traveled, we must add up tiny lengths \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. We return to this question in . First, the same curve derivatives let us revisit the surface grids from Chapter 4.

subsection.title: Velocities along a surface grid
subsection.p: In , we described a surface by \mathbf r(s,t) and drew its grid curves by holding one parameter fixed. We can now find the velocities along those curves. Each calculation uses an ordinary derivative of a function with just one changing input.

Choose an interior parameter pair (s_0,t_0), so that either parameter can vary a little in both directions. The two grid curves through P=\mathbf r(s_0,t_0) are \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=\mathbf r(s,t_0),\qquad \boldsymbol\beta(t)=\mathbf r(s_0,t). In the first curve t_0 is a constant; in the second s_0 is a constant. Their velocities at P are \boxed{\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\alpha'(s_0),\qquad \mathbf w=\boldsymbol\beta'(t_0).} A nonzero velocity is a tangent vector to its grid curve, based at P. The parameters need not measure physical time: velocity here means change of position per unit change of the parameter.

example.title: Two velocities on a bowl

statement.p: For \mathbf r(s,t)=(s,t,s^2+t^2), freezing one input gives \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s,t_0,s^2+t_0^2),\qquad \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(s_0,t,s_0^2+t^2). Differentiate these one-variable functions component by component: \mathbf v=(1,0,2s_0),\qquad \mathbf w=(0,1,2t_0). The vectors cannot be parallel: their first two coordinates already give two independent directions. Their cross product is \mathbf v\times\mathbf w=(-2s_0,-2t_0,1), perpendicular to both grid-curve tangents and never zero.

definition.title: Regular parameter point and a normal vector

statement.p: Suppose the two grid-curve velocities exist at an interior pair (s_0,t_0). The parametrization is regular at this parameter point when the velocities are linearly independent, equivalently when \boxed{\mathbf v\times\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0.} When they are dependent, the parameter point is nonregular. Thus regularity is a property of the chosen parametrization at a parameter pair, not just a test on the coordinates of its image point.

For surface geometry we work with parametrizations whose grid-curve velocities exist nearby and vary continuously as the two parameters vary. At a regular point they span the tangent plane to the local surface sheet; a normal vector to this sheet at P is \boxed{\mathbf N=\mathbf v\times\mathbf w.} Any nonzero multiple of \mathbf N is also normal. Swapping the two velocities changes its sign. The cross-product rule proves perpendicularity to both grid tangents immediately; the full justification that their plane describes the local sheet is given in .

subsection.p: The nearby-continuity assumption rules out erratic behavior between the grid curves; two derivatives at a single pair alone do not control an entire surface. For the polynomial and trigonometric parametrizations here, the displayed velocity formulas vary continuously. On a surface that crosses itself, the normal belongs to the sheet selected by the parameter pair.

example.title: A grid that collapses at a cone vertex

statement.p: Consider \mathbf r(s,t)=(s\cos t,s\sin t,s),\qquad s,t\in\mathbb R. Its image is the double cone x^2+y^2=z^2. Positive and negative s describe its upper and lower halves. Both inputs can vary on either side of every chosen value, including s=0.

Freezing t=t_0 gives a straight grid line \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s\cos t_0,s\sin t_0,s). Freezing s=s_0 gives a circular grid curve \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(s_0\cos t,s_0\sin t,s_0). Their velocities are \mathbf v=(\cos t_0,\sin t_0,1),\qquad \mathbf w=(-s_0\sin t_0,s_0\cos t_0,0). Hence \boxed{\mathbf N=(-s_0\cos t_0,-s_0\sin t_0,s_0).} The parametrization is regular exactly when s_0\ne0. At (0,t_0), the circular grid curve is the constant curve \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(0,0,0), so \mathbf w=\mathbf0 and \mathbf N=\mathbf0. The zero vector supplies no normal direction.

For this cone the vertex really has no single tangent plane. The straight grid lines with t_0=0,\pi/2,\pi have velocities (1,0,1),(0,1,1),(-1,0,1). Their determinant is 2, so these three directions cannot lie in one plane. This geometric argument says more than merely observing a zero cross product.

figure.caption: Grid curves on the double cone. The blue straight grid line and orange circular grid curve meet at the regular point P; the arrows show their velocities \mathbf v,\mathbf w and a normal \mathbf N, scaled for visibility. At the red vertex O, the circular grid has collapsed to a point. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: Double cone with grid curves, tangent velocities and a normal at a regular point, and a red nonregular vertex.

subsection.p: A nonregular parametrization does not always mean that the image itself has a sharp point. For example, \mathbf q(s,t)=(s^3,t,0) covers the ordinary xy-plane. Its grid velocities at (s_0,t_0) are (3s_0^2,0,0) and (0,1,0), so their cross product vanishes when s_0=0. The first grid curve simply has zero velocity there. The same plane has the regular parametrization \widetilde{\mathbf q}(a,b)=(a,b,0), whose grid velocities are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0).

statement.p: For the bowl \mathbf r(s,t)=(s,t,s^2+t^2), write the two frozen-parameter grid curves through the parameter pair (1,-1). Find their velocities and a normal at the image point. Is the parametrization regular there? What happens to the normal if the two velocities are exchanged?

hint.p: In one curve set t=-1; in the other set s=1. Differentiate each curve in its remaining variable, then use the cross product.

solution.p: The curves are \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s,-1,s^2+1) and \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(1,t,1+t^2). At P=(1,-1,2) their velocities are (1,0,2) and (0,1,-2). Their cross product (-2,2,1) is nonzero, so the parameter point is regular and this vector is normal. Exchanging the velocities gives the opposite normal (2,-2,-1).

subsection.p: The ordinary derivatives of two grid curves have given us two tangent directions and, at regular points, a normal. will collect the same velocities in a matrix and explain their role in a local linear approximation. We next return to a single moving point and measure its speed and distance traveled.

section.title: Arc length and speed
section.p: ended with a warning. The integral of velocity gives displacement: \int_a^b \mathbf r'(t)\,dt=\mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a). But displacement is not the same as distance traveled. A runner who completes one lap around a track has returned to the starting point, so the displacement is zero. The run was not zero meters long.

subsection.title: Distance traveled versus displacement
subsection.p: Picture a circular track of radius 50 meters. A runner completes one lap in 40 seconds. A convenient position function is \mathbf r(t)=\left(50\cos\frac{2\pi t}{40},50\sin\frac{2\pi t}{40}\right),\qquad 0\le t\le 40. At t=0, \mathbf r(0)=(50,0). At t=40, \mathbf r(40)=(50,0). So the displacement is \mathbf r(40)-\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf 0.
But the distance traveled is the circumference: 2\pi(50)=100\pi. The displacement remembers only the start and finish. Distance traveled remembers the whole path.

figure.caption: A closed trip can have zero displacement and positive distance traveled.

subsection.p:
Differentiate the runner's position: \mathbf r'(t)=\left(-50\frac{2\pi}{40}\sin\frac{2\pi t}{40},50\frac{2\pi}{40}\cos\frac{2\pi t}{40}\right). Its length is
\|\mathbf r'(t)\| \amp= 50\frac{2\pi}{40}\sqrt{\sin^2\frac{2\pi t}{40}+\cos^2\frac{2\pi t}{40}} \amp= \frac{5\pi}{2}.
So the runner's speed is constant: \frac{5\pi}{2}\text{ meters per second}. Distance traveled is speed multiplied by time: \frac{5\pi}{2}\cdot 40=100\pi. Equivalently, \int_0^{40}\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt=\int_0^{40}\frac{5\pi}{2}\,dt=100\pi.
The vector integral \int_0^{40}\mathbf r'(t)\,dt cancels the forward and backward changes in position. The scalar integral \int_0^{40}\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt does not cancel. Speed is never negative.

exercise.title: Why is the trip at least as long as the shortcut?

statement.p: Explain in your own words why the total distance traveled along a path is always at least as large as the magnitude of the displacement \|\mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a)\|. When are the two quantities equal?

hint.p: Think about the difference between the scalar integral \int_a^b\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt and the vector integral \int_a^b\mathbf r'(t)\,dt. The vector version lets backward steps cancel forward ones; the scalar version never does. What kind of path would have nothing to cancel?

subsection.p: That is the key idea.

statement.p: If \mathbf r(t) is a differentiable position function, then its velocity is \mathbf v(t)=\mathbf r'(t), and its speed is \boxed{\|\mathbf v(t)\|=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|.} Velocity is a vector. Speed is a number.

subsection.p: Velocity knows direction. Speed only knows how fast the point is moving.

subsection.title: The arc length integral
subsection.p: For a short time interval from t to t+\Delta t, the displacement is approximately \mathbf r'(t)\Delta t. The distance traveled during that short time is approximately \|\mathbf r'(t)\Delta t\|=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\Delta t. Adding these small distances suggests \text{length}=\int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.
This is exactly the same idea as single-variable integration. Break the quantity into tiny pieces, approximate each piece, and pass to a limit.

example.title: Length of a helix

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=\left(2\cos t,\;2\sin t,\;\frac{t}{3}\right),\qquad 0\le t\le 6\pi. This curve winds around a cylinder of radius 2 while rising.

Differentiate: \mathbf r'(t)=\left(-2\sin t,\;2\cos t,\;\frac13\right). The speed is
\|\mathbf r'(t)\| \amp= \sqrt{(-2\sin t)^2+(2\cos t)^2+\left(\frac13\right)^2} \amp= \sqrt{4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t+\frac19} \amp= \sqrt{4+\frac19} \amp= \frac{\sqrt{37}}{3}.
So the length of the helix is
L \amp= \int_0^{6\pi}\frac{\sqrt{37}}{3}\,dt \amp= \frac{\sqrt{37}}{3}(6\pi) \amp= 2\pi\sqrt{37}.
Let \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n be a continuously differentiable curve. Its arc length from t=a to t=b is \boxed{L=\int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.}

subsection.p: The symbol ds denotes the arc-length integration element. For an increasing parameter t, its notation means \boxed{ds=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.} So the length integral may also be written L=\int_a^b ds.
In the plane, where \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)), this becomes \boxed{ds=\sqrt{(x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2}\,dt.} In space, \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)), and \boxed{ds=\sqrt{(x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2+(z'(t))^2}\,dt.}

The meaning is ordinary single-variable integration of speed. For a small positive time increment \Delta t, the coordinate increments are approximately x'(t)\Delta t, y'(t)\Delta t, and z'(t)\Delta t; their Euclidean length is approximately \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\Delta t. Reversing travel does not change length: under a new parameter, use the speed with respect to that parameter. Thus ds measures unsigned length and is not a signed coordinate measurement such as dx from Chapter 2.

subsection.title: Why the formula comes from polygons
subsection.p: Before trusting the integral formula, it is helpful to see where it comes from.

Take a curve \mathbf r(t),\qquad a\le t\le b, and choose a partition a=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=b. Connect the points \mathbf r(t_0),\mathbf r(t_1),\ldots,\mathbf r(t_N) by straight segments. The length of this polygonal path is L_P=\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf r(t_i)-\mathbf r(t_{i-1})\|. For a fine partition, each small piece of the curve is nearly straight.

figure.caption: Arc length is the limit of polygonal lengths.

subsection.p: On a small interval [t_{i-1},t_i], the displacement is approximately \mathbf r'(t_i^*)\Delta t_i for some point t_i^* in the interval. Its length is approximately \|\mathbf r'(t_i^*)\|\Delta t_i. So the polygonal length is approximately \sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf r'(t_i^*)\|\Delta t_i. As the partition gets finer, this Riemann sum becomes \int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n be continuously differentiable. Then the arc length of the curve is \boxed{L=\int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.} If the curve is only piecewise continuously differentiable, the same formula holds by splitting the interval into smooth pieces and adding the lengths.

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p: On a very short interval, a differentiable curve is well approximated by its tangent line: \mathbf r(t+\Delta t)-\mathbf r(t)\approx\mathbf r'(t)\Delta t. Taking lengths gives \|\mathbf r(t+\Delta t)-\mathbf r(t)\|\approx\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\Delta t. Adding these approximations over the whole interval gives a Riemann sum for \int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. The continuity of \mathbf r' makes the approximation behave uniformly as the subintervals shrink.

subsection.p: The smoothness condition is there to keep the tangent approximation honest.

example.title: A corner must be treated piece by piece

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(|t|,t),\qquad -1\le t\le1. This curve has a corner at t=0. It is not differentiable there.

For t<0, \mathbf r(t)=(-t,t), so \mathbf r'(t)=(-1,1),\qquad \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt2. For t>0, \mathbf r(t)=(t,t), so \mathbf r'(t)=(1,1),\qquad \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt2. The curve is made of two straight segments, each of length \sqrt2. Therefore L=2\sqrt2.

We could not apply the smooth theorem on the whole interval at once, because the velocity does not exist at t=0. But the curve is piecewise smooth, so we split it: L=\int_{-1}^0\sqrt2\,dt+\int_0^1\sqrt2\,dt=2\sqrt2. The moral is simple: one corner is not a disaster, but it must be acknowledged.

subsection.title: Arc length does not depend on the clock
subsection.p: Here a change of clock means a continuously differentiable, strictly monotone reparametrization with nonzero derivative, covering the same traversal once. By the componentwise single-variable chain rule, \|d\mathbf r(t(u))/du\|=\|\mathbf r'(t(u))\||t'(u)|; ordinary substitution in the length integral proves invariance, also when the direction is reversed. Traversing a curve twice instead of once doubles the distance traveled.
The same path can be traced slowly or quickly. Its length should not change.
Consider the unit circle traced once: \mathbf r_1(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Its speed is \|\mathbf r_1'(t)\|=\|(-\sin t,\cos t)\|=1. So its length is L_1=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi.

Now trace the same circle using the faster clock \mathbf r_2(u)=(\cos(2u),\sin(2u)),\qquad 0\le u\le\pi. This also goes once around the circle. Its velocity is \mathbf r_2'(u)=(-2\sin(2u),2\cos(2u)), and its speed is \|\mathbf r_2'(u)\|=2. So L_2=\int_0^\pi 2\,du=2\pi. The second clock runs over a shorter interval, but the speed with respect to that clock is larger. The product gives the same length.
This is the reason arc length is geometric. It belongs to the curve, not to a particular clock.

exercise.title: Why does the clock not matter?

statement.p: When we sped up the clock so the same circle was traced over a shorter interval, the speed \|\mathbf r'\| grew but the arc length stayed 2\pi. Explain why changing how fast you traverse a curve never changes its length.

hint.p: Arc length is built from the product \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. A faster clock increases the speed but compresses the interval by the same factor. Picture walking and running along the same hallway: which one covers more floor?

subsection.title: The unit tangent vector
subsection.p: Velocity gives both speed and direction. If we want only the direction of motion, we divide by the speed.

For the circle \mathbf r(t)=(50\cos t,50\sin t), the velocity is \mathbf r'(t)=(-50\sin t,50\cos t). The speed is \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=50. So the direction of motion is \frac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}=(-\sin t,\cos t). This vector has length 1, and it is tangent to the circle.

statement.p: If \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf 0, then the unit tangent vector is \boxed{\mathbf T(t)=\frac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}.} It is the unit vector pointing in the direction of motion.

subsection.p: The condition \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf 0 matters. If the velocity vector is zero, then there is no direction to divide by.

example.title: A stopped particle has no unit tangent at that instant

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t^2,0),\qquad -1\le t\le1. This point moves left along the x-axis until t=0, stops, and then moves right along the same line.
The velocity is \mathbf r'(t)=(2t,0). For t<0, \mathbf T(t)=(-1,0). For t>0, \mathbf T(t)=(1,0). At t=0, \mathbf r'(0)=(0,0), so \frac{\mathbf r'(0)}{\|\mathbf r'(0)\|} is meaningless.
The geometric path lies on the x-axis, but the moving point stops and reverses. There is no single direction of motion at the stopping time.

subsection.p: A curve with \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf 0 is often called regular. Regular curves do not stop. They may turn, but they always have a well-defined direction of motion.

subsection.title: Reparametrization by arc length
subsection.p: Sometimes the clock t is inconvenient. A curve may speed up and slow down even when its shape is simple. Arc length gives a more geometric parameter.

Let \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. The speed is \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=2. The distance traveled from 0 to t is s(t)=\int_0^t 2\,du=2t. So t=\frac{s}{2}. Substituting into the curve gives \mathbf R(s)=\mathbf r\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)=\left(2\cos\frac{s}{2},2\sin\frac{s}{2}\right),\qquad 0\le s\le4\pi. Now s measures distance traveled along the circle. Differentiate: \mathbf R'(s)=\left(-\sin\frac{s}{2},\cos\frac{s}{2}\right). Thus \|\mathbf R'(s)\|=1. The curve is now traveled at unit speed.

statement.p: For a continuously differentiable curve \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n, the arc length function starting at a is \boxed{s(t)=\int_a^t \|\mathbf r'(u)\|\,du.} It measures the distance traveled from time a to time t.

subsection.p: By the single-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \frac{ds}{dt}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|. So s increases at the speed of the moving point.

exercise.title: What makes arc length the natural parameter?

statement.p: After reparametrizing a regular curve by arc length to get \mathbf R(s), what is its speed \|\mathbf R'(s)\|? Explain why that value is exactly what you should expect when the parameter s itself measures distance traveled.

hint.p: Speed is the rate at which distance is covered per unit of the parameter. If the parameter is distance, how much distance passes for each unit of s? You do not need to compute anything; reason from what s measures.

statement.p: Suppose \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n is continuously differentiable and \|\mathbf r'(t)\|>0 for all t\in[a,b]. Define s(t)=\int_a^t \|\mathbf r'(u)\|\,du. Then s(t) is strictly increasing, so it has an inverse t=t(s). The reparametrized curve \mathbf R(s)=\mathbf r(t(s)) has unit speed: \boxed{\left\|\frac{d\mathbf R}{ds}\right\|=1.}

proof.p: Since \frac{ds}{dt}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|>0, the function s(t) is strictly increasing and therefore invertible.

Using the chain rule, \frac{d\mathbf R}{ds}=\frac{d\mathbf r}{dt}\frac{dt}{ds}. But \frac{dt}{ds}=\frac{1}{ds/dt}=\frac{1}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}. Therefore \frac{d\mathbf R}{ds}=\frac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}=\mathbf T(t). Taking lengths gives \left\|\frac{d\mathbf R}{ds}\right\|=1.

subsection.p: The assumption \|\mathbf r'(t)\|>0 is not decoration. If the curve stops for a while, arc length cannot serve as a clock.

example.title: If the particle waits, arc length cannot recover the time

statement.p: During the waiting time, \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=0. So s(t)=0 for every 0\le t\le1. The arc length function is not one-to-one. Knowing s=0 does not tell us whether t=0.2,\quad t=0.7,\quad \text{or}\quad t=1. So t cannot be recovered from s. Strictly positive continuous speed guarantees a smooth arc-length parametrization, as the preceding theorem shows. Waiting on an interval prevents recovery of the old clock; an isolated zero of speed requires separate analysis.

subsection.p: Arc length solves the first problem raised by motion: how far did the point travel? But it does not tell us how the curve bends. Two roads can have the same length while one is nearly straight and the other twists through sharp turns. The unit tangent vector \mathbf T records direction; the next question is how quickly that direction changes as we move along the curve. That rate of turning is called curvature.

section.title: Curvature and normal direction
section.p: Arc length gave us a fair way to measure progress along a curve. It removed the arbitrary clock. Now we can ask a geometric question: \text{How much does the curve turn per meter traveled?} That question leads to curvature.

subsection.title: How sharply a curve turns
subsection.p: A bicycle moving around a small traffic circle must turn sharply. A bicycle moving around a large roundabout turns gently. Both paths are circles, but their radii are different.

Start with a circle of radius R: \mathbf r(t)=(R\cos t,R\sin t). Its velocity is \mathbf r'(t)=(-R\sin t,R\cos t), and its speed is \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=R. The unit tangent vector is \mathbf T(t)=\frac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}=(-\sin t,\cos t). Differentiate: \mathbf T'(t)=(-\cos t,-\sin t). The length of this derivative is \|\mathbf T'(t)\|=1.

But this is the rate of change of \mathbf T with respect to t, not with respect to distance. Since \frac{ds}{dt}=R, we have \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\frac{d\mathbf T/dt}{ds/dt}=\frac{\mathbf T'(t)}{R}. Therefore \left\|\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}\right\|=\frac1R.
A circle of radius R has curvature \frac1R. Small radius means large curvature. Large radius means small curvature.

statement.p: In your own words, what does curvature \kappa measure about a curve? Using that description, explain why a straight line has curvature \kappa=0 no matter how fast a particle travels along it.

hint.p: Curvature watches the direction of \mathbf T, not its length, and it measures change per unit distance rather than per unit time. On a straight line, which way is \mathbf T pointing as you move along?

figure.caption: Curvature measures turning per unit distance, not turning per unit time.

subsection.p: This example tells us what the definition should be.
The letter \kappa is the Greek letter kappa.
Curvature has units of \frac{1}{\text{length}}. For example, a circle of radius 50 meters has curvature \frac{1}{50}\text{ per meter}.

subsection.title: Computing curvature from any parameter
subsection.p: Curvature is defined using arc length s, but most curves are given with some other parameter t. The chain rule converts between them.

Since \frac{ds}{dt}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|, we have \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\frac{d\mathbf T/dt}{ds/dt}=\frac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}. Therefore \boxed{\kappa(t)=\frac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}.}

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t) be a C^2 regular curve, meaning that its first two derivatives are continuous and its velocity is nonzero. Then \boxed{\kappa(t)=\frac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|},} where \mathbf T(t)=\frac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}.

proof.p: The definition is \kappa=\left\|\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}\right\|. By the chain rule, \frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}=\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}\frac{ds}{dt}. Since \frac{ds}{dt}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|, we get \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\frac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}. Taking lengths gives the formula.

subsection.p: The word regular is essential. If \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf 0, then \mathbf T(t) is not defined.

example.title: Curvature fails at a stopping time

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t^2,0). For t<0, the unit tangent vector is \mathbf T(t)=(-1,0). For t>0, it is \mathbf T(t)=(1,0). At t=0, the velocity is zero: \mathbf r'(0)=(0,0). So the unit tangent is undefined there, and the curvature formula cannot be used at that instant.
The path lies on a straight line, but the parametrized motion stops and reverses. The regularity condition prevents this kind of ambiguity.

subsection.title: A useful plane formula
subsection.p: For a plane curve \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)), there is a compact curvature formula: \boxed{\kappa(t)=\frac{|x'(t)y''(t)-y'(t)x''(t)|}{\left((x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2\right)^{3/2}}.}

This formula is easier to remember if we recognize the numerator as a signed area measurement: x'y''-y'x''=\det\begin{pmatrix} x' \amp x''\\ y' \amp y'' \end{pmatrix}. It measures the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf r'(t)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbf r''(t). In the language that will later become differential forms, it is the same alternating measurement behind dx\wedge dy.

example.title: Curvature of a parabola

statement.p:
Let \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2). Then x(t)=t,\qquad y(t)=t^2. So x'(t)=1,\qquad y'(t)=2t, and x''(t)=0,\qquad y''(t)=2. The curvature is
\kappa(t) \amp= \frac{|x'y''-y'x''|}{\left((x')^2+(y')^2\right)^{3/2}} \amp= \frac{|1\cdot2-(2t)\cdot0|}{\left(1+4t^2\right)^{3/2}} \amp= \frac{2}{(1+4t^2)^{3/2}}.
At the vertex, t=0, the curvature is \kappa(0)=2. Farther away from the vertex, the denominator grows, so the curvature decreases. The parabola bends most sharply at its vertex.

subsection.p: The denominator in the curvature formula must not be zero. That denominator is \left((x')^2+(y')^2\right)^{3/2}=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3. So the plane formula has the same regularity requirement: \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf 0.

subsection.title: Unit normal vector in the plane
subsection.p: The tangent vector tells us the direction of motion. When the curve turns, the tangent vector changes. The direction in which \mathbf T changes is the normal direction.

For the circle \mathbf r(t)=(R\cos t,R\sin t), we found \mathbf T(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t). Then \mathbf T'(t)=(-\cos t,-\sin t). This points inward, toward the center of the circle. Its length is 1, so the unit normal vector is \mathbf N(t)=(-\cos t,-\sin t).

statement.p: If \mathbf T'(t)\ne\mathbf 0, then the unit normal vector is \boxed{\mathbf N(t)=\frac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.} It points in the direction the curve is turning.

subsection.p: For a plane curve, \mathbf T and \mathbf N are perpendicular. To see why, notice that \mathbf T(t)\cdot\mathbf T(t)=1 for all t. Differentiate: 2\mathbf T(t)\cdot\mathbf T'(t)=0. Thus \mathbf T(t)\cdot\mathbf T'(t)=0. So \mathbf T'(t), and therefore \mathbf N(t), is perpendicular to \mathbf T(t).

exercise.title: Why does \mathbf N point into the turn?

statement.p: The unit normal \mathbf N always points toward the inside of a turn, never toward the outside. Why should that be? Think about which way the tip of the unit tangent \mathbf T is being pulled as the curve bends.

hint.p: \mathbf N points in the direction of \mathbf T', the direction \mathbf T is changing. As you round a bend, the arrow \mathbf T swings toward the inside of the curve. Picture the circle \mathbf T' we computed: which way did it point relative to the center?

figure.caption: The normal vector points toward the side where the tangent direction is changing.

subsection.p: The condition \mathbf T'(t)\ne\mathbf 0 also matters.

example.title: A straight line has no preferred normal direction

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t,0). Then \mathbf T(t)=(1,0) for every t. Therefore \mathbf T'(t)=\mathbf 0. The curve is not turning, so there is no direction in which the tangent is changing.

Geometrically, the line has many perpendicular unit vectors, such as (0,1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(0,-1). But neither is chosen by the curve. The normal vector \mathbf N is only defined where the curve is actually turning.

subsection.p: When \kappa>0, we can write \boxed{\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N.} This is a compact way to read curvature and normal direction at once: \text{change of tangent per unit length}=\text{amount of turning}\times\text{direction of turning}.

subsection.title: Curvature in space
subsection.p: A space curve can bend without staying in one plane. The definition of curvature does not change: \kappa=\left\|\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}\right\|. The normal vector is still \mathbf N=\frac{d\mathbf T/ds}{\|d\mathbf T/ds\|} when \kappa>0.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t) be a C^2 regular curve in \mathbb R^3. Then \boxed{\kappa(t)=\frac{\|\mathbf r'(t)\times \mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.}

proof.p:
Let \sigma(t)=\|\mathbf r'(t)\| be the speed. Then \mathbf r'(t)=\sigma(t)\mathbf T(t). Differentiate: \mathbf r''(t)=\sigma'(t)\mathbf T(t)+\sigma(t)\mathbf T'(t). Now take the cross product with \mathbf r'(t)=\sigma\mathbf T:
\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'' \amp= \sigma\mathbf T\times\bigl(\sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma\mathbf T'\bigr) \amp= \sigma\sigma'(\mathbf T\times\mathbf T)+\sigma^2(\mathbf T\times\mathbf T') \amp= \sigma^2(\mathbf T\times\mathbf T').
Since \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf T=1, we have \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf T'=0. Thus \mathbf T and \mathbf T' are perpendicular, and \|\mathbf T\|=1. Hence \|\mathbf T\times\mathbf T'\|=\|\mathbf T'\|. Therefore \|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|=\sigma^2\|\mathbf T'\|. But \kappa=\frac{\|\mathbf T'\|}{\|\mathbf r'\|}=\frac{\|\mathbf T'\|}{\sigma}. So \|\mathbf T'\|=\kappa\sigma. Substitute: \|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|=\sigma^2(\kappa\sigma)=\kappa\sigma^3. Therefore \kappa=\frac{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|}{\|\mathbf r'\|^3}.

subsection.p: The hypothesis \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf 0 again appears in the denominator. A stopped particle has no unit tangent, so it has no curvature as a parametrized motion at that instant.

example.title: Curvature of a helix

statement.p:
Let \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t). Then \mathbf r'(t)=(-2\sin t,2\cos t,1), and \mathbf r''(t)=(-2\cos t,-2\sin t,0). The speed is \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t+1}=\sqrt5. Compute the cross product:
\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t) \amp= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i \amp \mathbf j \amp \mathbf k\\ -2\sin t \amp 2\cos t \amp 1\\ -2\cos t \amp -2\sin t \amp 0 \end{vmatrix} \amp= (2\sin t,\;-2\cos t,\;4).
Its length is \sqrt{4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t+16}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5. Therefore \kappa(t)=\frac{2\sqrt5}{(\sqrt5)^3}=\frac{2}{5}. The curvature is constant. A circular helix bends the same amount at every point.

subsection.p: A circular helix bends the same amount at every point, but it also twists through space instead of remaining in one fixed plane. Curvature does not measure this second effect. introduces the osculating plane and the torsion that measures its rotation.

subsection.title: Tangential and normal components of acceleration
subsection.p: Velocity can change in two different ways.
It can change length. That means the object speeds up or slows down.
It can change direction. That means the object turns.
Acceleration sees both.
When curvature is zero, the principal normal is undefined, but the normal acceleration vector is zero and \mathbf a=\sigma'\mathbf T. The scalar formula a_N=\kappa\sigma^2 still gives zero.

exercise.title: Why does acceleration split in two?

statement.p: Acceleration breaks neatly into a tangential part a_T\mathbf T and a normal part a_N\mathbf N. Explain conceptually why velocity can only change in these two ways, and which physical effect each part is responsible for.

hint.p: Velocity \mathbf r'=\sigma\mathbf T carries two pieces of information: a length \sigma (speed) and a direction \mathbf T. When you differentiate a product, what change in each factor does each resulting term record?

subsection.p: The first term, \sigma'(t)\mathbf T(t), is tangential acceleration. It changes speed.
The second term, \kappa(t)\sigma(t)^2\mathbf N(t), is normal acceleration. It changes direction.
The formula says something physical. Turning at high speed requires large normal acceleration because the speed is squared: a_N=\kappa\sigma^2. This is why taking a sharp curve too fast is dangerous.

example.title: A car on a circular track

statement.p: A car moves around a circular track of radius 30 meters at constant speed 12\text{ m/s}. The curvature of the track is \kappa=\frac{1}{30}. Because the speed is constant, a_T=0. The normal acceleration is a_N=\kappa\sigma^2=\frac{1}{30}(12)^2=\frac{144}{30}=4.8. So the acceleration has magnitude 4.8\text{ m/s}^2 and points inward, toward the center of the track.
The car is not speeding up, but it is accelerating because its direction is changing.

example.title: Acceleration on a helix

statement.p: For \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t), we found \sigma=\sqrt5,\qquad\kappa=\frac25. The speed is constant, so a_T=\sigma'=0. The normal acceleration is a_N=\kappa\sigma^2=\frac25\cdot5=2. Directly, \mathbf r''(t)=(-2\cos t,-2\sin t,0), whose length is 2. So all of the acceleration is normal. The moving point is not speeding up or slowing down; it is being pulled toward the axis of the helix.

subsection.p: There is also a useful dot-product formula for the tangential component. Since \mathbf v=\sigma\mathbf T, we have \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=\sigma\mathbf T\cdot(a_T\mathbf T+a_N\mathbf N). Because \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf T=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbf T\cdot\mathbf N=0, this gives \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=\sigma a_T. Therefore \boxed{a_T=\frac{\mathbf r'(t)\cdot\mathbf r''(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}.} In space, the normal component can be computed from \boxed{a_N=\frac{\|\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}.} This follows from a_N=\kappa\sigma^2 and \kappa=\frac{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|}{\|\mathbf r'\|^3}.

example.title: A path with both kinds of acceleration

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2),\qquad t>0. Then \mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t),\qquad\mathbf r''(t)=(0,2). The speed is \sigma(t)=\sqrt{1+4t^2}. So a_T=\sigma'(t)=\frac{4t}{\sqrt{1+4t^2}}. The curvature of this parabola is \kappa(t)=\frac{2}{(1+4t^2)^{3/2}}. Thus a_N=\kappa\sigma^2=\frac{2}{(1+4t^2)^{3/2}}(1+4t^2)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+4t^2}}. The acceleration vector \mathbf r''(t)=(0,2) has a tangential part and a normal part. Part of it makes the point move faster; part of it bends the motion upward.

subsection.p: This decomposition is useful because it separates two effects that are mixed together inside the raw vector \mathbf a=\mathbf r''.

Curvature tells us how a path bends, and the tangential-normal decomposition tells us how motion responds to that bending. A space curve can still change in a way that curvature does not record: the plane in which the curve is bending can rotate as the point moves. completes the moving frame and measures this twisting.

section.title: Torsion and the Frenet frame
section.p: measured how strongly a curve bends. A curve in space can do one more thing: it can twist out of the plane in which it is bending.

To see what that means, compare two curves. The circle given by the vector function
\mathbf c(t) = \left(\frac52\cos t,\frac52\sin t,0\right)
has curvature \kappa=\frac{1}{5/2}=\frac25. The helix from , \mathbf h(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t), also has curvature \kappa=\frac25. The two curves bend at the same rate, and yet they are not the same shape. The circle stays inside one plane. The helix does not lie in any plane at all.

Here is one way to visualize the difference. Take a piece of wire and bend it. If you keep bending it the same way, the wire stays flat: first an arc, then a circle. To make a coil spring instead, you must keep rotating the plane of bending about the wire. That rotation is what we call twisting, and curvature does not record it. So a curve in space raises two questions rather than one.

li.p: How fast is the curve bending? Curvature answers this.
How fast is the plane of bending turning? Torsion will answer this.

section.p: Curvature came from the turning of \mathbf T. To measure the second effect, we first complete \mathbf T and \mathbf N to a moving frame of three perpendicular unit vectors.

subsection.title: The binormal and the osculating plane
subsection.p: For the rest of this section, let \mathbf r(s) be a C^3 curve (with three continuous derivatives) in \mathbb R^3, parametrized by arc length, and suppose \kappa(s)>0. Then the unit tangent and unit normal vectors are defined, and \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N. The vectors \mathbf T and \mathbf N are perpendicular unit vectors. Their cross product gives a third perpendicular unit vector: \boxed{\mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N.}

definition.title: Binormal, osculating plane, and Frenet frame

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(s) be a regular space curve with \kappa(s)>0.
The unit binormal vector is \boxed{\mathbf B(s)=\mathbf T(s)\times\mathbf N(s).}
The plane through \mathbf r(s) spanned by \mathbf T(s) and \mathbf N(s) is called the osculating plane. Its normal vector is \mathbf B(s).

subsection.p: The word osculating comes from the Latin for kissing. The tangent line touches the curve and matches its direction. The osculating plane does a little better: it holds the tangent direction and also the direction in which the tangent is turning. Of all planes through the point, it is the one that hugs the curve most closely.

Because \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N, the Frenet frame is right-handed. Its cross products follow the same cyclic pattern as \mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k:
\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\mathbf B, \qquad \mathbf N\times\mathbf B=\mathbf T, \qquad \mathbf B\times\mathbf T=\mathbf N.
Reversing the order reverses the sign. For example, \mathbf T\times\mathbf B=-\mathbf N. That sign will matter when we derive the formulas for the moving frame.

exercise.title: Why is the binormal perpendicular to the osculating plane?

statement.p: Explain why \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N is perpendicular to the osculating plane. Why does the order \mathbf T\times\mathbf N, rather than \mathbf N\times\mathbf T, matter?

hint.p: The osculating plane is spanned by \mathbf T and \mathbf N. Recall what the cross product does and how reversing its factors changes its sign.

figure.caption: The Frenet frame moves with the helix. The vectors \mathbf T and \mathbf N span the osculating plane, while \mathbf B is perpendicular to it. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The frame is attached to the curve, not to the fixed coordinate axes, so all three vectors may turn as the point moves. Curvature already measures how fast \mathbf T turns. Since \mathbf B is the normal vector of the osculating plane, watching \mathbf B turn is the same as watching that plane turn. That is the measurement we want next.

subsection.title: Torsion: how the osculating plane turns
subsection.p: The derivative of \mathbf B has very little freedom. Two short computations show that only one direction is left for it.
First, \mathbf B\cdot\mathbf B=1. Differentiating with respect to arc length gives 2\mathbf B\cdot\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=0. Thus \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\perp\mathbf B.

Also, \mathbf B\cdot\mathbf T=0. Differentiate:
\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\cdot\mathbf T + \mathbf B\cdot\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds} =0.
Since \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N and \mathbf B\cdot\mathbf N=0, we get \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\cdot\mathbf T=0. Therefore d\mathbf B/ds is perpendicular to both \mathbf T and \mathbf B. The only direction left in the frame is \mathbf N, so d\mathbf B/ds must be a scalar multiple of \mathbf N.
The scalar multiple is written as -\tau rather than \tau. The minus sign is only a convention, chosen so that a right-handed helix rising along the z-axis has positive torsion.

Curvature is nonnegative because it is defined as a length. Torsion is signed. Its magnitude is \boxed{|\tau|=\left\|\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\right\|.} Thus |\tau| measures how quickly the binormal, and therefore the osculating plane, turns per unit distance traveled. The sign tells us which way the curve twists: a right-handed twist gives \tau>0, and a left-handed twist gives \tau<0.
Like curvature, torsion has units \frac{1}{\text{length}}. A plane curve has a fixed binormal vector, so its torsion is zero wherever its Frenet frame is defined.

statement.p: Curvature is always nonnegative, while torsion may be positive or negative. Explain what is different about the two definitions and what geometric information the sign of torsion records.

hint.p: Curvature is defined using a norm. Torsion is defined as a signed coefficient in d\mathbf B/ds=-\tau\mathbf N.

subsection.title: The Frenet–Serret formulas
subsection.p: We now know how two of the three frame vectors change: \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N, and \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=-\tau\mathbf N. The derivative of \mathbf N is then forced on us by these two formulas.
The three equations form one system.
The formulas separate two geometric effects.
The coefficient \kappa couples \mathbf T and \mathbf N. It records bending inside the osculating plane.
The coefficient \tau couples \mathbf N and \mathbf B. It records twisting of the osculating plane through space.

Both coefficients describe rotation, but about different axes. The \kappa term turns the frame about \mathbf B, which moves \mathbf T and \mathbf N within the osculating plane and leaves the plane where it is. The \tau term turns the frame about \mathbf T, which leaves the tangent alone and tips the plane. Indeed d\mathbf B/ds=-\tau\mathbf N is the same as \tau\,\mathbf T\times\mathbf B, which is exactly how a vector rotating about \mathbf T at rate \tau behaves.

subsection.title: Computing the frame and torsion from any parameter
subsection.p: Arc length gives the cleanest definitions, but a curve usually arrives written as \mathbf r(t) for some other parameter. We now rewrite the definitions as formulas we can apply directly to \mathbf r(t), without changing parameter first.

Let \sigma(t)=\|\mathbf r'(t)\| be the speed. Since \mathbf r'(t)=\sigma\mathbf T, we have
\mathbf r''(t) \amp= \sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma\frac{d\mathbf T}{dt}
\amp= \sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma^2\kappa\mathbf N.
Taking the cross product with \mathbf r'=\sigma\mathbf T gives
\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'' \amp= \sigma\mathbf T \times \bigl(\sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma^2\kappa\mathbf N\bigr)
\amp= \sigma^3\kappa\mathbf B.
When \kappa>0, this gives the binormal directly:
\boxed{ \mathbf B(t) = \frac{\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)} {\|\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\|}. }
Then \boxed{\mathbf N(t)=\mathbf B(t)\times\mathbf T(t).} The order matters. The cross product \mathbf T\times\mathbf B would give -\mathbf N.
Torsion has an equally compact formula.

proof.p:
We already found \mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''=\sigma^3\kappa\mathbf B. Also, \mathbf r''=\sigma'\mathbf T+\sigma^2\kappa\mathbf N. Differentiate this expression with respect to t. Most resulting terms lie in the span of \mathbf T and \mathbf N. The only term that can have a binormal component comes from differentiating \mathbf N: \sigma^2\kappa\frac{d\mathbf N}{dt}. By the chain rule and the Frenet–Serret formula,
\frac{d\mathbf N}{dt} \amp= \frac{d\mathbf N}{ds}\frac{ds}{dt}
\amp= \bigl(-\kappa\mathbf T+\tau\mathbf B\bigr)\sigma.
Therefore the binormal component of \mathbf r''' is \sigma^3\kappa\tau\mathbf B. Taking the dot product with \mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''=\sigma^3\kappa\mathbf B gives (\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''=\sigma^6\kappa^2\tau. On the other hand, \|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2=\sigma^6\kappa^2. Dividing gives the formula for \tau.

subsection.p: The numerator is a scalar triple product, and a scalar triple product is a signed volume. This is where the sign of the torsion comes from: the three derivative vectors sit in space with a handedness, and reversing that handedness reverses the sign of \tau.

remark.title: A practical computation order
remark.p:
For a C^3 curve with \mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\ne\mathbf 0, compute
\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \mathbf T \amp= \frac{\mathbf r'}{\|\mathbf r'\|},\\ \mathbf B \amp= \frac{\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''} {\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|},\\ \mathbf N \amp= \mathbf B\times\mathbf T,\\ \kappa \amp= \frac{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|} {\|\mathbf r'\|^3},\\ \tau \amp= \frac{(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''} {\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2}. \end{aligned} }

subsection.title: The circular helix revisited
subsection.p: We can now work out the whole frame, together with both curvature and torsion, for the helix from .

example.title: The Frenet frame and torsion of a helix

statement.p:
Let \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t). We already know that \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt5 and \kappa=\frac25. The first three derivatives are \mathbf r'(t)=(-2\sin t,2\cos t,1), \mathbf r''(t)=(-2\cos t,-2\sin t,0), and \mathbf r'''(t)=(2\sin t,-2\cos t,0). Also, \mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)=(2\sin t,-2\cos t,4). The numerator in the torsion formula is
(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r''' \amp= (2\sin t,-2\cos t,4) \cdot (2\sin t,-2\cos t,0)
\amp= 4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t
\amp= 4.
The denominator is
\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2 \amp= 4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t+16
\amp= 20.
Therefore \boxed{\tau=\frac4{20}=\frac15.}

We can check the torsion sign directly. Differentiate \mathbf B:
\frac{d\mathbf B}{dt} = \frac1{\sqrt5}(\cos t,\sin t,0).
Since \frac{ds}{dt}=\sqrt5, we have
\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds} \amp= \frac{d\mathbf B/dt}{ds/dt}
\amp= \frac15(\cos t,\sin t,0)
\amp= -\frac15\mathbf N.
Thus the defining equation \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=-\tau\mathbf N indeed gives \tau=\frac15.

The circle of radius 5/2 and this helix have the same curvature, \kappa=\frac25, but their torsions are different:
\text{circle:}\amp\qquad \tau=0, \text{helix:}\amp\qquad \tau=\frac15.
Curvature separates straightness from bending. Torsion separates planar bending from spatial twisting.

subsection.p:
More generally, the circular helix
\mathbf r(t)=(a\cos t,a\sin t,bt), \qquad a>0,
has
\boxed{ \kappa=\frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \qquad \tau=\frac{b}{a^2+b^2}. }
Changing the sign of b reverses the handedness of the helix. This reverses the sign of \tau and leaves \kappa unchanged.

subsection.title: Zero torsion and plane curves
subsection.p: This brings us back to the wire. The circle had zero torsion and stayed flat, while the helix had positive torsion and climbed out of every plane. That was not a coincidence. Whenever the Frenet frame is defined, zero torsion is exactly the condition for a curve to be flat.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(s) be a C^3 regular curve on a connected interval, parametrized by arc length, and suppose \kappa(s)>0 throughout the interval. Then the image of \mathbf r lies in a fixed plane if and only if \tau(s)=0 throughout the interval.

proof.p: Suppose first that the curve lies in a fixed plane. Let \mathbf b be a fixed unit normal to that plane. Both \mathbf T and \mathbf N lie in the plane, so \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N is either \mathbf b or -\mathbf b. Because \mathbf B varies continuously on a connected interval, it cannot jump from one choice to the other. Thus \mathbf B is constant. Hence \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=\mathbf 0, so \tau=0.

Conversely, suppose \tau=0. The third Frenet–Serret formula gives \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=\mathbf 0. Therefore \mathbf B is a fixed vector. Since \frac{d\mathbf r}{ds}=\mathbf T and \mathbf T\cdot\mathbf B=0, we have
\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(\mathbf r(s)\cdot\mathbf B\bigr) \amp= \mathbf T(s)\cdot\mathbf B
\amp= 0.
Thus \mathbf r(s)\cdot\mathbf B=c for some constant c. This is the equation of one fixed plane with normal \mathbf B. The entire curve lies in that plane.

subsection.p: The assumption \kappa>0 is doing real work in this theorem, as the next example shows.

example.title: Why nonzero curvature is required

statement.p: Consider the straight line \mathbf r(s)=(s,0,0). It is certainly planar, and its curvature is \kappa=0. But \frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\mathbf 0, so the curve does not choose a principal normal \mathbf N. Without \mathbf N, the binormal \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N and the torsion are not defined by the Frenet construction.
The theorem assumes \kappa>0 not because a straight line fails to be planar, but because the Frenet frame itself needs a direction in which the tangent is turning.

subsection.p:
Curvature and torsion now give two independent rates:
\text{curvature }\kappa = \text{bending per unit length},
\text{torsion }\tau = \text{signed twisting per unit length}.
The Frenet–Serret equations show how these two functions control the motion of the whole frame. A theorem we will not prove here says more: when \kappa>0, the two functions \kappa(s) and \tau(s) determine the curve completely, up to a translation and a rotation. Curvature and torsion together are a fingerprint of the shape.

aside.title: Looking ahead
aside.p: The Frenet frame moves because the curve bends and twists. uses a different moving frame, the polar vectors \mathbf e_r and \mathbf e_\theta, which move because the coordinate directions themselves change. In both cases the lesson is the same: when a basis moves, its derivatives carry geometric information.

section.title: Motion in special coordinate systems
section.p: described a moving orthonormal frame (\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B) attached to a space curve. Curvature and torsion record how that frame turns as distance is traveled. Polar coordinates use a different moving frame, (\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta), whose directions rotate as the point moves.

Rectangular coordinates are not always the friendliest language. A boat tracked by radar is naturally described by distance and angle. A planet moving around the sun is naturally described by distance from the sun and angle swept around it. For such motions, polar coordinates do not merely shorten formulas. They reveal structure.

subsection.title: Velocity in polar coordinates
subsection.p: A rescue boat leaves a harbor at sunset. Its radar position is recorded by r(t)=4+t, \qquad \theta(t)=\frac{t}{2}, where r is measured in kilometers and t is measured in hours. The boat is moving outward because r'(t)=1. It is also turning counterclockwise because \theta'(t)=\frac12.
At time t, an increase in r moves the boat directly away from the harbor. An increase in \theta moves the boat sideways along a circle centered at the harbor.

At t=0, r=4. The radial speed is r'=1. The sideways speed is not just \theta'. An angular change of \theta' radians per hour along a circle of radius r gives tangential speed r\theta'=4\cdot\frac12=2. So at t=0, the velocity is made from two perpendicular pieces: \text{radial part } 1, \qquad \text{angular part } 2. The speed is therefore \sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt5.

At t=2, r=6. The radial speed is still 1, but the sideways speed is now r\theta'=6\cdot\frac12=3. So the speed is \sqrt{1^2+3^2}=\sqrt{10}. The angular rate stayed the same, but the boat was farther from the center, so the sideways motion became faster.
This example already contains the polar velocity formula.

statement.p: In the boat example, the velocity has a radial part pointing away from the harbor and a transverse part pointing along a circle. Without computing anything, explain in words why two different motions of the boat are needed to account for its velocity. What does each piece describe about how the boat is moving?

hint.p: Picture holding the angle fixed and only letting r grow, then holding r fixed and only letting \theta grow. Where does the boat go in each case, and how could it ever move in just one of these ways alone?

subsection.p: To write it cleanly, define two unit vectors that move with the point: \boxed{ \mathbf e_r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta), \qquad \mathbf e_\theta=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta). } The vector \mathbf e_r points outward from the origin. The vector \mathbf e_\theta points in the direction of increasing angle.

figure.caption: The unit vector \mathbf e_r points outward, and \mathbf e_\theta points in the direction of increasing angle.

subsection.p: The position vector is \mathbf R(t)=r(t)\mathbf e_r(t). Here \mathbf R is the actual position vector, while r(t) is the scalar distance from the origin.

As \theta changes, the polar unit vectors rotate. Differentiating \mathbf e_r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta) gives \frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt} = \theta'(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta) = \theta'\mathbf e_\theta. Similarly, \frac{d\mathbf e_\theta}{dt} = -\theta'\mathbf e_r.

Now differentiate the position:
\mathbf v \amp= \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(r\mathbf e_r\bigr) \amp= r'\mathbf e_r+r\frac{d\mathbf e_r}{dt} \amp= r'\mathbf e_r+r\theta'\mathbf e_\theta.

proof.p: The first formula follows from the product rule: \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(r\mathbf e_r\bigr) = r'\mathbf e_r+r\mathbf e_r'. Since \mathbf e_r'=\theta'\mathbf e_\theta, we get \mathbf v=r'\mathbf e_r+r\theta'\mathbf e_\theta. The vectors \mathbf e_r and \mathbf e_\theta are perpendicular unit vectors, so the length of the velocity is found by the Pythagorean theorem: \|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{(r')^2+(r\theta')^2}.

subsection.p: The hypotheses matter. We need r(t) and \theta(t) to be differentiable, and we need a polar description that behaves well. The origin is a special danger point.

example.title: The origin has no preferred angle

statement.p: The motion \mathbf R(t)=(0,0) for all t is perfectly still. Its velocity is \mathbf v(t)=\mathbf 0. But in polar coordinates this same motion can be written as r(t)=0, \qquad \theta(t)=t^2, or r(t)=0, \qquad \theta(t)=\sin\frac1t for t\ne0, or with almost any other angle function. The angle does not describe anything real when r=0.
So polar formulas must be used with care at the origin. A point at the origin has no well-defined radial direction and no well-defined angular direction.

subsection.p: There is a second warning. A geometric path may be smooth while a bad polar description is not.

example.title: A bad polar clock can create a fake problem

statement.p: The line motion \mathbf R(t)=(t,0) is smooth. Its velocity is \mathbf R'(t)=(1,0) for every t.

If we insist on r(t)\ge0, then one polar description is r(t)=|t|, \qquad \theta(t)= \begin{cases} \pi, \amp t<0,\\ 0, \amp t>0. \end{cases} At t=0, this polar description has a corner in r and a jump in \theta. The problem is not the original motion. The problem is the polar coordinate description at the origin.
Coordinates are tools. At their singular points, they can misbehave.

subsection.title: Acceleration in polar coordinates
subsection.p: Velocity in polar coordinates has two pieces: \mathbf v=r'\mathbf e_r+r\theta'\mathbf e_\theta. Acceleration comes from differentiating this formula. Because the basis vectors \mathbf e_r and \mathbf e_\theta rotate as the point moves, the result contains more than just r'' and \theta''.

Differentiate:
\mathbf a \amp= \frac{d}{dt}\left(r'\mathbf e_r+r\theta'\mathbf e_\theta\right) \amp= r''\mathbf e_r+r'\mathbf e_r' +(r'\theta'+r\theta'')\mathbf e_\theta +r\theta'\mathbf e_\theta'.
Use \mathbf e_r'=\theta'\mathbf e_\theta, \qquad \mathbf e_\theta'=-\theta'\mathbf e_r. Then
\mathbf a \amp= r''\mathbf e_r +r'\theta'\mathbf e_\theta +(r'\theta'+r\theta'')\mathbf e_\theta -r(\theta')^2\mathbf e_r \amp= \bigl(r''-r(\theta')^2\bigr)\mathbf e_r + \bigl(r\theta''+2r'\theta'\bigr)\mathbf e_\theta.

statement.p: Suppose \mathbf R(t)=r(t)\mathbf e_r(t) is a plane motion with r(t) and \theta(t) twice differentiable. Then \boxed{ \mathbf a(t) = \bigl(r''-r(\theta')^2\bigr)\mathbf e_r + \bigl(r\theta''+2r'\theta'\bigr)\mathbf e_\theta. }

subsection.p: The twice differentiable condition is not decoration. Acceleration is a second derivative. At an instant where the second derivative does not exist, this acceleration formula cannot be applied. A reversal by itself need not be a problem: a smooth motion can stop and reverse.

example.title: A corner in angle destroys velocity at the corner

statement.p: Let r(t)=1, \qquad \theta(t)=|t|. The position is \mathbf R(t)=(\cos|t|,\sin|t|). For t>0, the point moves counterclockwise on the unit circle. For t<0, it moves clockwise. At t=0, the point is (1,0), but the velocity from the left points downward while the velocity from the right points upward.
So \mathbf R'(0) does not exist. The formula for acceleration cannot be used at t=0. The hypothesis that r and \theta are differentiable is doing real work.

subsection.title: Circular motion and angular velocity
subsection.p: Circular motion is the cleanest polar motion. The radius is constant: r(t)=R. The angle changes: \theta=\theta(t). The angular velocity is \boxed{ \omega(t)=\theta'(t). }
From the polar velocity formula, \mathbf v=R\omega\,\mathbf e_\theta. So the speed is \boxed{ \|\mathbf v\|=R|\omega|. } A larger circle gives a larger speed for the same angular velocity.

The acceleration formula gives \boxed{ \mathbf a=-R\omega^2\mathbf e_r+R\omega'\mathbf e_\theta. } The radial term -R\omega^2\mathbf e_r points inward. The tangential term R\omega'\mathbf e_\theta appears only when the angular velocity changes.

statement.p: A rider on the wheel moves at constant speed, so \omega never changes. Yet the acceleration -R\omega^2\mathbf e_r is not zero. How can something accelerate while its speed stays the same? What is actually changing from one instant to the next?

hint.p: Acceleration measures the change in the velocity vector, not just in the speed. Watch the direction of \mathbf e_\theta as the rider goes around: does the velocity vector ever stop turning?

example.title: A spinning observation wheel

statement.p: Since \omega is constant, \omega'=0. So the acceleration is purely inward: \mathbf a=-R\omega^2\mathbf e_r. Its magnitude is R\omega^2 = 20\left(\frac{\pi}{30}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{45}. The rider is not speeding up, but the rider is accelerating because the direction of motion is continuously changing.

subsection.p: This agrees with . A circle of radius R has curvature \kappa=\frac1R. The speed is \sigma=R|\omega|. So the normal acceleration is a_N=\kappa\sigma^2 = \frac1R(R^2\omega^2) = R\omega^2. The same fact has appeared twice: once from curvature, and once from polar coordinates.

example.title: Circular motion that speeds up
