statement.p: Let r(t)=3, \qquad \theta(t)=t^2. Then \omega(t)=2t, \qquad \omega'(t)=2. The velocity is \mathbf v=3(2t)\mathbf e_\theta=6t\mathbf e_\theta. The acceleration is \mathbf a = -3(2t)^2\mathbf e_r+3(2)\mathbf e_\theta = -12t^2\mathbf e_r+6\mathbf e_\theta. For t\ge0, the inward part grows as t^2, because the speed is increasing. The tangential part is constant, because the angular velocity increases at a constant rate.

subsection.title: Planetary motion as a guiding example
subsection.p: Put the sun at the origin. Suppose the planet has position \mathbf R(t)=r(t)\mathbf e_r. Gravity pulls along the line from the planet to the sun. That means the acceleration has no \mathbf e_\theta component. In polar coordinates, \mathbf a = \bigl(r''-r(\theta')^2\bigr)\mathbf e_r + \bigl(r\theta''+2r'\theta'\bigr)\mathbf e_\theta. So a central force gives r\theta''+2r'\theta'=0. Multiply by r: r^2\theta''+2rr'\theta'=0. But the left side is the derivative of r^2\theta': indeed, \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(r^2\theta'\bigr) = 2rr'\theta'+r^2\theta''. Therefore \boxed{ r^2\theta'=h } for some constant h.
This quantity is the angular momentum per unit mass. It is also the key to a beautiful area fact.

subsection.title: The area swept out by a radius vector
subsection.p: Imagine the planet at two nearby times. The radius vector from the sun to the planet sweeps out a thin wedge. For a small angle change \Delta\theta, the area is approximately \frac12 r^2\Delta\theta. So the rate at which area is swept should be \frac12 r^2\theta'. The calculation above says this rate is constant for central-force motion.

statement.p: Under a central force the quantity r^2\theta' stays constant, so the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times. When the planet swings close to the sun and r shrinks, what must \theta' do to keep the swept-area rate \tfrac12 r^2\theta' unchanged? Use that to explain why a nearby planet races along and a distant one dawdles.

hint.p: Think of \tfrac12 r^2\theta' as a fixed budget. If r drops, the only way to keep the product the same is for \theta' to compensate. Which direction must it move?

figure.caption: A radius vector sweeps out area as the angle changes.

statement.p: For a plane motion \mathbf R(t)=(x(t),y(t)), the signed area swept out by the radius vector from time a to time b is \boxed{ A=\frac12\int_a^b \bigl(x(t)y'(t)-y(t)x'(t)\bigr)\,dt. } In polar coordinates this becomes \boxed{ A=\frac12\int_a^b r(t)^2\theta'(t)\,dt. }

subsection.p: Here is the polar calculation. If x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta, then x'=r'\cos\theta-r\theta'\sin\theta,\qquad y'=r'\sin\theta+r\theta'\cos\theta. Expanding and canceling the rr' terms gives xy'-yx'=r^2\theta'. Substitution into the single-variable integral above proves the polar formula.

This is our first clear appearance of a 1-form that measures an area swept along a curve: \boxed{ \omega_A=\frac12(x\,dy-y\,dx). } At a fixed point (x,y), this is a linear measurement of a displacement vector (a,b), with value (xb-ya)/2, using the coordinate measurements from Chapter 2. Evaluating it on the velocity gives (xy'-yx')/2. This optional notation anticipates line integrals; the computations here use the displayed ordinary single-variable integrals.

theorem.title: Kepler's second law for central acceleration

statement.p: Suppose a twice continuously differentiable plane motion, with twice continuously differentiable polar coordinates, satisfies r(t)>0 and has acceleration always parallel to \mathbf e_r. Then r(t)^2\theta'(t) is constant. Therefore the signed area swept out per unit time, \boxed{ \frac{dA}{dt}=\frac12r(t)^2\theta'(t), } is constant.
In words: equal time intervals sweep out equal signed areas.

proof.p: If the acceleration is always radial, then its \mathbf e_\theta-component is zero: r\theta''+2r'\theta'=0. Since r>0, multiply by r: r^2\theta''+2rr'\theta'=0. But \frac{d}{dt}(r^2\theta') = r^2\theta''+2rr'\theta'. So \frac{d}{dt}(r^2\theta')=0. Thus r^2\theta' is constant. Since \frac{dA}{dt}=\frac12r^2\theta', the swept area rate is also constant.

subsection.p: The condition that the acceleration be radial is essential.

example.title: Tangential acceleration breaks equal areas

statement.p: Let r(t)=1, \qquad \theta(t)=t^2. Then r^2\theta'=2t, which is not constant. The signed swept area rate is \frac{dA}{dt}=\frac12(2t)=t. The radius vector sweeps area faster as time passes.

The polar acceleration has \mathbf e_\theta-component r\theta''+2r'\theta'=1\cdot2+0=2. So the acceleration is not purely radial. There is tangential acceleration, and equal areas in equal times fail.

subsection.p: There is also a warning about the word signed.

example.title: Signed swept area can cancel

statement.p: Let r(t)=1, \qquad \theta(t)=\sin t, \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then \theta'(t)=\cos t. The signed swept area is A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\cos t\,dt=0. But the radius vector did move. It swept forward and then backward, and the signed areas canceled.

So the formula \frac12\int r^2\theta'\,dt measures signed swept area. If a ray backtracks, total swept area counted with repetitions is obtained by integrating the absolute value of the area rate. This need not equal the area of the union of the swept regions, which counts overlapping regions only once.

subsection.p: Special coordinates have now done two things for us. They shortened computations, and they exposed hidden quantities: angular velocity, inward acceleration, and swept area. The chapter has one more job: gather the whole toolbox and see how it works in larger motion problems, from projectiles with air resistance to the curvature of roads.

introduction.p: Chapter 5 began with a moving point \mathbf r(t). From that one object came velocity, acceleration, speed, arc length, curvature, normal direction, osculating plane, binormal, Frenet frame, torsion, polar motion, angular velocity, and swept area. The chapter studies both how a curve bends and how it twists. The point moved through a curve, but the calculus happened through one variable: time.

subsection.title: The formula map
subsection.p: Here are the main tools of the chapter. Use continuous first derivatives for the length formula, a nonzero velocity for the unit tangent, continuous second derivatives for curvature, and positive curvature wherever the principal normal is used. The Frenet and torsion formulas additionally require three continuous derivatives.

table.title: The main formulas of Chapter 5

cell.m: \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N=\dfrac{\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''}{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|}

subsection.p: The formulas are less separate than they look. The speed \sigma is the bridge from time to distance: ds=\sigma\,dt. Curvature measures bending per unit length: \kappa=\left\|\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}\right\|. Torsion measures signed twisting per unit length: \tau=-\frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}\cdot\mathbf N. The Frenet frame (\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B) is attached to the curve. Polar coordinates use a different moving frame, (\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\theta), whose directions rotate with the coordinates rather than with the bending of the path. The swept-area form \frac12(x\,dy-y\,dx) quietly points toward the next big subject: integrating forms along paths.

subsection.title: A complete review example
subsection.p: Consider the helix \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t,4t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. This is one turn around a cylinder of radius 3, rising 8\pi units in height.
First, \mathbf r'(t)=(-3\sin t,3\cos t,4), so the speed is \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{9\sin^2t+9\cos^2t+16}=5. The length of one turn is L=\int_0^{2\pi}5\,dt=10\pi.

The unit tangent vector is \mathbf T(t)=\frac15(-3\sin t,3\cos t,4). Since the speed is constant, the tangential acceleration is a_T=0. The acceleration is \mathbf r''(t)=(-3\cos t,-3\sin t,0). Its length is \|\mathbf r''(t)\|=3. Because the speed is constant, all acceleration is normal, so a_N=3.

Now compute curvature: \mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)=(12\sin t,-12\cos t,9). Thus \|\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\|=\sqrt{144\sin^2t+144\cos^2t+81}=15. Therefore \kappa(t)=\frac{15}{5^3}=\frac{3}{25}. This agrees with a_N=\kappa\sigma^2, because \frac{3}{25}\cdot 25=3.

The unit tangent is already in hand. The binormal is the unit vector in the direction of \mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'':
\mathbf B(t) = \frac1{15}(12\sin t,-12\cos t,9) = \left(\frac45\sin t,-\frac45\cos t,\frac35\right).
Then
\mathbf N(t) = \mathbf B(t)\times\mathbf T(t) = (-\cos t,-\sin t,0).

To obtain torsion, differentiate once more: \mathbf r'''(t)=(3\sin t,-3\cos t,0). The numerator of the torsion formula is (\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''=36, and the denominator is \|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2=225. Therefore \boxed{\tau=\frac{36}{225}=\frac4{25}.}

This 3-4-5 helix has constant \kappa=\frac3{25},\qquad\tau=\frac4{25}. The same integers that made the speed equal to 5 now reappear in the curvature and torsion. The helix has constant speed, constant curvature, and constant torsion. It bends the same amount at every point, and it twists the same amount at every point.

subsection.title: Skill summary
subsection.p: By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to do the following.

li.p: Read a vector-valued function as a moving point: \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)).
Differentiate and integrate component by component: \mathbf r'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t),z'(t)), and \int_a^b \mathbf v(t)\,dt=\left(\int_a^b v_1(t)\,dt,\int_a^b v_2(t)\,dt,\int_a^b v_3(t)\,dt\right).
Find tangent lines: \mathbf L(s)=\mathbf r(a)+s\mathbf r'(a), when \mathbf r'(a)\ne\mathbf 0.
Compute distance traveled: L=\int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.
Reparametrize simple curves by arc length when the speed never vanishes.
Compute the unit tangent vector: \mathbf T=\frac{\mathbf r'}{\|\mathbf r'\|}.

Compute the Frenet frame (\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B) of a space curve with positive curvature, using
\mathbf T=\frac{\mathbf r'}{\|\mathbf r'\|}, \qquad \mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''}{\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|}, \qquad \mathbf N=\mathbf B\times\mathbf T.
Identify the osculating plane as the plane through the point spanned by \mathbf T and \mathbf N, with normal \mathbf B.

Compute torsion from the derivatives \mathbf r', \mathbf r'', and \mathbf r''':
\tau = \frac{(\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''} {\|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2}.

Use and interpret the Frenet–Serret formulas
\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}=\kappa\mathbf N, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf N}{ds}=-\kappa\mathbf T+\tau\mathbf B, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf B}{ds}=-\tau\mathbf N.
Recognize that, under the hypothesis \kappa>0 on a connected interval, zero torsion characterizes a planar curve.
Split acceleration into tangential and normal parts: \mathbf a=a_T\mathbf T+a_N\mathbf N,\qquad a_T=\sigma',\qquad a_N=\kappa\sigma^2.
Use polar coordinates for motion: \mathbf v=r'\mathbf e_r+r\theta'\mathbf e_\theta.
Recognize the central-force area law: \text{radial acceleration}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^2\theta'=\text{constant}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{dA}{dt}=\text{constant}.

exercises.title: Project: projectile motion with air resistance

introduction.p: Without air resistance, a projectile follows a parabola. With air resistance, it does not. But vector-valued functions still organize the motion.

Let the z-axis point upward. A projectile has position \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)) and velocity \mathbf v(t)=\mathbf r'(t). Assume m>0 and c>0. Assume gravity is -g\mathbf k and air resistance is proportional to velocity: -c\mathbf v. If the mass is m, Newton's law gives m\mathbf v'=-mg\mathbf k-c\mathbf v. Set k=\frac{c}{m}. Then \boxed{\mathbf v'=-k\mathbf v-g\mathbf k.}
This project can be explored in stages.

statement.p: Verify by differentiating that the formulas for v_x,v_y,v_z satisfy \mathbf v'=-k\mathbf v-g\mathbf k.
Verify by differentiating that the formulas for x,y,z satisfy \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf v(t).
Choose numerical values, such as g=9.8,\qquad k=0.15,\qquad \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1),\qquad \mathbf v(0)=(20,0,18). Find the time when z(t)=0. This equation usually needs numerical solving.
Compare the horizontal distance traveled with and without air resistance.
Plot the path (x(t),z(t)) in the vertical plane. The no-drag path is a parabola. The drag path is not.

conclusion.p: The point of the project is not that every motion has a simple formula. The point is that velocity and acceleration still give the right language, even when the path stops looking like the clean parabolas from single-variable calculus.

exercises.title: Project: curvature of a road or roller coaster track

introduction.p: A road designer cares about curvature because curvature controls normal acceleration. If a car moves with speed \sigma along a road of curvature \kappa, then a_N=\kappa\sigma^2. The speed is squared. This is why doubling speed is not twice as demanding on a curve; it is four times as demanding.

Suppose a road centerline in the plane is modeled by y=f(x). A convenient parametrization is \mathbf r(x)=(x,f(x)). Then \mathbf r'(x)=(1,f'(x)),\qquad \mathbf r''(x)=(0,f''(x)). The plane curvature formula becomes \boxed{\kappa(x)=\frac{|f''(x)|}{\left(1+(f'(x))^2\right)^{3/2}}.}
If the allowed normal acceleration is A, then a safe speed should satisfy \kappa\sigma^2\le A. So, where \kappa>0, \boxed{\sigma\le \sqrt{\frac{A}{\kappa}}.}

example.title: A simple speed estimate

statement.p: Suppose a road near its sharpest bend is modeled by y=0.005x^2, where x and y are measured in meters. Then f'(x)=0.01x,\qquad f''(x)=0.01. At x=0, \kappa(0)=0.01. If a comfortable normal acceleration is A=3\text{ m/s}^2, then \sigma\le \sqrt{\frac{3}{0.01}}=\sqrt{300}\approx17.3\text{ m/s}. The curvature calculation has turned a geometric bend into a speed recommendation.

introduction.p: A fuller project can use real data.

statement.p: Choose a road, bike path, running track, or roller coaster curve.
Model its centerline by a parametrized curve \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)) or \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)).
Compute or numerically estimate \kappa(t).
Find where the curvature is largest.
Use a_N=\kappa\sigma^2 to estimate a speed limit or a required banking design.
Explain the physical meaning of the largest curvature point. Is it a tight turn, a sudden vertical bend, or a combination?

If the track is genuinely three-dimensional, compute or numerically estimate torsion along the track. Identify where the osculating plane rotates most rapidly, and explain how this differs from finding the point of greatest curvature.

conclusion.p: This project is a good test of the whole chapter. The curve gives position. The first derivative gives direction and speed. The second derivative reveals turning. Curvature turns that geometry into a physical constraint.

statement.p: For \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,\ln t),\qquad t>0, find \mathbf v(t), \mathbf a(t), and the speed.
Find the tangent line to \mathbf r(t)=(e^t,\cos t,\sin t) at t=0.
Compute the length of \mathbf r(t)=(4\cos t,4\sin t,3t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.
Find the unit tangent vector for \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2) at t=1.
Compute the curvature of the parabola \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2) at t=0 and at t=1. Where is the curve bending more sharply?
Let \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t). Find the speed, the Frenet frame (\mathbf T,\mathbf N,\mathbf B), the curvature, the torsion, the tangential acceleration, and the normal acceleration.
For the polar motion r(t)=1+t,\qquad \theta(t)=t^2, find the radial and angular components of velocity.
For the polar motion r(t)=3,\qquad \theta(t)=t^3, find the radial and angular components of acceleration.
A point moves with r^2\theta'=12. Find the signed area swept out from t=1 to t=5.
Show that if a motion has constant speed, then its acceleration is perpendicular to its velocity.
A car moves at 15 m/s along a road with curvature 0.02. Find its normal acceleration.
A curve has speed 4 and curvature 0.5 at a certain instant. Find the normal component of acceleration at that instant.
Let \mathbf r(t)=(t^2,t^3). Show that \mathbf r'(0)=\mathbf 0. What does this say about the unit tangent formula at t=0?
Let \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t) for 0\le t\le4\pi. What is the displacement? What is the distance traveled?
For the circle \mathbf r(t)=(R\cos t,R\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, compute A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\bigl(x(t)y'(t)-y(t)x'(t)\bigr)\,dt. What area does this recover?
For \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,0), compute the torsion wherever the Frenet frame is defined. Explain why the answer agrees with the fact that the curve lies in the xy-plane.

For the circular helix
\mathbf r(t)=(a\cos t,a\sin t,bt),\qquad a>0,
derive
\kappa=\frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \qquad \tau=\frac{b}{a^2+b^2}.
What changes geometrically when b is replaced by -b?

conclusion.p: A regular space curve with positive curvature carries one tangent direction and a Frenet frame that records its bending and twisting. A surface is different. At a point on a sheet of paper, a hillside, or a sphere, there are many possible directions to move. The next chapter begins there: not with motion along one path, but with functions whose inputs fill a region. A single tangent direction and a single slope number will no longer be enough.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

introduction.p: A function may take several coordinates as inputs and return a number or a vector. Graphs and level sets help visualize such functions; limits and continuity require estimates that control all nearby inputs. We examine path tests, their limitations, and the hypotheses that make continuity useful.

section.title: Functions from \mathbb R^n to \mathbb R^m
section.p: followed a moving point: \mathbf r(t). The input was time, and the output was a vector. Now the input will often be a point in the plane or in space. A room temperature depends on where you stand. A pressure inside a tank depends on position. A wind velocity assigns an arrow to each point on a map.
The word function stays the same. What changes is the shape of the input and the shape of the output.

subsection.title: A temperature field on a room floor
subsection.p: Picture a rectangular room. The floor coordinates are measured in meters, with 0\le x\le 6, \qquad 0\le y\le 4. A heater sits near (2,1), and a cold window runs along the north wall. A simple model for the temperature on the floor is T(x,y)=20+\frac{6}{1+(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2}-\frac{y}{2}. The input is a point (x,y) on the floor. The output is one number, T(x,y), the temperature in degrees Celsius.
At the heater location, T(2,1)=20+\frac{6}{1+0+0}-\frac12=25.5. Near the far cold corner, T(5,4)=20+\frac{6}{1+9+9}-2=18+\frac{6}{19}\approx 18.32.
So T takes a point in the floor and returns a number. That is a scalar-valued function of two variables.

figure.caption: A scalar-valued function can assign one number, such as temperature, to each point in a region.

subsection.p: The same input region could also carry arrows. Suppose the air in the room slowly circulates around a ceiling fan. A simple two-dimensional model for the horizontal air velocity is \mathbf W(x,y)=\left(-\frac{y-2}{5},\frac{x-3}{5}\right). At the point (3,0), \mathbf W(3,0)=\left(\frac25,0\right), so the air is moving to the right. At the point (6,2), \mathbf W(6,2)=\left(0,\frac35\right), so the air is moving upward.
Now the input is still a point (x,y), but the output is a vector. This is a vector-valued function of two variables.

statement.p: A function F:D\subseteq \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^m assigns to each input \mathbf x\in D exactly one output F(\mathbf x)\in \mathbb R^m.
The set D is called the domain. The set of all possible outputs is called the range.

subsection.p: If m=1, the output is a number. We call the function scalar-valued. If m>1, the output is a vector. We call the function vector-valued.

statement.p: A scalar-valued function on a region in the plane or in space is often called a scalar field.
A vector-valued function on a region in the plane or in space is often called a vector field.

subsection.p: A temperature field is a scalar field. A wind field is a vector field. Later, line integrals and surface integrals will live inside this language.

subsection.title: Scalar-valued and vector-valued functions
subsection.p: Here are several common shapes of functions.

table.title: Common shapes of functions of one and several variables.

subsection.p: The notation F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m records the actual domain D, which may be a smaller region of input space. Writing simply F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m specifies all of \mathbb R^n as the domain. A formula and a model may have different domains, so state the restriction when it matters.

For example, the temperature model above is not meant for all of \mathbb R^2. It is meant for the rectangle D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 6,\ 0\le y\le 4\}. Outside the room, the formula may still produce a number, but the model no longer describes the room.

example.title: A vector-valued function from

statement.p: The helix \mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t) is a function \mathbf r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3. It has one input and three output components. It is vector-valued, but it is not a function of several variables. The input is still one-dimensional.

example.title: A parametrized surface

statement.p: A circular cylinder of radius 2 can be parametrized by \mathbf s(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z). Here \mathbf s:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3. The input has two variables, \theta and z. The output is a point in space.
If we restrict 0\le \theta\le 2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le 5, then the domain is a rectangle in the (\theta,z)-plane, and the image is the side of a cylinder of height 5.

subsection.p: The same notation covers scalar fields, vector fields, motion, and parametrized surfaces. The input dimension tells us how many independent variables we choose. The output dimension tells us what kind of object the function returns.

statement.p: Two functions can both take a point of the plane as input, yet feel completely different. What single feature of the output tells you whether a function is a scalar field or a vector field, and why does it matter that the output of a vector field carries more than one number?

hint.p: Look at m in F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m. Ask what you would draw at a single point in each case: a temperature reading, or an arrow with a direction.

subsection.title: Domains in the plane and in space
subsection.p: Sometimes a domain comes from a physical situation. Sometimes it comes from the formula itself.

example.title: A dome over a circular floor

statement.p: A glass dome over a circular courtyard has height h(x,y)=\sqrt{16-x^2-y^2}. The square root requires 16-x^2-y^2\ge 0. Therefore x^2+y^2\le 16. The natural domain is the disk D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le 16\}. The formula describes the upper half of a sphere of radius 4.

example.title: A formula with a missing plane

statement.p: Let g(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{z-y}. The denominator cannot be zero, so z-y\ne0. The domain is D=\{(x,y,z):z\ne y\}. This is all of space except the plane z=y.

example.title: A logarithm in space

statement.p: Let q(x,y,z)=\ln(8-z). The logarithm requires 8-z>0, so z<8. The domain is the open half-space below the plane z=8: D=\{(x,y,z):z<8\}.

example.title: A swirling field with a missing point

statement.p: The vector field \mathbf V(x,y)=\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}(-y,x) is defined whenever x^2+y^2\ne0. So its domain is \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. The origin is missing. This small hole will matter later: fields defined on regions with holes can behave in surprising ways.

subsection.p: The word domain is therefore not a decoration. It is part of the function. Changing the domain can change the meaning of the problem.

statement.p: Suppose two friends both write down the rule z\mapsto z, but one is thinking of a function on the line and the other of a function on space. Why can the dimension of the domain change the meaning of a function just as much as the rule itself does?

hint.p: Think about how many independent variables you are free to vary, and what region the inputs sweep out. The same algebraic expression can live over a line, a plane, or all of space.

subsection.title: Examples from temperature, pressure, cost, and motion
subsection.p: A function of several variables often begins as a story before it becomes a formula.

example.title: Pressure in a tank

statement.p: Suppose z measures height in meters, and pressure decreases linearly as height increases: p(x,y,z)=120-3z. This is a scalar field in space. It does not depend on x or y, only on height. All points with the same z-coordinate have the same pressure.

example.title: A cost function with two inputs

statement.p: A bakery makes two kinds of loaves. Let u be the number of sourdough loaves and v the number of rye loaves made in one day. A simplified cost model is C(u,v)=400+3u+4v+0.01uv. The term 400 is a fixed daily cost. The terms 3u and 4v are direct production costs. The mixed term 0.01uv models the extra scheduling cost of producing both types in the same day.
The physical domain is u\ge0,\qquad v\ge0. Strictly speaking, u and v should be whole numbers. Calculus treats them as continuous variables because that approximation lets us study rates of change.

example.title: A deformation of the plane

statement.p: A flexible sheet is pulled so that each point (x,y) moves to F(x,y)=(x+0.2y,\ y). This is a vector-valued function F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2. It shears the plane: points higher up move farther to the right.

This example is also a linear transformation, so it belongs to . The new point is that transformations are functions too. They take points or vectors as inputs and return points or vectors as outputs.

subsection.title: Functions as fields of values
subsection.p: A scalar field covers a region with numbers. A vector field covers a region with arrows.

statement.p: A formula like \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x) already gives every value exactly. So why is it still useful to imagine the function as a whole field of values spread across its domain, rather than as one input-output computation at a time?

hint.p: A single value tells you about one point. A field lets you see how the values change from place to place, so patterns like swirling or flowing become visible at a glance.

subsection.p: For example, the vector field \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x) assigns an arrow to every point in the plane. At (1,0), \mathbf W(1,0)=(0,1). At (0,1), \mathbf W(0,1)=(-1,0). The arrows circulate counterclockwise around the origin.

figure.caption: A vector field assigns an arrow to each point.

subsection.p: This field will return later when we study circulation. For now, it gives a clear contrast:

table.title: Scalar fields versus vector fields.

subsection.p: A scalar field can be visualized in several ways. We can make a graph, if the input is two-dimensional. We can draw a contour map, like a topographic map. We can draw level surfaces, if the input is three-dimensional. Each picture shows the same function from a different angle.
A formula gives exact values, but a picture tells us how those values are arranged. That arrangement is what we look at next.

section.title: Graphs, level curves, and level surfaces
section.p: gave us scalar fields and vector fields. Vector fields are best drawn with arrows. Scalar fields need a different kind of picture.
For a scalar-valued function f(x,y), the input lives in the plane and the output is a number. We can use the output as a height. That turns the function into a surface in space.

subsection.title: Graphs of functions z=f(x,y)
subsection.p: A market stall has a flat rectangular floor, 0\le x\le 4,\qquad 0\le y\le 3. A slanted canopy above it has height f(x,y)=2+\frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{6}. At the corner (0,0), f(0,0)=2. At the corner (4,3), f(4,3)=2+1+\frac12=3.5. The canopy is higher as we move in the positive x-direction and also higher as we move in the positive y-direction.
To draw the graph, we place the point (x,y,f(x,y)) above each floor point (x,y).

figure.caption: The graph of z=f(x,y) is made by placing height f(x,y) above each input point (x,y).

definition.title: Graph of a function of two variables

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. The graph of f is the set of points in \mathbb R^3 \boxed{\{(x,y,z): (x,y)\in D,\ z=f(x,y)\}.} In the examples considered here, this set describes the surface z=f(x,y).

subsection.p: This definition is the direct descendant of the graph of a single-variable function. For y=f(x), we placed the output y above the input x. Now we place the output z above the input point (x,y).

exercise.title: Why does the graph need a third dimension?

statement.p: The domain of f(x,y) is a flat region in the plane, yet we draw its graph as a surface floating in three-dimensional space. Where does the extra dimension come from, and what does a single point (x,y,f(x,y)) of the graph record about the function?

hint.p: Two coordinates locate the input, but the output f(x,y) still has to go somewhere. Picture stacking that output as a height above the floor point (x,y).

example.title: A dome as a graph

statement.p: The function h(x,y)=\sqrt{16-x^2-y^2} has domain x^2+y^2\le 16. Its graph is z=\sqrt{16-x^2-y^2}. Squaring gives x^2+y^2+z^2=16, with z\ge0. So the graph is the upper half of a sphere of radius 4.

subsection.p: Graphs are useful, but they have limits. A function of three variables f(x,y,z) would have a graph made of points (x,y,z,f(x,y,z)). That graph lives in four-dimensional space. We cannot draw it in the same direct way.
For scalar fields in the plane, there is another picture that is often even more useful than the graph: the contour map.

subsection.title: Contour maps and level curves
subsection.p: A hiker does not need a three-dimensional plastic model of a mountain to plan a route. A topographic map is usually better. It joins points of equal height.

Consider a hill whose height is H(x,y)=120-x^2-4y^2, where height is measured in meters. The highest point is at (0,0), where H(0,0)=120. The set of points at height 116 satisfies 120-x^2-4y^2=116, so x^2+4y^2=4. This is an ellipse.
The set of points at height 104 satisfies x^2+4y^2=16. The set of points at height 84 satisfies x^2+4y^2=36. Each height gives an ellipse around the summit.

figure.caption: Level curves of a stretched hill. The long direction of the ellipses shows that the hill changes more slowly east-west than north-south.

subsection.p: The picture tells a story. To lose the same amount of height, you can travel farther in the x-direction than in the y-direction. So the hill is gentler east-west and steeper north-south.
Now we name the idea.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. For a constant c, the level curve of f at level c is the set \boxed{\{(x,y)\in D:f(x,y)=c\}.} A contour map is a drawing of several level curves, usually labeled by their values of c.

subsection.p: The word curve is traditional, but it comes with a warning. A level set may be a curve, several curves, a point, or even empty.

example.title: A level curve can shrink to a point or disappear

statement.p: For H(x,y)=120-x^2-4y^2, the level c=120 gives x^2+4y^2=0. The only solution is (0,0). So this level set is just one point.
The level c=130 gives 120-x^2-4y^2=130, or x^2+4y^2=-10. There are no real solutions. So this level set is empty.

example.title: Level curves of a plane

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=6-3x-2y. The level curve at height c is 6-3x-2y=c. Rearranging, 3x+2y=6-c. So the level curves are parallel lines.
This makes sense: the graph of f is a plane. Slicing a tilted plane by horizontal planes gives parallel lines.

example.title: A saddle seen from above

statement.p: Let S(x,y)=y^2-x^2. The level curve S(x,y)=0 is y^2-x^2=0, so (y-x)(y+x)=0. Thus y=x \qquad\text{or}\qquad y=-x. The zero level set is two crossing lines.
For c>0, the curves y^2-x^2=c are hyperbolas opening upward and downward. For c<0, they open left and right. This crossing pattern is a top-down signal of a saddle surface.

subsection.p: Level curves are not merely flat drawings. They are the shadows of horizontal slices of the graph.

theorem.title: Level curves are horizontal slices of the graph

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. The intersection of the graph z=f(x,y) with the horizontal plane z=c is \{(x,y,c):(x,y)\in D,\ f(x,y)=c\}. Thus it is the level curve f(x,y)=c, lifted to height c.

proof.p: A point (x,y,z) lies on the graph exactly when z=f(x,y). It also lies in the horizontal plane z=c exactly when z=c. Both conditions hold exactly when f(x,y)=c and z=c. So the intersection is the level curve f(x,y)=c, placed in the plane z=c.

subsection.p: This is why a contour map can help us imagine a surface. Draw several level curves, then imagine each one lifted to its labeled height.

exercise.title: How can a flat map hold a whole hill?

statement.p: A contour map is flat, yet its labels convey heights on a three-dimensional hill. Explain how. Why does a finite collection of contours leave some information between the curves undetermined? If neighboring contours have equal height increments, what does close spacing tell you about the average height change across them?

hint.p: Each curve carries a label c, so a height is attached to it even though the drawing is flat. Now think about moving across two nearby labels: if the labels differ by a lot but the curves are only a tiny distance apart, how fast must the height be changing?

subsection.title: Level surfaces
subsection.p: For a function of three variables, f(x,y,z), the graph would live in four dimensions. But the level sets live in ordinary three-dimensional space.

example.title: Pressure levels in a tank

statement.p: Let p(x,y,z)=120-3z. The level surface p(x,y,z)=90 satisfies 120-3z=90. So z=10. That level surface is a horizontal plane.
More generally, p(x,y,z)=c gives z=\frac{120-c}{3}. So the pressure levels are horizontal planes stacked above one another.
Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R. For a constant c, the level surface of f at level c is the set \boxed{\{(x,y,z)\in D:f(x,y,z)=c\}.}

example.title: Distance from a radio beacon

statement.p: A radio beacon is located at B=(1,-2,3). The squared distance from the beacon is R(x,y,z)=(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2+(z-3)^2. The level surface R(x,y,z)=9 is (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2+(z-3)^2=9. This is a sphere centered at (1,-2,3) with radius 3.
More generally, R(x,y,z)=c is a sphere of radius \sqrt c when c>0, a single point when c=0, and empty when c<0.

figure.caption: Level surfaces of squared distance are spheres centered at the source.

subsection.p: Level surfaces are the three-dimensional version of contour lines. Instead of drawing curves of equal height on a map, we draw surfaces on which a quantity stays constant.

subsection.title: Reading geometry from level sets
subsection.p: Level sets let us read geometry without always drawing the graph.
Here are three important habits.

First, when successive levels differ by the same amount, level curves that are close together indicate rapid change across them. On a topographic map, tightly packed contour lines mean a steep slope. Widely spaced contour lines mean a gentle slope.

Second, the shape of a level curve tells us which directions change slowly. For H(x,y)=120-x^2-4y^2, the level curves are long in the x-direction and short in the y-direction. That means the hill changes more slowly east-west and more quickly north-south.
Third, different level curves of the same function cannot cross. If one point lay on both f(x,y)=10 and f(x,y)=12, then the same input (x,y) would have two outputs. That is not a function.

The warning is that one level set can have several pieces. For S(x,y)=y^2-x^2, the level set S=0 is the pair of lines y=x \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=-x. Those two lines meet, but they belong to the same level value. There is no contradiction.

A graph, a contour map, and a formula are three ways of seeing the same scalar field. Each has strengths. The formula computes. The graph shows height. The level curves show how height is arranged across the input region.

exercise.title: Reading steepness and shape from contours?

statement.p: You are handed a contour map you have never seen before, with no formula attached. Using both the labels and the spacing, how would you estimate where height changes most rapidly across neighboring contours? What happens to the function value if you travel along one level curve?

hint.p: Compare the change in labeled height with the distance between contours. Along a single contour the height is constant; the shape of one contour alone does not determine rates across it.

subsection.p: But pictures can also hide danger. A surface can look calm from several straight-line approaches to a point and still behave badly along a curved approach. Once inputs can approach a point from infinitely many directions, the old one-dimensional idea of a limit needs a sharper eye. That is the next problem.

section.title: Limits in several variables
section.p: gave us graphs, level curves, and level surfaces. Those pictures help us see scalar fields, but a picture is still a promise made from a distance. Limits ask a more delicate question: \text{What happens as the input gets very close to one point?}

In single-variable calculus, x\to a meant approaching from the left and from the right. In the plane, a point can approach from every direction: along lines, curves, spirals, parabolas, and paths we have not thought to name.

subsection.title: Approaching a point along many paths
subsection.p: Consider the function A(x,y)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). The formula is not defined at the origin. But we can ask whether the values settle down as (x,y) approaches (0,0).
Approach along the x-axis. Then y=0, so A(x,0)=\frac{x^2}{x^2}=1 for x\ne0. Along this path, the values approach 1.
Approach along the y-axis. Then x=0, so A(0,y)=\frac{-y^2}{y^2}=-1 for y\ne0. Along this path, the values approach -1.
The same point gives two different limiting answers: 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad -1. So the function has no limit at the origin.

figure.caption: A two-variable limit must survive every possible approach to the point.

subsection.p: This is the main new issue. A two-variable limit is not a left-right test. It is an all-paths test.

statement.p: In single-variable calculus, checking a limit means looking from just two sides: the left and the right. As a point (x,y) approaches (0,0) in the plane, how many genuinely different ways can it approach? Why does this make a two-variable limit harder to confirm than a one-variable limit?

hint.p: Picture every line, curve, spiral, and wandering path that ends at the point. On a line you have only two directions; in the plane you have a whole circle of directions, and curved paths beyond those. Think about how many of these the function must satisfy at once.

definition.title: Limit of a function of two variables

statement.p: All nearby inputs must lie in D. We assume that points of D other than (a,b) occur arbitrarily close to (a,b); such a point is called an accumulation point of D. The point (a,b) does not have to be in the domain of f. A limit is about nearby points, not necessarily the point itself.

subsection.p: The phrase whenever (x,y) is sufficiently close means from every direction and along every path. If even one path gives a different answer, the limit fails.

subsection.title: Path tests for nonexistence of a limit
subsection.p: A path is a curve approaching the point. If a limit exists, every path must see the same limiting value.
The quickest way to disprove a limit is to find two paths that disagree.

example.title: A family of straight paths

statement.p: Let B(x,y)=\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). Along the x-axis, B(x,0)=0. So along that path, the values approach 0.
Along the line y=x, we get B(x,x)=\frac{x^2}{x^2+x^2}=\frac12. So along that path, the values approach \frac12.

subsection.p:
The same function shows something stronger. Along the line y=mx, we get
B(x,mx) \amp= \frac{x(mx)}{x^2+(mx)^2} \amp= \frac{mx^2}{(1+m^2)x^2} \amp= \frac{m}{1+m^2},
for x\ne0. Different slopes m give different limiting values. The origin is not approached by one road; it is approached by infinitely many roads.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. Suppose two paths \mathbf r_1(t)\to(a,b), \qquad \mathbf r_2(t)\to(a,b) as t\to0, and suppose that, for sufficiently small nonzero t, the paths stay in the domain of f and avoid (a,b).
If \lim_{t\to0} f(\mathbf r_1(t)) and \lim_{t\to0} f(\mathbf r_2(t)) exist but are different, then \lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y) does not exist.

proof.p: If the two-variable limit were L, then f(x,y) would approach L whenever (x,y) approaches (a,b). In particular, it would approach L along every path to (a,b).
Two different path limits would force the same limit to equal two different numbers. That is impossible.

subsection.p: The theorem is a tool for showing that a limit does not exist. It is not a tool for proving that a limit exists.

exercise.title: Why is disproving easier than proving?

statement.p: Finding two paths that approach (a,b) with different limiting values settles the matter: the limit does not exist. Yet finding two paths that agree tells us almost nothing about whether the limit exists. Why is there this asymmetry between the two situations?

hint.p: A limit must equal the same number along every approach. To break that, one conflict is enough. To confirm it, no finite collection of agreeing paths can speak for all the infinitely many paths you did not test — an untested path might still disagree.

subsection.p: Here is the trap.

example.title: All straight paths agree, but the limit still fails

statement.p:
Define C(x,y)=\frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). First approach along a straight line y=mx. If m=0, then C(x,0)=0. If m\ne0, then
C(x,mx) \amp= \frac{x^2(mx)}{x^4+m^2x^2} \amp= \frac{mx^3}{x^2(x^2+m^2)} \amp= \frac{mx}{x^2+m^2}.
As x\to0, \frac{mx}{x^2+m^2}\to0. The vertical line x=0 also gives zero. So every straight-line path gives the limiting value 0.

But now approach along the parabola y=x^2. Then
C(x,x^2) \amp= \frac{x^2(x^2)}{x^4+(x^2)^2} \amp= \frac{x^4}{2x^4} \amp= \frac12.
Along this curved path, the limiting value is \frac12.
So the full limit does not exist, even though every straight-line test gave 0. Straight roads are not enough.

subsection.p: The moral is important:

subsection.title: Polar-coordinate tests near the origin
subsection.p: Near the origin, polar coordinates are built for limits. Every point near (0,0) can be written as x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta, where r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Approaching the origin means r\to0. The angle \theta may stay fixed, change, or spin wildly. A good polar argument must work no matter what \theta does.

example.title: A polar-coordinate proof of a limit

statement.p: Let D(x,y)=\frac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). We want to find \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}D(x,y).

subsection.p: The key was not merely rewriting in polar coordinates. The key was finding a bound that did not depend on \theta.

theorem.title: Polar squeeze test near the origin

statement.p: Suppose f(x,y) is defined near (0,0), except possibly at (0,0). Write x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta. If there is a function g(r) such that |f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)-L|\le g(r) for all sufficiently small r\gt0 and all angles \theta, and if \lim_{r\to0^+}g(r)=0, then \boxed{ \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f(x,y)=L. }

proof.p: The distance from (x,y) to the origin is r. As (x,y)\to(0,0), we have r\to0^+. The inequality |f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)-L|\le g(r) holds for every angle, so it controls every possible approach to the origin. Since g(r)\to0, the difference |f(x,y)-L| must also go to 0.

subsection.p: The phrase for all angles \theta is the heart of the theorem. Without it, a path could hide in the angle dependence.

example.title: Polar coordinates can also reveal failure

statement.p:
Return to A(x,y)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}. In polar coordinates,
A(x,y) \amp= \frac{r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta}{r^2} \amp= \cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta \amp= \cos(2\theta).
The expression does not depend on r at all. It depends only on the angle.
Along \theta=0, A=1. Along \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}, A=-1. No matter how close we get to the origin, the angle still controls the value. So the limit does not exist.

subsection.p: To use polar coordinates near another point (a,b), shift the point to the origin: u=x-a,\qquad v=y-b. Then write u=r\cos\theta,\qquad v=r\sin\theta. Approaching (a,b) is the same as r=\sqrt{(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2}\to0.

subsection.title: The formal limit definition in \mathbb R^n
subsection.p: The words nearby inputs give nearby outputs are right, but sometimes we need the exact sentence behind them.
For a function F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, both the input and the output may be vectors. Distance measures closeness in both spaces.

statement.p: We assume \mathbf a is an accumulation point of the domain: for every \delta>0, some \mathbf x\in D satisfies 0<\|\mathbf x-\mathbf a\|<\delta.
For every \varepsilon\gt0, there is a \delta\gt0 such that whenever 0\lt\|\mathbf x-\mathbf a\|\lt\delta and \mathbf x\in D, we have \|F(\mathbf x)-\mathbf L\|\lt\varepsilon.

subsection.p: This definition is just the precise version of the all-paths idea. The condition 0\lt\|\mathbf x-\mathbf a\|\lt\delta says that the input is close to \mathbf a, but not equal to \mathbf a. The condition \|F(\mathbf x)-\mathbf L\|\lt\varepsilon says that the output is close to \mathbf L.

statement.p: Checking a few paths, or even infinitely many along one family, can never list every possible approach. What does the \varepsilon-\delta definition require that path-checking cannot guarantee? In particular, think about what the single number \delta must control.

hint.p: The condition 0\lt\|\mathbf x-\mathbf a\|\lt\delta describes a whole punctured disk around \mathbf a, not a curve. So one \delta must force \|F(\mathbf x)-\mathbf L\|\lt\varepsilon for all points in that disk at once — every path through it included.

example.title: A direct limit proof for a linear function

statement.p:
Let f(x,y)=3x-2y. We claim that \lim_{(x,y)\to(1,4)} f(x,y)=f(1,4)=-5. Compute the difference:
|f(x,y)-(-5)| \amp= |3x-2y+5| \amp= |3(x-1)-2(y-4)|.
Using the triangle inequality, |3(x-1)-2(y-4)| \le 3|x-1|+2|y-4|. Also, |x-1|\le \sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-4)^2}, and |y-4|\le \sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-4)^2}. Therefore |f(x,y)-(-5)| \le 5\sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-4)^2}. If \sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-4)^2}\lt\delta, then |f(x,y)-(-5)|\lt5\delta. To make this less than \varepsilon, choose \delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{5}. So the formal definition confirms what geometry already suggested: a linear function has no sudden behavior. Its values move continuously with its inputs.

subsection.p: Vector-valued limits work component by component, just as they did for the one-variable vector-valued functions in .

statement.p: Let F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m be written in components as F(\mathbf x)= \bigl(F_1(\mathbf x),F_2(\mathbf x),\ldots,F_m(\mathbf x)\bigr). Let \mathbf L=(L_1,L_2,\ldots,L_m). Then \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}F(\mathbf x)=\mathbf L if and only if \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}F_i(\mathbf x)=L_i for every component i=1,2,\ldots,m.

proof.p: If the vector F(\mathbf x) approaches \mathbf L, then the distance between them goes to 0. Each component difference is no larger in absolute value than that distance, so each component approaches its limiting value.

example.title: A vector-valued limit

statement.p: Let F(x,y)= \left( x+y,\; \frac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2} \right), \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). As (x,y)\to(0,0), x+y\to0. From the polar-coordinate example above, \frac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}\to0. Therefore \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}F(x,y)=(0,0).

subsection.p: A limit does not care what happens at the point itself. That is both useful and a little dangerous.

For example, define G(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}, & (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm] 17, & (x,y)=(0,0). \end{cases} The limit at the origin is still 0. But the actual value at the origin is 17. So the surface has a perfectly good limiting height, but the function has placed the point at the wrong height.
That mismatch is exactly what continuity is designed to catch. A limit asks what the nearby values want the answer to be. Continuity asks whether the function actually listens.

section.title: Continuity
section.p: ended with a mismatch. The nearby values of \frac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2} wanted to approach 0 at the origin, but we could still define the value at the origin to be 17. Limits notice what happens nearby. Continuity asks whether the function agrees with its own nearby behavior.

subsection.title: Continuity as nearby inputs give nearby outputs
subsection.p: A temperature field should not usually jump suddenly. If you move a few centimeters across a room, the temperature should change only a little. A formula can express that kind of steadiness.
At an accumulation point of the domain, the limit formulation contains three requirements at once:

li.p: F(\mathbf a) must be defined.
\displaystyle \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}F(\mathbf x) must exist.
\displaystyle \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}F(\mathbf x) must equal F(\mathbf a).

subsection.p: If any one of these fails, continuity fails.

statement.p: In your own words, what does it mean intuitively for a function f(x,y) to be continuous at a point \mathbf a? Try to describe it without writing the limit equation, using everyday language about nearby inputs and nearby outputs.

hint.p: Picture wiggling the input a tiny bit. If the output is only allowed to wiggle a tiny bit too, with no sudden jumps and no holes, what does that tell you about how nearby inputs and nearby outputs are related?

example.title: A removable discontinuity

statement.p: Define f(x,y)=\frac{x^2+y^2}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}},\qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). For (x,y)\ne(0,0), f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Thus \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} f(x,y)=0. But the original formula is not defined at (0,0). So f is not continuous at the origin.
If we define f(0,0)=0, then the repaired function becomes continuous at the origin. The discontinuity was only a missing value.

example.title: A discontinuity that cannot be repaired

statement.p: Let h(x,y)=\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2},\qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). Along the x-axis, h(x,0)=0. Along the line y=x, h(x,x)=\frac{x^2}{2x^2}=\frac12. The limit at the origin does not exist. No choice of h(0,0) can make the function continuous there.
A missing value can be repaired only when the limit exists.

subsection.p: For vector-valued functions, continuity is componentwise, just as limits are.

statement.p: Let F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m be written as F(\mathbf x)=\bigl(F_1(\mathbf x),F_2(\mathbf x),\ldots,F_m(\mathbf x)\bigr). Then F is continuous at \mathbf a if and only if each component function F_i:D\to\mathbb R is continuous at \mathbf a.

proof.p: This follows directly from the componentwise limit theorem in . The vector limit \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}F(\mathbf x)=F(\mathbf a) holds exactly when every component limit satisfies \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}F_i(\mathbf x)=F_i(\mathbf a).

example.title: A continuous vector field

statement.p: The swirling field \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x) is continuous everywhere in the plane. Its components -y\qquad\text{and}\qquad x are continuous functions.

The field \mathbf V(x,y)=\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}(-y,x) is continuous on its domain \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. It is not continuous at the origin because it is not even defined there. The missing point is not a small detail; it will matter later when we study circulation around holes.

subsection.title: Algebra of continuous functions
subsection.p: Most continuous functions are built from simpler continuous functions.

For example, suppose the pressure in a tank is modeled by p(x,y,z)=\frac{100+2z}{1+x^2+y^2}. The numerator 100+2z is continuous. The denominator 1+x^2+y^2 is continuous and never equals 0. So the quotient behaves continuously everywhere in space.
This example is so common that we turn it into a theorem.

statement.p: Suppose f,g:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R are continuous at \mathbf a\in D, and let c be a constant. Then the following functions are continuous at \mathbf a: f+g,\qquad f-g,\qquad cf,\qquad fg. If g(\mathbf a)\ne0, then \frac{f}{g} is also continuous at \mathbf a.

proof.p: The scalar limit laws have the same proof as in one variable: the input distance replaces |x-a|, while the output estimates are unchanged. For sums use |(f+g)-(L+M)|\le|f-L|+|g-M|. For products use |fg-LM|\le|f||g-M|+|M||f-L|, with |f|\le|L|+1 sufficiently near the point. These estimates give \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}(f+g)(\mathbf x)=f(\mathbf a)+g(\mathbf a), and similarly for differences, constant multiples, and products.

For quotients with M\ne0, take inputs close enough that |g|>|M|/2. The estimate |1/g-1/M|\le2|g-M|/|M|^2, followed by the product limit law just justified, proves the quotient limit law. Here the limiting denominator is nonzero: \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}g(\mathbf x)=g(\mathbf a)\ne0. Thus \lim_{\mathbf x\to\mathbf a}\frac{f(\mathbf x)}{g(\mathbf x)}=\frac{f(\mathbf a)}{g(\mathbf a)}.

subsection.p: We required g(\mathbf a)\ne0 for a reason.

example.title: Why the denominator condition matters

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=1,\qquad g(x,y)=x^2+y^2. Both functions are continuous everywhere. But \frac{f(x,y)}{g(x,y)}=\frac{1}{x^2+y^2} is not continuous at the origin. It is not even defined there, and its values become unbounded as (x,y)\to(0,0).
So a quotient of continuous functions is continuous only where the denominator is not zero.

example.title: A formula continuous on its natural domain

statement.p: The square root requires 4-x^2-y^2\ge0, so x^2+y^2\le4. The denominator requires 1+xy\ne0. Therefore q is continuous on \{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le4,\ xy\ne -1\}.

subsection.p: This gives a practical habit:
subsection.md: \text{A formula made from continuous pieces is continuous wherever it is allowed to be.}
subsection.p: The suspicious points are the places where the formula is not allowed: zero denominators, square roots of negative numbers, logarithms of nonpositive numbers, and special piecewise definitions.

subsection.title: Continuity of compositions
subsection.p: A function can feed into another function.

statement.p: Suppose F is continuous and G is continuous. Explain, intuitively, why feeding the output of F into G should produce a continuous function G\circ F. What do you think could go wrong if one of the two pieces had a jump?

hint.p: Trace a small change in the input through both stages. The first function turns a small nudge into a small nudge; then think about what the second function does to that already small nudge. Where in this chain would a jump sneak in?

subsection.p:
For example, the height of a dome over a circular floor is h(x,y)=\sqrt{16-x^2-y^2}. In polar coordinates, x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta. Substituting gives
h(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \amp= \sqrt{16-r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta} \amp= \sqrt{16-r^2}.
The coordinate map \Phi(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) is continuous. The height function h is continuous on its disk. Their composition h\circ \Phi is continuous wherever 16-r^2\ge0.

statement.p: Let F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m be continuous at \mathbf a, and let G:E\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^k be continuous at F(\mathbf a). If F(D)\subseteq E, then the composition G\circ F is continuous at \mathbf a.

proof.p: Since F is continuous at \mathbf a, F(\mathbf x)\to F(\mathbf a)\qquad\text{as}\qquad\mathbf x\to\mathbf a. Since G is continuous at F(\mathbf a), G(\mathbf y)\to G(F(\mathbf a))\qquad\text{as}\qquad\mathbf y\to F(\mathbf a). Taking \mathbf y=F(\mathbf x), we get G(F(\mathbf x))\to G(F(\mathbf a)). So G\circ F is continuous at \mathbf a.

subsection.p: The continuity hypotheses are real. If either piece has a jump in the wrong place, the composition can have a jump.

example.title: A discontinuous outer function can break the composition
A discontinuous inner function can also break the composition

subsection.title: Continuous functions on closed and bounded regions
subsection.p: Single-variable calculus has a comforting theorem: a continuous function on a closed interval [a,b] has a maximum and a minimum. Multivariable calculus has the same idea, but the interval becomes a closed and bounded region.
First, an example.
Let H(x,y)=120-x^2-4y^2 on the rectangle D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le3,\ 0\le y\le2\}. This is the height function from our contour-map hill, restricted to a rectangular park.
The function is largest at (0,0), where H(0,0)=120. It is smallest at (3,2), where H(3,2)=120-9-16=95. So this hill has both a highest point and a lowest point on the park.
The rectangle matters. It contains its edges, and it does not stretch to infinity.

statement.p: A set D\subseteq\mathbb R^n is bounded if it fits inside some large ball. That is, there is a number M such that \|\mathbf x\|\le M for every \mathbf x\in D.

A set D\subseteq\mathbb R^n is closed if it contains all of its boundary points. A boundary point is a point whose every open ball meets both D and its complement; an open ball of radius r centered at \mathbf a consists of points with \|\mathbf x-\mathbf a\|<r.
In this book, the most important examples are regions described by non-strict inequalities, such as x^2+y^2\le 9 or 0\le x\le 3,\qquad 0\le y\le 2.

subsection.p: The disk x^2+y^2\le1 is closed and bounded. The open disk x^2+y^2\lt 1 is bounded but not closed, because it leaves out its boundary circle. The whole plane \mathbb R^2 is closed but not bounded.

theorem.title: Extreme Value Theorem in several variables

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be continuous. If D is nonempty, closed, and bounded, then f attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on D.
That means there are points \mathbf p,\mathbf q\in D such that f(\mathbf p)\le f(\mathbf x)\le f(\mathbf q) for every \mathbf x\in D.

proof.title: Idea of the proof
proof.p: A closed and bounded region has no missing boundary point and no escape to infinity. These observations motivate the theorem, but do not constitute a proof. In particular, the theorem does not require the region to be connected.

The full proof belongs to a later analysis course. For this course, the theorem is a tool: on a closed and bounded region, a continuous function cannot merely approach its maximum or minimum. It must attain them.

subsection.p: Each hypothesis matters.

statement.p: A continuous function on a closed and bounded region is guaranteed to attain a maximum and a minimum. Intuitively, why are both words needed? Describe what can go wrong if the region is bounded but not closed, and separately what can go wrong if it is closed but not bounded.

hint.p: Think about a value the function keeps approaching but never reaches. Dropping closed lets the region leave out the very edge point where the best value would live; dropping bounded lets the region run off to infinity so the values never settle. Which missing word causes which kind of escape?

example.title: Why boundedness matters

statement.p: The function f(x,y)=x is continuous on all of \mathbb R^2. The domain \mathbb R^2 is closed, but it is not bounded.
There is no maximum, because x can be made as large as we like. There is no minimum, because x can be made as negative as we like.

example.title: Why closedness matters

statement.p: The function f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 is continuous on the open disk D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\lt 1\}. The domain is bounded, but it is not closed.
The values satisfy 0\le f(x,y)\lt 1. The function has a minimum at (0,0), but it has no maximum. The value 1 is approached near the boundary circle, but the boundary circle is not included.

example.title: Why continuity matters

statement.p: As (x,y)\to(0,0), the values \frac{1}{x^2+y^2} become arbitrarily large. So u has no maximum on D. Closed and bounded domains do not protect us from discontinuities.

subsection.p: Continuity is a powerful promise, but it is also easy to assume too quickly. A formula may look harmless from a few straight paths and still hide a thin ridge, a missing point, or a sudden jump. Before we move on to slopes in many directions, it is worth collecting the main traps in one place.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: Limits and continuity in several variables have one central difficulty: there are too many ways to approach a point. The examples in this section are not rare tricks. They are the warning signs that tell us how to think.

subsection.title: A function with different limits along different paths
subsection.p: Let A(x,y)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). Along the x-axis, A(x,0)=1. Along the y-axis, A(0,y)=-1. So \lim_{x\to0}A(x,0)=1 but \lim_{y\to0}A(0,y)=-1. The two paths disagree. Therefore \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}A(x,y) does not exist.

In polar coordinates, A(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)=\frac{r^2\cos^2\theta-r^2\sin^2\theta}{r^2}=\cos(2\theta). The value depends only on the angle. Getting closer to the origin does not force the function toward one number.

figure.caption: Different path limits disprove a two-variable limit.

subsection.p: The moral is simple:

p.md: \text{One disagreement is enough to destroy a limit.}

subsection.title: A function whose path limits agree along lines but whose limit still fails
subsection.p: Now comes the more dangerous trap. Sometimes every straight-line test gives the same answer, but the full limit still fails.

Let C(x,y)=\frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). Approach along the line y=mx. If m=0, then C(x,0)=0. If m\ne0, then
C(x,mx) \amp= \frac{x^2(mx)}{x^4+m^2x^2} \amp= \frac{mx^3}{x^2(x^2+m^2)} \amp= \frac{mx}{x^2+m^2}.
As x\to0, \frac{mx}{x^2+m^2}\to0. The vertical line x=0 also gives zero. So every straight line gives the limiting value 0.

But along the parabola y=x^2, we get
C(x,x^2) \amp= \frac{x^2(x^2)}{x^4+(x^2)^2} \amp= \frac{x^4}{2x^4} \amp= \frac12.
The curved path gives a different value. Therefore the limit does not exist.

figure.caption: All straight paths can agree while a curved path disagrees.

subsection.p: The moral is sharper now:
To prove a limit, we need a bound that controls all paths at once.

statement.p: Suppose you check every straight-line approach to a point and they all give the same value. Why isn't this enough to guarantee that the two-variable limit exists? What is it about approaching a point in the plane that straight lines simply cannot capture?

hint.p: Think about how many roads lead to the origin. Lines are not the only ones. Recall the parabola y=x^2 in the example above, and ask what other shapes a path could take.

subsection.title: Separate continuity does not imply continuity
subsection.p: There is another tempting shortcut. If a function is continuous in x when y is held fixed, and continuous in y when x is held fixed, should it be continuous as a function of both variables?
No.
First hold y fixed. If y=0, then S(x,0)=0, which is continuous in x. If y=y_0\ne0, then S(x,y_0)=\frac{xy_0}{x^2+y_0^2}, which is a continuous function of x.
So S is continuous in x when y is held fixed.

statement.p: Being continuous in x alone and continuous in y alone only tests the function along horizontal and vertical lines through a point. Why doesn't passing both of these tests guarantee that the function is continuous as a function of both variables together?

hint.p: The two separate tests only walk you in along the coordinate directions. Picture all the other directions and curves you could slide in along, such as y=x, and ask whether the function has to agree with them too.

subsection.p: Similarly, holding x fixed gives a continuous function of y. The function is continuous in each variable separately.
But as a two-variable function, S is not continuous at the origin. Along the line y=x, S(x,x)=\frac{x^2}{2x^2}=\frac12. Along the x-axis, S(x,0)=0. So the limit at the origin does not exist.
This example will matter again in . Partial derivatives look at coordinate directions. Coordinate directions are important, but they are not the whole plane.

subsection.title: Why pictures can mislead near a singular point
subsection.p: Graphs and contour maps are powerful, but they have a weakness: a very thin feature can be invisible at normal scale.

Along any line y=mx, the function eventually equals 0 near the origin. To see why, suppose m\ne0. The condition 0\lt mx\lt x^4 would imply |m||x|<|x|^4, hence |m|<|x|^3, which is impossible for all sufficiently small nonzero x. For sufficiently small x, no fixed nonzero slope can fit inside the narrow strip. The lines y=0 and x=0 also give M=0.
So every straight-line test gives the value 0.

statement.p: A plotted graph or contour map near the origin can make it look as though M(x,y) settles down to a single value. Why can a picture fool you here, and when a drawing and a careful calculation seem to disagree about a limit, which one should you trust?

hint.p: A feature as thin as the strip 0\lt y\lt x^4 can be far too narrow to see at ordinary scale. Ask yourself what a finite-resolution picture can never show, and which tool gives an exact answer.

subsection.p: But along the curve y=\frac{x^4}{2}, we have 0\lt\frac{x^4}{2}\lt x^4 for every x\ne0. Therefore M\left(x,\frac{x^4}{2}\right)=1. This curved path approaches the origin while the function stays equal to 1. Hence the limit at the origin does not exist.

figure.caption: A thin curved strip can be missed by every straight-line test.

subsection.p: This is the geometric reason line tests are dangerous. A line is only one kind of road. A function can hide its bad behavior between all the straight roads.

The chapter began with functions as fields of values. It ends with a warning: fields can be subtle near a point. The next chapter asks a new question. When a scalar field is continuous enough to behave well, how fast is it changing? In one variable there was one derivative. On a surface, there are many possible directions to move, so the word slope has to split into several ideas.

introduction.p: This chapter changed the shape of calculus. A function no longer has to take one number as input. Its input may be a point in the plane or in space, and its output may be a number or a vector.
The new difficulty was not the algebra. It was approach. In one variable, a limit only had to survive left and right. In several variables, it must survive every path.

table.title: Chapter map

row.cell: A function with n input coordinates and m output coordinates.
A function whose output is one number, such as temperature or height.
A function whose output is a vector, such as wind velocity or force.
A surface made by placing height f(x,y) above each input point.
A set f(x,y)=c, showing where a scalar field has one fixed value.
A set f(x,y,z)=c, the three-dimensional version of a contour line.
The value a function approaches as the input approaches a point from every path.
The function's actual value agrees with the value forced by nearby inputs.

statement.p: Explain the difference between a scalar field and a vector field. Give one physical example of each.
A function has notation F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3. What is the shape of its input? What is the shape of its output?
Why is the domain part of the meaning of a function, not just a technical detail?
Explain how a level curve of f(x,y) is related to a horizontal slice of the graph z=f(x,y).
Can two level curves of the same function with different level values cross? Explain.
Why can checking the x-axis and y-axis be enough to disprove a limit, but not enough to prove one?
What does polar coordinates change about a limit near the origin?
State the three things that must be true for f to be continuous at a point \mathbf a.
Why does the Extreme Value Theorem require the domain to be closed and bounded?
Give an example of a function that has a limit at a point but is not continuous there.

introduction.p: Find the natural domain of each function. Describe the domain in words or with a sketch when possible.

exercises.title: Skills: graphs, level curves, and level surfaces

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=4-x-y. Find the level curves f(x,y)=0,1,2,3. What kind of surface is the graph z=f(x,y)?
Let H(x,y)=100-x^2-9y^2. Find the level curves H=99,\qquad H=91,\qquad H=64. Which direction is steeper, the x-direction or the y-direction?
Let R(x,y,z)=(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2+z^2. Describe the level surfaces R=1, R=4, and R=9.
Describe the level surfaces z^2-x^2-y^2=c for c=0,\qquad c=1,\qquad c=-1.
Let f(x,y)=xy. Sketch the level curves xy=-2,\quad xy=-1,\quad xy=0,\quad xy=1,\quad xy=2. What happens at the level 0?
Let f(x,y)=x^2+y^2. Explain why the level curves are circles. What happens to the spacing between the curves if the levels are 1,\quad 4,\quad 9,\quad 16?

introduction.p: Evaluate each limit or show that it does not exist.

statement.p: Let F(x,y)= \left( x+y,\, \frac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2} \right), \qquad (x,y)\ne(0,0). Find \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}F(x,y), if it exists.
Define f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}, & (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm] k, & (x,y)=(0,0). \end{cases} Find the value of k that makes f continuous at the origin.
Define g(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}, & (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm] k, & (x,y)=(0,0). \end{cases} Show that no value of k makes g continuous at the origin.
Let f(x,y)=\ln(9-x^2-y^2), and let \Phi(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta). Find (f\circ\Phi)(r,\theta) and describe where it is continuous.
Let D=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}. Explain why every continuous function on D has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.

For each domain below, say whether it is closed, bounded, both, or neither:
x^2+y^2\lt 1, x^2+y^2\le1, y\ge x^2, 0\lt x\lt 1,\quad 0\lt y\lt 1.

exercise.title: A contour map from a table

statement.p: The table below gives measured temperatures, in degrees Celsius, on a square plate. The row label is y, and the column label is x.
Draw an approximate contour map for the levels 20,\qquad 22,\qquad 24,\qquad 28. Where does the plate appear hottest? Where are the contour lines closest together?

For M(x,y)= \begin{cases} 1, & 0\lt y\lt x^4,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} show that every straight-line path through the origin gives limiting value 0, but the path y=\frac{x^4}{2} gives limiting value 1. Explain why a computer graph of M might miss the problem near the origin.
Find a function f(x,y) whose limit at the origin fails because two parabolic paths give different limiting values. The two paths should not be straight lines.
Find a function f(x,y) that is not defined at the origin but has a limit there. Then define a new function F by assigning one value at the origin so that F becomes continuous at the origin.
Choose a small real data set that depends on two variables. Examples include temperature on a tabletop, light intensity in a room, elevation on a hiking map, or sound level at different locations.
Make a table of values, draw an approximate contour map, and write a paragraph answering these questions:

li.p: Where is the quantity largest?
Where is it smallest?
Where does it seem to change fastest?
What features of the contour map tell you that?

conclusion.p: A contour map shows where a function has the same value. Limits and continuity tell us when those values settle down near a point. But they do not yet tell us how fast the values change.

On a hillside, we can walk east, north, northeast, or along any path we choose. Each direction may give a different slope. The next chapter begins with the simplest version of that idea: hold all variables still except one, and take an ordinary single-variable derivative in that slice. These are called partial derivatives, and they are the first step toward the full multivariable derivative.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

introduction.p: Partial derivatives use ordinary derivatives along coordinate slices. Directional derivatives, the gradient, and the total derivative then describe change in all input directions. We distinguish the existence of partial derivatives from a valid linear approximation, and organize vector-valued derivatives into Jacobian matrices.

section.title: Partial derivatives
section.p: A contour map tells us where a function has the same value. It does not tell us, by itself, how fast the function changes when we step east or north. To measure that, we return to the single-variable derivative, but we use it on one slice at a time.

subsection.title: Slicing a surface by holding variables fixed
subsection.p: Picture a grassy hill behind an observatory. Let x measure distance east and y measure distance north, and suppose the height of the hill is modeled by H(x,y)=80+3x-y-\frac14 x^2-\frac12 y^2. The height is measured in meters. The input point (x,y) is a point on the map.
At the point P=(2,1), the height is H(2,1)=80+6-1-1-\frac12=\frac{169}{2}=84.5.

Now stand at P and walk directly east. That means y stays fixed at 1, while x changes. Along this east-west slice, the height becomes the one-variable function g(x)=H(x,1). Compute:
g(x) \amp= 80+3x-1-\frac14 x^2-\frac12 \amp= \frac{157}{2}+3x-\frac14 x^2.
The slope of this slice at x=2 is g'(x)=3-\frac12 x, so g'(2)=3-1=2. At P, walking east raises the height at a rate of 2 meters per unit of eastward distance.

Now stand at the same point and walk directly north. This time x stays fixed at 2, while y changes. Along this north-south slice, k(y)=H(2,y). Compute:
k(y) \amp= 80+6-y-1-\frac12y^2 \amp= 85-y-\frac12y^2.
Thus k'(y)=-1-y, and k'(1)=-2. At P, walking north lowers the height at a rate of 2 meters per unit of northward distance.
The same point has two different coordinate slopes: \text{east slope}=2, \qquad \text{north slope}=-2.

figure.caption: To measure coordinate slopes, freeze one coordinate and let the other move.

subsection.p: This is the whole idea of a partial derivative. We do not try to measure all possible directions at once. We take one coordinate direction and use the ordinary derivative there.

statement.p: When we hold y fixed and let only x move, the surface z=H(x,y) becomes a single curve. Why does measuring the slope of that one curve with an ordinary one-variable derivative give us exactly the partial derivative we want, and what role does fixing y play in making this work?

hint.p: Think about what the graph looks like once y is frozen. You are walking along a single trail carved through the hillside, not wandering the whole surface.

subsection.title: The meanings of f_x, f_y, and f_z
subsection.p: The east slope of H at (2,1) came from differentiating with respect to x, while treating y as constant: \frac{\partial H}{\partial x}(2,1)=2. The north slope came from differentiating with respect to y, while treating x as constant: \frac{\partial H}{\partial y}(2,1)=-2.
The symbol \partial reminds us that only part of the input is allowed to move.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. The partial derivative of f with respect to x at (a,b) is \boxed{ f_x(a,b) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)}{h}, } when this limit exists.

subsection.p: These are ordinary derivatives hidden inside a two-variable function.

statement.p: When you compute f_x, which variable is held fixed, and which one is allowed to change? Explain why this makes f_x a rate of change in just one direction, rather than a measure of how f changes overall.

hint.p: Look back at the limit defining f_x(a,b): notice which input is nudged by h and which input never moves at all.

subsection.p: For the hill H(x,y)=80+3x-y-\frac14 x^2-\frac12 y^2, we compute H_x(x,y)=3-\frac12x, because y is treated as constant. Also, H_y(x,y)=-1-y, because x is treated as constant.

example.title: A canopy with two coordinate slopes

statement.p: A slanted fabric canopy over a market stall has height C(x,y)=2+\frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{6}. Then C_x(x,y)=\frac14, \qquad C_y(x,y)=\frac16. So moving one meter east raises the canopy by \frac14 meter, while moving one meter north raises it by \frac16 meter.
This canopy is a plane, so the coordinate slopes are the same at every point.

example.title: A curved surface has slopes that change from point to point

statement.p: Let B(x,y)=10-\frac{x^2}{4}-y^2. Then B_x(x,y)=-\frac{x}{2}, \qquad B_y(x,y)=-2y. At the top point (0,0), B_x(0,0)=0, \qquad B_y(0,0)=0. The surface is level in both coordinate directions.
At the point (2,1), B_x(2,1)=-1, \qquad B_y(2,1)=-2. There, the surface is descending eastward and descending more steeply northward.

subsection.title: Units and interpretation in applications
subsection.p: A partial derivative is a rate. Its units tell the story.
Recall the bakery cost model from : C(u,v)=400+3u+4v+0.01uv, where u is the number of sourdough loaves and v is the number of rye loaves. The output C(u,v) is measured in dollars.
Differentiate with respect to u: C_u(u,v)=3+0.01v. This means: C_u(u,v) = \text{approximate extra cost per additional sourdough loaf,} while the number of rye loaves is held fixed.
Differentiate with respect to v: C_v(u,v)=4+0.01u. This means: C_v(u,v) = \text{approximate extra cost per additional rye loaf,} while the number of sourdough loaves is held fixed.
At (u,v)=(200,100), we get C_u(200,100)=3+1=4, and C_v(200,100)=4+2=6. Near that production level, one more sourdough loaf costs about 4 dollars, while one more rye loaf costs about 6 dollars.
The phrase holding the other variable fixed is not decoration. It is part of the meaning of the derivative.

subsection.title: Partial derivatives in three variables
subsection.p: For a function of three variables, f(x,y,z), there are three coordinate partial derivatives: f_x,\qquad f_y,\qquad f_z. Each one measures the rate of change when one coordinate moves and the other two stay fixed.

example.title: Temperature in a storage room

statement.p: Let T(x,y,z)=18+\frac{4}{1+x^2+y^2}-0.7z, where z is height above the floor in meters. The last term says that higher shelves are cooler.
The partial derivative with respect to z is T_z(x,y,z)=-0.7. So, at every point, increasing height by one meter lowers the temperature by about 0.7^\circC.
The x-partial derivative is T_x(x,y,z) = -\frac{8x}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}. The y-partial derivative is T_y(x,y,z) = -\frac{8y}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}. Those rates depend on where you are horizontally.

subsection.p: A vector-valued function can also have partial derivatives. We differentiate each component.

example.title: Partial derivatives of a vector field

statement.p: The swirling field \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x) has two components: W_1(x,y)=-y, \qquad W_2(x,y)=x. So \mathbf W_x(x,y) = \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(-y),\frac{\partial}{\partial x}x\right) = (0,1), and \mathbf W_y(x,y) = \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(-y),\frac{\partial}{\partial y}x\right) = (-1,0). These vector partial derivatives tell us how the output arrow changes as the input point moves east or north.
Later, in , we will arrange these component derivatives into a matrix. That matrix is the Jacobian.

subsection.title: A warning: coordinate slopes are not the whole surface
subsection.p: It is tempting to believe that if the two coordinate slopes exist, then the function must behave nicely near the point. That is false.
For the x-partial, S_x(0,0) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{S(h,0)-S(0,0)}{h}. But S(h,0)=0 for h\ne0. Therefore S_x(0,0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{0-0}{h}=0.
Similarly, S_y(0,0) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{S(0,h)-S(0,0)}{h} = 0.
So both partial derivatives exist at the origin, and both are 0.
