But the function is not continuous at the origin. Along the line y=x, S(x,x)=\frac{x^2}{2x^2}=\frac12 for x\ne0. Along the x-axis, S(x,0)=0. The two path limits disagree.
So the coordinate slices missed the problem. The function looks flat along the two axes, but it does not settle down near the origin.

statement.p: The two partials f_x and f_y report only the east and north slopes. Why is it that knowing these two numbers does not, by itself, tell you the slope you would feel walking in a diagonal direction such as northeast?

hint.p: A diagonal step changes x and y at the same time. The example above shows a surface whose coordinate slopes are both 0, yet which is far from flat along the line y=x.

subsection.p: This is the derivative version of the warning from : checking only coordinate directions does not check the whole plane.

Partial derivatives give the east and north slopes. But a hiker is not limited to east and north. If the trail points northeast, the slope along the trail mixes the two coordinate slopes. The next question is how to measure the rate of change in a chosen direction.

section.title: Directional derivatives
section.p: measured the change in a function when we moved along one coordinate axis. On a real hill, a trail almost never points exactly east or exactly north. It points in some direction of its own.
A directional derivative measures the slope in that chosen direction.

subsection.title: Rate of change in a chosen direction
subsection.p: Return to the hill H(x,y)=80+3x-y-\frac14x^2-\frac12y^2. At P=(2,1), we found H_x(2,1)=2, \qquad H_y(2,1)=-2. So east is uphill and north is downhill.

Now suppose a trail through P points in the direction \mathbf u=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right). This is a unit vector because \left(\frac35\right)^2+\left(\frac45\right)^2=1. Moving a signed distance t along the trail gives the point (x(t),y(t))=(2,1)+t\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)=\left(2+\frac35t,\;1+\frac45t\right). The height along the trail is the one-variable function g(t)=H\left(2+\frac35t,\;1+\frac45t\right). The slope of the hill along the trail at P is g'(0).

We can differentiate g(t) directly:
g(t) \amp= 80+3\left(2+\frac35t\right)-\left(1+\frac45t\right) \amp\qquad -\frac14\left(2+\frac35t\right)^2-\frac12\left(1+\frac45t\right)^2.
Only the derivative at 0 is needed:
g'(0) \amp= 3\left(\frac35\right)-\frac45-\frac12(2)\left(\frac35\right)-(1)\left(\frac45\right) \amp= \frac95-\frac45-\frac35-\frac45 \amp= -\frac25.
So the trail slopes downward at \frac25 meter per unit distance.

figure.caption: A direction need not be a coordinate direction.

subsection.p: The calculation used only single-variable calculus after we turned the path into a one-variable function.

subsection.title: Directional derivatives from parametrized lines
subsection.p: The same construction works for any scalar field.

Start at a point \mathbf p=(a,b) and choose a unit direction \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2). The line through \mathbf p in direction \mathbf u is \mathbf r(t)=\mathbf p+t\mathbf u=(a+tu_1,b+tu_2). The function along the line is g(t)=f(\mathbf r(t))=f(a+tu_1,b+tu_2). The directional derivative is g'(0).

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R, let \mathbf p=(a,b), and let \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2) be a unit vector.
The directional derivative of f at \mathbf p in the direction \mathbf u is \boxed{D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(\mathbf p+t\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf p)}{t},} when this limit exists.

subsection.p: The same definition works in space. If \mathbf p=(a,b,c) and \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3) is a unit vector, then \boxed{D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(\mathbf p+t\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf p)}{t}.}
The vector \mathbf u is required to have length 1 so that t measures signed distance along the line. Otherwise the number would depend on how fast we chose to walk through the same direction.

example.title: Why the direction vector should be a unit vector

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=x. At the origin, moving in the direction (1,0) gives \frac{f(t,0)-f(0,0)}{t}=\frac{t}{t}=1. So D_{(1,0)}f(0,0)=1.

If we tried to use the non-unit vector (2,0), then the same line would be parametrized by (x,y)=(2t,0). The quotient would be \frac{f(2t,0)-f(0,0)}{t}=\frac{2t}{t}=2. The direction did not change, but the answer doubled. That is not a direction effect. It is a speed effect.
Using unit vectors removes this ambiguity.

subsection.title: The gradient formula for directional derivatives
subsection.p: For the hill H, the directional derivative along \mathbf u=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right) was -\frac25. There is a faster way to compute it.

At P=(2,1), H_x(2,1)=2,\qquad H_y(2,1)=-2. Then
H_x(2,1)\frac35+H_y(2,1)\frac45 \amp= 2\cdot\frac35+(-2)\cdot\frac45 \amp= \frac65-\frac85 \amp= -\frac25.
This matches the direct calculation.

The two partial derivatives have combined with the two components of the direction vector: \left(H_x(2,1),H_y(2,1)\right)\cdot\left(\frac35,\frac45\right). The vector of partial derivatives has a name.

statement.p: For a scalar-valued function f(x,y), the gradient of f is \boxed{\nabla f(x,y)=\left(f_x(x,y),f_y(x,y)\right).}
For a scalar-valued function f(x,y,z), the gradient is \boxed{\nabla f(x,y,z)=\left(f_x(x,y,z),f_y(x,y,z),f_z(x,y,z)\right).}

subsection.p:
For the hill, 
abla H(x,y)=\left(3- rac12x,\,-1-yight). At (2,1), 
abla H(2,1)=(2,-2). Thus D_{\mathbf u}H(2,1)=
abla H(2,1)\cdot\mathbf u.
That formula is not an accident. It works whenever the function is smooth enough near the point.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. Suppose f_x and f_y exist in a small disk around \mathbf p=(a,b), and suppose f_x and f_y are continuous at \mathbf p.

proof.p:
Look at the change from (a,b) to (a+tu_1,b+tu_2). Split it into two coordinate changes:
\amp f(a+tu_1,b+tu_2)-f(a,b) \amp\qquad = \bigl[f(a+tu_1,b+tu_2)-f(a,b+tu_2)\bigr]+\bigl[f(a,b+tu_2)-f(a,b)\bigr].

For the first bracket, only x changes. By the one-variable Mean Value Theorem applied to the x-slice, there is a number \theta_t between 0 and 1 such that f(a+tu_1,b+tu_2)-f(a,b+tu_2)=tu_1\,f_x(a+\theta_ttu_1,b+tu_2). For the second bracket, only y changes. Again by the one-variable Mean Value Theorem, there is a number \eta_t between 0 and 1 such that f(a,b+tu_2)-f(a,b)=tu_2\,f_y(a,b+\eta_ttu_2). Divide by t:
\frac{f(a+tu_1,b+tu_2)-f(a,b)}{t} \amp= u_1\,f_x(a+\theta_ttu_1,b+tu_2) \amp\qquad + u_2\,f_y(a,b+\eta_ttu_2).
As t\to0, the points inside f_x and f_y approach (a,b). Since the partial derivatives are continuous at (a,b), f_x(a+\theta_ttu_1,b+tu_2)\to f_x(a,b), and f_y(a,b+\eta_ttu_2)\to f_y(a,b). Therefore D_{\mathbf u}f(a,b)=u_1f_x(a,b)+u_2f_y(a,b).

exercise.title: Why does one dot product capture every direction?

statement.p: Assume the partial derivatives exist near \mathbf p and are continuous there. The gradient stores only the two coordinate slopes f_x(\mathbf p) and f_y(\mathbf p), yet the formula D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u recovers the slope in every direction \mathbf u. Why should two numbers be enough to determine the rate of change along infinitely many directions?

hint.p: Write a unit direction as \mathbf u=u_1\mathbf i+u_2\mathbf j and think about how a small step t\mathbf u splits into an x-step and a y-step. What does continuity of the partials let you say about combining those two coordinate changes?

subsection.title: Why the continuity hypothesis is there
subsection.p: The theorem required the partial derivatives to be continuous near the point. Having the two partial derivatives at the point is not enough.

Along the x-axis, f(h,0)=0, so f_x(0,0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h}=0. Along the y-axis, f(0,h)=0, so f_y(0,0)=0. Thus \nabla f(0,0)=(0,0). If we tried to use the gradient formula without its hypotheses, it would predict D_{\mathbf u}f(0,0)=0 in every direction.
The moral is precise:
subsection.md: \text{Partial derivatives at one point do not automatically combine into a true slope formula.}
subsection.p: The continuity of the partial derivatives is one way to make sure the coordinate slices fit together into one consistent local picture. will name that picture: the total derivative.

subsection.title: Fastest increase and steepest descent
subsection.p: The gradient formula says D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u. This turns a question about slopes into a question about the dot product.

For the hill at P=(2,1), we found 
abla H(2,1)=(2,-2). The gradient points east and south. Its length is \|
abla H(2,1)\|=\sqrt{2^2+(-2)^2}=2\sqrt2. If we walk in the unit direction \mathbf u= rac{
abla H(2,1)}{\|
abla H(2,1)\|}=\left( rac1{\sqrt2},- rac1{\sqrt2}ight), then
D_{\mathbf u}H(2,1) \amp= 
abla H(2,1)\cdot\mathbf u \amp= \|
abla H(2,1)\| \amp= 2\sqrt2.
That is the steepest uphill direction.

exercise.title: Why the gradient, and why its length?

statement.p: The steepest uphill direction turns out to be the gradient's own direction, and the steepest rate equals \|\nabla f(\mathbf p)\|. Using D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u, explain why pointing \mathbf u any other way can only give a smaller rate.

hint.p: Rewrite the dot product as \|\nabla f(\mathbf p)\|\cos\theta, where \theta is the angle between \mathbf u and the gradient. Which value of \theta makes \cos\theta as large as it can be?

subsection.p: If we walk in the opposite direction, -\mathbf u=\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2}\right), then D_{-\mathbf u}H(2,1)=-2\sqrt2. That is the steepest downhill direction.

proof.p:
For any unit vector \mathbf u, D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=
abla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u. By the dot product formula, 
abla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u=\|
abla f(\mathbf p)\|\,\|\mathbf u\|\cos	heta, where 	heta is the angle between 
abla f(\mathbf p) and \mathbf u. Since \|\mathbf u\|=1, this becomes D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\|
abla f(\mathbf p)\|\cos	heta. The largest possible value of \cos	heta is 1, when the two vectors point in the same direction. The smallest possible value is -1, when they point in opposite directions.

subsection.p: If \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\mathbf 0, then the gradient formula gives D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=0 for every unit direction \mathbf u. In that case the first-order test sees no uphill or downhill direction. The point might be a peak, a valley, a saddle, or something flatter. We will need second derivatives later to tell those apart.

subsection.title: The gradient and contour maps
subsection.p: The gradient also explains a feature of contour maps.

Suppose f has continuous first partial derivatives near a point \mathbf p, and a differentiable level curve \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)) passes through \mathbf p=\mathbf r(t_0) with \mathbf r'(t_0)\ne\mathbf0. We must relate change along this curved path to change along its tangent line.

Use the same coordinate-increment decomposition as in the proof above, now with \Delta x=x(t_0+h)-x(t_0) and \Delta y=y(t_0+h)-y(t_0). The one-variable Mean Value Theorem writes the change in f as f_x at a nearby point times \Delta x, plus f_y at a nearby point times \Delta y. Divide by h and let h\to0. Continuity of the partials and differentiability of the curve give 0=\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))\bigg|_{t=t_0}=f_x(\mathbf p)x'(t_0)+f_y(\mathbf p)y'(t_0)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf r'(t_0). The left side is zero because f is constant on the curve. For the unit tangent \mathbf t=\mathbf r'(t_0)/\|\mathbf r'(t_0)\|, this says \nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf t=0. If the gradient is nonzero, it therefore points perpendicular to the tangent. This special case uses the same one-variable argument; the general chain rule will be developed in Chapter 8.

exercise.title: Why does the gradient cut straight across a contour?

statement.p: Under the smoothness and nonzero-gradient assumptions just stated, walking along a level curve keeps the value of f constant, so the rate of change along the curve is 0. Explain why this single fact forces the gradient to be perpendicular to the level curve, rather than tilted at some other angle to it.

hint.p: If \mathbf t is a unit tangent to the level curve, then \nabla f\cdot\mathbf t=0. What does a zero dot product say about the angle between two nonzero vectors?

subsection.md: \text{The gradient points across contour lines, not along them.}

figure.caption: On a contour map, the gradient points in the direction of fastest increase, perpendicular to the level curve.

subsection.p: This matches how hikers read contour maps. Closely spaced contour lines mean steep ground. The steepest path crosses the contours as directly as possible.

The gradient packages the coordinate slopes into a vector. Directional derivatives use that vector to predict slopes along lines. But the counterexample above left a gap: when do the coordinate slopes really fit together into one reliable linear approximation?

That question leads to the main idea of multivariable differentiation. Near a good point, a curved surface should look like a plane, just as a curved graph in single-variable calculus looked like a line. The next section turns that sentence into a formula.

section.title: The total derivative as the best linear approximation
section.p: measured slopes in chosen directions. The gradient formula said that, at a good point, D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot \mathbf u. That formula is really a shadow of a larger idea. Near a good point, the whole function should be predicted by one linear rule.

subsection.title: Why partial derivatives alone are not yet the derivative
subsection.p: Return to the hill H(x,y)=80+3x-y-\frac14x^2-\frac12y^2. At P=(2,1), we found H_x(2,1)=2, \qquad H_y(2,1)=-2. These two numbers tell us the east slope and the north slope. But a small step on the map may mix east and north.

Let the small displacement be (\Delta x,\Delta y). Then the new point is (2+\Delta x,\;1+\Delta y). Compute the height change: H(2+\Delta x,1+\Delta y)-H(2,1). Since H(2,1)=\frac{169}{2}, we get
\amp H(2+\Delta x,1+\Delta y)-H(2,1) \amp\qquad = 2\Delta x-2\Delta y-\frac14(\Delta x)^2-\frac12(\Delta y)^2.
The first part, 2\Delta x-2\Delta y, is linear in the displacement. The remaining part, -\frac14(\Delta x)^2-\frac12(\Delta y)^2, is quadratic. For a small step, the quadratic terms are much smaller than the linear terms.

For example, take \Delta x=0.10, \qquad \Delta y=0.20. The linear prediction is 2(0.10)-2(0.20)=-0.20. The quadratic error is -\frac14(0.10)^2-\frac12(0.20)^2 = -0.0025-0.0200 = -0.0225. So the actual height change is -0.2225. The linear part predicted most of the change. The error was smaller because it involved squares of the step sizes.

This is what we want from a derivative in several variables. It should not be only a list of coordinate slopes. It should be a linear machine that takes a small displacement as input and returns the predicted change in the function.

statement.p: Suppose you stand at a point and you know both partial derivatives f_x and f_y exist there. Why does that still not guarantee the function is differentiable? Think about which displacements those two numbers actually report on, and which ones they say nothing about.

hint.p: A partial derivative only watches the function along a single coordinate line. A small step like (\Delta x,\Delta y) with both parts nonzero travels along none of those lines.

subsection.p: For the hill at P, that machine is L(\Delta x,\Delta y)=2\Delta x-2\Delta y.

subsection.title: Linear approximation in two variables
subsection.p: The same pattern appears for any well-behaved function f(x,y). Near a point (a,b), a small displacement (\Delta x,\Delta y) should give f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b) approximately equal to a linear function of (\Delta x,\Delta y). If the partial derivatives fit together correctly, that linear function is f_x(a,b)\Delta x+f_y(a,b)\Delta y.
So the local linear approximation is \boxed{ f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y) \approx f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)\Delta x+f_y(a,b)\Delta y. }
Equivalently, if x=a+\Delta x, \qquad y=b+\Delta y, then \boxed{ f(x,y) \approx f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b). }
For the hill, H(2+\Delta x,1+\Delta y) \approx H(2,1)+2\Delta x-2\Delta y. Since H(2,1)=\frac{169}{2}, this says H(2+\Delta x,1+\Delta y) \approx \frac{169}{2}+2\Delta x-2\Delta y.
The approximation is not merely a formula. It is a plane pretending, for a short distance, to be the curved surface.

subsection.title: Differentiability and the total derivative
subsection.p: The word differentiable means that this linear prediction is genuinely the first part of the change.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R, and suppose (a,b) is an interior point of D. We say that f is differentiable at (a,b) if there is a linear function L:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R such that \boxed{ f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y) = f(a,b)+L(\Delta x,\Delta y)+R(\Delta x,\Delta y), } where the error satisfies \boxed{ \lim_{(\Delta x,\Delta y)\to(0,0)} \frac{|R(\Delta x,\Delta y)|} {\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}} = 0. }
The linear function L is called the total derivative of f at (a,b). We write L=Df(a,b).

subsection.p: The error condition says more than R(\Delta x,\Delta y)\to0. It says the error is small compared with the step length \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}. That is why the linear part is truly the first-order part of the change.

There is only one possible linear function L. If two linear functions both made the error small in this sense, their difference would be a linear function that is smaller than first order in every direction. A nonzero linear function cannot do that. Along any direction where it is not zero, it grows exactly like the step length.

exercise.title: What does the limit buy you?

statement.p: The total derivative needs more than the partial derivatives merely existing. In the definition, what is the extra demand placed on the error R(\Delta x,\Delta y), and why is it stronger than just asking that R\to 0?

hint.p: Look at what R is divided by before the limit is taken. The error must shrink faster than the step length \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}, and it must do so for every direction of approach at once.

subsection.p: So it makes sense to say the total derivative.

theorem.title: The total derivative uses the partial derivatives

statement.p: If f is differentiable at (a,b), then the partial derivatives f_x(a,b),\qquad f_y(a,b) exist, and \boxed{ Df(a,b)(\Delta x,\Delta y) = f_x(a,b)\Delta x+f_y(a,b)\Delta y. }

proof.p: Because f is differentiable, f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y) = f(a,b)+Df(a,b)(\Delta x,\Delta y)+R(\Delta x,\Delta y), where \frac{|R(\Delta x,\Delta y)|}{\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}}\to0.

First move only in the x-direction. Set \Delta y=0. Then f(a+\Delta x,b)-f(a,b) = Df(a,b)(\Delta x,0)+R(\Delta x,0). Divide by \Delta x: \frac{f(a+\Delta x,b)-f(a,b)}{\Delta x} = \frac{Df(a,b)(\Delta x,0)}{\Delta x} + \frac{R(\Delta x,0)}{\Delta x}. Since Df(a,b) is linear, Df(a,b)(\Delta x,0)=\Delta x\,Df(a,b)(1,0). Also, \frac{R(\Delta x,0)}{\Delta x}\to0. Therefore f_x(a,b)=Df(a,b)(1,0).
The same argument with \Delta x=0 gives f_y(a,b)=Df(a,b)(0,1).

Now use linearity. Since (\Delta x,\Delta y)=\Delta x(1,0)+\Delta y(0,1), we get
Df(a,b)(\Delta x,\Delta y) \amp= \Delta x\,Df(a,b)(1,0)+\Delta y\,Df(a,b)(0,1) \amp= f_x(a,b)\Delta x+f_y(a,b)\Delta y.

subsection.p: This theorem says that if the total derivative exists, then its formula is forced. The partial derivatives are the coefficients of the best linear approximation.
The converse is false. Partial derivatives can exist without fitting together into a true linear approximation.

subsection.title: A warning: partial derivatives can fail to stitch together
subsection.p: But along the diagonal path y=x, we have f(x,x)=\frac{x^3}{2x^2}=\frac{x}{2} for x\ne0. The error, compared with the zero linear approximation, is R(x,x)=\frac{x}{2}. The step length is \sqrt{x^2+x^2}=\sqrt2\,|x|. Thus \frac{|R(x,x)|}{\sqrt{x^2+x^2}} = \frac{|x|/2}{\sqrt2\,|x|} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}. This does not approach 0.
So f is not differentiable at the origin.

The partial derivatives at the origin saw only the two coordinate slices. The total derivative asks for one linear approximation that works for all small displacements at once. That is a stronger demand.

subsection.title: Directional derivatives from the total derivative
subsection.p: The total derivative explains why the gradient formula worked in .

Suppose f is differentiable at \mathbf p, and let \mathbf u be a unit vector. For small t, f(\mathbf p+t\mathbf u) = f(\mathbf p)+Df(\mathbf p)(t\mathbf u)+R(t\mathbf u). By linearity, Df(\mathbf p)(t\mathbf u)=t\,Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf u). So \frac{f(\mathbf p+t\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf p)}{t} = Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf u)+\frac{R(t\mathbf u)}{t}. The error term goes to 0, because \frac{|R(t\mathbf u)|}{|t|}\to0. Therefore \boxed{ D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf u). }
In two variables, Df(a,b)(u_1,u_2) = f_x(a,b)u_1+f_y(a,b)u_2, so \boxed{ D_{\mathbf u}f(a,b) = \nabla f(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u. }
The gradient formula is therefore not the definition of differentiability. It is a consequence of differentiability.

subsection.title: The tangent plane as a linear model
subsection.p: For a function of one variable, differentiability means that the graph has a good tangent line approximation: f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x. For a function of two variables, the graph is a surface, and the linear approximation is a plane.

statement.p: Suppose z=f(x,y) and f is differentiable at (a,b). The tangent plane to the graph of f at (a,b,f(a,b)) is \boxed{ z= f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b). }

subsection.p: For the hill H, at (a,b)=(2,1), we have H(2,1)=\frac{169}{2}, \qquad H_x(2,1)=2, \qquad H_y(2,1)=-2. So the tangent plane is z=\frac{169}{2}+2(x-2)-2(y-1). Simplifying, \boxed{ z=\frac{165}{2}+2x-2y. }

figure.caption: A differentiable surface is locally modeled by its tangent plane. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The tangent plane does not claim that the surface is actually flat. It says that, under a magnifying glass centered at the point, the surface becomes harder and harder to distinguish from this plane.

statement.p: The two partial derivatives already give you a slope going east and a slope going north. Why does differentiability promise something more, namely a single genuine tangent plane rather than just two tangent lines crossing at the point?

hint.p: Two tangent lines fix the plane's tilt, but a plane also has to approximate the surface along every direction in between. Differentiability is exactly the condition that makes one plane do that job for all small displacements at once.

subsection.title: Differentiability in \mathbb R^n
subsection.p: The definition does not depend on the plane. It works in any number of input variables.

definition.title: Differentiability for scalar fields on \mathbb R^n

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, and let \mathbf p be an interior point of D. We say that f is differentiable at \mathbf p if there is a linear function L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R such that \boxed{ f(\mathbf p+\mathbf h) = f(\mathbf p)+L(\mathbf h)+R(\mathbf h), } where \boxed{ \lim_{\mathbf h\to\mathbf 0} \frac{|R(\mathbf h)|}{\|\mathbf h\|}=0. } The linear function L is called the total derivative: L=Df(\mathbf p).

subsection.p: If \mathbf p=(a_1,\ldots,a_n), then differentiability forces \boxed{ Df(\mathbf p)(h_1,\ldots,h_n) = f_{x_1}(\mathbf p)h_1+\cdots+f_{x_n}(\mathbf p)h_n. }

example.title: A three-variable temperature model

statement.p: Recall the storage-room temperature model T(x,y,z)=18+\frac{4}{1+x^2+y^2}-0.7z. At the point (1,0,2), the temperature is T(1,0,2)=18+\frac{4}{2}-1.4=18.6. The partial derivatives are T_x(x,y,z)= -\frac{8x}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}, T_y(x,y,z)= -\frac{8y}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}, and T_z(x,y,z)=-0.7. Thus T_x(1,0,2)=-2, \qquad T_y(1,0,2)=0, \qquad T_z(1,0,2)=-0.7. The total derivative at (1,0,2) is the linear function DT(1,0,2)(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z) = -2\Delta x-0.7\Delta z. A small move (\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)=(0.02,-0.03,0.10) therefore changes the temperature by about -2(0.02)-0.7(0.10) = -0.11. So the model predicts a drop of about 0.11^\circ\text{C}.

subsection.p: A three-variable scalar field has no ordinary graph in three-dimensional space, because its graph would live in four dimensions: (x,y,z,T(x,y,z)). But the total derivative still exists as a linear approximation. The picture is no longer a tangent plane we can draw. The idea is the same: a nonlinear function is replaced, near one point, by its best linear part.

The notation Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf h) is honest, but it is a little heavy. The linear function Df(\mathbf p) eats a small displacement \mathbf h and returns the predicted change in f. There is an older notation that says the same thing in a way that will later become the language of line integrals: df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy. To make that formula more than a symbol, we have to decide what dx and dy are. We already met them as coordinate-reading linear functions. Now they return as the first examples of 1-forms.

section.title: Differentials
section.p: made the total derivative into a linear function: Df(\mathbf p)(\Delta\mathbf x). It takes a small displacement and returns the predicted change in f. already gave us the simplest linear functions: dx,\qquad dy,\qquad dz. They read off components of a vector. Differentials combine these component-readers with the partial derivatives.

subsection.title: The differential as a linear function of small changes
subsection.p: Return to the bakery cost model from : C(u,v)=400+3u+4v+0.01uv, where u is the number of sourdough loaves and v is the number of rye loaves.

We computed C_u(u,v)=3+0.01v, \qquad C_v(u,v)=4+0.01u. At (u,v)=(200,100), these become C_u(200,100)=4, \qquad C_v(200,100)=6. So the total derivative at this production level is DC(200,100)(\Delta u,\Delta v) = 4\Delta u+6\Delta v.
Suppose the bakery changes production by \Delta u=4, \qquad \Delta v=3. The linear prediction is 4(4)+6(3)=34. So the cost should increase by about 34 dollars.

The exact change is
\amp C(200+\Delta u,100+\Delta v)-C(200,100) \amp\qquad = 4\Delta u+6\Delta v+0.01\Delta u\Delta v.
For \Delta u=4,\qquad \Delta v=3, this gives 34+0.01(4)(3)=34.12. The differential predicted the first-order part. The extra 0.12 came from the product of the two small changes.

statement.p: If f is differentiable at \mathbf p, then the differential of f at \mathbf p is the total derivative: \boxed{ df_{\mathbf p}=Df(\mathbf p). } Thus df_{\mathbf p} is a linear function of a small displacement.

subsection.p: For the bakery, dC_{(200,100)}(\Delta u,\Delta v) = 4\Delta u+6\Delta v.
The letter d is not decoration. It means: take the first-order change.

statement.p: We could have defined df_{\mathbf p} as the single number 34 we got from the bakery, the predicted cost change for one particular move. Instead we kept it as the whole linear function df_{\mathbf p}(\Delta u,\Delta v)=4\Delta u+6\Delta v. Why is the function the better object? What would we lose if we collapsed df_{\mathbf p} down to a tiny number?

hint.p: A single number answers one question; a function answers infinitely many at once. Ask yourself what changes (and what stays the same) if the bakery picks a different step (\Delta u,\Delta v).

subsection.title: The notation df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy

figure.caption: The linear functions dx and dy read off the components of a displacement.

example.title: The hill differential

statement.p: For H(x,y)=80+3x-y-\frac14x^2-\frac12y^2, we have H_x(x,y)=3-\frac12x, \qquad H_y(x,y)=-1-y. At (2,1), H_x(2,1)=2, \qquad H_y(2,1)=-2. So \boxed{ dH_{(2,1)}=2\,dx-2\,dy. }

If the trail direction is \mathbf u=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right), then
dH_{(2,1)}(\mathbf u) \amp= 2\,dx(\mathbf u)-2\,dy(\mathbf u) \amp= 2\left(\frac35\right)-2\left(\frac45\right) \amp= -\frac25.
This is exactly the directional derivative found in .

subsection.p: The gradient and the differential contain the same coefficients, but they play different roles: \nabla f(a,b)=\bigl(f_x(a,b),f_y(a,b)\bigr) is a vector, while df_{(a,b)}=f_x(a,b)\,dx+f_y(a,b)\,dy is a linear function that acts on displacement vectors.
The dot product connects them: df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf h)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot \mathbf h.

subsection.title: Error estimates and small-change calculations
subsection.p: The differential is useful because it is the part of the change we can compute quickly. If f is differentiable at \mathbf p, then f(\mathbf p+\Delta\mathbf x)-f(\mathbf p) = df_{\mathbf p}(\Delta\mathbf x)+R(\Delta\mathbf x), where \frac{|R(\Delta\mathbf x)|}{\|\Delta\mathbf x\|}\to0. So for small changes, \boxed{ \Delta f\approx df. }
This is the multivariable version of the single-variable estimate \Delta y\approx f'(a)\Delta x.

exercise.title: When does \Delta f\approx df hold up?

statement.p: In the line f(\mathbf p+\Delta\mathbf x)-f(\mathbf p)=df_{\mathbf p}(\Delta\mathbf x)+R(\Delta\mathbf x), the remainder satisfies |R|/\|\Delta\mathbf x\|\to0. Explain in your own words why this makes df a good estimate for a small step. Then describe a situation where you should not trust \Delta f\approx df, even though the formula is still technically true.

hint.p: The condition only says R shrinks faster than \|\Delta\mathbf x\| as the step goes to zero, it promises nothing for a large step. Think about the leftover 0.12 and 0.000194 terms in the worked examples, and what happens to them when the step is no longer small.

subsection.p: In a numerical small-change calculation, the customary notation dx=0.02 abbreviates the value of the coordinate measurement on the chosen displacement: dx(\Delta\mathbf x)=\Delta x=0.02. Similarly, a numerical df means df_{\mathbf p}(\Delta\mathbf x), the predicted change for that displacement. The underlying differential remains a linear function, not an infinitesimal number.

example.title: Measuring the volume of a storage bin

statement.p: A rectangular storage bin has side lengths x,\qquad y,\qquad z in meters. Its volume is V(x,y,z)=xyz. Then V_x=yz, \qquad V_y=xz, \qquad V_z=xy. At (x,y,z)=(2,3,5), we get V_x=15, \qquad V_y=10, \qquad V_z=6. So dV_{(2,3,5)} = 15\,dx+10\,dy+6\,dz.

Suppose the measured side lengths change by dx=0.02, \qquad dy=-0.01, \qquad dz=0.03. Then
dV \amp= 15(0.02)+10(-0.01)+6(0.03) \amp= 0.30-0.10+0.18 \amp= 0.38.
So the volume changes by about 0.38\ \text{m}^3.
The exact change is (2.02)(2.99)(5.03)-30 = 0.380194. The differential gives the first-order part. The missing 0.000194 comes from products of the small side-length changes.

subsection.p: Differentials are often used this way in measurements. If the inputs have small errors, the differential estimates the resulting output error.

example.title: Temperature sensitivity

statement.p: For the storage-room temperature model T(x,y,z)=18+\frac{4}{1+x^2+y^2}-0.7z, we found at (1,0,2) dT_{(1,0,2)}=-2\,dx-0.7\,dz. There is no dy term at that point because T_y(1,0,2)=0. A small move dx=0.02,\qquad dy=-0.03,\qquad dz=0.10 therefore gives dT=-2(0.02)-0.7(0.10)=-0.11. The dy-change does not affect the first-order estimate at this particular point.

subsection.p: A differential tells us which input errors matter most near the point. The coefficient of dx measures sensitivity to x. The coefficient of dy measures sensitivity to y. The coefficient of dz measures sensitivity to z.

subsection.title: Differentials as the first examples of 1-forms
subsection.p: The expression df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy is a special kind of object. It is a rule that assigns, at each point, a linear function of small displacements.
That is exactly the concrete meaning of a 1-form.

exercise.title: What does df eat, and what does it return?

statement.p: People often call a 1-form like df a machine: feed it a direction (a small displacement) at a point and it hands back a single number. Using df_{(2,1)}=2\,dx-2\,dy as your example, say in plain words what you must supply to the machine and what it gives you back. In what sense is df therefore a different kind of object than the function f itself?

hint.p: The function f eats a point and returns a value; df at a point eats a direction and returns a rate of change. Notice that dx and dy are themselves such machines, they just read off one component of the displacement you feed in.

statement.p: A 1-form on a region D\subseteq\mathbb R^2 is an expression \boxed{ \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy. } At a point \mathbf p=(x,y), it acts on a displacement \Delta\mathbf x=(\Delta x,\Delta y) by \boxed{ \omega_{\mathbf p}(\Delta\mathbf x) = P(x,y)\Delta x+Q(x,y)\Delta y. }

subsection.p: A differential df is a 1-form: \boxed{ df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy } in the plane, and \boxed{ df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz } in space.

statement.p: A 1-form \omega is called exact if there is a function f such that \omega=df.

subsection.p: For example, \omega=2x\,dx+2y\,dy is exact, because \omega=d(x^2+y^2). But a general 1-form need not come from a function. The swirling form \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy is built from the vector field \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x). At each point it measures how much a small displacement points with the swirl: \omega_{(x,y)}(\Delta x,\Delta y) = -y\Delta x+x\Delta y. Whether such a form is a differential of some scalar field is a separate question. We will need line integrals and curl before we can answer it well.
For now, df is the bridge between ordinary functions and 1-forms. A function has values. Its differential measures first-order change. A 1-form is ready to be added along a curve.

There is one more piece in this chapter before curves return. A scalar function has one differential: df. A transformation F=(F_1,F_2,\ldots,F_m) has one differential for each component: dF_1,\quad dF_2,\quad \ldots,\quad dF_m. Stacking these linear functions into rows gives the matrix of the total derivative. That matrix is the Jacobian, and it tells how a nonlinear map moves small grids near a point.

section.title: The Jacobian matrix
section.p: turned the derivative of a scalar function into a 1-form: df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy. That was one linear function. But many transformations have several output components. Each component has its own differential, and those differentials want to be stacked.
That stack is the Jacobian matrix.

subsection.title: A rubber sheet map
subsection.p: Imagine a square grid printed on a thin rubber sheet. The sheet is pulled so that a point (x,y) moves to a new point F(x,y)=(X(x,y),Y(x,y)). Suppose the rule is \boxed{ F(x,y)= \left( x+\frac15xy,\; y+\frac1{10}x^2 \right). } This is not a linear transformation, because of the terms xy and x^2. But near one point it should look almost linear if the point is viewed closely enough.
Take P=(2,1). Then F(2,1)= \left( 2+\frac25,\; 1+\frac4{10} \right) = \left(\frac{12}{5},\frac75\right).

Now make a small step (\Delta x,\Delta y) from P. The new point is (2+\Delta x,\;1+\Delta y). Compute the change in the first output:
X(2+\Delta x,1+\Delta y)-X(2,1) \amp= \left(2+\Delta x+\frac15(2+\Delta x)(1+\Delta y)\right)-\frac{12}{5} \amp= \frac65\Delta x+\frac25\Delta y+\frac15\Delta x\,\Delta y.
The linear part is \frac65\Delta x+\frac25\Delta y.

Now compute the change in the second output:
Y(2+\Delta x,1+\Delta y)-Y(2,1) \amp= \left(1+\Delta y+\frac1{10}(2+\Delta x)^2\right)-\frac75 \amp= \frac25\Delta x+\Delta y+\frac1{10}(\Delta x)^2.
The linear part is \frac25\Delta x+\Delta y.

That matrix is the derivative of the transformation F at P. Write its columns as F_x(P)=(6/5,2/5) and F_y(P)=(2/5,1): these are the componentwise rates of change when only the indicated input varies. The image displacements predicted for steps of sizes \Delta x and \Delta y are \Delta x\,F_x(P) and \Delta y\,F_y(P).

figure.caption: Near one point, a nonlinear map sends a small square almost to a parallelogram. The derivative matrix gives that parallelogram.

subsection.title: Derivatives of transformations
subsection.p: A scalar function has one output. A transformation F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m has m output components: F(\mathbf x)= \bigl(F_1(\mathbf x),F_2(\mathbf x),\ldots,F_m(\mathbf x)\bigr). Each component F_i is a scalar-valued function.
The derivative should be the best linear map from input displacements to output displacements.

statement.p: Let F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, and let \mathbf p be an interior point of D. We say that F is differentiable at \mathbf p if there is a linear map A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m such that \boxed{ F(\mathbf p+\mathbf h) = F(\mathbf p)+A\mathbf h+\mathbf R(\mathbf h), } where \boxed{ \lim_{\mathbf h\to\mathbf 0} \frac{\norm{\mathbf R(\mathbf h)}}{\norm{\mathbf h}}=0. } The linear map A is called the total derivative of F at \mathbf p, and we write A=DF(\mathbf p).

subsection.p: This is the vector-valued version of the definition in . The only change is that the error is now a vector, so we measure its size with a norm.
If F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m) is differentiable at \mathbf p, then each component F_i is differentiable at \mathbf p. Its differential gives one row of the derivative matrix.

subsection.title: The Jacobian matrix
subsection.p: Let F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m have component functions F_1,\ldots,F_m. Use input coordinates x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n. The partial derivatives form an m\times n matrix: \boxed{ J_F(\mathbf p) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf p) \amp \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_2}(\mathbf p) \amp \cdots \amp \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf p) \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf p) \amp \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial x_2}(\mathbf p) \amp \cdots \amp \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf p) \\ \vdots \amp \vdots \amp \ddots \amp \vdots \\[1mm] \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf p) \amp \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_2}(\mathbf p) \amp \cdots \amp \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf p) \end{pmatrix}. } This matrix is called the Jacobian matrix of F at \mathbf p. It is also called the Jacobi matrix.

statement.p: A map F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m sends inputs to outputs, yet its derivative turns out to be a whole m\times n matrix of partial derivatives rather than a single number. Where do the m rows and the n columns come from? What is each partial derivative \partial F_i/\partial x_j actually keeping track of?

hint.p: Think about what you must specify to predict an output change: there are m separate output components to track, and each one can respond to a nudge in any of the n input directions.

subsection.p: For the rubber sheet map, F(x,y)= \left( x+\frac15xy,\; y+\frac1{10}x^2 \right), we have F_1(x,y)=x+\frac15xy, \qquad F_2(x,y)=y+\frac1{10}x^2. The partial derivatives are \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x}=1+\frac15y, \qquad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}=\frac15x, and \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x}=\frac15x, \qquad \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y}=1. So \boxed{ J_F(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 1+\frac15y \amp \frac15x\\[1mm] \frac15x \amp 1 \end{pmatrix}. } At P=(2,1), \boxed{ J_F(2,1) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac65 \amp \frac25\\[1mm] \frac25 \amp 1 \end{pmatrix}. } This is exactly the matrix found by expanding the map near P.

subsection.title: Rows as differentials of component functions
subsection.p: The row viewpoint is the one that connects directly to differentials.

For F=(F_1,F_2), the component differentials are dF_1=F_{1x}\,dx+F_{1y}\,dy, and dF_2=F_{2x}\,dx+F_{2y}\,dy. At a point P, these become dF_{1,P}=F_{1x}(P)\,dx+F_{1y}(P)\,dy, dF_{2,P}=F_{2x}(P)\,dx+F_{2y}(P)\,dy. Stacking them gives \boxed{ J_F(P) = \begin{pmatrix} \text{coefficients of }dF_{1,P}\\ \text{coefficients of }dF_{2,P} \end{pmatrix}. }
For the rubber sheet map at P=(2,1), dF_{1,P}=\frac65\,dx+\frac25\,dy, and dF_{2,P}=\frac25\,dx+dy. Therefore J_F(P) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac65 \amp \frac25\\[1mm] \frac25 \amp 1 \end{pmatrix}.
Rows measure how each output coordinate changes.

Columns tell a different story. The first column is the output rate of change per unit step in the x-direction: F_x(P)= \begin{pmatrix} F_{1x}(P)\\ F_{2x}(P) \end{pmatrix}. The second column is the output rate of change per unit step in the y-direction: F_y(P)= \begin{pmatrix} F_{1y}(P)\\ F_{2y}(P) \end{pmatrix}. A step of size \Delta x therefore produces approximately \Delta x\,F_x(P), and similarly for \Delta y. So the rows are differentials of component functions, while the columns are images of unit coordinate directions under the derivative.
Both views are useful.

subsection.title: Local linearization of nonlinear maps

statement.p: The local linearization says F(\mathbf p+\mathbf h)\approx F(\mathbf p)+J_F(\mathbf p)\mathbf h. In plain words, what is the Jacobian matrix J_F(\mathbf p) telling you about how the map behaves in a tiny neighborhood of \mathbf p? What kind of map does F look like up close, and why does the curving part of F not appear in this picture?

hint.p: Imagine zooming in on \mathbf p until the bending of F is too small to notice. What is left of the map is captured entirely by J_F(\mathbf p) acting on the displacement \mathbf h.

example.title: A small displacement through the rubber map

statement.p:
Use F(x,y)= \left( x+\frac15xy,\; y+\frac1{10}x^2 \right) at P=(2,1), and take \mathbf h=(0.03,-0.04). The linear prediction is
J_F(P)\mathbf h \amp= \begin{pmatrix} \frac65 \amp \frac25\\[1mm] \frac25 \amp 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0.03\\ -0.04 \end{pmatrix} \amp= \begin{pmatrix} \frac65(0.03)+\frac25(-0.04)\\[1mm] \frac25(0.03)-0.04 \end{pmatrix} \amp= \begin{pmatrix} 0.020\\ -0.028 \end{pmatrix}.
So F(2.03,0.96) \approx F(2,1)+(0.020,-0.028). Since F(2,1)=\left(\frac{12}{5},\frac75\right)=(2.4,1.4), the prediction is F(2.03,0.96)\approx(2.420,1.372).

The exact value is
F(2.03,0.96) \amp= \left( 2.03+\frac15(2.03)(0.96),\; 0.96+\frac1{10}(2.03)^2 \right) \amp= (2.41976,\;1.37209).
The Jacobian gave the first-order change. The remaining error came from products and squares of the small displacement components.

subsection.title: A parametrized surface and its Jacobian
subsection.p: The Jacobian matrix also works when the output dimension is larger than the input dimension.

In , holding one parameter fixed produced a coordinate curve. In , we found its tangent velocity by taking an ordinary derivative while the other parameter stayed fixed. The partial-derivative notation from now names exactly that operation. For \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)), the notation means \mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)=(x_u,y_u,z_u)(u_0,v_0)=\left.\frac{d}{du}\mathbf r(u,v_0)\right|_{u=u_0}, and \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0)=(x_v,y_v,z_v)(u_0,v_0)=\left.\frac{d}{dv}\mathbf r(u_0,v)\right|_{v=v_0}. These vectors are the two columns of J_{\mathbf r}. If \mathbf r is differentiable at (u_0,v_0), its linear approximation is \mathbf r(u_0+\Delta u,v_0+\Delta v)-\mathbf r(u_0,v_0)\approx\Delta u\,\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)+\Delta v\,\mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). Continuous first partial derivatives near the point are sufficient, by applying the scalar differentiability criterion component by component. The next section proves that criterion. A nonzero column is tangent to its coordinate curve; two independent columns span a tangent plane. The systematic regularity conditions are developed in .

Let \mathbf s(u,v)= \left( u,\; v,\; 2+\frac{u^2}{4}-\frac{v^2}{9} \right). This is a parametrized surface: \mathbf s:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3. The component functions are s_1(u,v)=u, \qquad s_2(u,v)=v, \qquad s_3(u,v)=2+\frac{u^2}{4}-\frac{v^2}{9}. The Jacobian matrix is \boxed{ J_{\mathbf s}(u,v) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 1\\[1mm] \frac{u}{2} \amp -\frac{2v}{9} \end{pmatrix}. } This is a 3\times2 matrix. It cannot have a determinant, because it is not square.

Its columns are \mathbf s_u(u,v)= \left(1,0,\frac{u}{2}\right), and \mathbf s_v(u,v)= \left(0,1,-\frac{2v}{9}\right). These are independent tangent directions on this smooth graph. A step of size \Delta u produces approximately \Delta u\,\mathbf s_u; a step of size \Delta v produces approximately \Delta v\,\mathbf s_v.

At (u,v)=(2,3), the tangent directions are \mathbf s_u(2,3)=(1,0,1), and \mathbf s_v(2,3)=\left(0,1,-\frac23\right). So near the surface point \mathbf s(2,3)= \left(2,3,2+1-1\right)=(2,3,2), the surface is locally approximated by \boxed{ \mathbf s(2+\Delta u,3+\Delta v) \approx (2,3,2) + \Delta u(1,0,1) + \Delta v\left(0,1,-\frac23\right). } This is a tangent plane written in vector form.

subsection.title: The Jacobian determinant as local area or volume scaling
subsection.p: A determinant appears only when the Jacobian matrix is square: F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n. Then \det J_F(\mathbf p) measures the signed scaling of the derivative when F is differentiable.

For a map F(x,y)=(X(x,y),Y(x,y)), the Jacobian determinant is \boxed{ \frac{\partial(X,Y)}{\partial(x,y)} = \det \begin{pmatrix} X_x \amp X_y\\ Y_x \amp Y_y \end{pmatrix} = X_xY_y-X_yY_x. } At a point, this number tells how a tiny signed area is scaled.

statement.p: When F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n is differentiable at \mathbf p, the number \det J_F(\mathbf p) appears. What does this single number tell you about how the map treats a tiny region near \mathbf p? And what extra information is carried by its sign that its size alone does not?

hint.p: A tiny square or cube near \mathbf p gets pushed to a tiny parallelogram or parallelepiped. Think about how its area or volume changes, and about whether the map flips the region over or keeps its orientation.

subsection.p: For the rubber sheet map, J_F(2,1) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac65 \amp \frac25\\[1mm] \frac25 \amp 1 \end{pmatrix}. Therefore \boxed{ \det J_F(2,1) = \frac65\cdot1-\frac25\cdot\frac25 = \frac{26}{25}. } So a very small area near P=(2,1) is expanded by a factor of about \frac{26}{25}=1.04. The determinant is positive, so the local orientation is preserved.

The same fact can be written using the algebra from . Here dX and dY mean differentials of the component functions on the input plane, evaluated at one fixed input point. Thus every measurement below acts on input vectors. Since dX=X_x\,dx+X_y\,dy and dY=Y_x\,dx+Y_y\,dy, we get
dX\wedge dY \amp= (X_x\,dx+X_y\,dy)\wedge(Y_x\,dx+Y_y\,dy) \amp= X_xY_y\,dx\wedge dy+X_yY_x\,dy\wedge dx \amp= (X_xY_y-X_yY_x)\,dx\wedge dy.
Thus \boxed{ dX\wedge dY = \det(J_F)\,dx\wedge dy. } The determinant is the coefficient that converts the old signed area form into the new signed area form.
In three variables, \det J_F likewise measures the signed volume scaling of the linear derivative. The corresponding volume-form formula will be explained in .

This is why the Jacobian determinant will appear in change of variables for double and triple integrals. A coordinate change does not merely rename points. It stretches tiny areas and volumes, and the determinant measures that stretching.

The Jacobian matrix is a promise: near a point, the transformation behaves like this linear map. But the promise is only true when the partial derivatives really stitch together into a total derivative. The next question is practical and sharp: when can we trust the matrix of partial derivatives to be the derivative?

section.title: Sufficient conditions and warning examples
section.p: The Jacobian matrix in was built from partial derivatives. That is natural, but it hides a danger. Partial derivatives are measured along coordinate slices. The total derivative must work for every small displacement at once.
So we need a test that says when the slices fit together.

subsection.title: A safe example first
subsection.p: Return to the rubber sheet map F(x,y)=\left(x+\frac15xy,\;y+\frac1{10}x^2\right). Its partial derivatives are F_{1x}=1+\frac15y,\qquad F_{1y}=\frac15x, and F_{2x}=\frac15x,\qquad F_{2y}=1. These are polynomial functions. They are continuous everywhere.

That means the entries of the Jacobian matrix do not jump or oscillate near the point. A nearby point has nearby coordinate slopes. The local grid is not being asked to change its linear behavior abruptly at microscopic scale.
This is the good situation. In it, the Jacobian matrix is the total derivative.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R, and let (a,b) be an interior point of D. Suppose f_x and f_y exist in a small disk around (a,b), and suppose both partial derivatives are continuous at (a,b). Then f is differentiable at (a,b), and \boxed{Df(a,b)(\Delta x,\Delta y)=f_x(a,b)\Delta x+f_y(a,b)\Delta y.}

proof.p:
We compare f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y) to f(a,b). Split the change into two coordinate moves:
\amp f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b) \amp\qquad = \bigl[f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b+\Delta y)\bigr]+\bigl[f(a,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b)\bigr].
For the first bracket, only x changes. By the one-variable Mean Value Theorem, there is a number \theta between 0 and 1 such that f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b+\Delta y)=\Delta x\,f_x(a+\theta\Delta x,b+\Delta y). For the second bracket, only y changes. There is a number \eta between 0 and 1 such that f(a,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b)=\Delta y\,f_y(a,b+\eta\Delta y). Subtract the proposed linear part: f_x(a,b)\Delta x+f_y(a,b)\Delta y. The error is
R(\Delta x,\Delta y) \amp= \Delta x\bigl[f_x(a+\theta\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f_x(a,b)\bigr] \amp\qquad + \Delta y\bigl[f_y(a,b+\eta\Delta y)-f_y(a,b)\bigr].
Let r=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}. Since |\Delta x|\le r,\qquad |\Delta y|\le r, we get
\frac{|R(\Delta x,\Delta y)|}{r} \amp\le \left|f_x(a+\theta\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f_x(a,b)\right| \amp\qquad+ \left|f_y(a,b+\eta\Delta y)-f_y(a,b)\right|.
As (\Delta x,\Delta y)\to(0,0), the points inside f_x and f_y approach (a,b). Since f_x and f_y are continuous at (a,b), the right side approaches 0. Therefore \frac{|R(\Delta x,\Delta y)|}{r}\to0, which is exactly differentiability.

subsection.p: The same test works in any finite number of variables and for vector-valued maps.

statement.p: Let F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m have component functions F_1,\ldots,F_m. Suppose all first partial derivatives \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j} exist in a small ball around \mathbf p, and suppose all of them are continuous at \mathbf p. Then F is differentiable at \mathbf p, and \boxed{DF(\mathbf p)(\mathbf h)=J_F(\mathbf p)\mathbf h.}

subsection.p: The proof is just the scalar theorem applied to each component. The component errors are each smaller than first order, so the vector error is also smaller than first order.

This theorem is one of the most useful tests in the course. For polynomials, trigonometric functions, exponentials, logarithms on their domains, and rational functions away from zero denominators, the partial derivatives are continuous. In those settings, the Jacobian matrix really is the derivative.
Now come the warnings.

subsection.title: Continuous partials are sufficient, not necessary
subsection.p: The theorem gives a reliable test. It is not an if-and-only-if statement. A function can be differentiable even when its partial derivatives are not continuous.

Define f(x,y)=\begin{cases}x^2\sin\left(\dfrac1x\right), & x\ne0,\\[2mm]0, & x=0.\end{cases} This function does not depend on y. At the origin, f_x(0,0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{h^2\sin(1/h)-0}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}h\sin(1/h)=0, and f_y(0,0)=0. So the candidate total derivative at the origin is the zero linear function.

To check differentiability, estimate the error: |f(x,y)|=\left|x^2\sin\left(\frac1x\right)\right|\le x^2 when x\ne0, and the same inequality is true when x=0. Since x^2\le x^2+y^2, we get \frac{|f(x,y)-0|}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\to0. Therefore f is differentiable at the origin.

But f_x is not continuous at the origin. For x\ne0, f_x(x,y)=2x\sin\left(\frac1x\right)-\cos\left(\frac1x\right). The term \cos\left(\frac1x\right) oscillates as x\to0. So f_x(x,y) does not approach f_x(0,0)=0.
The moral is one-way:
The theorem is a safe test, not the only possible route.

statement.p: The continuous-partials test is a sufficient condition for differentiability, not a necessary one. In your own words, what is the difference between a sufficient condition and a necessary condition, and why does that distinction matter when you fail the test? If a function's partial derivatives turn out not to be continuous at a point, what may you conclude about differentiability there?

hint.p: A sufficient condition is enough to guarantee the conclusion; a necessary condition is one the conclusion cannot do without. Try filling in the implication arrow: \text{continuous partials} \Rightarrow \text{differentiable}. Does the arrow run the other way too? Think about what the x^2\sin(1/x) example just showed you.

subsection.title: Partial derivatives can exist without continuity
subsection.p: A sharper warning comes from the function S(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}, & (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm]0, & (x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases} We met this kind of example when studying limits. Along the x-axis, S(x,0)=0. Along the y-axis, S(0,y)=0. Therefore S_x(0,0)=0,\qquad S_y(0,0)=0. Both partial derivatives exist at the origin.
But S is not continuous at the origin. Along the diagonal y=x, S(x,x)=\frac{x^2}{2x^2}=\frac12 for x\ne0. Along the x-axis, S(x,0)=0. The function does not settle down to one value near the origin.

Differentiability implies continuity: the linear part satisfies |Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf h)|\le\|\nabla f(\mathbf p)\|\,\|\mathbf h\| by CauchySchwarz, and both it and the remainder tend to zero with \mathbf h. Therefore S cannot be differentiable at the origin.
So partial derivatives at a point do not even guarantee continuity. They only check two coordinate slices.

subsection.title: Partial derivatives can exist without differentiability
subsection.p: The previous example failed because the function was not continuous. The next one is more subtle: the function is continuous, and the partial derivatives exist, but the total derivative still fails.

Define G(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}, & (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm]0, & (x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases} First, G is continuous at the origin. For (x,y)\ne(0,0), |G(x,y)|=\frac{|x|^2|y|}{x^2+y^2}\le|y|. Since |y|\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}, we get |G(x,y)|\to0 as (x,y)\to(0,0). Thus G(x,y)\to G(0,0).

Now compute the partial derivatives at the origin. Along the x-axis, G(h,0)=0, so G_x(0,0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{G(h,0)-G(0,0)}{h}=0. Along the y-axis, G(0,h)=0, so G_y(0,0)=0. If G were differentiable at the origin, its total derivative would have to be DG(0,0)(\Delta x,\Delta y)=0. The tangent plane formula would predict z=0.

Now test the diagonal path y=x. For x\ne0, G(x,x)=\frac{x^3}{2x^2}=\frac{x}{2}. The proposed linear approximation is 0, so the error along this path is R(x,x)=\frac{x}{2}. The input step length is \sqrt{x^2+x^2}=\sqrt2\,|x|. Therefore \frac{|R(x,x)|}{\sqrt{x^2+x^2}}=\frac{|x|/2}{\sqrt2\,|x|}=\frac1{2\sqrt2}. This does not approach 0.
So G is not differentiable at the origin.

exercise.title: Both partials exist, yet no derivative?

statement.p: For this G, both partial derivatives exist at the origin, yet the function is not differentiable there. How can that happen? What does each partial derivative actually measure, and what does it miss? Explain why knowing the behavior along the two coordinate axes is not enough to pin down the behavior in every direction at once.

hint.p: A partial derivative only watches the function along one coordinate slice, where the other variable is held fixed. Differentiability is a stronger demand: a single linear map must approximate the change for every small displacement. Look at what the diagonal path y=x did that the axes could not see.

subsection.p: The function is continuous. The two coordinate partial derivatives exist. But no linear approximation works in all small directions at once.

subsection.title: The tangent plane formula can fail without differentiability
subsection.p: The graph of G gives the geometric warning.

Since G_x(0,0)=0,\qquad G_y(0,0)=0, the formal tangent plane formula would give z=0. Along the coordinate axes, that plane looks correct: G(x,0)=0,\qquad G(0,y)=0. But along the diagonal, G(x,x)=\frac{x}{2}. The graph rises with a nonzero first-order slope along a direction that the coordinate slices missed.

A tangent plane is not a plane that matches two coordinate traces. It is a plane that matches the whole surface to first order. That is why differentiability is the real condition behind the tangent plane.

exercise.title: Why might the plane not be tangent?

statement.p: The plane z=0 is built from the partial derivatives G_x(0,0)=0 and G_y(0,0)=0, and it hugs the graph perfectly along both coordinate axes. Yet it is not a genuine tangent plane. Why can a plane assembled from the partials fail to be tangent to the surface? What would a true tangent plane have to do that this one does not?

hint.p: The partials only certify the fit along two special directions. A true tangent plane must match the surface to first order in all directions. Ask yourself how the graph behaves along the diagonal y=x: does the plane z=0 still cling to the surface there, or does the surface peel away with a nonzero slope?

subsection.p: For (x,y)\ne(0,0), the partial derivatives of G are G_x(x,y)=\frac{2xy^3}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, and G_y(x,y)=\frac{x^2(x^2-y^2)}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. These partial derivatives are not continuous at the origin. For example, along y=x, G_x(x,x)=\frac12, while G_x(0,0)=0. So the continuous-partials theorem did not apply, and the failure was real.

subsection.title: What the test gives us
subsection.p: For most functions built from familiar smooth pieces, the Jacobian matrix can be trusted. For example, F(x,y,z)=\left(e^{xy}+z,\;\sin(xz)+y^2\right) has continuous partial derivatives everywhere. So F is differentiable everywhere, and DF(x,y,z)(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)=J_F(x,y,z)\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta z\end{pmatrix}. The Jacobian is \boxed{J_F(x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}ye^{xy} & xe^{xy} & 1\\z\cos(xz) & 2y & x\cos(xz)\end{pmatrix}.} This is a 2\times3 matrix because the input has three coordinates and the output has two.
Near any point, this matrix gives the first-order response of the two outputs to a small movement in space.

The chapter has now turned derivatives into linear maps. That viewpoint changes how the chain rule looks. If a moving particle passes through a temperature field, or if one coordinate change follows another, the nonlinear functions should first be replaced by their local linear parts. Linear parts compose by matrix multiplication. That is the next return of the single-variable chain rule, now written in the language of Jacobian matrices.

introduction.p:
This chapter began with coordinate slopes and ended with a matrix. The path was shorter than it may have looked:
\text{small change} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{linear prediction} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{matrix of that prediction}.
The derivative in several variables is not a number. It is the best linear rule for predicting what a function does to a small displacement.

subsection.title: A map of the chapter

li.p: The rate of change when x moves and y is held fixed.
The rate of change when y moves and x is held fixed.
The rate of change at \mathbf p in the unit direction \mathbf u.
The vector of partial derivatives. When the function is differentiable, D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u.
The total derivative: the linear function that gives the first-order change in f near \mathbf p.
Another name for Df(\mathbf p). Written as df_{\mathbf p}=f_x(\mathbf p)\,dx+f_y(\mathbf p)\,dy in two variables.

li.title: 1-form
li.p: A rule such as P\,dx+Q\,dy that eats a small displacement and returns a number. A differential df is the first example.

li.title: tangent plane
li.p: The graph of the linear approximation: z=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b).
The Jacobian matrix of a transformation F. Its rows are the differentials of the component functions.
For a map \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n, the signed local area or volume scaling factor.

subsection.p: The safest practical test was this:

p.alert: If the first partial derivatives are continuous near the point, then the function is differentiable there.

subsection.p: The warning was just as important:

p.alert: Partial derivatives at one point do not guarantee differentiability.

subsection.p: Coordinate slices can lie. The total derivative asks for one linear approximation that works in every small direction at once.

subsection.title: One model, four readings
subsection.p:
A vineyard has a thin protective canopy over a rectangular patch of young plants. The height of the canopy above the ground is modeled by
A(x,y) = 6+\frac25x-\frac15y-\frac{3}{100}x^2-\frac1{50}y^2,
where x and y are measured in meters, and A is measured in meters.

At the point P=(3,2), the height is
A(3,2) \amp= 6+\frac65-\frac25-\frac{27}{100}-\frac4{50} \amp= \frac{129}{20}.

First compute the partial derivatives: A_x(x,y)=\frac25-\frac{3}{50}x, and A_y(x,y)=-\frac15-\frac1{25}y. At P,
A_x(3,2)=\frac{11}{50}, \qquad A_y(3,2)=-\frac7{25}.
The gradient is \nabla A(3,2)=\left(\frac{11}{50},-\frac7{25}\right).

The differential is the linear function
\boxed{ dA_{(3,2)}= \frac{11}{50}\,dx-\frac7{25}\,dy. }
If a worker moves by
\Delta x=0.20, \qquad \Delta y=-0.10,
then the first-order height change is
dA_{(3,2)}(0.20,-0.10) \amp= \frac{11}{50}(0.20)-\frac7{25}(-0.10) \amp= 0.044+0.028 \amp= 0.072.

The exact height change is
0.072-\frac{3}{100}(0.20)^2-\frac1{50}(-0.10)^2 = 0.0706.
The differential predicted the first-order part. The missing -0.0014 came from the quadratic terms.

Now take the unit direction \mathbf u=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right). The directional derivative at P is
D_{\mathbf u}A(3,2) \amp= \nabla A(3,2)\cdot \mathbf u \amp= \frac{11}{50}\cdot\frac35 - \frac7{25}\cdot\frac45 \amp= \frac{33}{250}-\frac{56}{250} \amp= -\frac{23}{250}.
So moving in that direction lowers the canopy at about 0.092 meter per meter.

These are four different readings of the same first-order data:
A_x,\ A_y, \qquad \nabla A, \qquad dA, \qquad \text{tangent plane}.
They are not four separate ideas. They are four ways of seeing the same local linear approximation.

title.q: The partial derivatives exist, so the function is differentiable.

li.p: False. Partial derivatives at one point only check coordinate slices. Differentiability requires a linear approximation that works in all small directions.

title.q: The directional derivative can use any direction vector.

li.p: Use a unit vector if the answer is meant to be rate per unit distance. A non-unit vector mixes direction with speed.

title.q: The gradient and the differential are the same object.

li.p: They have the same coefficients, but different roles. The gradient is a vector. The differential is a linear function: df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf h)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf h.

title.q: The tangent plane formula always works if f_x and f_y exist.

li.p: False. The formula is a tangent plane only when f is differentiable at the point.

title.q: The Jacobian matrix is always square.

li.p: No. If F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, then J_F is an m\times n matrix. It is square only when m=n.

title.q: Every Jacobian matrix has a determinant.

li.p: Only square matrices have determinants. A parametrized surface \mathbf s:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3 has a 3\times2 Jacobian, whose columns are tangent directions.

statement.p: Explain, in words, what f_x(a,b) measures. What is held fixed?
Explain the difference between a partial derivative and a directional derivative.
Why must the direction vector in D_{\mathbf u}f usually be a unit vector?
What does the gradient formula D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u say geometrically?
Suppose \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\mathbf 0. What does the gradient formula say about all directional derivatives at \mathbf p, assuming f is differentiable there?
What is the difference between the statement f(a+\Delta x,b+\Delta y)-f(a,b)\to0 and the differentiability error condition \frac{|R(\Delta x,\Delta y)|}{\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}}\to0?
Why does differentiability imply continuity?
Give a sentence explaining why continuous partial derivatives imply differentiability.
In the expression df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy, what do dx and dy do to a displacement vector?
For a transformation F=(F_1,F_2,F_3):\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3, what are the rows of J_F? What are the columns?
What does \det J_F(\mathbf p)\lt 0 mean geometrically for a map F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2 that is differentiable at \mathbf p?
For f(x,y)=x^2e^y-y\ln(1+x^2), find f_x(x,y),\qquad f_y(x,y). Then evaluate them at (1,0).
For h(x,y)=\sqrt{25-x^2-4y^2}, find h_x and h_y where they exist. Describe the domain of h.
For T(x,y,z)=18+\frac{4}{1+x^2+y^2}-0.7z, find T_x,\qquad T_y,\qquad T_z. Then evaluate them at (1,0,2).
For p(x,y,z)=\ln(x^2+y^2+z^2), find p_x,\qquad p_y,\qquad p_z. Where are these formulas valid?
Let C(u,v)=400+3u+4v+0.01uv. Find C_u(200,100),\qquad C_v(200,100). Interpret both numbers with units.
A surface has height M(x,y)=5+0.2x-0.4y+0.03xy. Find M_x and M_y. At (10,5), is the surface rising or falling as x increases? As y increases?
A vector field is \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x). Find \mathbf W_x(x,y),\qquad \mathbf W_y(x,y).
A transformation is F(x,y,z)=\left(x+y,\,yz,\,x^2-z\right). Find all first partial derivatives of its component functions.
Let f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2-xy. Find \nabla f(1,2). Then find the directional derivative at (1,2) in the direction of \mathbf v=(2,-1). Remember to normalize \mathbf v.
Let q(x,y)=e^{x-y}+xy. Find D_{\mathbf u}q(1,1) for \mathbf u=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right).
Let B(x,y)=10-\frac{x^2}{4}-y^2. At (2,1), find the direction of fastest increase and the maximum directional derivative.
For the same function B, find the direction of steepest descent at (2,1).
Let T(x,y,z)=18+\frac{4}{1+x^2+y^2}-0.7z. At (1,0,2), find the directional derivative in the unit direction \mathbf u=\left(0,\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right).
Let f(x,y,z)=x^2y+yz^2. Find \nabla f(1,-1,2). Then find the directional derivative at that point in the direction \mathbf v=(1,2,2).
Suppose f is differentiable at (3,4) and \nabla f(3,4)=(-2,5). Without knowing f, find the directional derivative at (3,4) in the direction \mathbf u=\left(\frac35,-\frac45\right).
Suppose \nabla f(\mathbf p)=(0,0,0). What does the gradient formula predict for every directional derivative at \mathbf p, assuming f is differentiable there?

exercises.title: Skills: differentials, linear approximation, and tangent planes

statement.p: Find the linear approximation to f(x,y)=e^{x-y}+xy at (1,1). Use it to estimate f(1.02,0.97).
Find the tangent plane to z=\sqrt{36-x^2-y^2} at the point where (x,y)=(2,3).
Let f(x,y,z)=x^2y+\sin z. Write df at a general point (x,y,z). Then evaluate df at (1,2,0).
A rectangular box has volume V(x,y,z)=xyz. At (x,y,z)=(2,3,5), use the differential to estimate the change in volume when dx=0.01,\qquad dy=-0.02,\qquad dz=0.04.
A sensor output is modeled by S(a,b)=\frac{a}{1+b^2}. Find dS_{(4,1)}. Use it to estimate the output change when da=-0.05,\qquad db=0.02.
Let f(x,y)=|x|+|y|. Do f_x(0,0) and f_y(0,0) exist? Is f differentiable at the origin? Explain.
Let F(x,y)=\left(x^2-y,\,xy+y^2\right). Find J_F(x,y). Then find the local linear approximation to F at (1,2).
Let G(x,y,z)=\left(x+y+z,\,x^2-yz\right). Find J_G(x,y,z). What is the size of this matrix, and why?
Let \mathbf s(u,v)=\left(u,\,v,\,2+\frac{u^2}{4}-\frac{v^2}{9}\right). Find J_{\mathbf s}(u,v). Then find the tangent vectors \mathbf s_u(2,3),\qquad \mathbf s_v(2,3).
Use the tangent vectors from the previous problem to write a vector equation for the tangent plane to the surface at \mathbf s(2,3).
Let F(x,y)=\left(2x+y,\,x+3y\right). Find \det J_F. By what factor does F scale signed area?
Let F(x,y)=\left(x^2-y,\,x+y\right). Find \det J_F(x,y). At which points does the local area scaling vanish?

Let X=r\cos\theta,\qquad Y=r\sin\theta. Find the Jacobian matrix of the transformation (r,\theta)\mapsto (X,Y). Then show that \det J = r. This number will return when polar coordinates are used in double integrals.
For the same polar transformation, compute dX\wedge dY and show that dX\wedge dY=r\,dr\wedge d\theta.
Let X=x+y,\qquad Y=x-y. Compute dX\wedge dY. What does the sign tell you about orientation?
Let F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3 be defined by F(u,v)=(u+v,u-v,uv). Find J_F(u,v). Why does it not make sense to ask for \det J_F?

exercises.title: Project: sensitivity analysis in a model with several inputs

introduction.p: A differential is a practical tool for sensitivity analysis. It tells which input errors or input changes matter most near a chosen operating point.
Here is one model to study.
A small aquarium has dissolved oxygen level O(T,p,s) measured in milligrams per liter. The variables are:

li.p: water temperature in degrees Celsius
pump setting in percent
stock density, in fish per cubic meter

introduction.p:
A simplified model near normal operating conditions is
O(T,p,s) = 8.4 -0.18(T-22) +0.035(p-60) -0.025(s-30) -0.002(T-22)(s-30).

Suppose the temperature increases by 2^\circC, the pump setting increases by 5 percentage points, and the stock density decreases by 3 fish per cubic meter. Then dT=2,\qquad dp=5,\qquad ds=-3. The differential predicts
dO \amp= -0.18(2)+0.035(5)-0.025(-3) \amp= -0.36+0.175+0.075 \amp= -0.11.
So the model predicts a drop of about 0.11\text{ mg/L}.
The exact change from the formula is -0.11-0.002(2)(-3)=-0.098. The difference, 0.012, comes from the product term -0.002(T-22)(s-30), which is second order in the simultaneous change of T and s.
Use this model, or build a similar one, and carry out the following steps.

statement.p: State the meaning and units of each input variable and of the output.
Choose a base point \mathbf p.
Compute the partial derivatives at \mathbf p.
Write the differential df_{\mathbf p}.
Choose a realistic small change \Delta\mathbf x. Use the differential to predict \Delta f.
Compute the exact change from the original formula, if possible. Compare it with the differential estimate.

Rank the input variables by their effect on the output near \mathbf p. Do this with realistic changes, not just by comparing the raw partial derivatives. For example, a change of 1^\circC and a change of 1 pump percentage point may not be equally likely or equally large in practice.
Write a short paragraph explaining what the model says and what it leaves out. For the aquarium model, possible missing factors include water volume, plants, time of day, and feeding schedule.

conclusion.p:
The point of the project is not that the model is perfect. It is that the differential gives a local sensitivity card:
\text{small input changes} \quad\longmapsto\quad \text{predicted output change}.
That card is often the most useful part of a multivariable model.

exercise.title: A function with all directional derivatives but no linear approximation
A zero Jacobian determinant can mean folding

statement.p: Let F(x,y)=(x^2,y). Find J_F(x,y) and \det J_F(x,y). Explain geometrically what happens near the line x=0.

exercise.title: A map that preserves area but changes shape

statement.p: Let F(x,y)=(x+ky,y) where k is a constant. Find \det J_F. Draw the image of the unit square for k=1 and k=2. How can area stay the same while the square changes shape?

exercise.title: Rows and columns tell different stories

statement.p: Let F(x,y)=\left(x+xy,\,y-x^2\right). At (1,2), compute J_F. Interpret the rows as differentials of output coordinates, and interpret the columns as images of the coordinate directions.

Create a function f(x,y) that is continuous at the origin and has f_x(0,0)=f_y(0,0)=0, but is not differentiable at the origin. Your example may use the function G from , or you may build a different one.
Let f(x,y)=x^2y-y^3. Compute df. Then evaluate df_{(2,1)} on the displacement \mathbf h=(0.1,-0.2). Explain why this is the first-order predicted change in f.

Let X=3x-y,\qquad Y=2x+4y. Compute dX\wedge dY. Then compute
\det \begin{pmatrix} X_x \amp X_y\\ Y_x \amp Y_y \end{pmatrix}.
Explain why the same number appears.

conclusion.p: A derivative is now a linear map. That sentence is the turning point.

Suppose a drone flies through a temperature field. Its path is \mathbf r(t), and the temperature is T(x,y,z). The temperature felt by the drone is the single-variable function T(\mathbf r(t)). A small time step first becomes a small displacement through the derivative of \mathbf r. Then that displacement becomes a temperature change through the differential of T. One linear map follows another.
Single-variable calculus called this the chain rule. In several variables, the same old rule returns with a new face: linear parts compose, and matrices multiply.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

introduction.p: The chain rule describes how derivatives compose, first along a curve and then for general maps. We apply it to differentials and coordinate changes, keeping signed determinant scaling distinct from ordinary size. The inverse and implicit function theorems explain when equations give local coordinates, with their hypotheses and proof status stated explicitly.

section.title: The chain rule along a curve
section.p: A curve from gives position: \mathbf r(t). A scalar field from gives a number at each point: f(x,y)\qquad\text{or}\qquad f(x,y,z). If a moving object passes through the field, then the object experiences the single-variable function f(\mathbf r(t)). The chain rule tells us how fast that experienced value changes.

subsection.title: Temperature along a moving path
subsection.p: A small robot rolls across a greenhouse floor. Let x measure meters east and y measure meters north. Suppose the floor temperature is T(x,y)=20+3x-y-\frac12x^2-\frac14y^2. At time t, the robot is at \mathbf r(t)=(1+2t,\;2-t). So the temperature recorded by the robot is the one-variable function A(t)=T(\mathbf r(t))=T(1+2t,\;2-t).

We can compute A'(0) directly. Substitute: A(t)=20+3(1+2t)-(2-t)-\frac12(1+2t)^2-\frac14(2-t)^2. Differentiate:
A'(t) \amp= 6+1-\frac12\cdot 2(1+2t)\cdot 2-\frac14\cdot 2(2-t)(-1) \amp= 7-2(1+2t)+\frac12(2-t).
At t=0, A'(0)=7-2+1=6. So, at that instant, the robot's thermometer reads a temperature increasing at 6^\circ\text{C per second}.
Now compute the same number without expanding the whole composition.

At t=0, the robot is at \mathbf r(0)=(1,2). Its velocity is \mathbf r'(t)=(2,-1), so \mathbf r'(0)=(2,-1). The gradient of the temperature field is 
abla T(x,y)=\left(3-x,\;-1- rac12yight). At the robot's position, 
abla T(1,2)=(2,-2). The dot product with the robot's velocity gives 
abla T(1,2)\cdot \mathbf r'(0)=(2,-2)\cdot(2,-1)=4+2=6. The same number appears.

This calculation has a plain meaning. The gradient says how the temperature changes per meter of displacement. The velocity says how many meters of displacement happen per second. Applying one to the other gives degrees per second.

subsection.title: The derivative of f(x(t),y(t))
subsection.p: The greenhouse computation suggests the general rule. Let z=f(x,y) and suppose x=x(t),\qquad y=y(t). Then z(t)=f(x(t),y(t)). A small time change dt produces the small coordinate changes dx=x'(t)\,dt,\qquad dy=y'(t)\,dt. The differential of f predicts dz=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy. Substituting the changes caused by time gives dz=f_x(x(t),y(t))x'(t)\,dt+f_y(x(t),y(t))y'(t)\,dt. Divide by dt: \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t),y(t))=f_x(x(t),y(t))x'(t)+f_y(x(t),y(t))y'(t).} This is the two-variable chain rule along a curve.

statement.p: The chain rule for f(x(t),y(t)) adds two pieces: f_x\,x'(t) and f_y\,y'(t). Why should we add the contribution from the changing x and the contribution from the changing y, rather than, say, multiply them or keep only the larger one?

hint.p: Picture a single small time step dt. It nudges both coordinates at once, and each nudge moves the value of f a little. Think about how the differential dz=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy accumulates those independent nudges into one total change.

example.title: A pressure reading along a pipe

statement.p: A sensor moves along a pipe laid across a factory floor. The pressure field is p(x,y)=50+xy-2y^2, and the sensor position is x(t)=2+t^2,\qquad y(t)=1-t. Find the rate of change of pressure at t=1.

First compute the partial derivatives: p_x(x,y)=y,\qquad p_y(x,y)=x-4y. At t=1, x(1)=3,\qquad y(1)=0. So p_x(3,0)=0,\qquad p_y(3,0)=3. Also, x'(t)=2t,\qquad y'(t)=-1, so x'(1)=2,\qquad y'(1)=-1. Therefore
\frac{d}{dt}p(x(t),y(t))\bigg|_{t=1} \amp= p_x(3,0)x'(1)+p_y(3,0)y'(1) \amp= 0\cdot2+3(-1) \amp= -3.
At t=1, the sensor sees pressure decreasing at 3 pressure units per second.

subsection.title: Gradient form of the chain rule
subsection.p: The formula becomes shorter if we use vectors. Write \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)). Then \mathbf r'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t)). Also, \nabla f(x,y)=\bigl(f_x(x,y),f_y(x,y)\bigr). The chain rule becomes \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))=\nabla f(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t).}

statement.p: The two-variable chain rule has two separate terms, f_x\,x'(t)+f_y\,y'(t), yet the gradient form collapses them into the single dot product \nabla f\cdot\mathbf r'(t). What feature of the dot product lets it carry exactly the same information as that sum of products?

hint.p: Write out \nabla f=(f_x,f_y) and \mathbf r'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t)) and recall how a dot product is defined component by component. The collapse is really just a name for a pattern you already know.

subsection.p: There is also a differential form version: \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))=df_{\mathbf r(t)}\bigl(\mathbf r'(t)\bigr).} Here df is the 1-form df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy in the plane, or df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz in space. The differential df eats the velocity vector and returns the observed rate of change.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be differentiable at the point \mathbf r(t_0), and let \mathbf r:I\to\mathbb R^n be differentiable at t_0, with \mathbf r(t_0)\in D. Then the composite t\longmapsto f(\mathbf r(t)) is differentiable at t_0, and \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))\bigg|_{t=t_0}=Df(\mathbf r(t_0))\bigl(\mathbf r'(t_0)\bigr).} In gradient notation, \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))\bigg|_{t=t_0}=\nabla f(\mathbf r(t_0))\cdot \mathbf r'(t_0).}

proof.p: Let \mathbf p=\mathbf r(t_0),\qquad \mathbf v=\mathbf r'(t_0). Since \mathbf r is differentiable at t_0, \mathbf r(t_0+h)=\mathbf p+h\mathbf v+\mathbf e(h), where \frac{\|\mathbf e(h)\|}{|h|}\to0. So the displacement \mathbf k(h)=\mathbf r(t_0+h)-\mathbf p satisfies \mathbf k(h)=h\mathbf v+\mathbf e(h).

Since f is differentiable at \mathbf p, f(\mathbf p+\mathbf k)=f(\mathbf p)+Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf k)+R(\mathbf k), where \frac{|R(\mathbf k)|}{\|\mathbf k\|}\to0\quad\text{as}\quad \mathbf k\to\mathbf 0. Apply this with \mathbf k=\mathbf k(h):
f(\mathbf r(t_0+h))-f(\mathbf r(t_0)) \amp= Df(\mathbf p)(h\mathbf v+\mathbf e(h))+R(\mathbf k(h)) \amp= h\,Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf v)+Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf e(h))+R(\mathbf k(h)).
Divide by h. The middle term approaches 0 because Df(\mathbf p) is linear and \mathbf e(h)/h\to\mathbf 0. The last term also approaches 0, because \mathbf k(h) is of size proportional to |h| for small h. Therefore \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(\mathbf r(t_0+h))-f(\mathbf r(t_0))}{h}=Df(\mathbf p)(\mathbf v).

subsection.p: The hypothesis says f is differentiable, not merely that its partial derivatives exist. gave the reason. Here is the same warning in chain-rule form.

example.title: Why partial derivatives are not enough

statement.p: Define Q(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}, \amp (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm]0, \amp (x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases} At the origin, Q_x(0,0)=0,\qquad Q_y(0,0)=0.
