subsection.p: In the language of differentials, the same statement is shorter. A tangent vector \mathbf v to the level surface must satisfy \boxed{dF_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=0.} Since dF=F_x\,dx+F_y\,dy+F_z\,dz, this says F_x(a,b,c)v_1+F_y(a,b,c)v_2+F_z(a,b,c)v_3=0. The tangent plane is the set of first-order motions that dF sends to zero.

subsection.title: Orthogonality of flow lines and contours
subsection.p: Contour maps show level curves. The gradient points across them.

If a hiker walks in the direction of steepest uphill motion, the velocity is parallel to \nabla h. If rainwater runs downhill, its velocity is often modeled as parallel to -\nabla h. Either way, the motion crosses contours at right angles, because each contour's tangent direction is perpendicular to the gradient.

statement.p: A path of steepest ascent moves along \nabla f, and steepest descent moves along -\nabla f. Explain why both kinds of path cross the contour lines at right angles, and why that makes intuitive sense for the path of fastest possible climb or descent.

hint.p:
Each contour's tangent direction is perpendicular to 
abla f. If your velocity is parallel to 
abla f (or -
abla f), how can it sit relative to that tangent direction? Sliding any bit along a contour would waste effort on motion that does not change height.

subsection.p:
A curve satisfying \mathbf r'(t)=
abla f(\mathbf r(t)) is called a gradient flow line. Along such a curve,
 rac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t)) \amp= 
abla f(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t) \amp= 
abla f(\mathbf r(t))\cdot 
abla f(\mathbf r(t)) \amp= \|
abla f(\mathbf r(t))\|^2.
So unless the gradient is zero, f increases along its own gradient flow.
For downhill flow, \mathbf r'(t)=-\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)), we get \frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))=-\|\nabla f(\mathbf r(t))\|^2. So f decreases unless the gradient is zero.

This is a beautiful place for the story to pause. Level curves show where the function is constant. Gradient flow lines show the directions where the function changes as fast as possible. But both descriptions lose their direction when \nabla f=\mathbf 0. At such a point, first-order motion goes silent. The point might be the top of a hill, the bottom of a bowl, or a mountain pass. Those silent points are where optimization begins.

section.title: Critical points
section.p: ended at the places where the gradient disappears. A gradient flow line has no direction there. A contour map may pinch, cross, or close up there. For optimization, those points are the first ones we must find.

subsection.title: A hill with a highest nearby point
subsection.p: Return to the hill h(x,y)=100+4x+3y-x^2-xy-y^2. Its gradient is \nabla h(x,y)=\left(4-2x-y,\ 3-x-2y\right). Set the gradient equal to zero: 4-2x-y=0, \qquad 3-x-2y=0. Equivalently, 2x+y=4, \qquad x+2y=3. Solving gives y=\frac23, \qquad x=\frac53. So first-order change disappears at P=\left(\frac53,\frac23\right).

At that point, h(P)=\frac{313}{3}. To see what kind of point it is, write x=\frac53+u, \qquad y=\frac23+v. A direct substitution gives \boxed{ h\left(\frac53+u,\frac23+v\right) = \frac{313}{3}-(u^2+uv+v^2). } Now u^2+uv+v^2 = \left(u+\frac12v\right)^2+\frac34v^2. This is always nonnegative, and it is zero only when u=0,\qquad v=0. Therefore every nearby point has height at most \frac{313}{3}, with equality only at P. The point P is a local maximum.
The gradient equation found the candidate. The completed square told us what kind of candidate it was.

subsection.title: Local maxima and minima
subsection.p: The word local means nearby. A local maximum does not have to be the highest point in the whole domain. It only has to be the highest point in some small region around the point.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R. A point \mathbf p\in D is a local maximum of f if there is some radius r\gt 0 such that f(\mathbf x)\le f(\mathbf p) for every \mathbf x\in D with \|\mathbf x-\mathbf p\|\lt r.
A point \mathbf p\in D is a local minimum of f if there is some radius r\gt 0 such that f(\mathbf x)\ge f(\mathbf p) for every \mathbf x\in D with \|\mathbf x-\mathbf p\|\lt r.
A local maximum or local minimum is called a local extremum.

example.title: A quiet spot in a sound model

statement.p: Suppose the loudness near a quiet spot in a room is modeled by L(x,y)=5+(x-2)^2+3(y+1)^2. At (2,-1), we have L(2,-1)=5. Every other nearby point gives (x-2)^2+3(y+1)^2\gt 0. So L(x,y)\gt 5 nearby, except at (2,-1) itself. Thus (2,-1) is a local minimum.
The gradient agrees: \nabla L(x,y)=\left(2(x-2),6(y+1)\right), so \nabla L(2,-1)=\mathbf 0.

subsection.title: Saddle points
subsection.p: A critical point does not have to be a maximum or a minimum.
Consider the mountain-pass model S(x,y)=80+x^2-y^2. The gradient is \nabla S(x,y)=(2x,-2y). At the origin, \nabla S(0,0)=\mathbf 0. But the origin is not a local maximum or a local minimum.
Along the x-axis, S(x,0)=80+x^2, which is larger than 80 when x\ne0. Along the y-axis, S(0,y)=80-y^2, which is smaller than 80 when y\ne0.
So every small disk around the origin contains points higher than the origin and points lower than the origin. This is a saddle point.

exercise.title: Why isn't a zero gradient enough?

statement.p: We just saw a point where \nabla f=\mathbf 0 that is neither a maximum nor a minimum. In your own words, why does \nabla f=\mathbf 0 fail to guarantee an extremum, and what feature of a saddle point makes it different from a peak or a valley?

hint.p: Walk away from the point in two different directions. At a saddle, what happens to the value of f along one direction compared with the other?

figure.caption: Near a saddle point, some directions go up and others go down.

statement.p: A point \mathbf p is a saddle point of f if \mathbf p is a critical point and every small ball around \mathbf p contains points where f is larger than f(\mathbf p) and points where f is smaller than f(\mathbf p).

subsection.p: The saddle point is the first warning that \nabla f=\mathbf 0 does not mean maximum or minimum. It means that the first-order test has gone silent. We need more information to classify the point.

subsection.title: Critical points from \nabla f=0
subsection.p: Single-variable calculus had Fermat's theorem: if a differentiable function has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point, then its derivative is zero. The same idea works in several variables by looking at one coordinate slice at a time.

theorem.title: Fermat's theorem for functions of several variables

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R. Suppose \mathbf p is an interior point of D, and suppose f has a local maximum or local minimum at \mathbf p.

proof.p: Write \mathbf p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n). Hold every variable fixed except x_i. This gives a one-variable slice through \mathbf p: g_i(t)=f(p_1,\ldots,p_{i-1},t,p_{i+1},\ldots,p_n). Since f has a local maximum or minimum at \mathbf p, the slice g_i has a local maximum or minimum at t=p_i. By the one-variable Fermat theorem, g_i'(p_i)=0. But g_i'(p_i)=f_{x_i}(\mathbf p). So every first partial derivative is zero.

subsection.p: This theorem gives necessary conditions, not sufficient ones. Local maxima and minima must occur among the points where the first-order test fails, but not every such point is an extremum.

exercise.title: Why does the gradient vanish at an interior peak?

statement.p: Suppose f has a local maximum or local minimum at an interior point \mathbf p, and all its first partial derivatives exist there. Why must \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\mathbf 0? Try to explain it in terms of one-variable slices through \mathbf p.

hint.p: Freeze every variable but one. What kind of point does the resulting single-variable slice have at \mathbf p, and what did Fermat's theorem say about its derivative there?

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R. An interior point \mathbf p\in D is called a critical point of f if either \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\mathbf 0, or one of the first partial derivatives fails to exist at \mathbf p.
When f is differentiable, the critical points are exactly the interior points where \nabla f=\mathbf 0.

subsection.p: The definition includes points where derivatives fail to exist because extrema can hide there.

example.title: A sharp peak

statement.p: The function f(x,y)=-|x|-|y| has a local maximum at the origin. But f_x(0,0) does not exist, since along the x-axis f(h,0)=-|h|. The one-variable derivative of -|h| at 0 does not exist.
So the origin must still be checked in an optimization problem, even though \nabla f(0,0) does not exist.

subsection.p: The hypotheses in Fermat's theorem cannot be dropped.

example.title: Why the point must be interior

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=x on the closed disk D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\}. The maximum value occurs at (1,0), because no point in the disk has x\gt 1. But \nabla f(1,0)=(1,0), not \mathbf 0.

There is no contradiction. The point (1,0) is a boundary point, not an interior point. At the boundary, many directions are not allowed. The function would increase if we moved farther east, but the disk does not allow that move.

example.title: Why the partial derivatives must exist

statement.p: The function f(x,y)=-|x|-|y| has a local maximum at the origin, but the first partial derivatives do not exist there. So Fermat's theorem does not apply.
The theorem says: if the derivatives exist at an interior local extremum, then they must be zero. If the derivatives do not exist, the point is still a candidate.

subsection.title: Finding and reading critical points
subsection.p: Here is a small example where the critical equation finds more than one point.
Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2. Then f_x(x,y)=3x^2-3, \qquad f_y(x,y)=2y. Set both equal to zero: 3x^2-3=0, \qquad 2y=0. Thus x=\pm1, \qquad y=0. The critical points are (1,0) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (-1,0).

At (1,0), write x=1+u,\qquad y=v. Then
f(1+u,v) \amp =(1+u)^3-3(1+u)+v^2 \amp =-2+3u^2+u^3+v^2 \amp =-2+u^2(3+u)+v^2.
For |u|\lt 1, 3+u\gt 0. So nearby, f(1+u,v)\ge -2, with equality only at u=v=0. Thus (1,0) is a local minimum.

At (-1,0), write x=-1+u,\qquad y=v. Then
f(-1+u,v) \amp =(-1+u)^3-3(-1+u)+v^2 \amp =2-3u^2+u^3+v^2.
Along the line u=0, f(-1,v)=2+v^2, which is larger than 2 for v\ne0. Along the line v=0, f(-1+u,0)=2-3u^2+u^3. For small nonzero u, this is less than 2. So (-1,0) is a saddle point.
This classification was possible by hand, but it took separate local algebra around each point. The next sections will build a faster tool for this job.

subsection.title: Boundary points must be checked separately
subsection.p: Critical points are interior candidates. Boundary points have their own rules, because not every direction is available.

A rectangular roof is described by 0\le x\le 4, \qquad 0\le y\le 3. Suppose sunlight intensity on the roof is modeled by B(x,y)=3x+2y. The gradient is \nabla B=(3,2), so there are no interior critical points.

But the function still has a maximum and a minimum on the rectangle. Since B(x,y) increases as x increases and also as y increases, the minimum occurs at (0,0), and the maximum occurs at (4,3). The values are B(0,0)=0, \qquad B(4,3)=18.
The maximum is not detected by \nabla B=\mathbf 0 because the maximum occurs at a corner. The direction of increasing sunlight points northeast, but at the corner (4,3) the roof ends.

exercise.title: Why examine the boundary on its own?

statement.p: The condition \nabla f=\mathbf 0 found no candidates here, yet the maximum is real and sits on the boundary. Why can a maximum or minimum live at a boundary point even when \nabla f is never zero, so that boundary points must be examined separately from interior critical points?

hint.p: Fermat's theorem needs the point to be interior, so that motion is allowed in every direction. At a boundary point, which directions are no longer available to you?

subsection.p: So an optimization problem on a region has two kinds of candidates:

table.title: Two kinds of optimization candidates.

subsection.p: For a rectangular boundary, this usually means checking four edges and four corners. For a circular boundary, it means optimizing along a circle. For a surface constraint, it means something subtler: the gradient of f may not be zero, but it must be perpendicular to every motion allowed by the constraint.

We have found the first-order candidates. What we do not yet have is a reliable way to tell peak from valley from saddle without inventing a new trick each time. The missing information is hidden in the second-order part of the local approximation. In one variable, that information was f''. In two variables, it becomes a matrix of second partials: the Hessian.

section.title: Second derivatives and the Hessian matrix
section.p: ended at critical points. In this section we study functions with continuous second partial derivatives near the point in question. At a critical point of such a function, df=\mathbf 0, so the first-order approximation stops talking. If a point is a peak, a valley, or a saddle, that information must come from the next visible part of the function.
That next part is second order.

subsection.title: The summit we already met
subsection.p: Return to the hill from and : h(x,y)=100+4x+3y-x^2-xy-y^2. Its critical point is P=\left(\frac53,\frac23\right). In , we wrote x=\frac53+u, \qquad y=\frac23+v, and found the exact formula h\left(\frac53+u,\frac23+v\right)=\frac{313}{3}-(u^2+uv+v^2). There is no linear part. The first visible change is -(u^2+uv+v^2).

That expression tells the shape. Since u^2+uv+v^2=\left(u+\frac12v\right)^2+\frac34v^2, it is positive unless u=v=0. So every nonzero nearby displacement lowers the height. The critical point is a local maximum.

Now look at the second derivatives: h_x=4-2x-y, \qquad h_y=3-x-2y. Differentiating again gives h_{xx}=-2, \qquad h_{xy}=-1, \qquad h_{yx}=-1, \qquad h_{yy}=-2. These four numbers arrange themselves into the matrix
H_h= \begin{pmatrix} -2 \amp -1\\ -1 \amp -2 \end{pmatrix}.
Then
\frac12 \begin{pmatrix}u\amp v\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -2 \amp -1\\ -1 \amp -2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix} = -(u^2+uv+v^2).
So the second-order part of the hill is stored in a matrix.
That matrix is called the Hessian.

subsection.title: Second partial derivatives
subsection.p: A first partial derivative measures a coordinate slope. A second partial derivative measures how that coordinate slope changes.

For a function f(x,y), we have four second partial derivatives: f_{xx}, \qquad f_{xy}, \qquad f_{yx}, \qquad f_{yy}. The notation means f_{xy}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(f_x\right). So f_{xy} means: first differentiate with respect to x, then differentiate the result with respect to y.

statement.p: Let f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R. The second partial derivatives of f are f_{xx}=(f_x)_x, \qquad f_{xy}=(f_x)_y, \qquad f_{yx}=(f_y)_x, \qquad f_{yy}=(f_y)_y, when these derivatives exist.

example.title: Changing marginal costs

statement.p: Recall the bakery cost model C(u,v)=400+3u+4v+0.01uv, where u is the number of sourdough loaves and v is the number of rye loaves.
The first partial derivatives are C_u=3+0.01v, \qquad C_v=4+0.01u. Now differentiate again: C_{uu}=0, \qquad C_{uv}=0.01, and C_{vu}=0.01, \qquad C_{vv}=0.

The number C_{uv}=0.01 says that if the bakery makes one more rye loaf, then the marginal cost of making sourdough rises by 0.01 dollars. The interaction term 0.01uv is responsible. Without it, the two products would not affect each other's marginal costs.

example.title: Second partials in three variables

statement.p: Let T(x,y,z)=18+\frac{4}{1+x^2+y^2}-0.7z. Then T_z=-0.7, so T_{zz}=0. The temperature changes linearly with height, so the height-slope does not change as height changes.
For the x-direction, T_x=-\frac{8x}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}. A second derivative such as T_{xy} measures how this x-slope changes as we move in the y-direction.

subsection.p: Second partial derivatives are rates of change of rates of change. They are the multivariable version of f''.

subsection.title: Mixed partials and why order usually does not matter
subsection.p: Two of the second partials are mixed: f_{xy} \qquad\text{and}\qquad f_{yx}. At first, they look like different operations. One changes x first and y second. The other changes y first and x second.
For ordinary smooth formulas, they are equal.

statement.p: The Hessian places f_{xy} in the top-right corner and f_{yx} in the bottom-left corner. Explain why the equality f_{xy}=f_{yx} is exactly the statement that the matrix equals its own reflection across the main diagonal — that is, why equal mixed partials force the Hessian to be symmetric.

hint.p: A matrix is symmetric when the entry in row i, column j matches the entry in row j, column i. Which two entries of the Hessian are the mixed partials, and where do they sit?

example.title: Two orders, one answer

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=x^2y+3xy^2. Then f_x=2xy+3y^2, so f_{xy}=2x+6y. Also, f_y=x^2+6xy, so f_{yx}=2x+6y. Thus f_{xy}=f_{yx}.

subsection.p: This equality is not a coincidence. It is a theorem, but the theorem needs a regularity condition.

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p:
Look at the small rectangle with corners (a,b),\quad (a+u,b),\quad (a,b+v),\quad (a+u,b+v). The quantity
\Delta \amp= f(a+u,b+v)-f(a+u,b) \amp\qquad -f(a,b+v)+f(a,b)
measures how much the change in one direction depends on moving in the other direction.

If we divide by the small signed area uv, \frac{\Delta}{uv}, we get an average mixed rate of change over the rectangle. The one-variable mean value theorem can read this average in two ways: as an average of f_{xy}, or as an average of f_{yx}. As the rectangle shrinks to (a,b), continuity forces both averages to approach the values at (a,b). Therefore the two values are equal.

subsection.p: The continuity assumption is not decoration. Without it, the two mixed partials can exist and still disagree.

example.title: Mixed partials can fail to agree

statement.p: So \boxed{F_{xy}(0,0)=-1, \qquad F_{yx}(0,0)=1.} The mixed partials exist, but they are not equal. The missing condition is continuity of the mixed partials near the origin.

subsection.p: The equality of mixed partials explains the symmetry of the Hessian below. Later, will express the same cancellation using a derivative of differential forms. That later operation is not needed for the matrix argument here.

subsection.title: The Hessian matrix
subsection.p:
At a point (a,b), collect the second partials into one matrix:
H_f(a,b) = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx}(a,b) \amp f_{xy}(a,b)\\ f_{yx}(a,b) \amp f_{yy}(a,b) \end{pmatrix}.

statement.p: At a critical point the gradient is zero, so the gradient alone cannot tell a peak from a valley from a saddle. What information about the shape of the surface does the Hessian carry that the gradient cannot? Describe, in your own words, the kind of geometric behavior the second partials are recording.

hint.p: The gradient measures slope — how fast f is rising. The second partials measure how that slope itself is changing. Think about bending or curvature rather than steepness.

example.title: The Hessian of the hill

statement.p:
For h(x,y)=100+4x+3y-x^2-xy-y^2, we found h_{xx}=-2, \qquad h_{xy}=-1, \qquad h_{yx}=-1, \qquad h_{yy}=-2. So
H_h= \begin{pmatrix} -2 \amp -1\\ -1 \amp -2 \end{pmatrix}.
This Hessian is constant because h is already a quadratic function.

example.title: A Hessian that changes from point to point

statement.p:
Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2. Then f_x=3x^2-3, \qquad f_y=2y. So f_{xx}=6x, \qquad f_{xy}=0, \qquad f_{yx}=0, \qquad f_{yy}=2. The Hessian is
H_f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 6x \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 2 \end{pmatrix}.
At the critical point (1,0),
H_f(1,0) = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 2 \end{pmatrix}.
At the critical point (-1,0),
H_f(-1,0) = \begin{pmatrix} -6 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 2 \end{pmatrix}.
The same function bends differently at its two critical points.

subsection.p: The Hessian is the matrix version of the second derivative. To see this, we need the second-order approximation.

subsection.title: Quadratic approximation near a critical point
subsection.p:
In one-variable calculus, Taylor's formula said that near a, f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+\frac12f''(a)h^2+\text{smaller terms}. In two variables, the same story has more directions. Near (a,b), write x=a+u, \qquad y=b+v. Then the second-order approximation is
f(a+u,b+v) \amp\approx f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)u+f_y(a,b)v \amp\qquad +\frac12\left(f_{xx}(a,b)u^2+2f_{xy}(a,b)uv+f_{yy}(a,b)v^2\right).
The first line is the linear approximation. The second line is the quadratic correction.

exercise.title: Why the Hessian is the quadratic term

statement.p: Compare the one-variable Taylor term \frac12 f''(a)h^2 with the two-variable quadratic correction \frac12\begin{pmatrix}u\amp v\end{pmatrix}H_f(a,b)\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}. Explain why the Hessian plays the role of f'' here — that is, why this matrix product is exactly the second-order piece of the local model of f.

hint.p: Multiply out the matrix product. Which second partials appear, and how do the factors of u and v match the powers u^2, uv, and v^2 you would expect in a quadratic?

example.title: A minimum seen through its quadratic part

statement.p:
Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2. At the critical point (1,0), write x=1+u, \qquad y=v. Then
f(1+u,v) \amp= (1+u)^3-3(1+u)+v^2 \amp= -2+3u^2+u^3+v^2.
The quadratic part is 3u^2+v^2. The Hessian at (1,0) is
H_f(1,0) = \begin{pmatrix} 6\amp 0\\ 0\amp 2 \end{pmatrix},
and
\frac12 \begin{pmatrix}u\amp v\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 6\amp 0\\ 0\amp 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix} = 3u^2+v^2.
So the Hessian gives exactly the quadratic part of the local expansion.

Suppose f(x,y) has continuous second partial derivatives near (a,b). Then
f(a+u,b+v) \amp= f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)u+f_y(a,b)v \amp\qquad +\frac12\left(f_{xx}(a,b)u^2+2f_{xy}(a,b)uv+f_{yy}(a,b)v^2\right)+R(u,v),
where the remainder R(u,v) is small compared with u^2+v^2:
\boxed{ \frac{R(u,v)}{u^2+v^2}\to0 \quad\text{as}\quad (u,v)\to(0,0). }
Equivalently,
\boxed{ f((a,b)+\mathbf u) = f(a,b) + df_{(a,b)}(\mathbf u) + \frac12\mathbf u^T H_f(a,b)\mathbf u + R(\mathbf u), }
with \frac{R(\mathbf u)}{\|\mathbf u\|^2}\to0.

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p:
Move from (a,b) to (a+u,b+v) along the straight path \mathbf r(t)=(a,b)+t(u,v), \qquad 0\le t\le1. The composite g(t)=f(\mathbf r(t)) is a one-variable function. Two applications of the one-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (or integration by parts) give the exact identity g(1)=g(0)+g'(0)+\int_0^1(1-t)g''(t)\,dt. The chain rule gives g'(0)=df_{(a,b)}(u,v), and a second use of the chain rule gives
g''(0) = \begin{pmatrix}u\amp v\end{pmatrix} H_f(a,b) \begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}.
Write \mathbf p=(a,b) and \mathbf u=(u,v). Subtracting the value of the Hessian at \mathbf p in the integral gives the remainder R(\mathbf u)=\int_0^1(1-t)\mathbf u^T \bigl(H_f(\mathbf p+t\mathbf u)-H_f(\mathbf p)\bigr)\mathbf u\,dt. By continuity, for every \varepsilon\gt0, all four matrix-entry differences have absolute value at most \varepsilon when \|\mathbf u\| is sufficiently small, uniformly for 0\le t\le1. Thus |R(\mathbf u)|\le\tfrac12\varepsilon(|u|+|v|)^2 \le\varepsilon(u^2+v^2). This proves the stated remainder limit in every direction at once.

subsection.p: At a critical point, the first-order part vanishes. The Hessian becomes the first visible shape. But a matrix is not yet an answer. We still need to know how to read \mathbf u^T H\mathbf u. Can it be positive in every nonzero direction? Negative in every direction? Positive in one direction and negative in another? Those three possibilities are the mechanism behind the second derivative test.

section.title: The second derivative test
section.p: showed what replaces f'' in several variables. Near a critical point, f(\mathbf p+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf p) is controlled first by \frac12\mathbf u^T H_f(\mathbf p)\mathbf u. So the question becomes a question about a quadratic expression.

p.md: \text{What signs can } \mathbf u^T H\mathbf u \text{ have?}

subsection.title: Reading the quadratic part
subsection.p: Consider the function B(x,y)=12+2x^2+xy+y^2. At the origin, B_x=4x+y,\qquad B_y=x+2y, so \nabla B(0,0)=\mathbf 0. The origin is a critical point.

The change from the origin is B(x,y)-B(0,0)=2x^2+xy+y^2. Complete the square: 2x^2+xy+y^2=2\left(x+\frac14y\right)^2+\frac78y^2. This is positive unless x=y=0. So B(x,y)\gt B(0,0) for every nearby nonzero point. The origin is a local minimum.
Now consider M(x,y)=12-2x^2-xy-y^2. Again the origin is a critical point, but M(x,y)-M(0,0)=-(2x^2+xy+y^2). So every nearby nonzero point gives a smaller value. The origin is a local maximum.

Finally consider S(x,y)=12+x^2-y^2. At the origin, 
abla S(0,0)=\mathbf 0. But S(x,0)=12+x^2\gt 12 for x
e0, while S(0,y)=12-y^2\lt 12 for y
e0. The origin is a saddle point.
The three quadratic parts behave differently:

table.title: Sign behavior of three quadratic parts.

row.cell: positive in some directions, negative in others

statement.p: Let H be a symmetric matrix, and define q(\mathbf u)=\mathbf u^T H\mathbf u.
The quadratic form q is called positive definite if q(\mathbf u)\gt 0 for every nonzero vector \mathbf u.
It is called negative definite if q(\mathbf u)\lt 0 for every nonzero vector \mathbf u.
It is called indefinite if it takes both positive and negative values.

subsection.p: The Hessian tells the local shape through its quadratic form.

statement.p: Near a critical point the change f(\mathbf p+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf p) is governed by the quadratic part \tfrac12\mathbf u^T H\mathbf u. Why should the sign behavior of this quadratic part settle whether the point is a maximum, a minimum, or a saddle? Think about what it would mean for the quadratic part to be positive in every nonzero direction, versus negative in every direction, versus positive in some directions and negative in others.

hint.p: A local minimum means the function goes up no matter which way you step away from \mathbf p; a saddle means you can find a direction that goes up and another that goes down. Match those phrases to the signs the quadratic part can take.

figure.caption: A definite quadratic form has one sign in every nonzero direction. An indefinite form has both signs.

subsection.title: The two-variable determinant shortcut
subsection.p: For a two-variable function, the Hessian at a point has the form H=\begin{pmatrix}A \amp B\\B \amp C\end{pmatrix}. Its quadratic form is q(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u \amp v\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A \amp B\\B \amp C\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}=Au^2+2Buv+Cv^2. The number \boxed{\Delta=AC-B^2} decides most cases.

If A\ne0, complete the square:
q(u,v)\amp=Au^2+2Buv+Cv^2 \amp=A\left(u+\frac{B}{A}v\right)^2+\left(C-\frac{B^2}{A}\right)v^2 \amp=A\left(u+\frac{B}{A}v\right)^2+\frac{\Delta}{A}v^2.
Now the sign is visible.
If A=0 and \Delta\lt0, then B\ne0 and q(u,1)=2Bu+C takes both signs. Thus the indefinite conclusion below also covers the case excluded from completing the square.

table.title: What the determinant decides.

subsection.p: The last case is the one where the quadratic part has a flat direction or disappears entirely. Then second order is not enough.

statement.p: Suppose you already know that \Delta = AC - B^2 \gt 0 at a critical point. What more does the sign of A = f_{xx} tell you, and why is one number not enough on its own? Try to say in words what \Delta\gt 0 rules out, and then what the sign of f_{xx} picks between.

hint.p: Look back at the completed square A\left(u+\tfrac{B}{A}v\right)^2+\tfrac{\Delta}{A}v^2. With \Delta\gt 0 both terms share the sign of A. So \Delta\gt 0 tells you the form is definite, and A tells you which way it is definite.

subsection.title: The second derivative test
subsection.p: Now put the quadratic-form reading together with the second-order approximation.

theorem.title: Second derivative test in two variables

statement.p: Let f(x,y) have continuous second partial derivatives near a point (a,b). Suppose (a,b) is a critical point: f_x(a,b)=0,\qquad f_y(a,b)=0. Set A=f_{xx}(a,b),\qquad B=f_{xy}(a,b),\qquad C=f_{yy}(a,b), and \Delta=AC-B^2.
Then:

table.title: Classification by the discriminant.

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p: At a critical point, the second-order approximation says f((a,b)+\mathbf u)-f(a,b)=\frac12\mathbf u^T H_f(a,b)\mathbf u+R(\mathbf u), where \frac{R(\mathbf u)}{\|\mathbf u\|^2}\to0.

If the quadratic form q is positive definite, the continuous function q(\cos\theta,\sin\theta) is positive on the closed interval [0,2\pi]. The one-variable extreme-value theorem gives a positive minimum m_0. Scaling any nonzero vector to the unit circle therefore gives q(\mathbf u)\ge m_0\|\mathbf u\|^2. The remainder limit gives |R(\mathbf u)|\le(m_0/4)\|\mathbf u\|^2 for all sufficiently small \mathbf u. Hence \tfrac12q(\mathbf u)+R(\mathbf u)\gt0 for every such nonzero vector, proving a strict local minimum.
If the quadratic form is negative definite, the same argument gives a local maximum.

If the quadratic form is indefinite, there is one direction where the quadratic part is positive and another direction where it is negative. Along sufficiently small motions in those two directions, the function takes values both above and below f(a,b). That is a saddle point.

subsection.p: The test is a sign test for the first nonzero visible part of the function.

example.title: A minimum and a saddle from the same function

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2. First find the critical points: f_x=3x^2-3,\qquad f_y=2y. Setting both equal to zero gives x=\pm1,\qquad y=0. So the critical points are (1,0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(-1,0).
The second partials are f_{xx}=6x,\qquad f_{xy}=0,\qquad f_{yy}=2.
At (1,0), A=6,\qquad B=0,\qquad C=2. Thus \Delta=AC-B^2=12\gt 0, and A\gt 0. So (1,0) is a local minimum.
At (-1,0), A=-6,\qquad B=0,\qquad C=2. Thus \Delta=(-6)(2)-0=-12\lt 0. So (-1,0) is a saddle point.

example.title: The hilltop from earlier sections

statement.p: For h(x,y)=100+4x+3y-x^2-xy-y^2, the critical point is P=\left(\frac53,\frac23\right). The second partials are h_{xx}=-2,\qquad h_{xy}=-1,\qquad h_{yy}=-2. So A=-2,\qquad B=-1,\qquad C=-2. Then \Delta=AC-B^2=(-2)(-2)-(-1)^2=4-1=3. Since \Delta\gt 0\qquad\text{and}\qquad A\lt 0, the Hessian is negative definite. Therefore \left(\frac53,\frac23\right) is a local maximum.
This matches the exact expansion h\left(\frac53+u,\frac23+v\right)=\frac{313}{3}-(u^2+uv+v^2).

example.title: A cross-term saddle

statement.p: Let s(x,y)=xy. Then s_x=y,\qquad s_y=x. The origin is a critical point.
The second partials are s_{xx}=0,\qquad s_{xy}=1,\qquad s_{yy}=0. So A=0,\qquad B=1,\qquad C=0. Then \Delta=AC-B^2=0-1=-1\lt 0. Therefore the origin is a saddle point.
The geometry is easy to see: s(t,t)=t^2\gt 0, but s(t,-t)=-t^2\lt 0. The function rises along one diagonal and falls along the other.

subsection.title: Why the critical-point condition is needed
subsection.p: A positive definite Hessian does not by itself mean minimum. The first-order part must be gone.
Consider g(x,y)=x+x^2+y^2. At the origin, H_g(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}2 \amp 0\\0 \amp 2\end{pmatrix}, which is positive definite.
But the origin is not a critical point: \nabla g(0,0)=(1,0). In fact, g(-t,0)=-t+t^2\lt 0=g(0,0) for small positive t. So the origin is not a local minimum.
The Hessian tells us how the function bends. If the function is still sloping, the slope can dominate the bending.

subsection.title: Why the continuity condition is needed
subsection.p: The second derivative test also needs the second-order approximation to be valid. A Hessian computed at one point can mislead us if nearby second derivatives behave badly.

Define \Phi(x,y)=\begin{cases}x^2+y^2-8\dfrac{x^2y^2}{x^2+y^2}, \amp (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[3mm]0, \amp (x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases} At the origin, \nabla \Phi(0,0)=\mathbf 0. Along the coordinate axes, \Phi(x,0)=x^2,\qquad \Phi(0,y)=y^2. A direct calculation gives \Phi_{xx}(0,0)=2,\qquad \Phi_{xy}(0,0)=0,\qquad \Phi_{yx}(0,0)=0,\qquad \Phi_{yy}(0,0)=2. So the Hessian at the origin is H_\Phi(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}2 \amp 0\\0 \amp 2\end{pmatrix}, which is positive definite.

If the second derivative test applied, it would predict a local minimum. But along the line y=x=t, we get
\Phi(t,t)\amp=t^2+t^2-8\frac{t^4}{2t^2} \amp=2t^2-4t^2 \amp=-2t^2.
So \Phi(t,t)\lt \Phi(0,0) for every nonzero t close to 0. The origin is not a local minimum.

The second partials exist at the origin, but they are not continuous near the origin. The quadratic approximation is not trustworthy here. The continuity condition in the test protects us from this kind of behavior.

subsection.title: Degenerate Hessians
subsection.p: If \Delta=0, the second derivative test gives no conclusion. This does not mean the point is unusual or impossible to classify. It means the quadratic part does not decide.

example.title: Degenerate Hessian with a minimum

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=x^4+y^4. At the origin, \nabla f(0,0)=\mathbf 0. The Hessian is H_f(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0 \amp 0\\0 \amp 0\end{pmatrix}. So \Delta=0. The second derivative test says nothing.
But the origin is clearly a local minimum, because x^4+y^4\ge0, with equality only at (0,0). Here the first nonzero part is fourth order, not second order.

example.title: The same degenerate Hessian with a saddle

statement.p: Let g(x,y)=x^4-y^4. Again \nabla g(0,0)=\mathbf 0, and again H_g(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0 \amp 0\\0 \amp 0\end{pmatrix}. The Hessian is exactly the same as in the previous example.
But now g(t,0)=t^4\gt 0, while g(0,t)=-t^4\lt 0. So the origin is a saddle point.
The same Hessian produced a minimum in one function and a saddle in another. A degenerate Hessian does not carry enough information.

subsection.p: When the test is degenerate, we look for another idea: higher-order terms, special factoring, restrictions to curves, or a direct inequality.

statement.p: The two examples x^4+y^4 and x^4-y^4 share the very same zero Hessian, yet one gives a minimum and the other a saddle. Use this to explain why the test must fall silent exactly when \Delta = 0. What information has the quadratic part lost in that case, and where does the deciding behavior now hide?

hint.p: When \Delta=0 the quadratic part is flat in at least one direction, so it no longer reports a definite sign. The behavior is then decided by the first higher-order terms that the Hessian never sees.

subsection.title: A practical checklist
subsection.p: For an interior optimization problem with a twice continuously differentiable function of two variables:

table.title: Checklist for interior critical points.

row.cell: Find critical points by solving f_x=0,\ f_y=0.
Use the sign of \Delta and A to classify when possible.

subsection.p: This checklist is for interior critical points. It does not check boundaries. It also does not handle constraints.

That limitation matters. A marble rolling on a circular track wrapped around a hill cannot move in every direction. The ordinary gradient may not be zero at the highest point on the track, because the steepest uphill direction may point off the track. To optimize when motion is restricted, we need a new first-order condition. It will look strange at first: \nabla f=\lambda \nabla g. The number \lambda is a Lagrange multiplier.

section.title: Constrained optimization and Lagrange multipliers
section.p: classified interior critical points. There the point was free to move in every direction, so a local extremum forced \nabla f=\mathbf 0. But many optimization problems do not allow every direction. A marble on a circular track cannot move off the track. A box with a fixed amount of material cannot choose any side lengths it wants. A point on a surface must stay on the surface.
The first-order condition changes from \nabla f=\mathbf 0 to a condition about the directions that are allowed.

subsection.title: A circular walking path across a sloped field
subsection.p: A park has a circular walking path of radius 5 meters, centered at the origin. The sunlight score at a point on the ground is modeled by S(x,y)=6x+8y. We want the brightest and darkest points on the circular path x^2+y^2=25.

Without calculus, we can already guess the answer. The function S(x,y)=6x+8y increases most strongly in the direction (6,8). The vector (6,8) has length \sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10. The point on the circle of radius 5 in that direction is 5\frac{(6,8)}{10}=(3,4). So the brightest point should be (3,4), and the darkest point should be the opposite point (-3,-4).
Now let us find the same points by looking at gradients.
The constraint function is g(x,y)=x^2+y^2. The circular path is the level curve g(x,y)=25. From , the gradient \nabla g(x,y)=(2x,2y) is normal to this circle.

At a highest or lowest point on the circle, motion along the circle cannot change S to first order. So the gradient of S must also be normal to the circle. Since 
abla S=(6,8), we should have 
abla S=\lambda 
abla g for some number \lambda. That is, (6,8)=\lambda(2x,2y). So 6=2\lambda x, \qquad 8=2\lambda y. If \lambda
e0, then x= rac{3}{\lambda}, \qquad y= rac{4}{\lambda}. Now use the constraint: x^2+y^2=25. Thus  rac{9}{\lambda^2}+ rac{16}{\lambda^2}=25, so  rac{25}{\lambda^2}=25. Therefore \lambda=\pm1. When \lambda=1, (x,y)=(3,4). When \lambda=-1, (x,y)=(-3,-4). The values are S(3,4)=18+32=50, and S(-3,-4)=-18-32=-50. So  oxed{	ext{maximum value }50	ext{ at }(3,4),} and  oxed{	ext{minimum value }-50	ext{ at }(-3,-4).}

figure.caption: On the circle, allowed motion is tangent to the circle. At a constrained maximum or minimum, the gradient of the objective is normal to the allowed motion.

subsection.p: The number \lambda is called a Lagrange multiplier. The important part is not the number itself yet. The important part is the geometry: \text{gradient of objective} \quad \text{is parallel to} \quad \text{gradient of constraint}.

subsection.title: Why the gradient is perpendicular to a constraint
subsection.p: Suppose the constraint is g(x,y)=c. A curve \mathbf r(t) lying on the constraint satisfies g(\mathbf r(t))=c. Differentiating gives \nabla g(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)=0. So every allowed tangent direction is perpendicular to \nabla g.

Now suppose f has a local maximum or minimum while the point is forced to stay on the constraint. Along every allowed curve through the point, the one-variable function f(\mathbf r(t)) has a local maximum or minimum. Therefore \frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))=0 at that point. By the chain rule, \nabla f\cdot \mathbf r'(t)=0. So \nabla f is also perpendicular to every allowed tangent direction.
If the constraint is a smooth curve in the plane, then there is one tangent line. Two vectors perpendicular to the same tangent line must be parallel. Therefore \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g.

statement.p: At a constrained maximum or minimum on a smooth curve, why must \nabla f be parallel to \nabla g? Try to say it in terms of the tangent direction the constraint allows, rather than by quoting the formula.

hint.p: Both gradients are perpendicular to the same allowed tangent direction. In the plane that tangent line is one-dimensional, so how much freedom is left for a vector forced to be perpendicular to it?

statement.p: Let f and g have continuous first partial derivatives near a point \mathbf p. Suppose \mathbf p is a local maximum or local minimum of f subject to the constraint g(\mathbf x)=c. Suppose also that \nabla g(\mathbf p)\ne\mathbf 0, so the constraint is a smooth level curve or level surface near \mathbf p.

proof.p: At the constrained extremum, f has zero first-order change in every tangent direction allowed by the constraint.

The allowed tangent vectors \mathbf v are the vectors satisfying dg_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=0. The extremum condition says df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=0 for all such \mathbf v. Since dg_{\mathbf p}
e0, the constraint has a well-defined normal direction. The linear-functional argument above therefore gives df_{\mathbf p}=\lambda\,dg_{\mathbf p} for some number \lambda. In gradient notation, this becomes 
abla f(\mathbf p)=\lambda
abla g(\mathbf p).

subsection.p: The condition \nabla g(\mathbf p)\ne\mathbf 0 is not a technical decoration. If the constraint gradient vanishes, the level set may not have an ordinary tangent direction.

example.title: Why the constraint gradient must not vanish

statement.p: Let g(x,y)=x^2+y^2. The constraint g(x,y)=0 contains only the point (0,0). Now take f(x,y)=x. On the constraint set, f has both a maximum and a minimum, because the constraint set has only one point.

But \nabla f(0,0)=(1,0), while \nabla g(0,0)=(0,0). There is no number \lambda such that (1,0)=\lambda(0,0). The multiplier condition fails because the constraint is singular. The level set is not a smooth curve near the origin.

subsection.title: One constraint in three variables
subsection.p: The same condition works for surfaces in space.

example.title: Closest point on a plane

statement.p: A sensor is located at A=(1,2,3). A flat metal sheet lies in the plane x+2y+2z=6. We want the point on the sheet closest to the sensor.

Instead of minimizing the distance, minimize the squared distance: f(x,y,z)=(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2+(z-3)^2. The constraint is g(x,y,z)=x+2y+2z=6. Compute the gradients: 
abla f= igl(2(x-1),2(y-2),2(z-3) igr), and 
abla g=(1,2,2). The multiplier equation is 
abla f=\lambda
abla g. So 2(x-1)=\lambda, 2(y-2)=2\lambda, and 2(z-3)=2\lambda. Thus x=1+ rac{\lambda}{2}, \qquad y=2+\lambda, \qquad z=3+\lambda. Use the constraint: x+2y+2z=6. Substitute: \left(1+ rac{\lambda}{2}ight)+2(2+\lambda)+2(3+\lambda)=6. So 11+ rac{9}{2}\lambda=6. Therefore \lambda=- rac{10}{9}. The closest point is x=1- rac59= rac49, y=2- rac{10}{9}= rac89, and z=3- rac{10}{9}= rac{17}{9}. So  oxed{P=\left( rac49, rac89, rac{17}{9}ight).}
Geometrically, the vector from the sheet to the sensor is normal to the sheet. The Lagrange equation is just that fact written in gradient form.

subsection.p: The multiplier method gives candidates. It does not, by itself, decide whether a candidate is a maximum, a minimum, or something else. In the closest-point example, the geometry tells us the answer: distance squared from a fixed point to a plane has a unique minimum.

subsection.title: Multiple constraints
subsection.p: Sometimes a point must satisfy more than one constraint.

A curve in space can be described as the intersection of two surfaces: g(x,y,z)=c, \qquad h(x,y,z)=d. At a point on the curve, the allowed tangent direction must be perpendicular to both 
abla g \qquad	ext{and}\qquad 
abla h. So the normal plane to the curve is spanned by 
abla g \quad	ext{and}\quad 
abla h, provided these two gradients are independent.

theorem.title: Lagrange multiplier condition: two constraints in space

statement.p: Let f,g,h have continuous first partial derivatives near a point \mathbf p\in\mathbb R^3. Suppose \mathbf p is a local maximum or local minimum of f subject to g(\mathbf x)=c, \qquad h(\mathbf x)=d. Suppose also that \nabla g(\mathbf p) \quad\text{and}\quad \nabla h(\mathbf p) are linearly independent.

example.title: Optimizing on a circle in space

statement.p: A sensor ring lies where the cylinder x^2+y^2=1 meets the plane z=1. On that ring, the signal strength is F(x,y,z)=x+2y+3z. Find the maximum and minimum signal values.

Let g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2, \qquad h(x,y,z)=z. The constraints are g=1, \qquad h=1. The gradients are 
abla F=(1,2,3), 
abla g=(2x,2y,0), and 
abla h=(0,0,1). The multiplier equation is (1,2,3)=\lambda(2x,2y,0)+\mu(0,0,1). So 1=2\lambda x, 2=2\lambda y, and 3=\mu. Thus x= rac{1}{2\lambda}, \qquad y= rac{1}{\lambda}. Use x^2+y^2=1. Then  rac{1}{4\lambda^2}+ rac{1}{\lambda^2}=1, so  rac{5}{4\lambda^2}=1. Therefore \lambda=\pm rac{\sqrt5}{2}.
When \lambda=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}, we get x=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}, \qquad y=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}, \qquad z=1. When \lambda=-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}, we get x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt5}, \qquad y=-\frac{2}{\sqrt5}, \qquad z=1.

The corresponding values are F\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt5},\frac{2}{\sqrt5},1\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}+\frac{4}{\sqrt5}+3=3+\sqrt5, and F\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt5},-\frac{2}{\sqrt5},1\right)=3-\sqrt5. The ring is closed and bounded, so a continuous function on it has an absolute maximum and minimum. Thus \boxed{\text{maximum value }3+\sqrt5} and \boxed{\text{minimum value }3-\sqrt5.}

subsection.title: Boundary constraints and compactness
subsection.p: Lagrange multipliers find candidates on smooth constraint pieces. Boundary points must still be checked separately.
The guiding theorem is the same extreme-value theorem from single-variable calculus, now used in the plane and in space.

statement.p: Let D be a closed and bounded set in \mathbb R^2 or \mathbb R^3. If f:D\to\mathbb R is continuous, then f attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on D.

subsection.p: Here closed and bounded is the practical meaning of compact in the spaces of this book. Closed means the boundary is included. Bounded means the set fits inside some large ball.
Each hypothesis matters.

exercise.title: Why a compact set guarantees a winner

statement.p: A continuous function on a closed and bounded constraint set is guaranteed to attain its maximum and minimum. Why does that guarantee let us simply compare the values of f at our finite list of candidate points and trust the largest and smallest we find?

hint.p: If an extreme value is certain to occur somewhere on the set, and every place it could occur is already on your candidate list, what could possibly be hiding between the candidates?

example.title: Why closed matters

statement.p: The function f(x)=x on the open interval 0\lt x\lt 1 has no maximum and no minimum. The values get close to 1 and close to 0, but the endpoints are missing.

example.title: Why bounded matters

statement.p: The function f(x)=x on the real line has no maximum and no minimum. The domain is closed, but it is not bounded.

example.title: Why continuity matters

statement.p: Define f(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac1x, \amp 0\lt x\le1,\\[2mm] 0, \amp x=0. \end{cases} The domain [0,1] is closed and bounded. But f is not continuous at 0, and it has no maximum: as x\to0^+, the values \frac1x grow without bound.

subsection.p: For practical optimization on a region, the candidate list usually has several parts:

table.title: Where to look for constrained extrema.

row.cell: use Lagrange multipliers or one-variable calculus

example.title: A semicircular courtyard

statement.p: A solar sensor can be placed anywhere in the upper half-disk D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le25,\ y\ge0\}. Its score is S(x,y)=6x+8y. Find the absolute maximum and minimum.
The domain is closed and bounded, and S is continuous. Therefore the absolute maximum and minimum exist.
There are no interior critical points, because \nabla S=(6,8)\ne\mathbf 0.

Now check the curved boundary x^2+y^2=25, \qquad y\ge0. Using g(x,y)=x^2+y^2, the multiplier equation is (6,8)=\lambda(2x,2y). As before, this gives (x,y)=(3,4) \qquad\text{or}\qquad (x,y)=(-3,-4). Only (3,4) lies on the upper semicircle.
Now check the flat boundary y=0, \qquad -5\le x\le5. There S(x,0)=6x. On the interval [-5,5], this has endpoint values S(5,0)=30, \qquad S(-5,0)=-30.
Compare the candidates: S(3,4)=50, S(5,0)=30, and S(-5,0)=-30. Therefore \boxed{\text{absolute maximum }50\text{ at }(3,4),} and \boxed{\text{absolute minimum }-30\text{ at }(-5,0).}
The minimum occurs at an endpoint of a boundary piece. It is not found by the smooth circle multiplier equation.

subsection.title: Interpreting the multiplier
subsection.p: The multiplier \lambda often has a useful meaning. It measures how the best value changes when the constraint level changes.

Return to the circular path problem: S(x,y)=6x+8y, \qquad x^2+y^2=25. More generally, suppose the constraint is x^2+y^2=c, where c\gt 0. This is a circle of radius \sqrt c. The maximum of S on that circle is M(c)=10\sqrt c, because the vector (6,8) has length 10.
Differentiate: M'(c)=\frac{5}{\sqrt c}. At c=25, we get M'(25)=1. That matches the multiplier at the maximum point (3,4), where \lambda=1.
So if the allowed squared radius c increases slightly, the maximum sunlight score increases by about 1 unit of score per unit of c.

statement.p: Beyond being a number that makes \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g work, what does the Lagrange multiplier \lambda actually measure about the constrained problem?

hint.p: Think of the constraint level c as a dial you could turn. How does \lambda relate to the rate at which the best value of f responds when you nudge that dial?

subsection.p: The unit matters. If instead we write the constraint as \sqrt{x^2+y^2}=R, then the maximum value is 10R. At R=5, its derivative is 10. The multiplier changes because the constraint parameter changed. One version measures change per unit of squared radius. The other measures change per unit of radius.

This is one reason Lagrange multipliers appear in economics, physics, and design problems. They do not only find candidates. They also tell how valuable it would be to relax a constraint. But the method is easy to over-trust. It speaks only under its hypotheses, and it speaks only about the pieces where those hypotheses hold. The next section collects the traps, because most wrong optimization solutions fail in exactly these places.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The tests in this chapter are powerful because they are conditional. They say: \text{if the hypotheses hold, then the conclusion follows.} A warning example shows what can happen when one of the hypotheses is missing, or when a test is used beyond what it says.

subsection.title: A critical point that is not an extremum
subsection.p: The equation \nabla f=\mathbf 0 does not mean maximum or minimum. It means first-order silence.
Let f(x,y)=x^2-y^2. Then f_x=2x,\qquad f_y=-2y. So \nabla f(0,0)=\mathbf 0. The origin is a critical point.
But along the x-axis, f(x,0)=x^2\gt0 for x\ne0. Along the y-axis, f(0,y)=-y^2\lt0 for y\ne0.
Thus every small disk around the origin contains points where f is larger than f(0,0) and points where f is smaller. The origin is a saddle point.
The gradient equation finds candidates. It does not classify them.

exercise.title: Why does \nabla f=\mathbf 0 not settle the question?

statement.p: At a critical point we have \nabla f=\mathbf 0, yet the point may be neither a maximum nor a minimum. In your own words, why can a vanishing gradient fail to tell a peak from a valley from a saddle?

hint.p: A zero gradient only reports that f is flat to first order. Think about what the two axes do in f(x,y)=x^2-y^2: along one direction the value rises, along another it falls.

subsection.title: A degenerate Hessian with a minimum
subsection.p: The second derivative test also has limits. If the Hessian is degenerate, second-order information may not decide the shape.

Let f(x,y)=x^4+y^4. Then \nabla f(x,y)=(4x^3,4y^3), so \nabla f(0,0)=\mathbf 0. The Hessian is H_f(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}12x^2 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 12y^2\end{pmatrix}. At the origin, H_f(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0\amp0\\ 0\amp0\end{pmatrix}. So \Delta=0. The second derivative test gives no conclusion.
But x^4+y^4\ge0 for all (x,y), with equality only at (0,0). Therefore the origin is a local minimum.
Here the first nonzero visible terms are fourth order, not second order.

subsection.title: A degenerate Hessian with a saddle point
subsection.p: Now change only one sign: g(x,y)=x^4-y^4. Again \nabla g(0,0)=\mathbf 0, and again H_g(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0\amp0\\ 0\amp0\end{pmatrix}. The Hessian at the origin is exactly the same as in the previous example.
But along the x-axis, g(t,0)=t^4\gt0 for t\ne0, while along the y-axis, g(0,t)=-t^4\lt0 for t\ne0.
So the origin is a saddle point.

The same degenerate Hessian led to a minimum in one example and a saddle point in the other. When \Delta=0, the second derivative test is not weak. It is honest: second-order information is not enough.

subsection.title: A constrained problem where the multiplier method misses an endpoint
subsection.p: Lagrange multipliers are for smooth constraint pieces. They do not automatically find endpoints or corners.

Find the maximum and minimum of f(x,y)=x on the line segment -1\le x\le1,\qquad y=0. The smooth constraint is g(x,y)=y=0. Then \nabla f=(1,0),\qquad \nabla g=(0,1). The multiplier equation would be (1,0)=\lambda(0,1), which has no solution.
That does not mean the problem has no extrema. The domain is the closed line segment. The maximum occurs at (1,0), and the minimum occurs at (-1,0).
The multiplier method found no interior point of the segment because the function is increasing all along the segment. The extrema live at the endpoints, where the allowed set stops.

exercise.title: Where can Lagrange multipliers look the other way?

statement.p: The Lagrange-multiplier method can miss extrema that occur at endpoints or corners of a constraint. What assumption about the constraint does the method quietly rely on, and why does that assumption break down exactly at an endpoint or a corner?

hint.p: The multiplier equation \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g compares directions, so it needs a well-defined tangent direction along the constraint. Ask yourself whether such a direction exists where the allowed set simply stops.

subsection.title: Mixed partials can fail to agree without regularity
subsection.p: For smooth functions, the mixed partials agree: f_{xy}=f_{yx}. But the continuity hypothesis in the mixed-partials theorem is not optional.

So \boxed{F_{xy}(0,0)=-1,\qquad F_{yx}(0,0)=1.} Both mixed partials exist at the origin, but they are not equal. The missing condition is regularity near the point, such as continuity of the mixed partials.

exercise.title: What has failed when f_{xy}\ne f_{yx}?

statement.p: Suppose at some point a function satisfies f_{xy}\ne f_{yx}. Which hypothesis of the mixed-partials theorem must have failed there, and what does its failure say about how trustworthy the order of differentiation is at that point?

hint.p: The theorem does not just ask that both mixed partials exist. Look at the regularity condition it requires near the point, and ask what guarantees the two orders of differentiation agree.

subsection.title: The common lesson
subsection.p: The warnings are different, but they share one pattern.

table.title: What each tool does not do.

row.cell: does not check endpoints, corners, or singular constraints
does not hold without enough regularity

subsection.p: This chapter has been about special points: peaks, valleys, saddles, and constrained extrema. The next chapter changes the question. Instead of asking where a function is largest or smallest, we will ask how to add its values over a whole region. A hill will no longer be judged by its highest point, but by the total amount of earth under it. That new operation is the double integral.

introduction.p: collected the traps. A zero gradient may hide a saddle. A degenerate Hessian may hide higher-order behavior. A Lagrange multiplier calculation may miss an endpoint. Those warnings do not weaken the tools. They tell us where each tool belongs.
This review gathers the chapter into one decision path.

subsection.title: The chapter in one picture
subsection.p: Optimization begins by asking what motions are allowed.

If a point is free to move in every direction, then an interior extremum forces df=\mathbf 0, or, in gradient notation, 
abla f=\mathbf 0. If the point must stay on a constraint g=c, then only tangent directions to the constraint are allowed. At a constrained extremum, df=\lambda\,dg, or 
abla f=\lambda
abla g.
After first-order candidates are found, the Hessian reads the second-order shape.

figure.caption: The first question is not Which formula do I use? but What motions are allowed?

subsection.p:
For a twice continuously differentiable function of two variables, the Hessian test at a critical point uses A=f_{xx}, \qquad B=f_{xy}, \qquad C=f_{yy}, and \Delta=AC-B^2.
\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Condition} \amp \text{Conclusion} \\ \hline \Delta\gt 0,\ A\gt 0 \amp \text{local minimum}\\[1mm] \Delta\gt 0,\ A\lt 0 \amp \text{local maximum}\\[1mm] \Delta\lt 0 \amp \text{saddle point}\\[1mm] \Delta=0 \amp \text{test gives no conclusion} \end{array}
The number \Delta is only reading the quadratic part. If the quadratic part is silent in some direction, the function may still be decided by third, fourth, or higher-order terms.

subsection.title: Worked review example: free critical points
subsection.p: Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2-4y. Find and classify the critical points.
First compute the gradient: f_x=3x^2-3, \qquad f_y=2y-4. Set both equal to zero: 3x^2-3=0, \qquad 2y-4=0. Thus x=\pm1, \qquad y=2. The critical points are (1,2) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (-1,2).
Now compute the second partials: f_{xx}=6x, \qquad f_{xy}=0, \qquad f_{yy}=2.
At (1,2), we have A=6,\qquad B=0,\qquad C=2. So \Delta=AC-B^2=12\gt 0, and A\gt 0. Therefore \boxed{(1,2)\text{ is a local minimum.}}
At (-1,2), we have A=-6,\qquad B=0,\qquad C=2. So \Delta=(-6)(2)-0=-12\lt 0. Therefore \boxed{(-1,2)\text{ is a saddle point.}}
The same function has both behaviors. The gradient found the silent points. The Hessian listened to the first nonzero shape near each one.

subsection.title: Worked review example: absolute extrema on a rectangle
subsection.p: Let f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2-4x-4y on the rectangle 0\le x\le 3, \qquad 0\le y\le 2. Find the absolute maximum and minimum.
The domain is closed and bounded, and f is continuous, so an absolute maximum and minimum exist.

First check the interior. The gradient is \nabla f=(2x-4,\;4y-4). Set it equal to zero: 2x-4=0, \qquad 4y-4=0. Thus x=2, \qquad y=1. This point lies inside the rectangle. Its value is f(2,1)=4+2-8-4=-6.
Now check the boundary.
On the left edge, x=0,\qquad 0\le y\le2. Then f(0,y)=2y^2-4y=2(y-1)^2-2. The minimum on this edge is -2, and the maximum is 0, reached at y=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2.
On the right edge, x=3,\qquad 0\le y\le2. Then f(3,y)=9+2y^2-12-4y=2(y-1)^2-5. The minimum on this edge is -5, and the maximum is -3.
On the bottom edge, y=0,\qquad 0\le x\le3. Then f(x,0)=x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4. The minimum on this edge is -4, and the maximum is 0, reached at x=0.
On the top edge, y=2,\qquad 0\le x\le3. Then f(x,2)=x^2+8-4x-8=x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4. The minimum on this edge is -4, and the maximum is 0, reached at x=0.

Compare all candidates:
\begin{array}{c|c} \text{candidate} \amp f(x,y) \\ \hline (2,1) \amp -6\\ (0,0) \amp 0\\ (0,2) \amp 0\\ \text{other boundary candidates} \amp -5,\,-4,\,-3,\,-2 \end{array}
The interior gradient found the minimum. The maximum lived on the boundary.

subsection.title: Worked review example: one smooth constraint
subsection.p: Find the maximum and minimum of p(x,y)=x+2y on the ellipse x^2+4y^2=16.

Let g(x,y)=x^2+4y^2. The constraint is g=16. The gradients are 
abla p=(1,2), \qquad 
abla g=(2x,8y). The Lagrange multiplier equation is 
abla p=\lambda
abla g. So 1=2\lambda x, \qquad 2=8\lambda y. Thus x= rac{1}{2\lambda}, \qquad y= rac{1}{4\lambda}. Substitute into the constraint: x^2+4y^2=16. This gives  rac{1}{4\lambda^2} + 4\cdot rac{1}{16\lambda^2} = 16, so  rac{1}{2\lambda^2}=16. Therefore \lambda^2= rac{1}{32}, and \lambda=\pm  rac{1}{4\sqrt2}.
When \lambda=\frac{1}{4\sqrt2}, we get x=2\sqrt2, \qquad y=\sqrt2. When \lambda=-\frac{1}{4\sqrt2}, we get x=-2\sqrt2, \qquad y=-\sqrt2.

The values are p(2\sqrt2,\sqrt2)=2\sqrt2+2\sqrt2=4\sqrt2, and p(-2\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)=-4\sqrt2. The ellipse is closed and bounded, so these are the absolute extrema: \boxed{\text{maximum }4\sqrt2\text{ at }(2\sqrt2,\sqrt2),} \boxed{\text{minimum }-4\sqrt2\text{ at }(-2\sqrt2,-\sqrt2).}

Geometrically, the level lines x+2y=c slide across the ellipse. At the largest and smallest values, the line just touches the ellipse. At those touching points, the normal direction to the line is parallel to the normal direction to the ellipse.

statement.p: Why is the gradient normal to a level curve?
What is the tangent line to f(x,y)=f(a,b) at a point where \nabla f(a,b)\ne\mathbf 0?
What is the tangent plane to F(x,y,z)=F(a,b,c) at a point where \nabla F(a,b,c)\ne\mathbf 0?
Why must an interior local maximum or minimum of a differentiable function satisfy \nabla f=\mathbf 0?
Why does \nabla f=\mathbf 0 not guarantee a maximum or minimum?
What information does the Hessian contain that the gradient does not?
In the two-variable second derivative test, what does \Delta=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2 measure?
What does it mean for a Hessian to be positive definite? What local shape does that suggest at a critical point?
Why does the second derivative test require the point to be critical?
Why does the test give no conclusion when \Delta=0?

Why does a constrained extremum usually satisfy 
abla f=\lambda
abla g instead of 
abla f=\mathbf 0?
What can go wrong if \nabla g=\mathbf 0 on the constraint?
Why must endpoints and corners be checked separately?
In the differential-form notation df=\lambda\,dg, what does the equation say about allowed tangent motions?
Let f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2. Find the tangent line to the level curve f(x,y)=3 at (1,1).
Let F(x,y,z)=x^2+2y^2+3z^2. Find the tangent plane to F(x,y,z)=9 at (1,1,\sqrt2).
Let h(x,y)=20+4x-y-x^2-2y^2. Find all critical points and classify them.
Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2-2y. Find all critical points and classify them.
Let q(x,y)=x^2+4xy+y^2. Classify the origin using the Hessian.
Let s(x,y)=x^2+xy+2y^2. Use the Hessian to decide whether the origin is a local maximum, local minimum, or saddle point.
Let f(x,y)=x^4+y^2. Explain why the second derivative test gives no conclusion at the origin, and then classify the origin directly.
Let g(x,y)=x^4-y^2. Explain why the origin is a saddle point even though the Hessian is degenerate.
Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x,y)=x+y on the closed disk x^2+y^2\le 9.
Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x on the rectangle -1\le x\le3, \qquad 0\le y\le2.
Use Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum and minimum of f(x,y)=3x+4y on the circle x^2+y^2=25.
Use Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum and minimum of f(x,y)=xy on the ellipse x^2+4y^2=16.
Find the point on the plane x+y+z=6 closest to the origin.
Find the point on the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=25 where f(x,y,z)=x+2y+2z is largest.
Find the maximum and minimum of f(x,y,z)=z on the curve where x^2+y^2+z^2=9, \qquad x+y=0.

Let f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 subject to y=x^2. Find the constrained critical points by reducing to one variable. Compare the descriptions g(x,y)=y-x^2=0 and h(x,y)=(y-x^2)^2=0 of this same smooth parabola. Explain why Lagrange multipliers apply to the first description, while the vanishing gradient of h makes its multiplier equation unreliable.

Let f(x,y)=x on the line segment -1\le x\le1, \qquad y=0. Explain why the Lagrange multiplier equation for the smooth line y=0 finds no candidate, even though the function has a maximum and a minimum on the segment.
Let f(x,y)=|x|+y^2. Does f have a local minimum at the origin? Is the gradient defined there?
Let f(x,y)=x^2-y^2+x^4. Classify the origin.
Let f(x,y)=x^4+y^4-4xy. Find all critical points. Use the Hessian where possible.
Let f(x,y)=e^{x+y}(x^2+y^2). Show that the origin is a critical point and classify it.
Let f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2+2xy-6x. Complete the square to classify its critical point. Then check your answer with the Hessian.
Give an example of a critical point where the Hessian is the zero matrix but the point is a local minimum.
Give an example of a critical point where the Hessian is the zero matrix but the point is a saddle point.

subsection.title: Discovery project: least squares and the geometry of best fit
subsection.p: A line rarely passes exactly through experimental data. Suppose a lab records four points: (0,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,2),\qquad (3,4). We want a line y=mx+b that fits them as well as possible.

For each data point (x_i,y_i), the vertical error is mx_i+b-y_i. Instead of minimizing the sum of errors, which can cancel positive and negative mistakes, minimize the sum of squared errors: \boxed{E(m,b)=\sum_{i=1}^4(mx_i+b-y_i)^2.} For these data, \boxed{E(m,b) = (b-1)^2+(m+b-2)^2+(2m+b-2)^2+(3m+b-4)^2.}
The best-fit line is found by minimizing E. This is an optimization problem in the two variables m \qquad\text{and}\qquad b.

subsubsection.title: Part 1. The normal equations
subsubsection.p: Differentiate: E_m=2\sum_{i=1}^4 x_i(mx_i+b-y_i), and E_b=2\sum_{i=1}^4 (mx_i+b-y_i). At the minimum, E_m=0, \qquad E_b=0. These are called the normal equations.

subsubsection.title: Part 2. Why this critical point is a minimum
subsubsection.p:
The Hessian of E is
H_E = 2 \begin{pmatrix} \sum x_i^2 \amp \sum x_i\\ \sum x_i \amp 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 28 \amp 12\\ 12 \amp 8 \end{pmatrix}.
Compute \Delta=28\cdot8-12^2=224-144=80\gt 0. Since A=28\gt 0, the Hessian is positive definite. Therefore the critical point is a local minimum.
Because E(m,b) is a quadratic function whose leading quadratic part is positive definite, this local minimum is the absolute minimum.

subsubsection.title: Part 3. The geometry of the residual
subsubsection.p: Let \mathbf y=(1,2,2,4) be the vector of measured y-values. Let \mathbf 1=(1,1,1,1), \qquad \mathbf x=(0,1,2,3). The predicted values from the line y=mx+b form the vector \widehat{\mathbf y}=m\mathbf x+b\mathbf 1. The residual vector is \mathbf r=\widehat{\mathbf y}-\mathbf y.

At the best-fit line, m=b=\frac9{10}. So \widehat{\mathbf y} = \left(\frac9{10},\frac{18}{10},\frac{27}{10},\frac{36}{10}\right), and \mathbf r = \left(-\frac1{10},-\frac2{10},\frac7{10},-\frac4{10}\right). Check that \boxed{\mathbf r\cdot \mathbf 1=0} and \boxed{\mathbf r\cdot \mathbf x=0.}

The residual is perpendicular to every change caused by adjusting b or adjusting m. This is the geometric meaning of the normal equations: the error left over is orthogonal to the space of possible predictions.

subsubsection.title: What to hand in
subsubsection.p: Write a short report with the following pieces.

li.p: A plot of the four data points and the best-fit line.
The error function E(m,b).
The two normal equations E_m=0,\qquad E_b=0.
The solution m=b=\frac9{10}.
The Hessian calculation showing that this point gives a minimum.
The residual vector and the two dot products \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf 1=0, \qquad \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf x=0.
A paragraph explaining why best fit means a perpendicular residual.

subsection.title: Discovery project: designing a container under constraints
subsection.p: A rectangular open-top container has base side lengths x,\qquad y and height z. It must have volume 32 cubic units: xyz=32. The amount of material needed is A(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz. The term xy is the base. The terms 2xz and 2yz are the four side walls. There is no top.
Find the dimensions that use the least material.

subsubsection.title: Part 1. Set up the Lagrange equations
subsubsection.p:
Let g(x,y,z)=xyz. The constraint is g=32. The gradients are 
abla A=(y+2z,\ x+2z,\ 2x+2y), and 
abla g=(yz,\ xz,\ xy). The Lagrange multiplier equation is 
abla A=\lambda
abla g. So y+2z=\lambda yz, x+2z=\lambda xz, 2x+2y=\lambda xy, together with xyz=32.

subsubsection.title: Part 2. Show that the base is square
subsubsection.p: Multiply the first equation by x: xy+2xz=\lambda xyz. Multiply the second equation by y: xy+2yz=\lambda xyz. Subtract: 2xz-2yz=0. Since z\gt 0, we get \boxed{x=y.}

Set x=y=a. The third Lagrange equation becomes 4a=\lambda a^2, so \lambda=\frac4a. The first equation becomes a+2z=\lambda az. Substitute \lambda=\frac4a: a+2z=4z. Therefore \boxed{a=2z.} So z=\frac a2.
Use the volume constraint: a^2z=32. Since z=\frac a2, we get a^2\cdot\frac a2=32, so a^3=64. Thus a=4, and z=2. The candidate is \boxed{x=4,\qquad y=4,\qquad z=2.}

subsubsection.title: Part 3. Check the minimum another way
subsubsection.p: The dimensions are \boxed{4\times4\times2.}
The answer is not a cube. Since the container has no top, it is cheaper to make the base wider and the height shorter.

subsubsection.title: What to hand in
subsubsection.p: Write a short report with the following pieces.

li.p: A diagram of the open-top box with side lengths x, y, and z.
The material function A(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz.
The constraint xyz=32.
The Lagrange multiplier equations.
The calculation showing that x=y.
The calculation showing that z=\frac{x}{2}.
The final dimensions.
A sentence explaining why the answer is shorter than a cube.

conclusion.p: This chapter asked where a function is largest, smallest, or level to first order. That is a pointwise question. We stood on a hill and asked for the summit. We walked around a constraint and asked where the allowed motion stopped improving the value. The tools were local: df, \qquad \nabla f, \qquad H_f.

But sometimes the most interesting question is not about one point. A farmer does not only ask where the field is tallest; she asks how much crop the whole field will produce. An engineer does not only ask where a plate is hottest; she asks how much heat energy is spread across the plate. A hill is not only its highest point; it also has a total volume of earth under it.

To answer questions like that, we stop searching for a best point and start adding tiny pieces over a region. The single-variable integral added pieces along an interval. The next chapter lets the pieces fill a rectangle, a disk, or a curved region in the plane.
That is the double integral.

part.title: Multiple Integrals and Change of Variables

chapter.title: Double Integrals

introduction.p: A double integral adds contributions over a plane region. We begin with rectangular sums, then use iterated integrals to compute them on regions described by slices. Polar coordinates provide a first geometric substitution rule. Throughout, ordinary area is nonnegative; an oriented area form records an additional choice of orientation.

section.title: From area to volume by slicing
section.p: The single-variable integral began with area under a curve. A double integral begins with the same idea, but the base is no longer an interval. The base is a region in the plane, and the graph above it is a surface.

subsection.title: Area as a limit of sums
subsection.p: Imagine a garden bed whose edge is curved. The owner wants its area, but the shape is not a rectangle, a triangle, or a circle. One practical method is to lay a square grid over the garden and count squares.
Large squares give a rough estimate. Smaller squares give a better one.

figure.caption: Area can be estimated by adding the areas of many small squares.

subsection.p: If each small square has area \Delta A, and N of them lie mostly inside the garden, then \operatorname{Area} \approx N\Delta A. This is only an estimate, because boundary squares are awkward. For the garden shapes considered here, the boundary consists of finitely many smooth arcs. The boundary squares lie in a strip whose area tends to zero as the grid is refined. Thus the boundary error tends to zero. Arbitrarily complicated boundaries require additional hypotheses.

exercise.title: Why does a finer grid help?

statement.p: We claim that shrinking the squares makes the estimate N\Delta A close in on the true area. The interior squares are not the problem; the trouble lives in the boundary squares, which are partly in and partly out. Why does refining the grid shrink that error toward zero?

hint.p: Think about where the error lives. The boundary squares form a thin band hugging the curved edge. As the squares shrink, how does the total area of that band compare with the area of the whole region?

subsection.p: The idea is not new. In single-variable calculus, we approximated area under a curve by rectangles: \sum f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x. Now each small piece has area \Delta A instead of length \Delta x.

For a plain area problem, every small piece contributes just its own area. So area is the limit of sums like \sum \Delta A. Equivalently, \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(R)=\iint_R 1\,dA.} This formula says: add the constant value 1 over every tiny area piece in R.

subsection.title: Volume under a surface
subsection.p: Now put a surface above the region. Suppose a slanted canopy covers a rectangular market stall: 0\le x\le 4,\qquad 0\le y\le 3. Its height in meters is f(x,y)=2+\frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{6}. We want the volume of air under the canopy.

Cut the floor into 1-meter by 1-meter squares. Over each small square, pretend the canopy height is constant and equal to the height at the center of that square. Then each piece is approximately a rectangular column: \text{volume of one column} \approx \text{height at center}\times \text{base area}.

The centers have x=0.5,1.5,2.5,3.5 and y=0.5,1.5,2.5. Since each small square has area 1, the volume estimate is \sum f(x_i^*,y_j^*)\cdot 1. Compute the sum:
\sum f(x_i^*,y_j^*) \amp= \sum\left(2+\frac{x_i^*}{4}+\frac{y_j^*}{6}\right) \amp= 12\cdot 2 + \frac14\left(3(0.5+1.5+2.5+3.5)\right) \amp\qquad + \frac16\left(4(0.5+1.5+2.5)\right) \amp= 24+\frac14(24)+\frac16(18) \amp= 24+6+3 \amp= 33.
So the estimated volume is 33\text{ m}^3.

figure.caption: A double integral adds many small column volumes. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: The same pattern works for a nonnegative continuous height function z=f(x,y) above a region R. Divide R into many small pieces. On each piece, choose a sample point (x^*,y^*). The small column has approximate volume f(x^*,y^*)\,\Delta A. Add all the columns: \sum f(x^*,y^*)\,\Delta A. If these sums settle down to one number as the pieces shrink, that number is the volume under the surface.

subsection.title: Riemann sums over rectangles
subsection.p: The market canopy computation had the same shape as a one-variable Riemann sum, but with area pieces instead of length pieces.
For a rectangle R=[a,b]\times[c,d], we cut the x-interval into pieces and the y-interval into pieces. This creates many small subrectangles.

A typical subrectangle has side lengths \Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta y_j, so its area is \Delta A_{ij}=\Delta x_i\,\Delta y_j. Choose a sample point (x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*) inside that subrectangle. Then the Riemann sum is \boxed{\sum_i\sum_j f(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A_{ij}.}
This expression has a simple meaning:

table.title: The meaning of each factor in the Riemann sum.

row.cell: height, density, temperature, or value on the piece

subsection.p: When the function is a height, the contribution is a small volume. When the function is a density, the contribution is a small mass. When the function is temperature, the contribution is temperature times area, which leads to average temperature after we divide by total area.

exercise.title: From thin columns to exact volume?

statement.p: Each flat-topped column only approximates the curved surface above its little rectangle, so every single term f(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A_{ij} is a bit wrong. Yet we claim the limit of these sums is the surface's exact volume. How can adding up many approximate pieces and taking a limit land on the true answer?

hint.p: Notice that on a tiny rectangle the surface barely changes height, so the gap between the flat top and the real surface is small compared to that piece. Picture all those gaps shrinking faster than the pieces themselves as \Delta A_{ij}\to 0.

subsection.p: The symbol dA means a tiny positive area piece.

There is also a differential-forms way to write the same object. In , the form dx\wedge dy measured signed area in the xy-plane. On the usual orientation of the plane, a tiny rectangle whose sides point in the positive x- and y-directions has signed area (dx\wedge dy)\bigl((\Delta x,0),(0,\Delta y)\bigr)=\Delta x\,\Delta y. The left side evaluates a bilinear form on two finite edge vectors; it is not an equality between a form and a number. For this standard orientation, we define the oriented notation for the same integral to be \boxed{\iint_R f(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy.} For ordinary area, volume, mass, and average value, we usually write f\,dA. When orientation matters, especially near Green's theorem, the wedge notation will return.

subsection.title: What a double integral measures
subsection.p: A double integral is not tied to one picture. It is an adding machine for quantities spread over a region.

statement.p: A double integral can give area, volume, mass, or total charge, all from the same symbol \iint_R f\,dA. If f need not be a height, what role does it actually play in each tiny piece, and why does that single idea cover so many different physical quantities?

hint.p: Look at the units of f\,dA in each row of the table. In every case f is some quantity per unit area; multiplying by dA turns it into a small amount of the thing you care about. What is being accumulated then?

table.title: A double integral as an adding machine for different quantities.

example.title: Mass of a thin plate

statement.p: A thin metal plate occupies a region R in the plane. Its density at (x,y) is \rho(x,y)\quad \text{kg/m}^2. A tiny area piece \Delta A near (x,y) has mass approximately \rho(x,y)\Delta A. Adding all such pieces gives \boxed{M=\iint_R \rho(x,y)\,dA.} The double integral is not a volume here. It is mass.

example.title: Signed volume can cancel

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=x-y on the unit square R=[0,1]\times[0,1]. Below the diagonal y=x, the function is positive. Above the diagonal, it is negative.

For every point (x,y), the reflected point (y,x) has value f(y,x)=y-x=-(x-y). The square is symmetric under this reflection. So the positive and negative contributions cancel: \boxed{\iint_R (x-y)\,dA=0.} This does not mean the surface is flat. It means the signed volume above the square equals the signed volume below it.

subsection.p: The idea is now visible: choose small area pieces, multiply each by the value sitting on it, and add. But the phrase small area pieces still needs a careful meaning. If two people choose different sample points, will they get the same answer? If the function jumps around wildly, can the sums refuse to settle? The next section turns the picture of columns into a definition strong enough to compute with.

section.title: Double integrals over rectangles
section.p: built the double integral from a picture: columns over small rectangles. Now we make the pieces precise. The goal is the same as in single-variable calculus: define the integral in a way that does not depend on a lucky choice of sample points.

subsection.title: Partitions and sample points
subsection.p: Start with a rectangle R=[a,b]\times[c,d]. A partition of the x-interval is a list a=x_0\lt x_1\lt\cdots\lt x_m=b. A partition of the y-interval is a list c=y_0\lt y_1\lt\cdots\lt y_n=d. Together they cut R into subrectangles R_{ij}=[x_{i-1},x_i]\times[y_{j-1},y_j]. The area of R_{ij} is \Delta A_{ij}=\Delta x_i\,\Delta y_j, where \Delta x_i=x_i-x_{i-1}, \qquad \Delta y_j=y_j-y_{j-1}.

figure.caption: A partition cuts a rectangle into smaller rectangles. A Riemann sum chooses one sample point in each piece.

example.title: A midpoint estimate on a rectangle

statement.p:
Let R=[0,4]\times[0,2], and let f(x,y)=3+x+\frac12y. Cut R into four rectangles of size 2\times1. The midpoint sample points are (1,0.5),\quad (3,0.5),\quad (1,1.5),\quad (3,1.5). Each subrectangle has area \Delta A=2. The midpoint Riemann sum is
S \amp= 2\Bigl[ f(1,0.5)+f(3,0.5)+f(1,1.5)+f(3,1.5) \Bigr] \amp= 2\Bigl[ \left(3+1+\frac14\right) +\left(3+3+\frac14\right) +\left(3+1+\frac34\right) +\left(3+3+\frac34\right) \Bigr] \amp= 2\left[ \frac{17}{4}+\frac{25}{4}+\frac{19}{4}+\frac{27}{4} \right] \amp= 2\cdot 22 \amp= 44.
So this grid estimates \iint_R f\,dA by 44.
