subsection.p: For this linear function, the midpoint estimate is already exact. We will prove such facts later using iterated integrals. For now, the sum is the object to understand.

exercise.title: Why do the sample points stop mattering?

statement.p: For a continuous function f, two friends compute Riemann sums over the same rectangle, but they pick different sample points (x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*) inside each subrectangle, so their sums disagree. As the grid is refined and every subrectangle shrinks, why should this disagreement shrink to 0, no matter how stubbornly each friend keeps choosing different points?

hint.p: Think about how much f can change across a single tiny subrectangle. Two sample points in the same cell can differ in value by at most the spread of f on that cell, and that contribution is weighted by \Delta A_{ij}.

subsection.title: Integrable functions, informally
subsection.p: A function is integrable over a rectangle when the Riemann sums settle down to one number as the rectangles get small.
The sample points should stop mattering. The exact shape of the grid should stop mattering. Only the function and the region should matter.

exercise.title: What kind of bad behavior breaks integrability?

statement.p: We just asked that the sample points stop mattering as the grid refines. Imagine a bounded function for which that never happens: no matter how fine the grid, you can still pick sample points that push the sum high and others that push it low. What would such a function have to be doing on every tiny subrectangle to keep the upper and lower estimates from closing in on each other?

hint.p: Integrability fails when f keeps oscillating wildly at every scale, so that even the smallest subrectangle still contains points with large values and points with small values. Picture a function whose graph never settles down, no matter how far you zoom in.

statement.p: A bounded function f:R\to\mathbb R on a rectangle R=[a,b]\times[c,d] is integrable over R if all Riemann sums \sum_i\sum_j f(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A_{ij} approach the same number as the largest side length of the subrectangles approaches 0.

subsection.p: There is another way to say the same thing. On each subrectangle, the function has a largest possible value and a smallest possible value, at least for the functions we first meet. If we use all the largest values, we get an upper estimate. If we use all the smallest values, we get a lower estimate.
If the upper and lower estimates can be forced close together by using a fine enough partition, then the function is integrable.

theorem.title: Continuous functions on rectangles are integrable

statement.p: If f is continuous on a rectangle R=[a,b]\times[c,d], then f is integrable over R.

proof.title: Idea of proof
proof.p: A continuous function on a closed rectangle cannot oscillate too much inside very small rectangles. If the partition is fine enough, then the largest and smallest values of f on each subrectangle are close. Multiplying those small differences by the areas of the subrectangles and adding them gives upper and lower sums that are close. So every reasonable Riemann sum is trapped between two nearly equal numbers.

subsection.p: We required continuity because it gives a clean guarantee. Without it, the conclusion can fail.

example.title: A bounded function that is not integrable

statement.p: The function is bounded, but not integrable. It jumps too wildly on every tiny piece.

subsection.p: The boundedness condition is also part of this definition.

example.title: An unbounded function needs a different treatment

statement.p: This function does not fit the ordinary rectangle definition above. Integrals of unbounded functions require a limiting process. Those are improper double integrals, which return in .

subsection.p: The rectangle itself also has finite area. If we try to integrate f(x,y)=1 over the whole plane, the sums do not approach a finite number. They grow with the area being covered. Infinite regions also need improper integrals.
For now, rectangles are finite, functions are bounded, and continuity is the safe condition that makes the integral exist.

subsection.title: Average value over a rectangle
subsection.p: Single-variable calculus defined the average value of a function on an interval by f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx. The denominator was the length of the interval.
For a rectangle, length is replaced by area.

exercise.title: Why does dividing by area give the average?

statement.p: Suppose f were a constant, say f(x,y)=7, on a rectangle R. What is \iint_R f\,dA in that case, and what do you get when you divide it by \operatorname{Area}(R)? Use that simplest case to explain why dividing a general integral by the area deserves to be called the average value of f.

hint.p: The average value should be the single constant height that, spread evenly over R, accumulates the same total \iint_R f\,dA. Setting (\text{height})\times\operatorname{Area}(R)=\iint_R f\,dA and solving for the height gives the formula.

subsection.p: The units work out exactly as they should. If f is temperature in degrees Celsius, then \iint_R f\,dA has units {}^\circ\text{C}\cdot \text{m}^2. Dividing by area leaves {}^\circ\text{C}.

example.title: Average height of the market canopy

statement.p: In , the canopy over the rectangle [0,4]\times[0,3] had estimated volume 33\text{ m}^3. The floor area is 4\cdot 3=12\text{ m}^2. So the average canopy height is \frac{33}{12}=\frac{11}{4}=2.75\text{ m}. The average height is the height of a flat roof over the same floor that would enclose the same volume.

subsection.p: That last sentence is often the best way to remember average value:

subsection.title: Numerical estimates from tables and contour maps
subsection.p: In applications, we often do not know a formula for f(x,y). We may only have measurements.
Suppose a greenhouse floor is 0\le x\le 6,\qquad 0\le y\le 4, and temperature is measured at the centers of six equal rectangles. Each rectangle has dimensions 2\times2, so each has area 4.

table.title: Measured temperatures at the centers of six subrectangles.

subsection.p:
The midpoint estimate for the integral is
\iint_R T\,dA \amp\approx 4(18+19+20+22+24+23) \amp= 4(126) \amp= 504.
The total area is 6\cdot4=24. So the estimated average temperature is T_{\text{avg}} \approx \frac{504}{24} = 21{}^\circ\text{C}.
This is a double integral computed from a table. The table supplies the sample values. The grid supplies the area pieces.
Contour maps give another kind of estimate. They do not give values at isolated points; they show curves of equal value. We can estimate by splitting the region into bands.

figure.caption: A contour map can be turned into an estimate by using the areas between contours.

example.title: Estimating water volume from depth bands

statement.p: A pond is divided by contour lines into depth bands. Suppose the estimated areas are:

table.title: Depth bands, typical depths, and estimated areas for the pond.

statement.p:
Then the water volume is estimated by
V \amp\approx 0.5(120)+1.5(200)+2.5(160)+3.5(60) \amp= 60+300+400+210 \amp= 970\text{ m}^3.
The pond area is 120+200+160+60=540\text{ m}^2. So the estimated average depth is \frac{970}{540}\approx 1.80\text{ m}.

subsection.p: Both the table method and the contour method are Riemann sums in disguise. Each small contribution has the form \text{value}\times\text{area}.

So far, our double integrals have been built by estimates. That is honest, but slow. Single-variable calculus became powerful when area sums turned into ordinary antiderivatives. The same thing happens here in a surprising way: a double integral over a rectangle can often be computed by doing two single-variable integrals, one after the other. The next step is to slice the rectangle into strips and let the old Fundamental Theorem of Calculus do part of the work.

section.title: Iterated integrals and Fubini's theorem
section.p: defined a double integral over a rectangle as a limit of sums: \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA. That definition tells us what the integral means. It adds tiny contributions f(x,y)\,\Delta A over many small rectangles.

But the definition is not always the best way to compute. In single-variable calculus, we did not evaluate every definite integral by taking a limit of Riemann sums. Once the integral was defined, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gave us a practical method.
Something similar happens here. A double integral can often be computed by doing two ordinary one-variable integrals, one after the other.

subsection.title: A roof sliced two ways
subsection.p: A market stall has a rectangular base 0\le x\le 4, \qquad 0\le y\le 3. The height of its slanted roof above the floor is modeled by h(x,y)=5+x+2y. The volume under the roof is V=\iint_R h(x,y)\,dA, where R=[0,4]\times[0,3].

Instead of adding tiny columns all at once, freeze x. Then y runs from 0 to 3, and the roof above that vertical strip has cross-sectional area A(x)=\int_0^3 (5+x+2y)\,dy. Compute the inner integral:
A(x) \amp= \int_0^3 (5+x+2y)\,dy \amp= \Bigl[(5+x)y+y^2\Bigr]_0^3 \amp= 3(5+x)+9 \amp= 24+3x.
So a slice at position x has area 24+3x. Now add those slice areas from x=0 to x=4:
V \amp= \int_0^4 A(x)\,dx \amp= \int_0^4 (24+3x)\,dx \amp= \Bigl[24x+\frac32x^2\Bigr]_0^4 \amp= 96+24 \amp= 120.
Thus \boxed{\iint_R (5+x+2y)\,dA=120.}

The same volume can be sliced the other way. Freeze y, let x run from 0 to 4, and compute B(y)=\int_0^4 (5+x+2y)\,dx. Then
B(y) \amp= \Bigl[5x+\frac12x^2+2yx\Bigr]_0^4 \amp= 20+8+8y \amp= 28+8y.
Now add these horizontal slice areas:
V \amp= \int_0^3 B(y)\,dy \amp= \int_0^3 (28+8y)\,dy \amp= \Bigl[28y+4y^2\Bigr]_0^3 \amp= 84+36 \amp= 120.
Both slicing methods give the same volume: \boxed{\int_0^4\int_0^3 (5+x+2y)\,dy\,dx = \int_0^3\int_0^4 (5+x+2y)\,dx\,dy.}

statement.p: We sliced the roof first into vertical strips (freezing x) and then into horizontal strips (freezing y), and both routes gave 120. Without doing any new arithmetic, explain why slicing the very same solid in two different directions must produce the same total volume.

hint.p: Picture chopping the solid into many tiny columns of volume h(x,y)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y. Vertical and horizontal slicing are just two ways of grouping the very same little columns before you add them.

figure.caption: A rectangle can be added by vertical slices or by horizontal slices.

subsection.p: The picture is simple, but the idea is important. A double integral over a rectangle can be computed by reducing it to ordinary integrals.

subsection.title: Iterated integrals
subsection.p: The expression \int_0^4\int_0^3 (5+x+2y)\,dy\,dx means this:
First, hold x fixed and integrate with respect to y: \int_0^3 (5+x+2y)\,dy. Then integrate the result with respect to x: \int_0^4 \left(\int_0^3 (5+x+2y)\,dy\right) dx.
This is called an iterated integral, because one integral is nested inside another.

statement.p: Let R=[a,b]\times[c,d]. The iterated integral \boxed{\int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx} means \boxed{\int_a^b \left(\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\right) dx.} In the inner integral, x is held constant and y is the variable.

subsection.p: The inner integral makes a slice. The outer integral adds the slices.

A small notation warning is useful here. The symbol dy\,dx in an iterated integral is an instruction for the order of calculation: \text{integrate in }y\text{ first, then in }x. It is not a wedge product.

With the standard orientation of the xy-plane, the corresponding area 2-form is dx\wedge dy. So, for a positively oriented rectangle, \iint_R f\,dA = \int_R f\,dx\wedge dy. But dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy. Thus the wedge product remembers orientation, while the ordinary area element dA remembers positive area.

subsection.title: Fubini's theorem for rectangles
subsection.p: The roof example showed that the two orders gave the same answer. Fubini's theorem tells us when this is guaranteed.

statement.p: Let R=[a,b]\times[c,d], and suppose f is continuous on R. Then \boxed{\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_c^d\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy.}

proof.title: Idea of the proof
proof.p: For each fixed x, define A(x)=\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy. Geometrically, A(x) is the signed cross-sectional area of the surface over the vertical line segment above x. Adding those cross-sections gives \int_a^b A(x)\,dx = \int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx. This adds the same tiny rectangular contributions that the double integral adds: f(x,y)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y.
Similarly, if B(y)=\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx, then \int_c^d B(y)\,dy = \int_c^d\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy adds the same tiny contributions, only grouped into horizontal slices instead of vertical ones.
Both methods refine to the same Riemann sum limit, so both give the double integral.

subsection.p: The continuity assumption is a safe hypothesis. It guarantees that the double integral exists and that slicing in either order gives the same total.

exercise.title: What does each inner integral measure?

statement.p: Fubini's theorem lets us compute \iint_R f\,dA in either order, dy\,dx or dx\,dy. For a fixed x, what does the inner integral \int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy represent geometrically, and why should adding those quantities over all x give the same answer as adding the inner integrals \int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx over all y?

hint.p: Think of each inner integral as the area of one cross-sectional slice of the surface above a single line. The outer integral stacks those slices. Both orders are stacking slices of the very same solid.

subsection.title: A separated example
subsection.p: Sometimes the integrand splits into an x-part and a y-part. Then the double integral factors.

Let R=[0,3]\times[0,\pi], and let f(x,y)=(1+x^2)(2+\sin y). Then \iint_R (1+x^2)(2+\sin y)\,dA = \int_0^3\int_0^\pi (1+x^2)(2+\sin y)\,dy\,dx. Since 1+x^2 is constant with respect to y,
\int_0^\pi (1+x^2)(2+\sin y)\,dy \amp= (1+x^2)\int_0^\pi (2+\sin y)\,dy \amp= (1+x^2)\Bigl[2y-\cos y\Bigr]_0^\pi \amp= (1+x^2)(2\pi+2).
Now integrate in x:
\iint_R (1+x^2)(2+\sin y)\,dA \amp= \int_0^3 (1+x^2)(2\pi+2)\,dx \amp= (2\pi+2)\Bigl[x+\frac{x^3}{3}\Bigr]_0^3 \amp= (2\pi+2)(3+9) \amp= 24\pi+24.
Equivalently, \boxed{\iint_R (1+x^2)(2+\sin y)\,dA = \left(\int_0^3 (1+x^2)\,dx\right) \left(\int_0^\pi (2+\sin y)\,dy\right).}
The double integral factors because the rectangle has independent limits and the integrand is a product: f(x,y)=g(x)h(y).

subsection.title: Choosing an order
subsection.p: Fubini's theorem says that both orders work. It does not say that both orders are equally pleasant.

Consider I= \int_0^1\int_0^1 2x e^{xy}\,dy\,dx. If we integrate with respect to y first, x is a constant:
\int_0^1 2x e^{xy}\,dy \amp= 2\int_0^1 x e^{xy}\,dy \amp= 2\Bigl[e^{xy}\Bigr]_{y=0}^{y=1} \amp= 2(e^x-1).
Then
I \amp= \int_0^1 2(e^x-1)\,dx \amp= 2\Bigl[e^x-x\Bigr]_0^1 \amp= 2(e-1)-2 \amp= 2e-4.
So \boxed{\int_0^1\int_0^1 2x e^{xy}\,dy\,dx=2e-4.}
The other order is possible, but less direct. The moral is simple: before computing, look for the order in which the inner integral has an easy antiderivative.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: Fubini's theorem is safe for continuous functions on rectangles. If we sneak in an unbounded singularity, the story can break.
Define f(x,y) = \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} away from the origin in the square 0\le x\le1, \qquad 0\le y\le1. This function is not continuous at (0,0), and it is unbounded there.
If we read the iterated integrals as improper integrals, the two orders give different answers.

For fixed x\gt 0, \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( \frac{y}{x^2+y^2} \right) = \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. Therefore
\int_0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}\,dy \amp= \left[ \frac{y}{x^2+y^2} \right]_0^1 \amp= \frac{1}{1+x^2}.
Then \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}.

But for fixed y\gt 0, \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( -\frac{x}{x^2+y^2} \right) = \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. So
\int_0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}\,dx \amp= \left[ -\frac{x}{x^2+y^2} \right]_0^1 \amp= -\frac{1}{1+y^2}.
Then \int_0^1 -\frac{1}{1+y^2}\,dy=-\frac{\pi}{4}.

The two answers are \frac{\pi}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad -\frac{\pi}{4}. This is not a contradiction. Fubini's theorem did not apply. The function was not continuous on the rectangle, and the ordinary double integral was not a proper double integral over the square.

statement.p: For this f the two orders of integration gave \tfrac{\pi}{4} and -\tfrac{\pi}{4}. What feature of this function caused swapping the order to change the answer, and which hypothesis of Fubini's theorem would you check first before trusting that two orders must agree?

hint.p: Look at what happens near (0,0). Fubini's theorem asks for a continuous (in particular bounded) integrand on the rectangle. Ask whether this f meets that requirement everywhere on the square.

subsection.p: The warning is not meant to make the theorem feel fragile. It is meant to protect the theorem from being used outside its home. For continuous functions on rectangles, the order may be chosen for convenience.

subsection.title: What comes next
subsection.p: Rectangles are clean. Their bounds do not change: a\le x\le b, \qquad c\le y\le d. But most regions are not rectangular. A pond has a curved shore. A triangular plate has a slanted edge. A disk has circular boundaries.
The next step is to let the limits of the inner integral depend on the outer variable.
That is how double integrals escape the rectangle.

section.title: Double integrals over general regions
section.p: A rectangle is easy to slice because every vertical slice has the same y-limits, and every horizontal slice has the same x-limits. A general region asks for more care.
The main rule is not a formula. It is a habit:
section.md: \boxed{\text{Draw the region before writing the integral.}}
section.p: The picture tells us the limits.

To give the integral a meaning before computing it by slices, enclose a bounded region D in a rectangle R. Extend f to be zero on the part of R outside D. When this extension is Riemann integrable, define \iint_D f\,dA as its integral over R. A larger enclosing rectangle adds only zeros. For the continuous functions and regions bounded by finitely many piecewise smooth arcs used below, the boundary cells contribute an error tending to zero, so this construction applies.

subsection.title: A triangular flower bed
subsection.p: A triangular flower bed is bounded by y=0, \qquad x=4, \qquad y=\frac{x}{2}. Suppose the height of a layer of mulch spread over the bed is modeled by m(x,y)=6-y. Find the total volume of mulch over the bed.
The region is D=\left\{(x,y):0\le x\le4,\ 0\le y\le \frac{x}{2}\right\}. For each fixed x, the vertical slice runs from the bottom edge y=0 to the slanted edge y=\frac{x}{2}.

figure.caption: For this triangle, a vertical slice has variable height x/2.

subsection.p:
Therefore V=\iint_D (6-y)\,dA becomes V=\int_0^4\int_0^{x/2} (6-y)\,dy\,dx. Compute the inner integral:
\int_0^{x/2} (6-y)\,dy \amp= \left[6y-\frac12y^2\right]_0^{x/2} \amp= 3x-\frac{x^2}{8}.
Now integrate in x:
V \amp= \int_0^4 \left( 3x-\frac{x^2}{8} \right)\,dx \amp= \left[ \frac32x^2-\frac{x^3}{24} \right]_0^4 \amp= 24-\frac{64}{24} \amp= 24-\frac{8}{3} \amp= \frac{64}{3}.
Thus \boxed{V=\frac{64}{3}.}
The only new feature was the upper limit \frac{x}{2}. The upper edge of the region became a limit of integration.

subsection.title: Type I regions
subsection.p: The triangular flower bed is an example of a region that is easy to slice vertically.

statement.p: A region D in the plane is called a Type I region if it can be written as \boxed{ D= \left\{ (x,y): a\le x\le b,\ \phi_1(x)\le y\le \phi_2(x) \right\}. } Here the x-values run from a to b, and for each fixed x, the y-values run from a lower curve y=\phi_1(x) to an upper curve y=\phi_2(x).

subsection.p: For a Type I region, \boxed{ \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_{\phi_1(x)}^{\phi_2(x)} f(x,y)\,dy\,dx. }
The inner integral moves along a vertical slice. The outer integral moves those slices from left to right.

exercise.title: Why can the inner limits move?

statement.p: In a Type I setup, the outer limits a and b are plain constants, but the inner limits \phi_1(x) and \phi_2(x) are functions of x. Why must it be this way? What would go wrong if you tried to use constant y-limits for a region whose top and bottom edges are slanted?

hint.p: Picture two different vertical slices, one at a small x and one at a large x. Do they start and end at the same height? Think about what the inner limits are describing versus what the outer limits are describing.

figure.caption: A Type I region is described by vertical slices.

theorem.title: Double integral over a Type I region

statement.p: Suppose D= \left\{ (x,y): a\le x\le b,\ \phi_1(x)\le y\le \phi_2(x) \right\}, where \phi_1 and \phi_2 are continuous with \phi_1\le\phi_2 on [a,b], and suppose f is continuous on D. Then \boxed{ \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_{\phi_1(x)}^{\phi_2(x)} f(x,y)\,dy\,dx. }

proof.title: Idea of the proof
proof.p: For each fixed x, the vertical cross-section of D has y-values from \phi_1(x) to \phi_2(x). So the inner integral \int_{\phi_1(x)}^{\phi_2(x)} f(x,y)\,dy adds f along that vertical slice. The outer integral then adds all those slices from x=a to x=b.
This is the same slicing idea as Fubini's theorem, except now the slice endpoints can move with x.

subsection.title: Type II regions
subsection.p: Some regions are easier to slice horizontally.

statement.p: A region D in the plane is called a Type II region if it can be written as \boxed{ D= \left\{ (x,y): c\le y\le d,\ \psi_1(y)\le x\le \psi_2(y) \right\}. } Here the y-values run from c to d, and for each fixed y, the x-values run from a left curve x=\psi_1(y) to a right curve x=\psi_2(y).

subsection.p: For a Type II region, \boxed{ \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_c^d \int_{\psi_1(y)}^{\psi_2(y)} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy. }

figure.caption: A Type II region is described by horizontal slices.

theorem.title: Double integral over a Type II region

statement.p: Suppose D= \left\{ (x,y): c\le y\le d,\ \psi_1(y)\le x\le \psi_2(y) \right\}, where \psi_1 and \psi_2 are continuous with \psi_1\le\psi_2 on [c,d], and suppose f is continuous on D. Then \boxed{ \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_c^d \int_{\psi_1(y)}^{\psi_2(y)} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy. }

subsection.title: Drawing the region before integrating
subsection.p: The hardest part of many double integral problems is not the integration. It is setting up the bounds.
A reliable routine is:

li.p: Draw the boundary curves.
Mark the intersection points.
Decide whether vertical slices or horizontal slices are simpler.
Write the outer limits from the shadow of the region on the outer axis.
Write the inner limits from the slice.

subsection.p: The word shadow is useful. For a Type I setup, the region casts a shadow on the x-axis: a\le x\le b. For a Type II setup, it casts a shadow on the y-axis: c\le y\le d.

subsection.title: Reversing the order of integration
subsection.p: Sometimes one order leads to an integral we cannot evaluate with elementary functions. The other order may be easy.
Consider I= \int_0^1\int_y^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\,dy. The inner integral \int_y^1 e^{x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative. But the region may save us.
The bounds say 0\le y\le1, \qquad y\le x\le1. So the region is the triangle 0\le y\le x\le1. Equivalently, 0\le x\le1, \qquad 0\le y\le x.

figure.caption: The integral \int_0^1\int_y^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\,dy is over the triangle 0\le y\le x\le1.

subsection.p: The integral became possible not because the function changed, but because the slices changed.

statement.p: When you reverse the order of integration, it is tempting to simply exchange the inner and outer limits. Why doesn't that shortcut work? What information about the region would you miss if you never redrew the picture?

hint.p: The limits encode the shape of D, not just two numbers. Ask yourself: for a fixed x, where does a vertical slice begin and end? Is that the same as where a horizontal slice begins and ends for a fixed y?

subsection.title: A region that must be split
subsection.p: Not every region is Type I or Type II in one piece. Sometimes a slice hits the region in two separate intervals. Then one pair of limits would fill in space that is not really part of the region.
For example, let D= \bigl([0,1]\times[0,1]\bigr) \cup \bigl([0,1]\times[2,3]\bigr). This is two square islands with a gap between them.

statement.p: Some regions force you to break the integral into two or more pieces. What feature of a region tells you that a single pair of limits cannot describe it honestly? Why would one set of limits accidentally include points that aren't in the region?

hint.p: Run a single slice across the region and watch where it enters and leaves. If it leaves the region and then re-enters it, what does that say about the empty space in between?

subsection.p: A vertical slice at a fixed x hits 0\le y\le1 and also 2\le y\le3. It does not hit the gap 1\lt y\lt 2. So writing 0\le x\le1, \qquad 0\le y\le3 would describe the full rectangle, not the two islands.
The correct setup is a sum: \boxed{ \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dy\,dx + \int_0^1\int_2^3 f(x,y)\,dy\,dx. }
The principle is simple:
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{If one slice breaks into pieces, split the region.}}

subsection.title: Regions with holes
subsection.p: A hole is another reason to split or subtract.
Imagine an L-shaped floor: D= [0,3]\times[0,2] \setminus [1,3]\times[1,2]. It is a 3-by-2 rectangle with the upper-right rectangle removed.

Suppose f(x,y)=1+x is the density of a thin coating on the floor. The total amount of coating is \iint_D (1+x)\,dA. One method is to split the L-shape into two rectangles: D_1=[0,3]\times[0,1], and D_2=[0,1]\times[1,2]. Then \iint_D (1+x)\,dA = \int_0^3\int_0^1 (1+x)\,dy\,dx + \int_0^1\int_1^2 (1+x)\,dy\,dx. Compute:
\int_0^3\int_0^1 (1+x)\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^3 (1+x)\,dx \amp= \left[x+\frac12x^2\right]_0^3 \amp= 3+\frac92 \amp= \frac{15}{2}.
Also,
\int_0^1\int_1^2 (1+x)\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^1 (1+x)\,dx \amp= \left[x+\frac12x^2\right]_0^1 \amp= \frac32.
Therefore \boxed{ \iint_D (1+x)\,dA = \frac{15}{2}+\frac32 = 9. }

figure.caption: An L-shaped region is easiest to integrate over by splitting it into pieces.

subsection.p: Another method is subtraction: \iint_D (1+x)\,dA = \iint_{[0,3]\times[0,2]}(1+x)\,dA - \iint_{[1,3]\times[1,2]}(1+x)\,dA. The full rectangle contributes \int_0^3\int_0^2(1+x)\,dy\,dx = 2\int_0^3(1+x)\,dx = 15. The removed rectangle contributes \int_1^3\int_1^2(1+x)\,dy\,dx = \int_1^3(1+x)\,dx = 6. So again 15-6=9.
Both methods are correct. The good method is the one that makes the region easiest to describe.

subsection.title: The main lesson
subsection.p: For rectangles, the limits are constant: a\le x\le b, \qquad c\le y\le d. For general regions, one pair of limits often depends on the other variable: \phi_1(x)\le y\le\phi_2(x) or \psi_1(y)\le x\le\psi_2(y).
So the calculation is still based on one idea:
The only difference is that the slices may grow, shrink, split, or avoid holes.
The next obstacle is circular geometry. A disk can be described with x- and y-bounds, but the limits contain square roots. A circular ring is even less friendly in rectangular coordinates.
For circular regions, the natural slices are not vertical or horizontal. They are radial and angular.
That leads to polar coordinates.

section.title: Double integrals in polar coordinates
section.p: taught us how to integrate over regions that are not rectangles. The main tool was slicing. But circular regions still felt awkward in rectangular coordinates. A disk can be described by -a\le x\le a, \qquad -\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\le y\le \sqrt{a^2-x^2}, but those square roots are a sign that the coordinates are fighting the geometry.
For circular regions, the natural coordinates are x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta. The new question is not just how to rewrite the region. We must also understand how area changes.

subsection.title: A circular bowl
subsection.p: A shallow circular bowl has height z=9-x^2-y^2 above the circular floor x^2+y^2\le 9. The volume under the surface is V=\iint_D (9-x^2-y^2)\,dA, where D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le9\}.
In rectangular coordinates, the same integral becomes \int_{-3}^{3} \int_{-\sqrt{9-x^2}}^{\sqrt{9-x^2}} (9-x^2-y^2)\,dy\,dx. This is correct, but it does not look like the bowl.
In polar coordinates, x^2+y^2=r^2. The disk is simply 0\le r\le3, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. The height becomes 9-x^2-y^2=9-r^2.
The factor r is the new feature. Everything in polar integration depends on it.

subsection.title: Why the area element is r\,dr\,d\theta
subsection.p: A polar grid is made from circles and rays. If we fix r and let \theta change, we move around a circle. If we fix \theta and let r change, we move along a ray.

A small polar rectangle has two side lengths: \text{radial side length}\approx \Delta r, and \text{circular side length}\approx r\,\Delta\theta. The second formula is arc length: \text{arc length}=(\text{radius})(\text{angle}). Therefore \Delta A \approx (r\,\Delta\theta)(\Delta r) = r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta. More precisely, subtracting two circular-sector areas gives \Delta A=\tfrac12\bigl((r+\Delta r)^2-r^2\bigr)\Delta\theta =r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta+\tfrac12(\Delta r)^2\Delta\theta. On a bounded parameter region, the total error from the second term is bounded by a constant times the largest radial width. It therefore tends to zero as the grid is refined. This supplies the area factor directly, before the general substitution theorem.

figure.caption: A small polar rectangle has area approximately r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta.

subsection.p: There is also a differential-forms way to see the same factor.
This is the same factor we saw geometrically.

exercise.title: Where does the extra r come from?

statement.p: In rectangular coordinates a tiny cell has area dx\,dy, but in polar coordinates the area element is dA=r\,dr\,d\theta instead of just dr\,d\theta. Without computing anything, explain why a polar cell must pick up that extra factor of r. What is it about the shape of a polar grid that forces this?

hint.p: Two opposite sides of a polar cell are little arcs, not straight segments. Think about the arc-length rule (\text{length})=(\text{radius})(\text{angle}), and ask how the length of that arc depends on how far out you are.

subsection.title: Polar rectangles
subsection.p: A rectangle in the (r,\theta)-plane becomes a curved region in the xy-plane.

statement.p: A polar rectangle is a region described by \boxed{ a\le r\le b, \qquad \alpha\le\theta\le\beta. } In the xy-plane, this is the region between the circles r=a \qquad\text{and}\qquad r=b and between the rays \theta=\alpha \qquad\text{and}\qquad \theta=\beta.

subsection.p: For example, 1\le r\le3, \qquad 0\le\theta\le\pi is a half-annulus.

statement.p: Picture two polar rectangles with the same spans \Delta r and \Delta\theta: one hugging the origin, the other far out near the edge of a disk. Even though they share identical (r,\theta) dimensions, the far one encloses much more physical area. Why does a polar rectangle of fixed (r,\theta) size grow as it moves outward?

hint.p: The two slanted sides are rays through the origin, so they spread apart as r increases. How wide is the cell at radius r? Compare the arc r\,\Delta\theta near the origin with the same arc far away.

subsection.p:
Its area is
A \amp= \int_0^\pi\int_1^3 r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^\pi \left[ \frac12r^2 \right]_1^3 d\theta \amp= \int_0^\pi 4\,d\theta \amp= 4\pi.
This agrees with geometry: \frac12\pi(3^2)-\frac12\pi(1^2)=\frac92\pi-\frac12\pi=4\pi.

figure.caption: A polar rectangle can be a curved sector or annular sector.

subsection.title: The polar-coordinate formula
subsection.p: Now we can state the general rule.

statement.p: Suppose D is described in polar coordinates by S= \left\{ (r,\theta): \alpha\le\theta\le\beta,\ g(\theta)\le r\le h(\theta) \right\}, with D the image of this parameter region S in the xy-plane, where g and h are continuous, 0\le g(\theta)\le h(\theta), and the polar description covers the region once except possibly along boundary curves.

proof.title: Idea of the proof
proof.p: Divide the region into small polar rectangles. A small piece at radius r has area approximately r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta. On that piece, f(x,y)=f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta). So a Riemann sum looks like \sum f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta. As the polar pieces get small, this sum becomes \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{g(\theta)}^{h(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta. The differential calculation above records the same signed factor. The sector-area argument, rather than an unproved rule for integrating forms, justifies the integral here.

subsection.p: There are two warnings hidden in the theorem.

First, the function f is assumed continuous. This is a safe hypothesis that guarantees the usual Riemann integral exists. A wildly discontinuous function, such as the function that is 1 at rational-coordinate points and 0 at irrational-coordinate points inside a disk, is not Riemann integrable. Changing coordinates cannot fix a function whose ordinary integral is not defined.
Second, the polar description must not cover the region more than once.

For example, 0\le r\le1, \qquad 0\le\theta\le4\pi traces the unit disk twice. If we integrate 1, we get
\int_0^{4\pi}\int_0^1 r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{4\pi}\frac12\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi.
But the area of the unit disk is only \pi. The formula did not fail. The setup counted every point twice.

p.md: \boxed{ \text{A repeated polar description gives a repeated integral.} }

subsection.title: Radial symmetry
subsection.p: A function is radially symmetric if it depends only on the distance from the origin: f(x,y)=F(r), \qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. On a disk or annulus centered at the origin, polar coordinates make this especially simple.
The factor 2\pi comes from going all the way around the circle. The factor r still comes from area.

exercise.title: Why does symmetry simplify so much?

statement.p: When the integrand depends only on the distance from the origin, the polar double integral collapses to a single integral with a clean factor of 2\pi out front. Why does radial symmetry let one of the two integrations happen almost for free? What role does the choice of polar coordinates play in making this possible?

hint.p: If f=F(r), the integrand does not change as \theta sweeps around. Ask what the inner \theta-integral of a quantity that is constant in \theta must equal, and where the 2\pi comes from.

example.title: A radially symmetric mound

subsection.title: A shifted circle
subsection.p: Polar coordinates are not only for regions centered at the origin. They are often useful whenever a boundary has a simple polar equation.
Consider the disk D:\quad x^2+y^2\le2x. Complete the square: x^2-2x+y^2\le0, so (x-1)^2+y^2\le1. This is the disk of radius 1 centered at (1,0).

In polar coordinates, x^2+y^2=r^2, \qquad x=r\cos\theta. So the boundary x^2+y^2=2x becomes r^2=2r\cos\theta. For r\ge0, this gives r=2\cos\theta. This is nonnegative when -\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}. Thus the disk is -\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad 0\le r\le2\cos\theta.

figure.caption: The shifted disk (x-1)^2+y^2\le1 has polar boundary r=2\cos\theta.

subsection.p:
Now find \iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA. Since x^2+y^2=r^2, we get
\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA \amp= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_0^{2\cos\theta} r^2\,r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \left[ \frac14r^4 \right]_0^{2\cos\theta} d\theta \amp= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 4\cos^4\theta\,d\theta.
Using \cos^4\theta = \left(\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}\right)^2 = \frac38+\frac12\cos2\theta+\frac18\cos4\theta, we get
\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA \amp= 4\left[ \frac38\theta +\frac14\sin2\theta +\frac1{32}\sin4\theta \right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \amp= 4\cdot\frac{3\pi}{8} \amp= \frac{3\pi}{2}.
Thus \boxed{ \iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA=\frac{3\pi}{2}. }

subsection.title: A spiral region
subsection.p: Polar coordinates also describe regions bounded by spirals.

figure.caption: A spiral region can have very simple polar bounds.

subsection.title: The main lesson
subsection.p: Changing to polar coordinates does two things: x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta, and dA=r\,dr\,d\theta.
The first line changes the function and the region. The second line changes the area element.
So the safe routine is:

li.p: Draw the region.
Rewrite the boundary in polar form.
Rewrite the integrand using x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta.
Multiply by the area factor r.
Check that the polar description covers the region once.

subsection.p: The factor r is not optional. It is the price of using circular coordinates.

Now that we can integrate over many regions, we can ask what double integrals are good for besides volume. The same symbol \iint_D f\,dA can measure mass, center of mass, rotational inertia, probability, average temperature, rainfall, or elevation.
The integral is the same. The meaning of f changes.

section.title: Applications of double integrals
section.p: A double integral adds tiny pieces: f(x,y)\,\Delta A. If f is height, the pieces are tiny volumes. But f does not have to be height. It can be density, temperature, probability, or any quantity spread over a region.
This is why double integrals are useful. They turn a local measurement into a total quantity.

subsection.title: Mass from density
subsection.p: A thin metal sign occupies the rectangle D=[0,2]\times[0,1]. Because of a coating process, the sign is heavier toward the east. Its density is \sigma(x,y)=1+x kilograms per square meter.

statement.p: A thin plate in the plane is often called a lamina. If a lamina occupies a region D and has density \sigma(x,y) measured in mass per unit area, then its total mass is \boxed{ m=\iint_D \sigma(x,y)\,dA. } In form language, \boxed{ m=\int_D \sigma(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy. }

subsection.p: Density must be nonnegative for a physical mass distribution: \sigma(x,y)\ge0. Also, the total mass must be positive if we want to speak about a center of mass.

A signed function can still be integrated, but then it describes something like signed charge, not ordinary mass. For instance, on the symmetric rectangle [-1,1]\times[0,1], the signed density \sigma(x,y)=x has total integral \iint_D x\,dA=0. That may make sense as total charge. It does not make sense as a mass whose center we can find by dividing by total mass.

subsection.title: Center of mass
subsection.p: The same coated sign from above has density \sigma(x,y)=1+x on D=[0,2]\times[0,1]. Its mass is m=4.
Where should we balance it?
For a collection of point masses, the center of mass is a weighted average of positions. For a continuous lamina, the sums become integrals.

statement.p: The center of mass is built from \iint_D x\,\sigma\,dA divided by the total mass m, rather than just averaging the coordinates of the region. Why should the position of each tiny piece be weighted by its mass \sigma\,dA before we average? What would go wrong physically if we weighted every point equally instead?

hint.p: Picture a seesaw: a heavy child close to the pivot can balance a light child far away. Think about which pieces of the lamina "pull harder" on the balance point.

subsection.p: The x-coordinate of the center of mass should be the average of x, weighted by mass: \bar x = \frac{1}{m}\iint_D x\,\sigma(x,y)\,dA. The y-coordinate is \bar y = \frac{1}{m}\iint_D y\,\sigma(x,y)\,dA.

For our sign,
\iint_D x\sigma(x,y)\,dA \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 x(1+x)\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2 (x+x^2)\,dx \amp= \left[ \frac12x^2+\frac13x^3 \right]_0^2 \amp= 2+\frac83 \amp= \frac{14}{3}.
So \bar x=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{14}{3}=\frac76.

The answer makes sense. If the sign had uniform density, the center would be (1,1/2). Since the density is larger when x is larger, the center moves right to \bar x=\frac76\gt 1. But the density does not depend on y, so the vertical coordinate stays \bar y=\frac12.

figure.caption: The density increases to the right, so the center of mass shifts right.

subsection.p: The notation can feel backwards at first: M_y uses x, because x measures distance from the y-axis. Similarly, M_x uses y, because y measures distance from the x-axis.
If the density is constant, the center of mass is the geometric center of the region, called the centroid.

subsection.title: Moment of inertia
subsection.p: Mass tells us how hard it is to move an object in a straight line. Moment of inertia tells us how hard it is to rotate an object.
A small mass far from the axis of rotation matters more than the same mass near the axis. The distance is squared.

statement.p: For moment of inertia each piece of mass is weighted by r^2, its squared distance from the axis, not just by r. Suppose you move a small bead from distance r to distance 2r from the axle. How many times harder does that bead now make the object to spin up? Why does putting mass far from the axis matter so much more for rotation than for ordinary mass?

hint.p: A point at distance r traveling at angular speed \omega moves with speed r\omega, and its kinetic energy involves the square of its speed. See what that squaring does to the bead at 2r.

subsection.p: Consider a uniform circular disk of radius a, centered at the origin, with constant density \sigma_0. Find its moment of inertia about the origin, as if it were spinning around an axle through the center perpendicular to the disk.
This formula says that increasing the radius has a strong effect. The mass grows like a^2, but the moment of inertia about the center grows like a^4 if density stays fixed.

statement.p: Let a lamina occupy a region D, with density \sigma(x,y).

subsection.p: In polar coordinates, x^2+y^2=r^2, so moments of inertia about the origin often become especially simple: I_0=\iint_D r^2\sigma\,dA.

subsection.title: Probability density over a region
subsection.p: A probability density is another kind of density. Instead of mass per unit area, it measures probability per unit area.
Suppose a dart lands in the unit disk 0\le r\le1, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. The dart is more likely to land near the center than near the edge. A simple model is p(r)=C(1-r), where C is a constant.

To be a probability density, the total probability must be 1: \iint_D p\,dA=1. So
1 \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 C(1-r)\,r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi C\int_0^1(r-r^2)\,dr \amp= 2\pi C \left[ \frac12r^2-\frac13r^3 \right]_0^1 \amp= 2\pi C\left(\frac12-\frac13\right) \amp= \frac{\pi C}{3}.
Thus C=\frac{3}{\pi}. The density is p(r)=\frac{3}{\pi}(1-r).
For a uniform dartboard, the probability inside half the radius would be \frac{\pi(1/2)^2}{\pi(1)^2}=\frac14. Here it is larger because the density is concentrated near the center.
Both conditions matter.
If p(x,y)=2 on the unit square, then \iint_{[0,1]\times[0,1]}2\,dA=2, so it cannot be a probability density. Total probability would be 2, which is impossible.
If p(x,y)=-1 on any region of positive area, then probabilities over that region would be negative. That is also impossible.

subsection.title: Average value over a region
subsection.p: In single-variable calculus, the average value of f(x) on [a,b] was f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx. In two variables, we divide by area instead of length.

example.title: Average temperature in a circular pond

statement.p: A circular pond has radius 4 meters. Its surface temperature depends only on distance from the center: T(r)=20-r. The center is warmest, and the edge is coolest.

The area of the pond is 16\pi. The total temperature integral is
\iint_D T\,dA \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^4 (20-r)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^4(20r-r^2)\,dr \amp= 2\pi \left[ 10r^2-\frac13r^3 \right]_0^4 \amp= 2\pi \left( 160-\frac{64}{3} \right) \amp= \frac{832\pi}{3}.
Therefore
T_{\text{avg}} \amp= \frac{1}{16\pi}\cdot\frac{832\pi}{3} \amp= \frac{52}{3}.
So the average temperature is \boxed{ \frac{52}{3}^\circ\text{C}\approx 17.33^\circ\text{C}. }

subsection.p: The same formula can average rainfall, elevation, pollution concentration, light intensity, or any other scalar field over a region.

subsection.title: One integral, many meanings
subsection.p: The expression \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA has one mathematical structure: add local contributions over area.
Its meaning depends on what f measures.

statement.p: The single expression \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA can compute mass, total charge, a probability, or the quantity used for an average, with nothing changing except what f means. How can one calculation answer such different questions? What is the common idea, shared by all these settings, that the double integral is actually carrying out?

hint.p: Look at the building block f\,\Delta A by itself: it is "how much of the quantity sits on a tiny patch." Ask what the integral does with all those tiny patches, regardless of whether f is density, charge, or probability.

table.title: One integral, many meanings.

subsection.p: This is one of the strengths of integration. Once we know how to add over a region, many physical and geometric quantities become the same kind of calculation.

subsection.title: A compact summary of the main formulas
subsection.p: Let D be a region in the plane.
If \sigma(x,y) is density, then \boxed{ m=\iint_D \sigma\,dA. }
The moments are \boxed{ M_y=\iint_D x\sigma\,dA, \qquad M_x=\iint_D y\sigma\,dA. }
The center of mass is \boxed{ \bar x=\frac{M_y}{m}, \qquad \bar y=\frac{M_x}{m}. }
If p(x,y) is a probability density, then \boxed{ P((X,Y)\in A)=\iint_A p(x,y)\,dA. }
If f(x,y) is a scalar field, then its average value is \boxed{ f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\operatorname{Area}(D)} \iint_D f\,dA. }
Each formula is a weighted sum. The weight tells the integral what to measure.

subsection.title: What comes next
subsection.p: So far all our regions have lived in the plane. We have added over area: dA. But real objects fill space. A loaf of bread, a storm cloud, a storage tank, and a solid metal part occupy three-dimensional regions.
The next layer of the story is to add over volume: dV. That leads to triple integrals.

Before that, there is one warning worth understanding. Some regions are unbounded, and some functions blow up near a point. Then the ordinary double integral becomes an improper double integral. The same idea of adding tiny pieces remains, but convergence becomes the new question.

section.title: Improper double integrals
section.p: used double integrals to add mass, moments, probability, rainfall, temperature, and elevation over finite regions. The pieces were tiny, but the region itself was bounded, and the function stayed finite.

Some real quantities refuse to be that polite. Smoke can spread across a whole plain. A gravitational field can become very large near a point. A probability density may live on the entire plane. To handle these cases, we keep the same idea of adding tiny pieces, but the final answer now comes from a limit.

subsection.title: Unbounded regions
subsection.p: Imagine a thin layer of dust settling on a flat desert after a volcanic eruption. The dust is thickest near the source and thinner farther away. A simple radial model is \rho(x,y)=e^{-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, measured in grams per square meter.
The dust has no sharp edge in the model. It covers the whole plane. Still, the total mass might be finite because the density decreases fast.

Use polar coordinates: r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Then \rho=e^{-r}, \qquad dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. The mass inside a disk of radius A is
M(A) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^A e^{-r}r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^A re^{-r}\,dr.
Integrate by parts: \int re^{-r}\,dr=-re^{-r}-e^{-r}. So
M(A) \amp= 2\pi\left[-re^{-r}-e^{-r}\right]_0^A \amp= 2\pi\left(1-(A+1)e^{-A}\right).
As A\to\infty, we have (A+1)e^{-A}\to0. Therefore \boxed{M=\lim_{A\to\infty}M(A)=2\pi.}
The dust covers an infinite plane, but its total mass is finite.

exercise.title: What does convergence even mean here?

statement.p: When we say an integral over an infinite region converges, we are not adding up infinitely many things all at once. In your own words, what limiting process are we actually watching, and what would it mean for that process to fail to settle on a finite number?

hint.p: Look back at how M(A) was built: we measured the mass on a disk of radius A first, and only then asked what happens as A\to\infty. Picture the running total as the disk grows.

definition.title: Improper double integral over an unbounded region

statement.p: Let R be an unbounded region in the plane and let f\ge0 be integrable on each bounded truncation below. For A\gt 0, let R_A=R\cap\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le A^2\}. If the limit \boxed{\lim_{A\to\infty}\iint_{R_A} f\,dA} is finite, then we call it the convergent improper double integral of f over R, and we write \boxed{\iint_R f\,dA.}

subsection.p: For nonnegative functions, this definition matches the physical picture: measure more and more of the region, then see whether the accumulated total settles to a finite number.

figure.caption: Improper integrals use limits. For an unbounded region, the outer boundary moves outward. For a singular point, a small excluded disk shrinks inward.

subsection.p: The infinite size of the region does not automatically make the integral diverge. What matters is the balance between area growth and decay of the function.
Here is the simplest failure.

example.title: Infinite area gives infinite integral

statement.p: Let f(x,y)=1 on the whole plane. The integral over the disk of radius A is \iint_{x^2+y^2\le A^2}1\,dA=\pi A^2. As A\to\infty, this grows without bound. So \boxed{\iint_{\mathbb R^2}1\,dA} does not converge to a finite number.
The plane has infinite area, so adding 1 over the whole plane gives an infinite total.

subsection.p: A function can tend to 0 and still have infinite total.

example.title: Decay that is too slow

statement.p:
Let f(x,y)=\frac{1}{1+x^2+y^2} on the whole plane. In polar coordinates, f=\frac{1}{1+r^2}. The integral over the disk of radius A is
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^A \frac{1}{1+r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^A \frac{r}{1+r^2}\,dr \amp= \pi\ln(1+A^2).
As A\to\infty, the logarithm grows without bound. Therefore \boxed{\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{1}{1+x^2+y^2}\,dA} diverges.

subsection.p: The density \frac{1}{1+r^2} goes to 0, but not fast enough. The rings farther and farther away have larger circumference, and their combined contribution never settles down.

subsection.title: Unbounded functions
subsection.p: A different problem happens when the region is bounded, but the function becomes infinite at a point.

Imagine heat concentrated near the center of a thin circular plate. Let the plate be the unit disk D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\}. Suppose the heat density is modeled by h(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}. This function is unbounded at the origin. But the origin is only one point, so the total heat may still be finite.

In polar coordinates, h=\frac1r, \qquad dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. The product is simple: h\,dA=\frac1r\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=dr\,d\theta. To avoid the singularity at first, remove a tiny disk of radius \varepsilon. Then
\iint_{\varepsilon\le r\le1}\frac1r\,dA \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_\varepsilon^1 1\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi(1-\varepsilon).
Let \varepsilon\to0^+. Then \boxed{\iint_D\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\,dA=2\pi.} The function blows up at the center, but the total is finite.

definition.title: Improper double integral near a singular point

statement.p: Let R be a bounded region, and suppose f\ge0 is unbounded near a point \mathbf p\in R. Let R_\varepsilon=R\setminus B_\varepsilon(\mathbf p), where B_\varepsilon(\mathbf p) is the disk of radius \varepsilon centered at \mathbf p. If the limit \boxed{\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\iint_{R_\varepsilon} f\,dA} is finite, and f is integrable on each R_\varepsilon, then it is called the convergent improper double integral of f over R.

subsection.p: For a function that takes both signs, we will use an improper integral only when the corresponding integral of |f| is finite; this is absolute convergence. One then subtracts the finite integrals of its positive and negative parts. A limit using only centered disks can exist through cancellation even when absolute convergence fails; such a limit is a specified principal value, and is not enough to justify changing the order of integration or the shape of the truncations.

The power of r decides many singularities. Compare the previous example with k(x,y)=\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}. In polar coordinates, k=\frac1{r^2}. On the punctured disk,
\iint_{\varepsilon\le r\le1}\frac1{r^2}\,dA \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_\varepsilon^1 \frac1{r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_\varepsilon^1\frac1r\,dr \amp= 2\pi\ln\frac1{\varepsilon}.
As \varepsilon\to0^+, this grows without bound. So \boxed{\iint_D\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}\,dA} diverges.
The difference between \frac1r \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac1{r^2} is not small. The area element contributes a factor of r, and that factor saves \frac1r but not \frac1{r^2}.

subsection.title: Convergence and comparison
subsection.p: Most improper double integrals are not computed exactly. We often only need to know whether the total is finite.

Suppose a chemical concentration on the whole plane satisfies 0\le c(x,y)\le \frac{3}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}. The upper bound is easier to integrate. In polar coordinates, \iint_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{3}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}\,dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{3r}{(1+r^2)^2}\,dr\,d\theta. Use u=1+r^2, \qquad du=2r\,dr. Then
\int_0^\infty \frac{3r}{(1+r^2)^2}\,dr \amp= \frac32\int_1^\infty u^{-2}\,du \amp= \frac32.
Therefore \iint_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{3}{(1+x^2+y^2)^2}\,dA = 3\pi. Since c is squeezed below a function with finite integral, the total amount of chemical is also finite.

exercise.title: Why does comparing settle the question?

statement.p: We never computed the integral of c(x,y) itself, yet we still concluded it is finite. Why is it enough to know that c stays below a simpler function whose integral we can evaluate? What feature of nonnegative functions makes this trapping argument trustworthy?

hint.p: For a nonnegative function, the accumulated integral can only grow as the region expands. If it is forever held below a finite ceiling, where is the only place it can end up?

theorem.title: Comparison test for nonnegative double integrals

statement.p: Let 0\le f(x,y)\le g(x,y) on a region R, except possibly at singular points handled by improper limits, and assume both functions are integrable on the bounded nonsingular truncations.

li.p: If \iint_R g\,dA converges, then \iint_R f\,dA also converges.
If 0\le g(x,y)\le f(x,y) and \iint_R g\,dA diverges, then \iint_R f\,dA also diverges.

proof.title: Idea of proof
proof.p: For nonnegative functions, the accumulated integral over larger and larger pieces can only increase. If it is always bounded above by a finite number, it must settle to a finite limit. If it is always at least as large as a quantity that grows without bound, then it must also grow without bound.

subsection.p: The nonnegative condition is there because signed functions can cancel. Cancellation may be real, but it can also hide size.

For example, over the exterior region r\ge1, the radial function f(r,\theta)=\frac{\cos r}{r} has annular integral \int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^A \frac{\cos r}{r}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\int_1^A \cos r\,dr = 2\pi(\sin A-\sin 1). This has no limit as A\to\infty. It keeps oscillating. Positive comparison tests are designed for totals that do not cancel.
A useful rule of thumb comes from powers of r.
Near the origin, on a disk, \frac1{r^p} has integral like \int_0^1 r^{1-p}\,dr. This converges exactly when p\lt 2.
Far from the origin, on the outside of a large disk, \frac1{r^p} has integral like \int_1^\infty r^{1-p}\,dr. This converges exactly when p\gt 2.
The number 2 appears because area in polar coordinates carries the extra factor r. In three dimensions, that number will change.

subsection.title: The Gaussian integral
subsection.p: One of the most famous single-variable integrals has no elementary antiderivative: \int e^{-x^2}\,dx. But its improper integral over the whole real line has an exact value. The surprise is that a one-dimensional integral becomes easier after we square it and turn it into a double integral.

Let I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx. This integral is finite: for |x|\ge1, e^{-x^2}\le e^{-|x|}, whose tails converge. To justify squaring it without invoking an improper version of Fubini's theorem, set I_A=\int_{-A}^{A}e^{-x^2}\,dx. Finite-rectangle Fubini gives I_A^2=\iint_{[-A,A]^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA. The disk of radius A lies in this square, which lies in the disk of radius \sqrt2 A. Direct polar integration over a disk of radius B gives \pi(1-e^{-B^2}). Nonnegativity therefore yields \pi(1-e^{-A^2})\le I_A^2\le\pi(1-e^{-2A^2}). Both bounds tend to \pi, so I^2=\pi. The usual compact calculation below is justified by this bounded-domain argument:
I^2 \amp= \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx\right) \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-y^2}\,dy\right) \amp= \iint_{\mathbb R^2} e^{-x^2}e^{-y^2}\,dA \amp= \iint_{\mathbb R^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA.
Now use polar coordinates: x^2+y^2=r^2, \qquad dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. Then
I^2 \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr.
Use u=r^2, \qquad du=2r\,dr. Then
2\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr \amp= 2\pi\cdot\frac12\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du \amp= \pi.
Therefore I^2=\pi. Since I\gt 0, \boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi}.}
A single-variable antiderivative was missing, but the double integral found the value. The plane gave the problem a symmetry that the line could not show.

exercise.title: Why does polar make it work?

statement.p: On the line, \int e^{-x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative and resists every direct attack. After squaring it into a double integral and switching to polar coordinates, the computation suddenly goes through. What new factor appears in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta, and why is the extra r exactly the gift that makes \int e^{-r^2}r\,dr easy?

hint.p: Compare the missing antiderivative of e^{-x^2} with how cleanly the substitution u=r^2 handles e^{-r^2}r. Where did that helpful r come from?

subsection.p: That is a fitting ending for double integrals. They began as volume under a surface, then became a way to add density, probability, and mass across a region. Even a one-dimensional integral can become clearer after we let it spread into the plane. Before moving to space, it is worth gathering the whole chapter into one map.

introduction.p: Chapter began with the same idea that built single-variable integration: cut, multiply, add, and pass to a limit. The interval became a region. The tiny length dx became a tiny area dA, or, when orientation matters, dx\wedge dy.
The hardest part of most double integral problems is not the integration. It is deciding what the small pieces look like.

subsection.title: The chapter in one decision path
subsection.p: A double integral begins with a question: \text{What is being added, and over what region?}

If the region is a rectangle, iterated integrals usually go straight through. If the region has curved edges, draw it first. If the region is circular, polar coordinates may turn the picture into simple bounds. If the region is infinite or the function blows up, use an improper limit.

figure.caption: Most double integral problems are solved by matching the region to the right description.

subsection.p:
Here are the main formulas from the chapter.
\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Quantity} \amp \text{Double integral} \\ \hline \text{area of }R \amp \displaystyle \operatorname{Area}(R)=\iint_R 1\,dA \\[3mm] \text{volume under }z=f(x,y) \amp \displaystyle V=\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA \\[3mm] \text{average value} \amp \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{1}{\operatorname{Area}(R)}\iint_R f\,dA \\[4mm] \text{mass of a lamina} \amp \displaystyle M=\iint_R \rho\,dA \\[3mm] \text{moments} \amp \displaystyle M_y=\iint_R x\rho\,dA, \qquad M_x=\iint_R y\rho\,dA \\[4mm] \text{center of mass} \amp \displaystyle \bar x=\frac{M_y}{M}, \qquad \bar y=\frac{M_x}{M} \\[4mm] \text{moment of inertia about the origin} \amp \displaystyle I_O=\iint_R (x^2+y^2)\rho\,dA \\[4mm] \text{probability over }R \amp \displaystyle P((X,Y)\in R)=\iint_R p(x,y)\,dA \end{array}
For polar coordinates, \boxed{x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad dA=r\,dr\,d\theta.} The extra factor r is the area-scaling factor for a small polar rectangle.

subsection.title: Worked review example: drawing the region before integrating
subsection.p: Let R be the region bounded by y=x^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2x. Compute \iint_R y\,dA.

First find the intersection points: x^2=2x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(x-2)=0. So x=0\qquad\text{or}\qquad x=2. On 0\le x\le2, the line y=2x lies above the parabola y=x^2. Therefore R=\{(x,y):0\le x\le2,\ x^2\le y\le 2x\}. Set up the integral:
\iint_R y\,dA \amp= \int_0^2\int_{x^2}^{2x} y\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\left[\frac12y^2\right]_{x^2}^{2x}\,dx \amp= \frac12\int_0^2(4x^2-x^4)\,dx \amp= \frac12\left[\frac43x^3-\frac15x^5\right]_0^2 \amp= \frac12\left(\frac{32}{3}-\frac{32}{5}\right) \amp= \boxed{\frac{32}{15}}.

The same region can be described the other way. Since y=2x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac y2, and y=x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\sqrt y on the right-hand branch, the reversed description is R=\left\{(x,y):0\le y\le4,\ \frac y2\le x\le \sqrt y\right\}. So the same integral is \boxed{\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^4\int_{y/2}^{\sqrt y}y\,dx\,dy.} This is the same quantity with a different slicing direction.

subsection.title: Worked review example: a circular sprinkler pattern
subsection.p: A sprinkler waters a circular garden of radius 2 meters. The water density at a point depends only on distance from the center: w(r)=10-r,\qquad 0\le r\le2. Find the total water and the average water density over the garden.
The value \frac{26}{3} is less than 10, because most of the garden is not near the center. In polar coordinates, the factor r reminds us that larger rings contain more area.

statement.p: What does dA mean in a double integral?
Why is \iint_R 1\,dA the area of R?
What does the inner integral mean geometrically in an iterated integral?
Why does changing the order of integration require redrawing the region?
What is a Type I region? What is a Type II region?
Why does polar area have the factor r in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta?
When is polar integration likely to simplify a problem?
How are mass and density related by a double integral?
Why are the moments M_y=\iint_R x\rho\,dA,\qquad M_x=\iint_R y\rho\,dA named with the opposite coordinate?
What does the average value formula say in words?
How can a function be unbounded at one point but still have a finite double integral?
Why can a function that tends to 0 at infinity still have a divergent integral?
What does the comparison test require?

Let R be bounded by y=x^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad y=4. Set up and evaluate \iint_R x^2\,dA.

subsection.title: Project: estimating rainfall from gridded data
subsection.p: A storm passes over a rectangular watershed. The watershed is 0\le x\le8,\qquad 0\le y\le6, where x and y are measured in kilometers.

The region is divided into rectangles of size 2\text{ km}\times 2\text{ km}. Rainfall is measured at the center of each rectangle, in centimeters.
\begin{array}{c|cccc} \amp x=1 \amp x=3 \amp x=5 \amp x=7 \\ \hline y=5 \amp 3.2 \amp 4.1 \amp 4.6 \amp 3.8\\ y=3 \amp 2.4 \amp 3.5 \amp 5.0 \amp 4.2\\ y=1 \amp 1.1 \amp 2.0 \amp 3.1 \amp 2.7 \end{array}
Each grid cell has area 4\text{ km}^2.

subsubsection.title: Part 1. Estimate the total rainfall integral
Part 2. Convert to water volume
subsubsection.p: One centimeter of rain over one square kilometer equals 10{,}000\text{ m}^3 of water. Therefore the estimated water volume is \boxed{158.8(10{,}000)=1{,}588{,}000\text{ m}^3.}

subsubsection.title: Part 3. Estimate average rainfall
subsubsection.p: The watershed area is 8\cdot6=48\text{ km}^2. The average rainfall is \boxed{r_{\mathrm{avg}}\approx \frac{158.8}{48}\approx 3.31\text{ cm}.}

subsubsection.title: Part 4. What to hand in
subsubsection.p: Write a short report with the following pieces.

li.p: A sketch of the watershed grid.
The midpoint-sum estimate for \iint_R r(x,y)\,dA.
The conversion from \text{cm}\cdot\text{km}^2 to cubic meters.
The estimated average rainfall.
A contour-style sketch showing where the rainfall appears largest.
A paragraph explaining one possible source of error in the estimate. For example, what if the heaviest rain fell between two sensors?

conclusion.p: A double integral sees a thin region: a floor, a plate, a map, a lamina. But many objects are not thin. Air fills a room. Charge fills a solid ball. Density can vary from one shelf of a tank to another. The same adding idea is waiting there too, but the tiny pieces are no longer small rectangles. They are small boxes, and the bounds must describe a three-dimensional body. One more coordinate turns the double integral into a triple integral.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

introduction.p: Triple integrals extend the slicing and summation methods of Chapter 10 to solids. Cylindrical and spherical coordinates from Chapter 4 organize familiar regions, and their volume factors account for the sizes of small coordinate boxes. An optional section extends the same ideas to higher dimensions.

section.title: Triple integrals
section.p: A double integral adds over area. A triple integral adds over volume.
That one sentence is almost the whole idea. But it is worth seeing it first in the plainest possible place: a rectangular box.

subsection.title: Volume as a triple integral
subsection.p: Imagine a storage room whose dimensions are 4\text{ m}\times 3\text{ m}\times 2\text{ m}. Its volume is 4\cdot 3\cdot 2=24\text{ m}^3. Now suppose we forget that formula and rebuild the answer by adding small boxes.
Cut the room into unit cubes. Each cube has volume 1\text{ m}^3. There are 4\cdot3\cdot2=24 of them, so the total volume is 24\cdot1=24.

If the cubes were smaller, the idea would be the same. A small box with side lengths \Delta x,\qquad \Delta y,\qquad \Delta z has volume \Delta V=\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z. Adding all those small volumes gives the volume of the room: \sum \Delta V. In integral notation, \boxed{\operatorname{Volume}(E)=\iiint_E 1\,dV.} This says: add the constant value 1 throughout the solid E.

figure.caption: A triple integral begins by adding tiny volume pieces. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p: Now put a quantity inside the room. Suppose the density of a gas is \rho(x,y,z)=1+\frac z2 kilograms per cubic meter. The density is larger near the ceiling.
A small box near (x,y,z) has mass approximately \rho(x,y,z)\,\Delta V. Adding all small masses gives the total mass: \boxed{M=\iiint_E \rho(x,y,z)\,dV.}
The calculation did exactly what the story said. It added density times small volume throughout the room.

statement.p: We wrote \operatorname{Volume}(E)=\iiint_E 1\,dV. Why does adding the constant 1 throughout E measure volume, and what changes in the story when the constant 1 is replaced by a density f(x,y,z) so that the integral becomes \iiint_E f\,dV?

hint.p: Each tiny piece contributes (\text{value})\times \Delta V. Ask yourself what one small piece adds when the value is 1, and what it adds when the value is the local density.

statement.p: Let E be a solid region in space. If sums of the form \sum f(x_i^*,y_i^*,z_i^*)\,\Delta V_i approach one number as the small volume pieces shrink, independent of the sample points, then that number is called the triple integral of f over E, written \boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV.}

subsection.p: The symbol dV means a tiny positive volume piece.

There is also an oriented version. In , the form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz measured signed volume. For a small box whose edges point first in the positive x-direction, then the positive y-direction, then the positive z-direction, dx\wedge dy\wedge dz gives \Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z. So the oriented version of a triple integral is \boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.} For volume, mass, probability, and energy, we usually write dV, because those quantities use positive volume. The wedge notation remembers orientation, and that memory will matter when surfaces acquire a chosen side.

subsection.title: Integrals over boxes
subsection.p: A rectangular box has the form B=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f]. That means a\le x\le b,\qquad c\le y\le d,\qquad e\le z\le f.

To build a Riemann sum, cut the three coordinate intervals into pieces. A typical small box has side lengths \Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta y_j,\qquad \Delta z_k, so its volume is \Delta V_{ijk}=\Delta x_i\,\Delta y_j\,\Delta z_k. Choose a sample point (x_{ijk}^*,y_{ijk}^*,z_{ijk}^*) inside that small box. The Riemann sum is \boxed{\sum_i\sum_j\sum_k f(x_{ijk}^*,y_{ijk}^*,z_{ijk}^*)\,\Delta V_{ijk}.}
The table below gives the common meanings.

table.title: Common meanings of a triple integral.

example.title: Total charge in a box

statement.p: A solid block occupies B=[0,2]\times[0,1]\times[0,3]. Its charge density is q(x,y,z)=6+x+2y+3z. The total charge is Q=\iiint_B q(x,y,z)\,dV. Using the order dz\,dy\,dx, Q=\int_0^2\int_0^1\int_0^3 (6+x+2y+3z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.

First integrate with respect to z:
\int_0^3(6+x+2y+3z)\,dz \amp= \left[(6+x+2y)z+\frac32z^2\right]_0^3 \amp= 3(6+x+2y)+\frac{27}{2} \amp= \frac{63}{2}+3x+6y.

Then integrate with respect to y:
\int_0^1 \left(\frac{63}{2}+3x+6y\right)\,dy \amp= \frac{63}{2}+3x+3 \amp= \frac{69}{2}+3x.

subsection.p: The order dz\,dy\,dx tells us to integrate in z first, then y, then x. It is an instruction for computation.

The oriented volume form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is different. It remembers the orientation of ordered directions: dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=-dy\wedge dx\wedge dz. For ordinary triple integrals with dV, the order of calculation does not change the sign. The bounds and the differentials only tell us how to do the arithmetic.

subsection.title: Iterated triple integrals
subsection.p: The expression \int_a^b\int_c^d\int_e^f f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx means \int_a^b \left( \int_c^d \left( \int_e^f f(x,y,z)\,dz \right) dy \right) dx. In the innermost integral, x and y are held constant while z changes. After that, x is held constant while y changes. The outermost integral finally adds the results over x.

exercise.title: Why three integrals, one at a time?

statement.p: A triple integral asks us to add over a whole solid at once, yet we compute it by doing three ordinary single integrals in sequence. Why is it legitimate to peel the sum apart this way, holding two variables fixed while we integrate the third?

hint.p: Think about grouping the tiny contributions before adding them: first total a thin line in one direction, then collect those lines, then collect again. Holding two variables constant is just deciding which pieces to add first.

definition.title: Iterated triple integral over a box

statement.p: For a box B=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f], the iterated integral \boxed{\int_a^b\int_c^d\int_e^f f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx} means that z is integrated first, then y, then x.
Other orders are read the same way. The differential closest to the integrand is the first variable integrated.

subsection.p: Continuity is a safe condition. It guarantees that the volume sums settle down and that slicing in any coordinate order gives the same total. It is stronger than necessary. A density with a jump across a plane can still be integrable.

example.title: A jump can still be integrated

statement.p: On the box B=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,2], define f(x,y,z)= \begin{cases} 2, \amp 0\le z\lt 1,\\ 5, \amp 1\le z\le2. \end{cases} The function jumps across the plane z=1, so it is not continuous. But the integral is still easy. The lower half of the box contributes 2\cdot 1=2, and the upper half contributes 5\cdot 1=5. Thus \boxed{\iiint_B f\,dV=7.} So continuity is not the point by itself. The point is that the adding process must have a well-defined limit.

subsection.p: Here is what breaks when the adding process does not settle.

example.title: Why integrability is needed

statement.p: Define a function on B=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] by q(x,y,z)= \begin{cases} 1, \amp x\text{ is rational},\\ 0, \amp x\text{ is irrational}. \end{cases} Every small box contains points with rational x-coordinate and points with irrational x-coordinate. So on every small box, the largest possible value of q is 1, and the smallest possible value is 0.
The upper sums always give the full volume: 1. The lower sums always give 0. They cannot approach the same number. Therefore \iiint_B q\,dV does not exist as a Riemann integral.
This example is not a model for a physical density. It is a warning label for the theorem: before changing orders, there must be an integral to change.

proof.title: Idea of Fubini's theorem for boxes
proof.p: A triple integral over a box adds small contributions f(x,y,z)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z. An iterated integral groups those same small contributions into slices.
For example, if we integrate in z first, we add the thin vertical column above a fixed point (x,y). Then we add those columns over y, and finally over x.

If we integrate in x first, we group the same small boxes into slabs pointing in a different direction. The small contributions are the same; only the grouping changes. For continuous f, the limits of these grouped sums agree.

subsection.title: Order of integration in space
subsection.p: For a rectangular box, changing the order is mostly a matter of taste. The limits stay constant.

Return to the density \rho(x,y,z)=1+\frac z2 on B=[0,4]\times[0,3]\times[0,2]. The order dz\,dy\,dx gave \int_0^4\int_0^3\int_0^2 \left(1+\frac z2\right)\,dz\,dy\,dx. Since the density depends only on z, it may feel more natural to leave z for last:
M \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^3\int_0^4 \left(1+\frac z2\right)\,dx\,dy\,dz \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^3 4\left(1+\frac z2\right)\,dy\,dz \amp= \int_0^2 12\left(1+\frac z2\right)\,dz \amp= 12\left[z+\frac{z^2}{4}\right]_0^2 \amp= 36.
The same mass appears.

statement.p: There are exactly six orders in which we can integrate x, y, and z. Why are there six, and why should all six produce the very same number for a well-behaved integrand on a box?

hint.p: Count the ways to arrange three variables in a line. Then remember that each order only regroups the same little volume pieces f\,\Delta V before adding—the pieces themselves never change.

subsection.p: For boxes, all coordinate shadows are rectangles. That is why the limits are so calm. A real solid is rarely so polite. A room may have a slanted ceiling. A tank may have a curved side. A solid ball has no flat coordinate face at all. Then the bounds must describe the geometry, and changing the order becomes a drawing problem in three dimensions.
That is where the next section begins.

section.title: General solid regions
section.p: lived inside boxes. Boxes are a good first home because their bounds do not move: a\le x\le b,\qquad c\le y\le d,\qquad e\le z\le f. A general solid is different. One slice may be short, another tall, another empty. The limits have to tell that story.

subsection.title: Describing a solid by inequalities
subsection.p: Picture a small tent in the corner of a coordinate room. Its floor lies in the first quadrant of the xy-plane, and its sloping roof is the plane z=6-x-y. The tent touches the coordinate planes x=0,\qquad y=0,\qquad z=0. The solid inside the tent is E=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ x+y+z\le6\}.

The same solid can be described by nested inequalities. Choose x first: 0\le x\le 6. Once x is fixed, y can run from 0 to 6-x: 0\le y\le 6-x. Once x and y are fixed, z runs from the floor to the roof: 0\le z\le 6-x-y. So \boxed{E=\left\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le6,\ 0\le y\le 6-x,\ 0\le z\le 6-x-y\right\}.}

figure.caption: The solid x,y,z\ge0,\ x+y+z\le6 is a tetrahedron. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.p:
Its volume is \iiint_E 1\,dV. Using the bounds above,
\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x}\int_0^{6-x-y} 1\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x} (6-x-y)\,dy\,dx.
Compute the y-integral:
\int_0^{6-x} (6-x-y)\,dy \amp= \left[(6-x)y-\frac12y^2\right]_0^{6-x} \amp= \frac12(6-x)^2.
Therefore
\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= \int_0^6 \frac12(6-x)^2\,dx \amp= \frac12\left[-\frac{(6-x)^3}{3}\right]_0^6 \amp= 36.
So \boxed{\operatorname{Volume}(E)=36.}
The bounds were not guessed. They came from slicing the solid.

statement.p: We described the tetrahedron with the nested chain 0\le x\le6, then 0\le y\le 6-x, then 0\le z\le 6-x-y, and then simply copied those bounds into the integral \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x}\int_0^{6-x-y}\,dz\,dy\,dx. Why is the chain of nested inequalities already the integration limits, with no translation step in between?

hint.p: Think about what each inequality fixes. When you write 0\le z\le 6-x-y, the bounds on z are allowed to mention x and y because those are already chosen. Which variable is allowed to appear in which set of limits, and how does that ordering match the inside-to-outside order of the integral?

subsection.title: Slicing perpendicular to coordinate axes
subsection.p: The tent example used vertical slices. For each fixed point (x,y) in the shadow on the xy-plane, the z-coordinate ran from the bottom surface to the top surface.
That pattern is common enough to name.

For a z-simple solid, the triple integral is \boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \iint_D \left(\int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\,dz\right)dA.} After that, the double integral over D is handled by the methods of .
If D is Type I, D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \phi_1(x)\le y\le \phi_2(x)\}, then \boxed{\iiint_E f\,dV = \int_a^b \int_{\phi_1(x)}^{\phi_2(x)} \int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.}

theorem.title: Triple integral over a z-simple solid

statement.p: Suppose E=\left\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in D,\ g_1(x,y)\le z\le g_2(x,y)\right\}, where D is a bounded Type I or Type II region, or a finite union of such regions with disjoint interiors, and g_1,g_2 are continuous with g_1\le g_2 on D. Suppose f is continuous on E. Then \boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \iint_D \int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dA.}

proof.title: Idea of the proof
proof.p: For each fixed (x,y) in the shadow D, the vertical line through (x,y) cuts the solid in the interval g_1(x,y)\le z\le g_2(x,y). The inner integral adds f along that vertical slice. The outer double integral adds all the vertical slices over the shadow D.
This is the same slicing idea as Fubini's theorem, except now the slice endpoints depend on position.

exercise.title: Why a slice drops a dimension?

statement.p: For a z-simple solid we computed \iiint_E f\,dV by first integrating along each vertical slice, \int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f\,dz, and then doing a double integral over the shadow D. Why does integrating along the vertical line segments parallel to the z-axis leave a double integral over D, instead of leaving you with three integrals to do all at once?

subsection.p: The word z-simple matters. A vertical line must hit the solid in one interval. If it hits the solid in two separated pieces, one pair of z-limits cannot describe the solid without filling in empty space.

example.title: Why one slice must be one interval

statement.p: Let E=\bigl([0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1]\bigr)\cup\bigl([0,1]\times[0,1]\times[2,3]\bigr). This solid is two square shelves with a gap between them.
