For each point (x,y) in the unit square, the vertical line meets the solid in 0\le z\le1 and also in 2\le z\le3. It does not meet the gap 1\lt z\lt2. If we wrote 0\le z\le3, we would describe a full box of volume 3, not two shelves of total volume 2.

subsection.p: There are also x-simple and y-simple solids.

An x-simple solid has the form E=\left\{(x,y,z):(y,z)\in D_{yz},\ h_1(y,z)\le x\le h_2(y,z)\right\}. A y-simple solid has the form E=\left\{(x,y,z):(x,z)\in D_{xz},\ k_1(x,z)\le y\le k_2(x,z)\right\}. The same solid may be simple in more than one direction. The best direction is the one that makes the bounds easiest.

subsection.title: Regions bounded by surfaces
subsection.p: Many solids are described as the region between two surfaces above a plane region.

example.title: A layer between two slanted surfaces

statement.p:
A layer of insulation fills the region above the rectangle 0\le x\le2,\qquad 0\le y\le1. Its lower surface is z=1+x, and its upper surface is z=5-y. Since 1+x\le 5-y on this rectangle, the solid is E=\left\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le1,\ 1+x\le z\le 5-y\right\}. Its volume is
\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1\int_{1+x}^{5-y}1\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \bigl((5-y)-(1+x)\bigr)\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 (4-x-y)\,dy\,dx.
Now compute:
\int_0^1(4-x-y)\,dy \amp= 4-x-\frac12 \amp= \frac72-x.
Thus
\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= \int_0^2 \left(\frac72-x\right)\,dx \amp= 7-2 \amp= 5.
So \boxed{\operatorname{Volume}(E)=5.}

subsection.p: The inner integral with respect to z simply subtracts top minus bottom: (5-y)-(1+x). So for volume between two graphs, \boxed{\iiint_E 1\,dV = \iint_D \bigl(\text{top}-\text{bottom}\bigr)\,dA.} This is exactly the double-integral volume idea from . Triple integrals did not erase that idea; they placed it inside a larger one.

example.title: A nonconstant density between surfaces

statement.p:
Use the same solid 0\le x\le2,\qquad 0\le y\le1,\qquad 1+x\le z\le 5-y, but suppose the density is \rho(x,y,z)=z. Then
M \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1\int_{1+x}^{5-y} z\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left[\frac12 z^2\right]_{1+x}^{5-y}\,dy\,dx \amp= \frac12 \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left((5-y)^2-(1+x)^2\right)\,dy\,dx.
Compute the two pieces: \int_0^1(5-y)^2\,dy = \left[-\frac{(5-y)^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{125-64}{3} = \frac{61}{3}, and \int_0^2(1+x)^2\,dx = \left[\frac{(1+x)^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac{27-1}{3} = \frac{26}{3}. Since the first term is integrated over x\in[0,2] and the second over y\in[0,1],
M \amp= \frac12 \left(2\cdot\frac{61}{3} - 1\cdot\frac{26}{3}\right) \amp= \frac12\cdot\frac{96}{3} \amp= 16.
So \boxed{M=16.}

subsection.p: The bounds describe the solid. The integrand describes what is spread through it.

subsection.title: Changing the order of integration in space
subsection.p: Changing the order in two dimensions meant redrawing a region in the plane. Changing the order in three dimensions means redrawing a solid, or at least redrawing its shadow on a coordinate plane.

exercise.title: Why not just shuffle the limits?

statement.p: When we switched from \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x}\int_0^{6-x-y}\,dz\,dy\,dx to an order with x innermost, the new limits 0\le z\le6-y and 0\le x\le6-y-z were not the old limits rearranged. Why does changing the order force us to re-describe the solid from scratch, rather than simply permuting the limits we already had?

hint.p: Each set of limits answers the question “given the variables chosen so far, where can the next one go?” Changing the order changes which variables are chosen first, so it changes which surface bounds the slice and which coordinate plane the shadow lives on. Try sketching the shadow in the yz-plane versus the xy-plane and compare.

subsection.p: Return to the tetrahedron E=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ x+y+z\le6\}. One order was \boxed{\iiint_E f\,dV = \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x}\int_0^{6-x-y} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.} This order uses vertical z-slices. The shadow lies in the xy-plane: 0\le x\le6,\qquad 0\le y\le6-x.

Now choose x as the innermost variable. Then the shadow lies in the yz-plane. For fixed y and z, x runs from the plane x=0 to the slanted plane x=6-y-z. The yz-shadow is the triangle 0\le y\le6,\qquad 0\le z\le6-y. So the same integral can be written as \boxed{\iiint_E f\,dV = \int_0^6\int_0^{6-y}\int_0^{6-y-z} f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.}

A third order is \boxed{\iiint_E f\,dV = \int_0^6\int_0^{6-z}\int_0^{6-z-x} f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dx\,dz.} All three describe the same solid. The only difference is which coordinate direction is used for the innermost slice.

figure.caption: Changing the innermost variable changes the coordinate shadow we must draw.

subsection.p: Sometimes changing order is not only possible; it is the difference between a hard integral and an easy one.

example.title: Changing order to avoid a hard antiderivative

statement.p: Consider I=\int_0^1\int_0^1\int_y^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\,dz\,dy. The inner integral \int_y^1 e^{x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative.
The solid did not change. The grouping of its slices changed.

subsection.p: The habit from still works: \boxed{\text{Draw the shadow before writing the bounds.}} For a triple integral, choose the innermost variable first. Then draw the shadow on the plane of the two outer variables.

subsection.title: A compact guide to setting up bounds
subsection.p: When setting up a triple integral, use the following routine.

li.p: Decide which variable goes inside.
Look along that coordinate direction and describe the first and last surfaces hit.
Project the solid onto the plane of the two remaining variables.
Describe that shadow using the two-dimensional methods from .
Write the integral from inside to outside.

subsection.p: For example, if z goes inside, use \int\int\int_{\text{bottom}}^{\text{top}} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dA. If the xy-shadow is Type I, this becomes \int_a^b \int_{\phi_1(x)}^{\phi_2(x)} \int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.
If x goes inside, use \int\int\int_{\text{left}}^{\text{right}} f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dA_{yz}. If y goes inside, use \int\int\int_{\text{back}}^{\text{front}} f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dA_{xz}.
The names left, right, front, and back depend on the picture. The mathematics is the inequality.

Rectangular coordinates are good for boxes, wedges, slabs, and planes. But they are not always the natural language of space. A can, a pipe, a cone, and a ball all ask for distances and angles. If we describe a circular cylinder with x and y, square roots appear everywhere. If we describe it by radius, angle, and height, the solid becomes almost as simple as a box.
There is a price: a small coordinate box in radius and angle is not a true rectangular box in space. Its volume has a scale factor. The next section finds that factor: r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz.

section.title: Cylindrical coordinates in integrals
section.p: ended with a warning. Rectangular coordinates are not always the natural language of a solid. A box likes x, y, and z. A can, a pipe, a cone, and a round tank ask for radius, angle, and height.

Cylindrical coordinates keep the height z, but replace x and y by polar coordinates: x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad z=z. Here r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} is the distance from the z-axis, and \theta is the angle around that axis.

The new coordinates make circular solids easier to describe. They also change the small volume piece. A tiny box in r,\theta,z is not a rectangular box in ordinary space. That is why the factor r appears.

subsection.title: The volume element r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz
subsection.p: Start with the simplest round solid: a cylinder of radius 3 and height 5: x^2+y^2\le 9,\qquad 0\le z\le5. In cylindrical coordinates this becomes 0\le r\le3,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le5.

At radius r, an angular change \Delta\theta gives an arc length approximately r\,\Delta\theta. So the small piece has volume approximately \Delta V \approx (\Delta r)(r\,\Delta\theta)(\Delta z) = r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta\,\Delta z. Thus the cylindrical volume element is \boxed{dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz.}

exercise.title: Where does the r come from?

statement.p: A small cylindrical piece spans \Delta r, \Delta\theta, and \Delta z. Two such pieces share the same three numbers, but one sits near the z-axis and the other sits far from it. Why are their volumes different, and why does that difference force the factor r into dV=r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta?

hint.p: Think about the arc swept out by a fixed angle \Delta\theta. How long is that arc at radius r? The wider arc far from the axis is exactly what the factor r records.

figure.caption: The angular side of a small polar rectangle has length approximately r\,\Delta\theta, not \Delta\theta.

subsection.p:
Now compute the cylinder's volume:
V \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_0^5 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3 5r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{45}{2}\,d\theta \amp= 45\pi.
This agrees with the familiar formula \pi r^2h=\pi(3)^2(5)=45\pi.

The factor r is not optional. If we forgot it, we would get \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_0^5 1\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=30\pi, which is not the volume of the cylinder. The error comes from pretending that angular pieces near the axis and angular pieces far from the axis have the same width. They do not.

The same fact can be written with forms. In the following substitution calculation, dx abbreviates the differential of the scalar function x(r,\theta,z) on the parameter domain; dy is interpreted in the same way. Thus all the forms being equated live on that domain. will introduce explicit pullback notation for this convention. Since x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta, we have dx=\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta, and dy=\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta. Therefore
dx\wedge dy \amp= (\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta) \wedge (\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta) \amp= r\cos^2\theta\,dr\wedge d\theta + r\sin^2\theta\,dr\wedge d\theta \amp= r\,dr\wedge d\theta.
So \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = r\,dr\wedge d\theta\wedge dz.} For ordinary positive volume, we write this as dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz. The wedge version remembers orientation. The dV version remembers positive volume.

subsection.title: Cylinders, cones, and rotational symmetry
subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates are especially good when equations contain x^2+y^2. The translation is x^2+y^2=r^2.
For example, the circular cylinder x^2+y^2=9 becomes r=3. The solid inside the cylinder becomes 0\le r\le3.
The calculation was short because the solid did not care about the angle \theta. Every vertical slice through the z-axis looked the same.

exercise.title: Why do round shapes feel at home here?

statement.p: Cylinders, cones, and paraboloids all become tidy equations like r=3, z=4-r, or z=r^2 in cylindrical coordinates, while a plain box turns awkward. What do these round solids have in common that makes a coordinate built from r, \theta, and z describe them so cleanly?

hint.p: Ask what happens to each solid if you spin it around the z-axis. Which variable does its boundary equation quietly ignore?

subsection.p: When the solid and the integrand do not depend on \theta, we can usually factor out the full turn: \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta=2\pi. For a rotationally symmetric solid, E=\{(r,\theta,z):0\le\theta\le2\pi,\ a\le r\le b,\ g_1(r)\le z\le g_2(r)\}, and an integrand depending only on r and z, we get \boxed{\iiint_E f\,dV = 2\pi\int_a^b\int_{g_1(r)}^{g_2(r)} f(r,z)\,r\,dz\,dr.} The factor 2\pi comes from going once around the axis. The factor r comes from the widening of angular pieces.

example.title: A radially denser pipe

statement.p: A metal pipe has inner radius 1, outer radius 2, and length 5. Its density is \delta(r)=4+r kilograms per cubic meter. The density is larger near the outer wall.

subsection.title: Choosing bounds in cylindrical coordinates
subsection.p: For cylindrical coordinates, the shadow is usually drawn in the xy-plane using polar coordinates. Then z runs from a lower surface to an upper surface.
A useful routine is:

li.p: Rewrite the equations using x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad x^2+y^2=r^2.
Describe the shadow in the xy-plane by bounds on r and \theta.
Describe the vertical bounds for z.
Insert the factor r.

subsection.p: For a solid of the form \alpha\le\theta\le\beta, \qquad a(\theta)\le r\le b(\theta), \qquad g_1(r,\theta)\le z\le g_2(r,\theta), the integral becomes \boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)} \int_{g_1(r,\theta)}^{g_2(r,\theta)} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta.}

example.title: A cylinder cut by a slanted roof

statement.p: Let E be the solid inside the cylinder x^2+y^2\le4, above the floor z=0, and below the plane z=3+x. In cylindrical coordinates, x=r\cos\theta. So the top surface is z=3+r\cos\theta. Since 0\le r\le2, this top height is at least 1, so it stays above the floor.

The shadow is the disk 0\le r\le2,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Therefore \boxed{V = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^{3+r\cos\theta} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta.} Compute:
V \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 (3+r\cos\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \left[ \frac32 r^2+\frac13r^3\cos\theta \right]_0^2 d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 6+\frac83\cos\theta \right)d\theta \amp= 12\pi.
The slanted part averages out around the full circle: \int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,d\theta=0.

subsection.p: The bounds can also count too much if we are careless. For the full cylinder, the bounds 0\le\theta\le4\pi go around the same solid twice. The integral then gives twice the volume. Coordinate seams are harmless when they only repeat a boundary, such as \theta=0 and \theta=2\pi. They are not harmless when they repeat a whole three-dimensional region.

subsection.title: Applications to solids of revolution and tubes
subsection.p: A solid of revolution is often easiest to describe by drawing its rz-profile. The angle \theta then spins that profile around the z-axis.

example.title: A vase from a rotating profile

statement.p: A small vase has height 3. At height z, its radius is R(z)=1+\frac z3. So it widens linearly from radius 1 at the bottom to radius 2 at the top.

subsection.p: This example also explains why the old disk method from single-variable calculus worked. At height z, the cross-section is a disk of radius R(z), so its area is \pi R(z)^2. Cylindrical coordinates produce the same expression: \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{R(z)} r\,dr\,d\theta = \pi R(z)^2. The factor r is exactly what makes the circular area come out correctly.

A tube is similar, except the radial interval does not start at 0. If the inner radius is a and the outer radius is b, then a\le r\le b. A washer cross-section comes from the same idea: \int_0^{2\pi}\int_a^b r\,dr\,d\theta = \pi(b^2-a^2).

statement.p: A solid of revolution is made by spinning a flat profile around the z-axis. If you slice the result into thin cylindrical tubes, each tube has a radius r and a tiny thickness. Why does this picture of nested tubes match a solid of revolution so naturally, and where in the volume integral does the factor r for each tube appear?

hint.p: Imagine the surface of one thin tube at radius r. As you go once around in \theta, how far does that surface travel? That circumference is what the r in r\,dr\,d\theta is keeping track of.

subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates solve every problem whose geometry is organized around an axis. But they still treat height z differently from the other two coordinates. A ball does not have a preferred height direction. Its natural coordinate is distance from the center. Once we use that distance, two angles are needed to say which way we are looking. The price is another scale factor: \rho^2\sin\phi.

section.title: Spherical coordinates in integrals
section.p: Cylindrical coordinates made cans, pipes, and cones look simple. A ball is still awkward in cylindrical coordinates, because the top and bottom surfaces involve z=\pm\sqrt{a^2-r^2}. A ball wants a coordinate that measures distance from its center.
That coordinate is \rho. To locate a point in space, distance alone is not enough. We also need two angles.

subsection.title: The volume element \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta
subsection.p: Spherical coordinates use \rho,\qquad \phi,\qquad \theta. The convention in this book is as follows.

table.title: The spherical coordinates and their meanings.

row.cell: angle around the z-axis, measured in the xy-plane
angle down from the positive z-axis

subsection.p: Thus 0\le \rho, \qquad 0\le \phi\le \pi. The coordinate \theta usually runs through an interval of length 2\pi.
The conversion formulas are \boxed{x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta, \qquad y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta, \qquad z=\rho\cos\phi.} The distance from the z-axis is r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\rho\sin\phi.

figure.caption: The spherical volume element is bounded by small changes in \rho, \theta, and \phi.

subsection.p: Now find the small volume element.

A small spherical coordinate box has three side lengths, approximately: d\rho in the radial direction, \rho\,d\phi in the direction that changes \phi, and \rho\sin\phi\,d\theta in the direction that goes around the z-axis.
Multiplying these gives dV = d\rho\cdot \rho\,d\phi\cdot \rho\sin\phi\,d\theta. So \boxed{dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.}

The factor \rho^2 says that shells farther from the origin are larger. The factor \sin\phi says that angular pieces shrink near the poles. Near \phi=0, all values of \theta crowd around the positive z-axis.

statement.p: Without computing any integral, explain why the spherical volume element carries the factor \rho^2\sin\phi, so that dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta. Where does each piece of that factor come from geometrically?

hint.p: Picture the three edges of a tiny spherical box. One edge has length d\rho, but the other two are arcs whose radii are not 1. How long is the arc that sweeps through an angle d\phi, and how long is the arc that goes around the z-axis through d\theta? Notice that the second arc lives on a circle of radius \rho\sin\phi, not \rho.

subsection.p: In form language, substituting the scalar coordinate functions x(\rho,\phi,\theta), y(\rho,\phi,\theta), and z(\rho,\phi,\theta) gives the following identity on the parameter domain. Here dx,dy,dz mean the differentials of those functions, as in the cylindrical calculation; they are not unchanged target-coordinate covectors. The signed determinant calculation in gives \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = \rho^2\sin\phi\, d\rho\wedge d\phi\wedge d\theta.} This order is (\rho,\phi,\theta). Interchanging the two angular variables gives the negative signed determinant in order (\rho,\theta,\phi); ordinary volume uses the absolute value in either order. For positive volume, we write dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.

example.title: Volume of a ball

statement.p:
Let B be the ball of radius 4 centered at the origin: x^2+y^2+z^2\le16. In spherical coordinates, this is simply 0\le\rho\le4,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Therefore
\operatorname{Volume}(B) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^4 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= \left(\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\right)\left(\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_0^4\rho^2\,d\rho\right) \amp= (2\pi)(2)\left(\frac{64}{3}\right) \amp= \frac{256\pi}{3}.
This matches \frac43\pi(4)^3=\frac{256\pi}{3}.

subsection.p: Again, the scale factor is not optional. If we computed the unit ball without \sin\phi, we would get \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho^2\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}, not \frac{4\pi}{3}. The missing \sin\phi would give too much weight to tiny angular pieces near the poles.

subsection.title: Balls, shells, and cones
subsection.p: Spherical coordinates turn spheres into constant-\rho surfaces: x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \rho=a. So balls and shells become very simple.

exercise.title: Why are balls and shells so easy?

statement.p: In spherical coordinates, why are a solid ball and a spherical shell almost trivial to set up, while the same regions felt awkward in cylindrical coordinates? Think about what happens to the bounds on \rho, \phi, and \theta.

hint.p: A region is easiest when every bound is a constant rather than a function of the other variables. What do the surfaces \rho=2 and \rho=5 look like, and do the angular limits \phi and \theta depend on \rho at all here?

example.title: A spherical shell

statement.p:
The shell between radius 2 and radius 5 is 2\le\rho\le5. With full angular range, 0\le\phi\le\pi,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Its volume is
V \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_2^5 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= (2\pi)(2)\left[\frac{\rho^3}{3}\right]_2^5 \amp= 4\pi\cdot\frac{125-8}{3} \amp= 156\pi.

subsection.p: Cones also become simple, because a cone with vertex at the origin is a constant-angle surface. For example, z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} becomes \rho\cos\phi=\rho\sin\phi. Away from the origin, this gives \cos\phi=\sin\phi, so \phi=\frac{\pi}{4}. The inside of the upper cone is 0\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{4}.

example.title: A ball cut by a cone

subsection.p: A sphere fixes \rho. A cone fixes \phi. A vertical half-plane fixes \theta. That is the basic geometry of spherical bounds.

subsection.title: Choosing the angular bounds
subsection.p: The angle \theta is the same azimuth angle used in cylindrical coordinates. It describes the shadow in the xy-plane.
The angle \phi describes how far down from the positive z-axis the point lies. It controls vertical opening.

table.title: Conditions and their spherical meanings.

example.title: The first octant of a ball

statement.p:
The first octant means x\ge0,\qquad y\ge0,\qquad z\ge0. For the ball \rho\le4, the bounds are 0\le\rho\le4, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad 0\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}. The volume is
V \amp= \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^4 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)(1)\left(\frac{64}{3}\right) \amp= \frac{32\pi}{3}.
This is one eighth of the full ball volume \frac{256\pi}{3}.

subsection.p: Spherical coordinates can also describe caps, where the radial lower bound is not zero.

example.title: A spherical cap

statement.p:
Find the volume inside the sphere \rho\le3 and above the plane z=1. The plane becomes \rho\cos\phi=1. Along a ray with angle \phi, the plane is reached at \rho=\sec\phi. For the ray to reach the sphere after crossing the plane, we need \sec\phi\le3, or \cos\phi\ge\frac13. Thus 0\le\phi\le\arccos\frac13. The bounds are 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\arccos\frac13, \qquad \sec\phi\le\rho\le3. So \boxed{V= \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{\arccos(1/3)} \int_{\sec\phi}^{3} \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.} Compute:
V \amp= 2\pi\int_0^{\arccos(1/3)} \left[\frac{\rho^3}{3}\right]_{\sec\phi}^3 \sin\phi\,d\phi \amp= 2\pi\int_0^{\arccos(1/3)} \left(9-\frac13\sec^3\phi\right)\sin\phi\,d\phi.
Let \alpha=\arccos\frac13. Then \cos\alpha=\frac13, \qquad \tan^2\alpha=8. Also, \int_0^\alpha 9\sin\phi\,d\phi = 9(1-\cos\alpha)=6, and \frac13\int_0^\alpha \sec^3\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi = \frac13\int_0^\alpha \tan\phi\,\sec^2\phi\,d\phi = \frac16\tan^2\alpha = \frac43. Therefore V=2\pi\left(6-\frac43\right)=\frac{28\pi}{3}.

subsection.p: The angular bounds come from looking along rays from the origin. A ray either enters the solid immediately, enters after crossing a surface, or misses the solid. Spherical coordinates make us answer that ray question.

subsection.title: Applications to gravitational and radial densities
subsection.p:
Many three-dimensional densities depend only on distance from a central point. A planet model, a gas cloud, and a radially symmetric charge distribution all have this shape: \delta=\delta(\rho). For a ball of radius a, the total mass is
M \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^a \delta(\rho)\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= 4\pi\int_0^a \delta(\rho)\rho^2\,d\rho.
So \boxed{M=4\pi\int_0^a \delta(\rho)\rho^2\,d\rho.} The angular part contributes 4\pi, and the radial part carries the real information.

exercise.title: Why does the angular part split off?

statement.p: When the density depends only on \rho, the mass integral collapses to a single radial integral times the constant 4\pi. Explain why a density of the form \delta=\delta(\rho) lets the \phi and \theta integrals factor out, and why that would fail for a density like \delta=\delta(\rho,\phi).

hint.p: A product integrates as a product of integrals only when each variable appears in its own separate factor. Group the integrand \delta(\rho)\,\rho^2\sin\phi: which pieces involve \theta, which involve \phi, and which involve \rho? Does any factor mix two of the variables together?

example.title: A simple model planet

subsection.p:
The same scale factor explains a familiar feature of inverse-square laws. Suppose an energy density in a spherical shell is u(\rho)=\frac{10}{\rho^2}, \qquad 1\le\rho\le4. The total energy in the shell is
E \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_1^4 \frac{10}{\rho^2}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= 10(2\pi)(2)\int_1^4 d\rho \amp= 120\pi.
The \rho^2 in the volume element cancels the 1/\rho^2 in the density. Each unit of radial thickness contributes the same amount. Later, when we study flux, the same geometric growth of spherical area will help explain why gravitational and electric fields often have inverse-square form.

Cylindrical and spherical coordinates changed the shape of dV, but not the meaning of the integral. A triple integral still adds tiny contributions through a solid. Once we can add density, the next questions are natural: Where is the mass balanced? How far is it spread from an axis? How much charge or energy does the solid contain? Those are the applications that turn triple integrals from volume machines into physical measuring tools.

section.title: Applications of triple integrals
section.p: – taught us how to add over a solid. The geometry changed from boxes to wedges, cylinders, cones, balls, and shells, but the basic contribution always had the same shape: \text{value near a point}\times \text{tiny volume}. Now the value near the point becomes physical. It may be mass density, charge density, energy density, or probability density.
Because spherical coordinates already use the letter \rho, this section writes mass density as \delta(x,y,z).

subsection.title: Mass and density in space
subsection.p: Imagine a clear gel block in a laboratory. A chemical additive has settled unevenly, so the density is larger near the top. The block occupies E=[0,4]\times[0,3]\times[0,2], and its density is \delta(x,y,z)=2+z grams per cubic centimeter.

statement.p: If a solid E has mass density \delta(x,y,z), then its mass is \boxed{ M=\iiint_E \delta(x,y,z)\,dV. }

subsection.p: In oriented form notation, the same integral can be written \iiint_E \delta(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, when the solid is given the standard orientation. For mass, however, we usually write dV, because mass uses positive volume.

example.title: Mass of a cone with density depending on height

statement.p:
A solid cone has height 4, radius 4, and density \delta(x,y,z)=1+z. The cone has equation 0\le z\le 4-r in cylindrical coordinates. Thus 0\le \theta\le 2\pi, \qquad 0\le r\le4, \qquad 0\le z\le4-r. The mass is
M \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^4\int_0^{4-r} (1+z)r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^4 \left[z+\frac{z^2}{2}\right]_0^{4-r} r\,dr \amp= 2\pi\int_0^4 \left((4-r)+\frac12(4-r)^2\right)r\,dr.
Expand: (4-r)+\frac12(4-r)^2 = 4-r+8-4r+\frac12r^2 = 12-5r+\frac12r^2. So
M \amp= 2\pi\int_0^4 \left(12r-5r^2+\frac12r^3\right)\,dr \amp= 2\pi \left[ 6r^2-\frac53r^3+\frac18r^4 \right]_0^4 \amp= 2\pi \left( 96-\frac{320}{3}+32 \right) \amp= 2\pi\cdot\frac{64}{3} \amp= \frac{128\pi}{3}.
Thus \boxed{ M=\frac{128\pi}{3}. }

subsection.p: The density decides how much each small volume piece counts. The geometry decides where the pieces are.

subsection.title: Center of mass
subsection.p: Mass tells us how much matter there is. The center of mass tells us where that matter balances.

Return to the gel block E=[0,4]\times[0,3]\times[0,2], with density \delta(x,y,z)=2+z. The density depends only on height. So symmetry already tells us \bar x=2, \qquad \bar y=\frac32. But the z-coordinate of the center should be above the geometric middle z=1, because the block is denser near the top.

To find it, we compute the first moments: N_x=\iiint_E x\delta\,dV, \qquad N_y=\iiint_E y\delta\,dV, \qquad N_z=\iiint_E z\delta\,dV. For this block,
N_x \amp= \int_0^4\int_0^3\int_0^2 x(2+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \left(\int_0^4 x\,dx\right) \left(\int_0^3 dy\right) \left(\int_0^2(2+z)\,dz\right) \amp= 8\cdot3\cdot6 \amp= 144.
Similarly,
N_y \amp= \left(\int_0^4 dx\right) \left(\int_0^3 y\,dy\right) \left(\int_0^2(2+z)\,dz\right) \amp= 4\cdot\frac92\cdot6 \amp= 108.
For the height moment,
N_z \amp= \int_0^4\int_0^3\int_0^2 z(2+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= 12\int_0^2(2z+z^2)\,dz \amp= 12\left[z^2+\frac{z^3}{3}\right]_0^2 \amp= 12\left(4+\frac83\right) \amp= 80.
Since M=72, the center of mass is \boxed{ (\bar x,\bar y,\bar z) = \left( \frac{N_x}{M},\frac{N_y}{M},\frac{N_z}{M} \right) = \left(2,\frac32,\frac{10}{9}\right). } As expected, \bar z=\frac{10}{9}\gt 1.

figure.caption: When density increases with height, the center of mass moves upward.

statement.p: Let E be a solid with density \delta(x,y,z), and suppose M=\iiint_E \delta\,dV\gt 0. Define the first moments N_x=\iiint_E x\delta\,dV, \qquad N_y=\iiint_E y\delta\,dV, \qquad N_z=\iiint_E z\delta\,dV. Then the center of mass is \boxed{ (\bar x,\bar y,\bar z) = \left( \frac{N_x}{M}, \frac{N_y}{M}, \frac{N_z}{M} \right). }

subsection.p: The condition M\gt 0 matters. A real mass density is nonnegative, and if there is any material at all, then M\gt 0. But for signed quantities, such as electric charge, the same formula can break.

example.title: Why positive total mass is needed

statement.p: Suppose a cube contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge. A signed charge density q might satisfy \iiint_E q\,dV=0. The expression \frac{\iiint_E xq\,dV}{\iiint_E q\,dV} then tries to divide by zero. There may be a meaningful center of positive charge and a meaningful center of negative charge, but there is no center of total signed charge given by this quotient.
So the center of mass formula belongs to a positive finite mass distribution.

subsection.title: Moment of inertia
subsection.p: Center of mass measures balance. Moment of inertia measures resistance to rotation.
A point mass far from an axis is harder to spin than the same point mass near the axis. The distance is squared, so far-away material counts strongly.

statement.p: In a moment of inertia I=\iiint_E s^2\delta\,dV, the symbol s is the distance from a point to the rotation axis, not the distance to the origin. Why should the axis, rather than the origin, be the thing we measure distance to? Picture a point sitting directly on the spin axis but far below the origin: how fast is it actually moving as the solid turns, and what does that say about its share of the resistance to rotation?

hint.p: Ask what each little piece is physically doing while the solid spins. A piece right on the axis traces a circle of radius zero, so it barely moves no matter how far it is from the origin.

subsection.p: If a small volume piece has mass \delta\,dV and its distance from the axis is s, then its small contribution to moment of inertia is s^2\delta\,dV.

definition.title: Moment of inertia about an axis

statement.p: For a solid E with density \delta(x,y,z), the moment of inertia about an axis is \boxed{ I=\iiint_E s^2\delta(x,y,z)\,dV, } where s is the distance from (x,y,z) to the axis.

example.title: A solid cylinder spinning around its axis

statement.p: A solid cylinder has radius 2, height 3, and constant density 5. It spins around its central z-axis.
The mass of the cylinder is M=5\pi(2)^2(3)=60\pi. So I_z=\frac12M(2)^2, which matches the familiar physics formula for a solid cylinder.

figure.caption: For rotation about the z-axis, the distance factor is r^2=x^2+y^2.

subsection.p: Moment of inertia is an integral because a solid is made of many tiny masses, each at its own distance from the axis.

subsection.title: Total charge and total energy
subsection.p: Mass density is nonnegative. Charge density can be positive or negative. Energy density is usually nonnegative.

example.title: Positive and negative charge can cancel

statement.p: A charged cylinder has radius 1, height 2, and charge density q(x,y,z)=z-1. The lower half has negative charge, and the upper half has positive charge.

In cylindrical coordinates, 0\le r\le1, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le z\le2. The total charge is
Q \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^2 (z-1)r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \left(\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\right) \left(\int_0^1 r\,dr\right) \left(\int_0^2(z-1)\,dz\right).
But \int_0^2(z-1)\,dz = \left[\frac{z^2}{2}-z\right]_0^2 = 2-2 = 0. Therefore \boxed{ Q=0. } The cylinder is not uncharged everywhere. Its total signed charge is zero because the positive and negative parts cancel.

example.title: Energy stored in a spherical battery material

statement.p: A ball of radius 2 has energy density depending only on distance from the center: u(\rho)=10\left(1-\frac{\rho}{2}\right), \qquad 0\le \rho\le2. The density is largest at the center and drops to 0 at the surface.

subsection.p: The same triple integral notation covers mass, charge, and energy. The units of the integrand tell us what is being added.

statement.p: Mass is \iiint_E \delta\,dV, total charge is \iiint_E q\,dV, and total energy is \iiint_E u\,dV — the same triple integral each time, with only the integrand renamed. What is the integral really doing in all three cases, and why does swapping the meaning of the density (mass per volume, charge per volume, energy per volume) automatically change what the total represents, without changing a single step of the computation?

hint.p: Look at the building block (\text{density})\times(\text{tiny volume}). The integral only knows how to add up those little pieces; the units you attach to the density decide whether each piece is a bit of mass, a bit of charge, or a bit of energy.

table.title: Densities and their total quantities.

subsection.title: Probability in three dimensions
subsection.p: A probability density is another kind of density. Instead of mass per volume or charge per volume, it gives probability per volume.

If a random point is chosen in a solid region E, a probability density p(x,y,z) must satisfy two conditions: p(x,y,z)\ge0 and \iiint_E p(x,y,z)\,dV=1. Then the probability that the point lies in a smaller region A\subseteq E is \boxed{ \operatorname{Prob}(A)=\iiint_A p(x,y,z)\,dV. }

example.title: A random point more likely near the top of a box

statement.p:
Now find the probability that z\le\frac12. This is
\operatorname{Prob}\left(z\le\frac12\right) \amp= \int_0^1\int_0^1\int_0^{1/2} \frac23(1+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \frac23 \left[z+\frac{z^2}{2}\right]_0^{1/2} \amp= \frac23\left(\frac12+\frac18\right) \amp= \frac{5}{12}.
So \boxed{ \operatorname{Prob}\left(z\le\frac12\right)=\frac{5}{12}. } Even though the lower half of the cube has half the volume, it has less than half the probability, because the density increases with z.

subsection.p: The conditions p\ge0, \qquad \iiint_E p\,dV=1 are not cosmetic. Without them, the word probability loses its meaning.

statement.p: A probability density must satisfy \iiint_E p\,dV=1 over all of space. Why must the total come out to exactly 1, and not 2 or \tfrac12? Think about what event the integral over all of space is describing: if you pick a random point, how sure are you that it lands somewhere, and what number should that certainty correspond to?

hint.p: The integral over the whole region is the probability that the point lands somewhere in it — an event that is guaranteed to happen. A probability of 1 is the language we use for “certain.”

example.title: Why probability densities must be nonnegative and normalized

statement.p: On the unit cube, the function p(x,y,z)=2 is nonnegative, but \iiint_E 2\,dV=2. It assigns total probability 2, not 1, so it is not a probability density.
The function q(x,y,z)=2z-1 has total integral 0, and it is negative when z\lt 1/2. It cannot describe probability, because some regions would receive negative probability.
A probability density is an ordinary density with two extra promises: no negative amounts, and total amount exactly 1.

subsection.p: This last example points beyond three dimensions. A random point might have four coordinates, or ten, or a hundred. A gas molecule has position and velocity. A data point may have many measured features. The adding idea does not stop at three coordinates. What changes is harder to draw: a tiny piece is no longer a rectangle or a box we can picture. It is still a product of tiny coordinate lengths.

section.title: Higher-dimensional integrals
section.p: The probability example at the end of did not really care that the random point had three coordinates. A system may have many coordinates: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n. A triple integral is the case n=3. Higher-dimensional integrals follow the same adding rule, but the pictures become less trustworthy.
This optional section uses ordinary unsigned volume notation. We write dV_n for positive n-dimensional volume.

subsection.title: What changes in \mathbb R^n
subsection.p: A point in \mathbb R^n is written \mathbf x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n). A rectangular box in \mathbb R^n has the form B=[a_1,b_1]\times[a_2,b_2]\times\cdots\times[a_n,b_n]. Its side lengths are b_1-a_1,\quad b_2-a_2,\quad \ldots,\quad b_n-a_n. Its n-dimensional volume is \boxed{\operatorname{Vol}_n(B)=(b_1-a_1)(b_2-a_2)\cdots(b_n-a_n).}

A small coordinate box has side lengths \Delta x_1,\Delta x_2,\ldots,\Delta x_n. Its small volume is \Delta V_n=\Delta x_1\Delta x_2\cdots\Delta x_n. So the Riemann sum for a function f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) has the form \sum f(\mathbf x_i^*)\,\Delta V_{n,i}. If these sums settle to a single value, we write \boxed{\int_E f(\mathbf x)\,dV_n.}

example.title: A four-dimensional quality-control box

statement.p: A machine produces parts with four measured deviations: x_1,\quad x_2,\quad x_3,\quad x_4. Suppose each deviation is allowed to lie between -1 and 1. The acceptable region is the four-dimensional box B=[-1,1]^4. Its volume is \operatorname{Vol}_4(B)=2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=16.

If all points in B are equally likely, the probability density is constant: p=\frac1{16}. The probability that every deviation lies between -1/2 and 1/2 is
\operatorname{Prob}\left([-1/2,1/2]^4\right) \amp= \int_{[-1/2,1/2]^4}\frac1{16}\,dV_4 \amp= \frac1{16}\cdot(1\cdot1\cdot1\cdot1) \amp= \frac1{16}.
Each coordinate range was cut in half, but the four-dimensional volume was cut by \left(\frac12\right)^4. This is the first hint that high-dimensional size shrinks faster than our eyes expect.

subsection.p: For n=1, this is an ordinary single-variable integral. For n=2, it is a double integral. For n=3, it is a triple integral.

statement.p: Moving from \mathbb R^3 to \mathbb R^n for large n, the integral is still built by chopping the region into tiny boxes and adding up f(\mathbf x_i^*)\,\Delta V_{n,i}. Which parts of this story stay exactly the same, and which parts (the pictures, the geometry, the sizes of things) stop matching your three-dimensional intuition?

hint.p: Separate the bookkeeping of the integral (Riemann sums, Fubini, the adding rule) from the geometry it describes. One of these is dimension-blind; the other is not.

subsection.title: Product regions and Fubini's theorem
subsection.p: The easiest higher-dimensional regions are boxes and product regions, because each coordinate has its own interval.
For example, let B=[0,2]\times[0,3]\times[0,1]\times[0,4]. Then \operatorname{Vol}_4(B)=2\cdot3\cdot1\cdot4=24.

Now compute I=\int_B (x_1+x_4)\,dV_4. Using iterated integrals, I=\int_0^2\int_0^3\int_0^1\int_0^4(x_1+x_4)\,dx_4\,dx_3\,dx_2\,dx_1. Split the integral into two pieces: I=\int_B x_1\,dV_4+\int_B x_4\,dV_4. For the x_1-piece,
\int_B x_1\,dV_4 \amp= \left(\int_0^2 x_1\,dx_1\right)\left(\int_0^3 dx_2\right)\left(\int_0^1 dx_3\right)\left(\int_0^4 dx_4\right) \amp= 2\cdot3\cdot1\cdot4 \amp= 24.
For the x_4-piece,
\int_B x_4\,dV_4 \amp= \left(\int_0^2 dx_1\right)\left(\int_0^3 dx_2\right)\left(\int_0^1 dx_3\right)\left(\int_0^4 x_4\,dx_4\right) \amp= 2\cdot3\cdot1\cdot8 \amp= 48.
Thus \boxed{I=72.} The average value of x_1+x_4 over the box is \frac{72}{24}=3. That is the average of x_1, which is 1, plus the average of x_4, which is 2.

theorem.title: Fubini's theorem for boxes in \mathbb R^n

statement.p: Let B=[a_1,b_1]\times\cdots\times[a_n,b_n], and suppose f is continuous on B. Then \boxed{\int_B f(\mathbf x)\,dV_n} can be computed as an iterated integral in any order.
For example, \boxed{\int_B f\,dV_n=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}\cdots\int_{a_n}^{b_n}f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_n\cdots dx_1.}

subsection.p: Continuity is a safe condition. It is stronger than necessary, but it keeps the adding process well-behaved.

example.title: A nonintegrable function still breaks the story

statement.p: On the unit box [0,1]^n, define q(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\begin{cases}1, \amp x_1\text{ is rational},\\0, \amp x_1\text{ is irrational}.\end{cases} Every small n-dimensional box contains points with rational x_1 and points with irrational x_1. The upper sums are always 1, and the lower sums are always 0.
So the Riemann integral does not exist. Fubini's theorem cannot rescue an integral that was never there.

subsection.p: There is a useful special case when the function factors. If f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=g_1(x_1)g_2(x_2)\cdots g_n(x_n), then on a box, \boxed{\int_B f\,dV_n=\left(\int_{a_1}^{b_1}g_1(x_1)\,dx_1\right)\cdots\left(\int_{a_n}^{b_n}g_n(x_n)\,dx_n\right).} The integral separates because the variables separate.

example.title: A separated density

statement.p:
Let f(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=e^{-x_1}(1+x_2)x_3^2 on [0,1]\times[0,2]\times[0,3]\times[0,4]. The function does not depend on x_4, so the x_4-integral contributes a factor of 4. We get
\int f\,dV_4 \amp= \left(\int_0^1e^{-x_1}\,dx_1\right)\left(\int_0^2(1+x_2)\,dx_2\right)\left(\int_0^3x_3^2\,dx_3\right)\left(\int_0^4 dx_4\right) \amp= (1-e^{-1})(4)(9)(4) \amp= 144(1-e^{-1}).

subsection.p: The arithmetic looks familiar because Fubini turns one higher-dimensional adding problem into several one-dimensional ones.

subsection.title: Volumes of higher-dimensional balls and boxes
subsection.p: Boxes are easy in every dimension: \operatorname{Vol}_n([0,L]^n)=L^n. Balls are subtler.

statement.p: Take the cube [-1,1]^n and shrink it toward its center by halving each side, giving the smaller cube [-1/2,1/2]^n. As n grows, why does almost all of the big cube's volume end up near its surface, far from the center, leaving the inner cube with a vanishing share?

hint.p: Compare the two volumes as a ratio. The inner cube keeps only a factor of \left(\tfrac12\right)^n of the volume, and that fraction goes to 0. Ask what is left over, and where it must sit.

subsection.p:
The n-dimensional ball of radius R is B_n(R)=\left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2\le R^2\right\}. For the first few dimensions:
\begin{array}{c|c|c} n \amp B_n(R) \amp \operatorname{Vol}_n(B_n(R)) \\ \hline 1 \amp \text{interval} \amp 2R\\[1mm] 2 \amp \text{disk} \amp \pi R^2\\[1mm] 3 \amp \text{solid ball} \amp \dfrac43\pi R^3 \end{array}
The four-dimensional ball cannot be drawn, but it can be sliced.

Let B_4(1)=\{(x,y,z,w):x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2\le1\}. Fix w. Then the remaining variables satisfy x^2+y^2+z^2\le1-w^2. That is a three-dimensional ball of radius \sqrt{1-w^2}. Its volume is \frac43\pi(1-w^2)^{3/2}. So \operatorname{Vol}_4(B_4(1))=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac43\pi(1-w^2)^{3/2}\,dw. Use w=\sin u. Then dw=\cos u\,du,\qquad (1-w^2)^{3/2}=\cos^3u, and u runs from -\pi/2 to \pi/2. Therefore \operatorname{Vol}_4(B_4(1))=\frac43\pi\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^4u\,du. Since \cos^4u=\frac{3+4\cos(2u)+\cos(4u)}{8}, we have \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^4u\,du=\frac{3\pi}{8}. Thus \boxed{\operatorname{Vol}_4(B_4(1))=\frac43\pi\cdot\frac{3\pi}{8}=\frac{\pi^2}{2}.}

The pattern continues:
\begin{array}{c|c} n \amp \operatorname{Vol}_n(B_n(R)) \\ \hline 1 \amp 2R\\[1mm] 2 \amp \pi R^2\\[1mm] 3 \amp \dfrac43\pi R^3\\[2mm] 4 \amp \dfrac{\pi^2}{2}R^4\\[2mm] 5 \amp \dfrac{8\pi^2}{15}R^5 \end{array}
The formula has a compact version involving the gamma function, but the main idea is already visible: higher-dimensional balls can be studied by slicing them into lower-dimensional balls.

subsection.title: Why high-dimensional geometry feels surprising
subsection.p: High-dimensional geometry often disagrees with three-dimensional intuition. The reason is not mysterious. Powers grow and shrink quickly.

For an n-dimensional ball, scaling the radius by a scales volume by a^n. So the ball of half the radius has volume fraction \boxed{\left(\frac12\right)^n.} In three dimensions, that fraction is \frac18. In ten dimensions, it is \frac1{1024}. In one hundred dimensions, it is 2^{-100}. More generally, for any fixed 0\lt\varepsilon\lt1, the fraction inside radius 1-\varepsilon is (1-\varepsilon)^n\to0. This precise statement says that most volume lies in an outer shell of any fixed positive relative thickness.

We can also justify what happens to the whole unit-ball volume. Write V_n=\operatorname{Vol}_n(B_n(1)). For n\ge3, fix the last two coordinates, with polar radius r. The remaining slice is an (n-2)-ball of radius \sqrt{1-r^2}, hence volume V_{n-2}(1-r^2)^{(n-2)/2}. Slicing and the already proved planar polar formula give V_n=2\pi V_{n-2}\int_0^1r(1-r^2)^{(n-2)/2}\,dr =\frac{2\pi}{n}V_{n-2}. Once n\ge13, each step of two dimensions multiplies the volume by less than 1/2. Both the even and the odd subsequences therefore tend to zero. No gamma-function formula is needed for this conclusion.

statement.p: The volumes 2R, \pi R^2, \tfrac43\pi R^3, \tfrac{\pi^2}{2}R^4, \tfrac{8\pi^2}{15}R^5 seem to keep growing. Yet for a fixed radius such as R=1, the volume of the unit ball eventually decreases toward 0 as the dimension n grows. How can adding more dimensions make the unit ball smaller?

hint.p: A new dimension adds a slicing variable that ranges only over |x|\le 1, and each slice is itself a ball of radius \sqrt{1-x^2}\le 1 in one fewer dimension. Picture stacking many slices that are each smaller than the one you started with. Does the stack have to grow?

subsection.p: The cube gives another surprise. The cube [-1,1]^n has volume 2^n. Its corners have distance \sqrt{1^2+1^2+\cdots+1^2}=\sqrt n from the origin. As n grows, the corners move farther and farther away, even though every coordinate still lies between -1 and 1.

In four dimensions, the ball of radius 1 inside the cube [-1,1]^4 has volume \frac{\pi^2}{2}. The cube has volume 16. So the fraction occupied by the ball is \frac{\pi^2/2}{16}=\frac{\pi^2}{32}\approx 0.31. Already by dimension 4, much of the cube lies outside the inscribed ball, toward the corners.

These facts matter in probability, statistics, data science, and physics. A point with many coordinates does not behave like a point in a drawing. Volume migrates toward boundaries, corners, and shells.

But the integral itself has not changed. It still adds tiny contributions. The hard part is describing how a small coordinate box in one system becomes a small piece in another system. We have already met two answers: dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz and dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta. Those factors were not tricks for cylinders and spheres. They are examples of a single rule. finds that rule by looking at how a coordinate map stretches tiny boxes, and the determinant returns as the scale factor.

introduction.p: Chapter took the adding idea one dimension higher. A double integral adds over a region in the plane: f(x,y)\,dA. A triple integral adds over a solid: f(x,y,z)\,dV. The tiny pieces changed from rectangles to boxes. The story did not change: \text{value near a point}\times \text{tiny volume}.
The hard part is rarely the antiderivative. The hard part is describing the solid without counting too much or too little.

subsection.title: Skills: triple integrals in several coordinate systems

figure.caption: Choose coordinates by listening to the shape of the solid.

subsection.p:
The main volume elements are:
\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Coordinates} \amp \text{Conversion} \amp \text{Volume element} \\ \hline \text{rectangular} \amp (x,y,z) \amp dV=dx\,dy\,dz \\[2mm] \text{cylindrical} \amp x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad z=z \amp dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz \\[2mm] \text{spherical} \amp x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\quad y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\quad z=\rho\cos\phi \amp dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \end{array}

The oriented version of rectangular volume is dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. For ordinary volume, mass, probability, and energy, we use positive volume: dV. For orientation-sensitive integrals later in the book, the wedge notation will remember the order of the directions.

Here are the main application formulas from the chapter.
\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Quantity} \amp \text{Triple integral} \\ \hline \text{volume of }E \amp \displaystyle \operatorname{Vol}(E)=\iiint_E 1\,dV \\[3mm] \text{mass from density }\delta \amp \displaystyle M=\iiint_E \delta\,dV \\[3mm] \text{center of mass} \amp \displaystyle (\bar x,\bar y,\bar z) = \left( \frac{\iiint_E x\delta\,dV}{M}, \frac{\iiint_E y\delta\,dV}{M}, \frac{\iiint_E z\delta\,dV}{M} \right) \\[5mm] \text{moment of inertia about the }z\text{-axis} \amp \displaystyle I_z=\iiint_E (x^2+y^2)\delta\,dV \\[4mm] \text{total charge from charge density }q \amp \displaystyle Q=\iiint_E q\,dV \\[3mm] \text{total energy from energy density }u \amp \displaystyle \mathcal E=\iiint_E u\,dV \\[3mm] \text{probability of a region }A \amp \displaystyle \operatorname{Prob}(A)=\iiint_A p\,dV \end{array}
A probability density must satisfy p\ge0 and \iiint_E p\,dV=1.

subsection.title: Worked review example: a wedge with density
subsection.p: A storage wedge has rectangular floor 0\le x\le2,\qquad 0\le y\le1, and slanted roof z=4-x-y. The floor is z=0. Its density is \delta(x,y,z)=1+z. Find the mass.

The solid is E=\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le1,\ 0\le z\le4-x-y\}. So
M \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1\int_0^{4-x-y} (1+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left[ z+\frac12z^2 \right]_0^{4-x-y} \,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left( (4-x-y)+\frac12(4-x-y)^2 \right)dy\,dx.
Expand the integrand: (4-x-y)+\frac12(4-x-y)^2 = 12-5x-5y+\frac12x^2+xy+\frac12y^2. Now integrate in y:
\int_0^1 \left( 12-5x-5y+\frac12x^2+xy+\frac12y^2 \right)dy \amp= \frac{29}{3}-\frac92x+\frac12x^2.
Then
M \amp= \int_0^2 \left( \frac{29}{3}-\frac92x+\frac12x^2 \right)dx \amp= \frac{58}{3}-9+\frac43 \amp= \frac{35}{3}.
Thus \boxed{ M=\frac{35}{3}. }
The bounds came from the geometry. The integrand came from the density. The calculation only came after both were clear.

subsection.title: Worked review example: a round tank in cylindrical coordinates
subsection.p: A round tank has radius 2. Its floor is z=0, and its roof height depends on distance from the central axis: z=3+\frac r2. The density is \delta(r,z)=1+r. Find the mass.

The solid is rotationally symmetric, so cylindrical coordinates fit: 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le r\le2, \qquad 0\le z\le 3+\frac r2. Remember the volume factor: dV=r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta. So
M \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^{3+r/2} (1+r)r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^2 (1+r)r\left(3+\frac r2\right)dr.
Expand: (1+r)r\left(3+\frac r2\right) = 3r+\frac72r^2+\frac12r^3. Thus
M \amp= 2\pi\int_0^2 \left( 3r+\frac72r^2+\frac12r^3 \right)dr \amp= 2\pi \left[ \frac32r^2+\frac76r^3+\frac18r^4 \right]_0^2 \amp= 2\pi \left( 6+\frac{28}{3}+2 \right) \amp= \frac{104\pi}{3}.
So \boxed{ M=\frac{104\pi}{3}. }
The factor r is doing real work. Rings near r=2 contain more volume than rings near the central axis.

subsection.title: Worked review example: probability in a spherical cone
subsection.p: A random point is chosen in the solid inside the sphere \rho\le2 and inside the cone 0\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{3}. The probability density is proportional to distance from the origin: p(\rho,\phi,\theta)=C\rho. Find C. Then find the probability that \rho\le1.
The ball of half the radius has much less than half the probability. Part of the reason is geometry: volume grows like \rho^2. Another part is density: this density also grows like \rho.

statement.p: What does dV mean in a triple integral?
Why is \iiint_E 1\,dV the volume of E?
What is the difference between dV and dx\wedge dy\wedge dz?
What does it mean for a solid to be z-simple?
Why does the innermost variable determine the coordinate shadow we should draw?
In cylindrical coordinates, why does dV contain the factor r?
In spherical coordinates, why does dV contain both \rho^2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sin\phi?
What angle does \phi measure in the spherical-coordinate convention used in this book?
Give one example of a solid that is better described in cylindrical coordinates than in rectangular coordinates.
Give one example of a solid that is better described in spherical coordinates than in cylindrical coordinates.
Why can the same solid have several correct iterated-integral descriptions?
Why does the center of mass require M\gt0?
What is the distance factor for moment of inertia about the z-axis?
What two conditions must a probability density satisfy?
In \mathbb R^n, why does scaling every coordinate by a scale volume by a^n?
Compute \int_0^2\int_0^1\int_0^3 (x+y+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.
Find the volume of the solid E=\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le x,\ 0\le z\le x+y\}.
Let E=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ x+2y+3z\le6\}. Write an iterated integral for \iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV in the order dz\,dy\,dx.
For the same solid in , compute its volume.
Describe the solid represented by \int_0^4\int_0^{\sqrt{16-x^2}}\int_0^{x+y} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx. Use words and inequalities.
Rewrite \int_0^1\int_0^{1-x}\int_0^{1-x-y} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx with x as the innermost variable.
A box occupies 0\le x\le3,\qquad 0\le y\le2,\qquad 0\le z\le1. Its density is \delta(x,y,z)=2+x. Find its mass.
For the box in , find \bar x. Use symmetry to explain \bar y and \bar z.
A solid cylinder has radius a, height h, and constant density \delta_0. Use cylindrical coordinates to show that its moment of inertia about the central axis is I_z=\frac12Ma^2.
Find the volume inside the cylinder x^2+y^2\le9 and between the planes z=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad z=4. Use cylindrical coordinates.
Find the volume inside the cone z=5-r above the floor z=0.
A pipe has inner radius 1, outer radius 3, and height 4. Its density is \delta(r)=\frac{1}{r}. Find its mass.
A round tank is inside r\le2 and below the slanted roof z=5+r\cos\theta. It is above the floor z=0. Set up and evaluate the volume integral.
Find the volume inside the sphere \rho\le3 and above the cone \phi=\frac{\pi}{4}.
Find the volume of the first octant part of the sphere \rho\le5.
Write a spherical-coordinate integral for the volume inside \rho\le4 and below the cone \phi=\frac{2\pi}{3}. Be careful: below the cone means farther down from the positive z-axis.
A ball of radius 2 has density \delta(\rho)=3+\rho. Find its mass.
A spherical shell satisfies 2\le\rho\le5. Its energy density is u(\rho)=\frac{12}{\rho^2}. Find the total energy.
A probability density on the unit cube is p(x,y,z)=C(x+y+z). Find C. Then find \operatorname{Prob}(z\le1/2).
A probability density on the ball \rho\le1 is p(\rho)=C. Find C. Then find the probability that \rho\le\frac12.
Decide which coordinate system you would use first: rectangular, cylindrical, or spherical. Give a reason. x^2+y^2\le4,\qquad 0\le z\le 7.
Decide which coordinate system you would use first: rectangular, cylindrical, or spherical. Give a reason. x^2+y^2+z^2\le9,\qquad z\ge0.
Decide which coordinate system you would use first: rectangular, cylindrical, or spherical. Give a reason. 0\le x\le2,\qquad 0\le y\le3,\qquad 0\le z\le 4-x.
The four-dimensional box B=[0,2]\times[0,1]\times[0,3]\times[0,4] has constant density 5. Find its total mass.
Find the volume of the four-dimensional ball of radius 3, using \operatorname{Vol}_4(B_4(R))=\frac{\pi^2}{2}R^4.
A point is chosen uniformly from the cube [-1,1]^6. Find the probability that every coordinate lies between -1/2 and 1/2.
Explain why the bounds 0\le\theta\le4\pi,\qquad 0\le r\le2,\qquad 0\le z\le1 describe the same cylinder twice.
Write the oriented volume form in rectangular coordinates, and then write its positive-volume version.

subsection.title: Project: comparing volume formulas numerically
subsection.p: A unit ball has volume \frac{4\pi}{3}. That formula is familiar, but this chapter gives several ways to approach the same number. The goal of this project is to compare three numerical estimates of the unit ball volume.
The unit ball is B=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2+z^2\le1\}.

subsubsection.title: Method 1. Counting small cubes
subsubsection.p: Divide the cube -1\le x\le1,\qquad -1\le y\le1,\qquad -1\le z\le1 into N^3 equal small cubes. Each small cube has side length \Delta x=\frac{2}{N} and volume \Delta V=\left(\frac{2}{N}\right)^3. Use the center of each small cube as a test point. Count how many centers satisfy x^2+y^2+z^2\le1. If that number is K_N, then \boxed{ V_N^{\mathrm{box}} = K_N\left(\frac{2}{N}\right)^3. }

subsubsection.title: Method 2. Cylindrical slices
subsubsection.p: In cylindrical coordinates, the ball is 0\le r\le1, \qquad -\sqrt{1-r^2}\le z\le \sqrt{1-r^2}, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Its volume is V= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_{-\sqrt{1-r^2}}^{\sqrt{1-r^2}} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta. After integrating in z and \theta, this becomes V=4\pi\int_0^1 r\sqrt{1-r^2}\,dr. Use a midpoint sum with r_i^*=\left(i-\frac12\right)\Delta r, \qquad \Delta r=\frac1N. Then \boxed{ V_N^{\mathrm{cyl}} = 4\pi\sum_{i=1}^N r_i^*\sqrt{1-(r_i^*)^2}\,\Delta r. }

subsubsection.title: Method 3. Spherical shells
subsubsection.p: In spherical coordinates, the unit ball is simply 0\le\rho\le1,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. The volume is V= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta = 4\pi\int_0^1\rho^2\,d\rho. Use a midpoint sum with \rho_i^*=\left(i-\frac12\right)\Delta\rho, \qquad \Delta\rho=\frac1N. Then \boxed{ V_N^{\mathrm{sph}} = 4\pi\sum_{i=1}^N (\rho_i^*)^2\,\Delta\rho. }

subsubsection.title: Sample results
subsubsection.p:
The exact value is \frac{4\pi}{3}\approx 4.18879. Here are typical midpoint estimates.
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} N \amp V_N^{\mathrm{box}} \amp V_N^{\mathrm{cyl}} \amp V_N^{\mathrm{sph}} \\ \hline 4 \amp 4.00000 \amp 4.34530 \amp 4.12334\\ 8 \amp 4.37500 \amp 4.24276 \amp 4.17243\\ 16 \amp 4.25000 \amp 4.20738 \amp 4.18470\\ 32 \amp 4.21289 \amp 4.19522 \amp 4.18777 \end{array}

The spherical estimate improves quickly because the spherical bounds match the ball. The cube-counting estimate also improves, but its boundary is rough: small cubes do not fit a sphere very naturally.

subsubsection.title: What to hand in
subsubsection.p: Write a short report with the following pieces.

li.p: A picture or description of the three methods.
A table of your estimates for at least four values of N.
The absolute error for each method: \left|V_N-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right|.
A paragraph explaining which method converges fastest in your computation.
A paragraph explaining why the coordinate system matters even though all three methods are estimating the same volume.

subsubsection.p: The last paragraph is the point of the project. A coordinate system is not just notation. It shapes the pieces being added.

subsection.title: Hook: coordinate changes need a systematic scale factor
subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates gave dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz. Spherical coordinates gave dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta. We found those factors by looking carefully at tiny coordinate boxes. That worked because cylinders and spheres have familiar geometry.

But there are many other coordinate changes. A square can be sheared into a parallelogram. A rectangle can be bent into a curved patch. A box can be stretched, tilted, or folded by a transformation. We need one rule that tells us the correct scale factor every time.

That rule is not new. It has been waiting since the determinant appeared as signed area and signed volume. In Chapter , the determinant returns as the automatic correction factor for changing variables. In the language of forms, it is what appears when dx\wedge dy \qquad\text{or}\qquad dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is pulled back through a coordinate map.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

introduction.p: The total derivative from Chapter 7 approximates a coordinate map by a linear transformation. The determinant from Chapter 3 measures the resulting local area or volume scale. We develop substitution formulas and then define pullbacks of area and volume forms explicitly, keeping nonnegative measure separate from signed orientation.

section.title: The geometry of substitution
section.p: A substitution is a change of language. In single-variable calculus, we replaced x by a new variable u. In double integrals, we replace (x,y) by new variables (u,v). The new variables may straighten a slanted region, unwrap a circular region, or turn a difficult boundary into a rectangle.
But changing language changes the size of the small pieces. That is the whole issue.

subsection.title: Single-variable substitution remembered
subsection.p:
Start with the one-dimensional story. Compute \int_0^4 \sqrt{x}\,dx. Let x=u^2. Since x runs from 0 to 4, and we choose u\ge0, the new variable runs from u=0 \qquad\text{to}\qquad u=2. Also, dx=2u\,du. So
\int_0^4 \sqrt{x}\,dx \amp= \int_0^2 \sqrt{u^2}\,(2u)\,du \amp= \int_0^2 2u^2\,du \amp= 2\left[\frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^2 \amp= \frac{16}{3}.
The factor 2u did not appear by magic. It measures how much an interval in u-space is stretched when it becomes an interval in x-space.

Near a particular value u, a small interval of length \Delta u becomes an interval of length approximately \Delta x\approx \frac{dx}{du}\Delta u. For x=u^2, this says \Delta x\approx 2u\,\Delta u. Near u=2, a small u-interval is stretched by about 4. Near u=1/10, it is stretched by about 1/5.
So the one-dimensional substitution rule is really a measurement rule: \boxed{ \text{new small length in }x = \text{stretch factor}\cdot \text{old small length in }u. }

exercise.title: Why a stretch factor at all?

statement.p: We could imagine simply renaming x as u and copying the integral across unchanged. Why does honest accounting force the factor dx/du to appear, rather than letting the integrand alone carry the whole story?

hint.p: Picture two equal steps in u near u=1/10 and near u=2. Do they cover equal amounts of x?

subsection.p: In symbols, dx=\frac{dx}{du}\,du. For ordinary positive length, the scale factor is \left|\frac{dx}{du}\right|. For oriented integrals, the sign is allowed to stay. A negative derivative means the substitution reverses direction.
The same idea will guide us in the plane. The only difference is that small intervals become small parallelograms.

subsection.title: From small intervals to small parallelograms
subsection.p: Suppose a square tile in the (u,v)-plane is sent to the (x,y)-plane by T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u+2v,\;3u+v). The point (0,0) goes to (0,0). The unit step in the u-direction goes to T(1,0)-T(0,0)=(1,3). The unit step in the v-direction goes to T(0,1)-T(0,0)=(2,1). So the unit square in the (u,v)-plane becomes the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf a=(1,3), \qquad \mathbf b=(2,1).
Its signed area is \det[\mathbf a\ \mathbf b] = \begin{vmatrix} 1\amp2\\ 3\amp1 \end{vmatrix} = 1\cdot1-3\cdot2 = -5. The ordinary area is 5.

figure.caption: A linear change of variables sends a square to a parallelogram. The determinant measures the signed area of that parallelogram.

subsection.p: This is the two-dimensional version of the factor dx/du. A small square of area \Delta u\,\Delta v is turned into a parallelogram whose area is 5\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. The number 5 is the area scale factor.

The sign -5 also matters. It says the ordered directions have been flipped. The u-direction followed by the v-direction becomes a clockwise ordered pair in the (x,y)-plane. Ordinary area ignores that sign. Oriented area remembers it.

subsection.title: Local linearization of a coordinate map
subsection.p: The previous map was linear, so every square became a true parallelogram. Most useful coordinate maps are not linear.

For example, take T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u,\;uv). This map changes the spacing and angles of the (u,v)-grid. A rectangle with u\gt0 becomes a trapezoid: fixed u gives a vertical line and fixed v gives a line y=vx. Nonlinear maps can also produce curved edges, but this particular example has straight edges.

For a continuously differentiable map, sufficiently small images are described to first order by its derivative, as in . The two side vectors of the approximating parallelogram are the partial derivatives of T multiplied by the corresponding parameter increments.

statement.p: For a nonlinear map, a large rectangle's image can have bent sides, and its local area scale can vary across the tile. Yet near a point we use a single Jacobian determinant. In what sense does shrinking the tile rescue the parallelogram picture, and what would go wrong if we trusted that picture for a big tile?

hint.p: Think about how the curvature of the image edges compares to the side lengths as \Delta u,\Delta v shrink toward zero.

subsection.p: For T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)), define T_u=(x_u,y_u), \qquad T_v=(x_v,y_v). These are the two velocity vectors of the coordinate grid: one obtained by changing u, the other by changing v.

For T(u,v)=(u,uv), we have T_u(u,v)=(1,v), \qquad T_v(u,v)=(0,u). At the point (u,v)=(2,3), these become T_u(2,3)=(1,3), \qquad T_v(2,3)=(0,2). So a tiny rectangle near (2,3), with side lengths \Delta u and \Delta v, maps approximately to the parallelogram spanned by (1,3)\Delta u \qquad\text{and}\qquad (0,2)\Delta v. The signed area scale factor is \det \begin{pmatrix} 1\amp0\\ 3\amp2 \end{pmatrix} = 2. So the image area is approximately 2\,\Delta u\,\Delta v.

Let us check this with a small actual rectangle: 2\le u\le2.01, \qquad 3\le v\le3.01. Since x=u, \qquad y=uv, the vertical height of the image at a fixed u is u(3.01)-u(3)=0.01u. Therefore the exact image area is
\int_{2}^{2.01} 0.01u\,du \amp= 0.01\left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_{2}^{2.01} \amp= 0.01\cdot\frac{2.01^2-2^2}{2} \amp= 0.0002005.
The local linear estimate gives 2(0.01)(0.01)=0.0002. The agreement is close because the rectangle is small.

statement.p: For a differentiable coordinate map T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)), the Jacobian determinant of T is \boxed{ J_T(u,v) = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} x_u \amp x_v\\ y_u \amp y_v \end{vmatrix} = x_u y_v-x_v y_u. }

subsection.p: The notation \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} means: the determinant of the derivative matrix of the map from (u,v) to (x,y).

subsection.title: Why determinants appear
subsection.p: The determinant appears because two variables create area, and area is measured by a two-input object.

The side vectors of a tiny image tile are approximately T_u\,du \qquad\text{and}\qquad T_v\,dv. The signed area form dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of those two vectors:
(dx\wedge dy)(T_u,T_v) \amp= \begin{vmatrix} x_u \amp x_v\\ y_u \amp y_v \end{vmatrix} \amp= J_T(u,v).
So the determinant is not a random correction factor. It is the signed area of the parallelogram made by the two coordinate velocity vectors.

exercise.title: Why a determinant, not a product?

statement.p: The two coordinate velocity vectors T_u and T_v each have a length, so a tempting guess for the area factor would be the product of those lengths. Why is the determinant the right measure of how area is rescaled, while that product is not?

hint.p: Imagine the two vectors nearly parallel: their lengths stay positive, but how much area does the parallelogram they span enclose?

subsection.p:
The same fact can be written in differential form notation. In the following substitution equations, dx and dy denote the differentials of the scalar functions x(u,v) and y(u,v) on the parameter plane. Thus these are identities on one domain, not literal identifications of covectors on two different planes. Since x=x(u,v), \qquad y=y(u,v), we have dx=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv, and dy=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv. Then
dx\wedge dy \amp= (x_u\,du+x_v\,dv)\wedge(y_u\,du+y_v\,dv) \amp= x_u y_v\,du\wedge dv+x_v y_u\,dv\wedge du \amp= (x_u y_v-x_v y_u)\,du\wedge dv.
Thus \boxed{ dx\wedge dy = J_T(u,v)\,du\wedge dv. } This is the form version of the change in signed area.

There is one condition hidden in the phrase local linearization. The map must have a good derivative at the point. If T(u,v)=(|u|,v), then at the origin the map has a crease. Approaching from the right, the u-direction goes to (1,0). Approaching from the left, it goes to (-1,0). There is no single linear map that describes the behavior from all sides. So there is no single determinant at the origin that explains every tiny tile crossing the crease.
Away from the crease, the determinant picture works again.

For a nonlinear coordinate map, the determinant may change from point to point. That is why polar coordinates have the factor r, and spherical coordinates have the factor \rho^2\sin\phi. Before letting the scale factor vary, it is worth studying the case where it stays constant. Linear maps are the cleanest laboratory: every tiny square is stretched by the same determinant, and the curved-tile approximation becomes exact.

section.title: Linear changes of variables
section.p: found the local rule: \text{area scale factor}=\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|. For a linear map, this factor is constant. There is no approximation to manage. A square becomes a parallelogram, a rectangle becomes a parallelogram, and every small piece is scaled by the same amount.

subsection.title: Parallelograms from squares
subsection.p:
Let T(u,v)=(x,y)=(2u+v,\;u+3v). The unit square 0\le u\le1,\qquad 0\le v\le1 has two edge directions: \mathbf e_u=(1,0), \qquad \mathbf e_v=(0,1). Under T, these become T(1,0)-T(0,0)=(2,1), and T(0,1)-T(0,0)=(1,3). So the unit square becomes the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf a=(2,1), \qquad \mathbf b=(1,3). Its signed area is
\det[\mathbf a\ \mathbf b] = \begin{vmatrix} 2 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6-1 = 5.
Thus the ordinary area is 5.

The matrix of the map is
A= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp 3 \end{pmatrix}.
Its determinant is \det A=5. The columns of A are exactly the images of the two coordinate directions: \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}. So \det A measures the signed area of the image of the unit square.

statement.p: We read the area scale factor straight off the matrix A, yet A is just a box of numbers. What is it about the columns of A that lets them carry the geometry of the unit square, no matter which square we start with?

hint.p: Ask what A does to the two coordinate directions \mathbf e_u=(1,0) and \mathbf e_v=(0,1), and where those images show up inside A.

figure.caption: The determinant of a linear map is the signed area of the image of the unit square.

subsection.p: If the original square had side length 0.1, its area would be 0.01, and the image area would be 5(0.01)=0.05. If the original rectangle had area 7, the image area would be 5(7)=35. A linear map uses the same scale factor everywhere.

subsection.title: Area scaling by |\det A|
subsection.p: The translation moves the region. It does not change its area. The matrix A does the stretching, shearing, rotating, reflecting, or collapsing.
The coordinate directions become \mathbf a=(a,c), \qquad \mathbf b=(b,d). The signed area of the parallelogram spanned by them is \det A=ad-bc. So the ordinary area scale factor is |\det A|.

theorem.title: Area scaling by a linear map

statement.p: Let T(\mathbf u)=A\mathbf u+\mathbf p_0 be a linear change followed by a translation, where A is a 2\times2 matrix with \det A\ne0. If S is a region in the (u,v)-plane and R=T(S) is its image in the (x,y)-plane, then \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(R)=|\det A|\,\operatorname{Area}(S).} More generally, for any function f for which the integrals exist, \boxed{\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_S f(T(u,v))\,|\det A|\,du\,dv.}

proof.p: Cut S into many small rectangles. A rectangle with side lengths \Delta u,\qquad \Delta v has area \Delta u\,\Delta v. The map T sends its side directions to \mathbf a\,\Delta u \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf b\,\Delta v. The image is a parallelogram with ordinary area |\det[\mathbf a\ \mathbf b]|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v = |\det A|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. Adding these image pieces gives the area formula.

For the integral formula, the contribution from one small image piece is approximately f(T(u^*,v^*))\,|\det A|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. Adding all pieces and passing to the integral gives \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_S f(T(u,v))\,|\det A|\,du\,dv.

subsection.p: The condition \det A\ne0 is the condition that the map does not collapse the plane.

Here is what breaks without it. Let
A= \begin{pmatrix} 1 \amp 1\\ 2 \amp 2 \end{pmatrix}.
Then T(u,v)=(u+v,\;2u+2v). The unit square in the (u,v)-plane does not become a two-dimensional region. It collapses onto the line segment y=2x, \qquad 0\le x\le2. The determinant is \det A=1\cdot2-1\cdot2=0. A two-dimensional area has been crushed to area 0. This is not a valid two-dimensional change of variables for a double integral over a region with area.

statement.p: The formula \operatorname{Area}(R)=|\det A|\,\operatorname{Area}(S) still gives an answer when \det A=0 -- it just says the image has area 0. So why is \det A=0 forbidden for a change of variables, rather than simply being an interesting special case?

hint.p: A change of variables has to be reversible: every point of R should come from exactly one point of S. What happens to that requirement when a whole region is crushed onto a line?

subsection.title: Orientation and the sign of the determinant
subsection.p: Ordinary area uses |\det A|. Oriented area uses \det A.

The simplest example is reflection across the x-axis: T(u,v)=(u,-v). Here
A= \begin{pmatrix} 1 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det A=-1.
The unit square still has ordinary area 1. Its image still has ordinary area 1. But the orientation has reversed.

The ordered pair \mathbf e_u,\mathbf e_v turns counterclockwise in the (u,v)-plane. Its image is (1,0),(0,-1), which turns clockwise in the (x,y)-plane. That is why the signed area scale factor is -1.

statement.p: For computing ordinary area we throw the sign away and use |\det A|. So what information is the sign of \det A actually recording about the map, and why might we want to hold on to it rather than discard it?

hint.p: Picture the ordered pair of arrows \mathbf e_u,\mathbf e_v before and after the map. The sign is not about how big the image is -- it is about which way it turns.

subsection.p: This is the oriented change-of-variables rule. The ordinary area rule takes absolute value: \boxed{dA=|\det A|\,du\,dv.}
The sign is not an inconvenience. It carries information. Later, when we integrate forms over oriented curves and surfaces, this sign will become the reason boundary orientation works cleanly.

subsection.title: Examples with rotated and skewed regions
subsection.p: A linear change of variables is useful when the region is a parallelogram, a rotated rectangle, or any shape whose boundaries become simpler after a linear transformation.

example.title: A density over a skewed floor tile

statement.p: Let R be the parallelogram spanned by (2,1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (1,3), starting at the origin. Find \iint_R (x+y)\,dA.

Use the square S=\{(u,v):0\le u\le1,\ 0\le v\le1\} and the map x=2u+v, \qquad y=u+3v. Then
A= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad |\det A|=5.
Also, x+y=(2u+v)+(u+3v)=3u+4v. Therefore
\iint_R (x+y)\,dA \amp= \int_0^1\int_0^1 (3u+4v)\,5\,dv\,du \amp= 5\int_0^1\left[3uv+2v^2\right]_{0}^{1}\,du \amp= 5\int_0^1(3u+2)\,du \amp= 5\left(\frac32+2\right) \amp= \frac{35}{2}.
So \boxed{\iint_R (x+y)\,dA=\frac{35}{2}.} The parallelogram became a square, and the determinant supplied the area correction.

example.title: A rotated rectangle

statement.p:
A rectangle has been rotated by 45^\circ. Instead of describing its slanted sides in x and y, use coordinates u and v along the rotated axes: x=\frac{u-v}{\sqrt2}, \qquad y=\frac{u+v}{\sqrt2}. This is a rotation, so it should preserve area. The determinant confirms it:
A= \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt2 \amp -1/\sqrt2\\ 1/\sqrt2 \amp 1/\sqrt2 \end{pmatrix},
and \det A = \frac12+\frac12 = 1.

Let R be the image of 0\le u\le3, \qquad 0\le v\le1. Compute \iint_R (x^2+y^2)\,dA. Under the rotation,
x^2+y^2 \amp= \left(\frac{u-v}{\sqrt2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{u+v}{\sqrt2}\right)^2 \amp= u^2+v^2.
Since |\det A|=1,
\iint_R (x^2+y^2)\,dA \amp= \int_0^3\int_0^1 (u^2+v^2)\,dv\,du \amp= \int_0^3\left(u^2+\frac13\right)\,du \amp= 9+1 \amp= 10.
So \boxed{\iint_R (x^2+y^2)\,dA=10.} The region was slanted in x,y, but rectangular in u,v.

subsection.p: Linear maps are now under control. Their scale factor is constant because their grid lines stay straight and evenly spaced. But polar coordinates do not behave that way. Near the origin, angular wedges are tiny; far from the origin, the same angle covers a long arc. The determinant must change from point to point. The next step is to let the matrix of partial derivatives vary across the region and to trust the same local parallelogram idea everywhere at once.

section.title: Nonlinear changes of variables in the plane
section.p: treated linear changes of variables. A square became a parallelogram, and one number, |\det A|, scaled every area in the same way.

Now the grid is allowed to bend. A small square may become a small curved tile. But if the square is tiny, the curved tile is almost a parallelogram, and the determinant still measures its area. The only difference is that the determinant may change from point to point.

subsection.title: The change-of-variables theorem in two dimensions
subsection.p: Start with a map that is nonlinear, but still easy to see: T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u,uv). Let S=\{(u,v):1\le u\le3,\ 0\le v\le2\}. Since x=u,\qquad y=uv, the image region R=T(S) satisfies 1\le x\le3, \qquad 0\le y\le 2x. So a rectangle in the (u,v)-plane becomes a wedge-shaped region in the (x,y)-plane.

figure.caption: The nonlinear map T(u,v)=(u,uv) sends a rectangle to a wedge.

subsection.p: Let us find the area of R in two ways.

In x,y-coordinates, the region is 1\le x\le3,\qquad 0\le y\le2x. So
\operatorname{Area}(R) \amp= \int_1^3\int_0^{2x}1\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_1^3 2x\,dx \amp= \left[x^2\right]_1^3 \amp= 8.

Now compute the same area from the rectangle S. The derivative vectors of the map are T_u=(1,v), \qquad T_v=(0,u). The signed area scale factor is J_T(u,v) = \det \begin{pmatrix} 1\amp0\\ v\amp u \end{pmatrix} = u. Since u\ge1 on S, the ordinary area scale factor is |J_T(u,v)|=u. Therefore
\operatorname{Area}(R) \amp= \int_1^3\int_0^2 u\,dv\,du \amp= \int_1^3 2u\,du \amp= 8.

The computation says something geometric. The vertical v-direction is stretched by the factor u. When u=1, a step of size \Delta v has image length |\Delta v|. When u=3, the same step has length 3|\Delta v|. The grid spreads out as u increases.
The determinant is no longer one constant number. It is a function: J_T(u,v)=u.

exercise.title: Why does the scale factor wander?

statement.p: For a linear change of variables the area scale factor |\det A| was a single number, but here |J_T(u,v)|=u changes from point to point.
