What is it about a map that makes its scale factor depend on where you are? Is such variation inevitable for every nonlinear map, or only possible? Check the shear (u,v)\mapsto(u,v+u^2).

hint.p: Think about the derivative vectors T_u and T_v. For a linear map they are the same everywhere; for a nonlinear map, how do they behave as you move from one point to another?

subsection.p: The change-of-variables theorem says that this local scale factor can be added over the whole region.

theorem.title: Change of variables in the plane

statement.p: Let S be a compact region in the (u,v)-plane whose boundary consists of finitely many piecewise smooth arcs, and let T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)) be a coordinate map from S to a region R in the (x,y)-plane.
Assume:

li.p: T has continuous first partial derivatives on an open neighborhood of S;
T is one-to-one on the interior of S, except possibly along boundary pieces;
J_T(u,v)\ne0 on the interior of S.

statement.p: If f is continuous on R=T(S), then \boxed{ \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_S f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|J_T(u,v)|\,du\,dv. }

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p: Cut S into many tiny rectangles. Near a point (u,v), the map T is well approximated by its derivative: T(u+\Delta u,v+\Delta v) \approx T(u,v)+T_u\,\Delta u+T_v\,\Delta v. So a tiny rectangle in the (u,v)-plane maps almost to a parallelogram spanned by T_u\,\Delta u \qquad\text{and}\qquad T_v\,\Delta v. The area of that parallelogram is approximately |J_T(u,v)|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. Thus a small contribution in the image is approximately f(T(u,v))\,|J_T(u,v)|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. Adding all pieces and letting the rectangles shrink gives the formula.

subsection.p: The theorem has hypotheses because the determinant is a local story. It measures how one tiny tile is stretched near one point. A global change of variables must also avoid overlapping the same image region more than once.

subsection.title: The Jacobian determinant
subsection.p: The map T(u,v)=(u,uv) was chosen because the geometry was visible. Now use the theorem on a real integral.

Notice the two substitutions that happened at once: x+y \quad\longrightarrow\quad u+uv, and dA \quad\longrightarrow\quad u\,du\,dv. The first substitution changes the function. The second changes the tiny area piece.

subsection.title: One-to-one conditions and splitting regions
subsection.p: The one-to-one condition is easy to underestimate. A determinant can measure the right local scale and still give the wrong global answer if the map covers the same region twice.

Consider T(u,v)=(u^2,v) on the rectangle S=[-1,1]\times[0,1]. The image is the unit square R=[0,1]\times[0,1]. The Jacobian determinant is J_T(u,v) = \det \begin{pmatrix} 2u\amp0\\ 0\amp1 \end{pmatrix} = 2u. If we blindly integrate the area scale factor over all of S, we get
\iint_S |2u|\,du\,dv \amp= \int_0^1\int_{-1}^1 |2u|\,du\,dv \amp= 2.
But the image square has area 1. The formula counted most of the image twice: once from u\gt0, and once from u\lt0.

statement.p: The Jacobian determinant correctly measured how each tiny tile was stretched, yet the integral came out as 2 instead of the true area 1. How can a quantity be right about every small piece and still give the wrong total?

hint.p: The Jacobian only knows about one tile at a time. It cannot tell whether two different tiles land on the same spot in the image. What does the one-to-one condition guarantee that the determinant alone cannot?

subsection.p:
The fix is not to throw away the Jacobian. The fix is to choose a one-to-one branch. For example, on 0\le u\le1,\qquad 0\le v\le1, the same map covers the unit square once, and
\iint_{[0,1]\times[0,1]} 2u\,du\,dv \amp= 1.
The determinant was right locally. The region was wrong globally.

A second warning is smoothness. Take T(u,v)=(u,\ v+|u|). This map is one-to-one, but it has a crease along u=0. On the right side, where u\gt0, T(u,v)=(u,v+u). On the left side, where u\lt0, T(u,v)=(u,v-u). The derivative changes suddenly across the crease. There is no single linear map that describes T at points with u=0.

A tile crossing the crease does not have one clean tangent parallelogram. To use the change-of-variables theorem, split the domain into two pieces: u\ge0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad u\le0. Each piece is smooth. Then compute on the pieces separately.

The nonzero-Jacobian condition also has a geometric meaning. If J_T=0 throughout a patch, then tiny area can be crushed to zero area. For example, T(u,v)=(u,0) sends the whole unit square onto a line segment. Its Jacobian determinant is 0, and the image has no two-dimensional area.

A zero Jacobian at a boundary point is often harmless. Polar coordinates have J=r, which vanishes at r=0. That single point does not ruin the area formula. But a coordinate change should not collapse a whole two-dimensional piece if we want it to describe a two-dimensional region.

subsection.title: Polar coordinates revisited as a theorem, not a trick
subsection.p: Polar coordinates are the most familiar nonlinear change of variables: x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta. Before, the factor r came from the length of a circular arc: \text{arc length}\approx r\,\Delta\theta. Now the same factor comes automatically from the Jacobian determinant.

Compute: x_r=\cos\theta, \qquad x_\theta=-r\sin\theta, and y_r=\sin\theta, \qquad y_\theta=r\cos\theta. Therefore
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} \amp= \det \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta \amp -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta \amp r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \amp= r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta \amp= r.
So \boxed{ dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. } This is the old polar area element, now explained by the same determinant rule used for every coordinate change.

statement.p: The factor r in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta once came from the length of a small circular arc, and now it falls out of the Jacobian determinant. Why should these two very different-looking arguments produce the very same r?

hint.p: Both are measuring the area of one tiny tile of the polar grid. Picture the little patch between radii r and r+\Delta r and angles \theta and \theta+\Delta\theta — how do its two side lengths depend on r?

example.title: Dye in a circular spill

statement.p: A circular spill occupies the disk x^2+y^2\le4. The dye concentration at (x,y) is q(x,y)=12-x^2-y^2. Find the total amount of dye.

subsection.p: Polar coordinates are nearly one-to-one on the usual rectangle 0\le r\le a,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. The only overlaps occur on the boundary: \theta=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \theta=2\pi, and all points with r=0 become the origin. These boundary overlaps do not change the integral.
But if we use 0\le\theta\le4\pi, then the disk is traced twice. The integral will be twice as large unless we intend to count multiplicity. This is the same one-to-one warning in a familiar disguise.

The plane story is now complete enough to trust. A nonlinear map bends a grid, but each tiny tile is still governed by a determinant. In space, the same idea has one more edge: tiny boxes become tiny parallelepipeds, and the determinant becomes a 3\times3 volume scale factor.

section.title: Changes of variables in space
section.p: turned a tiny square into a tiny parallelogram. The area scale factor was the absolute value of a 2\times2 determinant.
A spatial coordinate change turns a tiny box into a tiny parallelepiped. The volume scale factor is the absolute value of a 3\times3 determinant.

subsection.title: Volume scaling by the Jacobian determinant
subsection.p: Begin with a transformation that turns a box into a solid with a curved ceiling: T(u,v,w)=(x,y,z)=(u,\ v,\ uvw). Let S=\{(u,v,w):1\le u\le2,\ 1\le v\le3,\ 0\le w\le1\}. Since x=u,\qquad y=v,\qquad z=uvw, the image E=T(S) is 1\le x\le2, \qquad 1\le y\le3, \qquad 0\le z\le xy. So the simple box in u,v,w-coordinates becomes the solid under the surface z=xy over the rectangle 1\le x\le2,\ 1\le y\le3.

Compute the volume directly:
\operatorname{Vol}(E) \amp= \int_1^2\int_1^3\int_0^{xy}1\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_1^2\int_1^3 xy\,dy\,dx \amp= \left[\int_1^2 x\,dx\right]\left[\int_1^3 y\,dy\right] \amp= \frac32\cdot4 \amp= 6.
Now compute the same volume by the transformation.

The derivative matrix is
DT(u,v,w) = \begin{pmatrix} x_u\amp x_v\amp x_w\\ y_u\amp y_v\amp y_w\\ z_u\amp z_v\amp z_w \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\amp 0\amp 0\\ 0\amp 1\amp 0\\ vw\amp uw\amp uv \end{pmatrix}.
Its determinant is J_T(u,v,w)=uv. Therefore
\operatorname{Vol}(E) \amp= \int_1^2\int_1^3\int_0^1 uv\,dw\,dv\,du \amp= \left[\int_1^2 u\,du\right]\left[\int_1^3 v\,dv\right]\left[\int_0^1 1\,dw\right] \amp= \frac32\cdot4\cdot1 \amp= 6.

Again the determinant is the scale factor. Here w measures the fraction of the way from the floor z=0 to the ceiling z=xy. A small w-step corresponds to a vertical z-step of length approximately xy\,\Delta w=uv\,\Delta w. That is why the factor is uv.

statement.p: A tiny coordinate box gets carried to a tiny parallelepiped. Why is the absolute value of the determinant exactly the right number to measure how much that box's volume is stretched or squeezed, rather than, say, the sum or product of the edge lengths of T_u\,\Delta u, T_v\,\Delta v, and T_w\,\Delta w?

hint.p: Think back to what a 3\times3 determinant computes for three vectors. The edge lengths alone cannot see how the edges are tilted relative to one another.

figure.caption: A simple coordinate box can become a solid whose height depends on position.

statement.p: Let S be a compact solid in the (u,v,w)-space with piecewise smooth boundary, and let T(u,v,w)=(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)) map S to a solid E in (x,y,z)-space.
Assume:

li.p: T has continuous first partial derivatives on an open neighborhood of S;
T is one-to-one on the interior of S, except possibly along boundary pieces;
J_T(u,v,w)\ne0 on the interior of S.

statement.p:
If f is continuous on E=T(S), then
\boxed{ \iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \iiint_S f(T(u,v,w))\,|J_T(u,v,w)|\,du\,dv\,dw. }

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p:
Cut S into tiny boxes. Near one point (u,v,w), the transformation is almost linear:
T(u+\Delta u,v+\Delta v,w+\Delta w) \approx T(u,v,w)+T_u\Delta u+T_v\Delta v+T_w\Delta w.
So a small coordinate box maps almost to the parallelepiped spanned by T_u\,\Delta u, \qquad T_v\,\Delta v, \qquad T_w\,\Delta w. The volume of that parallelepiped is |J_T(u,v,w)|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v\,\Delta w. A small contribution to the integral is therefore f(T(u,v,w))\,|J_T(u,v,w)|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v\,\Delta w. Adding the contributions and shrinking the boxes gives the formula.

subsection.p: The same warnings from the plane remain. If a map covers the same solid twice, the integral counts twice. If it has a crease, split the domain into smooth pieces. If its Jacobian vanishes on a whole three-dimensional patch, it is crushing volume.

For example, cylindrical coordinates with 0\le\theta\le4\pi trace the same cylinder twice. The factor r is correct locally, but the chosen domain is not one-to-one. The integral gives twice the ordinary volume.
The map T(u,v,w)=(u,v,0) has J_T=0 everywhere. It sends a solid box to a flat rectangle in the plane z=0. A three-dimensional volume has been crushed to zero.

subsection.title: Cylindrical and spherical coordinates revisited

example.title: Mass in a cylinder

statement.p: A solid cylinder has radius 3 and height 4: x^2+y^2\le9,\qquad 0\le z\le4. Its density is \delta(x,y,z)=z. Find its mass.

subsection.p: Spherical coordinates are x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta, y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta, and z=\rho\cos\phi. Here \rho is distance from the origin, \phi is the angle down from the positive z-axis, and \theta is the angle around the z-axis.

The three coordinate direction vectors are T_\rho,\qquad T_\phi,\qquad T_\theta. Their lengths are 1,\qquad \rho,\qquad \rho\sin\phi, and they are mutually perpendicular. With the order (\rho,\phi,\theta), the signed Jacobian determinant is \rho^2\sin\phi. So \boxed{dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.}

statement.p: The spherical factor \rho^2\sin\phi drops to 0 when \rho=0 or when \phi=0 or \phi=\pi. Geometrically, what is happening to a small coordinate box at those places that makes its volume shrink to nothing?

hint.p: Picture the three coordinate edges and their lengths 1, \rho, and \rho\sin\phi. Where do points with different \theta pile up on top of one another?

subsection.p: This is the spherical scale factor from , now obtained from the same determinant rule.

example.title: A radially denser ball

statement.p: A ball of radius 2 has density \delta(x,y,z)=1+\rho, where \rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. Find its mass.

subsection.title: General transformations in \mathbb R^3
subsection.p: Not every useful transformation has a special name like cylindrical or spherical. Sometimes the geometry of the region suggests its own variables.

Consider the ellipsoid \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2\le1. The denominators are not obstacles. They are instructions. They suggest x=2u, \qquad y=3v, \qquad z=w. Then \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2 = u^2+v^2+w^2. So the ellipsoid becomes the unit ball u^2+v^2+w^2\le1. The Jacobian determinant is
\det \begin{pmatrix} 2\amp 0\amp 0\\ 0\amp 3\amp 0\\ 0\amp 0\amp 1 \end{pmatrix} = 6.
Therefore the volume of the ellipsoid is
\operatorname{Vol} \amp= \iiint_{u^2+v^2+w^2\le1}6\,du\,dv\,dw \amp= 6\cdot \frac{4\pi}{3} \amp= 8\pi.
So
\boxed{ \operatorname{Vol}\left( \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2\le1 \right) = 8\pi. }
This example is linear, but the habit is the same for nonlinear maps: read the boundary equations and ask what variables would make them simple.

statement.p: In the ellipsoid example, the substitution came from the boundary of the region, not from the function being integrated. Why is the shape of the region so often a better guide to a good change of variables than the integrand is?

hint.p: A change of variables earns its keep mostly by turning awkward limits of integration into simple ones. Ask what makes a triple integral hard to set up in the first place.

subsection.title: Choosing transformations from geometry
subsection.p: A good change of variables is usually not guessed from the integrand alone. It is read from the shape of the region.

table.title: Reading useful variables from the shape of a region.

subsection.p: The last entry is exactly what happened in the first example of this section. The solid 0\le z\le xy became simple after setting z=xyw. The new variable w measured the fraction of the way from the bottom to the top.
Here is another example of that idea.

example.title: A solid with a variable ceiling

statement.p: Let E=\{(x,y,z):1\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le1,\ 0\le z\le x(1+y)\}. Use x=u,\qquad y=v,\qquad z=u(1+v)w. Then 1\le u\le2,\qquad 0\le v\le1,\qquad 0\le w\le1. The ceiling has become the flat coordinate face w=1.

The Jacobian matrix is
\begin{pmatrix} 1\amp 0\amp 0\\ 0\amp 1\amp 0\\ (1+v)w\amp uw\amp u(1+v) \end{pmatrix},
so J_T(u,v,w)=u(1+v). The volume is
\operatorname{Vol}(E) \amp= \int_1^2\int_0^1\int_0^1 u(1+v)\,dw\,dv\,du \amp= \left[\int_1^2u\,du\right]\left[\int_0^1(1+v)\,dv\right]\left[\int_0^1dw\right] \amp= \frac32\cdot\frac32\cdot1 \amp= \frac94.

subsection.p: The formula is now powerful, but it hides one subtle difference. Ordinary area and volume use |J|. Oriented forms use J with its sign. That sign seemed like a nuisance when we only wanted mass or volume. But it is not a nuisance. It is the bookkeeping that makes orientation work in line integrals, surface integrals, and the theorems still ahead. To see that bookkeeping clearly, we need to look not only at dA and dV, but at the forms dx\wedge dy \qquad\text{and}\qquad dx\wedge dy\wedge dz as they are pulled back through a coordinate map.

section.title: Pullbacks of area and volume elements
section.p: gave one rule for changing variables in space: dV=|J|\,du\,dv\,dw. The absolute value is right for ordinary volume. But it hides a sign.

That sign is not decoration. It tells us whether the coordinate change preserves or reverses orientation. To see the sign instead of hiding it, we return to the forms from : dx\wedge dy \qquad\text{and}\qquad dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. These measure signed area and signed volume.

subsection.title: What happens to dx\,dy under a change of variables
subsection.p: The notation dx\,dy is useful in ordinary iterated integrals, but it does not show orientation. The form dx\wedge dy does. It measures signed area, and it changes sign when the two directions are swapped.
Consider the coordinate change T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u+v,\;u-v). Start with the unit square S=\{(u,v):0\le u\le1,\ 0\le v\le1\}. Its image is a parallelogram in the xy-plane.

The two coordinate directions become T_u=(1,1), \qquad T_v=(1,-1). The signed area scale factor is \det \begin{pmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&-1 \end{pmatrix} = -2. So the image parallelogram has ordinary area 2, but the orientation induced by the ordered variables (u,v) is opposite to the usual orientation of the xy-plane.

figure.caption: The map T(u,v)=(u+v,u-v) sends the positive uv-orientation to the opposite orientation in the xy-plane.

subsection.p:
Now watch the same fact through differentials. The symbol T^*, called pullback, expresses a form on the target plane as a form on the parameter plane. For a differentiable map it works by applying the derivative to the input vectors: (T^*dx)_{(u,v)}(\mathbf a)=dx_{T(u,v)}(DT_{(u,v)}\mathbf a). Thus T^*(dx)=d(x(u,v)), the scalar differential already studied in . In this example, x=u+v, \qquad y=u-v. So T^*(dx)=du+dv, and T^*(dy)=du-dv. For an area form we apply DT to both input vectors; by the definition of the wedge of two linear measurements this gives
T^*(dx\wedge dy) \amp= (du+dv)\wedge(du-dv) \amp= du\wedge du-du\wedge dv+dv\wedge du-dv\wedge dv \amp= -du\wedge dv-du\wedge dv \amp= -2\,du\wedge dv.
Thus \boxed{ T^*(dx\wedge dy)=-2\,du\wedge dv. } Both sides are now forms on the same parameter plane; dx\wedge dy alone lives on the target plane.
The determinant has appeared as the coefficient of the pulled-back area form.

For ordinary area, we use the positive scale factor: \operatorname{Area}(T(S)) = \int_0^1\int_0^1 2\,du\,dv = 2. For signed area using the orientation induced by the parametrization T, we keep the sign. On a parameter region with the standard (u,v) orientation, define the integral of h(u,v)\,du\wedge dv to be the ordinary double integral of its coefficient h: \int_S T^*(dx\wedge dy) = \int_0^1\int_0^1 (-2)\,du\,dv = -2.
Both answers are correct. They answer different questions.

statement.p: The same map gave area 2 but signed area -2. In words, what extra piece of information does the form dx\wedge dy record that the plain area does not, and why might you want to keep it?

hint.p: Think about what changes if you list the coordinate directions in the opposite order. Does ordinary area notice? Does the sign?

subsection.title: The determinant as the coefficient of a pulled-back area element
subsection.p: The word pullback means that we express a form from the target coordinates back in the parameter coordinates.

If T is continuously differentiable and T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)), then pulling back dx means replacing it by the differential of x(u,v): T^*(dx)=d(x(u,v))=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv. Similarly, T^*(dy)=d(y(u,v))=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv.
This is the signed version of the change-of-variables rule.

In particular, for the linear map from , T(u,v)=(au+bv,cu+dv), this calculation gives T^*(dx\wedge dy)=(a\,du+b\,dv)\wedge(c\,du+d\,dv) =(ad-bc)\,du\wedge dv. The differential calculation therefore gives the same signed factor as the finite parallelogram calculation there. The corresponding ordinary area factor is |ad-bc|.

statement.p: Let T be continuously differentiable, with T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)). For a 2-form \omega=g(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy, its pullback by T is \boxed{ T^*\omega = g(x(u,v),y(u,v)) \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \,du\wedge dv. }

subsection.p: The pullback does two things at once: g(x,y)\quad\longrightarrow\quad g(x(u,v),y(u,v)), and dx\wedge dy\quad\longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\,du\wedge dv.

Under the one-to-one and regularity hypotheses of , ordinary area integrals use the absolute value of the second factor: \boxed{ \iint_R g(x,y)\,dA = \iint_S g(T(u,v)) \left| \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \right| du\,dv. } For oriented 2-form integrals, the sign stays: \boxed{ \iint_R g(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy = \iint_S g(T(u,v)) \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \,du\wedge dv, } when T is used to orient the image.

example.title: A chemical spread over a quarter disk

statement.p: A thin chemical film has areal density g(x,y)=3+x. Let R be the quarter disk x^2+y^2\le4, \qquad x\ge0,\qquad y\ge0. Use polar coordinates: x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta, with 0\le r\le2, \qquad 0\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}.

subsection.p: Here the polar Jacobian r is nonnegative on the chosen domain, so the signed and ordinary area factors agree. The coordinate map degenerates at the origin, where both factors are zero.

subsection.title: Pulling back volume elements
subsection.p: The same idea works in space. Let T(u,v,w)=(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)). For a continuously differentiable T, T^*(dx)=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv+x_w\,dw, T^*(dy)=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv+y_w\,dw, and T^*(dz)=z_u\,du+z_v\,dv+z_w\,dw. Here the wedge of three linear scalar measurements is the alternating trilinear measurement (\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c) =\det\begin{pmatrix} \alpha(\mathbf a)\amp\alpha(\mathbf b)\amp\alpha(\mathbf c)\\ \beta(\mathbf a)\amp\beta(\mathbf b)\amp\beta(\mathbf c)\\ \gamma(\mathbf a)\amp\gamma(\mathbf b)\amp\gamma(\mathbf c) \end{pmatrix}. The determinant is linear in each row, changes sign when two rows are exchanged, and is zero when two rows coincide. Grouped expressions such as (\alpha\wedge\beta)\wedge\gamma denote this same triple wedge. These facts justify distributing the wedge, swapping factors, and discarding repeated factors in the following expansion. When we wedge these three expressions together, every repeated differential vanishes, and the surviving coefficient is the 3\times3 determinant: \boxed{ T^*(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz) = \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} \,du\wedge dv\wedge dw. }

exercise.title: Where did the other terms go?

statement.p: When the three differentials are wedged together, six terms can survive; together they give one multiple of du\wedge dv\wedge dw. What is it about \wedge that makes every term with a repeated differential disappear, and why does that leave exactly the determinant behind rather than some other combination?

hint.p: Recall how du\wedge du behaves, and how swapping two factors changes the sign. The pattern of surviving signs is the same pattern that defines a determinant.

subsection.p: For a 3-form \Omega=h(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, the pullback is \boxed{ T^*\Omega = h(T(u,v,w)) \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} \,du\wedge dv\wedge dw. }

example.title: A skewed box with reversed orientation

statement.p: If S=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1], then T(S) is a skewed prism. Its ordinary volume is 2. But its oriented volume using the parametrization T is -2. The minus sign says that the ordered coordinate directions T_u,\quad T_v,\quad T_w have the opposite orientation from the usual x,y,z-orientation.

subsection.p: Under the substitution hypotheses of , the ordinary volume rule is \boxed{ \iiint_E h(x,y,z)\,dV = \iiint_S h(T(u,v,w)) \left| \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} \right| du\,dv\,dw. } For oriented 3-form integrals, the sign stays, with E carrying the orientation induced by T and the parameter domain carrying the (u,v,w) orientation: \boxed{ \iiint_E h(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = \iiint_S h(T(u,v,w)) \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} \,du\wedge dv\wedge dw. }

subsection.title: Orientation versus absolute value
subsection.p: There are now two languages.

statement.p: Ordinary integration uses |J|, while oriented integration with dx\wedge dy uses J itself. Conceptually, why does measuring plain size force us to throw away the sign, and what question are we no longer able to answer once we do?

hint.p: A length or an area can never come out negative. So if the determinant is negative, something has to give. Ask which of the two readings still remembers the flip.

table.title: Ordinary and oriented elements and their Jacobian factors.

subsection.p: The ordinary symbols dA,\qquad dV forget orientation. They count size only.
The wedge forms dx\wedge dy,\qquad dx\wedge dy\wedge dz remember orientation. They count size with sign.
This is why the same determinant appears in two slightly different ways: \text{ordinary integration uses } |J|, while \text{oriented integration uses } J.

If J\gt 0, the coordinate change preserves orientation. If J\lt 0, it reverses orientation. If J=0, then the derivative crushes area or volume at that point, and the coordinate change may stop being a genuine coordinate system there.

The notation T^*\omega is useful because it keeps the sign. But the same sign is also where mistakes begin. A determinant can be negative, zero, or locally correct while the map still covers the same region more than once. The next examples are traps worth meeting before the formula becomes a habit.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The determinant is a local measurement. It knows how one tiny tile changes near one point. It does not know whether another tile lands on top of the same place.
That is why the change-of-variables theorem had hypotheses: smoothness, one-to-one behavior, and nonzero Jacobian in the interior. The examples below show what those conditions are protecting.

subsection.title: A transformation that is not one-to-one
subsection.p: Polar coordinates give the cleanest warning.

Use x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta. The Jacobian determinant is J=r. Now choose the parameter region S=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le1,\ 0\le\theta\le4\pi\}. This region traces the unit disk twice. The angles from 0 to 2\pi cover the disk once. The angles from 2\pi to 4\pi cover it again.

If we blindly compute \iint_S r\,dr\,d\theta, we get
\int_0^{4\pi}\int_0^1 r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{4\pi}\frac12\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi.
But the ordinary area of the unit disk is \pi. The answer is twice too large because the disk was counted twice.

figure.caption: The determinant r is correct locally, but the chosen parameter region covers the disk twice.

subsection.p: The formula did not fail locally. It counted exactly what the parametrization did: one disk with multiplicity 2.

exercise.title: Where did the extra area come from?

statement.p: The Jacobian J=r was correct at every single point, yet the integral over 0\le\theta\le4\pi reported twice the area of the disk. Which hypothesis of the change-of-variables theorem was quietly violated here, and why can a perfectly correct local measurement still add up to the wrong total?

hint.p: The determinant only ever looks at one tiny tile near one point. Ask yourself whether two different parameter points were allowed to land on the same place in the disk.

subsection.p: For ordinary area of the image, use a one-to-one parameter region, such as 0\le r\le1, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Then \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r\,dr\,d\theta=\pi.

subsection.title: A transformation with zero Jacobian at a point
subsection.p: A zero Jacobian means that the derivative has crushed area or volume at that point. Sometimes this is harmless for integration. Polar coordinates have J=r, which vanishes at r=0, and the origin is only one point. That single collapse does not ruin the area formula.
But a zero Jacobian often warns us that the map is not a clean coordinate system near that point.

Consider T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u^2-v^2,\;2uv). This is the complex squaring map: x+iy=(u+iv)^2. The derivative matrix is
DT(u,v)= \begin{pmatrix} 2u&-2v\\ 2v&2u \end{pmatrix}.
Its determinant is
J_T(u,v) \amp= (2u)(2u)-(-2v)(2v) \amp= 4u^2+4v^2 \amp= 4(u^2+v^2).
So J_T(0,0)=0.

To see the geometry, write u=s\cos\alpha, \qquad v=s\sin\alpha. Then x = s^2\cos^2\alpha-s^2\sin^2\alpha = s^2\cos(2\alpha), and y = 2s^2\cos\alpha\sin\alpha = s^2\sin(2\alpha). So the map sends \text{radius }s \quad\longmapsto\quad \text{radius }s^2, and \text{angle }\alpha \quad\longmapsto\quad \text{angle }2\alpha.

A tiny circle around the origin is sent to an even tinier circle, and it is traced twice. The map folds directions together near the origin. There is no smooth inverse coordinate system through that point.

exercise.title: What is the vanishing Jacobian trying to tell us?

statement.p: At the origin the determinant collapses to J_T(0,0)=0. We saw that for polar coordinates a vanishing Jacobian at a single point did no harm. Here it does signal real trouble. What is the geometric difference between the two situations, and what does a zero Jacobian say about whether T can serve as a coordinate system near that point?

hint.p: A genuine coordinate chart needs a smooth inverse nearby. Think about what happens to two directions leaving the origin once the map doubles every angle.

subsection.p:
If D_a is the disk u^2+v^2\le a^2, then T(D_a) is the disk x^2+y^2\le a^4. Its ordinary area is \pi a^4. But integrating the absolute Jacobian over the full parameter disk gives
\iint_{D_a}4(u^2+v^2)\,du\,dv \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^a 4s^2\,s\,ds\,d\alpha \amp= 2\pi a^4.
Again the answer is twice the image area, because the disk is covered twice.

The zero Jacobian at the origin is not the only problem. The global problem is the double covering. But the zero Jacobian is a visible warning: the map is not a regular coordinate chart at the origin.

subsection.title: Why absolute value appears for ordinary area and volume
subsection.p: Now take a map that is perfectly one-to-one and has nonzero determinant everywhere: T(u,v)=(x,y)=(u,\;1-v). It sends the unit square 0\le u\le1,\qquad 0\le v\le1 onto the unit square 0\le x\le1,\qquad 0\le y\le1. The image area is plainly 1.

The Jacobian matrix is
DT= \begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&-1 \end{pmatrix},
so J_T=-1. If ordinary area used J_T instead of |J_T|, it would give \int_0^1\int_0^1 (-1)\,dv\,du=-1. That cannot be ordinary area.
The correct ordinary area computation is \int_0^1\int_0^1 |{-1}|\,dv\,du=1. So the absolute value is not a technical afterthought. It is what turns signed area into ordinary area.

The same thing happens for volume. The reflection T(u,v,w)=(u,v,-w) has J_T=-1. It preserves ordinary volume, but it reverses orientation. So dV=du\,dv\,dw, while T^*(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)=-du\wedge dv\wedge dw.

subsection.title: Why oriented integrals remember the sign
subsection.p: The sign becomes useful as soon as orientation matters.
Return to T(u,v)=(u,1-v). Pull back the signed area form: T^*(dx)=du, and T^*(dy)=-dv. Therefore T^*(dx\wedge dy)=du\wedge(-dv)=-du\wedge dv. So the parametrized unit square has signed area -1.
Why negative? Follow the boundary induced by the parameter square.

The positive boundary of the uv-square goes counterclockwise: (0,0)\to(1,0)\to(1,1)\to(0,1)\to(0,0). Under T, these points become (0,1)\to(1,1)\to(1,0)\to(0,0)\to(0,1). That path goes clockwise around the xy-square.

exercise.title: Why must we keep the minus sign?

statement.p: This map is one-to-one and its Jacobian never vanishes, so it breaks none of the hypotheses that caused the earlier failures. Yet ordinary area uses |J_T|=1 while the oriented form keeps J_T=-1. What information would be thrown away if oriented integrals also took the absolute value, and why does the boundary's reversed direction make that information worth keeping?

hint.p: Notice that the counterclockwise uv-loop became a clockwise xy-loop. If both loops gave the same answer, how would an integral ever tell the two directions apart?

figure.caption: The reflection y=1-v reverses the orientation of the square and its boundary.

subsection.p: The negative sign in T^*(dx\wedge dy)=-du\wedge dv is the same negative sign seen by walking around the boundary in the opposite direction.

This is why oriented integrals do not use absolute value. If we replaced J by |J|, then clockwise and counterclockwise parametrizations would give the same answer. That would destroy the bookkeeping needed for the theorems ahead.

The change-of-variables formula has taught us how areas and volumes transform inside a region. But the last example hints at another kind of transformation: the boundary itself changes direction. The next time orientation appears, it will be attached not to a tiny parallelogram, but to a curve we walk along. That is where vector fields, work integrals, and 1-forms begin.

introduction.p: Chapter answered the scale-factor question left by Chapter . Cylindrical coordinates needed the factor r, and spherical coordinates needed the factor \rho^2\sin\phi. Those were not special tricks. They were Jacobian determinants.

subsection.title: Skills: choosing and using substitutions
subsection.p: A good substitution usually comes from the boundary equations.
If the boundary contains x+y=1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x+y=4, then the expression u=x+y is asking to become a coordinate.
If the boundary contains xy=1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad xy=5, then u=xy may be a natural coordinate.
If the region is circular, polar coordinates are listening. If the solid is spherical, spherical coordinates are listening. If the object is an ellipsoid, a stretched ball is often hiding inside it.

table.title: Natural substitutions suggested by the geometry

subsection.p: The absolute value is for size. The sign is for orientation.

figure.caption: A substitution is both a geometric choice and a measurement correction.

subsection.title: Worked review example: a slanted window
subsection.p: A thin glass window occupies the parallelogram-like region R=\{(x,y):1\le x+y\le3,\ 0\le x-y\le2\}. The density of tint on the glass is q(x,y)=x+y. Find the total amount of tint: \iint_R (x+y)\,dA.
The boundary equations suggest u=x+y, \qquad v=x-y. Then R becomes the rectangle 1\le u\le3, \qquad 0\le v\le2.

Solve for x and y: x=\frac{u+v}{2}, \qquad y=\frac{u-v}{2}. The Jacobian determinant is
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \amp= \det\begin{pmatrix} 1/2\amp 1/2\\ 1/2\amp -1/2\end{pmatrix} \amp= -\frac14-\frac14 \amp= -\frac12.
So the ordinary area factor is \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac12. The integrand becomes x+y=u. Therefore
\iint_R (x+y)\,dA \amp= \int_1^3\int_0^2 u\cdot\frac12\,dv\,du \amp= \int_1^3 u\,du \amp= \left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_1^3 \amp= 4.
Thus \boxed{\iint_R (x+y)\,dA=4.}

The signed Jacobian was negative. That means the ordered variables (u,v) reverse the usual orientation of the xy-plane. The glass does not have negative area, so the ordinary integral uses the absolute value.

subsection.title: Worked review example: a curved plate between hyperbolas
subsection.p: A thin metal plate lies in the first quadrant. Its edges are xy=1,\qquad xy=4, and \frac{y}{x}=1,\qquad \frac{y}{x}=3. Its density is \delta(x,y)=xy. Find its mass.
The boundary equations almost name the new variables: u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}. Then the plate becomes the rectangle 1\le u\le4, \qquad 1\le v\le3.

Because we are in the first quadrant, x\gt0 and y\gt0. From u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}, we get y=vx. Then u=x(vx)=vx^2, so x=\sqrt{\frac{u}{v}}. Also, y=vx=\sqrt{uv}. Thus x=\sqrt{\frac{u}{v}}, \qquad y=\sqrt{uv}.

Compute the Jacobian. A quick way is to compute the determinant of the forward map (x,y)\longmapsto (u,v). Since u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}, we have \frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=\det\begin{pmatrix} y\amp x\\ -y/x^2\amp 1/x\end{pmatrix}. Therefore
\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} \amp= y\cdot\frac1x - x\left(-\frac{y}{x^2}\right) \amp= \frac{y}{x}+\frac{y}{x} \amp= 2\frac{y}{x} \amp= 2v.
So \boxed{\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\frac{1}{2v}.} The density becomes \delta(x,y)=xy=u. Thus
M \amp= \iint_R xy\,dA \amp= \int_1^4\int_1^3 u\cdot\frac{1}{2v}\,dv\,du \amp= \frac12 \left(\int_1^4 u\,du\right)\left(\int_1^3 \frac{1}{v}\,dv\right) \amp= \frac12 \left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_1^4 \left[\ln v\right]_1^3 \amp= \frac12\cdot\frac{15}{2}\cdot\ln 3 \amp= \frac{15}{4}\ln 3.
So \boxed{M=\frac{15}{4}\ln 3.}
The region looked awkward in x,y. It was a rectangle in the variables its own edges were already using.

subsection.title: Worked review example: a stretched ball
subsection.p: Let E be the ellipsoid \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2\le1. Its density is \delta(x,y,z)=1+\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2. Find the mass.
The ellipsoid is a stretched unit ball. Use x=2u, \qquad y=3v, \qquad z=w. Then \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2=u^2+v^2+w^2. So the solid E becomes the unit ball B=\{(u,v,w):u^2+v^2+w^2\le1\}.

The Jacobian determinant is \det\begin{pmatrix} 2\amp0\amp0\\ 0\amp3\amp0\\ 0\amp0\amp1\end{pmatrix}=6. The density becomes \delta=1+u^2+v^2+w^2. Therefore
M \amp= \iiint_E \left(1+\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2\right)dV \amp= \iiint_B 6(1+u^2+v^2+w^2)\,du\,dv\,dw.
Two coordinate changes worked together. The first turned the ellipsoid into a ball. The second used spherical coordinates because the new ball had radial symmetry.

subsection.title: Project: Gaussian integrals and polar coordinates
subsection.p: The integral \int e^{-x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative. That is a single-variable problem. The surprising way through it is to square the integral and make it two-dimensional.
Let I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx. This integral is positive, so if we can find I^2, then we can find I.

subsubsection.title: Part 1. Square the integral
subsubsection.p: Write I^2=\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx\right)\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-y^2}\,dy\right). The bounded-square Fubini argument and disk comparison in justify the limiting step. The second variable is called y so the two copies can be combined as a double integral: \boxed{I^2=\iint_{\mathbb R^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA.} The integrand is now radial: e^{-(x^2+y^2)}=e^{-r^2}. The region is the whole plane. Polar coordinates fit both the integrand and the region.

subsubsection.title: Part 2. Change to polar coordinates
subsubsection.p:
In polar coordinates, dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. Therefore I^2=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta. The inner integral uses the substitution s=r^2, \qquad ds=2r\,dr. So
\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr \amp= \frac12\int_0^\infty e^{-s}\,ds \amp= \frac12.
Thus
I^2 \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\frac12\,d\theta \amp= \pi.
Since I\gt0, \boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi}.}
This is one of the most famous uses of polar coordinates. A one-variable antiderivative was unavailable, but a two-dimensional symmetry solved the definite integral.

subsubsection.title: Part 3. A careful finite-radius version
subsubsection.p:
For a radius R\gt0, define G(R)=\iint_{x^2+y^2\le R^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA. Use polar coordinates:
G(R) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\left[-\frac12e^{-r^2}\right]_0^R \amp= \pi(1-e^{-R^2}).
So \boxed{G(R)=\pi(1-e^{-R^2}).} As R\to\infty, G(R)\to\pi. That is the polar-coordinate shadow of I^2=\pi.

subsubsection.title: Part 4. A scaled Gaussian
Part 5. Normalizing the normal density
subsubsection.p: A probability density on the real line must integrate to 1. The bell-shaped density with mean 0 and spread parameter \sigma\gt0 has the form p(x)=C e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}. Find C.

Using the scaled Gaussian formula with a=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}, we get \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}=\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}. Therefore 1=C\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}, so \boxed{C=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}.} Thus the normalized density is \boxed{p(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}.}

subsubsection.title: What to hand in
subsubsection.p: Write a short report with the following pieces.

li.p: Explain why the single-variable antiderivative is not the point of this problem.
Show how squaring the integral produces a double integral over \mathbb R^2.
Evaluate the double integral using polar coordinates.
Compute \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-ax^2}\,dx for a\gt0.
Use the result to find the normalizing constant for C e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}.
Write one paragraph explaining why polar coordinates were the right coordinates for the squared integral.

p.em: The boundary of a region now begins to matter.

conclusion.p: Change of variables taught us to respect the inside of a region. Tiny squares became parallelograms. Tiny boxes became parallelepipeds. The determinant kept track of how much size changed, and the wedge product kept track of orientation.

But the warning examples kept pointing toward the boundary. A square reflected by (u,v)\mapsto (u,1-v) did not change its ordinary area, but it reversed the direction in which its boundary was walked. A polar rectangle with 0\le\theta\le4\pi did not describe a larger disk; it walked around the same disk twice.

So far, the boundary has mostly helped us write bounds. Soon it will become an object we integrate over. A force field can do work along a path. A swirling fluid can have circulation around a closed curve. A 1-form P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is built to be added along such a path.

part.title: Vector Fields, Line Integrals, and Surface Integrals

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

introduction.p: A vector field assigns an arrow to each point. Integrating along a curve produces two different measurements: a scalar line integral uses arc length, while a work integral uses directed displacement. Differential 1-forms express the second measurement, and potentials explain when its value depends only on the endpoints.

section.title: Vector fields
section.p: A scalar field attaches one number to each point. A temperature field says, at this point, the temperature is 21^\circ\text{C}. A height field says, at this point, the height is 80 meters.

A vector field attaches an arrow to each point. A wind field says, at this point, the air is moving northeast at this speed. A force field says, at this point, a particle would be pulled in this direction with this strength.

subsection.title: A vector attached to every point
subsection.p: Picture a shallow circular fountain. Water swirls around the center. Put the center at the origin, and suppose the horizontal velocity of the water at the point (x,y) is \mathbf V(x,y)=\frac14(-y,x). At a few points,

table.title: Sample values of the fountain field \mathbf V(x,y)=\frac14(-y,x).

subsection.p: So water on the right side moves upward, water at the top moves left, water on the left moves downward, and water at the bottom moves right. The arrows circle around the origin.

figure.caption: A vector field attaches an arrow to every point of its domain.

subsection.p: This picture is not one moving particle. It is a whole instruction book. If a tiny floating leaf reaches the point (2,3), the field tells the leaf what velocity to have there: \mathbf V(2,3)=\frac14(-3,2)=\left(-\frac34,\frac12\right).

exercise.title: An instruction book, not a journey?

statement.p: We said the picture of \mathbf V is a whole instruction book rather than the path of one moving particle. What does it mean that the field assigns a vector to a point like (2,3) even if no leaf ever floats there? Why might it be misleading to read the arrows as if they trace out a single trajectory?

hint.p: Think about how many points the domain has, and ask what the arrow at (2,3) is promising: a velocity for whatever arrives there, not a record of where anything has been.

statement.p: A vector field on a region D in the plane is a function \mathbf F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2. Usually we write \mathbf F(x,y)=(P(x,y),Q(x,y)).
A vector field on a region D in space is a function \mathbf F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3, usually written \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(P(x,y,z),Q(x,y,z),R(x,y,z)).

subsection.p: The input is a point. The output is a vector. We draw the output vector with its tail placed at the input point.

The domain matters. The formula \mathbf F(x,y)=\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}(-y,x) looks like a swirling field, but it is not defined at the origin. Its domain is \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. That missing point will become important later, when we study conservative fields. A tiny hole can change the behavior of every closed curve around it.

subsection.title: Velocity fields, force fields, and gradient fields
subsection.p: Vector fields appear in several different roles.
A velocity field tells how a fluid or moving crowd flows. The fountain field \mathbf V(x,y)=\frac14(-y,x) is a velocity field. It assigns a velocity vector to every point in the water.

A force field tells what force would act on a particle placed at each point. For example, a simplified gravitational field pointing toward the origin has the form \mathbf G(x,y,z)=-\frac{k}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}(x,y,z), where k\gt 0. The vector (x,y,z) points away from the origin, so the negative sign points back toward the origin. The denominator says the field weakens with distance.
A gradient field comes from a scalar field. If f(x,y) is a differentiable scalar field, then \nabla f(x,y)=\bigl(f_x(x,y),f_y(x,y)\bigr) is a vector field.

For example, let h(x,y)=100+4x+3y-x^2-y^2. This could be a simple height model for a hill. Its gradient field is \nabla h(x,y)=(4-2x,\;3-2y). At the point (1,1), \nabla h(1,1)=(2,1). A hiker standing there sees the steepest uphill direction pointing roughly east and slightly north.

exercise.title: Why is a gradient field special?

statement.p: A force field or a wind field is just an arrow at every point. A gradient field \nabla f is also an arrow at every point, yet we say it is tied to the contour map of f. What extra information does a gradient field carry that a generic vector field need not, and why does that matter when you look at its arrows?

hint.p: Recall that \nabla f points across level curves at right angles and toward increasing f. Could you reconstruct something about the underlying surface from its gradient arrows alone? Could you do that for an arbitrary field of arrows?

example.title: A field that is not a gradient field, at least not obviously

statement.p: The swirling field \mathbf V(x,y)=(-y,x) has arrows tangent to circles centered at the origin. If it were the gradient of some height function, its arrows would be perpendicular to that height function's level curves. But these arrows go around in circles. They look more like rotation than uphill motion.
Later we will learn a test that detects this difference. Some fields are gradients in disguise. Others carry genuine circulation.

subsection.title: Sketching vector fields
subsection.p: A vector field drawing cannot show every arrow. There are infinitely many points. A sketch chooses representative points and draws enough arrows to reveal the pattern.
Here are four basic fields in the plane.

table.title: Four basic vector fields in the plane.

row.cell: arrows point away from the origin

subsection.p: The length of an arrow matters, but only up to the scale of the drawing. If one arrow is too long, it can hide the rest of the picture. It is common to shorten all arrows while preserving their directions, or to draw only direction arrows. A sketch is meant to show structure, not to be a measuring device.

example.title: Sketching a saddle-like field

statement.p: Consider \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,-y). On the x-axis, where y=0, \mathbf F(x,0)=(x,0). So arrows point away from the origin along the x-axis.
On the y-axis, where x=0, \mathbf F(0,y)=(0,-y). So arrows point toward the origin along the y-axis.
This field pushes outward in one direction and inward in the perpendicular direction. The origin is a saddle-type equilibrium: motion near it is attracted from some directions and repelled in others.

subsection.p: A few practical rules help when drawing a field.

table.title: Practical steps for sketching a vector field.

row.cell: Evaluate the field at simple points.
Look along axes or symmetry lines.
Notice whether arrows point outward, inward, around, or across.
Scale arrows so the pattern can be seen.

subsection.p: The points where \mathbf F(\mathbf p)=\mathbf 0 are called equilibrium points. If the field is a velocity field, a the constant curve at such a point satisfies the velocity equation. This observation does not by itself prove that every solution starting there must remain there; uniqueness requires additional hypotheses on the field.

subsection.title: Flow lines and qualitative behavior
subsection.p: A vector field tells a moving particle what velocity it should have at each point. A path that obeys the field is called a flow line.

For the fountain field \mathbf V(x,y)=(-y,x), the circle \mathbf r(t)=(R\cos t,R\sin t) is a flow line. Its velocity is \mathbf r'(t)=(-R\sin t,R\cos t). But \mathbf V(\mathbf r(t))=\mathbf V(R\cos t,R\sin t)=(-R\sin t,R\cos t). So \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf V(\mathbf r(t)). The particle follows the arrows exactly.

statement.p: Let \mathbf F be a vector field. A differentiable curve \mathbf r(t) is called a flow line of \mathbf F if \boxed{\mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))} for every t in its interval of definition.

subsection.p: The equation \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) says that the curve's velocity at each moment equals the arrow assigned by the field at the curve's current position.

exercise.title: What does the flow-line equation really say?

statement.p: The definition asks that \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) at every instant. In plain words, why does this single equation force the curve to obey the field? And why does it matter that the right-hand side is evaluated at the curve's current position \mathbf r(t) rather than at some fixed point?

hint.p: Imagine reading the field like a set of directions handed to you wherever you happen to stand. If you stepped off the path even slightly, the instruction you receive would change. Along a proposed flow line, compare its instantaneous velocity with the arrow assigned by the field at that same point.

example.title: Flow lines of a radial field

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,y). If a particle starts at \mathbf r(0)=(a,b), then \mathbf r(t)=(ae^t,be^t) is a flow line, because \mathbf r'(t)=(ae^t,be^t)=\mathbf r(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)). The particle moves along the ray through (a,b), away from the origin. The origin is an equilibrium point, but nearby points are pushed outward.

example.title: Flow lines of a saddle field

statement.p: For \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,-y), a flow line through (a,b) is \mathbf r(t)=(ae^t,be^{-t}). Then \mathbf r'(t)=(ae^t,-be^{-t})=\mathbf F(ae^t,be^{-t}). If ab\ne0, the product of the coordinates along the flow is x(t)y(t)=ae^t\cdot be^{-t}=ab. So the flow lines lie on hyperbolas xy=\text{constant}.

subsection.p: A vector field drawing is therefore a prediction device. It tells us where motion is fast or slow, where it turns, where it settles, and where it circulates.

But motion is only one thing we can do with a curve. A curve can also carry material. A wire can have density. A trail can have snow depth. A cable can have temperature. Those quantities are not arrows, but they still need to be added along a path. Before we let vector fields do work, we need the simpler integral that adds scalar quantities along curves.

section.title: Line integrals of scalar functions
section.p: A vector field attaches arrows to points. A scalar field attaches numbers. When a curve passes through a scalar field, it collects numbers along its length.
That idea sounds like ordinary integration, but the domain is no longer an interval. The domain is a curve.

subsection.title: Accumulating density along a curve
subsection.p: A thin copper wire is bent into the upper half of a circle of radius 3. Its shape is x^2+y^2=9, \qquad y\ge0. The wire is not uniform. Its linear density at the point (x,y) is \rho(x,y)=2+\frac{x}{3} grams per centimeter.
The right side of the wire is denser, because x\gt 0. The left side is lighter, because x\lt 0.
Parametrize the upper semicircle by \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le \pi. Then \rho(\mathbf r(t)) = 2+\frac{3\cos t}{3} = 2+\cos t.

figure.caption: A scalar line integral adds density along the length of a curve.

subsection.p: This is the seed of the definition. We multiply the scalar value on the curve by a tiny length element and add: \sum \rho\,\Delta s.

subsection.title: The arc length element ds
subsection.p: The symbol ds means a tiny piece of arc length.

If a curve is parametrized by \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)), then over a small time interval \Delta t, the displacement is approximately \mathbf r'(t)\Delta t. Its length is approximately \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\Delta t. So \boxed{ ds=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. } In the plane, \boxed{ ds= \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt. } In space, \boxed{ ds= \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{dz}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt. }
This is the same speed from . Arc length is distance traveled: L=\int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. A scalar line integral simply weights this distance by a scalar field.

definition.title: Line integral of a scalar function

statement.p: Let C be a piecewise smooth curve parametrized by \mathbf r(t),\qquad a\le t\le b. Let f be a continuous scalar function on C. The line integral of f with respect to arc length is \boxed{ \int_C f\,ds = \int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. }

subsection.p: The notation \int_C f\,ds says: add the values of f along the curve, weighted by length.
If f=1, then \int_C 1\,ds = \int_a^b \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt, which is the length of the curve.

statement.p: The factor \|\mathbf r'(t)\| turns dt into a piece of arc length ds. In plain words, what does this factor measure about how the curve is being traced, and why would leaving it out give the wrong total?

hint.p: Think about the difference between clock time dt and distance on the wire. If the parametrization speeds up, one second of t covers more length.

subsection.title: Mass of a wire
subsection.p: A scalar line integral is often a mass integral.

example.title: A straight wire in space

statement.p: A wire runs from (0,0,0) to (2,2,1). Parametrize it by \mathbf r(t)=(t,t,t/2), \qquad 0\le t\le2. Suppose its density is \rho(x,y,z)=1+z kilograms per meter.

subsection.p: The computation has three steps:
The last step is the one students most often forget. The parameter t is not necessarily arc length. The factor \|\mathbf r'(t)\| converts dt into length.

exercise.title: Is t the same as distance?

statement.p: The text warns that the parameter t is not necessarily arc length. What would have to be true about a parametrization for t itself to measure distance along the curve, so that the speed factor became simply 1?

hint.p: Ask what value \|\mathbf r'(t)\| would need to have at every instant. A curve traced at unit speed has a special name.

example.title: The same segment with a different clock

statement.p:
The same line segment from (0,0,0) to (2,2,1) can also be written as \mathbf q(u)=(2u,2u,u), \qquad 0\le u\le1. Along this parametrization, \rho(\mathbf q(u))=1+u, and \mathbf q'(u)=(2,2,1), so \|\mathbf q'(u)\|=3. The mass is
M \amp= \int_0^1 (1+u)3\,du \amp= 3\left[u+\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_0^1 \amp= \frac92.
The answer is the same. The new clock moves along the same wire over a different parameter interval, and the speed factor corrects for that.

subsection.title: Why parametrization does not change the value
subsection.p: The last example was not an accident. A scalar line integral depends on the curve as a traced geometric object, not on the particular clock used to trace it.

theorem.title: Scalar line integrals are unchanged by reparametrization

statement.p: Let C be a curve parametrized by \mathbf r(t),\qquad a\le t\le b. Let t=\phi(u),\qquad \alpha\le u\le \beta, where \phi is continuously differentiable and traces the interval [a,b] exactly once, either forward or backward. Then \mathbf q(u)=\mathbf r(\phi(u)) parametrizes the same curve once, and \boxed{ \int_\alpha^\beta f(\mathbf q(u))\|\mathbf q'(u)\|\,du = \int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. }

proof.p: By the chain rule, \mathbf q'(u)=\mathbf r'(\phi(u))\phi'(u). Therefore \|\mathbf q'(u)\| = \|\mathbf r'(\phi(u))\|\,|\phi'(u)|. So f(\mathbf q(u))\|\mathbf q'(u)\| = f(\mathbf r(\phi(u)))\|\mathbf r'(\phi(u))\|\,|\phi'(u)|. If \phi traces the interval forward, then \phi'(u)\ge0 except possibly at isolated points, and this is the ordinary substitution rule. If \phi traces the interval backward, the absolute value reverses the sign that would have come from dt. Either way, length is positive, and the same total is obtained.

subsection.p: This is why orientation does not affect scalar line integrals. If you walk along a wire from left to right or right to left, its mass is the same.

statement.p: A scalar line integral such as mass gives the same value whether the curve is traced one way or the other, yet later in the chapter work will change sign when you reverse direction. What is it about adding up f\,ds that makes orientation simply not register?

hint.p: Notice that ds is always a positive length, never a signed displacement. Reversing the trace reorders the pieces but does not turn any of them negative.

subsection.p: But the theorem contains the phrase exactly once for a reason.

example.title: Same image, different multiplicity

statement.p: Let C be the unit circle and let f(x,y)=1. Tracing the circle once by \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, gives \int_C 1\,ds = \int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt = 2\pi.

Tracing the same geometric circle twice by \mathbf q(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le4\pi, gives \int 1\,ds = \int_0^{4\pi}1\,dt = 4\pi. The image is the same set of points, but the traced curve is not the same. The second parametrization counts the wire twice.

subsection.p: The phrase piecewise smooth also matters. It rules out curves whose length is not controlled by ordinary calculus.

example.title: A continuous curve can have too much length

statement.p: So continuity alone is not enough for the line integrals in this chapter. Piecewise smooth curves keep the geometry tame enough that arc length can be computed by \int \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt.

subsection.p: The scalar field also needs to be reasonable along the curve.

example.title: A density too wild to integrate

statement.p: This is why the definition assumes f is continuous on the curve. Continuous densities do not jump between two values at every scale.

subsection.title: Average value along a curve
subsection.p: For a scalar function on a region, average value means \frac{\text{total}}{\text{size of domain}}. Along a curve, the size of the domain is length.

statement.p: Let C have length L=\int_C 1\,ds. The average value of a scalar function f along C is \boxed{ f_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_C f\,ds. }

example.title: Average density on the semicircular wire

statement.p: For the upper semicircle of radius 3, L=3\pi. Earlier we found \int_C \rho\,ds=6\pi. Therefore the average density is \rho_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{1}{3\pi}(6\pi) = 2. This makes sense. The density \rho(x,y)=2+\frac{x}{3} is larger on the right side and smaller on the left side. The upper semicircle is symmetric, so the x/3 part averages to 0.

example.title: Average temperature along a straight cable

subsection.p: Scalar line integrals add quantities that do not care which way the curve is traveled. Mass, length, and average temperature are unchanged if we reverse direction.

A force field is different. If a force helps you move one way, it resists you in the opposite direction. To measure work, we cannot multiply by the unsigned length ds. We must measure how much of the force points along the actual displacement. That is where \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r enters, and it will lead us directly to the 1-form P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.

section.title: Work integrals of vector fields
section.p: added scalar quantities along a curve. Density, temperature, and length used ds, so direction did not matter. Walking along a wire from left to right or right to left does not change its mass.
Force is different. A force that helps you move one way resists you in the opposite way. So a work integral cannot use only the unsigned length ds. It must remember the actual displacement.

subsection.title: Force dotted with displacement
subsection.p:
Start with a constant force. A cart is pulled across a warehouse floor by the force \mathbf F=(4,1) newtons. The cart moves from A=(0,0) to B=(3,2). Its displacement is \Delta \mathbf r=B-A=(3,2). The work done by the force is
W \amp= \mathbf F\cdot \Delta \mathbf r \amp= (4,1)\cdot(3,2) \amp= 12+2 \amp= 14.
The force has a large eastward component and a small northward component. Both help this displacement.
If the same cart moves backward from B to A, the displacement is -\Delta \mathbf r=(-3,-2). The work becomes \mathbf F\cdot(-\Delta \mathbf r)=-14. The same force now resists the motion.
This is the first difference between scalar line integrals and work integrals:

p.md: \boxed{\text{Scalar line integrals ignore orientation. Work integrals remember it.}}

subsection.p: Now let the force vary from point to point, and let the cart move along a curved track.
Suppose the force field is \mathbf F(x,y)=(2x,1). The eastward force grows as x increases, and the northward force is constantly 1.

Let the track be \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2), \qquad 0\le t\le2. A tiny time step dt produces the tiny displacement d\mathbf r\approx \mathbf r'(t)\,dt. Since \mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t), and \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=\mathbf F(t,t^2)=(2t,1), the tiny work is approximately
dW \amp= \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt \amp= (2t,1)\cdot(1,2t)\,dt \amp= (2t+2t)\,dt \amp= 4t\,dt.
Adding all the tiny work pieces gives
W \amp= \int_0^2 4t\,dt \amp= \left[2t^2\right]_0^2 \amp= 8.

figure.caption: Work adds the component of the force in the direction of motion.

subsection.p: The dot product is doing the physical filtering. Only the part of the force pointing along the displacement contributes positive work. The part perpendicular to the motion does no work.

statement.p: Suppose at every instant the force \mathbf F happens to point exactly perpendicular to the direction the cart is moving. Without computing anything, what should the total work be, and why does the dot product give you that answer automatically?

hint.p: Think about \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r at a single instant when the two vectors are at right angles. What does the dot product of perpendicular vectors equal, and what does adding up many copies of that give you?

subsection.p: The previous computation is the model for the definition.

Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(P(x,y),Q(x,y)) be a vector field in the plane, and let \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)), \qquad a\le t\le b, parametrize an oriented curve C. Then \mathbf r'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t)). The force at the point \mathbf r(t) is \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)). The tiny displacement is d\mathbf r=\mathbf r'(t)\,dt. So the tiny work is \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt.

definition.title: Work integral of a vector field

statement.p: Let C be a piecewise smooth oriented curve parametrized by \mathbf r(t), \qquad a\le t\le b. Let \mathbf F be a continuous vector field on C. The work integral of \mathbf F along C is \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt. }

subsection.p: In the plane, this means \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \left[ P(x(t),y(t))x'(t) + Q(x(t),y(t))y'(t) \right]dt. }

In space, if \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(P(x,y,z),Q(x,y,z),R(x,y,z)) and \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)), then \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \left[ P x'(t)+Q y'(t)+R z'(t) \right]dt, } where P,Q,R are evaluated at (x(t),y(t),z(t)).
The notation d\mathbf r is a reminder of the tiny displacement. Along a parametrized curve, d\mathbf r=\mathbf r'(t)\,dt.

example.title: Work along a helix

statement.p: A particle moves along the helix \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. A force field is \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,2). Find the work done along the helix.

First, \mathbf r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t,1). Along the curve, \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = \mathbf F(\cos t,\sin t,t) = (-\sin t,\cos t,2). Therefore
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t) \amp= (-\sin t,\cos t,2)\cdot(-\sin t,\cos t,1) \amp= \sin^2t+\cos^2t+2 \amp= 3.
So \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_0^{2\pi}3\,dt = 6\pi. } The rotational part of the force helps the circular motion, and the constant vertical force helps the upward motion.

subsection.title: Parametrization and orientation of a curve
subsection.p: A scalar line integral used ds=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. The absolute value hidden in the norm erased direction. Work integrals use d\mathbf r=\mathbf r'(t)\,dt. No absolute value appears. Direction survives.

statement.p: A scalar line integral uses ds=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt, but a work integral uses d\mathbf r=\mathbf r'(t)\,dt with no norm. In words, why does keeping the velocity vector itself (instead of just its length) make the integral able to tell forward travel from backward travel?

hint.p: A norm can never be negative, so it forgets which way the arrow points. Ask yourself what happens to \mathbf r'(t) when you walk the same road the other way.

subsection.p: Return to the curved track \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2), \qquad 0\le t\le2, with force field \mathbf F(x,y)=(2x,1). We found \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=8.

Now use a different clock: \mathbf q(u)=(2u,4u^2), \qquad 0\le u\le1. This traces the same curve in the same direction. Along this parametrization, \mathbf q'(u)=(2,8u), and \mathbf F(\mathbf q(u))=(4u,1). Therefore
\int_0^1 \mathbf F(\mathbf q(u))\cdot\mathbf q'(u)\,du \amp= \int_0^1 (4u,1)\cdot(2,8u)\,du \amp= \int_0^1 16u\,du \amp= 8.
The value did not change.

Now reverse the curve: \overline{\mathbf r}(t)=\mathbf r(2-t) = (2-t,(2-t)^2), \qquad 0\le t\le2. Then \overline{\mathbf r}'(t)=(-1,-2(2-t)). Also, \mathbf F(\overline{\mathbf r}(t))=(2(2-t),1). Thus
\int_0^2 \mathbf F(\overline{\mathbf r}(t))\cdot \overline{\mathbf r}'(t)\,dt \amp= \int_0^2 \left[ -2(2-t)-2(2-t) \right]dt \amp= \int_0^2 -4(2-t)\,dt \amp= -8.
Reversing the path reversed the sign.

theorem.title: Effect of reparametrization on work integrals

statement.p: Let \mathbf r(t),\qquad a\le t\le b, parametrize a piecewise smooth curve C, and let \mathbf q(u)=\mathbf r(\phi(u)), \qquad \alpha\le u\le\beta, where \phi is continuously differentiable and traces [a,b] exactly once, and \mathbf F is continuous along the curve.

If \phi is increasing, then \mathbf q gives the same orientation and \boxed{ \int_\alpha^\beta \mathbf F(\mathbf q(u))\cdot\mathbf q'(u)\,du = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt. }

If \phi is decreasing, then \mathbf q gives the opposite orientation and \boxed{ \int_\alpha^\beta \mathbf F(\mathbf q(u))\cdot\mathbf q'(u)\,du = - \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt. }

proof.p:
By the chain rule, \mathbf q'(u)=\mathbf r'(\phi(u))\phi'(u). Therefore
\mathbf F(\mathbf q(u))\cdot\mathbf q'(u) \amp= \mathbf F(\mathbf r(\phi(u)))\cdot \bigl(\mathbf r'(\phi(u))\phi'(u)\bigr) \amp= \left[ \mathbf F(\mathbf r(\phi(u)))\cdot \mathbf r'(\phi(u)) \right]\phi'(u).
If \phi is increasing, the substitution t=\phi(u) preserves the order of the limits. If \phi is decreasing, the substitution reverses the order of the limits, which introduces the minus sign.

subsection.p: The phrase exactly once matters. If the same curve is traced twice, the work is counted twice.

example.title: Same image, different multiplicity

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x) and trace the unit circle by \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t). For one counterclockwise trip, 0\le t\le2\pi, we have \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=(-\sin t,\cos t) and \mathbf r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t). Thus \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)=1, so \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt = 2\pi.

If the same formula is used on 0\le t\le4\pi, the image is still the unit circle, but it is traced twice. The integral becomes \int_0^{4\pi}1\,dt=4\pi. The work integral sees the traveled curve with its multiplicity, not just the set of points.

subsection.p: The continuity assumption on the vector field is also there for a reason.

example.title: Why the field should be integrable along the path

statement.p: On the line segment \mathbf r(t)=(t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le1, define \mathbf F(x,y)=(D(x),0), where D(x)= \begin{cases} 1, \amp x \text{ rational},\\ 0, \amp x \text{ irrational}. \end{cases} Then \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)=D(t). This function has no Riemann integral on [0,1], because every interval contains rational and irrational numbers. The work sums can be forced toward different values by different sample points.
Continuity is more than a comfort condition. It prevents this kind of microscopic jumping along the curve.

subsection.p: The curve itself must also be tame enough to have a velocity on finitely many smooth pieces. Corners are allowed; infinitely wild motion is not part of the basic theory here.

subsection.title: Circulation around a closed curve
subsection.p: When the curve is closed, work has a special name.

The circle on the integral sign reminds us that the curve is closed. In the plane, a counterclockwise orientation is usually called positive. As you walk, the region inside the curve stays on your left.

example.title: A swirling field has positive circulation

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x). This field points tangent to circles centered at the origin. Around the unit circle, parametrized counterclockwise by \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, we already computed \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)=1. Therefore \boxed{ \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi. }
The arrows of the field point with the motion all the way around the circle.

figure.caption: The field (-y,x) circulates counterclockwise around the origin.

example.title: A radial field has zero circulation around a circle

statement.p: The radial field points outward. The circular motion is tangent. A perpendicular force does no work along the curve.

subsection.p: The two fields (-y,x) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (x,y) look equally simple, but their closed-curve behavior is completely different. One carries circulation. The other does not.

statement.p: The swirling field (-y,x) has nonzero circulation around a circle, while the radial field (x,y) has zero. Geometrically, what is it about how each field sits relative to the direction of travel around the circle that explains the difference?

hint.p: Picture the arrows of each field at a point on the circle and compare them with the tangent direction of motion. Only the part of the field along the path does any work.

subsection.p: The dot-product notation \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r has brought us far enough to compute work. But it is hiding the actual integrand. When \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) and d\mathbf r=(dx,dy,dz), the expression is really P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. That object is not quite a vector field. It is a 1-form, and it is built from the start to be integrated along a curve.

section.title: Differential 1-forms
section.p: defined work by \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r. If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) and \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)), then the integrand is P x'(t)+Q y'(t)+R z'(t). But x'(t)\,dt=dx,\qquad y'(t)\,dt=dy,\qquad z'(t)\,dt=dz. So the work integrand is really P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.
Here we study 1-forms as integrands along curves, continuing the use of area and volume forms in .

subsection.title: Work written as P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz
subsection.p: Return to the swirling field \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x). The work expression is \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = (-y,x)\cdot(dx,dy) = -y\,dx+x\,dy. So instead of writing \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r, we can write \int_C -y\,dx+x\,dy.

The calculation is the same as the work integral, but the notation has changed. The expression -y\,dx+x\,dy is the object being integrated. It knows how to eat tiny steps along a curve: multiply the tiny x-step by -y, multiply the tiny y-step by x, and add.

The symbols dx,\qquad dy,\qquad dz are the coordinate-reading 1-forms. They measure components of a displacement: dx(v_1,v_2,v_3)=v_1, dy(v_1,v_2,v_3)=v_2, and dz(v_1,v_2,v_3)=v_3. So at a point \mathbf p, the 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz acts on a displacement vector \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3) by \boxed{ \omega_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v) = P(\mathbf p)v_1+Q(\mathbf p)v_2+R(\mathbf p)v_3. }
A 1-form is therefore a field of linear measuring rules. At each point, it takes a tiny displacement and returns a number.

exercise.title: What does the form actually eat?

statement.p: We keep saying that a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is a machine that eats a tiny displacement vector and returns a number. Why is it important that the input is a vector (a direction and size of a step) rather than just a point? What information would be missing if you only handed \omega a location and no step?

hint.p: Look at the rule \omega_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=P(\mathbf p)v_1+Q(\mathbf p)v_2. The point \mathbf p fixes the coefficients, but what role do the components v_1,v_2 still have to play before a number comes out?

subsection.title: Why a 1-form naturally integrates along a curve
subsection.p: A curve supplies tiny displacements: d\mathbf r=(dx,dy,dz). A 1-form is built to measure those tiny displacements: P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. That is why 1-forms are the natural integrands along curves.

example.title: A form along a parabolic track

statement.p: Something interesting happened here. The answer is 1, which is also the change in xy from the beginning of the curve to the end: xy\big|_{(1,1)}-xy\big|_{(0,0)}=1-0=1. That is not a coincidence. The next section will name the reason.

subsection.p: A 1-form does not need a length element ds. It does not ask how long the motion was. It asks how much x, y, and z changed, with coefficients attached to those changes.
That is why orientation matters. Reverse a curve, and dx,\ dy,\ dz all reverse sign.

statement.p: An arc-length integral carries a length element ds, but the integral of a 1-form does not. In your own words, why does a 1-form not need to know how long the path was? What is it measuring along the curve instead of length, and how does that explain why reversing the curve flips the sign?

hint.p: A 1-form reads tiny steps (dx,dy,dz), and a step has a direction. Distance ds is always positive no matter which way you walk, but a directed step is not. Which of these two notions changes sign when you turn around?

subsection.title: Pulling a 1-form back to a parameter interval
subsection.p: A curve turns a 1-form into an ordinary single-variable integrand.

Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz and let \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)), \qquad a\le t\le b. Along the curve, dx=x'(t)\,dt, \qquad dy=y'(t)\,dt, \qquad dz=z'(t)\,dt. So \omega becomes \left[ P(\mathbf r(t))x'(t) + Q(\mathbf r(t))y'(t) + R(\mathbf r(t))z'(t) \right]dt.

definition.title: Pullback of a 1-form to a curve

statement.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be a 1-form, and let \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)). The pullback of \omega by \mathbf r is the 1-variable form \boxed{ \mathbf r^*\omega = \left[ P(\mathbf r(t))x'(t) + Q(\mathbf r(t))y'(t) + R(\mathbf r(t))z'(t) \right]dt. } The line integral of \omega along C is \boxed{ \int_C \omega = \int_a^b \mathbf r^*\omega. }

subsection.p: The word pullback means that the form has been pulled back from the curve in space to the parameter interval on the t-line. Once that happens, the integral is an ordinary single-variable integral.

example.title: Pulling back a space form

statement.p:
Let \omega=z\,dx+x\,dy+y\,dz. Let the curve be \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,1-t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then dx=dt, \qquad dy=2t\,dt, \qquad dz=-dt. Also, x=t,\qquad y=t^2,\qquad z=1-t. So
\mathbf r^*\omega \amp= (1-t)\,dt+t(2t\,dt)+t^2(-dt) \amp= (1-t+2t^2-t^2)\,dt \amp= (1-t+t^2)\,dt.
Therefore
\int_C \omega \amp= \int_0^1(1-t+t^2)\,dt \amp= \left[t-\frac{t^2}{2}+\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \amp= 1-\frac12+\frac13 \amp= \frac56.

subsection.p: The same hypotheses from work integrals remain. The curve should be piecewise smooth, and the coefficients of the form should be continuous along the curve. Otherwise the pulled-back integrand may not be integrable.

example.title: A 1-form too wild along a path

statement.p: Let \omega=D(x)\,dx, where D(x)= \begin{cases} 1, \amp x \text{ rational},\\ 0, \amp x \text{ irrational}. \end{cases} Along the line segment \mathbf r(t)=(t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le1, we get dx=dt, so \mathbf r^*\omega=D(t)\,dt. This is not Riemann integrable. The problem is not the curve. The problem is that the coefficient jumps between 0 and 1 at every scale.

subsection.p: Tracing a curve more than once also matters.

example.title: The same image counted twice

statement.p:
On the punctured plane \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, consider the form \omega=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}. On the unit circle \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), we have dx=-\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=\cos t\,dt, so
\mathbf r^*\omega \amp= \frac{-(\sin t)(-\sin t\,dt)+(\cos t)(\cos t\,dt)}{\cos^2t+\sin^2t} \amp= dt.
One counterclockwise trip gives \int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi. Two counterclockwise trips give \int_0^{4\pi}dt=4\pi. The image is the same circle, but the traveled curve is different.

subsection.p: This form will return. It measures change in angle. It is locally called d\theta, but the whole punctured plane has no single continuous angle function \theta. That small fact is the source of a large surprise later.

subsection.title: Vector fields and 1-forms: related but not identical
subsection.p: A vector field assigns an arrow to each point. A 1-form assigns a measuring rule to each point.

In ordinary Cartesian coordinates, the dot product lets us turn a vector field into a 1-form. If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), then the associated work form is \boxed{ \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. } For every displacement vector \mathbf v, \omega_{\mathbf F}(\mathbf v)=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v. So \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_C \omega_{\mathbf F}. }
That is why vector fields and 1-forms look almost the same in this chapter. But they are not the same kind of object.
The distinction becomes visible in polar coordinates.

A small displacement in the plane can be written as d\mathbf r=\mathbf e_r\,dr+\mathbf e_\theta\,r\,d\theta. The factor r appears because a small angular change d\theta at radius r sweeps out an arc of length r\,d\theta.

If a vector field is written in polar unit vectors as \mathbf F=F_r\,\mathbf e_r+F_\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta, then its work form is \boxed{ \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = F_r\,dr+F_\theta\,r\,d\theta. } The angular part gets a factor of r.

example.title: The angular unit vector and the angle form

statement.p: The unit angular vector field is \mathbf e_\theta=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta) = \left(-\frac{y}{r},\frac{x}{r}\right), where r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Its associated work form is \omega_{\mathbf e_\theta} = -\frac{y}{r}\,dx+\frac{x}{r}\,dy. Since d\theta= \frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{r^2}, we have \boxed{ \omega_{\mathbf e_\theta}=r\,d\theta. }

On a circle of radius R, r\,d\theta=R\,d\theta. So \int_{\text{circle}} \omega_{\mathbf e_\theta} = \int_0^{2\pi}R\,d\theta = 2\pi R. That is the circumference. A unit tangent force does one unit of work per unit of arc length.
But the form d\theta itself gives \int_{\text{circle}}d\theta=2\pi. It measures angle swept out, not distance traveled.
