The vector field corresponding to d\theta by the Cartesian dot product is \left(-\frac{y}{r^2},\frac{x}{r^2}\right), whose length is \frac1r. So d\theta is not the work form of the unit angular vector field. It is the work form of a field whose arrows get weaker as the radius grows.

subsection.p: This example is worth keeping. The vector field \mathbf e_\theta is an arrow field. The form d\theta is an angle-measuring rule. In Cartesian coordinates, a dot product connects arrows and measuring rules, but the connection uses the geometry of the plane.
For line integrals, the 1-form is the cleaner object: \int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. It says exactly what is added along the curve.

statement.p: In Cartesian coordinates a vector field and its work 1-form look almost identical, yet in polar coordinates the angular part of the form picks up a factor of r while the vector field does not. What does this mismatch reveal about the difference between an arrow (a vector field) and a measuring rule (a 1-form)? Why should we trust the form, not the dot product, as the thing being integrated along a curve?

hint.p: The dot product that turns \mathbf F into \omega_{\mathbf F} secretly uses the geometry of the plane (how long the basis vectors are). The line integral \int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy never asks about that geometry. Think about which object is defined without reference to lengths and angles.

subsection.p: Some 1-forms have a special origin. The form y\,dx+x\,dy from the earlier example is d(xy). It is the differential of a function. That is why its integral along the parabola quietly became an endpoint difference.

But the angle form \frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} also looks like it should be d\theta, and its integral around a closed circle is 2\pi, not 0. How can a differential around a closed loop fail to cancel?
The answer depends not only on the formula, but on the domain. A missing point can change everything. That is where conservative vector fields and exact 1-forms begin.

section.title: Conservative vector fields and exact 1-forms
section.p: ended with a small mystery. The form y\,dx+x\,dy quietly became an endpoint difference, because y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy). But the angle form \frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} looked like it wanted to be d\theta, while its integral around a circle was not zero. So the question is now unavoidable: \text{When is a line integral really just an endpoint difference?}

subsection.title: Potential functions
subsection.p: Start with a force field on a factory floor: \mathbf F(x,y)=(y,x). Its work form is \omega=\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=y\,dx+x\,dy.

Move a cart from A=(0,0) to B=(2,1). First take the straight path \mathbf r(t)=(2t,t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Along this path, x=2t,\qquad y=t, so dx=2\,dt,\qquad dy=dt. Therefore
\omega \amp= y\,dx+x\,dy \amp= t(2\,dt)+(2t)(dt) \amp= 4t\,dt.
The work is \int_0^1 4t\,dt=2.
Now take a broken path: first go east from (0,0) to (2,0), then go north from (2,0) to (2,1).
On the eastward segment, y=0,\qquad dy=0, so y\,dx+x\,dy=0. On the northward segment, x=2,\qquad dx=0, so y\,dx+x\,dy=2\,dy. Thus \int_0^1 2\,dy=2. Both paths give the same work.

figure.caption: For the form y\,dx+x\,dy, these two paths from A to B give the same integral.

subsection.p: The reason is not the shape of the paths. The reason is that y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy). Let \phi(x,y)=xy. Then d\phi=y\,dx+x\,dy. So the integral becomes \int_C d\phi. It measures the change in \phi along the path: \phi(2,1)-\phi(0,0)=2-0=2.
The function \phi is called a potential function.

definition.title: Potential function, conservative field, exact form

statement.p: Let D be a region in the plane or in space.
A scalar function \phi is called a potential function for a vector field \mathbf F on D if \boxed{ \mathbf F=\nabla \phi } on D. In that case, \mathbf F is called a conservative vector field.
A 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy or \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is called exact on D if there is a function \phi on D such that \boxed{ \omega=d\phi. }

subsection.p: The two languages are the same in Cartesian coordinates. If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), then \mathbf F=\nabla\phi means P=\phi_x,\qquad Q=\phi_y,\qquad R=\phi_z. The associated work form is P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz=d\phi.

In physics, one often writes a conservative force as \mathbf F=-\nabla U, where U is potential energy. The minus sign is a convention: the force points downhill in potential energy. In this book, when we say a vector field has a potential \phi, we mean \mathbf F=\nabla\phi.

example.title: A potential in space

statement.p: Let \phi(x,y,z)=xz+y^2. Then d\phi=z\,dx+2y\,dy+x\,dz. So the vector field \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(z,2y,x) is conservative, with potential \phi.

If a particle moves from A=(1,2,0) to B=(3,1,4), then the work done by \mathbf F along any path for which the integral is defined is
\phi(B)-\phi(A) \amp= \bigl(3\cdot4+1^2\bigr)-\bigl(1\cdot0+2^2\bigr) \amp= 13-4 \amp= 9.
The path does not have to be known.

subsection.title: The fundamental theorem for line integrals
subsection.p: The last example is the line-integral version of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
In one variable, \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). For a curve, the derivative f'(x)\,dx becomes the differential d\phi. The interval endpoints a,b become the initial and final points of the curve.

statement.p: Let \phi be a C^1 function on a region D, and let C be a piecewise smooth oriented curve in D, starting at A and ending at B. Then \boxed{ \int_C d\phi=\phi(B)-\phi(A). } Equivalently, if \mathbf F=\nabla\phi, then \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(B)-\phi(A). }

proof.p:
First suppose C is smoothly parametrized by \mathbf r(t), \qquad a\le t\le b, with \mathbf r(a)=A,\qquad \mathbf r(b)=B. By the chain rule from , \frac{d}{dt}\phi(\mathbf r(t)) = d\phi_{\mathbf r(t)}(\mathbf r'(t)). In coordinates, this is \frac{d}{dt}\phi(\mathbf r(t)) = \nabla\phi(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t). Therefore
\int_C d\phi \amp= \int_a^b d\phi_{\mathbf r(t)}(\mathbf r'(t))\,dt \amp= \int_a^b \frac{d}{dt}\phi(\mathbf r(t))\,dt \amp= \phi(\mathbf r(b))-\phi(\mathbf r(a)) \amp= \phi(B)-\phi(A).
If C is piecewise smooth, apply this argument on each smooth piece. The endpoint values at the internal break points cancel.

subsection.p: The theorem has real hypotheses.

First, the form must actually be exact. The form \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy is not exact on the plane. Around the unit circle, \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, we get \eta=dt. Thus \oint_C \eta=2\pi. If \eta=d\phi on the whole plane, the fundamental theorem would force every closed curve integral to be 0. This one is not.

Second, the curve must stay inside the domain where the potential is defined. For example, d(\ln x)=\frac1x\,dx on the half-plane x\gt 0. The formula cannot be used on a curve that crosses the line x=0, because neither \ln x nor \frac1x\,dx is defined there. A potential is not only a formula. It is a formula on a domain.

statement.p: The text insists that a potential is a formula on a domain, not just a formula. For the angle form \alpha=(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2), the integral \oint_C \alpha=2\pi around the counterclockwise unit circle is nonzero even though \alpha looks locally like d\theta. This differs from the earlier form \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy. What goes wrong if we pretend \theta is a single potential defined on the whole punctured plane?

hint.p: Imagine walking once around the origin and asking what value \theta hands back to you when you return to your starting point. Does it agree with where you began?

subsection.title: Path independence
subsection.p: The factory-floor example showed two paths with the same endpoints and the same integral. Exact forms always behave that way.

statement.p: A line integral \int_C \omega is called path independent in a region D if its value depends only on the initial and final points of C, not on the particular path connecting them.
If \omega=d\phi for a C^1 function \phi on a region D, then \int_C \omega is path independent on D. In fact, for every piecewise smooth curve C from A to B, \boxed{ \int_C \omega=\phi(B)-\phi(A). }

subsection.p: There is also a converse. It is one of the best reasons to care about path independence.

exercise.title: What does the converse buy us?

statement.p: One direction is easy: an exact form is automatically path independent. The converse says path independence alone produces a potential \phi(X)=\int_A^X\omega. Why is the converse the more surprising and useful half? What does it let you conclude when you have not been handed a formula for \phi?

hint.p: Think about what you can check directly about a field versus what you would love to know. Which one is easier to observe, and which one does the converse promise to deliver from it?

statement.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy be a continuous 1-form on an open path-connected region D in the plane. Suppose the integral of \omega is path independent in D. Choose a base point A\in D, and define \boxed{ \phi(X)=\int_A^X \omega, } where the integral is taken along any piecewise smooth path in D from A to X. Then \boxed{ d\phi=\omega. } So \omega is exact.

proof.p: Such paths exist: cover a continuous path from A to X by open balls lying in D. Compactness of the parameter interval gives a finite subdivision whose successive path pieces lie in these balls. Replace each piece by its straight chord, which stays in the same ball. The resulting polygonal path is piecewise smooth.
Path independence makes \phi(X) well-defined. The value does not depend on the path chosen from A to X.

Let X=(x,y). To compute \phi_x(x,y), compare \phi(x+h,y) and \phi(x,y). Because of path independence, we may go from (x,y) to (x+h,y) along the horizontal segment. Openness of D keeps that segment in D for sufficiently small |h|. Along it, dy=0, so \omega=P\,dx. Therefore \phi(x+h,y)-\phi(x,y) = \int_x^{x+h}P(s,y)\,ds. Divide by h and let h\to0. Since P is continuous, \phi_x(x,y)=P(x,y). Similarly, moving along a small vertical segment gives \phi_y(x,y)=Q(x,y). Thus d\phi=P\,dx+Q\,dy=\omega.

subsection.p: The same idea works in space: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. If the integral is path independent, define \phi(X)=\int_A^X\omega. Small coordinate segments show \phi_x=P,\qquad \phi_y=Q,\qquad \phi_z=R.

subsection.title: Closed curves and zero work
subsection.p: A path-independent integral has no reason to accumulate anything around a closed loop. The beginning and the end are the same point.
If C is closed and \omega=d\phi, then \oint_C \omega=\phi(A)-\phi(A)=0.

theorem.title: Equivalent ways to recognize path independence

statement.p: Let \omega be a continuous 1-form on an open path-connected region D. Then the following statements are equivalent: \begin{array}{ll} 1. \amp \displaystyle \int_C\omega \text{ is path independent in }D.\\[2mm] 2. \amp \displaystyle \oint_C\omega=0 \text{ for every closed piecewise smooth curve }C \text{ in }D.\\[2mm] 3. \amp \omega \text{ is exact on }D. \end{array}

proof.p: If \omega=d\phi, then the fundamental theorem for line integrals gives path independence. So 3\Rightarrow1.
If the integral is path independent, then any closed curve starts and ends at the same point, so its integral must be 0. Thus 1\Rightarrow2.

Now suppose every closed curve integral is 0. Let C_1 and C_2 be two paths from A to B. Travel along C_1, then return from B to A along C_2 with the opposite orientation. This makes a closed curve. Therefore \int_{C_1}\omega-\int_{C_2}\omega=0. So \int_{C_1}\omega=\int_{C_2}\omega. The integral is path independent. Hence 2\Rightarrow1.
Finally, the previous theorem showed that path independence produces a potential. So 1\Rightarrow3.

subsection.p: This theorem explains the word conservative. A conservative field can transfer energy between forms, but it does not create net work around a closed loop. Go out, come back, and the potential returns to its starting value.

exercise.title: Why must the loop give zero?

statement.p: For a conservative field, \oint_C \omega=0 around every closed loop, no matter how large or twisted. Explain in your own words why this has to be true, using the idea of a potential rather than any computation. If a field gave nonzero work around some closed loop, what would that say about whether a potential can exist?

hint.p: A closed loop ends where it began, so A=B. Look at what the fundamental theorem reports for \phi(B)-\phi(A) in that case, and ask whether a single-valued \phi could ever produce a nonzero answer.

subsection.title: Exact forms as differentials df
subsection.p: In practice, finding a potential is often a matching game.
Suppose \omega=(2xy+3)\,dx+(x^2+2y)\,dy. We want to know whether \omega=d\phi for some \phi(x,y). If so, then \phi_x=2xy+3, and \phi_y=x^2+2y.

Start with the first equation: \phi_x=2xy+3. Integrate with respect to x, treating y as constant: \phi(x,y)=x^2y+3x+g(y). The extra term g(y) is allowed because it disappears when differentiating with respect to x.

Now use the second equation: \phi_y=x^2+g'(y). We need this to equal x^2+2y. So g'(y)=2y, and therefore g(y)=y^2+C. One potential is \boxed{ \phi(x,y)=x^2y+3x+y^2. } The constant C does not matter, because dC=0.

Now the line integral of \omega is immediate. From A=(0,1) to B=(2,3), any path gives
\int_C \omega \amp= \phi(2,3)-\phi(0,1) \amp= (4\cdot3+6+9)-(0+0+1) \amp= 27-1 \amp= 26.

example.title: Finding a potential in space

statement.p: Let \omega=yz\,dx+xz\,dy+xy\,dz. If \omega=d\phi, then \phi_x=yz. Integrating with respect to x, \phi=xyz+g(y,z). Now \phi_y=xz+g_y(y,z). Since the coefficient of dy is xz, we need g_y=0. So g depends only on z: g(y,z)=h(z). Finally, \phi_z=xy+h'(z). Since the coefficient of dz is xy, we need h'(z)=0. Thus one potential is \boxed{ \phi(x,y,z)=xyz. } So yz\,dx+xz\,dy+xy\,dz=d(xyz).

subsection.p: The matching method is useful, but it leaves a practical question. In the last two examples, we were lucky: the pieces fit. How can we tell, before searching for a potential, whether the pieces are even compatible? If P=\phi_x \qquad\text{and}\qquad Q=\phi_y, then P_y and Q_x are both trying to be the same mixed derivative \phi_{xy}. That small observation becomes the first curl test.

section.title: Curl tests in the plane and in space
section.p: showed the reward for finding a potential: line integrals become endpoint differences. But finding a potential by guessing is not a method. We need a test that can say, quickly, whether a field could be conservative.
The test begins with mixed partial derivatives.

subsection.title: The test P_y=Q_x in the plane
subsection.p: Suppose \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is exact. Then \omega=d\phi for some potential \phi. That means P=\phi_x, \qquad Q=\phi_y. Differentiate the first equation with respect to y: P_y=\phi_{xy}. Differentiate the second equation with respect to x: Q_x=\phi_{yx}. If the mixed partial derivatives are continuous, then \phi_{xy}=\phi_{yx}. So every smooth exact form must satisfy \boxed{P_y=Q_x.}

example.title: A form that passes the test

statement.p: Let \omega=(2xy+3)\,dx+(x^2+2y)\,dy. Here P(x,y)=2xy+3, \qquad Q(x,y)=x^2+2y. Then P_y=2x, \qquad Q_x=2x. The test passes. In , we found the potential \phi(x,y)=x^2y+3x+y^2.

example.title: A swirling form that fails the test

statement.p: Let \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy. Then P=-y, \qquad Q=x. So P_y=-1, \qquad Q_x=1. The test fails. Therefore \eta is not exact on the plane.
This agrees with what we already know: \oint_{\text{unit circle}} -y\,dx+x\,dy=2\pi\ne0.

subsection.p: The difference Q_x-P_y is called the scalar curl of the plane field \mathbf F=(P,Q). So the condition P_y=Q_x is the same as \boxed{Q_x-P_y=0.}

statement.p: A C^1 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is called closed if \boxed{Q_x-P_y=0.} Equivalently, P_y=Q_x.

subsection.p: Exact forms are closed, provided the coefficients are smooth enough. This is the first appearance of a pattern that will return later as d^2=0.

exercise.title: Which way does the arrow point?

statement.p: We just argued that every exact form satisfies P_y=Q_x. Suppose a friend computes P_y=Q_x for some form and announces, “Great, so it’s exact!” What is the logical gap in that announcement, and why does the implication we proved only run in one direction?

hint.p: Reread the theorem as “exact \Rightarrow closed.” Passing the test is a necessary condition. Ask yourself whether necessary and sufficient are the same thing here—and recall that the upcoming rectangle theorem needs an extra hypothesis before it can turn the arrow around.

theorem.title: Exact implies closed in the plane

statement.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy be a C^1 1-form on a region D. If \omega=d\phi for a C^2 potential \phi, then \boxed{P_y=Q_x} throughout D.

proof.p: Since \omega=d\phi, we have P=\phi_x, \qquad Q=\phi_y. Therefore P_y=\phi_{xy}, \qquad Q_x=\phi_{yx}. The mixed partial derivatives of a C^2 function are equal, so P_y=Q_x.

subsection.p: The smoothness condition is real. Without it, mixed partials can misbehave.

example.title: Why smoothness matters in the mixed-partial test

statement.p: Define \Phi(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{xy(x^2-y^2)}{x^2+y^2}, \amp (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm] 0, \amp (x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases} This function has first partial derivatives at the origin, and we may form d\Phi=\Phi_x\,dx+\Phi_y\,dy. So d\Phi is exact wherever these derivatives are defined.

But the mixed partials at the origin are not equal. First compute \Phi_x(0,y)=-y, so \Phi_{xy}(0,0)=\lim_{y\to0}\frac{\Phi_x(0,y)-\Phi_x(0,0)}{y}=\lim_{y\to0}\frac{-y}{y}=-1. Also, \Phi_y(x,0)=x, so \Phi_{yx}(0,0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\Phi_y(x,0)-\Phi_y(0,0)}{x}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x}{x}=1. Thus \Phi_{xy}(0,0)\ne \Phi_{yx}(0,0).
The problem is not exactness. The problem is lack of sufficient smoothness. The coefficient functions of d\Phi are not C^1 near the origin.

subsection.p: On a rectangle, the curl test is not only necessary. It is sufficient. Its proof uses the following differentiation rule for an integral with a parameter.

lemma.title: Differentiating an integral with a parameter

statement.p: Suppose q(x,t) and q_x(x,t) are continuous on a neighborhood of [a,b]\times[c,d]. For a\lt x\lt b, H(x)=\int_c^d q(x,t)\,dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H'(x)=\int_c^d q_x(x,t)\,dt. The same conclusion holds for any fixed subinterval of [c,d].

proof.p: Fix x. Continuity of q_x makes q_x(x+s,t)-q_x(x,t) uniformly small for all c\le t\le d when s is small. To justify the word uniformly, first use continuity near each (x,t_0) to bound both values by their difference from q_x(x,t_0). The closed interval [c,d] is covered by finitely many of these neighborhoods, so the smallest of their allowed positive bounds on |s| works for the entire interval. This is the usual finite-cover argument behind uniform continuity on a closed bounded interval.

The one-variable Mean Value Theorem, applied with t fixed, now gives \left|\frac{q(x+h,t)-q(x,t)}{h}-q_x(x,t)\right|\le\varepsilon for all t\in[c,d] and all sufficiently small nonzero h. Integrating this inequality yields \left|\frac{H(x+h)-H(x)}{h}-\int_c^d q_x(x,t)\,dt\right| \le(d-c)\varepsilon. Letting h\to0 proves the derivative formula. Thus the interchange is justified by the stated continuity hypotheses, not by a formal movement of symbols.

statement.p: Let R=[a,b]\times[c,d] be a rectangle, and let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy be a C^1 1-form on an open neighborhood of R. If \boxed{P_y=Q_x} throughout that neighborhood, then \omega is exact on R.

proof.p:
Choose the lower-left corner (a,c) as a base point, and define \phi(x,y)=\int_a^x P(s,c)\,ds+\int_c^y Q(x,t)\,dt. Then \phi_y(x,y)=Q(x,y). For the x-partial derivative, apply with y held fixed:
\phi_x(x,y) \amp= P(x,c)+\int_c^y Q_x(x,t)\,dt \amp= P(x,c)+\int_c^y P_y(x,t)\,dt \amp= P(x,c)+\bigl(P(x,y)-P(x,c)\bigr) \amp= P(x,y).
So d\phi=P\,dx+Q\,dy=\omega.

subsection.p: This proof also tells us why the condition works. The equality P_y=Q_x makes the two ways of building \phi compatible.

subsection.title: Curl zero in space
subsection.p: In space, a 1-form has three coefficients: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. If it is exact, then \omega=d\phi for some potential \phi, so P=\phi_x,\qquad Q=\phi_y,\qquad R=\phi_z. The mixed partial derivatives force three compatibility conditions: \boxed{P_y=Q_x,\qquad P_z=R_x,\qquad Q_z=R_y.}

statement.p: A C^1 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is called closed if \boxed{\nabla\times(P,Q,R)=\mathbf 0.} Equivalently, P_y=Q_x,\qquad P_z=R_x,\qquad Q_z=R_y.

example.title: A space field with zero curl

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(yz,xz,xy). Then P=yz,\qquad Q=xz,\qquad R=xy. Compute: R_y=x,\qquad Q_z=x, P_z=y,\qquad R_x=y, and Q_x=z,\qquad P_y=z. Therefore \nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0. In fact, \mathbf F=\nabla(xyz), because d(xyz)=yz\,dx+xz\,dy+xy\,dz.

example.title: A space field with nonzero curl

statement.p:
Let \mathbf G(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0). Then P=-y,\qquad Q=x,\qquad R=0. The curl is
\nabla\times\mathbf G \amp= \left(R_y-Q_z,\, P_z-R_x,\, Q_x-P_y\right) \amp= (0-0,\ 0-0,\ 1-(-1)) \amp= (0,0,2).
So \mathbf G is not conservative on all of space. Its arrows rotate around the z-axis, and the curl sees that rotation.

subsection.p: A useful sufficient condition for the reverse direction is a geometric condition on the domain.

subsection.title: Simply connected regions
subsection.p: A curl test is local. It looks at what happens in tiny neighborhoods. But a line integral can feel the shape of the whole domain.

A region D is called simply connected if it is path connected (any two points can be joined by a continuous path in D) and every closed curve in D can be shrunk continuously to a point while staying inside D.
For the regions in this book, this means: \boxed{\text{connected, with no holes that a closed curve can wrap around.}}
Examples of simply connected regions include:

table.title: Simply connected regions.

subsection.p: Examples that are not simply connected include:

table.title: Regions that are not simply connected.

row.cell: a disk with a smaller disk removed

subsection.p: The hole matters because a closed curve can wrap around it and refuse to shrink to a point.

exercise.title: What does the hole actually break?

statement.p: The curl test P_y=Q_x only looks inside tiny neighborhoods, yet the conclusion we want—“\omega is exact on all of D”—is a statement about the whole region. In your own words, why should the presence of a hole be able to spoil a global conclusion even when the local test passes at every single point?

hint.p: Think about a closed curve that wraps around the hole. Simple connectivity is exactly the permission to shrink such a curve to a point. If you cannot shrink it, what guarantee about line integrals over closed loops are you no longer entitled to?

theorem.title: Curl test on simply connected regions

statement.p: Let D be an open simply connected region.
In the plane, let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy be a C^1 1-form on D. If P_y=Q_x throughout D, then \omega is exact on D.
In space, let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a C^1 vector field on D. If \nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0 throughout D, then \mathbf F is conservative on D.

subsection.p: The rectangle case was proved above by constructing a potential directly. We state the full simply connected theorem here for use, with its proof postponed to . That proof constructs potentials on balls and then uses a subdivided continuous contraction to show that every closed curve has zero integral. Green's theorem and Stokes' theorem give related geometric interpretations; merely saying that a loop shrinks is not yet the proof in space.

Without the simply connected condition, the test can pass and still fail to produce a global potential. Simple connectivity is sufficient to guarantee a potential for every curl-free field on the domain; it is not necessary for a particular field. For example, (2x,2y)=\nabla(x^2+y^2) has a potential even on the punctured plane.

subsection.title: Local versus global potentials
subsection.p: Return to the form \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} on the punctured plane D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. Here P(x,y)=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q(x,y)=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. A calculation gives P_y=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, and Q_x=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. So P_y=Q_x everywhere in the punctured plane.
The local curl test passes.

But around the unit circle, \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, we have \alpha=dt. Therefore \boxed{\oint_C \alpha=2\pi.} If \alpha were exact on the whole punctured plane, every closed curve integral would be zero. So \alpha is not exact on D.

figure.caption: The form \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} has zero curl away from the origin, but its integral around a loop enclosing the origin is 2\pi.

subsection.p: So what is going on?

Locally, \alpha really is a differential. On the right half-plane x\gt 0, define \theta=\arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right). Then \theta_x=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad \theta_y=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. Therefore \boxed{d\theta=\alpha} on the right half-plane.
The same thing works on many other smaller patches. We can choose a continuous angle function on a patch that does not wrap all the way around the origin.

But there is no single continuous angle function on the whole punctured plane. After one full counterclockwise trip around the origin, the angle has increased by 2\pi. It has not returned to its original value as an ordinary single-valued function should.
This is the difference between local and global.

statement.p: On every small patch, \alpha equals d\theta for an honest potential, so the curl test passes everywhere and local potentials genuinely exist. What goes wrong when you try to stitch all these local angle functions into one continuous potential on the whole punctured plane, and how does this story show that zero curl alone does not guarantee a global potential on every domain?

hint.p: Follow \theta once around the origin and watch its value when you return to the start. A single-valued function must come back to where it began—does the angle? The missing point is what prevents the loop from shrinking, and that is precisely the failure of simple connectivity.

p.md: \boxed{\begin{aligned} \amp\text{Zero curl gives local potentials.}\\ \amp\text{A simply connected domain lets those local potentials glue into one global potential.}\\ \amp\text{A hole can prevent the gluing.} \end{aligned}}

subsection.p: The scalar curl Q_x-P_y is therefore a local measurement. It detects tiny rotation. It cannot, by itself, see a missing point that a large loop winds around. The next chapter supplies the missing global bookkeeping: Green's theorem will add the local curl over a region and compare it to circulation around the boundary. That is where the hidden hole finally has to show itself.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: gave a useful test: P_y=Q_x in the plane, or \nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0 in space. But it also gave a warning: this test is local. It checks tiny rotation near each point. It does not, by itself, know the shape of the whole domain.
This section collects the traps in one place. They are worth seeing slowly, because most mistakes with conservative fields come from forgetting one of them.

subsection.title: Curl zero but no global potential on a punctured plane
subsection.p: Consider the 1-form \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} on the punctured plane D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. The origin is missing, so the denominator is never zero on D.

Write \alpha=P\,dx+Q\,dy, where P(x,y)=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q(x,y)=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. Compute:
P_y \amp= \frac{-(x^2+y^2)+2y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} \amp= \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2},
and
Q_x \amp= \frac{(x^2+y^2)-2x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} \amp= \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.
Thus P_y=Q_x everywhere on D.
So the local curl test passes.

exercise.title: What did the test not check?

statement.p: The condition P_y=Q_x only looks at derivatives at each individual point. Why is it possible for this point-by-point test to pass everywhere on D and still leave room for a loop integral like \oint_C\alpha=2\pi to be nonzero? What feature of D is the local test simply unable to notice?

hint.p: A derivative only knows what happens in a tiny neighborhood of a point. Ask yourself whether any such neighborhood can ever “feel” the missing origin, and what a whole loop can sense that a single point cannot.

subsection.p: If \alpha were exact on all of D, then \alpha=d\phi for some potential \phi, and every closed-curve integral would be zero: \oint_C d\phi=0. But this closed-curve integral is 2\pi. So \alpha is not exact on the punctured plane.

figure.caption: The form \alpha has zero curl away from the origin, but a loop around the missing origin has integral 2\pi.

subsection.p: The moral is not that the curl test is wrong. The moral is that the curl test is local. A loop can detect a hole that no tiny derivative sees.

subsection.title: A path-dependent integral with the same endpoints
subsection.p: Path independence is a strong property. It says that every path from A to B gives the same integral. Here is a simple field where that fails.
Let \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy. Move from A=(0,0) to B=(1,1).
First take the straight path C_1:\quad \mathbf r(t)=(t,t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then x=t,\qquad y=t,\qquad dx=dt,\qquad dy=dt. So \eta=-t\,dt+t\,dt=0. Therefore \boxed{\int_{C_1}\eta=0.}
Now take the broken path C_2: first go east from (0,0) to (1,0), then go north from (1,0) to (1,1).
On the eastward segment, y=0,\qquad dy=0, so -y\,dx+x\,dy=0. On the northward segment, x=1,\qquad dx=0, so -y\,dx+x\,dy=dy. Thus \int_{C_2}\eta = \int_0^1 dy = 1. So \boxed{\int_{C_2}\eta=1.}
The endpoints are the same, but the integrals are different: \int_{C_1}\eta=0, \qquad \int_{C_2}\eta=1. So \eta is not exact, and its integral is not path independent.
The curl test sees the problem immediately: P=-y,\qquad Q=x, so Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2. This form carries rotation everywhere.

figure.caption: The same endpoints can give different work when the field is not conservative.

subsection.p: A conservative field has no memory of the route. This one does.

subsection.title: A vector field with a singularity hidden at the origin
subsection.p: The most dangerous mistake is to compute a curl on the points where a field is defined and then silently pretend the field is defined everywhere.
Return to \mathbf A(x,y)= \left( \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \frac{x}{x^2+y^2} \right). This is the vector field associated with \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}. It is not defined at the origin.

Around a circle of radius R\gt 0, \mathbf r(t)=(R\cos t,R\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, we have dx=-R\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=R\cos t\,dt. The numerator becomes
-y\,dx+x\,dy \amp= -(R\sin t)(-R\sin t\,dt)+(R\cos t)(R\cos t\,dt) \amp= R^2\,dt.
The denominator is x^2+y^2=R^2. So \alpha=dt, and therefore \boxed{\oint_{C_R}\alpha=2\pi} for every radius R\gt 0.
This is strange at first. The circle can be tiny: R=10^{-6}. The circulation is still 2\pi.

The reason is that the field gets stronger near the missing point. Its length is \|\mathbf A(x,y)\| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}. On a circle of radius R, the field has size 1/R. The circumference is 2\pi R. Their product stays roughly \frac1R\cdot 2\pi R=2\pi.
The origin is not a harmless missing point. It is where the circulation is hiding.

statement.p: We found \oint_{C_R}\alpha=2\pi for every radius R\gt 0, no matter how tiny. If we could only contract the loop down to a single point, the integral would have to vanish. Conceptually, why can't we ever finish shrinking the loop here, and what does that stubborn 2\pi reveal about the hole at the origin?

hint.p: Imagine pulling the loop tighter and tighter toward the center. Is the point you are trying to reach actually part of the domain? A loop that cannot be shrunk to a point inside D is exactly what detects something the formula alone hides.

subsection.p: So the statement \nabla\times\mathbf A=\mathbf 0 is true only on the punctured plane. It is not a statement about the whole disk containing the origin, because \mathbf A is not a vector field there. \boxed{\text{Before applying any theorem, check the domain of the field.}}

subsection.title: Why the domain matters as much as the formula
subsection.p: The same formula can behave differently on different domains.

statement.p: On the right half-plane D_+ the form \alpha is exact, with potential \theta=\arctan(y/x), yet on the punctured plane D the identical formula is closed but not exact. The local rule never changed. Conceptually, what is it about D_+ that lets a single-valued potential exist, and what does the hole in D do to that same potential?

hint.p: Think about whether you can loop all the way around the origin while staying inside D_+. Then picture following \theta continuously once around the origin in D and ask whether you arrive back at the same value you started with.

subsection.p: Again take \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}.

On the right half-plane D_+=\{(x,y):x\gt 0\}, define \theta(x,y)=\arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right). Then \theta_x= \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad \theta_y= \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. So \boxed{d\theta=\alpha} on D_+. On the right half-plane, the form is exact.
But on the punctured plane D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, the same formula is not exact, because \oint_{\text{unit circle}}\alpha=2\pi.
And on the whole plane \mathbb R^2, the same formula does not even define a 1-form, because it is undefined at (0,0).

table.title: The status of \alpha depends on its domain.

subsection.p: This is why we never say only \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. We say: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy \quad\text{on a domain }D.

The formula tells us the local measuring rule. The domain tells us which paths are allowed, which loops can shrink, and which singularities have been removed. A potential function is not just a formula. It is a formula that works continuously and single-valuedly on the whole domain.

These warnings look like exceptions, but they are really pointing toward a theorem. The form \alpha has no local curl away from the origin, yet a loop around the origin detects something global. To connect local curl with boundary circulation, we need a theorem that adds curl over a whole region. That theorem is Green's theorem.

introduction.p: Chapter began with arrows attached to points and ended with a warning: arrows are not enough. The domain matters, orientation matters, and a line integral can remember the path.
Here are the main tools in one place.

subsection.title: Skills: line integrals and potentials
subsection.p: There are two different kinds of line integrals in this chapter.

table.title: Two kinds of line integrals

subsection.p: For a parametrized curve \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)), \qquad a\le t\le b, the scalar line integral is \boxed{ \int_C f\,ds = \int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. } The speed \|\mathbf r'(t)\| turns parameter time into arc length.

For a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, the line integral is \boxed{ \int_C \omega = \int_a^b \left[ P(\mathbf r(t))x'(t) + Q(\mathbf r(t))y'(t) + R(\mathbf r(t))z'(t) \right]dt. } Here dx=x'(t)\,dt,\qquad dy=y'(t)\,dt,\qquad dz=z'(t)\,dt. No norm appears. Orientation survives.

table.title: Which tool answers which question

row.cell: What is the mass of a wire?
What work does a force field do?
Is the integral only an endpoint difference?
Is a plane form locally compatible with a potential?
Is a space field locally compatible with a potential?

subsection.p: The exact case is the easiest case, once we recognize it. If \omega=d\phi, then \boxed{ \int_C \omega=\phi(B)-\phi(A), } where A is the starting point and B is the ending point.
This is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in curve form.

subsubsection.title: A final worked review problem
subsubsection.p: Let \omega=(2xy+z)\,dx+(x^2+3z)\,dy+(x+3y)\,dz. Find \int_C \omega along any path from A=(0,0,1) to B=(2,1,3), if the integral is path independent.

First look for a potential \phi. If \omega=d\phi, then \phi_x=2xy+z. Integrate with respect to x: \phi=x^2y+xz+g(y,z). Now differentiate this with respect to y: \phi_y=x^2+g_y(y,z). We need \phi_y=x^2+3z, so g_y=3z. Thus g(y,z)=3yz+h(z). Now \phi=x^2y+xz+3yz+h(z). Differentiate with respect to z: \phi_z=x+3y+h'(z). We need \phi_z=x+3y. So h'(z)=0. One potential is \boxed{ \phi(x,y,z)=x^2y+xz+3yz. }

Therefore
\int_C \omega \amp = \phi(B)-\phi(A) \amp = \phi(2,1,3)-\phi(0,0,1) \amp = (2^2\cdot1+2\cdot3+3\cdot1\cdot3)-0 \amp = 4+6+9 \amp = 19.
So \boxed{ \int_C \omega=19. } No parametrization of C was needed.

subsubsection.title: The exterior derivative thread
subsubsection.p: This chapter also prepared the next step in the differential-forms story.
A function is a 0-form. Its exterior derivative is d\phi=\phi_x\,dx+\phi_y\,dy+\phi_z\,dz. This is the 1-form version of the gradient.
For a plane C^1 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy, we now define its exterior derivative in this case by \boxed{ d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. } The coefficient Q_x-P_y is the scalar curl.

So the plane curl test Q_x-P_y=0 can be written as d\omega=0. If \phi has continuous second partial derivatives, its exact form satisfies \omega=d\phi, and the definition gives d\omega=(\phi_{yx}-\phi_{xy})\,dx\wedge dy=0 by equality of mixed partials from . This proves the local, planar instance of the rule \boxed{ d^2=0. }

subsection.title: Project: work done in a nonconservative field
subsection.p: The field \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x) is the simplest rotational field. Its work form is \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy. It is not conservative, because Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2. So a particle can return to where it started and still have nonzero total work done by the field.
This project reveals a pattern that is too beautiful to be accidental.

subsubsection.title: A rectangle
subsubsection.p: Let R be the rectangle 0\le x\le a, \qquad 0\le y\le b. Orient its boundary counterclockwise. That means the rectangle stays on your left as you walk around it.
Compute \oint_{\partial R} -y\,dx+x\,dy.
There are four sides.
On the bottom side, y=0,\qquad dy=0, so -y\,dx+x\,dy=0.
On the right side, x=a,\qquad dx=0,\qquad 0\le y\le b, so -y\,dx+x\,dy=a\,dy. The contribution is \int_0^b a\,dy=ab.
On the top side, y=b,\qquad dy=0, and the path goes from x=a to x=0. The form becomes -b\,dx. The contribution is \int_a^0 -b\,dx=ab.
On the left side, x=0,\qquad dx=0, so -y\,dx+x\,dy=0.

figure.caption: The rotational field (-y,x) does positive work around a positively oriented rectangle.

subsubsection.p: The coefficient 2 is not a coincidence. It is the scalar curl: Q_x-P_y=2.

subsubsection.title: A circle
A polygon and the shoelace formula
subsubsection.p: Try the same integral around a polygon with vertices (x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2),\ldots,(x_n,y_n), listed counterclockwise, with (x_{n+1},y_{n+1})=(x_1,y_1). On the straight edge from (x_i,y_i) to (x_{i+1},y_{i+1}), a parametrization is x(t)=x_i+t(x_{i+1}-x_i), y(t)=y_i+t(y_{i+1}-y_i), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then dx=(x_{i+1}-x_i)\,dt, \qquad dy=(y_{i+1}-y_i)\,dt. Substitution gives -y\,dx+x\,dy = \bigl(x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i\bigr)\,dt. So the edge contribution is x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i. Adding all edges, \boxed{ \oint_{\partial P}-y\,dx+x\,dy = \sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i\bigr). } This suggests the shoelace area formula \boxed{ \operatorname{Area}(P) = \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i\bigr) } for a simple counterclockwise polygon. We will prove it from Green's theorem in . Once established, it gives \boxed{ \oint_{\partial P}-y\,dx+x\,dy = 2\,\operatorname{Area}(P). }
The rotational field has become an area-measuring device. By doing work only around the boundary, it finds the area inside.
That is the surprise Green's theorem will explain.

subsection.title: Hook: circulation becomes a two-dimensional integral
subsection.p: The rectangle, circle, and polygon computations all point to the same hidden rule: a boundary integral can equal an interior integral.

For \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy, we found d\eta=2\,dx\wedge dy. The boundary integral measured \oint_{\partial R}\eta, while the interior integral measured \iint_R d\eta = \iint_R 2\,dx\wedge dy. For the rectangle and circle we have proved directly that \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\eta = \iint_R d\eta. }

The next chapter shows that this is not a trick of one special field. For a large class of regions R and 1-forms \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy, Green's theorem says \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R} \omega = \iint_R d\omega = \iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. }
The curl that was only a test in this chapter becomes something we can add over an area. A curve around the boundary will know what happened throughout the region inside it.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

introduction.p: Green's theorem connects the line integrals of Chapter 13 with the double integrals of Chapter 10. Circulation around a boundary measures the accumulated scalar curl inside; outward flux measures accumulated divergence. We track the orientation of every boundary component and use a locally defined exterior derivative to express both statements in the same notation.

section.title: Circulation around a small rectangle
section.p: A line integral of a 1-form adds tiny measurements along a curve. When the curve is closed, the integral is called a circulation integral. It measures the net tendency of the field to push us around the loop.
The simplest loop is a small rectangle. On that rectangle we can see the whole theorem before naming it.

subsection.title: Local rotation from boundary motion
subsection.p: Suppose a flat fluid moves with velocity field \mathbf F(x,y)=(P(x,y),Q(x,y)). The associated work form is \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. If we walk counterclockwise around a tiny rectangle, a positive integral means the field helps that counterclockwise motion more than it resists it.
Start with a field whose calculation is exact: \omega=(3-y)\,dx+2x\,dy. Let R=[a,a+h]\times[b,b+k], where h>0 and k>0. Give \partial R the counterclockwise orientation.
There are four sides.

paragraphs.title: Bottom side
paragraphs.p:
Here y=b, dy=0, and x goes from a to a+h. So
\int_{\text{bottom}}\omega \amp= \int_a^{a+h}(3-b)\,dx \amp= (3-b)h.

paragraphs.title: Right side
paragraphs.p:
Here x=a+h, dx=0, and y goes from b to b+k. So
\int_{\text{right}}\omega \amp= \int_b^{b+k}2(a+h)\,dy \amp= 2(a+h)k.

paragraphs.title: Top side
paragraphs.p:
Here y=b+k, dy=0, and x goes backward from a+h to a. So
\int_{\text{top}}\omega \amp= \int_{a+h}^{a}(3-b-k)\,dx \amp= -(3-b-k)h.

paragraphs.title: Left side
paragraphs.p:
Here x=a, dx=0, and y goes backward from b+k to b. So
\int_{\text{left}}\omega \amp= \int_{b+k}^{b}2a\,dy \amp= -2ak.

subsection.p: The number 3 came from how the field changes across the rectangle. The constant parts canceled. Only two differences survived: \text{right side} - \text{left side} and \text{bottom side} - \text{top side}.
Those are the two ways a field can help counterclockwise motion: the upward push can be stronger on the right than on the left, and the rightward push can be weaker at the top than at the bottom.

statement.p: The constant parts of the field canceled, and only the differences between opposite sides survived. What is it about a constant push that makes it unable to drive any net circulation around the loop, no matter how strong it is?

hint.p: Picture walking the rectangle once around. A truly uniform push helps you on one side and hinders you equally on the side you traverse in the opposite direction.

figure.caption: Circulation around a small rectangle compares opposite sides.

subsection.title: The scalar curl in the plane
subsection.p: The rectangle calculation generalizes. On a small rectangle, the circulation of \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is controlled by two rates: Q_x,\qquad P_y.

The right side and left side involve Q\,dy. If Q increases as x increases, then the upward contribution on the right side is larger than the downward contribution on the left side. This contributes approximately Q_x\,hk.

The bottom and top involve P\,dx. The top is walked in the negative x-direction. If P increases as y increases, then the top contribution cancels too much of the bottom contribution. This contributes approximately -P_y\,hk.
This coefficient gets its own name.

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(P(x,y),Q(x,y)) be a vector field in the plane, and let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy be its associated 1-form. The scalar curl of \mathbf F, or of \omega, is \boxed{\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf F = Q_x-P_y.}

subsection.p: The word scalar matters. In three-dimensional space, curl will be a vector. In the plane, the rotation axis points out of the page, so only one signed number is needed: positive for counterclockwise tendency, negative for clockwise tendency.

exercise.title: Why one number in the plane?

statement.p: In space the curl will need three numbers, but in the plane a single signed number Q_x-P_y is enough. What feature of motion confined to a flat plane makes one number capture the entire rotational behavior at a point?

hint.p: Ask yourself where the axis of any in-plane spinning has to point, and how many independent directions remain for it once the motion is trapped in the page.

subsection.p: For the form in the first example, P=3-y,\qquad Q=2x. So Q_x-P_y=2-(-1)=3, which matches the exact rectangle computation.

In the language of forms, the same coefficient appears in \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.} Here dx\wedge dy measures signed area. So d\omega is the signed circulation per unit area. This is why kept pairing curl with the exterior derivative.

example.title: A shear field

statement.p: Let \omega=x\,dy. Then P=0,\qquad Q=x, so Q_x-P_y=1. Around any small positively oriented rectangle, the circulation is approximately its area.

For the rectangle [a,a+h]\times[b,b+k], the computation is exact. The bottom and top contribute nothing because dy=0. The right side contributes (a+h)k, and the left side, walked downward, contributes -ak. So \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}x\,dy=hk=\operatorname{Area}(R).} This simple form will become an area-measuring tool in Green's theorem.

subsection.title: Positive orientation of a plane region
subsection.p: The sign of circulation depends on the direction of travel. If we reverse a curve, then dx,\qquad dy reverse sign along the curve, and every 1-form integral changes sign.
For a rectangle, the counterclockwise direction is the positive one. For a general plane region, the same idea is stated without mentioning clockwise or counterclockwise:

statement.p: A boundary curve is positively oriented if, as you walk along it, the region stays on your left.

subsection.p: For a region without holes, positive orientation usually means counterclockwise. For a region with a hole, this rule has two effects:

table.title: Positive orientation of boundary components.

subsection.p: The clockwise direction on the inner boundary can feel surprising at first. But if you walk around a hole clockwise, the actual region, the material outside the hole, stays on your left.

figure.caption: Positive orientation means the region stays on the left. Inner boundaries are oriented clockwise.

subsection.p: Orientation is not a convention we can ignore. It is part of the theorem's sign.

subsection.title: From many small rectangles to one boundary curve
subsection.p: Now tile a region with many small rectangles. Around each small rectangle, \oint_{\partial R_i} \omega \approx (Q_x-P_y)\,\Delta A_i. Add these approximations over all rectangles: \sum_i \oint_{\partial R_i}\omega \approx \sum_i (Q_x-P_y)\,\Delta A_i.
The right side is becoming a double integral: \sum_i (Q_x-P_y)\,\Delta A_i \longrightarrow \iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dA.

The left side has a different kind of magic. Every interior edge is walked twice: once in one direction by one rectangle, and once in the opposite direction by the neighboring rectangle. Since line integrals reverse sign when orientation reverses, the two interior edge contributions cancel.

statement.p: When all the interior edges cancel and only the outer boundary survives, the messy inside of the region seems to vanish from the bookkeeping. What is this telling us about the relationship between the total circulation of the field and the field's behavior strictly along the outer edge?

hint.p: Notice that the inside still matters through the accumulated curl. The cancellation says two very different-looking sums are secretly measuring the same thing.

subsection.p: Only the outside boundary survives.

figure.caption: Adding circulation around small rectangles cancels all shared interior edges.

subsection.p: This cancellation is the beginning of Stokes' idea. A sum of many tiny boundary integrals becomes one large boundary integral. A sum of many tiny curls becomes an area integral.
The small-rectangle calculation has shown the mechanism. The next step is to state the theorem that says the limiting version is exact.

section.title: Green's theorem: circulation form
section.p: showed the engine: local circulation is measured by Q_x-P_y, and shared interior edges cancel when rectangles are added. Green's theorem says that this engine works for a whole region, not only for a grid of rectangles.
Before the theorem, here is one complete example where both sides can be computed by hand.

subsection.title: A triangle that already contains the theorem
subsection.p: Let T be the triangle with vertices (0,0),\qquad (2,0),\qquad (0,1), listed counterclockwise. Let \omega=(x-y)\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy. Then P=x-y, \qquad Q=x+2y, so Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2. The area of the triangle is \frac12(2)(1)=1. So the interior curl integral is \boxed{ \iint_T (Q_x-P_y)\,dA = \iint_T 2\,dA =2. }
Now compute the boundary integral directly.
On the edge from (0,0) to (2,0), we have y=0 and dy=0, so \int_0^2 x\,dx=2.

On the edge from (2,0) to (0,1), use x=2-2t, \qquad y=t, \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then dx=-2\,dt, \qquad dy=dt. Also x-y=2-3t, \qquad x+2y=2. So
\int_{\text{slanted edge}}\omega \amp= \int_0^1\bigl[(2-3t)(-2)+2\bigr]dt \amp= \int_0^1(-2+6t)\,dt \amp= 1.
On the edge from (0,1) down to (0,0), we have x=0, dx=0, and y goes from 1 to 0. Thus \int_1^0 2y\,dy=-1.
That is Green's theorem in one triangle.

subsection.title: Statement of the theorem
subsection.p: A region good enough for Green's theorem may have a curved boundary and may have holes, but its boundary should be made from finitely many smooth pieces. The field should be differentiable on the region and slightly around it, so no singularity is hidden on an edge or just inside the boundary.

statement.p: Let R be a bounded closed plane region whose boundary \partial R consists of finitely many disjoint piecewise smooth simple closed curves. Give \partial R the positive orientation, so the region stays on the left as the boundary is traversed.

Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy be a 1-form whose coefficient functions P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing R. Then \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R} P\,dx+Q\,dy = \iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dA. } Equivalently, \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\omega = \iint_R d\omega, \qquad d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. }

subsection.p: The first boxed formula is the classical vector-calculus version. The second boxed formula is the differential-forms version. They say the same thing, but the forms version shows the pattern that will later become Stokes' theorem.

statement.p: The boxed identity says a boundary integral \oint_{\partial R}\omega equals a double integral \iint_R(Q_x-P_y)\,dA over the whole inside. One number comes from walking the edge; the other adds up something at every interior point. What does it mean that these two very different-looking quantities are always equal?

hint.p: Think about the cancellation picture: each tiny piece of interior curl is really a tiny loop, and neighboring loops share edges. Where do those shared edges go?

subsection.p: The proof idea is the cancellation from . Prove the formula on rectangles. Cut a more complicated region into many small rectangles. The interior edge integrals cancel in pairs. The small rectangle sums become the double integral of Q_x-P_y. The remaining edge pieces approach the boundary integral around \partial R. proves the theorem for finite unions of simple regions and explains the approximation idea for the general statement. The general approximation argument there is explicitly a sketch.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses are doing work
subsection.p: Each condition in the theorem protects the formula from a specific mistake.

subsubsection.title: Orientation cannot be reversed silently
subsubsection.p: For the triangle example above, \oint_{\partial T}\omega=2 when \partial T is positively oriented. If the same triangle is walked clockwise, then the line integral becomes -2. The interior integral is still \iint_T 2\,dA=2. So Green's theorem would fail with the wrong sign. The boundary orientation is part of the statement, not a drawing choice.

subsubsection.title: A jump inside the region cannot be ignored
subsubsection.p: Let R=[-1,1]\times[0,1] and define \omega=Q(x,y)\,dy, \qquad Q(x,y)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x\le0,\\ 1, \amp x\gt 0. \end{cases} The form jumps along the vertical line x=0. It does not have continuous first partial derivatives on R.

Compute the boundary integral directly. On the bottom and top edges, dy=0. On the right edge, Q=1 and y goes from 0 to 1, giving \int_0^1 dy=1. On the left edge, Q=0. Therefore \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\omega=1. }

Away from the jump line, Q_x=0. If we illegally pretended the curl were zero everywhere, we would get \iint_R 0\,dA=0, which is not the boundary integral. The missing derivative along the jump line is where the contribution lives. The smoothness condition prevents this kind of hidden edge inside the region.

subsubsection.title: A singularity inside the region changes the answer
subsubsection.p: The form \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} is defined on the punctured plane, but not at the origin. On every point where it is defined, Q_x-P_y=0. Around the unit circle C, oriented counterclockwise, \oint_C \alpha=2\pi.

If someone tried to apply Green's theorem to the disk bounded by C, the right side would seem to be \iint_{\text{disk}}0\,dA=0, but the left side is 2\pi. The theorem did not fail. Its hypothesis failed: the form is not defined on an open region containing the disk. The origin is where the circulation is hiding.

statement.p: For \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} the scalar curl Q_x-P_y is zero at every point where \alpha is defined, yet the boundary integral around the circle is 2\pi, not 0. If the curl vanishes everywhere we can see, what is the boundary integral actually detecting?

hint.p: Green's theorem needs the form to be smooth on all of the inside, including the origin. Ask what the region of the disk includes that the region where \alpha lives does not.

subsection.title: Examples over simple regions
subsection.p: Green's theorem is often useful because the boundary integral is hard while the area integral is easy.

example.title: A messy boundary integral around a disk

statement.p: Let D be the unit disk x^2+y^2\le1, with positively oriented boundary. Compute \oint_{\partial D}(e^x-y^3)\,dx+(x^2+\sin y)\,dy.

Here P=e^x-y^3, \qquad Q=x^2+\sin y. So Q_x=2x, \qquad P_y=-3y^2. Therefore Q_x-P_y=2x+3y^2. Green's theorem gives
\oint_{\partial D}(e^x-y^3)\,dx+(x^2+\sin y)\,dy \amp= \iint_D(2x+3y^2)\,dA.
By symmetry, \iint_D 2x\,dA=0. Also,
\iint_D y^2\,dA \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^2\sin^2\theta\,r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \left(\int_0^1 r^3\,dr\right) \left(\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\right) \amp= \frac14\cdot\pi \amp= \frac\pi4.
Thus \boxed{ \oint_{\partial D}(e^x-y^3)\,dx+(x^2+\sin y)\,dy = \frac{3\pi}{4}. }
The boundary integral would be unpleasant to compute directly. The curl integral is short.

example.title: A rectangle where only the curl matters

statement.p:
Let R=[0,3]\times[0,2] and \omega=(xy+\cos x)\,dx+(x^2+y^5)\,dy. Then P_y=x, \qquad Q_x=2x. So Q_x-P_y=x. Green's theorem gives
\oint_{\partial R}\omega \amp= \int_0^3\int_0^2 x\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^3 2x\,dx \amp= 9.
The terms \cos x and y^5 look large in the original form, but their contribution to circulation around a closed boundary disappears because they do not affect Q_x-P_y.

subsection.title: Using Green's theorem to compute area
subsection.p: If we choose a 1-form whose scalar curl is 1, then Green's theorem turns a boundary integral into area.

Three common choices are \omega=x\,dy, \omega=-y\,dx, and \omega=\frac12(-y\,dx+x\,dy). Each has Q_x-P_y=1. Therefore, for a positively oriented simple closed curve C=\partial R, \boxed{ \operatorname{Area}(R) = \oint_C x\,dy = -\oint_C y\,dx = \frac12\oint_C(-y\,dx+x\,dy). }

example.title: The area of an ellipse from its boundary

statement.p: Let C be the ellipse x=a\cos t, \qquad y=b\sin t, \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, where a\gt 0 and b\gt 0. This parametrization is counterclockwise.

Use \operatorname{Area}(R)=\oint_C x\,dy. Since dy=b\cos t\,dt, we get
\operatorname{Area}(R) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}(a\cos t)(b\cos t)\,dt \amp= ab\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2t\,dt \amp= ab\pi.
So \boxed{ \operatorname{Area}(\text{ellipse})=\pi ab. } A boundary integral has found the area inside the curve.

subsection.title: Holes and multiple boundary components
subsection.p: For a region with holes, \partial R means all boundary components with positive orientation. Leaving out an inner boundary changes the problem.
Let A be the annulus 1\le x^2+y^2\le4. Use again \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}. This form is defined everywhere on the annulus, and Q_x-P_y=0 on the annulus.
The positively oriented boundary has two pieces:

table.title: The two boundary components of the annulus.

subsection.p: Around any counterclockwise circle centered at the origin, \int \alpha=2\pi. Therefore \int_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\alpha=2\pi, while the clockwise inner boundary gives \int_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}\alpha=-2\pi. So \boxed{ \oint_{\partial A}\alpha=2\pi-2\pi=0. } This agrees with Green's theorem: \boxed{ \iint_A 0\,dA=0. }
If we had used only the outer circle, we would have obtained 2\pi, but that would not be the boundary of the annulus. The inner boundary is not optional. It is exactly what records the hole.

statement.p: For the annulus the two boundary circles are traversed in opposite directions, and their circulations 2\pi and -2\pi cancel to give 0. Why does Green's theorem insist on including the inner circle at all, instead of just the outer one we might naturally draw?

hint.p: The double integral only sees the material that is actually part of the region. Picture standing inside the region with the wall always on your left: which way does that force you to walk around the hole?

subsection.p: Green's theorem has now turned circulation into an area integral. But a vector field near a closed curve can do another thing besides circulate around it. It can cross the curve outward or inward. That second measurement is flux, and it leads to another face of the same theorem: divergence in the plane.

section.title: Green's theorem: flux form
section.p: measured circulation. A field could push us around a closed curve, and Green's theorem turned that boundary circulation into the area integral of the scalar curl: \oint_{\partial R} P\,dx+Q\,dy = \iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dA.

But a field near a boundary can do something else. It can cross the boundary. Fluid can flow out of a pond. Heat can leave a plate. Air can escape through a closed fence. This measurement is called flux.

subsection.title: Outward normal in the plane
subsection.p: The number 2 will soon get a name. It is the divergence of \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,y).

figure.caption: For the radial field \mathbf F=(x,y), the arrows point outward through the circle.

subsection.p: For a general positively oriented boundary curve, the outward normal has a simple formula.
This formula is useful because it removes the square root hidden in ds. It also reveals that flux is another 1-form integral.

statement.p: Let C be an oriented curve with a chosen unit normal \mathbf n, and let \mathbf F=(M,N) be a vector field. The flux of \mathbf F across C is \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds. } If C=\partial R, the normal is usually chosen to be the outward normal.

subsection.p: For a closed curve, outward flux is positive when more field leaves the region than enters it. It is negative when more field enters than leaves.

subsection.title: Divergence in two dimensions
subsection.p: Now look at a small rectangle S=[a,a+h]\times[b,b+k]. Let \mathbf F=(M,N). The horizontal component M contributes to flux through the vertical sides. The vertical component N contributes to flux through the horizontal sides.

On the right side, the outward normal points right, so the contribution is roughly M(a+h,b)\,k. On the left side, the outward normal points left, so the contribution is roughly -M(a,b)\,k. Together the vertical sides contribute approximately \bigl(M(a+h,b)-M(a,b)\bigr)k \approx M_x(a,b)\,h\,k.

On the top side, the outward normal points up, so the contribution is roughly N(a,b+k)\,h. On the bottom side, the outward normal points down, so the contribution is roughly -N(a,b)\,h. Together the horizontal sides contribute approximately \bigl(N(a,b+k)-N(a,b)\bigr)h \approx N_y(a,b)\,k\,h.
Adding all four sides, \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds \approx (M_x+N_y)\,\Delta A. }
This coefficient is the local net outflow per unit area.

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(M(x,y),N(x,y)) be a vector field in the plane. The divergence of \mathbf F is \boxed{ \operatorname{div}\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf F = M_x+N_y. }

exercise.title: What does zero divergence really say?

statement.p: Suppose a field has \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=0 at a point. Does that mean nothing is happening there, or could the field still be doing something interesting near that point? Explain in your own words what the zero is actually measuring.

hint.p: Remember that \operatorname{div}\mathbf F records net outflow per unit area. Think about a tiny box: what must be true about what enters versus what leaves, and is that the same as the field being still?

subsection.p: For the radial source \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,y), we get \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=1+1=2, which matches the circle computation: \text{outward flux}=2\cdot\text{area}.

The divergence measures source strength. Positive divergence means local net outflow. Negative divergence means local net inflow. Zero divergence means that, to first order, what flows into a tiny region also flows out.

example.title: A field with circulation but no divergence

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x). Then \operatorname{div}\mathbf F = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(-y) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x) = 0. This field circulates around the origin, but it has no local source or sink.

subsection.title: Green's theorem in flux form
subsection.p: The small-rectangle calculation suggests the theorem. The flux through the boundary should equal the integral of divergence over the inside.

statement.p: Let R be a bounded closed plane region whose boundary \partial R consists of finitely many disjoint piecewise smooth simple closed curves. Give \partial R the positive orientation, and let \mathbf n be the outward unit normal.

Let \mathbf F=(M,N) be a vector field whose component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing R. Then \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds = \iint_R (M_x+N_y)\,dA. } Equivalently, \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R} M\,dy-N\,dx = \iint_R (M_x+N_y)\,dA. }

The flux form and the circulation form of Green's theorem look like two different results, yet the text obtains one from the other just by changing the 1-form being integrated. Why is it reasonable that a single theorem can describe both circulation and flux?

hint.p: Look at what both boundary integrals have in common. Each turns a measurement along \partial R into an integral of a derivative density over R. What is the object that is really being integrated around the boundary?

subsection.p: This is not a separate miracle from the circulation form of Green's theorem. It is the same theorem applied to the 1-form \omega=-N\,dx+M\,dy. For this form, P=-N, \qquad Q=M. So Q_x-P_y = M_x-(-N_y) = M_x+N_y. The circulation form says \oint_{\partial R} -N\,dx+M\,dy = \iint_R (M_x+N_y)\,dA, which is exactly the flux form.

example.title: A steady wind through a closed fence

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(5,2) be a constant wind field. Then \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=0+0=0. For any region R to which Green's theorem applies, \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=0. } This does not mean no wind crosses the fence. Wind enters one side and leaves another. The theorem says the total entering and total leaving cancel.

example.title: Flux through an ellipse without parametrizing the ellipse

statement.p: Let E be the elliptical region \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\le 1, where a,b\gt0. Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(x+\sin y,\;y+e^x). A direct flux integral around the ellipse would be unpleasant. Green's theorem makes it short.

Here M=x+\sin y, \qquad N=y+e^x. Therefore M_x=1, \qquad N_y=1. So \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=2. Hence
\oint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds \amp= \iint_E 2\,dA \amp= 2\,\operatorname{Area}(E) \amp= 2\pi ab.
Thus \boxed{ \oint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=2\pi ab. } The extra terms \sin y and e^x affect the boundary arrows, but they do not change the divergence in this example.

example.title: A sink

statement.p:
Let R=[0,2]\times[0,1] and \mathbf F(x,y)=(-2x,-3y). Then \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=-2-3=-5. Green's theorem gives
\oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds \amp= \iint_R (-5)\,dA \amp= -5\cdot 2 \amp= -10.
So \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=-10. } The negative sign says that, in total, more field enters the rectangle than leaves it.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses are doing work
subsection.p: The flux form has the same kind of hypotheses as the circulation form. They keep hidden sources and hidden boundaries from being smuggled into the region.

exercise.title: Where could a hidden source hide?

statement.p: The hypotheses ask \mathbf F to have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing R. If we quietly ignored a singularity or a jump inside R, why might the interior integral of \operatorname{div}\mathbf F come out too small compared to the true boundary flux?

hint.p: A place where the field is not smooth can act like an extra, unseen boundary. Ask yourself where flux could be entering or leaving that the integral over the smooth part of R never gets to count.

subsubsection.title: The outward normal cannot be replaced by the inward normal
subsubsection.p: For \mathbf F=(x,y) on the disk of radius a, \oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=2\pi a^2 with the outward normal. If we use the inward normal instead, the answer becomes -2\pi a^2. The interior integral \iint_R 2\,dA does not change. The theorem is about outward flux.

subsubsection.title: A jump inside the region can hide a source line
subsubsection.p: Let R=[-1,1]\times[0,1] and define \mathbf F(x,y)= \begin{cases} (0,0), \amp x\le0,\\ (1,0), \amp x\gt0. \end{cases} This field jumps across the line x=0. It is not C^1.

The boundary flux is easy. The right side has outward normal (1,0), so it contributes 1. The left side has field (0,0), and the top and bottom have normals perpendicular to the field. Therefore \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=1. }

Away from the jump line, M_x+N_y=0. If we illegally ignored the jump and integrated 0, we would get \iint_R 0\,dA=0. The missing contribution lives on the internal jump line. The smoothness hypothesis prevents an unseen boundary from appearing inside the region.

subsubsection.title: A singularity can hide a point source
subsubsection.p: Consider the radial field \mathbf F(x,y)=\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}(x,y). It is defined on the punctured plane, but not at the origin. Away from the origin, \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=0. On the unit circle, \mathbf F=(\cos t,\sin t)=\mathbf n, and ds=dt. So \boxed{ \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds=2\pi. } If we tried to apply Green's theorem to the whole unit disk, the right side would seem to be 0, while the boundary flux is 2\pi. The theorem did not fail. The field is not defined on an open region containing the disk. The origin is a hidden source.

If we instead use the annulus \varepsilon\le x^2+y^2\le1, then the field is defined on the region. The outer boundary contributes 2\pi, and the inner boundary, whose outward normal points into the hole, contributes -2\pi. The total flux is 0, exactly matching \iint_{\text{annulus}}0\,dA=0. The inner boundary is what records the missing point.

subsection.title: Source, sink, and net outflow interpretations
subsection.p: For a small region around a point, \operatorname{div}\mathbf F is the net outward flux per unit area.
If \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\gt0, the point behaves like a source. More field leaves a tiny box than enters it.
If \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\lt0, the point behaves like a sink. More field enters than leaves.
If \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=0, there is no first-order net creation or loss. The field may still move, shear, stretch, or rotate, but it is not locally adding or removing material.

Green's theorem now has two faces:
\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Boundary measurement} \amp \text{Interior density} \amp \text{Name}\\ \hline \displaystyle \oint_{\partial R} P\,dx+Q\,dy \amp \displaystyle Q_x-P_y \amp \text{circulation / curl}\\[3mm] \displaystyle \oint_{\partial R} M\,dy-N\,dx \amp \displaystyle M_x+N_y \amp \text{flux / divergence} \end{array}

The two formulas look different, but the boundary integrals are both 1-form integrals. The real unifying object is not the vector field. It is the form being integrated around the boundary. Once we focus on that form, Green's theorem becomes one sentence.

section.title: Green's theorem in differential-form language
section.p: The circulation form and the flux form of Green's theorem are two costumes for the same idea. In both cases, a 1-form is integrated around a boundary, and its exterior derivative is integrated over the region inside.

Here \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy denotes the plane 1-form from . For continuously differentiable coefficients, we define the plane operation d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. It produces a signed area form, called the exterior derivative of \omega. For the standard orientation of R, the notation \int_R h\,dx\wedge dy=\iint_R h\,dA integrates its coefficient; reversing the orientation changes the sign, as in . The boundary \partial R carries the corresponding positive orientation described in the preceding sections.
The notation is shorter: \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. But the meaning is the same story we have been building: boundary accumulation equals interior accumulation of a derivative.

subsection.title: A 1-form on the boundary
subsection.p: Recall from that a 1-form in the plane has the form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. It is built to be integrated along a curve. At each tiny step, it reads the x-change and y-change, weights them by P and Q, and adds.
For a vector field \mathbf F=(M,N), there are two natural 1-forms one might build.
The work or circulation form is \boxed{\omega_{\mathrm{work}}=M\,dx+N\,dy.} It measures motion along the curve: \int_C \omega_{\mathrm{work}}=\int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.

The flux form is \boxed{\omega_{\mathrm{flux}}=M\,dy-N\,dx.} When C=\partial R is positively oriented, it measures outward crossing: \int_{\partial R}\omega_{\mathrm{flux}}=\oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds.
So the same vector field can give two different boundary measurements. The difference is not in the field alone. It is in the 1-form we choose to integrate.

statement.p: The vector field (M,N) never changes, yet swapping M\,dx+N\,dy for M\,dy-N\,dx turns a circulation measurement into a flux measurement. In your own words, what is the 1-form actually deciding when you choose one over the other?

hint.p: Think about what each form reads at a single tiny step along the curve: a step's motion along the boundary versus its motion through the boundary.

table.title: Two 1-forms built from one vector field.

subsection.p: This is why forms are useful. They remember the actual integrand.

subsection.title: The exterior derivative in the plane
subsection.p: Take the form \omega=(x-y)\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy. This is the form from the triangle example in . There, P=x-y,\qquad Q=x+2y. The coefficient that appeared in Green's theorem was Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2. So the interior form was 2\,dx\wedge dy. That is the exterior derivative of \omega: \boxed{d\omega=2\,dx\wedge dy.}
Now write the general rule.

statement.p: Let \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy be a C^1 1-form in the plane. Its exterior derivative is the 2-form \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

subsection.p: The coefficient Q_x-P_y is the scalar curl of the form P\,dx+Q\,dy. The factor dx\wedge dy is the signed area form.

We can verify a useful way of writing this locally defined operation using only scalar differentials and the wedge algebra. Since dP=P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy, and dQ=Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy, we compute
dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy \amp= (P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy)\wedge dx+(Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy)\wedge dy \amp= P_y\,dy\wedge dx+Q_x\,dx\wedge dy \amp= -P_y\,dx\wedge dy+Q_x\,dx\wedge dy \amp= (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy=d\omega.
This checks the identity against our definition; it does not assume a general product rule for exterior derivatives, which will be developed later. The terms involving dx\wedge dx\qquad\text{and}\qquad dy\wedge dy vanish because a parallelogram with two identical directions has zero signed area.

example.title: The area-measuring form

statement.p: Let \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy. Then P=-y,\qquad Q=x. So d\eta=(1-(-1))\,dx\wedge dy=2\,dx\wedge dy. Green's theorem says \oint_{\partial R}\eta=\iint_R 2\,dx\wedge dy. Thus \oint_{\partial R}(-y\,dx+x\,dy)=2\,\operatorname{Area}(R) for a positively oriented simple boundary. This is exactly the pattern discovered before Green's theorem gave it a name.

subsection.title: Green's theorem as one formula
subsection.p: Now the circulation form of Green's theorem becomes a single statement.

statement.p: Let R be a bounded plane region whose boundary consists of finitely many piecewise smooth simple closed curves, with positive orientation.

subsection.p: The symbol \int_R d\omega means an integral of the 2-form d\omega over the oriented region R. For the standard counterclockwise orientation of the plane, dx\wedge dy agrees with positive area, so this is the same number as \iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dA.

figure.caption: Green's theorem says that a boundary integral of a 1-form equals an interior integral of its exterior derivative.

subsection.p: The two versions of Green's theorem now sit in one table.

table.title: The circulation and flux forms in one place.

subsection.p: The same vector field (M,N) can be used in either row. The form decides what kind of boundary measurement we are making.

example.title: Flux as a form calculation

statement.p:
Let \mathbf F=(M,N)=(x+\sin y,\;y+e^x). The flux form is \omega_{\mathrm{flux}}=M\,dy-N\,dx=(x+\sin y)\,dy-(y+e^x)\,dx. Written as P\,dx+Q\,dy, this has P=-(y+e^x),\qquad Q=x+\sin y. Therefore
d\omega_{\mathrm{flux}} \amp= (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy \amp= (1-(-1))\,dx\wedge dy \amp= 2\,dx\wedge dy.
So for any positively oriented region R, \oint_{\partial R}\omega_{\mathrm{flux}}=\iint_R 2\,dx\wedge dy=2\,\operatorname{Area}(R). This is the flux theorem again, because M_x+N_y=1+1=2.

subsection.title: The warnings are part of the formula
subsection.p: The compact formula \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega is easy to remember. It is also easy to misuse.
The form must be defined and smooth on a region containing R. The boundary must carry the correct orientation. All boundary components must be included.

The punctured-plane form \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} is the cleanest warning. On the punctured plane, d\alpha=0. But on the unit circle, \oint_C \alpha=2\pi. We cannot apply Green's theorem to the whole disk because \alpha is not defined at the origin.

exercise.title: How can d\alpha=0 yet the loop integral not vanish?

statement.p: For the punctured-plane form we have d\alpha=0 everywhere it is defined, but \oint_C\alpha=2\pi around the unit circle. If Green's theorem says the boundary integral equals \int_R d\omega, why does this not force the loop integral to be zero?

hint.p: The equation \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega only speaks about a region R on which the form is defined and smooth. Ask whether the disk bounded by the circle is such a region.

subsection.p: If the region is an annulus around the origin, then the theorem works. The positively oriented boundary has two pieces: the outer circle counterclockwise and the inner circle clockwise. The two integrals are 2\pi\qquad\text{and}\qquad -2\pi, so the total is 0. That agrees with \int_R d\alpha=\int_R 0=0. The short formula is trustworthy only when its hypotheses are present.

subsection.title: Why this is already Stokes' theorem in disguise
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus can be written in the same shape.

On an interval [a,b], a function f has differential df=f'(x)\,dx. The boundary of the interval is the endpoint b with positive sign and the endpoint a with negative sign. So \int_{\partial [a,b]} f=f(b)-f(a). The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says \boxed{\int_{\partial [a,b]} f=\int_{[a,b]} df.} Written out, f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx.
Green's theorem says the same kind of thing one dimension higher: \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega.}

table.title: One sentence, two dimensions.

subsection.p: This is the beginning of Stokes' idea. The boundary of a region carries one kind of integrand. The inside carries its exterior derivative. The integral over the boundary equals the integral over the inside.
Later, a surface in space will have a boundary curve, and a solid in space will have a boundary surface. The same sentence will survive both times. What changes is the kind of form being integrated.

exercise.title: What stays the same as the dimension climbs?

statement.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Green's theorem both fit the single shape \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega, just one dimension apart. What is the common idea that this one sentence is expressing, the part that does not change as we move from an interval to a region to a surface?

hint.p: Focus on the relationship between a boundary and the derivative d\omega living inside it, rather than on the particular formulas. What role does the boundary play in every version?

subsection.p: The formula is beautiful enough to make us suspicious: why should all the interior information collapse to the boundary? The answer is not magic. Cut the region into many small rectangles. Every shared interior edge is walked twice, in opposite directions, and disappears. The proof of Green's theorem is the art of making that cancellation honest.

section.title: Why Green's theorem is true
section.p: compressed Green's theorem into one line: \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. The formula is short, but it is not magic. It comes from two old facts working together.

table.title: Two old facts behind Green's theorem.

section.p: Both facts can already be seen on one rectangle.

subsection.title: A rectangle with only vertical motion
subsection.p: Start with the form \omega=(x^2+y)\,dy on the rectangle R=[0,2]\times[0,1]. Only the vertical sides matter, because dy=0 along horizontal sides.

On the right side, x=2,\qquad 0\le y\le1, so
