\int_{\text{right}}\omega \amp= \int_0^1(4+y)\,dy \amp= 4+\frac12.
On the left side, positive orientation walks downward: x=0,\qquad 1\ge y\ge0. Thus
\int_{\text{left}}\omega \amp= \int_1^0 y\,dy \amp= -\frac12.
Therefore \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}(x^2+y)\,dy=4.}

What happened? The boundary integral compared the value of Q on the right side with the value of Q on the left side: Q(2,y)-Q(0,y). The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus rewrites that difference as Q(2,y)-Q(0,y)=\int_0^2 Q_x(x,y)\,dx. Then integrating over y gives the double integral.

subsection.title: The proof for a rectangle
subsection.p: Now let R=[a,b]\times[c,d], and let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy where P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives.
The rectangle proof is just the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applied once in the x-direction and once in the y-direction. The signs come from orientation.

subsection.title: Two rectangles and one disappearing edge
subsection.p: A single rectangle explains where Q_x-P_y comes from. The next idea explains why only the outside boundary survives.

Put two rectangles side by side: R_1=[0,1]\times[0,1],\qquad R_2=[1,2]\times[0,1]. They share the vertical edge E=\{1\}\times[0,1]. For R_1, positive orientation walks up along E. For R_2, positive orientation walks down along the same edge.

Along E, x=1,\qquad dx=0. So the contribution from R_1 is \int_0^1 Q(1,y)\,dy. The contribution from R_2 is \int_1^0 Q(1,y)\,dy. They add to zero. \boxed{\int_E Q\,dy+\int_{-E}Q\,dy=0.} The same cancellation happens for any shared edge. One rectangle walks the edge in one direction; the neighboring rectangle walks it in the opposite direction. A line integral changes sign when orientation reverses, so the two contributions cancel.

exercise.title: Why does the shared edge vanish?

statement.p: The two rectangles compute the same integrand Q(1,y) along the same edge E, yet the contributions add to zero. Without doing any new computation, explain what feature of the boundary, other than the integrand, is responsible for the cancellation.

hint.p: Ask what is different about how R_1 and R_2 each walk along E, and recall how a line integral responds to that difference.

figure.caption: Interior edges are walked twice in opposite directions.

subsection.p: Therefore \boxed{\oint_{\partial R_1}\omega+\oint_{\partial R_2}\omega = \oint_{\partial(R_1\cup R_2)}\omega.} The left side contains the shared edge twice. The right side contains only the outside boundary.

subsection.title: Regions made from many rectangles
subsection.p: Now tile a region S by finitely many nonoverlapping rectangles R_1,R_2,\ldots,R_N. Assume two rectangles meet only along whole edges or at corners. Green's theorem is true on each rectangle: \int_{\partial R_i}\omega=\int_{R_i}d\omega. Add all N formulas: \sum_{i=1}^N\int_{\partial R_i}\omega = \sum_{i=1}^N\int_{R_i}d\omega. On the right, \sum_{i=1}^N\int_{R_i}d\omega = \int_S d\omega. On the left, every shared interior edge cancels with its neighbor. Only the outside boundary remains: \sum_{i=1}^N\int_{\partial R_i}\omega = \int_{\partial S}\omega. Thus \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.} This is already Green's theorem for any region built from finitely many rectangles.

figure.caption: For a finite union of rectangles, all interior edges cancel in pairs.

subsection.p: This cancellation is the two-dimensional version of a familiar one-dimensional fact. When we add \int_{x_0}^{x_1}f'(x)\,dx + \int_{x_1}^{x_2}f'(x)\,dx + \cdots + \int_{x_{n-1}}^{x_n}f'(x)\,dx, the intermediate endpoint values cancel: f(x_1)-f(x_0)+f(x_2)-f(x_1)+\cdots+f(x_n)-f(x_{n-1}) = f(x_n)-f(x_0). Green's theorem does the same thing one dimension higher. Interior edges are the new intermediate endpoints.

exercise.title: What plays the role of the endpoints?

statement.p: In the one-dimensional sum, the intermediate values f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_{n-1}) cancel and only f(x_n)-f(x_0) survives. In the tiled region, what is the two-dimensional analogue of those vanishing intermediate values, and what survives in their place?

hint.p: Each interior edge belongs to exactly two rectangles, while each piece of the outer boundary belongs to only one. Let that asymmetry guide you.

subsection.title: Curved boundaries by slicing
subsection.p: Rectangles explain the theorem's engine. Curved boundaries require one more idea: slice the region into pieces where the one-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus can still see the edge differences.

Let R=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ g(x)\le y\le h(x)\}, where g and h are continuously differentiable and g(x)\le h(x). This is a vertically simple region. The coefficient functions are C^1 on an open neighborhood of its closure.

A vertically simple region need not also be horizontally simple. To finish its proof without that extra condition, set H(x)=\int_{g(x)}^{h(x)}Q(x,y)\,dy. Split H(x+s)-H(x) into the change over the fixed interval [g(x),h(x)] and the two short intervals created by the moving endpoints. The fixed-interval term is handled by ; the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the chain rule handle the endpoints. Thus H'(x)=\int_{g(x)}^{h(x)}Q_x(x,y)\,dy +Q(x,h(x))h'(x)-Q(x,g(x))g'(x). Directly parametrizing the four boundary pieces gives \oint_{\partial R}Q\,dy =H(b)-H(a)+\int_a^b \bigl(Q(x,g(x))g'(x)-Q(x,h(x))h'(x)\bigr)\,dx. Substitute H(b)-H(a)=\int_a^b H'(x)\,dx. The endpoint terms cancel, leaving \oint_{\partial R}Q\,dy=\iint_R Q_x\,dA. Together with the earlier P\,dx calculation, this proves the full formula for a vertically simple region. Interchanging the coordinates proves it for a horizontally simple region. Piecewise continuously differentiable boundary functions are handled by subdividing at their finitely many breakpoints.

Adding finitely many such pieces cancels their internal boundaries. This proves Green's theorem for regions admitting this decomposition, including the disks, ellipses, polygons, and annuli used in this chapter. At an endpoint where a graph representation of a circle or ellipse has an unbounded derivative, truncate just before that endpoint and pass to the limit: the removed boundary arc has length tending to zero, so its integral is bounded by that length times a bound for the field, and the removed area also tends to zero.

The theorem was stated for general piecewise smooth boundaries. The finite-piece proof above does not establish that every such boundary has the required decomposition; a smooth arc can oscillate infinitely often. The following approximation discussion explains the general theorem but is a proof sketch. We use the full standard theorem as stated, and do not claim that the sketch supplies all its approximation estimates.

subsection.title: Curved boundaries by approximation
subsection.p: There is another way to picture the last step. Overlay a fine grid on a curved region R. Keep the grid squares that lie inside. The result is a staircase region R_h made from finitely many rectangles. For R_h, \int_{\partial R_h}\omega=\int_{R_h}d\omega is already proved.
As the grid becomes finer, two things happen.

First, the area integral over R_h approaches the area integral over R: \int_{R_h}d\omega\longrightarrow \int_R d\omega. Continuity of Q_x-P_y keeps the values from jumping unpredictably in the thin strip near the boundary.

Second, the staircase boundary approaches the curved boundary. On a smooth arc, a tiny stair step has almost the same first-order effect as the tiny curve segment it replaces. Adding those small differences along the boundary makes the boundary integral approach \int_{\partial R}\omega.

figure.caption: A curved region can be approximated by regions made from rectangles.

subsection.p: This approximation picture is not a full proof by itself. It tells us where the hypotheses enter.

exercise.title: Where could the cancellation hide trouble?

statement.p: The cancellation of interior edges seems automatic, so why must we still insist that the boundary include every component of the region? Describe, conceptually, what could go wrong with the argument if a hole in the region were left without a boundary curve.

hint.p: A hole's edge is also an interior edge of the surrounding tiles. Think about whether that edge finds a partner to cancel with, or whether it should have remained as part of \partial S.

subsection.p: The boundary must be piecewise smooth so the staircase boundary really approaches a curve with well-defined line integrals. The partial derivatives must be continuous so the interior integral behaves predictably as the boundary strip shrinks. The boundary must include every component so cancellation does not leave a hidden edge behind.

Those words are carrying real work. If we reverse orientation, hide a singularity, forget a hole, or ask the theorem to handle a boundary too wild for our definition of line integral, the formula can give the wrong sign, the wrong number, or no number at all. The proof has shown us exactly where to look for the trouble.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The proof in was built from rectangles, cancellation, and limiting curved boundaries. Each hypothesis in Green's theorem protects one of those steps. The warnings below are not exceptions to the theorem. They are examples where the theorem's words have been changed.

subsection.title: Reversing orientation changes the sign
subsection.p: Take the unit square R=[0,1]\times[0,1], and the form \omega=x\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy, so \int_R d\omega=\operatorname{Area}(R)=1.

Now compute the boundary integral with positive orientation. The bottom and top edges have dy=0. The left edge has x=0. Only the right edge contributes. There, x=1, \qquad 0\le y\le1. So \oint_{\partial R}x\,dy = \int_0^1 1\,dy = 1. This matches Green's theorem.

If we walk the same boundary clockwise, the right edge is walked downward: 1\ge y\ge0. The integral becomes \int_1^0 1\,dy=-1. The interior integral is still \int_R dx\wedge dy=1. So the clockwise boundary gives the wrong sign: \boxed{\int_{-\partial R}\omega=-\int_{\partial R}\omega.}
The theorem did not fail. Its orientation condition was ignored. Positive orientation means the region stays on the left.

subsection.title: A singularity inside the region cannot be hidden
subsection.p: Now return to the angle form \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}. It is defined on the punctured plane \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, but not at the origin.

Where it is defined, write P(x,y)=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q(x,y)=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. A direct calculation gives Q_x=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} and P_y=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. Thus Q_x-P_y=0 away from the origin, so d\alpha=0 on the punctured plane.
If we tried to apply Green's theorem to the disk bounded by C, we would be tempted to write \oint_C\alpha = \iint_{\text{disk}}0\,dA = 0. But the boundary integral is 2\pi.

exercise.title: Where does the disk argument break?

statement.p: We found d\alpha=0 at every point where \alpha is defined, yet \oint_C\alpha=2\pi rather than 0. Which exact hypothesis of Green's theorem fails for the disk bounded by C, and why is it not enough that d\alpha=0 at every point except the origin?

hint.p: Read the theorem's domain requirement literally: it asks for the form to be defined and smooth on all of the region, not just on most of it. Where does \alpha live, and what single point sits inside the disk?

subsection.p: The missing hypothesis is not small. Green's theorem requires the form to be defined with continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing the whole disk. The origin is inside the disk, and \alpha is not defined there. The circulation is hiding at that missing point.

figure.caption: A singularity inside the region can carry circulation even when d\alpha=0 away from it.

subsection.title: A hole must be included in the boundary
subsection.p: A hole is not only missing area. It is also an extra boundary curve.

statement.p: Suppose you only adjusted for the missing area of the hole but kept integrating over the outer circle alone. Why would Green's theorem still disagree with you? In terms of the cancellation idea from the proof, what does the inner curve do that no other piece of the boundary can undo?

hint.p: Picture slicing the annulus into rectangles. Interior edges pair up and cancel, but the edge hugging the hole has no neighbor on the other side. What happens to a boundary piece that never finds a partner?

subsection.p: Let A be the annulus 1\le x^2+y^2\le4. Use the area-measuring boundary 1-form \omega=x\,dy. Since d\omega=dx\wedge dy, Green's theorem predicts \oint_{\partial A}x\,dy = \operatorname{Area}(A) = 4\pi-\pi = 3\pi.
The boundary of A has two pieces:

table.title: The two boundary components of the annulus.

subsection.p:
For the outer circle, x=2\cos t, \qquad y=2\sin t, \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dy=2\cos t\,dt, so
\int_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}x\,dy \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}(2\cos t)(2\cos t)\,dt \amp= 4\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2t\,dt \amp= 4\pi.

For the inner boundary, positive orientation is clockwise. Use x=\cos t, \qquad y=-\sin t, \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dy=-\cos t\,dt, and
\int_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}x\,dy \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}(\cos t)(-\cos t)\,dt \amp= -\pi.
If we used only the outer circle, we would get 4\pi, the area of the filled disk of radius 2, not the area of the annulus. The inner boundary subtracts the missing disk.

figure.caption: The boundary of an annulus has two components. The inner one is oriented clockwise.

subsection.p: This is the same cancellation idea from the proof. A hole creates a boundary that does not cancel with a neighboring piece. It must be counted.

subsection.title: A jump inside the region is a hidden edge
subsection.p: Green's theorem also requires P and Q to have continuous first partial derivatives. A jump inside the region behaves like a boundary we forgot to draw.
Let R=[-1,1]\times[0,1], and define \omega=Q(x,y)\,dy, \qquad Q(x,y)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x\le0,\\ 1, \amp x\gt0. \end{cases} The form jumps across the vertical line x=0. It is not C^1.

exercise.title: What does the jump act like?

statement.p: The coefficient Q has Q_x=0 everywhere it is differentiable, so the naive interior integral is 0, yet the boundary integral is 1. Which hypothesis of Green's theorem does the jump violate, and why does the section describe the line x=0 as a hidden edge rather than an ordinary interior point?

hint.p: The theorem assumes P and Q are C^1 on the whole region. Ask yourself what the missing contribution would look like if you redrew the region's boundary to run along the jump line.

subsection.p: Away from the jump line, Q_x=0. If we illegally pretended that d\omega=0 everywhere, then the interior integral would be \iint_R 0\,dA=0. That is not the boundary integral.
The missing contribution lives on the internal jump line. Smoothness prevents a hidden edge from appearing inside the region.

subsection.title: A boundary can be too rough for the theorem as stated
subsection.p: The boundary condition also matters. Green's theorem in this chapter is stated for boundaries made from finitely many piecewise smooth simple closed curves. That condition guarantees that \int_{\partial R}\omega is a finite sum of ordinary line integrals.

Consider a square pond from which infinitely many tiny circular islands have been removed. Let the outer square be S=[0,1]\times[0,1], and remove disjoint disks D_1,D_2,D_3,\ldots lying inside the square. Suppose their areas add to a finite number: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Area}(D_n)\lt 1. The remaining region is R=S\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}D_n.

For the form \omega=x\,dy, we have d\omega=dx\wedge dy. For a finite number of removed disks, Green's theorem says \oint_{\partial R_N}x\,dy = 1-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\operatorname{Area}(D_n), because the outer square contributes 1, and each clockwise inner circle subtracts the area of its disk.

If there are infinitely many islands, the expected answer would be 1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Area}(D_n). But now the boundary is not a finite collection of curves. It has infinitely many components: \partial S,\quad \partial D_1,\quad \partial D_2,\quad \partial D_3,\ldots The boundary integral is no longer a finite sum of line integrals. It needs an infinite series of boundary contributions, and convergence has to be checked.

So the elementary theorem stops before this example. The formula may still be true under extra assumptions, but it is no longer covered by the statement we proved. The word finitely is protecting us from an infinite boundary sum hidden in the notation \int_{\partial R}.

An even rougher boundary, such as a snowflake-shaped curve with infinite length and no ordinary tangent at most points, creates a different problem: the line integral along the boundary may not be defined by the piecewise smooth parametrizations introduced in . Again, Green's theorem has not failed. Its hypotheses have not been met.

subsection.title: What the warnings have in common
subsection.p: Each warning points back to the proof.

table.title: Each warning traced back to the step it breaks.

row.cell: the surviving boundary has the wrong sign
the form is not defined on the region
an uncanceled boundary component is missing
there is a hidden internal edge
the boundary integral is not a finite smooth sum

subsection.p: The proof was not only a justification. It was a diagnostic tool. It tells us what to check before trusting the formula.

Green's theorem is a theorem about flat regions. But its real message is larger: boundary measurements can equal interior measurements of a derivative. The next time that pattern appears, the inside will not be a plane region. It will be a surface in space. Then even the word boundary will need care, because a surface has two sides, and choosing one side will decide the sign of everything that crosses it.

introduction.p: Green's theorem began with a small rectangle. Opposite sides compared the field in two directions, and the surviving coefficient was Q_x-P_y. After adding many rectangles, every interior edge canceled. What remained was the boundary of the whole region.
That cancellation is the heart of the chapter: \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega.} The rest is learning to choose the right 1-form \omega, the right orientation, and the right region.

subsection.title: One theorem, several questions
subsection.p: A boundary curve can answer different questions. The same curve and the same vector field can ask for circulation, flux, or area. Green's theorem helps only after we know which question we are asking.
subsection.md: \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Question} \amp \text{Boundary form} \amp \text{Interior form} \\ \hline \text{circulation of } \mathbf F=(M,N) \amp M\,dx+N\,dy \amp (N_x-M_y)\,dx\wedge dy \\[2mm] \text{outward flux of } \mathbf F=(M,N) \amp M\,dy-N\,dx \amp (M_x+N_y)\,dx\wedge dy \\[2mm] \text{area of }R \amp x\,dy \amp dx\wedge dy \\[2mm] \text{area of }R \amp -y\,dx \amp dx\wedge dy \\[2mm] \text{area of }R \amp \dfrac12(-y\,dx+x\,dy) \amp dx\wedge dy \end{array}
subsection.p: The same theorem sits behind every row: \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. The form \omega decides what the boundary is measuring.

example.title: The same field, two different boundary questions

statement.p: Let R=[0,2]\times[0,1], with positive orientation, and let \mathbf F(x,y)=(M,N)=(xy,\;x^2-y).
The same field and the same rectangle gave two different answers because circulation and flux are different boundary measurements.

subsection.title: A checklist before using Green's theorem
subsection.p: Before applying \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega, pause long enough to check four things.

For a region without holes, positive orientation means counterclockwise. For a region with holes, the outer boundary is counterclockwise and each inner boundary is clockwise. That one rule says the same thing everywhere: \text{as you walk, the region stays on your left.}

subsection.title: Area from a boundary curve
subsection.p: Green's theorem can turn a boundary walk into an area calculation. Since d\left(\frac12(-y\,dx+x\,dy)\right)=dx\wedge dy, a positively oriented simple closed curve C=\partial R satisfies \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(R)=\frac12\oint_C(-y\,dx+x\,dy).}
This formula becomes especially useful when the boundary is known but the region is awkward.

example.title: The shoelace formula from Green's theorem

statement.p: A surveyor records the vertices of a small lot, in counterclockwise order: (0,0),\qquad (4,1),\qquad (5,4),\qquad (2,5),\qquad (-1,3). The boundary is made of straight line segments.

On one segment from (x_i,y_i)\quad\text{to}\quad(x_{i+1},y_{i+1}), write x(t)=x_i+t(x_{i+1}-x_i),\qquad y(t)=y_i+t(y_{i+1}-y_i),\qquad 0\le t\le1. Then dx=(x_{i+1}-x_i)\,dt,\qquad dy=(y_{i+1}-y_i)\,dt. So
\int_{\text{edge}}(-y\,dx+x\,dy) \amp= \int_0^1\Bigl[-(y_i+t\Delta y)\Delta x+(x_i+t\Delta x)\Delta y\Bigr]dt \amp= x_i\Delta y-y_i\Delta x \amp= x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i.
Adding all edges gives \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(R)=\frac12\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i)\right|,} where the last point is followed by the first: (x_{n+1},y_{n+1})=(x_1,y_1). This is the shoelace formula.

For the lot above,
\sum (x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i) \amp= (0\cdot1-4\cdot0) \amp\quad +(4\cdot4-5\cdot1) \amp\quad +(5\cdot5-2\cdot4) \amp\quad +(2\cdot3-(-1)\cdot5) \amp\quad +((-1)\cdot0-0\cdot3) \amp= 0+11+17+11+0 \amp= 39.
Therefore \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(R)=\frac{39}{2}.} A formula often taught as a polygon trick is really Green's theorem in disguise.

subsection.title: A polar area formula from the same boundary form
subsection.p: The same area-measuring boundary 1-form also explains the familiar polar area formula.

example.title: A rounded triangular lake

statement.p:
A drone traces the boundary of a lake whose polar equation is r(\theta)=3+\cos(3\theta),\qquad 0\le \theta\le2\pi. Since r(\theta)\gt 0 for all \theta, the curve does not pass through the origin. The area enclosed is
A \amp= \frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(3+\cos3\theta)^2\,d\theta \amp= \frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\left(9+6\cos3\theta+\cos^2 3\theta\right)d\theta.
Now \int_0^{2\pi}\cos3\theta\,d\theta=0 and \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 3\theta\,d\theta=\pi. Therefore
A \amp= \frac12(18\pi+\pi) \amp= \frac{19\pi}{2}.
So \boxed{A=\frac{19\pi}{2}.}

figure.caption: A polar boundary can give area without describing the region by inequalities.

exercises.title: Project: area from a measured boundary curve

introduction.p: A curve can be known from measurements instead of from a clean formula. This project uses Green's theorem to estimate area from boundary data.

Suppose a drone flies once counterclockwise around a pond and records points (x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2),\ldots,(x_n,y_n) at equally spaced times. Connect consecutive points by straight segments, and connect the last point back to the first.

statement.p: Use \operatorname{Area}=\frac12\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i y_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i)\right| to estimate the pond's area.
Explain why the estimate improves as the drone records more points, assuming the boundary is smooth.

Repeat the computation using \operatorname{Area}=\oint_C x\,dy. For a straight segment from (x_i,y_i) to (x_{i+1},y_{i+1}), show that \int_{\text{edge}}x\,dy=\frac{x_i+x_{i+1}}{2}(y_{i+1}-y_i). Then show that the result agrees with the shoelace formula.
Try the method on a boundary given parametrically by x(t)=3\cos t+\cos 2t,\qquad y(t)=2\sin t,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Use \operatorname{Area}=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\bigl(x(t)y'(t)-y(t)x'(t)\bigr)\,dt.

conclusion.p: The point is not the formula alone. The point is that area can be recovered from a walk around the edge.

statement.p: Let C be the positively oriented boundary of the rectangle [0,3]\times[0,2]. Compute \oint_C (x^2-y)\,dx+(xy+y^3)\,dy using Green's theorem.
Let C be the positively oriented unit circle. Compute \oint_C (e^x-y)\,dx+(x+\cos y)\,dy.
Let R be the triangle with vertices (0,0),\qquad (3,0),\qquad (0,2). For \mathbf F=(x+y,\;2x-y), compute the outward flux across \partial R.
Let A be the annulus 1\le x^2+y^2\le9. Compute \oint_{\partial A}x\,dy. Remember the orientation of the inner boundary.
Let \omega=(y^2+x)\,dx+(x^2-y)\,dy. Find d\omega. Then compute \int_{\partial R}\omega for R=[0,1]\times[0,2].
Let \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}. Explain why Green's theorem cannot be applied to \alpha on the unit disk. Then explain why it can be applied on the annulus \frac14\le x^2+y^2\le1.
A simple closed curve C is oriented clockwise. If \frac12\oint_C(-y\,dx+x\,dy)=-8, what is the area enclosed by C?
Find a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy such that d\omega=5\,dx\wedge dy. Use it to write an area-like boundary formula for 5\operatorname{Area}(R).

subsection.title: What Green's theorem cannot yet do
subsection.p: Green's theorem lives in the plane. Its region R is flat, and its boundary \partial R is a curve. The positive orientation rule is simple: walk so the region stays on your left.

But many boundaries in space are not edges of flat regions. A wire loop may bound a soap film. The film may bend. The same wire may bound many different surfaces. A dome has a top side and a bottom side. A sphere has an outside and an inside.

On a flat region, orientation could be described by left and right. On a surface in space, orientation becomes a choice of normal direction. Once that choice is made, the boundary direction has to match it.

That is the next problem. To carry Green's theorem into space, we need to understand surfaces, their area, their two possible sides, and how a boundary curve knows which side has been chosen. The surprising part is that the same short formula will survive: \int_{\partial(\text{something})}\omega=\int_{\text{something}}d\omega. The something will no longer be only a flat region. It will be a surface.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

introduction.p: We now combine the derivative and integration tools of Chapters 514. Parameter grids from Chapter 4 become regular surface patches, then surface area and oriented flux. Curl, divergence, and their integral theorems follow with their hypotheses stated.

section.title: Parametric surfaces and tangent planes
section.p: A curve needed one parameter: \mathbf r(t). A surface needs two. One parameter moves along one family of curves on the surface; the other moves along a crossing family. Together they form a coordinate grid on the surface. In , ordinary derivatives of these grid curves first gave us tangent velocities, regular parameter points, and normals. We now express the same construction with partial derivatives and justify the local tangent-plane approximation.

subsection.title: Two parameters make a surface
subsection.p: Think of a rectangular sheet of rubber. Before it is bent, a point on the sheet can be labeled by two numbers: (u,v). After the sheet is bent into space, the point has three coordinates: (x,y,z). So a bent sheet is naturally described by a function \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)).
The input (u,v) lives in a flat parameter region. The output \mathbf r(u,v) lives in space.

statement.p: A surface lives in three-dimensional space, yet we describe it using only two parameters (u,v). Why two and not three? What does this say about how a surface sits inside space?

hint.p: Think about how many directions you can actually walk while staying on the rubber sheet, before it is bent or after.

subsection.p: For example, a cylinder of radius 2 can be described by \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,\,2\sin\theta,\,z), where 0\le \theta\le 2\pi, \qquad 0\le z\le 5. The parameter \theta moves around the cylinder. The parameter z moves upward.

If \theta=\pi/3 and z=4, then \mathbf r\left(\frac{\pi}{3},4\right) = \left(1,\sqrt3,4\right). So the flat rectangle 0\le \theta\le 2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le5 has been wrapped into the side of a cylinder.

figure.caption: A parametrization turns a flat two-parameter domain into a surface. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

statement.p: A parametric surface in space is a function \mathbf r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3 of the form \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)). The set \{\mathbf r(u,v):(u,v)\in D\} is the image of the parametrization.

subsection.p: The parameters do not have to be called u and v. On a cylinder, it is more natural to use \theta and z. On a sphere, it is more natural to use two angles.

subsection.title: Coordinate curves on a surface
subsection.p: A parametrized surface comes with two families of curves.

For the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), hold z fixed and let \theta vary. We get a horizontal circle: \theta\longmapsto (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z_0). Hold \theta fixed and let z vary. We get a vertical line: z\longmapsto (2\cos\theta_0,2\sin\theta_0,z).
These two curve families form the grid on the surface.

example.title: Tangent directions on a cylinder

statement.p: For the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), differentiate with respect to \theta: \mathbf r_\theta(\theta,z)=(-2\sin\theta,2\cos\theta,0). This points around the cylinder.
Differentiate with respect to z: \mathbf r_z(\theta,z)=(0,0,1). This points straight upward.

At \theta=\frac{\pi}{3},\qquad z=2, the point on the cylinder is \mathbf r\left(\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) = (1,\sqrt3,2). The two tangent directions are \mathbf r_\theta\left(\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) = (-\sqrt3,1,0) and \mathbf r_z\left(\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) = (0,0,1). One direction goes around the pipe. The other goes up the pipe.

Let \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)). Assume its first partial derivatives exist. The two coordinate tangent vectors are \boxed{ \mathbf r_u=(x_u,y_u,z_u), \qquad \mathbf r_v=(x_v,y_v,z_v). } They are tangent to the coordinate curves obtained by holding one parameter fixed.

subsection.p: Independent coordinate tangent vectors describe two local directions of a sheet. Dependent vectors signal a defect in this parametrization; they do not by themselves prove that the geometric surface has a singularity.

subsection.title: Normal direction from the cross product
subsection.p: Two nonparallel tangent vectors determine a plane. A normal vector to that plane is given by their cross product: \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v.

For the cylinder, \mathbf r_\theta=(-2\sin\theta,2\cos\theta,0), \qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1). So
\mathbf r_\theta\times \mathbf r_z \amp= (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,0).
This vector points radially outward. At \theta=\pi/3, \mathbf r_\theta\times \mathbf r_z=(1,\sqrt3,0). That is exactly the outward normal direction at the point (1,\sqrt3,z).

figure.caption: The two parameter directions on a cylinder give two tangent directions \mathbf r_\theta (around) and \mathbf r_z (up); their cross product \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z is the outward normal. Arrows show directions and are scaled for visibility. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: A cylinder with two coordinate tangent directions and their outward cross product at one point.

subsection.p: The order matters. If we reverse the order, \mathbf r_z\times \mathbf r_\theta = -(\mathbf r_\theta\times \mathbf r_z), so the normal points inward instead of outward. This sign will become part of orientation and flux later.

statement.p: Swapping \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v for \mathbf r_v\times \mathbf r_u flips the normal to the other side of the surface. Geometrically, the surface itself has not changed at all. So what extra piece of information are we choosing when we pick an order for the cross product?

hint.p: The surface is the same either way, but you select which normal direction counts as positive. An arbitrary patch need not have an inside or an outside.

statement.p: A parametrization \mathbf r(u,v) is called smooth if its first partial derivatives are continuous.

It is called regular at (u,v) if \boxed{ \mathbf r_u(u,v)\times \mathbf r_v(u,v)\ne \mathbf 0. } At an interior parameter point, a smooth regular map describes a smooth sheet after restricting to a sufficiently small neighborhood. To justify the local-sheet claim, a nonzero component of the cross product is a nonzero 2\times2 minor of the derivative. Project onto those two output coordinates. The inverse function theorem from gives local inverse coordinates, in which the third output coordinate is a C^1 graph. Distinct parameter neighborhoods may still meet in the image; the tangent plane belongs to the selected local sheet.

exercise.title: What do the two tangents build?

statement.p: Holding v fixed and varying u gives one grid curve; holding u fixed and varying v gives another. Why does this produce two tangent vectors \mathbf r_u and \mathbf r_v at a point, and at a regular point, what geometric object does their cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v describe?

hint.p: Each parameter direction traces its own curve through the point, and each curve has its own tangent. Recall that a cross product is perpendicular to both factors. If \mathbf r_u and \mathbf r_v both lie in its tangent plane, where must \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v point?

subsection.p: The regularity condition says that the two parameter directions really make a little surface patch, not just a curve or a point.

subsection.title: Tangent planes to parametrized surfaces
subsection.p: At an interior point of a smooth regular patch, the tangent plane is spanned by \mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). If \mathbf p=\mathbf r(u_0,v_0), then a parametric equation for the tangent plane is \boxed{ \mathbf X=\mathbf p+s\,\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)+t\,\mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). } A normal vector is \mathbf n=\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)\times \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0), so the same plane can be written as \boxed{ \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf X-\mathbf p)=0. }

theorem.title: Tangent plane to a parametrized surface

statement.p: Let \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3 be smooth on a neighborhood of an interior point (u_0,v_0) and regular there. Set \mathbf p=\mathbf r(u_0,v_0). Then the tangent plane to this local sheet at \mathbf p is \boxed{ \mathbf X=\mathbf p+s\,\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)+t\,\mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). } Equivalently, if \mathbf n=\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)\times \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0), then \boxed{ \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf X-\mathbf p)=0. }

proof.p: The curve u\longmapsto \mathbf r(u,v_0) lies on the surface, and its velocity at u=u_0 is \mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0). So \mathbf r_u is tangent to the surface.
Similarly, the curve v\longmapsto \mathbf r(u_0,v) lies on the surface, and its velocity at v=v_0 is \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). So \mathbf r_v is also tangent.

By the local linear approximation in , \mathbf r(u_0+h,v_0+k)=\mathbf p+h\mathbf r_u+k\mathbf r_v+\mathbf E(h,k), \qquad \frac{\|\mathbf E(h,k)\|}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}\longrightarrow0. Thus this plane approximates all nearby parameter displacements to first order, not just the two coordinate curves. Regularity makes it a plane rather than a line; the cross product is normal to it.

example.title: A tangent plane to a cylinder

statement.p: For the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), take \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}, \qquad z=4. Then \mathbf p=(1,\sqrt3,4). The tangent vectors are \mathbf r_\theta=(-\sqrt3,1,0), \qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1). A normal vector is \mathbf n=\mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z=(1,\sqrt3,0). Therefore the tangent plane is (1,\sqrt3,0)\cdot\bigl((x,y,z)-(1,\sqrt3,4)\bigr)=0. That is x-1+\sqrt3(y-\sqrt3)=0, or \boxed{ x+\sqrt3\,y=4. } The tangent plane is vertical, as it should be for the side of a cylinder.

subsection.title: Graphs as parametrized surfaces
subsection.p: This agrees with the tangent-plane formula from . If \mathbf p=(a,b,g(a,b)), then z-g(a,b)=g_x(a,b)(x-a)+g_y(a,b)(y-b).

example.title: A tangent plane to a curved shade cloth

statement.p: A shade cloth over a courtyard has height g(x,y)=4+\frac{x}{3}-\frac{y}{4}-\frac{x^2}{12}. At the point (x,y)=(1,2), the height is g(1,2) = 4+\frac13-\frac12-\frac1{12} = \frac{15}{4}. The partial derivatives are g_x(x,y)=\frac13-\frac{x}{6}, \qquad g_y(x,y)=-\frac14. At (1,2), g_x(1,2)=\frac16, \qquad g_y(1,2)=-\frac14. So the tangent plane is \boxed{ z-\frac{15}{4} = \frac16(x-1)-\frac14(y-2). } In parametric-surface language, this is the same plane spanned by \mathbf r_x=\left(1,0,\frac16\right), \qquad \mathbf r_y=\left(0,1,-\frac14\right).

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: We asked for smoothness and regularity because tangent planes can fail in two different ways.

First, a surface can have a crease. Consider z=|x|. A natural parametrization is \mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,|x|). Along the line x=0, the surface folds like a roof ridge. Approaching from x>0, the surface has slope +1 in the x-direction. Approaching from x<0, it has slope -1. There is no single tangent plane along the crease.
The partial derivative with respect to x does not exist there. Smoothness was not a decoration; it prevented a hidden fold.

example.title: Why regularity matters: the tip of a cone

statement.p: The upper cone z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} has the parametrization \mathbf r(s,\theta) = (s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,s), \qquad s\ge0,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. For s\gt0, the parameters describe points away from the tip.

At the tip, s=0, all angles give the same point: \mathbf r(0,\theta)=(0,0,0). The tangent directions are \mathbf r_s=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,1), and \mathbf r_\theta=(-s\sin\theta,s\cos\theta,0). At s=0, \mathbf r_\theta=(0,0,0). So \mathbf r_s\times\mathbf r_\theta=\mathbf 0. The parametrization is not regular at the tip.

Geometrically, this matches what we see. The cone has a sharp point. The three straight generators with directions (1,0,1), (-1,0,1), and (0,1,1) all reach the tip. Their determinant is -2, so they do not lie in one plane. Thus no single tangent plane can contain all three directions.

subsection.p: Failure of regularity alone does not settle the geometry. The spherical coordinates of collapse at a pole, but near the north pole the same sphere has the regular graph patch \mathbf q(u,v)=(u,v,\sqrt{9-u^2-v^2}),\qquad u^2+v^2\lt9. At (0,0) its coordinate tangent vectors are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0). The sphere therefore has a tangent plane there. The cone's three independent generator directions, rather than merely a zero cross product, rule out a plane at its tip.

exercise.title: A coordinate defect or a sharp tip?

statement.p: Both the cone coordinates and the spherical coordinates have a zero cross product at a collapsed edge. Why does this fact alone not decide whether the image has a tangent plane? What additional argument distinguishes the cone?

hint.p: Use the regular graph patch for the sphere and the three independent generator directions for the cone.

subsection.p: So a smooth regular patch is the surface version of a smooth curve with nonzero velocity. It has a well-defined tangent plane and a normal direction.

But a normal direction is not yet an area. The vector \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v does two jobs at once: it points perpendicular to the surface, and its length measures how much a tiny parameter rectangle has been stretched. That length is the next piece of the story.

section.title: Surface area and scalar surface integrals
section.p: gave us the two tangent vectors \mathbf r_u,\qquad \mathbf r_v. Their cross product points normal to the surface. Its length has another meaning: it measures the area scale from parameter space. For a small parameter rectangle, its sides scale to \Delta u\,\mathbf r_u and \Delta v\,\mathbf r_v.
That is how surface area becomes a double integral.

subsection.title: A small parameter rectangle becomes a small parallelogram
subsection.p: Let \mathbf r(u,v) be a smooth surface patch. Take a tiny rectangle in the (u,v)-plane with side lengths \Delta u,\qquad \Delta v. Near a point (u_0,v_0), the two sides of its image are approximately \mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)\,\Delta u and \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0)\,\Delta v. So the tiny surface patch is approximately a parallelogram.

The area of a parallelogram spanned by vectors \mathbf a and \mathbf b is \|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\|. Therefore the tiny surface area is approximately \boxed{\Delta S\approx\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v.} In differential notation, \boxed{dS=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv.}

exercise.title: Why a length, not a vector?

statement.p: The cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v is a vector with a direction, yet the area element dS keeps only its length \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|. What goes wrong if you tried to call the whole vector the area? What is the length alone telling you about the little patch of surface?

hint.p: Think about what a number like area should and should not depend on. Where does the direction of \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v point, and is that the same kind of information as how big is the parallelogram?

figure.caption: The area scale factor is \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

subsection.title: Surface area from a parametrization
subsection.p: Assume the patch is regular on the interior and covers the surface once, apart from boundary curves, with continuous derivatives on the parameter closure. If we add all the tiny surface pieces, we get surface area: \sum \Delta S\approx\sum \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. Taking the limit gives the formula \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(S)=\iint_D \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv.}

example.title: The side area of a cylinder

statement.p:
The side of a cylinder of radius 2 and height 5 is parametrized by \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le5. We already computed \mathbf r_\theta=(-2\sin\theta,2\cos\theta,0),\qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1). Thus \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,0), and \|\mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z\|=2. So
\operatorname{Area}(S) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^5 2\,dz\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}10\,d\theta \amp= 20\pi.
This matches the familiar formula \text{circumference}\times\text{height}=(4\pi)(5)=20\pi.

subsection.p: The formula did not need us to remember the cylinder area formula. It found the same answer by measuring the stretching of the parameter rectangle.

subsection.title: Scalar surface integrals
subsection.p: Surface area adds 1\,dS over the surface. If a quantity varies across the surface, we multiply by its value before adding.
Suppose a thin shell has surface density \sigma(x,y,z) in kilograms per square meter. A small surface patch has mass approximately \sigma(x,y,z)\,\Delta S. Adding gives M=\iint_S \sigma\,dS.

statement.p: Let S be parametrized by a smooth regular map \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3 that covers the surface once, except possibly along boundary curves. For a scalar function f on S for which the integral below exists (in particular, a continuous function on a compact patch), the scalar surface integral of f over S is \boxed{\iint_S f\,dS=\iint_D f(\mathbf r(u,v))\,\|\mathbf r_u(u,v)\times\mathbf r_v(u,v)\|\,du\,dv.} When f=1, this gives the surface area of S.

example.title: Mass of a cylindrical shell

subsection.p: A scalar surface integral does not care which side of the surface is chosen. It uses positive area. That is why \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\| appears, not the vector \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v itself.

statement.p: To find the mass of a thin shell we compute \iint_S \sigma\,dS rather than just multiplying a single density value by the total area. Why does a varying density \sigma(x,y,z) force us to multiply inside the integral, patch by patch, instead of multiplying once at the end?

hint.p: Imagine the shell is heavy near the top and light near the bottom. Would one single number for density honestly describe every patch? Picture what each tiny \sigma\,\Delta S contributes before the sum.

subsection.title: Surface area of graphs
subsection.p: For a graph z=g(x,y), use the parametrization \mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,g(x,y)). Then \mathbf r_x=(1,0,g_x),\qquad \mathbf r_y=(0,1,g_y). Their cross product is \mathbf r_x\times \mathbf r_y=(-g_x,-g_y,1), so \|\mathbf r_x\times \mathbf r_y\|=\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}. Thus \boxed{dS=\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}\,dx\,dy.} For a graph over a region R in the xy-plane, \boxed{\operatorname{Area}(S)=\iint_R \sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}\,dA.}

example.title: Area of a slanted roof

statement.p:
A flat roof over the rectangle 0\le x\le6,\qquad 0\le y\le4 has height z=2+\frac{x}{3}-\frac{y}{4}. Here g_x=\frac13,\qquad g_y=-\frac14. So \sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}=\sqrt{1+\frac19+\frac1{16}}=\sqrt{\frac{169}{144}}=\frac{13}{12}. Therefore the roof area is
\operatorname{Area} \amp= \int_0^6\int_0^4 \frac{13}{12}\,dy\,dx \amp= \frac{13}{12}\cdot24 \amp= 26.
The flat floor area is 24. The roof area is larger because the roof is tilted.

subsection.p: The formula \sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2} is the local stretching factor from the floor to the graph. When the graph is nearly flat, this factor is close to 1. When the graph is steep, the surface uses more area over the same floor region.

subsection.title: Surface area in cylindrical and spherical coordinates
subsection.p: Many surfaces are easiest to describe with cylindrical or spherical coordinates.

subsubsection.title: A horizontal disk
subsubsection.p: A horizontal disk of radius a at height z=c can be parametrized by \mathbf r(s,\theta)=(s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,c), where 0\le s\le a,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Then \mathbf r_s=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0), and \mathbf r_\theta=(-s\sin\theta,s\cos\theta,0). So \|\mathbf r_s\times\mathbf r_\theta\|=s. Thus \boxed{dS=s\,ds\,d\theta.} This is the same area element used for polar coordinates in the plane.

subsubsection.title: The side of a cylinder
subsubsection.p: A cylinder of radius a has parametrization \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,z). Then \|\mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z\|=a, so \boxed{dS=a\,d\theta\,dz.}

subsubsection.title: A sphere
subsubsection.p: A sphere of radius a can be parametrized by \mathbf r(\phi,\theta)=(a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\,a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\,a\cos\phi), where 0\le \phi\le\pi,\qquad 0\le \theta\le2\pi. Here \phi is the angle down from the positive z-axis.

Compute: \mathbf r_\phi=(a\cos\phi\cos\theta,\,a\cos\phi\sin\theta,\,-a\sin\phi), and \mathbf r_\theta=(-a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\,a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\,0). A direct cross product gives \|\mathbf r_\phi\times\mathbf r_\theta\|=a^2\sin\phi. Therefore \boxed{dS=a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta.}

The area of the sphere is then
\operatorname{Area} \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\left[-a^2\cos\phi\right]_0^\pi d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}2a^2\,d\theta \amp= 4\pi a^2.

At the poles, where \phi=0 or \phi=\pi, the factor \sin\phi is 0. The longitude lines all meet there, so the parametrization collapses in the \theta-direction. This is not a problem for the area integral because the collapse happens only along the boundary of the parameter rectangle. It would be a problem if we tried to use this particular spherical-coordinate map as a regular patch with the pole as an interior point. A different graph patch is regular there; see the pole comparison.

subsection.title: When parametrizations count too much
subsection.p: The surface integral formula counts what the parametrization covers.

For the cylinder, if we used 0\le\theta\le4\pi instead of 0\le\theta\le2\pi, then the parametrization would wrap around the same cylinder twice. The formula would give 40\pi instead of 20\pi. The calculation is not broken. It has computed the area with multiplicity.

This is why the definition said that the parametrization should cover the surface once, except possibly along boundary curves. When the same physical sheet is covered twice by the parameter region, the integral counts it twice.

exercise.title: Whose fault is the extra area?

statement.p: Letting \theta run from 0 to 4\pi gave 40\pi for a cylinder whose true area is 20\pi. The physical cylinder never changed. So what did the integral actually measure, and what does this tell you about the difference between a surface and a way of sweeping it out?

hint.p: The formula faithfully adds up area for every (u,v) in the parameter region. Ask not is the answer wrong? but how many times did my map pass over each point of the cylinder?

subsection.title: Scalar area versus oriented area
subsection.p: The scalar surface integral uses dS=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv. The norm removes the sign. If we swap the order of the parameters, then \mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u=-\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v, but \|\mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u\|=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|. So surface area and mass do not depend on which side of the surface we call positive.
That will change for flux.

If water flows through a net, it matters whether we count flow through the net upward as positive or downward as positive. The scalar area element dS cannot remember that choice. The full vector \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v can.

The same cross product that measured area has been quietly carrying orientation all along. Once we decide which side of a surface is positive, a surface integral can count flow through the surface with a sign. That signed quantity is called flux.

introduction.p: measured surface area with dS=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv. That formula deliberately forgot the sign of \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. For mass and area, forgetting the sign was right. But for flow through a surface, the sign is the point.

A screen has two sides. Water can pass through it one way or the other. Air can move from outside to inside or from inside to outside. The same surface area is involved, but the sign changes when we change which side we call positive.

subsection.title: A surface has two normal directions
subsection.p: Start with the simplest possible screen: S=\{(x,y,1):0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le3\}. This is a horizontal rectangle at height z=1. Suppose air moves upward with constant velocity \mathbf F=(0,0,5). The surface has area 2\cdot3=6. If we choose the upward normal \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,1), then the air passes through the positive side of the screen at a rate \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=5. So the total flow through the screen is 5\cdot6=30.
If instead we choose the downward normal \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,-1), then \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=-5, and the total flow is -30.
The physical motion did not change. Only our choice of positive side changed.

figure.caption: Flux is signed. Reversing the chosen normal reverses the sign.

statement.p: An orientation of a smooth surface is a continuous choice of unit normal vector \widehat{\mathbf n} at each point of the surface.
A surface with such a continuous choice is called orientable.

subsection.p: A continuous normal chooses a consistent side. For a smooth regular parametrized patch \mathbf r(u,v), the cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v chooses a normal direction wherever it is nonzero. The corresponding unit normal is \boxed{\widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v}{\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|}.} If we swap the order of the parameters, the normal reverses: \mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u=-\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v.

Not every surface can be oriented. A Möbius strip has only one side. If you carry a normal vector once around the strip, it comes back pointing the opposite way. So there is no continuous global choice of positive side. We will return to this warning in . For now, the surfaces we use will be orientable.

statement.p: Choosing an orientation of a surface means making a consistent choice of normal direction, or equivalently a consistent choice of side. What goes wrong on a Möbius strip that prevents such a consistent choice from existing? Picture sliding a normal vector all the way around the strip and asking where it ends up.

hint.p: Imagine carrying a small normal arrow once around the Möbius strip without ever flipping it. When it returns to the starting point, which way is it pointing compared to how it began? What does that say about having a single well-defined side?

subsection.title: Flux as signed flow through a surface
subsection.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z) be a vector field. If \mathbf F is a fluid velocity field, then \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} measures the normal component of the velocity.

statement.p: Suppose the fluid is racing along quickly but everywhere stays tangent to the surface, so \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=0. The flux is zero even though nothing is standing still. What does a flux of zero actually tell you about how the surface experiences this flow?

hint.p: Think of the screen as a turnstile: flux counts what passes through it, not what glides past it. Which of those is happening here?

subsection.p: A small surface patch has area approximately \Delta S. The amount of fluid crossing it per unit time is approximately \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,\Delta S. Adding all patches gives the flux.

statement.p: Let S be an oriented smooth surface with chosen unit normal \widehat{\mathbf n}. The flux of a vector field \mathbf F through S is \boxed{\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS.}

exercise.title: Why does signed flux require an orientation?

statement.p: A Möbius strip has only one side, so it cannot be oriented. In your own words, why does the signed flux integral defined above fail to have a global meaning once we lose a continuous choice of positive side?

hint.p: Imagine sliding the unit normal \widehat{\mathbf n} once around the strip and asking which side counts as out. What happens to your answer when it returns to the start?

subsection.p: Reversing the chosen normal multiplies flux by -1. It leaves a scalar surface integral \iint_S f\,dS unchanged, because dS uses a norm. This parallels the distinction between work integrals and scalar arc-length integrals in .

If \mathbf F is velocity measured in meters per second and dS is measured in square meters, then flux has units \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\cdot \text{m}^2=\frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{s}}. So flux is volume per time.

subsection.title: The vector area element
subsection.p: The parametrization formula for flux comes from combining two things we already know: dS=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv and \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v}{\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|}. Multiplying them gives \widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv. This vector \widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS is called the oriented surface area element. It is area with a direction attached.

So, if the parametrization \mathbf r(u,v) has the chosen orientation, then \boxed{\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=\iint_D \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\bigl(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\bigr)\,du\,dv.} If \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v points opposite to the chosen orientation, then the right-hand side gives the negative of the desired flux.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3 be a smooth regular parametrization that covers an oriented surface S once, except possibly along boundary curves. Suppose the chosen orientation is the one determined by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. Then \boxed{\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=\iint_D \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot\bigl(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\bigr)\,du\,dv.}

proof.p: On a tiny parameter rectangle, \Delta u\,\Delta v, the surface patch is approximately the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf r_u\,\Delta u \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf r_v\,\Delta v. Its oriented area vector is approximately (\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. The flux across that tiny patch is therefore approximately \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,\Delta u\,\Delta v. Adding these contributions and taking the limit gives the formula.

subsection.p: The phrase covers once matters. If a parametrization wraps around the same surface twice, the flux integral counts the surface twice. The calculation is not wrong; it is computing flux with multiplicity.

subsection.title: A slanted skylight in a steady wind
subsection.p: A rectangular skylight lies in the plane z=1+\frac{x}{2}, above the rectangle 0\le x\le2,\qquad 0\le y\le3. Choose the upward orientation. A steady wind is modeled by \mathbf F=(2,1,5). Find the flux through the skylight.

Use the parametrization \mathbf r(u,v)=\left(u,v,1+\frac u2\right), \qquad 0\le u\le2,\quad 0\le v\le3. Then \mathbf r_u=\left(1,0,\frac12\right), \qquad \mathbf r_v=(0,1,0). So
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v \amp= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i\amp\mathbf j\amp\mathbf k\\ 1\amp0\amp1/2\\ 0\amp1\amp0 \end{vmatrix} \amp= \left(-\frac12,0,1\right).
This vector has positive z-component, so it gives the upward orientation.
The z-component of the wind contributes positively. The x-component reduces the flux because the upward normal leans slightly in the negative x-direction.
If we choose the downward orientation, the flux is -24.

subsection.title: Flux through the side of a cylinder
subsection.p: The side of a cylinder of radius a and height h is parametrized by \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,z), \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\quad 0\le z\le h. Then \mathbf r_\theta=(-a\sin\theta,a\cos\theta,0), \qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1). Their cross product is \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,0). This points outward.

Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,0). On the cylinder, \mathbf F(\mathbf r(\theta,z))=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,0). Therefore
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(\theta,z))\cdot(\mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z) \amp= (a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,0)\cdot(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,0) \amp= a^2.
So the outward flux through the side is
\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^h a^2\,dz\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi a^2h.
For the cylinder of radius 2 and height 5, \boxed{\text{outward flux}=40\pi.}

Now compare this with the swirling field \mathbf G(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0). On the cylinder, \mathbf G(\mathbf r(\theta,z))=(-a\sin\theta,a\cos\theta,0). This is tangent to the cylinder. Its dot product with the outward normal is (-a\sin\theta,a\cos\theta,0)\cdot(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,0)=0. So \boxed{\iint_S \mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=0.} The field moves around the cylinder, not through it.

statement.p: For \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), compute \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z. Does it point inward or outward?

subsection.title: Closed surfaces and outward orientation
subsection.p: A surface with no boundary is called a closed surface. A sphere is closed. The boundary of a solid box is closed. The side of a cylinder alone is not closed, because it has two circular boundary curves.
For a closed surface, the standard orientation is the outward orientation.

statement.p: If S is the boundary of a solid region E, the outward orientation chooses the normal direction that points away from the inside of E.

subsection.p: Flux through a closed surface measures net flow out of the region. Flow leaving counts positive. Flow entering counts negative.

exercise.title: What does zero net flux mean?

statement.p: A closed surface reports a total outward flux of zero. Does that force the field to be tangent to the surface everywhere, or could fluid still be streaming in and out? Explain what the single number zero is and is not promising you about the region inside.

hint.p: Zero is a balance, not an absence. Picture water entering the bottom of a box and leaving the top at the same rate.

example.title: A constant vertical field through a closed box

statement.p: Let B be a rectangular box, and let \mathbf F=(0,0,5). The outward flux through the top face is positive. The outward flux through the bottom face is negative with the same magnitude. The side faces have zero flux because the field is tangent to them.
So the total outward flux is \boxed{0.} The field passes through the box, but it does not create fluid inside the box. Whatever enters through the bottom leaves through the top.

example.title: Outward flux through a sphere

statement.p:
Let S be the sphere of radius a centered at the origin, with outward orientation. Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z). At every point on the sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{1}{a}(x,y,z). Thus \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=(x,y,z)\cdot\frac{1}{a}(x,y,z)=\frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a}=a. Therefore
\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iint_S a\,dS \amp= a\cdot 4\pi a^2 \amp= 4\pi a^3.
So \boxed{\iint_S (x,y,z)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=4\pi a^3.} The field points outward everywhere, and its strength grows with radius.

subsection.p: Flux is now a surface integral with a sign. But the formula \mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v) still hides something. The cross product has three components: y_u z_v-y_v z_u, \qquad z_u x_v-z_v x_u, \qquad x_u y_v-x_v y_u. Each one is a signed area of a shadow on a coordinate plane. That is exactly the kind of measurement that wedge products were built to remember. The next step is to write flux without hiding those signed areas inside a cross product.

section.title: Flux 2-forms
section.p:
The flux formula from is
\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iint_D \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot \bigl(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\bigr)\,du\,dv.
This is efficient, but it hides the signed-area pieces. In , the form dx\wedge dy measured oriented area in the xy-plane. A surface in space has three coordinate shadows, so flux needs three oriented area forms: dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx,\qquad dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: A wall perpendicular to the x-axis
subsection.p:
Take a flat wall x=2,\qquad 0\le y\le3,\qquad 0\le z\le4. Orient it in the positive x-direction. A natural parametrization is \mathbf r(y,z)=(2,y,z). Then
\mathbf r_y=(0,1,0), \qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1),
so \mathbf r_y\times\mathbf r_z=(1,0,0). For a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), the flux through this wall is
\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \int_0^3\int_0^4 \mathbf F(2,y,z)\cdot(1,0,0)\,dz\,dy \amp= \int_0^3\int_0^4 P(2,y,z)\,dz\,dy.
Only the x-component of the field crosses a wall whose positive normal points in the x-direction.
The area element on this wall is dy\wedge dz. So the flux integrand is P\,dy\wedge dz.
The other coordinate walls follow the same pattern.
The middle entry dz\wedge dx is not a typo. The ordered directions \mathbf k,\mathbf i have cross product \mathbf k\times\mathbf i=\mathbf j. That is the positive y-normal.

subsection.title: The flux form of a vector field
subsection.p: The coordinate-wall computation suggests the right 2-form.

statement.p:
Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a vector field in space. The flux 2-form associated to \mathbf F is
\boxed{ \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy. }

subsection.p: This form packages the three possible coordinate fluxes:
So the vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) and the 2-form \Phi_{\mathbf F} carry the same flux information.

subsection.title: The shadows of a surface patch
subsection.p:
The formula
P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy
is easier to trust after seeing what it does to one tiny surface patch.

Let
\mathbf a=(a_1,a_2,a_3), \qquad \mathbf b=(b_1,b_2,b_3)
be two tangent vectors spanning a tiny oriented parallelogram. The form dy\wedge dz measures the signed area of the shadow of this parallelogram on the yz-plane:
(dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) = \begin{vmatrix} a_2\amp b_2\\ a_3\amp b_3 \end{vmatrix} = a_2b_3-a_3b_2.
Similarly,
(dz\wedge dx)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) = a_3b_1-a_1b_3,
and
(dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) = a_1b_2-a_2b_1.
But these three numbers are exactly the components of the cross product:
\boxed{ \mathbf a\times\mathbf b = \bigl( (dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b),\, (dz\wedge dx)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b),\, (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \bigr). }
Therefore
\Phi_{\mathbf F}(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \amp= P(dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) + Q(dz\wedge dx)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \amp\qquad + R(dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \amp= (P,Q,R)\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b) \amp= \mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b).
So the flux 2-form is not a new kind of flux. It is the same flux, written as a signed-area measurement.

statement.p: The plane only needed a single oriented-area form, dx\wedge dy, but flux in space uses three: dy\wedge dz, dz\wedge dx, and dx\wedge dy. What is it about a surface sitting in \mathbb R^3 that makes one shadow insufficient, and why exactly three rather than two or four?

hint.p: A tiny tilted parallelogram in space casts a shadow on each of the three coordinate planes. Think about how many independent ways its orientation can lean.

subsection.title: Pulling a 2-form back to a parameter domain
subsection.p: Let \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)) parametrize an oriented surface. To integrate a 2-form over this surface, we rewrite the form in terms of du and dv. This substitution is called a pullback, written \mathbf r^*, as in . It evaluates the original form on the images of parameter vectors under the derivative of \mathbf r.

In the next calculation the source and target differentials are distinguished explicitly: \mathbf r^*(dx)=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv, \mathbf r^*(dy)=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv, and \mathbf r^*(dz)=z_u\,du+z_v\,dv. Now compute:
\mathbf r^*(dy\wedge dz) \amp= (y_u\,du+y_v\,dv)\wedge(z_u\,du+z_v\,dv) \amp= (y_u z_v-y_v z_u)\,du\wedge dv.
Similarly,
\mathbf r^*(dz\wedge dx) = (z_u x_v-z_v x_u)\,du\wedge dv,
and
\mathbf r^*(dx\wedge dy) = (x_u y_v-x_v y_u)\,du\wedge dv.

Thus the flux form pulls back to
\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \mathbf r^*\Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp= \Bigl[ P(\mathbf r)(y_u z_v-y_v z_u) + Q(\mathbf r)(z_u x_v-z_v x_u)\\ \amp\qquad + R(\mathbf r)(x_u y_v-x_v y_u) \Bigr]\,du\wedge dv. \end{aligned} }
The coefficient in brackets is exactly
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot \bigl(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\bigr).

statement.p:
Let S be an oriented surface parametrized by \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3 by a smooth map, regular in the interior, covering S once except along boundary curves, with integrable pulled-back coefficient and with the orientation determined by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. If \mathbf r^*\Phi=A(u,v)\,du\wedge dv, then
\boxed{ \iint_S \Phi = \iint_D A(u,v)\,du\,dv. }

subsection.p: The order (u,v) makes du\wedge dv positive on the ordered parameter directions. Swapping that order replaces it by dv\wedge du=-du\wedge dv, matching the reversed normal. In the computations below, equalities involving dx,dy,dz after substitution mean their pullbacks to the parameter domain; they do not identify covectors in two different spaces.

Reversing the orientation reverses the sign. Covering the same surface twice doubles the integral. These are not defects of the formula; they are reminders that 2-form integrals are integrals over oriented surfaces.

statement.p: When you flip a surface's orientation, the integral of \Phi_{\mathbf F} changes sign even though the surface occupies the very same points in space. What physical or geometric information is the sign keeping track of, and why should a measurement of flux care which way the surface faces?

hint.p: Imagine the field as flowing fluid. Crossing a window from inside to outside is not the same event as crossing from outside to inside.

subsection.title: The slanted skylight again
subsection.p:
Return to the skylight
z=1+\frac{x}{2}, \qquad 0\le x\le2,\quad 0\le y\le3,
with upward orientation, and the vector field \mathbf F=(2,1,5). The flux form is
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = 2\,dy\wedge dz + dz\wedge dx + 5\,dx\wedge dy.

Use the parametrization \mathbf r(u,v)=\left(u,v,1+\frac u2\right). Then dx=du,\qquad dy=dv,\qquad dz=\frac12\,du. Pull back each term:
dy\wedge dz = dv\wedge\frac12du = -\frac12\,du\wedge dv,
dz\wedge dx = \frac12du\wedge du = 0,
and
dx\wedge dy = du\wedge dv.
Therefore
\mathbf r^*\Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp= 2\left(-\frac12\,du\wedge dv\right) + 0 + 5\,du\wedge dv \amp= 4\,du\wedge dv.
So
\iint_S \Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^3 4\,dv\,du \amp= 24.
This matches the cross-product computation from .
The form calculation shows where the number 4 came from: 5\,dx\wedge dy gave the upward contribution, while 2\,dy\wedge dz subtracted 1 because the skylight has a yz-shadow with the opposite sign.

subsection.title: Graphs and a useful flux formula
subsection.p:
For a graph z=g(x,y), use the upward orientation and the parametrization \mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,g(x,y)). Then dz=g_x\,dx+g_y\,dy. Pull back the flux form
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.
We get
dy\wedge dz = dy\wedge(g_x\,dx+g_y\,dy) = -g_x\,dx\wedge dy,
and
dz\wedge dx = (g_x\,dx+g_y\,dy)\wedge dx = -g_y\,dx\wedge dy.
Therefore
\boxed{ \mathbf r^*\Phi_{\mathbf F} = \bigl(-P g_x-Q g_y+R\bigr)\,dx\wedge dy, }
where P,Q,R are evaluated at (x,y,g(x,y)). So the upward flux through a graph is
\boxed{ \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iint_R \bigl(-P(x,y,g)g_x-Q(x,y,g)g_y+R(x,y,g)\bigr)\,dx\,dy. }
This is the same as the cross-product formula, because \mathbf r_x\times\mathbf r_y=(-g_x,-g_y,1).

subsection.title: A cylinder in flux-form language
subsection.p:
Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,0). Then
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = x\,dy\wedge dz + y\,dz\wedge dx.
Parametrize the outward-oriented side of the cylinder of radius a and height h by
\mathbf r(\theta,z)=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta,z), \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\quad 0\le z\le h.
Then
x=a\cos\theta, \qquad y=a\sin\theta,
and
dx=-a\sin\theta\,d\theta, \qquad dy=a\cos\theta\,d\theta.
So
dy\wedge dz = a\cos\theta\,d\theta\wedge dz,
and
dz\wedge dx \amp= dz\wedge(-a\sin\theta\,d\theta) \amp= a\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge dz.
Pull back the flux form:
\mathbf r^*\Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp= a\cos\theta \bigl(a\cos\theta\,d\theta\wedge dz\bigr) + a\sin\theta \bigl(a\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge dz\bigr) \amp= a^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,d\theta\wedge dz \amp= a^2\,d\theta\wedge dz.
Thus
\iint_S \Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^h a^2\,dz\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi a^2h.
Again, this matches the classical flux calculation.

subsection.title: Why the 2-form notation matters
subsection.p: The cross product is fast in \mathbb R^3. The flux 2-form is more revealing.

statement.p: The cross product computes flux faster, yet the text insists the 2-form \Phi_{\mathbf F}=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy is more revealing. What does writing flux as a sum of wedge terms make visible that the single symbol \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS hides from you?

hint.p: Notice that the cross product is a trick special to three dimensions. Ask what each wedge term is separately telling you about how the field pierces a particular kind of oriented area.

subsection.p:
This form notation also prepares the next theorem. In the plane, Green's theorem said \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. The derivative of a plane 1-form became a 2-form: d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. In space, the derivative of a 1-form also becomes a 2-form, but now it has three pieces:
d(P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz) \amp= (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz \amp\quad+ (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx \amp\quad+ (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.
This is a preview of the space exterior derivative, developed in Chapter 17. Its three coefficients are the curl already defined in ; no general differentiation rule for forms is needed for the flux computations above.

So the next surface integral will look like flux, but it will come from circulation around a boundary curve. A wire loop can bound many different surfaces, and the same boundary integral will know how much curl passes through any one of them.

section.title: Curl and Stokes' theorem
section.p:
turned flux into a 2-form:
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.
At the end, a different kind of 2-form appeared. If \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is a work 1-form, then d\omega is also a 2-form. Its three coefficients form a vector. That vector is called the curl.
The meaning is simple but deep: curl measures local circulation per unit area.

subsection.title: A small paddle wheel in space
subsection.p: Picture a tiny paddle wheel floating in a moving fluid. If the fluid pushes harder on one side than the other, the wheel spins. In the plane, measured this tendency with the scalar curl Q_x-P_y. In space, the paddle wheel can face many directions. A wheel lying flat in the xy-plane detects spinning around the z-axis. A wheel in the yz-plane detects spinning around the x-axis. A wheel in the zx-plane detects spinning around the y-axis.
So curl in space needs three components.
Start with a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) and its work form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.
On a tiny rectangle in the xy-plane, the circulation density is Q_x-P_y. That is the z-component of curl.

On a tiny rectangle in the yz-plane, the positive normal direction is the x-direction. The relevant work form is Q\,dy+R\,dz. By the same rectangle argument as in , the circulation density is R_y-Q_z. That is the x-component of curl.

On a tiny rectangle whose ordered area form is dz\wedge dx, the positive normal direction is the y-direction, because \mathbf k\times \mathbf i=\mathbf j. The relevant circulation density is P_z-R_x. That is the y-component of curl.
These three numbers form one vector.

statement.p:
Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a vector field in space. The curl of \mathbf F is
\boxed{ \nabla\times \mathbf F = (R_y-Q_z,\;P_z-R_x,\;Q_x-P_y). }

subsection.p: The notation \nabla\times\mathbf F is classical vector notation. It is useful, but it hides the form story. The form story says that curl is the vector field whose flux 2-form is d\omega.
This is the bridge between circulation and flux.

statement.p: A paddle wheel in the plane reported a single circulation number, but in space the curl needs three components. What does each component actually measure, and why can't a single number capture spinning in space the way it did in the plane?

hint.p: Think about which way the paddle wheel faces. A wheel lying flat in the xy-plane feels a different swirl than one standing up in the yz-plane.

subsection.title: A first Stokes calculation: a circular wire
subsection.p:
Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac y2,\frac x2,0\right), so \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. The curl is
\nabla\times\mathbf F \amp= (0-0,\;0-0,\;\tfrac12-(-\tfrac12)) \amp= (0,0,1).
Equivalently, d\omega=dx\wedge dy.

Let C be the circle of radius a in the plane z=0, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above: \mathbf r(t)=(a\cos t,a\sin t,0),\qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi. Then dx=-a\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=a\cos t\,dt. Pull back \omega:
\omega \amp= -\frac{a\sin t}{2}(-a\sin t\,dt) + \frac{a\cos t}{2}(a\cos t\,dt) \amp= \frac{a^2}{2}(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt \amp= \frac{a^2}{2}\,dt.
Therefore
\oint_C \omega \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\frac{a^2}{2}\,dt \amp= \pi a^2.

Now let D be the flat disk bounded by C, with upward orientation. Since d\omega=dx\wedge dy, we get
\iint_D d\omega \amp= \iint_D dx\wedge dy \amp= \operatorname{Area}(D) \amp= \pi a^2.
So
\boxed{ \oint_C \omega=\iint_D d\omega. }
The left side walks around the wire. The right side measures how much curl passes through a surface spanning the wire.

subsection.title: Surface orientation and boundary orientation
subsection.p: A surface orientation chooses a normal direction. Once that normal is chosen, the positive direction around the boundary is forced.

For a parametrized surface \mathbf r(u,v) whose orientation is given by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v, the boundary orientation is the image of the positive boundary orientation of the parameter region. This is the most reliable rule.
There is also a hand rule. Point the thumb of your right hand in the chosen normal direction. Your curled fingers show the positive boundary direction.
For a flat disk with upward normal, the boundary is counterclockwise as seen from above. If the same disk is oriented downward, the positive boundary direction is clockwise.

figure.caption: For Stokes' theorem, the surface orientation and boundary orientation must match.

statement.p: Let S be an oriented surface with boundary \partial S. The boundary is given the compatible orientation if, near each boundary point, the surface lies on the left as seen from the chosen positive side of the surface.
Equivalently, for a parametrized oriented surface, \partial S receives the orientation induced from the positively oriented boundary of the parameter domain.

subsection.p: This compatibility is not bookkeeping. It controls the sign of the theorem.

subsection.title: Stokes' theorem
subsection.p: The circle computation was not a coincidence. It is the space version of Green's theorem.

proof.title: Proof for smooth patches; scope of the general statement
proof.p: First suppose one regular parametrization has continuous second partial derivatives and covers the surface once, with the usual boundary identifications. Parametrize this patch by \mathbf r:D\to S, where D is a compact planar region with piecewise smooth boundary, and the parametrization is C^2 on a neighborhood of D. Use the orientation given by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. The boundary of S is the image of the boundary of D, with the induced orientation.

Pull the 1-form \omega back to the parameter domain: \mathbf r^*\omega. This is now a 1-form on a region in the uv-plane. By Green's theorem, \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D d(\mathbf r^*\omega). Here is the required chain-rule calculation. Write \mathbf r^*\omega=A\,du+B\,dv,\qquad A=\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf r_u,\quad B=\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot\mathbf r_v. The product and chain rules give B_u-A_v=(D\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\mathbf r_u)\cdot\mathbf r_v -(D\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\mathbf r_v)\cdot\mathbf r_u. The terms \mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot(\mathbf r_{vu}-\mathbf r_{uv}) cancel by equality of continuous mixed partials. Expanding the remaining dot products gives B_u-A_v=(\nabla\times\mathbf F)(\mathbf r)\cdot (\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v). By the plane definition of d and the flux pullback formula of , this proves the particular identity d(\mathbf r^*\omega)=\mathbf r^*(d\omega) used here, without assuming its later general version. Therefore \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega). Translating back to the surface gives \int_{\partial S}\omega = \int_S d\omega.

For a surface divided into finitely many such patches, add these identities. The line integrals on shared edges cancel because the induced directions are opposite. This proves the result for that class of surfaces. The more general piecewise smooth statement above is accepted here; extending this argument to arbitrary admissible patches requires an approximation argument not supplied in this book. Chapter 18 develops the unified theorem and its local mechanism.

subsection.p: Stokes' theorem says that circulation around the boundary is caused by curl passing through the surface.

The surprise is that the boundary is enough. The surface can bend, stretch, or sag. As long as both surfaces and the field satisfy the theorem's hypotheses and have the same oriented boundary, the total curl flux is the same.

subsection.title: Changing the surface but keeping the boundary
subsection.p: Take again \mathbf F=\left(-\frac y2,\frac x2,0\right), so \nabla\times\mathbf F=(0,0,1).
Let C be the unit circle in the plane z=0: x^2+y^2=1,\qquad z=0, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above.
One surface spanning C is the flat disk D:\quad z=0,\qquad x^2+y^2\le1. The upward curl flux is \iint_D (0,0,1)\cdot(0,0,1)\,dS=\pi.
Now replace the flat disk by the curved cap S:\quad z=1-x^2-y^2,\qquad x^2+y^2\le1, with upward orientation. This cap has the same boundary C, because when x^2+y^2=1, z=1-1=0.
