For a graph z=g(x,y), the upward vector area element is (-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dx\,dy. Here g(x,y)=1-x^2-y^2, so (-g_x,-g_y,1)=(2x,2y,1). Thus
\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iint_{x^2+y^2\le1} (0,0,1)\cdot(2x,2y,1)\,dx\,dy \amp= \iint_{x^2+y^2\le1}1\,dx\,dy \amp= \pi.
The surface changed. The answer did not.

p.md: \boxed{ \iint_{\text{flat disk}}\nabla\times\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iint_{\text{curved cap}}\nabla\times\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r. }

subsection.p: This is often the easiest way to use Stokes' theorem. If the boundary is simple, compute the line integral. If the surface is annoying but another spanning surface is simpler, change the surface.

statement.p: The flat disk and the curved cap share the same boundary circle, and they returned the same curl flux \pi. In your own words, why should two such different surfaces be forced to agree? What does Stokes' theorem reveal about what the answer really depends on?

hint.p: The line integral on the right of Stokes' theorem only sees the boundary curve. If that curve is fixed, what freedom does the surface in the middle really have?

subsection.title: A surface with two boundary curves
subsection.p: A surface can have more than one boundary curve. Then every boundary component must be included, with the correct orientation.

Let A be the annulus 1\le x^2+y^2\le4,\qquad z=0, with upward orientation. Its boundary has two circles: C_{\text{outer}}:\quad x^2+y^2=4, and C_{\text{inner}}:\quad x^2+y^2=1. The compatible orientation is counterclockwise on the outer boundary and clockwise on the inner boundary.

Use \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy. So
\iint_A d\omega \amp= \operatorname{Area}(A) \amp= 4\pi-\pi \amp= 3\pi.
If we forgot the inner boundary, we would get 4\pi, not 3\pi. The hole has a rim, and Stokes' theorem counts every rim.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem needs more than a formula. It needs a surface, a compatible boundary orientation, and a vector field that is defined and differentiable where the theorem uses it.

subsubsection.title: Orientation must be compatible
subsubsection.p: Use the unit disk D, upward orientation, and \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. We know \iint_D d\omega=\pi. The compatible boundary direction is counterclockwise, and then \oint_{\partial D}\omega=\pi.

If instead we walk around the same circle clockwise, the line integral becomes -\pi. The surface integral has not changed. The sign mismatch is not a paradox. The boundary orientation is no longer compatible with the surface orientation.

subsubsection.title: The field must be defined on the surface
subsubsection.p:
Consider the vector field
\mathbf A(x,y,z) = \left( -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}, \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}, 0 \right).
It is defined away from the z-axis. Its work form is
\alpha= -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx + \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy.
Where it is defined, a direct calculation gives d\alpha=0.

Now integrate around the unit circle C:\quad (x,y,z)=(\cos t,\sin t,0),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=\cos t\,dt. On C, x^2+y^2=1, and
\alpha \amp= -\sin t(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt) \amp= (\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt \amp= dt.
So
\boxed{ \oint_C\alpha=2\pi. }

It may be tempting to say: d\alpha=0,\qquad \text{so } \oint_C\alpha=0. That would be wrong. The flat disk bounded by C contains the origin, and the field is not defined there. Stokes' theorem cannot be applied to that disk.
The missing point is not harmless. It carries circulation that the formula cannot see unless the singularity is removed and the new inner boundary is counted.

subsection.title: Reading Stokes' theorem in both languages
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem has two faces.
This is the same shape as Green's theorem. It is also the same shape as the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). The object changed, but the story did not.

statement.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, and Stokes' theorem all share the pattern \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. What is the single idea common to all three, and what role does taking a derivative d play in lifting the integral up by one dimension?

subsection.p: An interval has two boundary points. A plane region has a boundary curve. A surface has a boundary curve too. The derivative moves the integrand up by one dimension: 0\text{-form}\to1\text{-form},\qquad 1\text{-form}\to2\text{-form}.

But there is another kind of surface: a closed surface. A sphere has no boundary curve at all. Stokes' theorem then predicts no boundary circulation. Yet a closed surface can still have flux through it. A balloon can leak outward everywhere. A source can fill the inside.
The derivative that measures source strength is not curl. It is divergence.

section.title: Divergence and the divergence theorem
section.p: Stokes' theorem compares a boundary curve with a surface. Flux through a closed surface asks for a different comparison. A closed surface is the boundary of a solid region, so the inside is three-dimensional.
If curl measures local spinning, divergence measures local source strength.

subsection.title: Flux out of a small box
subsection.p: Start with a vector field whose flux through a box is easy to compute: \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,2y,3z). Let B be the rectangular box a\le x\le a+h, \qquad b\le y\le b+k, \qquad c\le z\le c+\ell. Give the boundary \partial B the outward orientation.
The box has six faces.

paragraphs.title: The two x-faces
paragraphs.p: On the right face, x=a+h, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf n}=(1,0,0). So \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=a+h. The face has area k\ell, so the outward flux through the right face is (a+h)k\ell.

On the left face, x=a, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf n}=(-1,0,0). So \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=-a. The flux through the left face is -ak\ell. Together, the two x-faces contribute (a+h)k\ell-ak\ell=hk\ell.

paragraphs.title: The two y-faces
paragraphs.p: On the face y=b+k, the outward normal is \mathbf j, and \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=2(b+k). On the face y=b, the outward normal is -\mathbf j, and \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=-2b. The area of each face is h\ell. The total contribution is 2(b+k)h\ell-2bh\ell=2hk\ell.

paragraphs.title: The two z-faces
paragraphs.p: On the face z=c+\ell, the outward normal is \mathbf k, and \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=3(c+\ell). On the face z=c, the outward normal is -\mathbf k, and \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=-3c. The area of each face is hk. The total contribution is 3(c+\ell)hk-3chk=3hk\ell.

subsection.p: The number 6 is not mysterious. It is \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2y) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(3z) = 1+2+3. Each component contributes the rate at which that component spreads outward in its own coordinate direction.

figure.caption: Divergence measures net outward flux per unit volume.

subsection.title: Divergence as source density
subsection.p: For a general field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), the same small-box argument gives \boxed{ \text{net outward flux through a tiny box} \approx (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,\Delta V. } The coefficient gets its own name.

statement.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a vector field in space. The divergence of \mathbf F is \boxed{ \nabla\cdot\mathbf F = P_x+Q_y+R_z. }

subsection.p: If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F>0, then the field has net outward flow from a small box. It behaves like a source.
If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F<0, then more flow enters a small box than leaves. It behaves like a sink.
If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0, then there is no net creation or loss at that point. Fluid may still move, swirl, and bend, but it is not locally expanding or compressing.

exercise.title: Can fluid move where divergence is zero?

statement.p: A friend says, If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0 at a point, then the fluid must be sitting still there. Is that right? Explain what \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0 actually tells you about the flow near that point, and what it does not tell you.

hint.p: Divergence measures net outward flow from a tiny box, not speed. Think about the swirling field (-y,x,0): things are clearly moving, yet nothing piles up or drains out.

example.title: A swirling field has zero divergence

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0). Then P=-y,\qquad Q=x,\qquad R=0. So \nabla\cdot\mathbf F = P_x+Q_y+R_z = 0+0+0 = 0. This field rotates around the z-axis, but it does not create net outward flow from small boxes.

example.title: A radial field has positive divergence

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z). Then \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1+1+1=3. Every small box has net outward flux approximately 3\,\Delta V. The field points away from the origin and expands space uniformly.

subsection.title: Divergence in form language
subsection.p: This is the next piece of the pattern:

table.title: The exterior derivative across degrees.

subsection.p: The derivative of a 2-form is a 3-form. Flux through a surface becomes source density inside a solid.

subsection.title: The divergence theorem
subsection.p: Now tile a solid region by many small boxes. On each small box, \text{outward flux} \approx (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\Delta V. Add all boxes.

On the left side, flux across interior faces cancels. One small box sees the shared face as outward, while the neighboring box sees the same face with the opposite normal. The two contributions have opposite signs.
Only the outer boundary remains.

exercise.title: Why does only the boundary survive?

statement.p: When we add up the outward flux over all the little boxes, the contributions from interior faces cancel and only the outer boundary is left over. Why does that cancellation have to happen? What feature of two neighboring boxes guarantees their shared face contributes equal and opposite amounts?

hint.p: Picture the single face shared by two boxes. Each box wants its own outward normal there. How do those two outward normals compare on that one shared wall?

subsection.p: On the right side, the sums become a triple integral: \sum(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\Delta V \longrightarrow \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV.
This gives the divergence theorem.

statement.p: Let E be a bounded solid region whose closure has piecewise smooth boundary \partial E. Give \partial E the outward orientation. Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing the closure of E. Then \boxed{ \iint_{\partial E} \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV. } In differential-form notation, \boxed{ \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf F} = \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf F}. }

subsection.p: The box argument explains cancellation and proves the result for boxes by one-variable integration on opposite faces. Passing from boxes to a general curved boundary needs a limit argument beyond this sketch. We use the stated divergence theorem with its hypotheses; the sketch is not a full proof of that general statement.
The theorem says: \boxed{ \text{net outward flux through the boundary} = \text{total source strength inside}. }
This is the three-dimensional cousin of Green's theorem and Stokes' theorem. Once again, an integral over a boundary equals an integral of a derivative over the inside.

subsection.title: Outward flux through a sphere
subsection.p: Let S be the sphere of radius a centered at the origin, with outward orientation. Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z). In , we computed this flux directly and found 4\pi a^3. Now the divergence theorem gives it almost immediately.

Let E be the ball x^2+y^2+z^2\le a^2. The divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=3. Therefore
\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iiint_E 3\,dV \amp= 3\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= 3\left(\frac43\pi a^3\right) \amp= 4\pi a^3.
So \boxed{ \iint_S (x,y,z)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=4\pi a^3. } The surface calculation became a volume calculation.

subsection.title: A closed cylinder
subsection.p: Let E be the solid cylinder x^2+y^2\le a^2, \qquad 0\le z\le h. Its boundary has three pieces:

table.title: The three boundary pieces of the closed cylinder.

subsection.p: We can see the pieces too.
On the side, showed that for (x,y,0) the outward side flux is 2\pi a^2h. The z-component is tangent to the side, so the same side flux holds for (x,y,z).
On the top, \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,1), so \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=h. The top area is \pi a^2, so the top flux is h\pi a^2.
On the bottom, \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,-1), but z=0, so \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=0. The bottom flux is 0.
Adding: 2\pi a^2h+\pi a^2h+0=3\pi a^2h. The divergence theorem found the total at once.

subsection.title: Using symmetry: a paraboloid cap
subsection.p: The divergence theorem is especially helpful when a surface integral would be awkward.
Let S be the curved paraboloid z=4-x^2-y^2, \qquad x^2+y^2\le4, oriented upward. Together with the disk D:\quad z=0,\qquad x^2+y^2\le4, it bounds a solid region E.
Let \mathbf F=(0,0,z). We want the flux through the curved paraboloid S.

The divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1. So the total outward flux through the closed surface S\cup D is \iiint_E 1\,dV=\operatorname{Volume}(E). The volume is
\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2(4-r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\left[2r^2-\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^2 \amp= 2\pi(8-4) \amp= 8\pi.
On the bottom disk, z=0, so \mathbf F=(0,0,0). The bottom flux is 0. Therefore the flux through the curved paraboloid is \boxed{ 8\pi. } The theorem let the solid volume do the work.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: The divergence theorem has three common traps: the surface must be closed, the normal must point outward, and the field must be defined throughout the solid.

paragraphs.title: A single open surface is not enough
paragraphs.p: Let D be the disk x^2+y^2\le1,\qquad z=0, oriented upward. Let \mathbf F=(0,0,1). The flux through the disk is \iint_D 1\,dS=\pi. But \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0.

This does not contradict the divergence theorem. The disk alone is not a closed surface. It is not the entire boundary of a solid. To use the theorem, we would need a closed surface, such as the boundary of a cylinder or a half-ball.

paragraphs.title: Outward orientation matters
paragraphs.p: Take the unit cube E=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] and the field \mathbf F=(x,0,0). The divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1. So the divergence theorem predicts outward flux \iiint_E 1\,dV=1.
Indeed, only the two x-faces contribute. On x=1, the outward normal is \mathbf i, and the flux is 1. On x=0, the field is zero. Total outward flux: 1.
If we choose inward normals instead, every sign reverses and the flux is -1. The theorem uses outward orientation.

paragraphs.title: The field must be defined inside
paragraphs.p: Consider the inverse-square radial field \mathbf G(x,y,z) = \frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}. This field is not defined at the origin.

Away from the origin, write r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. Then \mathbf G=\left(\frac{x}{r^3},\frac{y}{r^3},\frac{z}{r^3}\right). A direct calculation gives, for r>0,
\nabla\cdot\mathbf G \amp= \left(r^{-3}-3x^2r^{-5}\right) + \left(r^{-3}-3y^2r^{-5}\right) + \left(r^{-3}-3z^2r^{-5}\right) \amp= 3r^{-3}-3(x^2+y^2+z^2)r^{-5} \amp= 3r^{-3}-3r^2r^{-5} \amp= 0.

Now take the sphere S_a of radius a, oriented outward. On this sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a}, and \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}. Thus
\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} \amp= \frac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}\cdot \frac{(x,y,z)}{a} \amp= \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a^4} \amp= \frac{a^2}{a^4} \amp= \frac1{a^2}.
Therefore
\iint_{S_a}\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \frac1{a^2}\cdot 4\pi a^2 \amp= 4\pi.

It would be wrong to say: \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0, \qquad \text{so the flux through the sphere is }0. The field is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the sphere. The divergence theorem cannot be applied to the whole ball.

If we remove the singularity, the theorem works again. Let E be the spherical shell b\le r\le a, \qquad 0<b<a. On this shell, \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0. The boundary has two pieces. The outer sphere contributes 4\pi. On the inner sphere r=b, the outward normal for the shell points toward the center, so it is -\widehat{\mathbf r}. The inner flux is -4\pi. The total flux is 4\pi-4\pi=0, which matches \iiint_E 0\,dV=0.
The missing point was carrying the source.

subsection.title: Physical meaning: conservation and balance
subsection.p: If \mathbf F is a velocity field of a fluid, then \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} measures flow rate through a unit area. The flux through a closed surface measures net flow leaving the region.
The divergence theorem says that this net outflow can be computed by adding local source strengths: \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV.

If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0 throughout E, then \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=0. Fluid may pass through the region, but whatever enters also leaves. There is no net creation inside.
If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F>0 on average, more fluid leaves than enters. Something inside acts like a source.
If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F<0 on average, more fluid enters than leaves. Something inside acts like a sink.
This is the mathematical language behind conservation laws. To know how much quantity changes inside a region, look at what crosses the boundary and what is created or destroyed inside.

exercise.title: Reading the inside from the boundary

statement.p: The divergence theorem lets you compute the total source strength inside a region by measuring only the flux across its boundary. Why is it remarkable that you can learn what is happening throughout a solid without ever looking inside it? What does this say about how local sources and sinks relate to the boundary as a whole?

hint.p: Whatever a source creates deep inside has to get out somewhere, and the only exit is the boundary. Think about how a hidden source eventually announces itself on \partial E.

subsection.p:
We now have two space derivatives of vector fields: 
abla	imes\mathbf F \qquad	ext{and}\qquad 
abla\cdot\mathbf F. One measures spinning; the other measures spreading. They look unrelated in vector notation. But in form notation they are consecutive exterior derivatives: \omega \xrightarrow{\ d\ } d\omega \xrightarrow{\ d\ } d(d\omega). That raises a strange question. What happens if we take d twice? The answer is always zero, and it hides two famous vector-calculus identities: 
abla	imes(
abla f)=\mathbf 0, \qquad 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0. The next section explains why these are not two miracles. They are one fact wearing two costumes.

section.title: Classical vector-calculus identities
section.p: ended with two familiar-looking derivatives: \nabla\times \mathbf F \qquad\text{and}\qquad \nabla\cdot \mathbf F. In vector notation they look like separate operations. In form notation they are successive appearances of the same operation: d. That is why two famous identities are really one fact.

subsection.title: A gradient field has no local rotation
subsection.p: Suppose a metal plate has temperature T(x,y,z)=x^2y+yz+3z. The gradient field is \nabla T=(2xy,\ x^2+z,\ y+3). This field points in the direction of fastest temperature increase.

Compute its curl:
\nabla\times(\nabla T) \amp= \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y+3) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(x^2+z), \right. \amp\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(2xy) - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(y+3), \amp\qquad\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2+z) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy) \right) \amp= (1-1,\ 0-0,\ 2x-2x) \amp= \mathbf 0.

The cancellations are not an accident. A gradient field comes from a potential function. It points uphill. A tiny paddle wheel placed in a pure uphill field may be pushed, but it has no first-order tendency to spin.

statement.p: Let f have continuous second partial derivatives on a neighborhood of a small disk. Use the fundamental theorem for work integrals from to explain why \oint_C\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r=0 around its boundary C. How does this agree with the local paddle-wheel interpretation of curl?

hint.p: The integral is the final potential minus the initial potential. A closed path has the same starting and ending point.

subsection.p: In the language of 1-forms, the potential T has differential dT=T_x\,dx+T_y\,dy+T_z\,dz. For our example, dT=2xy\,dx+(x^2+z)\,dy+(y+3)\,dz. Taking d again gives d(dT)=0. That is the form version of \nabla\times(\nabla T)=\mathbf 0.

proof.p:
Write 
abla f=(f_x,f_y,f_z). Then 
abla	imes(
abla f) = (f_{zy}-f_{yz},\ f_{xz}-f_{zx},\ f_{yx}-f_{xy}). If the second partial derivatives are continuous, then the mixed partials agree: f_{zy}=f_{yz},\qquad f_{xz}=f_{zx},\qquad f_{yx}=f_{xy}. So every component is zero.

subsection.p: The hypothesis about continuous second partial derivatives is doing real work.

example.title: Why the smoothness hypothesis matters

statement.p: Define f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{xy(x^2-y^2)}{x^2+y^2}, \amp (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[2mm] 0, \amp (x,y)=(0,0). \end{cases} This function has second mixed partial derivatives at the origin, but they are not equal.

First compute f_x(0,y). For y\ne0,
f_x(0,y) \amp= \lim_{h\to0} \frac{f(h,y)-f(0,y)}{h} \amp= \lim_{h\to0} \frac{hy(h^2-y^2)}{h^2+y^2}\cdot\frac1h \amp= \lim_{h\to0} y\frac{h^2-y^2}{h^2+y^2} \amp= -y.
Also f_x(0,0)=0. Therefore f_{xy}(0,0) = \lim_{y\to0}\frac{f_x(0,y)-f_x(0,0)}{y} = \lim_{y\to0}\frac{-y}{y} = -1.

Now compute f_y(x,0). For x\ne0,
f_y(x,0) \amp= \lim_{h\to0} \frac{f(x,h)-f(x,0)}{h} \amp= \lim_{h\to0} \frac{xh(x^2-h^2)}{x^2+h^2}\cdot\frac1h \amp= \lim_{h\to0} x\frac{x^2-h^2}{x^2+h^2} \amp= x.
Also f_y(0,0)=0. Therefore f_{yx}(0,0) = \lim_{x\to0}\frac{f_y(x,0)-f_y(0,0)}{x} = \lim_{x\to0}\frac{x}{x} = 1.

So  oxed{ f_{xy}(0,0)=-1, \qquad f_{yx}(0,0)=1. } If we form the field 
abla f=(f_x,f_y,0), then at the origin the z-component of 
abla	imes(
abla f) would be f_{yx}(0,0)-f_{xy}(0,0)=2. The identity failed because the second partial derivatives were not continuous enough to force mixed partials to agree.

subsection.p: The moral is small but sharp: the identity \nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0 belongs to sufficiently smooth functions. It is not a purely formal trick with symbols.

subsection.title: A curl field has no source strength
subsection.p: Now look at a curl instead of a gradient.

Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(0,xz,0). Then
\nabla\times\mathbf F \amp= \left( 0-\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(xz), \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(0)-0, \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xz)-0 \right) \amp= (-x,0,z).
Now take its divergence:
\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F) \amp= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(-x) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(0) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(z) \amp= -1+0+1 \amp= 0.

A curl field represents local spinning. Spinning can move material around, but by itself it does not create source strength. In form language, if \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is the work form of \mathbf F, then d\omega is the flux form of 
abla	imes\mathbf F. Taking d again gives d(d\omega)=0. That is the form version of 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0.

statement.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) have continuous second partial derivatives on an open region. Then \boxed{ \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0. } Equivalently, if \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, then \boxed{ d(d\omega)=0. }

proof.p:
The curl is 
abla	imes\mathbf F = (R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y). Its divergence is

abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F) \amp= (R_y-Q_z)_x + (P_z-R_x)_y + (Q_x-P_y)_z \amp= R_{yx}-Q_{zx}+P_{zy}-R_{xy}+Q_{xz}-P_{yz}.
Regroup: (R_{yx}-R_{xy}) + (P_{zy}-P_{yz}) + (Q_{xz}-Q_{zx}). Each pair cancels because the second partial derivatives are continuous. Therefore 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0.

subsection.p: The same smoothness warning appears again.

example.title: A nonsmooth vector potential can break the cancellation

statement.p:
Use the function from the previous example: f(x,y)=  egin{cases} \dfrac{xy(x^2-y^2)}{x^2+y^2}, \amp (x,y)
e(0,0),\[2mm] 0, \amp (x,y)=(0,0). \end{cases} Define a vector field in space by \mathbf A(x,y,z)=(0,0,f(x,y)). Then 
abla	imes\mathbf A=(f_y,-f_x,0). At the origin,

abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A) \amp= (f_y)_x+(-f_x)_y \amp= f_{yx}-f_{xy} \amp= 1-(-1) \amp= 2.
So the identity 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A)=0 fails at the origin. The formal cancellation depends on the mixed partials being allowed to trade order.

subsection.title: The single fact: d^2=0
subsection.p: The two identities now have the same explanation.
For a function f, df is a 1-form. Its exterior derivative is d(df). The identity d(df)=0 is the statement \nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0.

For a work 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, the derivative d\omega is the flux 2-form of the curl: d\omega=\Phi_{
abla	imes\mathbf F}. The identity d(d\omega)=0 is the statement 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0.

A tiny piece of the algebra shows why. In two variables, df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy. Then
d(df) \amp= d(f_x)\wedge dx+d(f_y)\wedge dy \amp= (f_{xx}\,dx+f_{xy}\,dy)\wedge dx + (f_{yx}\,dx+f_{yy}\,dy)\wedge dy.
Now dx\wedge dx=0, \qquad dy\wedge dy=0, and dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy. So
d(df) \amp= f_{xy}\,dy\wedge dx+f_{yx}\,dx\wedge dy \amp= (f_{yx}-f_{xy})\,dx\wedge dy.
When the mixed partials agree, this is 0.
The wedge product supplies the sign. Equality of mixed partials supplies the cancellation.

statement.p: The computation of d(df) relied on two separate facts: the wedge product is antisymmetric (so dx\wedge dy=-\,dy\wedge dx), and the mixed partials are equal (f_{xy}=f_{yx}). What does each fact contribute, and why does the result fail to be zero if either one is missing?

hint.p: Picture the two surviving terms before cancellation. One ingredient lines them up as a difference; the other makes that difference vanish. Try removing each in turn and see which structure collapses.

subsection.title: Potentials and topology warnings
subsection.p: The identity \nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0 says every gradient field has zero curl.

The converse is more delicate. If \nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0, and \mathbf F has continuous first partial derivatives on an open region, then it has local potentials; on a simply connected domain it has a global potential by : \mathbf F=\nabla f. But holes can prevent a global potential.

Recall the field \mathbf A(x,y,z) = \left( -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}, \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}, 0 \right), defined away from the z-axis. A direct calculation gives \nabla\times\mathbf A=\mathbf 0 where the field is defined.

But around the unit circle \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, we get \mathbf A(\mathbf r(t))=(-\sin t,\cos t,0), and \mathbf r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t,0). Thus
\oint_C \mathbf A\cdot d\mathbf r \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} (-\sin t,\cos t,0)\cdot(-\sin t,\cos t,0)\,dt \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt \amp= 2\pi.
If \mathbf A were a global gradient field on its whole domain, every closed-loop integral would be 0. This nonzero integral proves that no such global potential exists.

statement.p: The field \mathbf A has zero curl everywhere it is defined, yet its loop integral around the circle is 2\pi rather than 0. Since the curl test is purely local, what is it about the shape of the domain—not the formula for \mathbf A—that lets a curl-free field still fail to have a global potential?

hint.p: A potential would make every closed-loop integral zero. Ask whether the loop could be shrunk to a point while staying inside the domain, and what the missing z-axis has to do with that.

subsection.p:
A similar warning appears one level higher. The identity 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A)=0 says every curl field has zero divergence. The converse asks whether every divergence-free field can be written as a curl: \mathbf F=
abla	imes\mathbf A. Again, topology can interfere.

Consider \mathbf G(x,y,z) =  rac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}, defined on \mathbb R^3\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}. Away from the origin, 
abla\cdot\mathbf G=0. But the outward flux through any sphere centered at the origin is 4\pi. If \mathbf G=
abla	imes\mathbf A for a smooth vector field \mathbf A defined on the punctured space, then the flux of \mathbf G through the sphere would be the flux of a curl through a closed surface. Stokes' theorem would give \iint_S(
abla	imes\mathbf A)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \int_{\partial S}\mathbf A\cdot d\mathbf r = 0, because a sphere has no boundary. But the flux is 4\pi. So no global vector potential exists on the punctured space.
These warnings are not exceptions to the identities. They say something more subtle: local derivative tests do not always decide global questions. Smoothness and domain shape both matter.
That is why the final section of the chapter collects the traps. The formulas are short, but the surface, the orientation, the boundary, and the domain decide whether the formula may be used.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The two integral theorems in this chapter are easy to state: \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega, \qquad \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi. Their hypotheses are where many mistakes happen. A surface may have no consistent normal direction. A field may be undefined at one hidden point. A boundary may be walked the wrong way. A region may have an inner boundary that should not be ignored.
Each warning below is a small failure of one of those hidden assumptions.

subsection.title: A nonorientable surface and why flux is not globally defined
subsection.p: A flux integral needs a chosen side: \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS. That means S must have a continuous unit normal vector field \widehat{\mathbf n} on the whole surface.
A sphere has two sides, inside and outside. A cylinder has two sides, inside and outside. A disk has two sides, up and down.
A Möbius strip does not.

One parametrization of a Möbius strip is \mathbf r(u,v)= \left( \left(2+v\cos\frac u2\right)\cos u,\, \left(2+v\cos\frac u2\right)\sin u,\, v\sin\frac u2 \right), where 0\le u\le2\pi, \qquad -\frac12\le v\le \frac12. The point at u=0 with parameter v is identified with the point at u=2\pi with parameter -v. That twist is the whole issue.
If you choose a normal vector at one point and slide it continuously around the center of the strip, it returns to the same physical point pointing the opposite way. The surface has only one side.

figure.caption: The Möbius strip is made by identifying opposite ends with a twist. A normal direction reverses after one trip around the strip.

subsection.p: A scalar surface integral still makes sense: \iint_S f\,dS. Area has no sign, so it does not need a side.

But flux is signed. It asks whether the field crosses the positive side or the negative side. On a Möbius strip there is no globally consistent positive side. So a global flux integral \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS is not defined.
The problem is not the vector field. The problem is the surface.

exercise.title: Why does area survive but flux does not?

statement.p: On a Möbius strip the scalar surface integral \iint_S f\,dS is perfectly well defined, yet the flux integral \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS is not. What feature of flux, which area simply does not have, is the one that fails on a one-sided surface?

hint.p: Think about what each integral asks at a point. Does measuring a little patch of area require you to know which way the patch faces?

subsection.title: A field with nonzero flux because of a hidden singularity
subsection.p: The divergence theorem says \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV. But the field must be defined and differentiable throughout the solid E, not only on its boundary.

Consider again \mathbf G(x,y,z) = \frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}. Away from the origin, \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0. Now take the sphere S_a of radius a, oriented outward. On the sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a}, and \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}. Therefore
\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} \amp= \frac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}\cdot\frac{(x,y,z)}{a} \amp= \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a^4} \amp= \frac{a^2}{a^4} \amp= \frac1{a^2}.
Thus
\iint_{S_a}\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \frac1{a^2}\cdot 4\pi a^2 \amp= 4\pi.
It would be tempting to say: \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0, \qquad \text{so the flux should be }0. That is not allowed. The origin is inside the sphere, and the field is not defined there.
The missing point behaves like a source. The divergence calculation sees zero everywhere it is allowed to look, but the flux through the sphere reveals that something has been hidden inside.

exercise.title: Which hypothesis did the origin break?

statement.p: Someone argues: since \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0 everywhere we computed it, the divergence theorem forces the flux to be 0, so the value 4\pi must be an arithmetic slip. Which exact hypothesis of the divergence theorem does this argument quietly assume, and where in E does that hypothesis fail?

hint.p: The theorem asks for something to be true throughout the solid, not just on the boundary. Look at the single point the sphere encloses.

subsection.title: Stokes' theorem with incompatible orientations
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem needs the orientation of the surface and the orientation of its boundary to match.

Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac y2,\frac x2,0\right). Then \nabla\times\mathbf F=(0,0,1). Let D be the unit disk in the plane z=0, oriented upward. Then
\iint_D(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iint_D(0,0,1)\cdot(0,0,1)\,dS \amp= \pi.
The upward orientation gives the boundary circle the counterclockwise orientation as seen from above. With that direction, \oint_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\pi.

But now walk around the same circle clockwise. A convenient parametrization is \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,-\sin t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then \mathbf r'(t)=(-\sin t,-\cos t,0), and \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = \left(\frac{\sin t}{2},\frac{\cos t}{2},0\right). So
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(\frac{\sin t}{2},\frac{\cos t}{2},0\right) \cdot (-\sin t,-\cos t,0) \,dt \amp= -\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt \amp= -\pi.

The line integral is now -\pi, but the upward surface integral is still \pi. There is no contradiction. The clockwise boundary is not compatible with the upward normal. It would be compatible with the downward normal.
The theorem did not fail. The orientation choice failed.

statement.p: Here the surface integral gave \pi while the boundary integral gave -\pi, and yet we insist Stokes' theorem is unharmed. What unstated compatibility condition between the surface's normal and the boundary's direction had to hold for the two numbers to be required to agree?

hint.p: Ask which boundary direction the upward normal actually pairs with. The clockwise loop is the boundary of which orientation?

subsection.title: The divergence theorem on a region with an inner boundary
subsection.p: A region with a hole has more than one boundary piece. The divergence theorem counts all of them.

Let E be the spherical shell b\le r\le a, \qquad 0\lt b\lt a, where r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. Its boundary has two pieces: S_a:\ r=a, \qquad S_b:\ r=b. The outward normal on the outer sphere S_a points away from the origin. The outward normal on the inner sphere S_b, for the shell, points toward the origin.

Take the field \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z). Then \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=3. The divergence theorem gives
\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iiint_E 3\,dV \amp= 3\left(\frac43\pi a^3-\frac43\pi b^3\right) \amp= 4\pi(a^3-b^3).
Now check the boundary pieces.
On S_a, \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a}, so \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=a. Thus \iint_{S_a}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = a\cdot4\pi a^2 = 4\pi a^3.

On the inner sphere S_b, the outward normal for the shell is -\frac{(x,y,z)}{b}. So \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} = (x,y,z)\cdot\left(-\frac{(x,y,z)}{b}\right) = -b. Thus \iint_{S_b}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = -b\cdot4\pi b^2 = -4\pi b^3. Adding both pieces gives 4\pi a^3-4\pi b^3 = 4\pi(a^3-b^3), exactly as the divergence theorem predicted.
If we forget the inner boundary, we get 4\pi a^3, which is wrong. A hole has a boundary, and its outward direction is the one that points out of the material region, not out of the hole's center.

subsection.title: The common pattern in the warnings
subsection.p: The warnings all say the same thing in different clothes.

table.title: The four warnings and what each one breaks.

subsection.p: The formulas are powerful because they are precise. They are also unforgiving for the same reason.
Now we can step back and put the chapter in one place: surface area, flux, curl, divergence, and the three-dimensional versions of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

introduction.p: Chapter ended with Green's theorem in the plane: \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. This chapter moved that same shape into space. First we learned how to measure curved surfaces. Then we learned how to orient them. Then flux, curl, and divergence became surface and volume integrals.

subsection.title: The main objects

p.md: \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Object} \amp \text{Classical notation} \amp \text{Form notation} \\ \hline \text{work along a curve} \amp \displaystyle \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \displaystyle \int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz \\[3mm] \text{flux through a surface} \amp \displaystyle \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp \displaystyle \iint_S P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy \\[3mm] \text{volume integral} \amp \displaystyle \iiint_E f\,dV \amp \displaystyle \iiint_E f\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \end{array}

subsection.p: For a parametrized surface \mathbf r(u,v), the scalar area element is \boxed{dS=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv.} The oriented vector area element is \boxed{\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv,} provided the orientation is the one determined by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v.

For a graph z=g(x,y), the upward vector area element is \boxed{(-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dx\,dy.} So the upward flux of \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) through the graph is \boxed{\iint_R \bigl(-Pg_x-Qg_y+R\bigr)\,dx\,dy,} with P,Q,R evaluated at (x,y,g(x,y)).

subsection.title: Curl and divergence
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), the curl is \boxed{\nabla\times\mathbf F=(R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).} It measures circulation density.
In form notation, \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz has derivative \boxed{d\omega=(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.} This is the flux form of \nabla\times\mathbf F.
The flux form \Phi_{\mathbf F}=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy has derivative \boxed{d\Phi_{\mathbf F}=(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}

subsection.title: The two big theorems in space
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem turns boundary circulation into curl flux through a surface.
The divergence theorem turns boundary flux into total source strength inside a solid.

subsection.title: Skill checklist
subsection.p: By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to do the following.

li.p: Parametrize a surface and find \mathbf r_u,\mathbf r_v.
Compute dS=\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,du\,dv.
Choose or check the orientation of a surface.
Compute scalar surface integrals such as mass and area.
Compute flux through parametrized surfaces and graphs.
Translate a vector field into its flux 2-form.
Compute curl and use Stokes' theorem.
Compute divergence and use the divergence theorem.
Recognize when a theorem cannot be used because of orientation, missing boundary pieces, or singularities.

subsection.title: A worked review problem: choose the easier surface
subsection.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,z). Let C be the circle x^2+y^2=4,\qquad z=3, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above. Compute \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.
The curve bounds many surfaces. The easiest is the flat disk D:\quad x^2+y^2\le4,\qquad z=3, oriented upward.

Compute the curl:
\nabla\times\mathbf F \amp= (R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y) \amp= (0-0,\ 0-0,\ 1-(-1)) \amp= (0,0,2).
On the upward disk, \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,1). So
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp= \iint_D(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iint_D 2\,dS \amp= 2\cdot \operatorname{Area}(D) \amp= 2\cdot4\pi \amp= 8\pi.
Thus \boxed{\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=8\pi.}
The z-component of the original field did not affect the answer. Curl, not the field itself, is what Stokes' theorem sends through the spanning surface.

subsection.title: A worked review problem: close the surface
subsection.p: Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=9,\qquad z\ge0, oriented upward and outward. Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,2z). Find the flux through S.
The surface S is not closed. Close it with the disk D:\quad x^2+y^2\le9,\qquad z=0, oriented downward, so that S\cup D is the outward boundary of the upper half-ball.
The divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1+1+2=4. The volume of the upper half-ball of radius 3 is \frac12\cdot\frac43\pi(3)^3=18\pi. So the total outward flux through S\cup D is 4\cdot18\pi=72\pi.

On the disk D, we have z=0, so \mathbf F=(x,y,0). The downward normal is (0,0,-1). Thus \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=0. The disk contributes no flux. Therefore the flux through the hemisphere is \boxed{72\pi.}
The open surface was handled by adding the missing piece and then subtracting its contribution.

exercises.title: Project: fluid flow through a surface

introduction.p: A thin curved screen is stretched above a square frame: 0\le x\le1,\qquad 0\le y\le1, with height z=g(x,y)=1+\frac15\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). Air moves through the screen with velocity field \mathbf V(x,y,z)=\left(1,\,\frac12,\,2-\frac z4\right). Use the upward orientation.

statement.p: Show that the upward vector area element is (-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dx\,dy.
Compute g_x(x,y)=\frac{\pi}{5}\cos(\pi x)\sin(\pi y), and g_y(x,y)=\frac{\pi}{5}\sin(\pi x)\cos(\pi y).
Write the flux integral \iint_S\mathbf V\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS as a double integral over the unit square.
Explain the meanings of the three terms in \mathbf V(x,y,g)\cdot(-g_x,-g_y,1). Which parts come from horizontal wind hitting a tilted surface? Which part comes from vertical flow?
Evaluate the integral exactly if possible, or estimate it numerically.

conclusion.p: This project is a good test of the graph formula for flux. It also shows why horizontal velocity matters when a surface is tilted.

exercises.title: Project: electric flux and Gauss's law

introduction.p: For a point charge at the origin, the electric field has the radial form \mathbf E(x,y,z)=kq\,\frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}, where q is the charge and k is a constant depending on units.

statement.p: Compute the flux through a sphere of radius a centered at the origin.
Show that the answer does not depend on a.
Explain why the divergence theorem cannot be applied to the full ball x^2+y^2+z^2\le a^2.
Apply the divergence theorem to the spherical shell b\le r\le a to show that the flux through the outer sphere equals the flux through the inner sphere, with orientations handled correctly.
In physical units, k=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}. Show that the flux through any sphere centered at the charge is \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}.

conclusion.p: The calculation says that the total electric flux detects the charge inside, not the radius of the measuring sphere. The singularity at the origin is not a nuisance here. It is the source.

statement.p: Parametrize the side of the cone z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\qquad 0\le z\le3. Find its surface area.
Let S be the graph z=4-x^2-y^2,\qquad x^2+y^2\le1. Compute \iint_S z\,dS. This is a scalar surface integral, not a flux integral.
Let \mathbf F=(x,0,z). Compute the outward flux through the closed cylinder x^2+y^2\le4,\qquad 0\le z\le5 using the divergence theorem.
Compute the same flux in Problem 3 by adding the flux through the side, top, and bottom.
Let \mathbf F=(yz,zx,xy). Compute \nabla\times\mathbf F and \nabla\cdot\mathbf F.
Let \mathbf F=(0,xz,0). Verify directly that \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0.
Let C be the boundary of the triangle with vertices (0,0,0),\qquad (1,0,0),\qquad (0,1,0), oriented counterclockwise as seen from above. Use Stokes' theorem to compute \oint_C(-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz).

Let S be the part of the plane x+y+z=1 in the first octant, oriented upward. For \mathbf F=(z,x,y), compute \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS. Then check the answer by integrating \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r around the boundary.
Let \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy. Compute d\Phi. Then use it to find the outward flux of (x,y,z) through the unit sphere.
Explain why the flux of a vector field through a Möbius strip is not globally defined, but the surface area of the same strip is defined.
Let \mathbf A=\left(-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2},\frac{x}{x^2+y^2},0\right). Compute its line integral around the circle x^2+y^2=9,\qquad z=0, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above.
Let \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}. Compute its outward flux through the sphere of radius 5. Explain why the divergence theorem cannot be applied to the ball of radius 5.

subsection.title: The same theorem in four disguises
subsection.p: The chapter ends where the story has been leading since the single-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

In one variable, \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). The right side is an integral over the boundary of the interval: \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}. So the theorem can be written as \int_{[a,b]}df=\int_{\partial[a,b]}f.
Green's theorem says \int_R d\omega=\int_{\partial R}\omega. Stokes' theorem says \int_S d\omega=\int_{\partial S}\omega. The divergence theorem says \int_E d\Phi=\int_{\partial E}\Phi.
The same pattern keeps appearing: \boxed{\text{integral of a derivative over a region}=\text{integral of the original object over the boundary}.}
Or, in the order we have usually written it, \boxed{\int_{\partial(\text{region})}\text{form}=\int_{\text{region}}d(\text{form}).}

Chapter takes that repeated pattern seriously. Instead of treating dx, dy, dz, wedge products, work forms, flux forms, and volume forms as separate tools, we will build them as one family of objects designed for integration. The payoff is that all these theorems become one theorem. The name sounds larger than the idea: \text{the generalized Stokes theorem.}

part.title: Differential Forms and the Unified Theorem

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

introduction.p: Chapters 13 and 15 introduced work and flux integrals, and Chapter 12 introduced pullbacks of area and volume forms. This chapter gives these examples a common algebra: covectors measure tangent vectors, wedge products measure oriented pairs and triples, and pullbacks express those measurements in parameters.

section.title: What is a differential form?
section.p: A curve gives tiny tangent arrows. A surface gives tiny oriented parallelograms. A solid gives tiny oriented boxes. A differential form is a rule that knows how to measure one of those tiny objects.

subsection.title: Forms as objects designed to be integrated
subsection.p: Think of four measurements in a small laboratory.

A temperature reading at one point is just a number: T(P). A force measurement along a wire uses tiny displacements: P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. A flow measurement through a screen uses tiny oriented area pieces: P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy. A density measurement throughout a box uses tiny volume pieces: \rho\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Each expression is designed for a different dimension.
The degree tells us the dimension of the object the form measures.

figure.caption: A k-form is built to be integrated over k-dimensional oriented objects.

subsection.p: This is the guiding idea: \boxed{\text{A differential form is an object designed to be integrated.}}
The symbols dx, dy, dz, and their wedge products are not decorations. They tell the form what kind of tiny geometric piece it is measuring.

subsection.title: 0-forms: functions
subsection.p: A 0-form is a function.
For example, on the real line, f(x)=x^2 is a 0-form. On the plane, T(x,y)=20+\frac{6}{1+(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2} is also a 0-form. It assigns one number to each point.

The unusual part is integration. A 0-form is integrated over oriented points. An oriented point is just a point with a sign attached: +P \qquad\text{or}\qquad -P. We define \int_{+P} f=f(P), \qquad \int_{-P} f=-f(P).

This may look strange until we remember the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The oriented boundary of the interval [a,b] is \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}. So \int_{\partial[a,b]} f = f(b)-f(a). That is exactly the boundary term in \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a).

statement.p: A 0-form just records a number at each point, so why do we bother attaching a sign to the point we integrate over? What would we lose if every point were treated as positive?

hint.p: Picture the two endpoints of an interval in \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). Which endpoint contributes with which sign, and what would happen to that formula if both came in positively?

example.title: A function on the boundary of an interval

statement.p:
Let f(x)=x^2+1 and let I=[1,4]. Then \partial I=\{4\}-\{1\}. Therefore
\int_{\partial I} f \amp= f(4)-f(1) \amp= 17-2 \amp= 15.
The signs on the endpoints matter. The right endpoint is positive, and the left endpoint is negative.

subsection.p: This is why functions belong in the forms family. They are the forms of degree zero. They do not measure length, area, or volume. They measure signed points.

statement.p: A 0-form on a region D is a scalar function f:D\to\mathbb R. It is integrated over oriented 0-dimensional objects, which are signed collections of points.

subsection.p: Later, the exterior derivative will turn a 0-form into a 1-form: f \quad\longmapsto\quad df. That is the form version of taking a derivative.

subsection.title: 1-forms: line-measuring objects
subsection.p: A 1-form measures one tangent direction at a time. That is why it is integrated along a curve.

The work form of a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) is \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. At each tiny step along a curve, it adds P(\text{tiny }x\text{-change}) + Q(\text{tiny }y\text{-change}) + R(\text{tiny }z\text{-change}).

example.title: A turnstile that charges by displacement

statement.p: A robot moves across a warehouse floor. The cost of a tiny move is \omega=3\,dx+2\,dy. Moving east by one meter costs 3 units. Moving north by one meter costs 2 units. Moving west or south gives a negative cost, because the displacement is oriented.

Let the robot move from (0,0) to (4,1) along the straight path \mathbf r(t)=(4t,t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then dx=4\,dt, \qquad dy=dt. So
\int_C \omega \amp= \int_0^1 \bigl(3(4\,dt)+2(dt)\bigr) \amp= \int_0^1 14\,dt \amp= 14.
The 1-form did not measure how long the path was. It measured the oriented coordinate changes along the path.

A 1-form on a region D\subseteq\mathbb R^2 is an expression \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy. A 1-form on a region D\subseteq\mathbb R^3 is an expression \omega=P(x,y,z)\,dx+Q(x,y,z)\,dy+R(x,y,z)\,dz. It is integrated over oriented curves.

subsection.p: A 1-form changes sign when the orientation of the curve is reversed: \int_{-C}\omega=-\int_C\omega. That sign is part of the object. A 1-form is not an unsigned length density like \rho\,ds. The form P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz cares which way the curve is traveled.

subsection.title: 2-forms: surface-measuring objects
subsection.p: A 2-form measures an oriented area piece. In the plane, the basic area form is dx\wedge dy. So a typical 2-form in the plane is \alpha=M(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy.
On a positively oriented region in the xy-plane, this acts like M\,dA. But the wedge notation remembers the sign: dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy.

statement.p: Ordinary area does not care about order, yet the wedge insists that dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy. What information is the form trying to hold onto by refusing to let these two be equal?

hint.p: Think about which way you sweep around a little patch of the plane. A 2-form measures oriented area, so swapping the two directions is like flipping the patch over.

example.title: A signed paint layer on a floor tile

statement.p:
Let \alpha=(2+x)\,dx\wedge dy on the rectangle R=[0,3]\times[0,2], with the usual orientation of the plane. Then
\int_R \alpha \amp= \int_0^3\int_0^2 (2+x)\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^3 2(2+x)\,dx \amp= \left[4x+x^2\right]_0^3 \amp= 21.
If we reverse the orientation of R, the same form gives -21. The physical amount of paint would not become negative, but the oriented integral does. A 2-form measures signed area.

subsection.p: In space, a surface can have shadows on three coordinate planes. The basic 2-forms are dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx,\qquad dx\wedge dy. A general 2-form in space has the shape \Phi=A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy.
Flux forms are the main example: \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy for a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R).

example.title: Flow through a coordinate screen

statement.p:
Let \Phi=5\,dy\wedge dz+2\,dz\wedge dx. Take the screen x=1, \qquad 0\le y\le2, \qquad 0\le z\le3, oriented in the positive x-direction. A parametrization is \mathbf r(y,z)=(1,y,z). On this screen, dy\wedge dz is the positive area form. Also, dx=0, so dz\wedge dx=0. Thus \mathbf r^*\Phi=5\,dy\wedge dz. Therefore
\int_S \Phi \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^3 5\,dz\,dy \amp= 30.
Only the dy\wedge dz part crosses a screen perpendicular to the x-axis.

A 2-form on a region in the plane has the form \alpha=M(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy. A 2-form on a region in space has the form \Phi=A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy. It is integrated over oriented surfaces or oriented plane regions.

subsection.p: Surface area integrals such as \iint_S f\,dS do not need an orientation. A 2-form integral does. That is why flux is the natural surface integral for forms.

subsection.title: 3-forms: volume-measuring objects
subsection.p: A 3-form measures oriented volume in space. The basic volume form is dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. A typical 3-form is \Omega=H(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

statement.p: In three-dimensional space the volume form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is the top of the ladder. Conceptually, why can there be no genuine 4-form here, in terms of the kind of tiny object a form is supposed to measure?

hint.p: A k-form is built to measure k-dimensional oriented pieces. Ask yourself what a 4-dimensional tiny object would even look like sitting inside ordinary space.

example.title: Density in a storage box

statement.p:
A gas fills the box E=[0,2]\times[0,1]\times[0,3]. Suppose its density form is \Omega=(5+z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Using the usual orientation of space,
\int_E \Omega \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1\int_0^3 (5+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left[5z+\frac{z^2}{2}\right]_0^3 \,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \frac{39}{2} \,dy\,dx \amp= 39.
So the total mass is 39. If we reverse the orientation of space, the form integral becomes -39. For physical mass we usually keep the standard orientation fixed and report the positive number.
A 3-form on a region in space is an expression \Omega=H(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. It is integrated over oriented solid regions.

subsection.p: The whole family now fits into one picture:
subsection.md: \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Degree} \amp \text{Typical form} \amp \text{Tiny object measured} \amp \text{Integral} \\ \hline 0 \amp f \amp \text{oriented point} \amp \int_{\partial I} f\\[1mm] 1 \amp P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz \amp \text{oriented tangent vector} \amp \int_C \omega\\[1mm] 2 \amp A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy \amp \text{oriented parallelogram} \amp \int_S \Phi\\[1mm] 3 \amp H\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \amp \text{oriented box} \amp \int_E \Omega \end{array}
subsection.p: The table hides one important question. A 1-form is built from dx, dy, and dz. But what are these symbols really? They are not tiny numbers. They are linear measuring rules for tangent vectors. Giving those rules their proper name, covectors, is the next step.

section.title: Covectors and differentials
section.p: treated forms as integrands. A 1-form measures tiny tangent arrows along a curve, and a 2-form measures tiny oriented parallelograms on a surface. To understand the pieces of those forms, we start with the simplest question: what does dx do to a vector?

subsection.title: Linear functions on vectors
subsection.p: Stand on a flat loading dock. A small cart can move east, north, and up. Write one displacement as \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z). Suppose a scanner assigns the number L(\mathbf v)=4v_x-v_y+2v_z to that displacement. A move one meter east counts 4. A move one meter north counts -1. A move one meter upward counts 2.

This scanner is linear. If the cart makes two displacements, \mathbf u \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf v, then L(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=L(\mathbf u)+L(\mathbf v). If the displacement is doubled, the reading doubles: L(2\mathbf v)=2L(\mathbf v).

For example, let \mathbf u=(1,3,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(2,-1,4). Then L(\mathbf u)=4(1)-3+0=1 and L(\mathbf v)=4(2)-(-1)+2(4)=17. Also, \mathbf u+\mathbf v=(3,2,4), so L(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=4(3)-2+2(4)=18. Indeed, 18=1+17.
This is the kind of object hiding behind dx, dy, and dz.

statement.p: A covector at a point is a linear function that takes a tangent vector at that point and returns a number.
In \mathbb R^3, a covector has the form a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz at a point, and it acts on \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z) by \boxed{(a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz)(\mathbf v)=av_x+bv_y+cv_z.}

subsection.p: A vector points. A covector measures.

statement.p: A vector and a covector in \mathbb R^3 are each described by three numbers, so it is tempting to call them the same thing. What is the genuine difference in their jobs, and why does that difference deserve two separate names?

hint.p: Ask what each one does. One of them is something you can travel along; the other is a machine you feed a displacement to in order to get a number out.

subsection.p: They are related, especially when a dot product is available, but they are not the same kind of object.

subsection.title: dx, dy, and dz as coordinate covectors
subsection.p: The coordinate covectors are the simplest measuring rules: dx(\mathbf v)=v_x, dy(\mathbf v)=v_y, dz(\mathbf v)=v_z. They read the coordinate components of a tangent vector.

figure.caption: dx reads the horizontal component, and dy reads the vertical component.

subsection.p: For instance, if \mathbf v=(3,-5,2), then dx(\mathbf v)=3, \qquad dy(\mathbf v)=-5, \qquad dz(\mathbf v)=2.
A general covector is a linear combination of these coordinate covectors.

example.title: A covector from its coordinate readings

statement.p:
Let \eta=4\,dx-dy+2\,dz. Then on \mathbf v=(3,-5,2), we get
\eta(\mathbf v) \amp= 4\,dx(\mathbf v)-dy(\mathbf v)+2\,dz(\mathbf v) \amp= 4(3)-(-5)+2(2) \amp= 21.

subsection.p: The next theorem is the covector version of a familiar fact: a linear rule is determined by what it does to the standard basis vectors.

theorem.title: Every covector is a linear combination of coordinate covectors

proof.p:
Every vector \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z) can be written as \mathbf v=v_x\mathbf i+v_y\mathbf j+v_z\mathbf k. Since \eta is linear,
\eta(\mathbf v) \amp= v_x\eta(\mathbf i)+v_y\eta(\mathbf j)+v_z\eta(\mathbf k).
Let a=\eta(\mathbf i), \qquad b=\eta(\mathbf j), \qquad c=\eta(\mathbf k). Then \eta(\mathbf v)=av_x+bv_y+cv_z. But this is exactly (a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz)(\mathbf v). The coefficients are unique because applying the covector to \mathbf i,\mathbf j, and \mathbf k forces them.

subsection.p: In the plane, the same statement says every covector has the form a\,dx+b\,dy.

subsection.title: Evaluating a 1-form on a tangent vector
subsection.p: A covector lives at one point. A 1-form is a covector field: it attaches a covector to every point.

For example, \omega=(x+y)\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz is a 1-form in space. At the point \mathbf p=(2,1,-1), its coefficients become x+y=3, \qquad x=2, \qquad z=-1. So at that point, \omega_{\mathbf p}=3\,dx+2\,dy-dz.

Now evaluate it on the tangent vector \mathbf v=(3,-4,2). We get
\omega_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v) \amp= 3\,dx(\mathbf v)+2\,dy(\mathbf v)-dz(\mathbf v) \amp= 3(3)+2(-4)-2 \amp= -1.
The subscript matters: \omega_{\mathbf p} means the covector obtained by freezing the coefficient functions at the point \mathbf p.

statement.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be a 1-form on a region in space. At a point \mathbf p, and on a tangent vector \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z), we define \boxed{\omega_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=P(\mathbf p)v_x+Q(\mathbf p)v_y+R(\mathbf p)v_z.}

subsection.p: This is the local measurement behind every line integral.

If a curve is \mathbf r(t), then its tangent vector is \mathbf r'(t). At time t, the 1-form measures that tangent vector: \omega_{\mathbf r(t)}(\mathbf r'(t)). The line integral is obtained by adding those measurements over time: \boxed{\int_C \omega=\int_a^b \omega_{\mathbf r(t)}(\mathbf r'(t))\,dt.}

example.title: A form along a circular path

statement.p:
Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy and let \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then \mathbf r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t). At the point \mathbf r(t), the form is \omega_{\mathbf r(t)}=-\sin t\,dx+\cos t\,dy. Evaluate on the tangent vector:
\omega_{\mathbf r(t)}(\mathbf r'(t)) \amp= (-\sin t)(-\sin t)+(\cos t)(\cos t) \amp= 1.
Therefore \int_C \omega=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi. The form gives 1 on the counterclockwise unit tangent all the way around the circle.

subsection.p: This language separates two jobs. The curve supplies tangent vectors. The form measures them.

statement.p: A 1-form attaches a covector \omega_{\mathbf p} to every point \mathbf p. Conceptually, why must the measuring rule be allowed to change from point to point, rather than being a single fixed covector everywhere?

hint.p: Picture walking along a curve where the wind or terrain changes as you move. Should the rule that scores your tangent direction stay the same at every location?

subsection.title: Why gradients require a dot product but differentials do not
subsection.p: The differential of a function is a covector.

Let f(x,y,z) be differentiable at a point \mathbf p=(a,b,c). The best linear prediction for the change in f is df_{\mathbf p}=f_x(\mathbf p)\,dx+f_y(\mathbf p)\,dy+f_z(\mathbf p)\,dz. On a tangent vector \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z), this gives \boxed{df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=f_x(\mathbf p)v_x+f_y(\mathbf p)v_y+f_z(\mathbf p)v_z.}
This formula does not mention length or angle. It only uses how the function changes under a displacement.

The gradient vector appears when we use the usual Euclidean dot product. With that dot product, \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\bigl(f_x(\mathbf p),f_y(\mathbf p),f_z(\mathbf p)\bigr), and \boxed{df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf v.}

theorem.title: The differential is represented by the gradient in Euclidean space

statement.p: Let f be differentiable at \mathbf p\in\mathbb R^3, and use the usual dot product. Then the covector df_{\mathbf p} is represented by the gradient vector: \boxed{df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf v} for every tangent vector \mathbf v.

proof.p: Write \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z). By the definition of df_{\mathbf p}, df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=f_x(\mathbf p)v_x+f_y(\mathbf p)v_y+f_z(\mathbf p)v_z. By the definition of the usual dot product, \nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf v=\bigl(f_x(\mathbf p),f_y(\mathbf p),f_z(\mathbf p)\bigr)\cdot(v_x,v_y,v_z), which is the same expression.

subsection.p: The phrase use the usual dot product is doing real work.

exercise.title: What does the dot product add?

statement.p: The differential df_{\mathbf p} already turns a tangent vector into a number all by itself. So what extra ingredient does choosing a dot product supply, and why is the gradient vector unavailable until that choice is made?

hint.p: The differential measures; it never needs lengths or angles. The gradient is meant to be a vector that reproduces that measurement through a dot product, so something has to decide how vectors and measurements correspond.

example.title: The same differential can have different gradient vectors

statement.p: Take the function f(x,y)=3x+4y. Its differential is \boxed{df=3\,dx+4\,dy.} This covector is fixed. On a vector \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y), it gives df(\mathbf v)=3v_x+4v_y.
With the usual dot product, (a,b)\cdot(v_x,v_y)=av_x+bv_y, the representing gradient vector is \nabla f=(3,4).

Now change only the dot product. Suppose the geometry of the floor measures vertical motion with four times the weight: \langle (a,b),(v_x,v_y)\rangle_*=av_x+4bv_y. The same differential df=3\,dx+4\,dy is now represented by the vector \mathbf g=(3,1), because \langle (3,1),(v_x,v_y)\rangle_*=3v_x+4v_y=df(\mathbf v). So the differential did not change: df=3\,dx+4\,dy. The gradient vector changed because the dot product changed.

subsection.p: This is the moral:

p.md: \boxed{df \text{ is a covector. The gradient is the vector that represents } df \text{ after a dot product is chosen.}}

subsection.p: In ordinary Euclidean coordinates, the distinction is easy to miss because df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz and \nabla f=(f_x,f_y,f_z) use the same coefficients. But they have different jobs. The differential measures tangent vectors directly. The gradient is a vector chosen so that the dot product with a tangent vector gives the same measurement.

This distinction becomes more valuable as soon as we multiply covectors. A single covector measures one direction. To measure an oriented parallelogram, we need two directions at once. The operation that combines covectors into area-measuring forms is the wedge product.

section.title: The wedge product
section.p: ended with covectors. A covector measures one tangent vector. But a surface patch gives two tangent vectors, and a tiny box gives three. To measure oriented area and oriented volume, we need a way to combine covectors.
That way is the wedge product.

subsection.title: Oriented area from two covectors
subsection.p: Start with a small parallelogram in the plane. Its first edge is \mathbf u=(3,1), and its second edge is \mathbf v=(1,4). The ordered pair (\mathbf u,\mathbf v) means that we travel first in the \mathbf u-direction and then in the \mathbf v-direction. That order gives the parallelogram an orientation.

figure.caption: The signed area of a parallelogram depends on the order of its two edge vectors.

subsection.p:
The signed area is the determinant
\begin{vmatrix} 3\amp1\\ 1\amp4 \end{vmatrix} = 3\cdot4-1\cdot1 = 11.
Now write the same computation using the coordinate covectors dx,\qquad dy. They read components:
dx(\mathbf u)=3, \qquad dy(\mathbf u)=1,
and
dx(\mathbf v)=1, \qquad dy(\mathbf v)=4.
The signed area is dx(\mathbf u)dy(\mathbf v)-dx(\mathbf v)dy(\mathbf u). For our two vectors, this gives 3\cdot4-1\cdot1=11.
The symbol dx\wedge dy is the basic oriented area form in the xy-plane. It eats two tangent vectors and returns their signed xy-area.

example.title: The same parallelogram with reversed order

statement.p:
Use the same vectors
\mathbf u=(3,1), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,4),
but feed them to dx\wedge dy in the opposite order:
(dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf v,\mathbf u) \amp= dx(\mathbf v)dy(\mathbf u)-dx(\mathbf u)dy(\mathbf v) \amp= 1\cdot1-3\cdot4 \amp= -11.
The geometric parallelogram is the same size, but its orientation has been reversed.

subsection.p: This example contains the whole idea. The wedge product is built to measure oriented parallelograms.

statement.p:
Let \alpha and \beta be covectors at a point. Their wedge product \alpha\wedge\beta is the rule that takes an ordered pair of tangent vectors (\mathbf u,\mathbf v) and returns
\boxed{ (\alpha\wedge\beta)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) = \alpha(\mathbf u)\beta(\mathbf v) - \alpha(\mathbf v)\beta(\mathbf u). }

subsection.p: The two terms are the two possible ways to match the covectors with the two vectors. The minus sign is what remembers orientation.

example.title: A wedge product that measures a slanted coordinate area

statement.p:
Let
\alpha=2\,dx+dy, \qquad \beta=dx+3\,dy.
Use the vectors
\mathbf u=(1,2), \qquad \mathbf v=(4,-1).
First evaluate the covectors:
\alpha(\mathbf u)=2(1)+2=4, \qquad \alpha(\mathbf v)=2(4)-1=7,
and
\beta(\mathbf u)=1+3(2)=7, \qquad \beta(\mathbf v)=4+3(-1)=1.
Therefore
(\alpha\wedge\beta)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= \alpha(\mathbf u)\beta(\mathbf v) - \alpha(\mathbf v)\beta(\mathbf u) \amp= 4\cdot1-7\cdot7 \amp= -45.
The negative sign says that the ordered measurements \alpha,\beta see the ordered vectors \mathbf u,\mathbf v with the opposite orientation.

subsection.p: A 1-form measures one vector. A wedge of two 1-forms measures two vectors at once. That is why it becomes a 2-form.

subsection.title: Antisymmetry: dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx
subsection.p:
The wedge product changes sign when its factors are swapped. Check this directly:
(\beta\wedge\alpha)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= \beta(\mathbf u)\alpha(\mathbf v) - \beta(\mathbf v)\alpha(\mathbf u) \amp= -\left[ \alpha(\mathbf u)\beta(\mathbf v) - \alpha(\mathbf v)\beta(\mathbf u) \right].
So
\boxed{ \beta\wedge\alpha=-\alpha\wedge\beta. }

example.title: The same area measured with dy\wedge dx

statement.p:
Return again to
\mathbf u=(3,1), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,4).
Then
(dy\wedge dx)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= dy(\mathbf u)dx(\mathbf v)-dy(\mathbf v)dx(\mathbf u) \amp= 1\cdot1-4\cdot3 \amp= -11.
But (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=11. So dy\wedge dx measures the same area with the opposite orientation.

subsection.p: This is the first algebra rule of wedge products:
That sign is not a bookkeeping trick. It is the algebraic form of a geometric fact: swapping the two edge directions of a parallelogram reverses its orientation.

exercise.title: What is the minus sign really saying?

statement.p: We found dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. Setting aside the algebra, what geometric fact about a parallelogram is this minus sign recording? Why should reversing the order of the two edge directions flip the sign of the area rather than its size?

hint.p: Picture walking around the parallelogram's boundary. What changes about the direction of that walk when you list the edges in the opposite order?

subsection.title: Why dx\wedge dx=0
subsection.p: The geometry is simple. A single coordinate reading repeated twice cannot measure area. Area needs two independent directions of measurement. Measuring the x-component twice collapses the picture onto one line.

exercise.title: Why must a covector wedged with itself vanish?

statement.p: We get dx\wedge dx=0, and more generally \alpha\wedge\alpha=0 for any covector \alpha. Without redoing the computation, explain why this has to happen. What does it mean to try to build an oriented area out of a single direction of measurement?

hint.p: Area needs two independent directions. If you only ever read the same component, how many genuinely different directions are you measuring?

example.title: Parallel edge vectors give zero area

statement.p:
Let
\mathbf u=(2,1), \qquad \mathbf v=(6,3).
The second vector is \mathbf v=3\mathbf u. The parallelogram has collapsed to a line segment, so its signed area should be 0. Indeed,
(dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= 2\cdot3-6\cdot1 \amp= 0.
The wedge product automatically detects the collapse.

subsection.p: This is one reason wedge notation is so useful. The rules dx\wedge dx=0 and dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx make repeated or reversed directions behave exactly as oriented area says they should.

subsection.title: Building 2-forms and 3-forms
subsection.p: In the plane, there is only one basic oriented area form: dx\wedge dy. So every 2-form in the plane has the shape M(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy.

In space, a small surface patch can cast shadows on three coordinate planes. That is why three basic 2-forms appear: dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx,\qquad dx\wedge dy. Each one measures a signed shadow.

example.title: A 2-form measuring a tilted surface patch

statement.p:
Suppose a small surface patch has tangent edge vectors
\mathbf u=(1,2,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,3).
Compute the three coordinate shadow areas:
(dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= 2\cdot3-1\cdot0 = 6, (dz\wedge dx)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= 0\cdot0-3\cdot1 = -3, (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= 1\cdot1-0\cdot2 = 1.
Now let \Phi=2\,dy\wedge dz-dz\wedge dx+4\,dx\wedge dy. Then
\Phi(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp= 2(6)-(-3)+4(1) \amp= 19.
The form did not measure ordinary surface area. It measured an oriented combination of coordinate-plane shadows.

subsection.p: A 3-form measures an oriented box. The basic one in space is dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. It eats three tangent vectors and returns the signed volume of the parallelepiped they span.

example.title: A 3-form measuring volume

statement.p:
Let
\mathbf u=(1,0,0), \qquad \mathbf v=(1,2,0), \qquad \mathbf w=(0,1,3).
Then
(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w) \amp= \det \begin{pmatrix} 1\amp1\amp0\\ 0\amp2\amp1\\ 0\amp0\amp3 \end{pmatrix} \amp= 6.
So the oriented volume of the box spanned by these three ordered vectors is 6. If we swap \mathbf u and \mathbf v, the value becomes -6.

exercise.title: Why three basic 2-forms in space but only one in the plane?

statement.p: In the plane a 2-form has just one piece, dx\wedge dy, yet in space we need three: dy\wedge dz, dz\wedge dx, and dx\wedge dy. What is it about a surface patch sitting in three dimensions that forces three measurements, when a patch in the plane needs only one?

hint.p: Think about the shadows a tilted patch casts onto the coordinate planes. How many coordinate planes are there to cast a shadow on in the plane, and how many in space?

subsection.title: Determinants as wedge-product coefficients
subsection.p: The wedge product explains why determinants keep appearing in multivariable calculus. They are the coefficients of oriented area and oriented volume.

Start in the plane. Let
\alpha=a\,dx+b\,dy, \qquad \beta=c\,dx+d\,dy.
Then
\alpha\wedge\beta \amp= (a\,dx+b\,dy)\wedge(c\,dx+d\,dy) \amp= ac\,dx\wedge dx +ad\,dx\wedge dy +bc\,dy\wedge dx +bd\,dy\wedge dy.
Now use
dx\wedge dx=0, \qquad dy\wedge dy=0,
and dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy. The result is
\boxed{ \alpha\wedge\beta=(ad-bc)\,dx\wedge dy. }
The coefficient ad-bc is a 2\times2 determinant:
\boxed{ ad-bc = \begin{vmatrix} a\amp b\\ c\amp d \end{vmatrix}. }

example.title: The determinant inside a wedge product

statement.p:
Let
\alpha=2\,dx+dy, \qquad \beta=dx+4\,dy.
Then
\alpha\wedge\beta \amp= (2\cdot4-1\cdot1)\,dx\wedge dy \amp= 7\,dx\wedge dy.
The number 7 is the signed area scale factor hidden in the two covectors.

subsection.p:
In space, wedge two 1-forms: \alpha=a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz, and \beta=p\,dx+q\,dy+r\,dz. A direct expansion gives
\boxed{ \alpha\wedge\beta = (br-cq)\,dy\wedge dz + (cp-ar)\,dz\wedge dx + (aq-bp)\,dx\wedge dy. }
The three coefficients are the components of the cross product of the coefficient vectors:
(a,b,c)\times(p,q,r) = (br-cq,\ cp-ar,\ aq-bp).
So the cross product is also hiding inside the wedge product. The wedge product keeps the result as a 2-form, while the cross product turns the same coefficients into a vector.

For three 1-forms, \alpha=a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz, \beta=p\,dx+q\,dy+r\,dz, and \gamma=m\,dx+n\,dy+s\,dz, the wedge product is
\boxed{ \alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma = \begin{vmatrix} a\amp b\amp c\\ p\amp q\amp r\\ m\amp n\amp s \end{vmatrix} dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

example.title: A triple wedge product

statement.p:
Let
\alpha=dx+dy, \qquad \beta=2\,dy+dz, \qquad \gamma=3\,dx-dz.
Then
\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma = \begin{vmatrix} 1\amp1\amp0\\ 0\amp2\amp1\\ 3\amp0\amp-1 \end{vmatrix} dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Compute the determinant:
\begin{vmatrix} 1\amp1\amp0\\ 0\amp2\amp1\\ 3\amp0\amp-1 \end{vmatrix} \amp= 1(2(-1)-1\cdot0) - 1(0(-1)-1\cdot3) \amp= -2-(-3) \amp= 1.
So
\boxed{ \alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma = dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

subsection.p: The wedge product has now given us the basic measuring objects. But forms in real integrals do not usually have constant coefficients. They have functions attached to them, and we need to add them, scale them, and multiply them without losing track of degree. That is the algebra of forms.

section.title: Algebra of forms
section.p: The wedge product gives the multiplication rule. Now we need the everyday algebra: adding forms, multiplying them by functions, and keeping signs straight. The main rule is simple: the degree tells us what kind of object the form measures, so the degree must be respected.

subsection.title: Adding forms of the same degree
subsection.p:
Two 1-forms can be added because both measure tangent vectors. For example, \omega_1=3\,dx-y\,dy and \omega_2=x\,dx+2\,dy combine to make
\omega_1+\omega_2 \amp= (3\,dx-y\,dy)+(x\,dx+2\,dy) \amp= (x+3)\,dx+(2-y)\,dy.
On any tangent vector, the new form gives the sum of the two old readings.

example.title: Two small meters along a path

statement.p: A cart moves in the plane. One meter charges \omega_1=2\,dx+dy, and another charges \omega_2=-dx+4\,dy. Together they charge \omega_1+\omega_2=dx+5\,dy. If the cart has tangent vector \mathbf v=(3,-1), then \omega_1(\mathbf v)=2(3)+(-1)=5, and \omega_2(\mathbf v)=-3+4(-1)=-7. The combined reading is 5+(-7)=-2. Using the combined form directly, (dx+5\,dy)(\mathbf v)=3+5(-1)=-2.

subsection.p: The same rule works for 2-forms. In space, \Phi_1=A_1\,dy\wedge dz+B_1\,dz\wedge dx+C_1\,dx\wedge dy and \Phi_2=A_2\,dy\wedge dz+B_2\,dz\wedge dx+C_2\,dx\wedge dy add to \boxed{\Phi_1+\Phi_2=(A_1+A_2)\,dy\wedge dz+(B_1+B_2)\,dz\wedge dx+(C_1+C_2)\,dx\wedge dy.} Two 3-forms add in the same way: H_1\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz+H_2\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=(H_1+H_2)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

We do not add a 1-form and a 2-form as a single form in this book. They measure different kinds of objects. The expression dx+dx\wedge dy contains a line-measuring part and an area-measuring part. Advanced books allow such mixed objects, but here we keep each degree separate.

exercise.title: Why can't we add a line and an area?

statement.p: We freely add two 1-forms, yet we refuse to add a 1-form and a 2-form into a single form. What is it about the meaning of a form's degree that makes the second sum a different kind of thing entirely?
Forms of the same degree are added coefficient by coefficient. The sum has the same degree.

subsection.title: Multiplying forms by functions
subsection.p: A function is a 0-form. It assigns a number to each point. Multiplying a form by a function scales the form point by point.
For example, if \omega=dx+2\,dy and f(x,y)=1+x^2, then \boxed{f\omega=(1+x^2)\,dx+2(1+x^2)\,dy.} At the point (2,1), the scaling factor is f(2,1)=5. So at that point, (f\omega)_{(2,1)}=5\,dx+10\,dy.

example.title: A position-dependent toll

statement.p: A robot moves across a warehouse floor. The basic motion charge is \omega=3\,dx+dy. Near a loading area, the cost is multiplied by f(x,y)=1+\frac{x}{10}. The actual cost form is f\omega=\left(1+\frac{x}{10}\right)(3\,dx+dy). So f\omega=\left(3+\frac{3x}{10}\right)dx+\left(1+\frac{x}{10}\right)dy. At x=0, the original cost is unchanged. At x=10, the whole form is doubled.

subsection.p: For 2-forms, f\left(A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy\right) means \boxed{fA\,dy\wedge dz+fB\,dz\wedge dx+fC\,dx\wedge dy.} For 3-forms, f\left(H\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz\right)=fH\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

definition.title: Multiplying a form by a function

statement.p: If f is a function and \omega is a k-form, then f\omega is the k-form obtained by multiplying every coefficient of \omega by f.
