subsection.title: Wedge products of forms of different degrees

table.title: Degree of a wedge product.

subsection.p: In \mathbb R^3, any product whose degree is greater than 3 is zero. There is no nonzero 4-dimensional volume in three-dimensional space.

exercise.title: Why does space itself set a ceiling?

statement.p: In \mathbb R^3 every form of degree greater than 3 collapses to zero, and in \mathbb R^n the ceiling sits at degree n. Why should the dimension of the space we live in decide the highest degree a nonzero form can have?

hint.p: A degree-k wedge is built from k basic 1-forms, each pointing along a coordinate direction. If k exceeds the number of independent directions available, some direction must repeat. Recall what a repeated factor does to a wedge.

subsection.p: The most useful new case is 1\text{-form}\wedge 2\text{-form}. Let \alpha=A\,dx+B\,dy+C\,dz and \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy. Then \alpha\wedge\Phi=(A\,dx+B\,dy+C\,dz)\wedge(P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy). Most terms contain a repeated factor, such as dx\wedge dz\wedge dx or dy\wedge dy\wedge dz. Those terms are zero. The surviving terms are AP\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, BQ\,dy\wedge dz\wedge dx, and CR\,dz\wedge dx\wedge dy. Both dy\wedge dz\wedge dx and dz\wedge dx\wedge dy are the same orientation as dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Therefore \boxed{\alpha\wedge\Phi=(AP+BQ+CR)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}

example.title: A 1-form wedged with a flux 2-form

statement.p:
Let \alpha=2\,dx-dy+3\,dz and \Phi=4\,dy\wedge dz+5\,dz\wedge dx+2\,dx\wedge dy. Then A=2,\qquad B=-1,\qquad C=3, and P=4,\qquad Q=5,\qquad R=2. So
\alpha\wedge\Phi \amp= (2\cdot4+(-1)\cdot5+3\cdot2)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \amp= 9\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
The product is a 3-form, so it is ready to be integrated over a solid.

subsection.p: There is a familiar pattern in the coefficient AP+BQ+CR. It looks like a dot product. That is not an accident. With the flux convention \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy, wedging a 1-form with \Phi pairs their coefficient triples by the dot product.

subsection.title: Sign rules and degree
subsection.p: The basic sign rule dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx comes from swapping two 1-forms. For larger forms, the same idea counts how many swaps are needed.

For example, (dy\wedge dz)\wedge dx=dy\wedge dz\wedge dx. To compare this with dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, move dx left past dz, then past dy. That is two swaps. Each swap changes the sign, so two swaps restore the sign: dy\wedge dz\wedge dx=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Thus \boxed{(dy\wedge dz)\wedge dx=dx\wedge(dy\wedge dz).} A 2-form and a 1-form commute in this case because two sign changes occur.
Here is the general rule.

statement.p: If \alpha is a k-form and \beta is an \ell-form, then \boxed{\beta\wedge\alpha=(-1)^{k\ell}\alpha\wedge\beta.}

proof.p: First expand each form as a sum of coefficient functions times wedges of coordinate 1-forms. It is enough, by distributivity, to compare one term from each sum. Such a term of \alpha has k basic 1-form factors, and a term of \beta has \ell factors. To move that term of \beta past \alpha, each of the \ell factors in \beta must pass each of the k factors in \alpha. That makes k\ell swaps. Each swap contributes a minus sign. Hence the total sign is (-1)^{k\ell}.

subsection.p: The common cases are the following.

table.title: Swap signs for common degrees.

subsection.p: The last line is rarely used in \mathbb R^3, because a 2-form wedged with a 2-form has degree 4, and every 4-form in \mathbb R^3 is zero.

example.title: One swap versus two swaps

statement.p: One swap changes sign: dy\wedge dx\wedge dz=-dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Two swaps do not: dz\wedge dx\wedge dy=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Indeed, move dz from the front to the end: dz\wedge dx\wedge dy=-dx\wedge dz\wedge dy=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

subsection.p: A repeated factor always kills a wedge product: dx\wedge dy\wedge dx=0. To see why, move the final dx left past dy: dx\wedge dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dx\wedge dy=0. Geometrically, two of the measurements are the same, so the oriented volume collapses.

exercise.title: What is the minus sign trying to tell us?

statement.p: The graded rule \beta\wedge\alpha=(-1)^{k\ell}\alpha\wedge\beta can feel like bookkeeping. But when swapping two factors flips the sign, what real feature of the geometry is that minus sign keeping track of, and why does a repeated factor then have to give zero?

hint.p: Think of the wedge as recording oriented volume. Swapping two directions reverses the orientation, the way exchanging two rows flips a determinant. Then ask what orientation an oriented region could possibly have if two of its directions coincide.

subsection.title: Common computations in \mathbb R^2 and \mathbb R^3
subsection.p: The following formulas are the ones that appear most often.
In the plane, if \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy and \eta=R\,dx+S\,dy, then \boxed{\omega\wedge\eta=(PS-QR)\,dx\wedge dy.}

example.title: A plane computation

statement.p:
Let \omega=(x+1)\,dx+2y\,dy and \eta=3\,dx+x\,dy. Then
\omega\wedge\eta \amp= \bigl((x+1)x-(2y)(3)\bigr)\,dx\wedge dy \amp= (x^2+x-6y)\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.p: In space, if \alpha=a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz and \beta=p\,dx+q\,dy+r\,dz, then \boxed{\alpha\wedge\beta=(br-cq)\,dy\wedge dz+(cp-ar)\,dz\wedge dx+(aq-bp)\,dx\wedge dy.}

example.title: Two 1-forms in space

statement.p: Let \alpha=2\,dx-dy+3\,dz, and \beta=dx+4\,dy-dz. Here (a,b,c)=(2,-1,3),\qquad (p,q,r)=(1,4,-1). The coefficients are br-cq=(-1)(-1)-3(4)=-11, cp-ar=3(1)-2(-1)=5, and aq-bp=2(4)-(-1)(1)=9. Therefore \boxed{\alpha\wedge\beta=-11\,dy\wedge dz+5\,dz\wedge dx+9\,dx\wedge dy.}

subsection.p: If \alpha=A\,dx+B\,dy+C\,dz and \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy, then \boxed{\alpha\wedge\Phi=(AP+BQ+CR)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.} Since a 1-form and a 2-form commute, \boxed{\Phi\wedge\alpha=\alpha\wedge\Phi.}

For three 1-forms, \alpha=a\,dx+b\,dy+c\,dz, \beta=p\,dx+q\,dy+r\,dz, and \gamma=m\,dx+n\,dy+s\,dz, we have \boxed{\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma=\begin{vmatrix}a\amp b\amp c\\p\amp q\amp r\\m\amp n\amp s\end{vmatrix}dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}

These formulas are enough for most computations in this book. They also explain why determinants, dot products, and cross products keep returning. They are different ways of reading wedge products through the coordinate system.

One problem remains before we can integrate forms fluently. A curve is usually given by a parameter t, and a surface by parameters u,v. The form may live in x,y,z-space, while the actual calculation happens in the parameter domain. The operation that carries a form back to the parameters is ordinary substitution with a better name: the pullback.

section.title: Pullbacks
section.p: ended with a practical problem. A form may be written in x,y,z-space, but the actual calculation may happen in a parameter domain. A curve uses a parameter t. A surface uses parameters u,v. A change of coordinates may use r,\theta,z or \rho,\phi,\theta.
So we need one operation that answers this question:
section.md: \text{How does a form look after we substitute the parametrization?}
section.p: That operation is called the pullback. The name sounds abstract, but the idea is ordinary substitution, done carefully enough to remember dx, dy, dz, and wedge products.

subsection.title: Substitution as the pullback idea
subsection.p: In the substitution calculations below, an equation such as dx=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv abbreviates T^*(dx)=d(x\circ T), where the x on the right is the target coordinate function. The coordinate covector dx lives in the target; its pullback lives in the parameter domain. These equations identify their measurements after substitution, not covectors on two different spaces without a map between them.

exercise.title: Why does the form move backward?

statement.p: The map T sends points forward, from the (u,v)-world to the (x,y)-world, yet T^* carries the form \omega the other way, from (x,y) back to (u,v). Why is it natural for a form to travel opposite to the points, rather than alongside them?

hint.p: Think about what a form does for a living: it waits to be fed a coordinate direction and report a number. If you only know how to build directions in the (u,v)-world, which world must the form end up living in so it can read them?

exercise.title: Where did the cross product come from?

statement.p: Nothing in the setup of \mathbf r^*\Phi mentioned a cross product, yet the three coefficients turned out to be exactly the components of \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. What is it about pulling back a 2-form through the wedge product that forces this cross product to appear on its own?

hint.p: Each basic 2-form like dy\wedge dz pulls back to a 2\times 2 determinant in the parameter derivatives. Recall how a cross product is assembled out of 2\times 2 determinants of the same columns.

subsection.p: The pullback is not just a computational convenience. It is what makes it possible to integrate a form over a curved surface by integrating an ordinary form over a flat parameter region.

subsection.title: The Jacobian determinant from wedge products
subsection.p: The Jacobian determinant is not a mysterious correction factor. It is the coefficient of a pulled-back volume form.

exercise.title: What does the Jacobian's sign mean?

statement.p: When T^*(dx\wedge dy) produces a negative Jacobian coefficient, the ordinary change-of-variables formula would simply take its absolute value. What information is the bare wedge product holding onto that the absolute value throws away, and why might we sometimes want to keep it?

hint.p: Ask what a sign could possibly be recording about the map T itself. Picture a small loop traced counterclockwise in the (u,v)-square and what happens to its turning direction after T sends it into the (x,y)-plane.

example.title: A reflection remembers its sign

statement.p: Let
Then
So
The map reflects the parameter square across a horizontal line. It preserves ordinary area but reverses orientation.
If we were computing unsigned area, the scale factor would be 1. But for an oriented 2-form, the scale factor is -1.

subsection.p: A pullback therefore does two jobs at once. It performs substitution, and it keeps track of how oriented length, area, or volume changes. Once a form has been pulled back to a parameter domain, the only remaining step is to integrate it.

section.title: Integrating forms
section.p: A pullback turns a form on a curve, surface, or solid into a form on a simple parameter domain. That is the bridge from geometry to calculation.
Now we define the integral of a form by crossing that bridge: \boxed{\text{pull back first, then integrate on the parameter domain.}}
This is the same procedure we have been using all along for line integrals, surface integrals, and change of variables. The difference is that the form notation lets us say all three at once.

subsection.title: Integrating 1-forms over oriented curves
subsection.p: Let C be an oriented curve in space, and let \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^3 be a parametrization that follows the chosen orientation of C. If \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, then \mathbf r^*\omega=\bigl[P(\mathbf r(t))x'(t)+Q(\mathbf r(t))y'(t)+R(\mathbf r(t))z'(t)\bigr]\,dt. We define \boxed{\int_C\omega=\int_a^b \mathbf r^*\omega.} In expanded form, \boxed{\int_C\omega=\int_a^b\bigl[P(\mathbf r(t))x'(t)+Q(\mathbf r(t))y'(t)+R(\mathbf r(t))z'(t)\bigr]\,dt.}

statement.p: A curve is one-dimensional, and the object we integrate over it is a 1-form. Looking at the definition above, what is it about the pullback \mathbf r^*\omega=g(t)\,dt that makes a 1-form exactly the right kind of thing to integrate over a curve, rather than a 2-form or a plain function?

hint.p: The parameter domain [a,b] is one-dimensional. Count how many dt factors you need before \int_a^b has something to act on.

definition.title: Integral of a 1-form over a curve

statement.p: Let C be an oriented piecewise smooth curve, and let \omega be a 1-form. Choose a parametrization \mathbf r(t) that traces C once in the chosen orientation. Then \boxed{\int_C\omega=\int \mathbf r^*\omega.} If the curve has corners, integrate over each smooth piece and add the results.

example.title: Circulation around a fountain

statement.p:
Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy. Let C be the circle of radius 3, oriented counterclockwise: \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-3\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=3\cos t\,dt. Also, x=3\cos t,\qquad y=3\sin t. So
\mathbf r^*\omega \amp= -(3\sin t)(-3\sin t\,dt)+(3\cos t)(3\cos t\,dt) \amp= 9(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt \amp= 9\,dt.
Therefore \boxed{\int_C\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}9\,dt=18\pi.} The same form on the unit circle gave 2\pi. On a circle of radius 3, the value is 9 times as large because this form measures twice the signed area swept out by the circle.

subsection.p: In vector language, if \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), then \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is the work form of \mathbf F, and \int_C\omega=\int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r. The form notation keeps the coordinate changes visible: dx,\ dy,\ dz are exactly the pieces that the parametrization pulls back to x'(t)\,dt,\ y'(t)\,dt,\ z'(t)\,dt.

subsection.title: Integrating 2-forms over oriented surfaces
subsection.p: Let S be an oriented surface, and let \mathbf r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3 be a parametrization that matches the chosen orientation. Matching the orientation means that the normal direction \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v points to the chosen side of the surface.

If \Phi=A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy, then \mathbf r^*\Phi is a 2-form on the parameter domain: \mathbf r^*\Phi=G(u,v)\,du\wedge dv. We define \boxed{\int_S\Phi=\iint_D \mathbf r^*\Phi.} In coefficient form, \boxed{\int_S\Phi=\iint_D G(u,v)\,du\,dv,} where
G(u,v) \amp= A(\mathbf r)(y_u z_v-y_v z_u)+B(\mathbf r)(z_u x_v-z_v x_u) \amp\qquad+C(\mathbf r)(x_u y_v-x_v y_u).

For a flux form \Phi_{\mathbf F}=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy, this becomes \boxed{\int_S\Phi_{\mathbf F}=\iint_D\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv.} That is the classical flux integral.

definition.title: Integral of a 2-form over a surface

statement.p: Let S be an oriented piecewise smooth surface, and let \Phi be a 2-form. Choose a parametrization \mathbf r:D\to S that covers the surface once, except possibly along boundary curves, and whose orientation agrees with the chosen orientation of S. Then \boxed{\int_S\Phi=\iint_D\mathbf r^*\Phi.} If the surface is made from several patches, integrate over the patches and add the results.

example.title: Flux through the side of a cylinder

statement.p: Let S be the side of the cylinder x^2+y^2=4,\qquad 0\le z\le3, oriented outward. Parametrize it by \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), where 0\le \theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le3. Then \mathbf r_\theta=(-2\sin\theta,2\cos\theta,0),\qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1), so \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,0), which points outward.

Take the flux form for the vector field \mathbf F=(x,y,z): \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy. We can use the flux formula: \mathbf F(\mathbf r(\theta,z))=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), and
\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot(\mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z) \amp= (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z)\cdot(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,0) \amp= 4\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta \amp= 4.
Thus \mathbf r^*\Phi=4\,d\theta\wedge dz. Therefore \boxed{\begin{aligned}\int_S\Phi\amp=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3 4\,dz\,d\theta\\ \amp=24\pi.\end{aligned}} The same answer would be called the outward flux of \mathbf F through the cylinder side in vector calculus notation.

subsection.p: The surface orientation is not optional. If the same cylinder were oriented inward, the normal vector would be reversed, and the integral would become -24\pi.

subsection.title: Integrating 3-forms over regions in space
subsection.p: A 3-form in space has the shape \Omega=H(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. With the standard orientation of space, we integrate it over a solid region E by \boxed{\int_E \Omega=\iiint_E H(x,y,z)\,dV.} Here dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is the standard oriented volume form.

If we use a coordinate map that covers the interior once and preserves the chosen orientation, T(u,v,w)=(x,y,z), then \int_E\Omega is computed by pulling back: \boxed{\int_E\Omega=\iiint_{D} T^*\Omega,} where D is the parameter region.

definition.title: Integral of a 3-form over a solid

statement.p: Let E be an oriented solid region in space, and let \Omega=H\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. With the standard orientation, \boxed{\int_E\Omega=\iiint_E H\,dV.} If E is described by a smooth coordinate map T:D\to E that is one-to-one and onto in the interiors, has nonzero Jacobian there, and carries the orientation of D to the chosen orientation of E, then \boxed{\int_E\Omega=\iiint_D T^*\Omega.}

example.title: A density form in a cylinder

subsection.p: For physical mass, we usually think of (1+z)\,dV as a positive density times positive volume. The form (1+z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is the oriented version. With the standard orientation, the numbers agree.

subsection.title: Parametrization independence
subsection.p: An integral over a curve or surface should depend on the oriented geometric object, not on the particular clock or grid used to describe it.
That statement is true when the new parametrization covers the same object exactly once and preserves orientation.

exercise.title: What is the integral really about?

statement.p: We say the integral depends on the oriented geometric object, not on the clock or grid used to describe it. In your own words, why should we expect a quantity like circulation or flux to be independent of the chosen parametrization, and what role does the substitution rule play in turning that expectation into a fact?

hint.p: Think about what the parametrization is and is not part of: it names the points, but it does not change which oriented curve or surface you are standing on. The Jacobian factor from the substitution rule is exactly what cancels the change of clock.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n parametrize an oriented curve C, and let \phi:[\alpha,\beta]\to[a,b] be smooth, one-to-one, onto, and increasing. In particular, \phi(\alpha)=a and \phi(\beta)=b. Then \widetilde{\mathbf r}(s)=\mathbf r(\phi(s)) parametrizes the same curve with the same orientation, and for every 1-form \omega, \boxed{\int_\alpha^\beta \widetilde{\mathbf r}^{\,*}\omega=\int_a^b \mathbf r^*\omega.}

proof.p: Suppose \mathbf r^*\omega=g(t)\,dt. Then \widetilde{\mathbf r}^{\,*}\omega=g(\phi(s))\phi'(s)\,ds. Therefore \int_\alpha^\beta \widetilde{\mathbf r}^{\,*}\omega=\int_\alpha^\beta g(\phi(s))\phi'(s)\,ds. By the single-variable substitution rule, this equals \int_a^b g(t)\,dt=\int_a^b \mathbf r^*\omega.

example.title: The same segment with a different clock

statement.p: Let C be the line segment from (0,0) to (1,1), and let \omega=x\,dy. First parametrize by \mathbf r(t)=(t,t),\qquad 0\le t\le1. Then x=t,\qquad dy=dt, so \mathbf r^*\omega=t\,dt. Hence \int_C\omega=\int_0^1 t\,dt=\frac12.

Now use the slower clock \widetilde{\mathbf r}(s)=\left(\frac{s}{2},\frac{s}{2}\right),\qquad 0\le s\le2. Then x=\frac{s}{2},\qquad dy=\frac12\,ds. So \widetilde{\mathbf r}^{\,*}\omega=\frac{s}{4}\,ds. Therefore \int_0^2 \frac{s}{4}\,ds=\frac12. The clock changed, but the oriented curve did not.

subsection.p: The hypotheses matter.

example.title: Tracing twice is not a harmless reparametrization

statement.p: Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy on the unit circle.

The once-around parametrization \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, gives \int_C\omega=2\pi. But the parametrization \widetilde{\mathbf r}(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le4\pi, traces the same circle twice. Its pullback is still dt, but now the interval has twice the length: \int_0^{4\pi}dt=4\pi. So the integral doubles.
This is why a parametrization used for a single integral must cover the oriented curve once, except for harmless endpoint repetitions.

subsection.p: For surfaces, the same idea uses a two-variable change of parameters.

statement.p: Let \mathbf r:D\to S parametrize an oriented surface, and let \psi:D'\to D be a smooth one-to-one change of parameters onto D, with positive Jacobian determinant in the interior. Then \widetilde{\mathbf r}=\mathbf r\circ\psi parametrizes the same surface with the same orientation, and for every 2-form \Phi, \boxed{\iint_{D'}\widetilde{\mathbf r}^{\,*}\Phi=\iint_D\mathbf r^*\Phi.}

subsection.p: The proof is the change-of-variables formula written in pullback language. If \mathbf r^*\Phi=G(u,v)\,du\wedge dv, and (u,v)=\psi(a,b), then \widetilde{\mathbf r}^{\,*}\Phi=G(\psi(a,b))\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(a,b)}\,da\wedge db. A positive Jacobian preserves orientation, so the oriented integral is unchanged.
If the Jacobian is negative, the surface orientation is reversed. Then the integral changes sign.

There is one more quiet condition: the parametrization must be regular, except possibly on boundary curves or isolated harmless sets. If a parametrization collapses a two-dimensional region to a curve, it is not describing a surface patch.

example.title: A collapsed parametrization is not a surface parametrization

statement.p: Consider \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,0,0). The whole (u,v)-rectangle maps to a line on the x-axis. The tangent vectors are \mathbf r_u=(1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf r_v=(0,0,0), so \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\mathbf 0. There is no small parallelogram on a surface. Every 2-form pulls back to zero because the image has no area.
The regularity condition \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\ne\mathbf 0 is what prevents this collapse.

subsection.title: Orientation reversal and sign
subsection.p: Forms are oriented integrands. Reversing orientation reverses the sign.

exercise.title: Where does the minus sign come from?

statement.p: Reversing the orientation of a curve, surface, or solid flips the sign of the integral, for example \int_{-C}\omega=-\int_C\omega. What does it mean to say a form is an oriented integrand, and why does this sign behavior feel natural once you remember that dx\wedge dy=-\,dy\wedge dx?

hint.p: Reversing orientation swaps the order of the basis pieces inside the wedge. Ask yourself what happens to a signed area or signed volume when you trace its boundary the other way around.

example.title: Reversing a curve

statement.p: Let C be the unit circle oriented counterclockwise, and let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy. We know \int_C\omega=2\pi. If -C is the same circle oriented clockwise, then \boxed{\int_{-C}\omega=-2\pi.} A clockwise trip turns the same geometric circle into the opposite oriented curve.

subsection.p: The cylinder example above gave \int_S\bigl(x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy\bigr)=24\pi for the outward orientation. With the inward orientation, the value is -24\pi.
For regions in space, reversing orientation means replacing dx\wedge dy\wedge dz by -dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. So \boxed{\int_{-E}\Omega=-\int_E\Omega.}

This sign behavior is the reason differential forms fit the boundary theorems so well. A boundary always comes with an induced orientation. The outer boundary of a plane region is counterclockwise, while the boundary around a hole is clockwise. The sign is not an afterthought; it is how the inside and outside agree.

We can now integrate 0-forms over points, 1-forms over curves, 2-forms over surfaces, and 3-forms over solids. Pullbacks tell us how to calculate those integrals using parameters. Orientation tells us the sign. One piece is still missing. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus did not only integrate forms; it integrated a derivative. For functions, that derivative was df. The next question is unavoidable: what is the derivative of a 1-form or a 2-form? The answer will be the exterior derivative, and it will turn gradient, curl, and divergence into one operation.

introduction.p: Section gave the practical rule for integration: \boxed{\text{pull the form back to the parameter domain, then integrate.}}

That rule now covers curves, surfaces, and solids. The form tells us what kind of tiny object it measures. The parametrization supplies those tiny objects. The pullback turns the geometric integral into an ordinary integral in the parameters.
This final section gathers the chapter into a translation table. The goal is not to add new machinery. It is to make the language feel usable.

subsection.title: Classical notation versus form notation
subsection.p: Classical notation often separates those pieces. Forms keep them in one object.

table.title: Vector-calculus notation and its differential-form cousin.

subsection.p: The word cousin is deliberate. The expressions are closely related, but they are not always identical.
The classical element dA is positive area. The form dx\wedge dy is signed area.
The classical element dS is positive surface area. A flux form such as P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy measures oriented surface pieces.
The classical element dV is positive volume. The form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is signed volume.
So forms are the natural language when orientation matters. That is why they fit boundary theorems so well.

subsection.title: One vector field, two different forms
subsection.p: A vector field in space has three components: \mathbf F=(P,Q,R). Those same three components can be used in two different ways.
The work form of \mathbf F is the 1-form \boxed{\omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.} It is integrated along curves: \int_C \omega_{\mathbf F} = \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.

The flux form of \mathbf F is the 2-form \boxed{\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.} It is integrated over surfaces: \int_S \Phi_{\mathbf F} = \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n\,dS.
The coefficient triple is the same, but the job is different.

table.title: The same components used as a work form and as a flux form.

subsection.p: This is an important warning. A vector field is not automatically a 1-form or a 2-form. We choose the form according to the measurement we want.

subsection.title: Work integrals as 1-form integrals
subsection.p: A 1-form measures tangent vectors. That is exactly what a work integral does.

Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(2x-y,\ x+y). Its work form is \omega=(2x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy. Let C be the parabolic path \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then x=t,\qquad y=t^2, and dx=dt,\qquad dy=2t\,dt. Pull back the form:
Therefore
The classical vector-calculus computation gives the same integrand. Along the path, \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=(2t-t^2,\ t+t^2) and \mathbf r'(t)=(1,2t). So
Thus \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_C\omega.
The form notation shows why this happens: dx \quad\text{pulls back to}\quad x'(t)\,dt, and dy \quad\text{pulls back to}\quad y'(t)\,dt. The dot product appears after the pullback.

subsection.title: Flux integrals as 2-form integrals
subsection.p: A 2-form measures oriented surface pieces. That is exactly what a flux integral does.

Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(3,1,z). Its flux form is \Phi = 3\,dy\wedge dz + dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy. Let S be the tilted screen \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,1+u+2v), where 0\le u\le2, \qquad 0\le v\le1. This parametrization has \mathbf r_u=(1,0,1), \qquad \mathbf r_v=(0,1,2), so \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=(-1,-2,1). The positive z-component tells us this is the upward orientation.
Now pull back the form. We have dx=du, \qquad dy=dv, \qquad dz=du+2\,dv. Therefore
Also,
Finally, \mathbf r^*(z\,dx\wedge dy) = (1+u+2v)\,du\wedge dv. Thus
So
The classical flux formula gives the same result: \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))=(3,1,1+u+2v), and \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=(-1,-2,1). Then
Again the pullback has produced the classical integrand.
The negative answer means the net flow crosses the chosen surface in the opposite direction from the chosen orientation. If we reversed the orientation of the screen, the answer would become 4.

subsection.title: Volume integrals as 3-form integrals
subsection.p: A 3-form measures oriented volume. In the standard orientation of space, H\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is the oriented version of H\,dV.
Let B=[0,1]\times[0,2]\times[0,3], and let \Omega=(2+x+z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Using the standard orientation, \int_B\Omega = \int_0^1\int_0^2\int_0^3 (2+x+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.
First integrate in z:
Then \int_0^2\left(\frac{21}{2}+3x\right)\,dy = 21+6x. Finally,
So \boxed{\int_B (2+x+z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=24.}

If the orientation of the box were reversed, the same form integral would be -24. For a physical mass calculation, we would usually fix the standard orientation and report the positive mass. The form integral keeps the orientation sign available.

subsection.title: Pullbacks are the calculation engine
subsection.p: Every computation in this chapter used the same pattern.
For a coordinate change T(u,v,w)=(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)), \boxed{T^*(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz) = \frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} \,du\wedge dv\wedge dw.}
The determinant is not an extra correction factor. It is what the wedge product gives when the volume form is pulled back.

subsection.title: Common sign checks
subsection.p: Most mistakes with forms are sign mistakes. The following checks catch many of them.

table.title: Sign rules that catch most form mistakes.

row.cell: use a coordinate change with negative Jacobian

subsection.p: For curves, the sign comes from direction of travel.

For surfaces, the sign comes from the chosen side. In a parametrization \mathbf r(u,v), the positive normal direction is \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. Swapping the parameters changes the normal to \mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u = -\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v.

For volume, the sign comes from the orientation of ordered directions. The standard orientation of space is dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Changing the order changes the sign according to how many swaps are needed.

example.title: A quick orientation check

statement.p: The form dz\wedge dx\wedge dy has the same orientation as dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Indeed, dz\wedge dx\wedge dy = -dx\wedge dz\wedge dy = dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Two swaps were needed, so the sign is positive.
But dy\wedge dx\wedge dz = -dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Only one swap was needed, so the sign is negative.

subsection.title: What forms do not replace
subsection.p: Forms do not erase the classical tools. They organize them.
Arc length integrals such as \int_C f\,ds are not 1-form integrals of the type \int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. The element ds measures unsigned length. It does not change sign when the curve is reversed.
Surface area integrals such as \iint_S f\,dS are not flux-form integrals. The element dS measures unsigned surface area. It does not require a choice of normal direction.
So there are two kinds of geometric integration living side by side:

table.title: Unsigned and oriented geometric integration side by side.

subsection.p: Neither kind is better. They answer different questions.
If you want length, mass of a wire, or surface area, use the unsigned element ds \quad\text{or}\quad dS. If you want work, circulation, flux, or a boundary theorem, use forms.

subsection.title: A compact chapter map
subsection.p: The chapter can be compressed into one ladder.

table.title: The chapter as one degree ladder.

subsection.p: The degree tells us the dimension of the object the form is built to measure.
The wedge product builds higher-degree measuring objects from 1-forms: dx\wedge dy \quad\text{measures signed area}, and dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \quad\text{measures signed volume}.

Pullbacks move forms from the geometric object to the parameter domain: \text{form in }x,y,z \quad\longmapsto\quad \text{form in }t for curves, \text{form in }x,y,z \quad\longmapsto\quad \text{form in }u,v for surfaces, and \text{form in }x,y,z \quad\longmapsto\quad \text{form in }u,v,w for coordinate changes in solids.
That is the whole computational machine of this chapter.

subsection.title: The missing derivative
subsection.p: One operation is still missing.
A function is a 0-form. Its differential df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz is a 1-form. So the derivative of a 0-form raises the degree by one: 0\text{-form} \quad\longrightarrow\quad 1\text{-form}.
Green's theorem suggests the next step. A 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy should have a derivative that is a 2-form: d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. That 2-form measures circulation density over area.

The divergence theorem suggests one more step. A flux 2-form \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy should have a derivative that is a 3-form: d\Phi=(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. That 3-form measures source density inside volume.
So the pattern is asking to be named:

The next chapter gives this degree-raising derivative its name: the exterior derivative. Once it is in place, gradient, curl, and divergence stop looking like three separate operations. They become one operation seen in three degrees. That is the doorway to the single theorem that has been hiding behind the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

introduction.p: The forms and pullbacks of Chapter 16 are now ready to be differentiated. Starting with the familiar differential of a function, we define the exterior derivative of work and flux forms and explain its relation to gradient, curl, and divergence. Continuous mixed partial derivatives explain why applying this derivative twice gives zero; the domain determines whether a closed form has a global potential.

section.title: The exterior derivative of a 0-form
section.p: A 0-form is a function. So the first case of the exterior derivative is the one we already know: f \longmapsto df. But now df is not just a symbol from single-variable calculus. It is a 1-form: a rule that measures tangent vectors.

subsection.title: From a function f to its differential df
subsection.p: Picture a metal plate on a laboratory table. The point (x,y) gives a location on the plate, measured in centimeters. The temperature is modeled by T(x,y)=18+4x-y-\frac12x^2+\frac13xy. At the point P=(2,3), the temperature is T(2,3)=23.

Now move a tiny amount (\Delta x,\Delta y)=(h,k) from P. The new point is (2+h,3+k). Substitute into T:
T(2+h,3+k) \amp= 18+4(2+h)-(3+k)-\frac12(2+h)^2+\frac13(2+h)(3+k) \amp= 23+3h-\frac13k+\frac13hk-\frac12h^2.
So the temperature change is T(2+h,3+k)-T(2,3)=3h-\frac13k+\frac13hk-\frac12h^2.
The first-order part is 3h-\frac13k. The other terms, \frac13hk-\frac12h^2, are smaller than the displacement when (h,k) is very small. So, near P, \Delta T\approx 3\,\Delta x-\frac13\,\Delta y.
This linear measuring rule is the differential at P: \boxed{dT_P=3\,dx-\frac13\,dy.} It measures a tiny tangent vector \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y) by dT_P(\mathbf v)=3v_x-\frac13v_y.

For example, suppose a small sensor is moving through P with velocity \mathbf v=(2,-3) centimeters per second. Then
dT_P(\mathbf v) \amp= 3(2)-\frac13(-3) \amp= 7.
So the sensor sees temperature increasing at 7^\circ\text{C per second}.

statement.p: We found dT_P=3\,dx-\frac13\,dy, and feeding it the velocity \mathbf v=(2,-3) returned the single number 7. So why do we call dT_P a 1-form rather than just saying the temperature is changing at 7^\circ per second at P?

hint.p: The number 7 belonged to one particular direction. Ask what dT_P would report for a different velocity, and what kind of object can answer that for every direction at once.

figure.caption: The parallel lines are levels of the affine approximation T_{\mathrm{lin}}(x,y)=23+3(x-2)-\frac13(y-3), not of the nonlinear temperature function itself. The blue arrow is the gradient vector \nabla T(P)=(3,-\frac13), perpendicular to those lines. The differential dT_P is the covector that measures displacement across them. The red vector spans seven unit level increments, illustrating dT_P(\mathbf v)=7.

subsection.p: The calculation did two things at once. It found the best linear approximation to the change in temperature, and it produced a 1-form. That is exactly what d does to a 0-form.
In one variable, the differential is df=f'(x)\,dx. That says a small change dx in the input produces the first-order output change df\approx f'(x)\,dx.
In two variables, there are two coordinate changes: dx \qquad\text{and}\qquad dy. So a differentiable function f(x,y) has differential \boxed{df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy.}

statement.p: Let f be a differentiable scalar function.
In the plane, \boxed{d f=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy.}
In space, \boxed{d f=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz.} The form df is called the exterior derivative of the 0-form f.

subsection.p: When f has continuous first partial derivatives, this formula behaves smoothly from point to point. We will often say that f is C^1. That means: f_x,\ f_y,\ f_z \quad\text{exist and are continuous} on the region under discussion.
The continuity condition is not just politeness. Partial derivatives at a single point do not automatically produce a true differential there.

example.title: Why partial derivatives alone are not enough

statement.p: Define f(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \amp (x,y)\ne(0,0),\\ 0, \amp (x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases} At the origin, the coordinate partial derivatives exist: f_x(0,0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h}=0, and f_y(0,0)=\lim_{k\to0}\frac{f(0,k)-f(0,0)}{k}=0. If those two numbers were enough, the differential at the origin would be df_{(0,0)}=0.

But along the diagonal path (t,t), f(t,t)=\frac{t^2}{\sqrt{2t^2}}=\frac{|t|}{\sqrt2}. The proposed linear approximation gives 0, and the error is \frac{|t|}{\sqrt2}. Compare this to the size of the displacement: \|(t,t)\|=\sqrt2\,|t|. The ratio is \frac{|t|/\sqrt2}{\sqrt2\,|t|}=\frac12. It does not approach 0.

So f is not differentiable at the origin. The partial derivatives exist there, but there is no true differential df_{(0,0)}. A differential is a linear approximation to all nearby directions at once, not only to the two coordinate directions.

subsection.p: This is the same warning from , now in the language of forms. The form f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy deserves to be called df at a point only when it really gives the first-order change of f there.

subsection.title: Relation to the gradient
subsection.p: The differential df is a 1-form. The gradient \nabla f is a vector.

In Euclidean space, the dot product lets us translate between them. If f=f(x,y,z), then df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz. On a tangent vector \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z), this gives df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=f_x(\mathbf p)v_x+f_y(\mathbf p)v_y+f_z(\mathbf p)v_z. The gradient vector is \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\bigl(f_x(\mathbf p),f_y(\mathbf p),f_z(\mathbf p)\bigr). Therefore \boxed{df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot \mathbf v.}

theorem.title: The gradient represents df when a dot product is chosen

statement.p: Let f be differentiable at a point \mathbf p\in\mathbb R^3, and use the usual Euclidean dot product. Then \boxed{df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf v} for every tangent vector \mathbf v.

proof.p: Write \mathbf v=(v_x,v_y,v_z). By the definition of df, df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=f_x(\mathbf p)v_x+f_y(\mathbf p)v_y+f_z(\mathbf p)v_z. By the definition of the dot product, \nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf v=\bigl(f_x(\mathbf p),f_y(\mathbf p),f_z(\mathbf p)\bigr)\cdot(v_x,v_y,v_z), which is the same number.

subsection.p: The theorem says the gradient and the differential contain the same coordinate numbers in ordinary Euclidean space. But they are different kinds of objects.
The dot product is the bridge between the two. Without a dot product, the covector df still makes sense. The gradient vector needs that extra geometric structure.

exercise.title: Why does the gradient need a dot product?

statement.p: The differential df happily measures tangent vectors without any mention of a dot product, yet to even speak of the gradient \nabla f we had to choose one. What does the dot product supply that turns the covector df into the vector \nabla f?

hint.p: A 1-form takes a vector and returns a number. To go the other way, from a measuring rule back to an arrow, you need a way to match directions with lengths and angles. Which structure carries that information?

subsection.title: Directional derivatives from evaluating df
subsection.p: More generally, if \mathbf v is a velocity vector, not necessarily a unit vector, then df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v) is the rate of change of f along motion with velocity \mathbf v.

exercise.title: What if you double your speed?

statement.p: Suppose you pass through \mathbf p along the same heading but twice as fast, so your velocity is 2\mathbf v instead of \mathbf v. Without recomputing anything, what does this say about df_{\mathbf p}(2\mathbf v) compared to df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v), and why is that exactly what a rate of change should do?

hint.p: Remember that df_{\mathbf p} is a linear measuring rule. Think about how the field looks the same along your path, but the clock is now running differently.

statement.p: Let f be differentiable at \mathbf p, and let \mathbf r(t) be a differentiable curve with \mathbf r(t_0)=\mathbf p. Then \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf r(t))\bigg|_{t=t_0}=df_{\mathbf p}\bigl(\mathbf r'(t_0)\bigr).}

proof.p: The curve supplies a tangent vector \mathbf r'(t_0). The differential df_{\mathbf p} is the best linear measurement of how f changes from \mathbf p. Applying that linear measurement to the curve's velocity gives the first-order rate of change along the curve. In coordinates, this is the chain rule: \frac{d}{dt}f(x(t),y(t),z(t))=f_xx'(t)+f_yy'(t)+f_zz'(t). The right side is exactly df_{\mathbf r(t)}(\mathbf r'(t)).

example.title: A drone flying through a concentration field

statement.p: A drone flies through a room where the concentration of smoke is modeled by C(x,y,z)=10+xz-y^2+\frac12x^2. The exterior derivative of C is dC=(z+x)\,dx-2y\,dy+x\,dz. At the point P=(1,2,3), this becomes dC_P=4\,dx-4\,dy+dz.

Suppose the drone passes through P with velocity \mathbf v=(2,1,-3) meters per second. Then the rate of change of the smoke concentration measured by the drone is
dC_P(\mathbf v) \amp= 4(2)-4(1)+1(-3) \amp= 1.
So, at that instant, the concentration reading is increasing at 1 concentration unit per second.
In gradient notation, this is the same computation: \nabla C(P)=(4,-4,1), and \nabla C(P)\cdot\mathbf v=(4,-4,1)\cdot(2,1,-3)=1.

subsection.p: A 0-form changes as we move along a curve, and df measures that change. But a 1-form is already something we integrate along curves. Its derivative should not measure change along a single tangent vector. It should measure what happens when we walk around a tiny loop. That is why the next form of d produces curl.

section.title: The exterior derivative of a 1-form
section.p: turned a function into a 1-form: f\longmapsto df. Now we ask what d does to a 1-form. The answer should be a 2-form, because the exterior derivative raises degree by one: 1\text{-form}\longrightarrow 2\text{-form}.
Green's theorem already told us what to expect. A 1-form can be integrated around a closed curve. Its derivative should measure the circulation density inside the loop.

subsection.title: Computing d(P\,dx+Q\,dy) in the plane
subsection.p: Recall the form from : \omega=(3-y)\,dx+2x\,dy. Around any small positively oriented rectangle, its circulation was 3\cdot\text{area}. So the derivative of \omega should be the 2-form 3\,dx\wedge dy.
The exterior derivative finds that number by differentiating the coefficient functions and wedging with the coordinate forms.
The first term is (3-y)\,dx. The coefficient has differential d(3-y)=-dy. So d\bigl((3-y)\,dx\bigr)=d(3-y)\wedge dx=(-dy)\wedge dx. Using dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy, we get (-dy)\wedge dx=dx\wedge dy.
The second term is 2x\,dy. The coefficient has differential d(2x)=2\,dx. So d(2x\,dy)=d(2x)\wedge dy=2\,dx\wedge dy.

Add the two pieces:
d\omega \amp= d\bigl((3-y)\,dx\bigr)+d(2x\,dy) \amp= dx\wedge dy+2\,dx\wedge dy \amp= 3\,dx\wedge dy.
This matches the rectangle calculation: \oint_{\partial R}\omega=\iint_R 3\,dx\wedge dy.

statement.p: We started with a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy and its exterior derivative came out as a multiple of dx\wedge dy, a 2-form. Thinking about what \omega integrates over and what d\omega should measure, why is it natural that the derivative of a 1-form is a 2-form rather than another 1-form?

hint.p: A 1-form is integrated along a curve; d\omega is meant to report what happens inside the loop. What is the dimension of the region a 2-form is built to be integrated over?

figure.caption: The exterior derivative of a plane 1-form measures circulation density.

subsection.p: The same computation works for every plane 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy.

Since dP=P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy and dQ=Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy, we get
d\omega \amp= dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy \amp= (P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy)\wedge dx+(Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy)\wedge dy.
Now use dx\wedge dx=0,\qquad dy\wedge dy=0, and dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy. Then
d\omega \amp= P_y\,dy\wedge dx+Q_x\,dx\wedge dy \amp= -P_y\,dx\wedge dy+Q_x\,dx\wedge dy \amp= (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

statement.p: Let \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy be a 1-form with C^1 coefficient functions. Its exterior derivative is the 2-form \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

subsection.p: The coefficient Q_x-P_y is the scalar curl from . So in the plane, \boxed{d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}(P,Q)\,dx\wedge dy.}

example.title: A zero exterior derivative

statement.p: Let \omega=(2x+y)\,dx+(x-3y)\,dy. Here P=2x+y,\qquad Q=x-3y. Then P_y=1,\qquad Q_x=1. Therefore d\omega=(1-1)\,dx\wedge dy=0.
This does not mean \omega itself is zero. For example, at (1,0), \omega=2\,dx+dy. It means the local circulation density is zero. Around very small loops, the leading circulation cancels.

subsection.title: Computing d(P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz) in space
subsection.p: In space, a 1-form has the shape \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. Its exterior derivative should be a 2-form. Since 2-forms in space have three basic pieces, dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx,\qquad dx\wedge dy, we should expect three coefficients.
Work through one example first.

Let \omega=z^2\,dx+xz\,dy+y^2\,dz. Then P=z^2,\qquad Q=xz,\qquad R=y^2. Differentiate the coefficients: dP=2z\,dz, dQ=z\,dx+x\,dz, and dR=2y\,dy. Now wedge each differential with its coordinate form:
d\omega \amp= dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy+dR\wedge dz \amp= (2z\,dz)\wedge dx+(z\,dx+x\,dz)\wedge dy+(2y\,dy)\wedge dz.
Rewrite in the standard order dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx,\qquad dx\wedge dy. We get
d\omega \amp= 2z\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy+x\,dz\wedge dy+2y\,dy\wedge dz \amp= (2y-x)\,dy\wedge dz+2z\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy.
So \boxed{d\omega=(2y-x)\,dy\wedge dz+2z\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy.}
The same pattern gives the general formula.

Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. Then d\omega=dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy+dR\wedge dz. Use dP=P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy+P_z\,dz, dQ=Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy+Q_z\,dz, and dR=R_x\,dx+R_y\,dy+R_z\,dz. After deleting repeated wedges and reordering signs, we get \boxed{d\omega=(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

statement.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be a 1-form in space with C^1 coefficient functions. Its exterior derivative is \boxed{d\omega=(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

subsection.p: The coordinate forms themselves have zero exterior derivative: d(dx)=d(dy)=d(dz)=0. The variation comes from the coefficient functions P,Q,R, not from the constant coordinate measuring rules.

subsection.title: Curl hidden inside d\omega
subsection.p: The formula for d\omega looks familiar if we compare it with curl.

For a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), the classical curl is \boxed{\nabla\times\mathbf F=(R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).} The exterior derivative of the work form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is \boxed{d\omega=(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

So d\omega is the flux 2-form associated with the curl vector field: \boxed{d\omega=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}.} Here \Phi_{\mathbf G}=G_1\,dy\wedge dz+G_2\,dz\wedge dx+G_3\,dx\wedge dy is the flux form of a vector field \mathbf G=(G_1,G_2,G_3).

theorem.title: Exterior derivative of a work form is curl as a flux form

statement.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a C^1 vector field in space, and let \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be its work 1-form. Then \boxed{d\omega_{\mathbf F}=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}.}

proof.p: The flux form of \nabla\times\mathbf F=(R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y) is (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. This is exactly the formula for d(P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz).

subsection.p: This theorem explains the word curl in a clean way. The curl is not a separate mystery operation. It is the exterior derivative of a 1-form, read through the three-dimensional flux-form dictionary.

exercise.title: Is curl really a new idea?

statement.p: We just saw that d\omega_{\mathbf F}=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}, so the curl is the exterior derivative of a work 1-form read through the flux-form dictionary. In your own words, what does this say about why curl shows up at all in vector calculus, and why it produces three components in space but only one scalar in the plane?

hint.p: Count the independent basic 2-forms in the plane versus in space (how many ways are there to write dx\wedge dy-type pieces?). The number of curl components is just the number of slots d\omega has to fill.

example.title: A rotating air flow in space

statement.p: Let \mathbf F=(-y,\ x,\ z). Its work form is \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz. Compute d\omega: P=-y,\qquad Q=x,\qquad R=z. Then R_y-Q_z=0-0=0, P_z-R_x=0-0=0, and Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2. Therefore \boxed{d\omega=2\,dx\wedge dy.} The curl vector is \nabla\times\mathbf F=(0,0,2). The field rotates around the z-axis, and the exterior derivative records that rotation as a 2-form measuring xy-oriented surface pieces.

subsection.title: Green's and Stokes' theorem previewed again
subsection.p: In the plane, the formula d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy turns Green's theorem into the short statement \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega.} The left side is circulation around the boundary. The right side is circulation density added over the inside.

statement.p: The compact statement \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega equates a boundary integral with an integral over the inside. Conceptually, why should circulation measured only along the edge equal circulation density summed throughout the interior? What would go wrong with this balance if the density d\omega were not the local version of the boundary circulation?

hint.p: Imagine tiling R with many tiny loops. Adjacent edges are traversed in opposite directions and cancel; only the outer boundary survives. What is left adding up the tiny loop circulations is exactly the interior sum of d\omega.

subsection.p: For example, with \omega=(3-y)\,dx+2x\,dy, we found d\omega=3\,dx\wedge dy. So Green's theorem says \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R 3\,dx\wedge dy=3\,\operatorname{Area}(R)} for every positively oriented plane region R to which the theorem applies.

In space, the same statement becomes Stokes' theorem: \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.} Now S is an oriented surface, and \partial S is its oriented boundary curve. The exterior derivative d\omega is the curl 2-form.

example.title: The same boundary with a curved surface

statement.p: Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz, so d\omega=2\,dx\wedge dy. Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=1,\qquad z\ge0, oriented upward. Its boundary is the unit circle in the xy-plane, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above.

Stokes' theorem predicts \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S 2\,dx\wedge dy. The form dx\wedge dy measures the signed xy-shadow of the surface. The upward-oriented upper hemisphere casts the unit disk as its positive shadow. Therefore \int_S 2\,dx\wedge dy=2\pi.

Check the boundary integral directly. Parametrize the boundary by \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=\cos t\,dt,\qquad dz=0. So
\mathbf r^*\omega \amp= -\sin t(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt)+0 \amp= dt.
Hence \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi.} The curved surface and the flat disk have the same boundary, and the same d\omega accounts for the boundary circulation.

subsection.p: The hypotheses behind Green's and Stokes' theorem matter. The form must be defined and smooth on a region containing the surface or plane region we integrate over. A missing point can break the conclusion.

example.title: A hidden singularity breaks the theorem

statement.p: Consider the 1-form \omega_0=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. It is defined on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, not at the origin.
Away from the origin, P=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2},\qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. A direct calculation gives Q_x-P_y=0, so d\omega_0=0 wherever the form is defined.

Now integrate around the unit circle C:\quad \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. On this circle, x^2+y^2=1, so \omega_0=-y\,dx+x\,dy. As before, \mathbf r^*\omega_0=dt. Therefore \boxed{\int_C\omega_0=2\pi.}

If we pretended Green's theorem applied to the whole disk, we would get \int_C\omega_0=\int_{\text{disk}}d\omega_0=0, which is false. The problem is the missing origin. The form is not defined on the disk bounded by C.
So the condition defined and smooth on the whole region is not a technical detail. It prevents a singularity from hiding inside the boundary.

subsection.p: The exterior derivative has now turned functions into 1-forms and 1-forms into 2-forms: f\longmapsto df,\qquad \omega\longmapsto d\omega. The next step is forced by the divergence theorem. A flux 2-form measures flow through a surface. Its derivative should measure source density inside a volume. That will be a 3-form, and the old vector name for its coefficient is divergence.

section.title: The exterior derivative of a 2-form
section.p: turned a work 1-form into a flux 2-form: \omega_{\mathbf F} \quad\longmapsto\quad d\omega_{\mathbf F} = \Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}. A 2-form is integrated over a surface. So its derivative should be integrated over a solid. That means the next exterior derivative should measure source strength inside volume.

subsection.title: Computing d(P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy)
subsection.p: Picture air flowing through a sealed box. The flux through the boundary tells us whether more air is leaving than entering. If more leaves than enters, something inside acts like a source. If more enters than leaves, something inside acts like a sink.
The flux 2-form of a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) is \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy. The three pieces measure flux through the three coordinate shadows:

table.title: The three pieces of a flux 2-form.

subsection.p: Start with the simple expanding field \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,2y,3z). Its flux form is \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+2y\,dz\wedge dx+3z\,dx\wedge dy. computed the outward flux of this field through a rectangular box and found \text{outward flux}=6\cdot\text{volume}. So its exterior derivative should be 6\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Now compute with d.

For the first term, d\bigl(x\,dy\wedge dz\bigr) = dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. For the second term, d\bigl(2y\,dz\wedge dx\bigr) = 2\,dy\wedge dz\wedge dx. The order dy\wedge dz\wedge dx is a cyclic shift of dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, so it has the same sign: dy\wedge dz\wedge dx=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Thus d\bigl(2y\,dz\wedge dx\bigr) = 2\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

For the third term,
d\bigl(3z\,dx\wedge dy\bigr) \amp= 3\,dz\wedge dx\wedge dy \amp= 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Again the order is cyclic, so the sign is positive.

Add the three pieces:
d\Phi \amp= dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + 2\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \amp= 6\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
So \boxed{ d\Phi=6\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. } The coefficient 6 is the source density. Every small volume box has net outward flux approximately 6\,\Delta V.

figure.caption: The exterior derivative of a flux 2-form measures net outward flux per unit volume.

subsection.p: The same calculation works for every flux 2-form in space.

Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy. Then d\Phi = dP\wedge dy\wedge dz + dQ\wedge dz\wedge dx + dR\wedge dx\wedge dy. Use dP=P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy+P_z\,dz. Only the P_x\,dx term survives, because dy\wedge dy=0, \qquad dz\wedge dz=0. So dP\wedge dy\wedge dz = P_x\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

Similarly, dQ=Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy+Q_z\,dz. Only the Q_y\,dy term survives:
dQ\wedge dz\wedge dx \amp= Q_y\,dy\wedge dz\wedge dx \amp= Q_y\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

Finally, dR=R_x\,dx+R_y\,dy+R_z\,dz. Only the R_z\,dz term survives:
dR\wedge dx\wedge dy \amp= R_z\,dz\wedge dx\wedge dy \amp= R_z\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Therefore \boxed{ d\Phi = (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

statement.p: Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy be a 2-form in space with C^1 coefficient functions. Its exterior derivative is the 3-form \boxed{ d\Phi = (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

subsection.p: The notation is compact, but the meaning is physical: \boxed{ d(\text{flux form})=\text{source density volume form}. }

subsection.title: Divergence hidden inside d\Phi
subsection.p: For a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), the classical divergence is \boxed{ \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=P_x+Q_y+R_z. } The flux form of \mathbf F is \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy. Taking its exterior derivative gives \boxed{ d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

theorem.title: Exterior derivative of a flux form is divergence as a volume form

statement.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a C^1 vector field in space, and let \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy be its flux 2-form. Then \boxed{ d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

proof.p: The coefficient of d\Phi_{\mathbf F} is P_x+Q_y+R_z, which is exactly \nabla\cdot\mathbf F.

subsection.p: The theorem completes the promised dictionary:

table.title: The exterior derivative across degrees.

subsection.p: Gradient, curl, and divergence are no longer three unrelated formulas. They are the same degree-raising operation d, read in degrees 0, 1, and 2.

statement.p: Gradient, curl, and divergence all turn out to be the single operation d applied in degrees 0, 1, and 2. What does it tell you about these three classical operators that they are really the same degree-raising step, just read on different kinds of forms?

hint.p: Think about what d always does: it raises a k-form to a (k+1)-form and measures how the form changes from the boundary of a small region to its interior. The classical name you read off depends only on the degree you started in.

example.title: A swirling field with no source

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0). Its flux form is \Phi_{\mathbf F} = -y\,dy\wedge dz + x\,dz\wedge dx. Then P=-y,\qquad Q=x,\qquad R=0. So P_x=0,\qquad Q_y=0,\qquad R_z=0. Therefore \boxed{ d\Phi_{\mathbf F}=0. } The field rotates around the z-axis, but it has no source strength. Air can swirl without being created.

example.title: A field with uniform source density

statement.p:
Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z). Then \Phi_{\mathbf F} = x\,dy\wedge dz + y\,dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy. The exterior derivative is
d\Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp= (1+1+1)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \amp= 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Every small box has net outward flux approximately 3\,\Delta V. The field expands uniformly in all three coordinate directions.

subsection.title: Flux balance as an exterior derivative statement
subsection.p: A 2-form is integrated over a surface: \int_S \Phi. Its derivative is a 3-form, so it is integrated over a solid: \int_E d\Phi.

For a rectangular box B and C^1 coefficients defined near it, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus on opposite faces gives the exact equality \boxed{ \int_{\partial B}\Phi = \int_B d\Phi. } The left side is the outward flux through the boundary. The right side is the source density added throughout the box.

exercise.title: What does the balance really claim?

statement.p: The relation \int_{\partial B}\Phi = \int_B d\Phi sets a boundary integral equal to an interior integral. In plain words, why should the flux leaking out through the skin of a box be the same as the source density piled up inside it? What would it mean physically if these two numbers disagreed?

hint.p: Imagine nothing is created or destroyed inside the box. Then anything that flows out of the boundary had to come from somewhere within. The interior integral of d\Phi is just the bookkeeping that adds up every tiny source.

subsection.p: For the expanding form \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+2y\,dz\wedge dx+3z\,dx\wedge dy, the equality is exact on every rectangular box: d\Phi=6\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. If B=[a,a+h]\times[b,b+k]\times[c,c+\ell], then \int_B d\Phi = \int_B 6\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = 6hk\ell. The boundary flux is also 6hk\ell, because the opposite faces contribute hk\ell,\qquad 2hk\ell,\qquad 3hk\ell. So \boxed{ \int_{\partial B}\Phi=\int_B d\Phi. }

For a general smooth field, the equality is already exact on each box. Approximating its volume integral by the divergence at one point times the box volume introduces an approximation. When boxes are added, their interior face integrals cancel; this cancellation is the starting point for the theorem on more general regions.
That is the same cancellation pattern we saw in Green's theorem. In the plane, small edge contributions cancel inside a region. In space, small face contributions cancel inside a solid.

subsection.title: The divergence theorem previewed again
subsection.p: The divergence theorem is the 2-form version of the same boundary principle.

statement.p: Let E be a solid region whose boundary is made from finitely many smooth surface pieces. Give \partial E the outward orientation. Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy have C^1 coefficient functions on a region containing E. Then \boxed{ \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi. } If \Phi=\Phi_{\mathbf F}, this is the classical formula \boxed{ \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV. }

subsection.p: The theorem has three sign-and-domain traps.

example.title: A disk is not a closed boundary

statement.p: Let D be the unit disk in the plane z=0, oriented upward, and let \mathbf F=(0,0,1). Its flux form is \Phi=dx\wedge dy. The flux through the disk is \int_D dx\wedge dy=\pi. But d\Phi=0. This does not contradict the divergence theorem. The disk alone is not the boundary of a solid. It has a rim. The theorem needs a closed boundary surface.

example.title: Outward orientation matters

statement.p: Let E=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] and \mathbf F=(x,0,0). Then \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1. So \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf F}=1. With outward orientation, the only nonzero flux is through the face x=1, and it is 1. With inward orientation, the same surface integral becomes -1. The theorem uses the outward orientation.

example.title: A hidden singularity can carry source strength

statement.p: Consider the inverse-square radial field \mathbf G(x,y,z) = \frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}, defined on \mathbb R^3\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}. Away from the origin, \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0, so d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0 where the form is defined.

Now integrate through the sphere S_a of radius a, oriented outward. On the sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a} and \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}. Thus \mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} = \frac{1}{a^2}. Therefore \int_{S_a}\Phi_{\mathbf G} = \iint_{S_a}\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \frac{1}{a^2}\cdot 4\pi a^2 = 4\pi.

It would be wrong to say d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0, \qquad \text{so the sphere flux is }0. The field is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the sphere. The missing point is carrying the source.

exercise.title: How can d\Phi=0 yet the flux be 4\pi?

statement.p: For the inverse-square field, d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0 everywhere the form is defined, and yet the outward flux through a sphere around the origin is 4\pi, not 0. What is it about the hole at the origin that lets a source hide there, even though the source density vanishes at every point you can actually evaluate?

hint.p: The divergence theorem trades a boundary integral for an interior integral only when the form is defined on the whole solid. Here the origin is missing, so the interior integral is not allowed to swallow that point. Ask where the theorem's hypothesis quietly fails.

subsection.p:
The exterior derivative has now moved through every degree available in ordinary space: 0\longrightarrow 1\longrightarrow 2\longrightarrow 3. There is no new ordinary spatial integrand after 3-forms. But we can still ask a different question: what happens if we apply d twice? The answer is always zero for smooth forms. That one fact explains both 
abla	imes(
abla f)=\mathbf 0 and 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0. It also has a geometric reason: a boundary has no boundary.

section.title: The rule d^2=0

subsection.title: Why second exterior derivatives vanish
subsection.p:
Start with a function. Let f(x,y,z)=x^2z+xy. Then df=(2xz+y)\,dx+x\,dy+x^2\,dz. Now take d again:
d(df) \amp= d(2xz+y)\wedge dx + d(x)\wedge dy + d(x^2)\wedge dz.
Compute the coefficient differentials: d(2xz+y)=2z\,dx+dy+2x\,dz, d(x)=dx, \qquad d(x^2)=2x\,dx. So
d(df) \amp= (2z\,dx+dy+2x\,dz)\wedge dx + dx\wedge dy + 2x\,dx\wedge dz.
The repeated wedge dx\wedge dx vanishes:
d(df) \amp= dy\wedge dx+2x\,dz\wedge dx + dx\wedge dy + 2x\,dx\wedge dz.
Now pair the terms: dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy, and dz\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dz. Thus
d(df) \amp= -dx\wedge dy-2x\,dx\wedge dz + dx\wedge dy + 2x\,dx\wedge dz \amp= 0.
The cancellation came from two facts: dx\wedge dx=0 and dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. The wedge product supplies the signs that make the second derivative cancel.

statement.p: In the computation above, the cancellation in d(df)=0 came from two features of the wedge product: dx\wedge dx=0 and dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. If the wedge were instead a symmetric product, with dx\wedge dy=+dy\wedge dx, would you still expect the second derivative to vanish? What does this tell you about where the rule d^2=0 really comes from?

hint.p: Trace which terms in the final sum relied on the minus sign to cancel. Ask what would survive without it, and notice it has nothing to do with the function f you chose.

subsection.p: The same thing happens to every sufficiently smooth function.

statement.p: Let f(x,y,z) have continuous second partial derivatives on an open region. Then \boxed{ d(df)=0. }

proof.p:
Write df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz. Then
d(df) \amp= d(f_x)\wedge dx+d(f_y)\wedge dy+d(f_z)\wedge dz.
Expand:
d(df) \amp= (f_{xx}\,dx+f_{xy}\,dy+f_{xz}\,dz)\wedge dx \amp\quad+ (f_{yx}\,dx+f_{yy}\,dy+f_{yz}\,dz)\wedge dy \amp\quad+ (f_{zx}\,dx+f_{zy}\,dy+f_{zz}\,dz)\wedge dz.
All repeated wedges vanish. The remaining terms are
d(df) \amp= (f_{yx}-f_{xy})\,dx\wedge dy \amp\quad+ (f_{xz}-f_{zx})\,dz\wedge dx \amp\quad+ (f_{zy}-f_{yz})\,dy\wedge dz.
Since the second partial derivatives are continuous, the mixed partials agree: f_{xy}=f_{yx}, \qquad f_{xz}=f_{zx}, \qquad f_{yz}=f_{zy}. Therefore d(df)=0.

subsection.p: The smoothness condition is doing real work. It lets us trade the order of mixed partials.

example.title: Why the C^2 hypothesis matters

statement.p: If we try to run the formula d(dg)=(g_{yx}-g_{xy})\,dx\wedge dy at the origin using these existing second partials, we get d(dg)=2\,dx\wedge dy there, not zero.
The theorem did not fail. Its hypothesis failed. The function is not C^2 at the origin, and the mixed partials are not forced to agree.

subsection.title: d(df)=0 and \nabla\times\nabla f=\mathbf 0
subsection.p: The identity d(df)=0 is the differential-form version of a classical vector identity.
This says a gradient field has no local rotation. It can push a particle uphill or downhill, but it does not create first-order spinning.

exercise.title: Why can't a hill make you spin?

statement.p: We just read \nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0 as saying a gradient field has no local rotation. In plain terms, why should the steepest-ascent directions of a surface refuse to swirl? Try to say what would be strange about a landscape whose uphill arrows curled around in little circles.

hint.p: Imagine walking a tiny closed loop on the hillside. A gradient measures change in height, and you return to the height you started at. Connect that round-trip with the absence of curl, no formula required.

example.title: A temperature gradient has zero curl

statement.p:
Let T(x,y,z)=20+xy+yz+xz^2. Then 
abla T=(y+z^2,\ x+z,\ y+2xz). Compute the curl:

abla	imes
abla T \amp= \left(  rac{\partial}{\partial y}(y+2xz) -  rac{\partial}{\partial z}(x+z), ight. \amp\qquad  rac{\partial}{\partial z}(y+z^2) -  rac{\partial}{\partial x}(y+2xz), \amp\qquad\left.  rac{\partial}{\partial x}(x+z) -  rac{\partial}{\partial y}(y+z^2) ight) \amp= (1-1,\ 2z-2z,\ 1-1) \amp= \mathbf 0.
The cancellations are mixed partials in disguise.

subsection.title: d(d\omega)=0 and \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0
subsection.p: Now start with a 1-form instead of a function.

Use the example from : \omega=z^2\,dx+xz\,dy+y^2\,dz. We found d\omega = (2y-x)\,dy\wedge dz + 2z\,dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy. Now take d again:
d(d\omega) \amp= d(2y-x)\wedge dy\wedge dz + d(2z)\wedge dz\wedge dx + d(z)\wedge dx\wedge dy.
Compute: d(2y-x)=2\,dy-dx, \qquad d(2z)=2\,dz, \qquad d(z)=dz. So
d(d\omega) \amp= (2\,dy-dx)\wedge dy\wedge dz + 2\,dz\wedge dz\wedge dx + dz\wedge dx\wedge dy.
Repeated wedges vanish: dy\wedge dy=0, \qquad dz\wedge dz=0. Therefore
d(d\omega) \amp= -dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + dz\wedge dx\wedge dy.
But dz\wedge dx\wedge dy=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, so \boxed{ d(d\omega)=0. }
The general identity is the 1-form case of d^2=0.

statement.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz have C^2 coefficient functions on an open region. Then \boxed{ d(d\omega)=0. }

proof.p:
From , d\omega = (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz + (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx + (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. Now apply d to this 2-form:
d(d\omega) \amp= \Bigl((R_y-Q_z)_x+(P_z-R_x)_y+(Q_x-P_y)_z\Bigr) \,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
The coefficient is R_{yx}-Q_{zx}+P_{zy}-R_{xy}+Q_{xz}-P_{yz}. Group the matching mixed partials: (R_{yx}-R_{xy}) + (P_{zy}-P_{yz}) + (Q_{xz}-Q_{zx}). Since the coefficient functions are C^2, each pair cancels. Hence d(d\omega)=0.

subsection.p: A curl field has no source strength. It can circulate, but it cannot be the whole story of a source.

example.title: A curl with zero divergence

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(0,xz,0). Then \nabla\times\mathbf F=(-x,0,z). Its divergence is \nabla\cdot(-x,0,z) = -1+0+1 = 0. The two surviving rates cancel. This cancellation is d^2=0 written in vector language.

subsection.p:
There is one last degree to check. If \Theta=H\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is a 3-form in ordinary space, then
d\Theta \amp= dH\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \amp= (H_x\,dx+H_y\,dy+H_z\,dz)\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Every term repeats one of dx,\qquad dy,\qquad dz. So \boxed{ d\Theta=0. } In three-dimensional space, there is no nonzero 4-form waiting after a 3-form.

subsection.title: Boundary of a boundary is zero
subsection.p: Start in one dimension. For an interval I=[a,b], the oriented boundary is \partial I=\{b\}-\{a\}. A point has no boundary, so \partial(\partial I)=0.

Now look at a rectangle with vertices A,B,C,D, oriented counterclockwise: \partial R=[A,B]+[B,C]+[C,D]+[D,A]. Take the boundary of each edge:
\partial(\partial R) \amp= (B-A)+(C-B)+(D-C)+(A-D) \amp= 0.
Every vertex appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign.

figure.caption: The boundary of a rectangle is a closed curve. Its boundary cancels at the corners.

subsection.p: For a solid box, the same cancellation happens one dimension higher. The boundary of the box is made of faces. The boundary of those faces is made of edges. Every edge belongs to two neighboring faces, and the two induced orientations are opposite. So all edges cancel.

This explains why d^2=0 belongs with Stokes-type theorems. The general pattern is \int_{\partial M}\alpha=\int_M d\alpha. Apply the same idea one more time: \int_{\partial(\partial M)}\alpha = \int_{\partial M}d\alpha = \int_M d(d\alpha). The left side is zero because \partial(\partial M)=0. The right side is zero because d(d\alpha)=0.

That is a small sentence with a large reach. It says every exact form has zero exterior derivative: \alpha=d\beta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d\alpha=0. But it does not answer the reverse question. If a form has zero exterior derivative, must it come from another form? On a region with no holes, often yes. Around a missing point or a missing axis, sometimes no. The next names are short, but they open the door to the topology hiding inside vector calculus: closed and exact.

statement.p: This section paired two statements: the algebraic rule d^2=0 and the geometric rule \partial^2=0, the boundary of a boundary is zero. In your own words, what does it mean that these are the same idea seen from two sides? Why is it satisfying, rather than a coincidence, that they appear together in \int_{\partial M}\alpha=\int_M d\alpha?

hint.p: Look at the chain that applies the Stokes pattern twice. Which rule kills the left end, and which kills the right end? Ask why a single equation can only stay true if both rules hold at once.

section.title: Closed and exact forms
section.p: Section ended with the identity d^2=0. That identity gives one direction for free: \text{if a form is already a derivative, then its next derivative is zero.} The reverse question is more delicate. If a form has zero exterior derivative, did it come from another form? Sometimes yes. Sometimes a hole in the domain stops it.

subsection.title: Exact forms: \omega=d\alpha
subsection.p: Start with a form whose origin is visible.
Let \phi(x,y,z)=xz+y^2. Then d\phi=z\,dx+2y\,dy+x\,dz. The 1-form \omega=z\,dx+2y\,dy+x\,dz is not just any 1-form. It is the exterior derivative of the 0-form \phi.
That gives it a special property. Along any curve from A to B, \int_C \omega = \int_C d\phi = \phi(B)-\phi(A). The integral is an endpoint difference. It does not remember the path.
This is the same exactness from Section , now placed in the larger forms ladder.
The word exact means that the form has a global antiderivative of the correct degree.
Here are the three main degrees in ordinary space.

example.title: An exact 1-form

statement.p: Let \phi(x,y,z)=xz+y^2. Then \boxed{d\phi=z\,dx+2y\,dy+x\,dz.} So z\,dx+2y\,dy+x\,dz is an exact 1-form.

example.title: An exact 2-form

statement.p:
Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz. Then
d\omega \amp= d(-y)\wedge dx+d(x)\wedge dy+d(z)\wedge dz \amp= (-dy)\wedge dx+dx\wedge dy+dz\wedge dz \amp= dx\wedge dy+dx\wedge dy+0 \amp= 2\,dx\wedge dy.
Therefore \boxed{2\,dx\wedge dy=d(-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz).} So 2\,dx\wedge dy is an exact 2-form.

example.title: An exact 3-form

statement.p: The ordinary volume form is exact on \mathbb R^3: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=d(x\,dy\wedge dz).} Indeed, d(x\,dy\wedge dz) = dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. So even a 3-form can be an exterior derivative.

subsection.p: Exactness is not only a formula. It is a formula on a domain. The antiderivative form has to exist on the whole domain where we want to use it.

subsection.title: Closed forms: d\omega=0
subsection.p: Now forget where the form came from and ask only what happens when we apply d.

For the exact 1-form \omega=z\,dx+2y\,dy+x\,dz=d(xz+y^2), we get d\omega=d(d\phi)=0. For the exact 2-form \Phi=2\,dx\wedge dy=d(-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz), we get d\Phi=0. For the exact 3-form \Theta=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=d(x\,dy\wedge dz), we also have d\Theta=0, because every 3-form in ordinary space has zero exterior derivative.
This property gets its own name.

statement.p: A form \alpha is called closed if \boxed{d\alpha=0.}

subsection.p: Closed means that the next exterior derivative vanishes.
For 1-forms in the plane, \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is closed exactly when \boxed{Q_x-P_y=0.} That is the scalar-curl test.
For 1-forms in space, \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz is closed exactly when \boxed{\nabla\times(P,Q,R)=\mathbf 0.}

So the old vector-calculus words fit into one table:
\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Form} \amp \text{Closed condition} \amp \text{Vector-language translation} \\ \hline P\,dx+Q\,dy \amp d\omega=0 \amp Q_x-P_y=0\\[1mm] P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz \amp d\omega=0 \amp \nabla\times(P,Q,R)=\mathbf 0\\[1mm] P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy \amp d\Phi=0 \amp \nabla\cdot(P,Q,R)=0 \end{array}

subsection.title: Exact implies closed
subsection.p: The identity d^2=0 is exactly the statement that every exact form is closed.

exercise.title: Why is exactness the strong condition?

statement.p: We just saw that exact always forces closed, but not the other way around. In your own words, why should “\alpha=d\beta” be a stronger demand than “d\alpha=0”? What does an antiderivative \beta give you that merely knowing d\alpha=0 does not?

hint.p: Closedness is a condition you can check by a local computation at each point. Exactness asks for a single object \beta that works everywhere at once. Which of those is easier to satisfy?

statement.p: Let \alpha be a form with smooth enough coefficients for the identity d^2=0 to apply. If \alpha is exact, then \alpha is closed.
In symbols, \boxed{\alpha=d\beta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d\alpha=0.}

proof.p: If \alpha=d\beta, then d\alpha=d(d\beta)=d^2\beta=0. So \alpha is closed.

subsection.title: Closed does not always imply exact
subsection.p: The reverse statement is the tempting one: d\alpha=0 \quad\stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow}\quad \alpha=d\beta. It is false on domains with holes.

exercise.title: What does the missing point actually break?

statement.p: The angle form satisfies d\alpha=0 at every single point of the punctured plane, yet it fails to be exact there. If the closedness test passes everywhere the form lives, what is it about the missing origin that can still spoil exactness?

hint.p: Picture building a potential \theta by integrating \alpha as you walk around a loop that encircles the hole. Do you arrive back at the same value you started with? An honest function cannot disagree with itself at one point.

subsection.p: The cleanest example is the angle form \alpha= \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+ \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy on the punctured plane D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. The origin is missing, so the formula is defined everywhere on D.

Let P=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. Then P_y = \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, and Q_x = \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. So Q_x-P_y=0, and therefore \boxed{d\alpha=0} on the punctured plane. The form is closed.

If \alpha were exact on D, then \alpha=d\theta for some single-valued function \theta on all of D. The fundamental theorem for line integrals would give \oint_C d\theta=0, because C starts and ends at the same point.
But the integral is 2\pi. Therefore \boxed{\alpha \text{ is closed but not exact on } \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}.}

figure.caption: A closed 1-form can fail to be exact when the domain has a hole.

subsection.p: This returns to the topology issue from . The formula d\alpha=0 is local. It checks tiny rectangles. Exactness is global. It asks whether one potential works on the whole domain.

subsection.title: Holes, topology, and conservative fields
subsection.p: For 1-forms, the old conservative-field language now becomes a special case of the closed-exact language.
