Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be the work form of a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R).

On open simply connected domains, including the interiors of rectangles, disks, boxes, and balls, a C^1 closed 1-form is exact. Here is the proof promised in . Simple connectivity is a sufficient domain condition; a particular field can also have a potential on a domain with holes.

theorem.title: Closed 1-forms on a simply connected domain

statement.p: Let D\subseteq\mathbb R^n, where n=2 or 3, be open, path connected, and simply connected. If the coefficients of \omega=\sum_{i=1}^n F_i\,dx_i are C^1 and d\omega=0 on D, then \omega=d\phi for a function \phi on D.

proof.p:
First work in an open ball B centered at a and contained in D. Every segment from a to x\in B stays in B. Define \phi_B(x)=\int_0^1\sum_{i=1}^n F_i(a+t(x-a))(x_i-a_i)\,dt. Closedness means \partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j. Differentiating under this integral is justified by , applied to each coordinate on a small closed neighborhood of x. With v=x-a, the product and chain rules give
\partial_j\phi_B(x)\amp=\int_0^1\left[F_j(a+tv)+t\sum_i v_i\partial_jF_i(a+tv)\right]dt \amp=\int_0^1\frac{d}{dt}\left[tF_j(a+tv)\right]dt=F_j(x).
Thus d\phi_B=\omega on B. By the fundamental theorem for line integrals, two piecewise smooth paths inside this ball with the same endpoints have the same integral.

Next let C:[0,1]\to D be a piecewise smooth closed path, based at p=C(0)=C(1). Simple connectivity supplies a continuous contraction H:[0,1]^2\to D with H(t,0)=C(t),\qquad H(t,1)=q,\qquad H(0,s)=H(1,s) for some q\in D. The common endpoint of the intermediate loops may move. We need not differentiate H, and its image need not be a regular surface.

Subdivide the parameter square finely enough that the image of each small closed rectangle lies in one open ball contained in D. The elementary compactness fact used here is that a continuous map on a closed square has this uniform local control. To see it directly, suppose arbitrarily small rectangles failed the condition. Their centers have a convergent subsequence in the closed square (apply the bounded-sequence subsequence theorem to the two coordinates). Their diameters tend to zero. Continuity at the limiting center then puts all their images, eventually, in a ball about its image contained in D, a contradiction. Include the finitely many corner parameters of C in the subdivision.

Send each grid vertex through H, and replace every grid edge by the straight segment joining the images of its endpoints. Each resulting four-edge path lies in its cell's ball, since balls are convex. Its integral is zero by the local potential. Add these zero integrals over all cells: every interior segment occurs twice with opposite directions and cancels. The top side is constant at q, while the two vertical sides give identical polygonal paths traversed in opposite directions, so they cancel. The bottom side is a polygonal replacement of C. On each bottom interval, the original arc of C and its replacement segment lie in the same ball and have the same integral. Hence \oint_C\omega=0.

Finally fix p\in D and define \phi(x) as the integral of \omega along a piecewise smooth path from p to x. Such paths exist: subdivide a continuous path into pieces in balls and replace them by segments, as above. Vanishing integrals around closed paths make \phi(x) independent of the path. In a small ball, differences of \phi equal differences of \phi_B, so d\phi=\omega.

subsection.p: The angle form \alpha is the model example. Away from the origin it has no local curl. But a loop around the missing origin measures 2\pi. The hole is invisible to d\alpha, but visible to integration.
That sentence is the main point: \boxed{d\alpha=0 \text{ is local; } \alpha=d\beta \text{ is global.}}

statement.p: The derivative d\alpha only inspects tiny rectangles, so it never sees a hole sitting far away. Why does that explain how a form can be closed (a purely local fact) and yet not exact (a global one)? What is the integral around a loop measuring that the local derivative cannot?

hint.p: Think of d\alpha=0 as a clue gathered point by point, and exactness as a verdict about the whole domain at once. The shape of the domain — whether a loop can be shrunk to a point — is the missing ingredient.

subsection.p: The same issue can happen one degree higher. A closed flux 2-form can have zero divergence everywhere it is defined and still fail to be the exterior derivative of a global 1-form. In the next warning examples, a loop around a missing point and a sphere around a missing point will both detect information that the local derivative cannot see.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The words closed and exact are short, but they hide the most common mistake in vector calculus: checking a derivative and forgetting the domain.
A derivative sees what happens near each point. An integral can walk around a hole. Those are different powers.

subsection.title: A closed 1-form on a punctured plane that is not exact
subsection.p: We already computed d\alpha=0 on D. So \alpha is closed.
But around the unit circle, C:\quad \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi, we get \mathbf r^*\alpha=dt. Hence \boxed{\oint_C\alpha=2\pi.}

This one number proves that \alpha is not exact on D. If \alpha=d\theta on all of D, then the integral around every closed curve would be zero: \oint_C d\theta=\theta(C_{\text{end}})-\theta(C_{\text{start}})=0. But C_{\text{end}}=C_{\text{start}}, and the integral is 2\pi.
So the form satisfies d\alpha=0 but fails \alpha=d\theta globally.
The missing point matters. The loop cannot shrink to a point without crossing the place where the form is not defined.

exercise.title: Why does the loop notice the hole?

statement.p: The derivative d\alpha=0 everywhere on D, yet the integral around the unit circle is not zero. Explain, in words, what the loop is detecting that the local condition d\alpha=0 simply cannot see.

hint.p: Ask yourself whether the loop could be shrunk down to a single point while staying inside D. What stands in the way?

subsection.title: A locally exact form with a global obstruction
subsection.p: The same form \alpha=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy really is an angle differential locally.

On the right half-plane D_+=\{(x,y):x\gt 0\}, define \theta(x,y)=\arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right). Then
\theta_x \amp= \frac{1}{1+(y/x)^2}\left(-\frac{y}{x^2}\right) \amp= \frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}\left(-\frac{y}{x^2}\right) \amp= \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2},
and
\theta_y \amp= \frac{1}{1+(y/x)^2}\left(\frac1x\right) \amp= \frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}\left(\frac1x\right) \amp= \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}.
Therefore \boxed{d\theta=\alpha} on D_+.
So \alpha is exact on the right half-plane.

The problem is not local. Near any point of the punctured plane, we can choose a small neighborhood and a continuous angle function there. On that small neighborhood, \alpha=d\theta. The problem is global. No single continuous angle function can be chosen on the whole punctured plane.

Here is the obstruction in one line. Suppose there were a global function \theta on D with d\theta=\alpha. Along the unit circle, \mathbf r^*(d\theta)=\mathbf r^*\alpha=dt,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\theta(\cos t,\sin t)=1. So \theta(\cos t,\sin t)=t+C. At t=0 and t=2\pi, the point on the circle is the same: (1,0). But the formula would give values differing by 2\pi: C\qquad\text{and}\qquad 2\pi+C. A single-valued function cannot do that.

figure.caption: The angle function works on a half-plane. It cannot be made single-valued around a full loop.

subsection.p: This is the difference between local and global exactness: \boxed{\begin{array}{c}\text{locally exact: potentials exist in small neighborhoods},\\[1mm]\text{globally exact: one potential works on the whole domain.}\end{array}}
A hole can prevent local potentials from gluing into one global potential.

subsection.title: A singular form that breaks the theorem if the singularity is ignored
subsection.p: The same warning appears in space, one degree higher.

Let r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}, and define the vector field \mathbf G(x,y,z)=\frac{(x,y,z)}{r^3} on \mathbb R^3\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}. Its flux 2-form is \boxed{\Phi=\frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz+\frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx+\frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy.}

Away from the origin, d\Phi=(\nabla\cdot\mathbf G)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Compute the divergence. Since \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{x}{r^3}\right)=\frac1{r^3}-\frac{3x^2}{r^5}, and similarly for y and z,
\nabla\cdot\mathbf G \amp= \left(\frac1{r^3}-\frac{3x^2}{r^5}\right)+\left(\frac1{r^3}-\frac{3y^2}{r^5}\right)+\left(\frac1{r^3}-\frac{3z^2}{r^5}\right) \amp= \frac3{r^3}-\frac{3(x^2+y^2+z^2)}{r^5} \amp= \frac3{r^3}-\frac{3r^2}{r^5} \amp= 0.
Thus \boxed{d\Phi=0} wherever \Phi is defined.

Now integrate over the sphere S_a of radius a, oriented outward. On that sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a}, and \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}. Therefore \mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a^4}=\frac{a^2}{a^4}=\frac1{a^2}. So \boxed{\int_{S_a}\Phi=\iint_{S_a}\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=\frac1{a^2}\cdot 4\pi a^2=4\pi.}
It is tempting to say: d\Phi=0,\qquad \text{so the flux through the sphere should be }0. That is the mistake. The form is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the sphere.
The divergence theorem cannot be applied to the whole ball x^2+y^2+z^2\le a^2, because \Phi is not smooth on that ball. It is not even defined at the center.

If we remove a small ball around the origin, the theorem works perfectly. Let E_{\varepsilon,a}=\{(x,y,z):\varepsilon\le r\le a\}. This is a spherical shell. Its boundary has two pieces: \partial E_{\varepsilon,a}=S_a- S_\varepsilon. The minus sign appears because the outward normal for the shell on the inner sphere points toward the origin.
Since d\Phi=0 on the shell, \int_{\partial E_{\varepsilon,a}}\Phi=\int_{E_{\varepsilon,a}}d\Phi=0. And indeed, \int_{S_a}\Phi-\int_{S_\varepsilon}\Phi=4\pi-4\pi=0.
The singularity is not a minor defect. It carries the missing flux.

exercise.title: Where does the flux come from?

statement.p: We found d\Phi=0 at every point where \Phi is defined, and yet the flux through the sphere is 4\pi. If the local source density vanishes everywhere, where is the flux coming from, and why does removing a tiny ball make the divergence theorem behave again?

hint.p: Think about the one point that the form refuses to talk about. Is it inside the sphere? Is it inside the shell?

figure.caption: Removing the singular point turns the ball into a shell. The boundary now has two spheres with opposite induced orientations.

subsection.title: Why zero derivative can hide global information
subsection.p: The two examples have the same shape.
In the punctured plane, \alpha=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy satisfies d\alpha=0, but \int_{\text{unit circle}}\alpha=2\pi.
In punctured space, \Phi=\frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz+\frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx+\frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy satisfies d\Phi=0, but \int_{\text{unit sphere}}\Phi=4\pi.
The word closed has two meanings in this discussion, and both matter.

exercise.title: Two kinds of closed, one role for the hole?

statement.p: A form being closed (d\omega=0) and a curve or surface being closed (\partial C=0) are different statements. Yet in both the plane and space examples, it is a closed object wrapped around a missing point that exposes the failure of exactness. Why is it precisely the hole that lets these two notions of closed meet and produce a nonzero answer?

hint.p: Imagine filling in the missing point. Could the closed loop or sphere then be the boundary of something living entirely inside the domain? What would that force the integral to be?

subsection.p: A form is closed when d\alpha=0. A curve or surface is closed when it has no boundary: \partial C=0,\qquad \partial S=0.

If a form is exact, then its integral over a closed object must vanish. For a closed curve, \int_C d\phi=0. For a closed surface, \int_S d\omega=0. The boundary of the boundary has nothing left to measure.
So a nonzero integral over a closed loop or closed surface is a certificate: \boxed{\text{the form is not exact on that domain.}}
The derivative d checks local density: local curl, local source, local change. A closed loop or surface can check something larger: whether the domain has a missing piece that the form winds around.

That is why the next theorem has to mention both objects: \text{a form}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\text{the boundary of the region where it is integrated.} The next section will put the whole chapter into one translation table. Then gives the single boundary theorem that explains why all these local and global pieces fit together: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.

introduction.p: ended with a warning. The equation d\alpha=0 is local. It checks what happens near each point where the form is defined. But integrals around closed loops and closed surfaces can detect something larger: a missing point, a missing axis, or a hole in the domain.
Now we collect the whole chapter into one dictionary.
The exterior derivative does one simple thing: \boxed{d \text{ raises degree by }1.}

In ordinary three-dimensional space, the ladder is 0\text{-forms} \xrightarrow{\ d\ } 1\text{-forms} \xrightarrow{\ d\ } 2\text{-forms} \xrightarrow{\ d\ } 3\text{-forms} \xrightarrow{\ d\ } 0. The last arrow gives zero because there are no nonzero 4-forms in ordinary three-dimensional space.
The practical rule is just as simple: \boxed{\text{Differentiate the coefficient, then wedge with the coordinate factors.}}
The wedge product then takes care of the signs: dx\wedge dx=0, \qquad dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx.

subsection.title: d on 0-forms: gradient information
subsection.p: A 0-form is a function. Its exterior derivative is the differential.
If f=f(x,y,z), then \boxed{df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz.} This 1-form measures tangent vectors: df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v) = f_x(\mathbf p)v_x+f_y(\mathbf p)v_y+f_z(\mathbf p)v_z.

example.title: A 0-form and its first-order change

statement.p: Let f(x,y,z)=x^2y+yz. Then f_x=2xy, \qquad f_y=x^2+z, \qquad f_z=y. So \boxed{df=2xy\,dx+(x^2+z)\,dy+y\,dz.}

At the point P=(1,2,3), this becomes df_P=4\,dx+4\,dy+2\,dz. If a particle passes through P with velocity \mathbf v=(2,-1,3), then
df_P(\mathbf v) \amp= 4(2)+4(-1)+2(3) \amp= 10.
So f is increasing at rate 10 along that motion.
In gradient notation, \nabla f(P)=(4,4,2), and \nabla f(P)\cdot \mathbf v = (4,4,2)\cdot(2,-1,3) = 10.

subsection.p: So the first row of the dictionary is: \boxed{\text{exterior derivative of a function} = \text{gradient information as a }1\text{-form}.}
But df is not mainly a vector. It is a covector, a measuring rule for tangent vectors. The gradient vector appears only after the dot product translates that measuring rule into a vector.

subsection.title: d on 1-forms: curl information
subsection.p: A 1-form is integrated along curves. Its exterior derivative is a 2-form, so it is integrated over surfaces. This is why d\omega measures circulation density.
In the plane, let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. Then \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.} The coefficient Q_x-P_y is the scalar curl in the plane.
So Green's theorem can be read as \text{circulation around the boundary} = \text{circulation density added over the inside}.
In space, let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. Then \boxed{d\omega = (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz + (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx + (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) and \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, then \boxed{d\omega_{\mathbf F}=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}.} In words: \boxed{\text{the exterior derivative of a work form is the curl as a flux form.}}

example.title: A 1-form and its curl 2-form

statement.p: Let \omega=(xy+z)\,dx+(y^2+xz)\,dy+(x^2-y)\,dz. Here P=xy+z, \qquad Q=y^2+xz, \qquad R=x^2-y. Compute the three curl coefficients: R_y-Q_z=-1-x, P_z-R_x=1-2x, and Q_x-P_y=z-x. Therefore \boxed{d\omega = (-1-x)\,dy\wedge dz + (1-2x)\,dz\wedge dx + (z-x)\,dx\wedge dy.}
If \mathbf F=(xy+z,\ y^2+xz,\ x^2-y), then \nabla\times\mathbf F=(-1-x,\ 1-2x,\ z-x), and d\omega is exactly the flux form of that curl.

subsection.p: The standard order dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx,\qquad dx\wedge dy is not accidental. These are the three coordinate area forms perpendicular to the x-, y-, and z-axes:

table.title: Coordinate area forms and the components they match

subsection.p: That is why the curl vector becomes a flux 2-form in exactly this order.

subsection.title: d on 2-forms: divergence information
subsection.p: A 2-form is integrated over surfaces. Its exterior derivative is a 3-form, so it is integrated over solids. This is why d\Phi measures source density.
In space, a flux 2-form has the shape \Phi = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy. Then \boxed{d\Phi = (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}

If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), then P_x+Q_y+R_z=\nabla\cdot\mathbf F. So \boxed{d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.} In words: \boxed{\text{the exterior derivative of a flux form is divergence as a volume form.}}

example.title: A 2-form and its source density

statement.p: Let \Phi = (x^2+yz)\,dy\wedge dz + (\sin y+xz)\,dz\wedge dx + (xy+e^z)\,dx\wedge dy. Here P=x^2+yz, \qquad Q=\sin y+xz, \qquad R=xy+e^z. Therefore P_x=2x, \qquad Q_y=\cos y, \qquad R_z=e^z. So \boxed{d\Phi=(2x+\cos y+e^z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.} The coefficient 2x+\cos y+e^z is the divergence of the vector field whose flux form is \Phi.

subsection.p: This is the third row of the dictionary: \boxed{\text{exterior derivative of a flux form} = \text{divergence information as a volume form}.}

subsection.title: The two forms attached to a vector field
subsection.p: A vector field in space can be turned into two different forms. They do different jobs.
If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), then its work form is \boxed{\omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.} This is integrated over curves.
The exterior derivative treats these two forms differently:

table.title: Work form and flux form of the same vector field

subsection.p: This is a common place to mix things up. The same vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) does not automatically tell us whether we are doing work or flux. The form tells us.

subsection.title: The whole dictionary
subsection.p: The chapter can now be compressed into one table.

table.title: The exterior derivative across all degrees in \mathbb R^3

subsection.p: The classical vector-calculus names are shadows of the same operation: \boxed{\begin{array}{ccl} f \amp \xrightarrow{\ d\ } \amp df \quad\text{contains gradient information},\\ \omega_{\mathbf F} \amp \xrightarrow{\ d\ } \amp \Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F} \quad\text{contains curl information},\\ \Phi_{\mathbf F} \amp \xrightarrow{\ d\ } \amp (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \quad\text{contains divergence information}. \end{array}}

figure.caption: Gradient, curl, and divergence are one operation, d, seen in different degrees.

subsection.title: Closed, exact, and the role of holes
subsection.p: The identity \boxed{d^2=0} says that every exact form is closed: \alpha=d\beta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d\alpha=0.
In forms language, both are the same statement: d(d(\text{something}))=0.
The reverse direction is the delicate one.

table.title: Closed, exact, and the warning between them

row.cell: usually caused by holes or singularities

subsection.p: The punctured-plane form \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx + \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy is closed where it is defined, but its integral around the unit circle is 2\pi. That nonzero integral proves it is not exact on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}.

The punctured-space flux form \frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz + \frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx + \frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy is closed where it is defined, but its integral over any sphere around the missing origin is 4\pi. That nonzero integral proves it is not exact on \mathbb R^3\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}.
So the slogan from is worth keeping: \boxed{d\alpha=0 \text{ is local; } \alpha=d\beta \text{ is global.}}
A derivative sees tiny neighborhoods. A closed loop or closed surface can see the shape of the domain.

p.em: Looking ahead: a form on a boundary and its derivative inside.

conclusion.p: has focused on the right-hand side of the future theorem: d\omega. We now know how to compute it. We know that it becomes gradient, curl, or divergence depending on the degree of the form. We also know that applying d twice gives zero.
The missing piece is the boundary.
The same pattern has already appeared several times:

table.title: A form on a boundary and its derivative inside

conclusion.p: The dimensions always match. If M is k-dimensional, then \partial M is (k-1)-dimensional. So a (k-1)-form can be integrated over the boundary, and its exterior derivative, a k-form, can be integrated over the inside.
That is the shape of the theorem: \boxed{\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.}
In one dimension, it is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^b df. In the plane, it is Green's theorem. On surfaces, it is Stokes' theorem. In solids, it is the divergence theorem.
The surprise is that these are not four separate miracles. They are one boundary principle wearing four different costumes.

will state that principle carefully. The signs will matter. The orientation of the boundary will matter. Smoothness and missing points will matter. But the heart of the proof is already visible: when a region is cut into many tiny pieces, the interior boundary contributions cancel in pairs. Only the outside boundary remains.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

introduction.p: Chapters 16 and 17 supplied forms, their integrals, and their exterior derivatives. We now specify the orientation induced on a boundary and state the theorem relating a boundary integral to an integral of the derivative inside. The familiar Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green, Stokes, and divergence theorems are its low-dimensional cases; the proof section distinguishes exact coordinate calculations from the general patching argument.

section.title: Boundaries and orientation
section.p: A form changes sign when orientation reverses. So before we state the theorem, we must make the signs automatic. The boundary of an interval, a region, a surface, or a solid should inherit its orientation from the object it bounds.

subsection.title: Oriented intervals and endpoints
subsection.p: Start with the old one-dimensional picture.

The interval I=[a,b] is oriented from left to right. Its boundary consists of two endpoints, but the endpoints do not have the same sign: \boxed{\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}.} The right endpoint is positive. The left endpoint is negative.
This is exactly the sign pattern in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). In forms language, f is a 0-form and \int_{\partial[a,b]} f=f(b)-f(a).

example.title: The boundary of an interval

statement.p:
Let I=[2,5] with the usual left-to-right orientation, and let f(x)=x^2+1. Then \partial I=\{5\}-\{2\}. So
\int_{\partial I} f \amp = f(5)-f(2) \amp = 26-5 \amp = 21.
If the same interval is given the opposite orientation, then its boundary becomes \{2\}-\{5\}, and the integral becomes -21.

subsection.p: A point by itself has no direction to walk. Its orientation is only a sign: +P \qquad\text{or}\qquad -P. That is enough for 0-forms.

The sign convention can be remembered by the word outward. At the right endpoint, the outward direction points in the positive direction of the interval. At the left endpoint, the outward direction points in the negative direction. So the right endpoint gets +, and the left endpoint gets -.

subsection.title: Oriented plane regions and boundary curves
subsection.p: A region in the xy-plane has the standard orientation dx\wedge dy. This means that the ordered pair of directions \text{positive }x\text{-direction first, positive }y\text{-direction second} is positive.
The boundary of such a region is oriented so that the region stays on your left as you walk along the boundary.
For a region without holes, this means counterclockwise.

figure.caption: A positively oriented plane boundary keeps the region on the left.

example.title: A rectangle and its positive boundary

statement.p: Let R=[0,4]\times[0,3], oriented by dx\wedge dy. Then \partial R is the rectangle walked counterclockwise: (0,0)\to(4,0)\to(4,3)\to(0,3)\to(0,0).

If \omega=x\,dy, then the bottom and top edges contribute 0, because dy=0 there. The right edge has x=4,\qquad 0\le y\le3, so \int_{\text{right edge}}x\,dy=\int_0^3 4\,dy=12. The left edge has x=0, so it contributes 0. Therefore \boxed{\int_{\partial R} x\,dy=12.} If we walk the rectangle clockwise, the answer becomes -12.

subsection.p: For a region with a hole, the same region on the left rule gives two different-looking directions.
The outer boundary is counterclockwise. The inner boundary is clockwise.

figure.caption: The inner boundary of a positively oriented annulus is walked clockwise.

subsection.p: This is not a special exception. It is the same rule. If you walk around the hole clockwise, the material of the annulus stays on your left.

exercise.title: Why does the hole turn the other way?

statement.p: The outer edge of the annulus is walked counterclockwise, but the inner edge around the hole is walked clockwise. Without computing anything, explain why these two opposite-looking directions are really the same rule. What single phrase ties them together?

hint.p: Stand on the boundary and ask: on which side does the gray material sit as you walk? Trace the inner circle clockwise in your mind and watch where the region lies.

definition.title: Positive boundary orientation in the plane

statement.p: Let R be a plane region oriented by dx\wedge dy. The positive orientation of \partial R is the one for which the region stays on the left as the boundary is traveled.
For a region without holes, this is counterclockwise. For an inner boundary around a hole, this is clockwise.

subsection.title: Oriented surfaces and boundary curves
subsection.p: A surface in space is oriented by choosing one of its two sides. Equivalently, we choose a continuous unit normal vector field \mathbf n on the surface.

For a parametrized surface \mathbf r(u,v), the normal direction attached to the parameter order (u,v) is \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v. Swapping the parameters reverses the orientation: \mathbf r_v\times \mathbf r_u = -\mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v.
Once the surface orientation is chosen, the boundary curve orientation is forced.

statement.p: We say that picking a side of the surface (a normal \mathbf n) forces the direction you walk the boundary. What would go wrong if you tried to flip the boundary direction while keeping the same normal \mathbf n? Why can't the two choices be made independently?

hint.p: Point your right thumb along \mathbf n and let your fingers curl. There is only one way they curl. Think about what Stokes' theorem \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega would say if the two sides disagreed by a sign.

example.title: A disk with two possible orientations

statement.p: Let D be the unit disk in the xy-plane: x^2+y^2\le1.
If D is oriented by the upward normal \mathbf n=\mathbf k, then its boundary circle is oriented counterclockwise when viewed from above: \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.
If D is oriented by the downward normal \mathbf n=-\mathbf k, then the same boundary circle is oriented clockwise when viewed from above: \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,-\sin t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.

subsection.p: The rule is the right-hand rule.
Point your right thumb in the chosen normal direction. Your fingers curl in the positive boundary direction.

figure.caption: Changing the surface normal reverses the boundary orientation.

subsection.p: There is also a version of the region on the left rule for surfaces.
Imagine standing on the surface with your head pointing in the chosen normal direction. Walk along the boundary in the positive direction. The surface should stay on your left.

definition.title: Boundary orientation of an oriented surface

statement.p: Let S be an oriented surface with chosen normal direction \mathbf n. The positive orientation of \partial S is the direction given by the right-hand rule: the thumb points in the direction of \mathbf n, and the fingers curl in the positive boundary direction.
Equivalently, when walking along the boundary with head in the normal direction, the surface stays on the left.

subsection.p: This is the orientation used in Stokes' theorem: \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. The sign of the boundary integral depends on the side of the surface we chose.

subsection.title: Oriented solids and boundary surfaces
subsection.p: A solid region in ordinary space has the standard orientation dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. The boundary of a solid is a surface, and its positive orientation is the outward one.
This is the orientation used for flux. A flux integral over the boundary of a solid uses the outward normal.

example.title: The boundary orientation of a box

statement.p:
Let E=[0,2]\times[0,3]\times[0,4]. The boundary \partial E has six faces. Each face is oriented by its outward normal.
\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Face} \amp \text{Outward normal} \amp \text{Positive area form on the face} \\ \hline x=2 \amp \mathbf i \amp dy\wedge dz\\[1mm] x=0 \amp -\mathbf i \amp dz\wedge dy\\[1mm] y=3 \amp \mathbf j \amp dz\wedge dx\\[1mm] y=0 \amp -\mathbf j \amp dx\wedge dz\\[1mm] z=4 \amp \mathbf k \amp dx\wedge dy\\[1mm] z=0 \amp -\mathbf k \amp dy\wedge dx \end{array}

For instance, the top face z=4 has outward normal \mathbf k, so its positive surface orientation is dx\wedge dy. The bottom face z=0 has outward normal -\mathbf k, so its positive surface orientation is dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy.

subsection.p: This sign pattern is not arbitrary. It comes from the same outward first rule that worked for intervals and plane regions.

subsection.title: The outward-first convention
subsection.p: All boundary orientations in this book come from one convention.

exercise.title: What is the boundary of a boundary?

statement.p: The boundary \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\} is a pair of signed points, and a point has no boundary at all, so \partial\partial[a,b] is empty. Looking at the outward-first picture, why should it be no accident that taking the boundary twice always leaves nothing behind? What does that say about the edges where two faces of the box meet?

hint.p: Each shared edge of the box belongs to two faces, and those two faces walk it in opposite directions. You don't need a formula here, just imagine the contributions of neighboring faces meeting along an edge.

statement.p: Let M be an oriented k-dimensional object, where k=1,2, or 3. At a smooth boundary point, let \nu_{\text{out}} be the outward direction normal to the boundary but tangent to M.

subsection.p: This convention may look abstract, so let us test it in the three familiar cases.
The theorem needs exactly these signs. If one sign is reversed, the two sides of Stokes' theorem disagree by a minus sign.
The boundary has now become a signed object. That is the missing piece. A form lives on the boundary, its derivative lives inside, and the orientations are ready to make the two integrals comparable.
The next step is to state the theorem that has been hiding behind the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem.

section.title: The theorem
section.p: fixed the signs on boundaries. fixed the meaning of d. The generalized Stokes theorem simply puts those two pieces in one sentence.
Before stating it, let us watch it work in one familiar rectangle.

subsection.title: A rectangle that already knows the theorem
subsection.p: Let R=[0,4]\times[0,3] with its standard orientation dx\wedge dy. Its boundary is oriented counterclockwise.
Take the 1-form \omega=x\,dy. We computed in that \int_{\partial R} x\,dy=12.

Now compute the exterior derivative: d\omega=d(x\,dy). Since dx\wedge dy is the area form, d(x\,dy)=dx\wedge dy. Therefore
\int_R d\omega \amp= \int_R dx\wedge dy \amp= \operatorname{Area}(R) \amp= 12.
So \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega.}
The boundary integral added x\,dy around the edge. The interior integral added dx\wedge dy across the rectangle. They gave the same number.

Nothing in this calculation depended on a hidden trick. The right edge of the rectangle carried all the boundary contribution, and the interior area had the same total size. For a more complicated 1-form, the same comparison happens locally on tiny rectangles. The exterior derivative measures the boundary circulation per unit area.

subsection.title: The statement
subsection.p: Here is the theorem in the form we will use.

statement.p: Let M be an oriented, compact, piecewise smooth k-dimensional object, with k=1,2, or 3. Give \partial M the induced boundary orientation from .

Let \omega be a C^1 differential form of degree k-1, defined on an open set containing M. Then \boxed{\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.} If \partial M=\emptyset, then the left side is defined to be 0.

subsection.p: We use this as a stated theorem. proves the rectangle and box cases and explains the patching argument; the estimates needed for a fully general piecewise smooth region are outlined there, not proved in full. The theorem is short, but every word is doing work.

table.title: What each word means.

row.cell: directions or sides have been chosen
finite, closed, bounded pieces in our examples
smooth pieces are allowed to meet at corners
d\omega can be integrated over M
there are no hidden singularities inside

subsection.title: What kind of object M is
subsection.p: The letter M is a common name for the object being integrated over. It does not force us into a new abstract world. In this book, M will be one of the following kinds of pieces.

table.title: The kinds of object M and their boundaries.

subsection.p: A rectangle, a disk, an annulus, a cylinder side, a hemisphere, a box, and a solid ball all fit this language.

Corners are allowed. A rectangle is not smooth at its four corners, but it is made of smooth sides. A box is not smooth along its edges, but it is made of smooth faces. That is what piecewise smooth means here.

A sphere considered as a surface has no boundary curve: \partial S=\emptyset. A solid ball has boundary: \partial E=\text{the sphere}. The same sphere can appear in two different roles, and the theorem reads it differently depending on the dimension of M.

subsection.title: What kind of object \omega is
subsection.p: The form \omega always has one degree less than M.
If M is one-dimensional, then \omega is a 0-form, which means a function. If M is two-dimensional, then \omega is a 1-form. If M is three-dimensional, then \omega is a 2-form.

table.title: Each row is a classical theorem in disguise.

cell.m: P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy

subsection.p: This table is the whole chapter in compressed form. The next sections will unpack each row.

statement.p: Each row of the table pairs \omega with an M whose dimension is exactly one more than the degree of \omega. Why must \omega always carry one fewer degree than the dimension of M for the statement \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega to even make sense? What would go wrong if the degrees did not line up this way?

hint.p: Ask where each object gets integrated: \omega over \partial M and d\omega over M. Compare the dimension of each domain with the degree of the form sitting on it.

subsection.title: Why the dimensions match
subsection.p: The theorem says \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. The two integrals live in different places, but their dimensions match perfectly.
If \dim M=k, then \dim(\partial M)=k-1. The form \omega has degree k-1, so it can be integrated over \partial M. The exterior derivative d\omega has degree k, so it can be integrated over M.
That is the reason d raises degree by one. The derivative inside the region must be one dimension higher than the form on the boundary.

statement.p: The diagram shows \omega living on \partial M and d\omega living on M. In your own words, why does it make conceptual sense that the operation d raises the degree of a form by one, rather than lowering it or leaving it unchanged?

hint.p: Think about what d\omega has to be ready for: it gets integrated over M, which is one dimension larger than \partial M. The form must match the size of the region it fills.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses are needed
subsection.p: The theorem is powerful because it is precise. If we drop its conditions carelessly, the formula can lose meaning or give the wrong sign.
The boundary orientation must be induced. Take the unit square R=[0,1]\times[0,1] with the usual orientation dx\wedge dy, and take \omega=x\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy, so \int_R d\omega=1.

With the induced boundary orientation, \partial R is counterclockwise and \int_{\partial R}\omega=1. But if we walk the boundary clockwise, then \int_{-\partial R}\omega=-1. So the formula would say -1=1, which is false.
The theorem did not fail. We used the wrong boundary orientation.

Every boundary component must be included. Let A=\{(x,y):1\le x^2+y^2\le4\} be the annulus between the circles of radius 1 and 2. Use the standard orientation dx\wedge dy, and again take \omega=x\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy, so \int_A d\omega=\operatorname{Area}(A)=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.
Now compute the boundary integral. The outer circle is counterclockwise, and the inner circle is clockwise.

On a counterclockwise circle of radius r, x=r\cos t,\qquad y=r\sin t, so dy=r\cos t\,dt. Thus
\int x\,dy \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} r^2\cos^2 t\,dt \amp= \pi r^2.
The outer circle contributes 4\pi. The inner circle is oriented clockwise, so it contributes -\pi. Therefore \int_{\partial A}\omega=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.
If we forgot the inner boundary, we would get 4\pi, which is wrong. Holes have boundary curves too, and their orientations matter.

The form must be defined on the whole region. Consider the 1-form on the punctured plane \eta=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. showed that this form is closed where it is defined: d\eta=0\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}.

On the unit circle x=\cos t,\qquad y=\sin t, we have dx=-\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=\cos t\,dt. So
\eta \amp= (-\sin t)(-\sin t\,dt)+(\cos t)(\cos t\,dt) \amp= dt.
Therefore \int_{x^2+y^2=1}\eta=\int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi.

A careless use of Stokes' theorem on the unit disk would say \int_{\partial D}\eta=\int_D d\eta=0. But this is not allowed. The form \eta is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the disk.
The missing point is not harmless. The boundary circle detects it.
The smoothness assumptions keep the integrals meaningful. The theorem asks for \omega to be C^1. This guarantees that d\omega exists and is continuous.

For example, \omega=|x|\,dy is not C^1 on any region crossing the line x=0. The derivative of |x| is not defined at x=0, so the expression d\omega is not defined by the rules of this book on that line.
Some rough cases can be handled by more advanced versions of Stokes' theorem. But the theorem stated here is a theorem for the objects we know how to integrate.

The same warning applies to the boundary. A polygon is fine, because it is made from smooth pieces. A cube is fine, because it is made from smooth faces. A wildly jagged fractal boundary has no tangent direction at most points, so our line integral along it has not been defined.

subsection.title: Why the theorem is believable
subsection.p: The proof idea is already visible in a grid.

Cut a plane region into many small rectangles. On each small rectangle, \int_{\partial(\text{small rectangle})}\omega measures the local boundary circulation. The exterior derivative d\omega measures the same local circulation per unit area, so \int_{\partial(\text{small rectangle})}\omega=\int_{\text{small rectangle}}d\omega for the ideal small piece.
Now add all small rectangles.
Every interior edge is walked twice, once in each direction. A 1-form changes sign when direction reverses, so the two contributions cancel. Only the outside boundary remains.

figure.caption: When small pieces are added, interior boundary contributions cancel.

subsection.p: The same cancellation happens for intervals, surfaces, and solids.
For intervals, the interior endpoints cancel: (f(x_1)-f(x_0))+(f(x_2)-f(x_1))+\cdots+(f(x_n)-f(x_{n-1}))=f(x_n)-f(x_0).
For surfaces, interior curves cancel. For solids, interior faces cancel. Boundary is what remains after all interior cancellations.

statement.p: When the small pieces are added up, every interior edge is walked twice and the two contributions cancel, leaving only the outer boundary. What does this cancellation tell you about why the equality \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega reaches across an entire region while only mentioning its boundary?

hint.p: Picture the information as flowing outward: anything happening between two adjacent cells is shared and cancels. Ask what is left that no neighbor can cancel.

subsection.p: That is the heart of the generalized Stokes theorem.

The next sections will open the theorem one disguise at a time. The first disguise is the oldest one: a function on an interval, whose derivative adds up to f(b)-f(a). The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus was already Stokes' theorem. We just did not yet have the language to say so.

section.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as Stokes
section.p: The generalized Stokes theorem says \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. The shortest nontrivial case happens when M is an interval. Then the boundary is only two signed endpoints, and \omega is only a function.
That case is not a new theorem. It is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

subsection.title: A changing temperature along a rod
subsection.p: Imagine a thin metal rod lying along the x-axis from x=1 \qquad\text{to}\qquad x=4. The temperature along the rod is T(x)=x^2+2x. Then dT=T'(x)\,dx=(2x+2)\,dx.

The interval I=[1,4] is oriented from left to right. Its boundary is \partial I=\{4\}-\{1\}. So the boundary integral of the 0-form T is
\int_{\partial I}T \amp= T(4)-T(1) \amp= (16+8)-(1+2) \amp= 21.
This is exactly Stokes' theorem: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega, with M=I, \qquad \omega=T.

subsection.title: A 0-form on an interval
subsection.p: A 0-form is a function. On an interval, \omega=f(x) is a 0-form, and its exterior derivative is the 1-form \boxed{d\omega=df=f'(x)\,dx.}
So the two sides of Stokes become \int_{\partial[a,b]}f and \int_{[a,b]}df.
The first one is an endpoint calculation. The second one is an ordinary integral.
If [a,b] is oriented from a to b, then \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}. Therefore \boxed{\int_{\partial[a,b]}f=f(b)-f(a).}
Meanwhile, \boxed{\int_{[a,b]}df=\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx.}
That is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

theorem.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as Stokes

subsection.p: The theorem is familiar, but the forms language shows its shape:
subsection.md: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Stokes language} \amp \text{One-variable language} \\ \hline M=[a,b] \amp \text{the interval of integration}\\[1mm] \partial M=\{b\}-\{a\} \amp \text{right endpoint minus left endpoint}\\[1mm] \omega=f \amp \text{a function}\\[1mm] d\omega=df=f'(x)\,dx \amp \text{the derivative times }dx\\[1mm] \displaystyle\int_{\partial M}\omega \amp f(b)-f(a)\\[3mm] \displaystyle\int_M d\omega \amp \displaystyle\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx \end{array}

subsection.title: The boundary signs are the whole point
subsection.p: The boundary of an interval is not just the set \{a,b\}. It is the signed set \{b\}-\{a\}. Without those signs, the theorem would not know the difference between f(b)-f(a) and f(a)+f(b).

exercise.title: Where does the minus sign come from?

statement.p: The boundary of [a,b] is written \{b\}-\{a\}, with a minus in front of the left endpoint. In what sense is one endpoint positive and the other negative, given that both are just points on a line? What information is the minus sign actually recording?

hint.p: Think about which way the interval is being traveled. The sign is not a property of the point alone, but of how the oriented interval meets that point.

example.title: Reversing the interval reverses the theorem

statement.p: Let f(x)=x^3 on the interval [0,2]. With the usual orientation, \partial[0,2]=\{2\}-\{0\}. So \int_{\partial[0,2]}f=f(2)-f(0)=8. Also \int_{[0,2]}df=\int_0^2 3x^2\,dx=8.

Now reverse the orientation. The same geometric interval is now traveled from 2 to 0. Its boundary is \{0\}-\{2\}. Therefore \int_{\partial(-[0,2])}f=f(0)-f(2)=-8. The integral through the interval also reverses: \int_{-[0,2]}df=\int_2^0 3x^2\,dx=-8. Both sides change sign together.

subsection.p: This is the first lesson about orientation:
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{Reversing orientation reverses both sides of Stokes' theorem.}}

subsection.title: A one-dimensional cancellation picture
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus already contains the cancellation idea behind all versions of Stokes' theorem.

Cut the interval [a,b] into smaller intervals: a=x_0<x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_n=b. On each small interval, [x_{j-1},x_j], the boundary is \{x_j\}-\{x_{j-1}\}. So its boundary contribution is f(x_j)-f(x_{j-1}).

Add all the small boundary contributions:
\amp\bigl(f(x_1)-f(x_0)\bigr)+\bigl(f(x_2)-f(x_1)\bigr)+\cdots+\bigl(f(x_n)-f(x_{n-1})\bigr) \amp\qquad = f(x_n)-f(x_0).
Every interior point appears twice with opposite signs: +f(x_1)-f(x_1), \qquad +f(x_2)-f(x_2), \qquad \ldots Only the outside boundary survives.

statement.p: When the small boundary contributions are added up, every interior point x_j appears twice and cancels, while only a and b survive. Why does each interior point pick up opposite signs, and what would break if neighboring pieces did not share their boundary signs this way?

hint.p: An interior point x_j is the right endpoint of one small interval and the left endpoint of the next. Ask what sign it gets in each role.

figure.caption: The one-dimensional cancellation behind the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

subsection.p: This same cancellation will reappear in the plane. Instead of interior endpoints, we will have interior edges. Instead of df, we will have d(P\,dx+Q\,dy).

subsection.title: Why the smoothness condition is not decorative
subsection.p: The theorem asked for f to be C^1. That is stronger than just being a function with endpoint values. The derivative df must exist and behave well throughout the interval.
Here is what can go wrong.

example.title: A hidden jump breaks the naive formula

statement.p: Away from x=0, the function is constant, so a careless person might say df=0 and conclude \int_{[-1,1]}df=0. That would give 1=0, which is false.

The problem is the jump at x=0. The function is not continuous there, and it is not C^1. In our rules, df is not a valid continuous 1-form on the whole interval. The theorem was never allowed to be used.
The missing smoothness is hiding an internal boundary.

subsection.p: A corner is less dangerous than a jump, but it still needs care.

example.title: A corner can be handled by splitting

statement.p: Let f(x)=|x| on [-1,1]. This function is continuous, but it is not differentiable at x=0. So the C^1 version of the theorem does not apply directly.

But if we split the interval into two smooth pieces, [-1,0] \qquad\text{and}\qquad [0,1], then f(x)=-x \quad\text{on }[-1,0], and f(x)=x \quad\text{on }[0,1]. Thus
\int_{-1}^{0}(-1)\,dx+\int_0^1 1\,dx \amp= -1+1 \amp= 0.
The endpoint difference is also f(1)-f(-1)=1-1=0.
The formula survives after splitting, because the function has no jump. But the single C^1 theorem did not cover the whole interval at once.

subsection.p: This is a useful pattern. Piecewise smooth objects are usually allowed, but the pieces and their boundary signs must be accounted for honestly.

subsection.title: The first Stokes theorem
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is often introduced as a theorem about antiderivatives. In this chapter, it is better to see it as the first boundary theorem.
It says:
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{the total derivative inside an interval equals the signed value on the boundary.}}
subsection.p: The phrase signed value on the boundary is the new part. Once we learn to hear it, the theorem no longer feels like a one-dimensional accident.

exercise.title: Why call it a boundary theorem?

statement.p: Calling the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus a boundary theorem reframes f(b)-f(a) as a value living on the boundary of the interval. What does this shift in viewpoint let you anticipate about a plane region, before you have seen Green's theorem at all?

hint.p: The boundary of an interval is two points; the boundary of a plane region is a curve. Picture what signed value on the boundary should become when the boundary is no longer just endpoints.

subsection.p: The interval has two boundary points. A plane region has a boundary curve. When the same idea moves from endpoints to curves, the derivative inside changes from df to d(P\,dx+Q\,dy). That is where Green's theorem enters the story.

section.title: Green's Theorem as Stokes
section.p: The previous section turned the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus into \int_{\partial[a,b]}f=\int_{[a,b]}df. Now the object M becomes a plane region R. Its boundary is no longer two endpoints. It is a closed curve.
The form on the boundary is no longer a function. It is a 1-form: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. Its derivative is a 2-form: d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. That is Green's theorem in Stokes form.

subsection.title: A triangular region that measures area from its boundary
subsection.p: Let R be the triangle with vertices (0,0),\qquad (3,0),\qquad (0,2), oriented by the standard area form dx\wedge dy. Then \partial R is walked counterclockwise.

Take the 1-form \omega=x\,dy. Its exterior derivative is d\omega=dx\wedge dy. So the right-hand side of Stokes should be \int_R dx\wedge dy=\operatorname{Area}(R)=3. Now compute the boundary integral directly.
The boundary has three sides.
Bottom side. Parametrize the bottom edge by \mathbf r_1(t)=(t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le3. Here dy=0, so \int_{\mathbf r_1}x\,dy=0.

Slanted side. Parametrize the slanted side from (3,0) to (0,2) by \mathbf r_2(t)=(3-3t,2t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Then x=3-3t, \qquad dy=2\,dt. Therefore
\int_{\mathbf r_2}x\,dy \amp= \int_0^1 (3-3t)\,2\,dt \amp= \int_0^1 (6-6t)\,dt \amp= 3.
Left side. Parametrize the left side from (0,2) back to (0,0) by \mathbf r_3(t)=(0,2-2t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. Here x=0, so \int_{\mathbf r_3}x\,dy=0.

figure.caption: For this triangle, the boundary integral of x\,dy measures area.

subsection.p: This example is Green's theorem in its cleanest form. The boundary form x\,dy turns into the area form dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Exterior derivative and scalar curl
subsection.p:
Let \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy be a 1-form on a plane region. To compute d\omega, use d(P\,dx)=dP\wedge dx, and d(Q\,dy)=dQ\wedge dy. Since dP=P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy, we get
d(P\,dx) \amp= (P_x\,dx+P_y\,dy)\wedge dx \amp= P_x\,dx\wedge dx+P_y\,dy\wedge dx \amp= -P_y\,dx\wedge dy.
Similarly,
d(Q\,dy) \amp= (Q_x\,dx+Q_y\,dy)\wedge dy \amp= Q_x\,dx\wedge dy+Q_y\,dy\wedge dy \amp= Q_x\,dx\wedge dy.
Therefore \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

The coefficient Q_x-P_y is the scalar curl in the plane. It measures local counterclockwise circulation per unit area. \boxed{\text{exterior derivative of a plane }1\text{-form}=\text{scalar curl}\times\text{area form}.}

statement.p: The number Q_x-P_y appears as the lone coefficient in d\omega. Without computing anything, what is this coefficient telling you about the flow described by \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy at a single point, and why is it sensible that the rest of d\omega is just the area form dx\wedge dy?

hint.p: Think of d\omega as a local rate. The area form supplies the per unit area part; the coefficient supplies the how much circulation part. What spinning motion would make this coefficient large and positive?

subsection.title: Green's theorem in circulation form
subsection.p: We can now read Green's theorem as one row of the generalized Stokes theorem.

statement.p: Let R be a compact, oriented, piecewise smooth plane region. Give \partial R the positive boundary orientation, so that R stays on the left as the boundary is traveled.

subsection.title: A rectangle with changing curl
subsection.p: Let R=[0,2]\times[0,1], with positive orientation, and let \omega=xy\,dx+x^2\,dy. Then P=xy, \qquad Q=x^2. So P_y=x, \qquad Q_x=2x. Therefore d\omega=(2x-x)\,dx\wedge dy=x\,dx\wedge dy.

The interior integral is
\int_R d\omega \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 x\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2 x\,dx \amp= 2.
Now check the boundary integral.
On the bottom edge, y=0 and dy=0, so \omega=0. The bottom contributes 0.
On the right edge, x=2, dx=0, and y goes from 0 to 1. Thus \omega=4\,dy, so the right edge contributes \int_0^1 4\,dy=4.
On the top edge, y=1, dy=0, and x goes from 2 back to 0. Thus \omega=x\,dx, so the top edge contributes \int_2^0 x\,dx=-2.
On the left edge, x=0, so \omega=0. The left edge contributes 0.

figure.caption: The boundary contributions add to the integral of d\omega=x\,dx\wedge dy inside the rectangle.

subsection.title: Why interior edges cancel
subsection.p: The proof idea is the same as in one dimension.
Cut R into many small rectangles. Apply Green's theorem on each small rectangle. Now add all the small boundary integrals.
Every interior edge is traveled twice: \text{once in one direction, once in the opposite direction.} A 1-form integral changes sign when the direction reverses. So the two contributions cancel.
Only the outer boundary remains.
That is the same cancellation we saw for an interval, where interior endpoints canceled. Green's theorem is the two-dimensional version of the same boundary bookkeeping.

subsection.title: Holes and boundary components
subsection.p: If a region has a hole, the boundary has more than one component. Green's theorem uses all of them.
The outer boundary is counterclockwise. The inner boundary is clockwise.

exercise.title: Why does the hole turn the other way?

statement.p: The outer rim is traveled counterclockwise, yet the rim of the hole is traveled clockwise. What goes wrong with the identity \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega if you instead orient both boundary circles the same way, and what is the shared rule about the region that both orientations are obeying?

hint.p: Picture walking along each boundary curve. The positive convention asks you to keep the region R on one fixed side the whole time. Stand inside the annulus and ask which way is region on your left for the inner circle.

subsection.p: Here is a compact example that shows why.

Let A=\{(x,y):1\le x^2+y^2\le4\} be the annulus between the circles of radius 1 and 2. Consider the 1-form \alpha=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. This form is defined on the annulus, because the origin is not included. On that domain, d\alpha=0. So Green's theorem predicts \int_{\partial A}\alpha=0.

Now compute the boundary. On a counterclockwise circle of radius r, x=r\cos t, \qquad y=r\sin t, \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-r\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=r\cos t\,dt. Substitute:
\alpha \amp= \frac{-r\sin t}{r^2}(-r\sin t\,dt)+\frac{r\cos t}{r^2}(r\cos t\,dt) \amp= \sin^2t\,dt+\cos^2t\,dt \amp= dt.
So a counterclockwise circle contributes \int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi.

The outer boundary of the annulus is counterclockwise, so it contributes 2\pi. The inner boundary is clockwise, so it contributes -2\pi. Thus \boxed{\int_{\partial A}\alpha=2\pi-2\pi=0,} which matches \int_A d\alpha=0.
If we forgot the inner boundary, we would get 2\pi, which would contradict the theorem. The theorem did not fail. The boundary was incomplete.

subsection.title: A singularity inside the region is not allowed
subsection.p: The same form \alpha=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy is closed wherever it is defined: d\alpha=0 \qquad \text{on }\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. But on the unit circle, \int_{x^2+y^2=1}\alpha=2\pi. A careless person might try to apply Green's theorem to the unit disk and say \int_{\partial D}\alpha=\int_D d\alpha=0. That is not allowed. The form is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the disk.
The missing point is exactly what the boundary circle detects.

p.md: \boxed{\text{Green's theorem requires the form to be defined on the whole region, not only on the boundary.}}

subsection.title: A jump in the coefficients creates a hidden edge
subsection.p: The C^1 condition on P and Q also matters. If the coefficients jump, the usual formula can miss an internal boundary.
If we ignore the jump and only look away from y=0, then H is constant on each side, so a careless computation would say d\omega=0. That would predict \int_{\partial R}\omega=0.

But the boundary integral is not zero. On the bottom edge y=-1, H(y)=0, so the bottom contributes 0. On the top edge y=1, the boundary is traveled from x=1 to x=-1, and H(y)=1. So the top contributes \int_1^{-1} dx=-2. The vertical sides have dx=0. Hence \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=-2.}
The jump along y=0 is hiding an internal edge. The ordinary C^1 theorem is not designed to handle it.

subsection.title: Flux form of Green's theorem
subsection.p: Green's theorem also has a flux version.
Let \mathbf F=(A,B) be a vector field in the plane. The outward flux of \mathbf F across a positively oriented boundary is represented by the 1-form \boxed{\phi=A\,dy-B\,dx.}

To see why, parametrize the boundary by \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)) in positive orientation. Then the tangent direction keeps the region on the left, so the outward normal points to the right. A right normal times ds is (dy,-dx). Therefore \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_{\text{out}}\,ds=(A,B)\cdot(dy,-dx)=A\,dy-B\,dx.

Now compute the exterior derivative:
d\phi \amp= d(A\,dy-B\,dx) \amp= dA\wedge dy-dB\wedge dx \amp= A_x\,dx\wedge dy+B_y\,dx\wedge dy \amp= (A_x+B_y)\,dx\wedge dy.
The coefficient A_x+B_y is the divergence of \mathbf F.

example.title: Flux out of a circular pond

statement.p: Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,y), the radial field pointing away from the origin. The flux form is \phi=x\,dy-y\,dx. Its exterior derivative is d\phi=2\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Two Green's theorems, one Stokes theorem
subsection.p: The circulation form of Green's theorem uses \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. It gives \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dA.}
The flux form uses \phi=A\,dy-B\,dx. It gives \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_{\text{out}}\,ds=\iint_R \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dA.}

They look like two different vector calculus formulas. In forms language, they are the same theorem: \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\text{form}=\int_R d(\text{form}).} The only difference is which 1-form we choose for the boundary measurement.

statement.p: The circulation form and the flux form look like two separate results, but here they collapse into the single statement \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. In your own words, what is the one structural fact that both forms share, and what is the only thing you actually changed to pass from one to the other?

hint.p: Both statements integrate something on \partial R on the left and its exterior derivative d\omega on R on the right. Look only at which 1-form you fed in: P\,dx+Q\,dy versus A\,dy-B\,dx.

subsection.p: Green's theorem is Stokes' theorem on a flat surface. But a boundary curve in space does not have to lie flat. A wire loop can bend and twist, and a soap film can stretch across it in many possible shapes. The boundary is still a curve, but the inside is now a surface. The next disguise of the same theorem is the one that carries curl from a flat region into space.

section.title: Classical Stokes' theorem as generalized Stokes
section.p: kept everything flat. A plane region R had a boundary curve \partial R, and Green's theorem became \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. Now the region is allowed to bend into space. The boundary is still a curve, but the inside is a surface.
This is classical Stokes' theorem.

subsection.title: A tilted sheet and a boundary integral
subsection.p: Start with a tilted rectangular sheet in space: \mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,u+2v), \qquad 0\le u\le2,\quad 0\le v\le1. The parameter rectangle is D=[0,2]\times[0,1]. The surface orientation is determined by \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. Since \mathbf r_u=(1,0,1), \qquad \mathbf r_v=(0,1,2), we get \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=(-1,-2,1).
Now take the 1-form \omega=z\,dy. This form is built to be integrated along the boundary curve of the tilted sheet.

Instead of parametrizing the four boundary curves directly in space, pull the form back to the parameter rectangle. On the surface, x=u,\qquad y=v,\qquad z=u+2v. So dy=dv, and \mathbf r^*\omega=(u+2v)\,dv.
The boundary of D is positively oriented counterclockwise. Compute the integral around its four sides.
On the bottom side v=0, dv=0, so the contribution is 0.
On the right side u=2, v goes from 0 to 1, so \int_{\text{right}}(u+2v)\,dv = \int_0^1(2+2v)\,dv = 3.
On the top side v=1, dv=0, so the contribution is 0.
On the left side u=0, v goes from 1 down to 0, so \int_{\text{left}}(u+2v)\,dv = \int_1^0 2v\,dv = -1.
Adding the four sides gives \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega = \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = 3-1 = 2. }

Now compute the surface side. Since \omega=z\,dy, we have d\omega=dz\wedge dy. Pull this back: dz=d(u+2v)=du+2\,dv, so
\mathbf r^*(d\omega) \amp= (du+2\,dv)\wedge dv\\ \amp= du\wedge dv.
Therefore
\int_S d\omega \amp= \int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega)\\ \amp= \int_D du\wedge dv\\ \amp= \operatorname{Area}(D)\\ \amp= 2.
So \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. }

figure.caption: A positively oriented parameter rectangle induces the compatible orientation on the boundary of the surface.

subsection.p: The computation contains the whole theorem. The boundary integral on the surface was turned into a boundary integral on the parameter rectangle. Then Green's theorem took over.

subsection.title: Pullback to a parameter domain
subsection.p: A C^2 regular parametrization, one-to-one in the interior and tracing the patch's boundary once, \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)) lets us translate forms in space into forms in the parameter plane.

For a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz, the pullback is \boxed{ \mathbf r^*\omega = P(\mathbf r(u,v))\,d x(u,v) + Q(\mathbf r(u,v))\,d y(u,v) + R(\mathbf r(u,v))\,d z(u,v). } Here dx=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv, dy=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv, and dz=z_u\,du+z_v\,dv.
The pullback does two jobs at once. It substitutes the parametrization into the coefficients, and it replaces dx,dy,dz by the coordinate changes caused by du and dv.
For boundary integrals, \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega, } provided the boundary orientation on S is induced from the boundary orientation on D.
The most important identity is \boxed{ d(\mathbf r^*\omega)=\mathbf r^*(d\omega). } This is the chain rule in form language. It says that pulling back and differentiating fit together.

Here is the coordinate justification. Write \omega=\sum_i F_i\,dx_i and \mathbf r^*\omega=A\,du+B\,dv, where A=\sum_i F_i(\mathbf r)(x_i)_u and B=\sum_i F_i(\mathbf r)(x_i)_v. The product and chain rules give B_u-A_v=\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jF_i)(\mathbf r) \bigl((x_j)_u(x_i)_v-(x_j)_v(x_i)_u\bigr). Terms containing (x_i)_{uv}-(x_i)_{vu} cancel because \mathbf r is C^2. The displayed coefficient is exactly the coefficient obtained by pulling back d\omega=\sum_{i,j}\partial_jF_i\,dx_j\wedge dx_i. This proves the identity used here without assuming Stokes' theorem.

Now apply Green's theorem on D: \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D d(\mathbf r^*\omega). Using d(\mathbf r^*\omega)=\mathbf r^*(d\omega), we get \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega). Translated back to the surface, this becomes \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.
That is Stokes' theorem.

subsection.title: Curl as the exterior derivative of a 1-form
subsection.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R) be a vector field, and let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be its work 1-form.

Compute d\omega:
d\omega \amp= dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy+dR\wedge dz\\ \amp= (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz\\ \amp\quad+ (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx\\ \amp\quad+ (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.
In words: \boxed{ \text{the exterior derivative of the work form is the flux form of the curl.} }
This is why the right side of classical Stokes' theorem contains curl.

exercise.title: Why does curl show up at all?

statement.p: The right-hand side of Stokes' theorem could have been any combination of derivatives of P,Q,R. Why is it exactly the curl that appears, rather than, say, the divergence or some other mixture? What feature of d\omega forces this particular answer?

hint.p: Look back at the coefficients that came out of computing d\omega for a work 1-form. Nobody chose them by hand — ask what produced them.

subsection.title: Boundary circulation equals surface curl
subsection.p: Now the theorem can be written in both languages.

theorem.title: Classical Stokes' theorem as generalized Stokes

statement.p: Let S be an oriented compact piecewise smooth surface in space, with piecewise smooth boundary \partial S. Give \partial S the boundary orientation compatible with the orientation of S.
Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz be a C^1 1-form on an open set containing S. Then \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. }

subsection.p: The forms statement is the generalized Stokes theorem with M=S, \qquad \omega\text{ a }1\text{-form}. The vector statement is the classical formula students often learn first.
The left side is boundary circulation. The right side is curl passing through the surface.

subsection.title: A curved surface with the same boundary
subsection.p: Let \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy.

Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2, \qquad z\ge0, oriented by the upward/outward normal. Its boundary is the circle C:\quad x^2+y^2=a^2,\qquad z=0, oriented counterclockwise as viewed from above.

Now compute the surface integral. Since d\omega=dx\wedge dy, the integral \int_S dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of the shadow of S on the xy-plane. With upward orientation, that shadow is the disk x^2+y^2\le a^2 with positive orientation. Therefore \boxed{ \int_S d\omega=\int_S dx\wedge dy=\pi a^2. } Again, \boxed{ \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. }
The hemisphere and the flat disk have the same boundary. For this form, both surfaces give the same answer because Stokes' theorem only sees the boundary.

exercise.title: What does “only sees the boundary” mean?

statement.p: We bent the surface from a flat disk into a dome, yet the value of \int_S d\omega did not budge. What is the theorem really telling us about which features of a surface affect the answer and which are irrelevant? Could you replace the hemisphere with a wildly crumpled sheet and still get \pi a^2?

hint.p: Both sides of \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega share one curve. Think about what would have to change for the answer to change.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem is a sign-sensitive theorem. It is also sensitive to holes and singularities.

p.em: The boundary orientation must be compatible.

subsection.p: Use the disk x^2+y^2\le1,\qquad z=0, with upward orientation, and use \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy, so \int_S d\omega=\pi.
The compatible boundary orientation is counterclockwise. With that orientation, \int_{\partial S}\omega=\pi.
If we walk the same boundary clockwise, the boundary integral becomes -\pi. The surface integral has not changed. The problem is not the theorem; the boundary orientation was wrong.

p.em: Every boundary component must be included.

subsection.p: Let A=\{(x,y,0):1\le x^2+y^2\le4\} be a flat annulus with upward orientation. Its boundary has two components: C_{\text{outer}}:\ x^2+y^2=4, and C_{\text{inner}}:\ x^2+y^2=1. The compatible orientation is counterclockwise on the outer circle and clockwise on the inner circle.
For \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy, we have d\omega=dx\wedge dy. Therefore \int_A d\omega=\operatorname{Area}(A)=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.
On a counterclockwise circle of radius r, \int\omega=\pi r^2. So the outer boundary contributes 4\pi, while the clockwise inner boundary contributes -\pi. Thus \int_{\partial A}\omega=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.
If we forgot the inner boundary, the left side would be 4\pi, not 3\pi. The hole has a rim, and Stokes' theorem counts that rim with its induced sign.

p.em: The form must be defined on the whole surface.

subsection.p: Consider \alpha= -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx + \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. This form is defined away from the z-axis. Where it is defined, d\alpha=0.

A careless use of Stokes' theorem on the flat unit disk would say \int_C\alpha=\int_D d\alpha=0. But the form is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies in the disk. Stokes' theorem cannot be used there.

If we remove a small disk around the origin, the theorem works again. The new surface is an annulus. Its outer boundary contributes 2\pi, and its inner boundary contributes -2\pi. The total boundary integral is 0, matching \int d\alpha=0 on the annulus.
The missing point was not harmless. It carried the circulation.

statement.p: The form \alpha satisfies d\alpha=0 everywhere it is defined, so its exterior derivative seems to contribute nothing. Yet the loop integral came out to 2\pi, not 0. How can a single excluded point at the origin be responsible for all of that circulation, when the surface integrand vanishes everywhere it exists?

hint.p: Stokes' theorem needs \alpha defined on the whole surface. Ask what the disk contains that the form refuses to live at.

subsection.p: Stokes' theorem compares a boundary curve with a surface. But some surfaces have no boundary curve at all. A sphere has no rim. A closed box surface has no edge. Still, flux can pass through them. To read that situation as Stokes' theorem, the object inside must be one dimension higher: a solid region, with a 2-form on its boundary.

section.title: The divergence theorem as generalized Stokes
section.p: used M=S, where S was a surface and \partial S was a curve. A 1-form lived on the boundary curve, and its exterior derivative lived on the surface: \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.
Now move up one dimension. Let M=E be a solid region. Its boundary is a surface. So the boundary integrand must be a 2-form.
That is the divergence theorem.

subsection.title: A 2-form on a box
subsection.p: Let E=[0,2]\times[0,1]\times[0,3] with the standard orientation dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. The boundary \partial E is oriented outward.
Take the 2-form \boxed{\Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy.} This is the flux 2-form of the vector field \mathbf F=(x,y,z).
Compute the boundary integral face by face.
On the face x=2, the outward normal is \mathbf i, and the positive surface form is dy\wedge dz. There, x=2, so the contribution is \int_{x=2}2\,dy\wedge dz=2(1)(3)=6.
On the face x=0, the coefficient x is zero, so the contribution is 0.
On the face y=1, the outward normal is \mathbf j, and the positive surface form is dz\wedge dx. There, y=1, so the contribution is \int_{y=1}1\,dz\wedge dx=1(3)(2)=6.
On the face y=0, the contribution is 0.
On the face z=3, the outward normal is \mathbf k, and the positive surface form is dx\wedge dy. There, z=3, so the contribution is \int_{z=3}3\,dx\wedge dy=3(2)(1)=6.
On the face z=0, the contribution is 0.
Adding the six faces gives \boxed{\int_{\partial E}\Phi=6+6+6=18.}

Now compute the interior side. Since \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy, we have
d\Phi \amp= dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + dy\wedge dz\wedge dx + dz\wedge dx\wedge dy \amp= 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
Therefore
\int_E d\Phi \amp= \int_E 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \amp= 3\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp= 3(2)(1)(3) \amp= 18.
So \boxed{\int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi.}

figure.caption: For a solid, the boundary is a surface. A 2-form is the correct boundary integrand.

subsection.p: The example has the same shape as every version of Stokes: \text{form on the boundary} \qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad \text{derivative of the form inside}.

subsection.title: Exterior derivative and divergence
subsection.p: In words: \boxed{\text{the exterior derivative of the flux form is the divergence volume form.}}

exercise.title: Why does the degree go up?

statement.p: The flux form \Phi_{\mathbf F} is a 2-form, but its exterior derivative d\Phi_{\mathbf F} is a 3-form. Why is it natural that differentiating a 2-form should produce something that measures volume rather than surface area, and how does that match the picture of flux leaving the boundary and accumulating inside?

hint.p: Think about what each degree counts: a 2-form responds to oriented surface pieces, a 3-form to oriented chunks of volume. Where does the boundary live, and where does its "source" live?

subsection.p: A 2-form measures oriented surface pieces. Its derivative is a 3-form, which measures oriented volume pieces. That is exactly the movement from boundary flux to interior source.

subsection.title: Boundary flux equals interior source
subsection.p: The divergence theorem is the generalized Stokes theorem in dimension 3.

statement.p: Let E be a compact solid region in space with the standard orientation and piecewise smooth boundary \partial E. Give \partial E the outward boundary orientation.

Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy be a C^1 2-form on an open set containing E. Then \boxed{\int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi.} Equivalently, for the vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), \boxed{\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{out}}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV.}

subsection.p: The forms statement is \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega with M=E, \qquad \omega=\Phi.
The vector statement says: \boxed{\text{net outward flux through the boundary} = \text{total source strength inside}.}

statement.p: The theorem equates a quantity living only on the surface \partial E with a quantity spread throughout the solid E. In your own words, how can a measurement taken entirely on the outer skin "know" about all the sources hidden deep inside? What does it mean that the interior detail is invisible from outside except through its total?

hint.p: Imagine two solids with very different source patterns inside but the same total source strength. What would an observer measuring only the boundary flux be able to distinguish?

subsection.title: Flux out of a spherical tank
subsection.p: The direct surface calculation says the same thing. On the sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{(x,y,z)}{a}. Thus (x,y,z)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a} = a. So the outward flux is a\cdot 4\pi a^2=4\pi a^3.
The divergence theorem turned a surface integral into the volume of the ball. The surface was curved, but the interior source density was constant: \nabla\cdot(x,y,z)=3.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: The divergence theorem is often misused in three ways: the surface is not closed, the orientation is not outward, or the field is not defined inside. A fourth warning is smoothness: jumps can hide internal sources.

paragraphs.title: The boundary surface must be closed
paragraphs.p: Let D be the unit disk x^2+y^2\le1, \qquad z=0, oriented upward. Take the constant field \mathbf F=(0,0,1), with flux form \Phi=dx\wedge dy. Then \int_D\Phi=\pi. But d\Phi=d(dx\wedge dy)=0.

This does not contradict the divergence theorem. The disk is not the full boundary of a solid. It has a boundary curve: x^2+y^2=1,\qquad z=0. The divergence theorem applies to closed surfaces such as spheres, boxes, and the full boundary of a cylinder, not to one open cap by itself.

paragraphs.title: The orientation must be outward
paragraphs.p: Take the unit cube E=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1], and the 2-form \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz. Then d\Phi=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. So \int_E d\Phi=1.

With outward orientation, only the face x=1 contributes: \int_{\partial E}\Phi=1. If every face is oriented inward instead, the boundary integral becomes -1. The theorem uses the boundary orientation induced from the solid. For a solid in ordinary space, that means outward.

paragraphs.title: The form must be defined throughout the solid
paragraphs.p: Let r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} and consider the inverse-square radial field \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{r^3}. Its flux form is \Psi= \frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz + \frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx + \frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy. This form is not defined at the origin.
Away from the origin, \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0, so d\Psi=0 wherever \Psi is defined.

It would be wrong to say: d\Psi=0, \qquad \text{so } \int_{S_a}\Psi=0. The form is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the sphere. The divergence theorem cannot be applied to the whole ball.

If we remove the origin, the theorem works. Let E=\{(x,y,z):b\le r\le a\}, \qquad 0\lt b\lt a. Then d\Psi=0 on E. The boundary has two spheres. The outer sphere contributes 4\pi. The inner sphere has the orientation outward from the shell, which points toward the origin, so it contributes -4\pi. The total boundary integral is 4\pi-4\pi=0, matching \int_E d\Psi=0.
The missing point was acting like a source.

paragraphs.title: The form must be smooth enough
paragraphs.p: Let E=[-1,1]\times[-1,1]\times[-1,1], and define H(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x\lt 0,\\ 1, & x\ge 0. \end{cases} Consider the flux form \Phi=H(x)\,dy\wedge dz. This form jumps across the plane x=0. It is not C^1 on E.

If we ignore the jump and only look on the two sides, then H is constant on each side, so a careless computation would say d\Phi=0. But the outward flux through the boundary is not zero. On the face x=1, H(1)=1, so the contribution is \int_{x=1}dy\wedge dz=4. On the face x=-1, H(-1)=0, so there is no contribution. The other faces do not contribute to dy\wedge dz. Thus \boxed{\int_{\partial E}\Phi=4.}
The jump across x=0 is hiding an internal source sheet. The C^1 theorem is not designed to handle that sheet. More advanced versions can treat it, but then the jump must be counted honestly.

subsection.title: Why closed surfaces have no boundary curve
subsection.p: A sphere has no boundary curve. A cube surface looks as if it has edges, but as an oriented surface it has no boundary curve. Each edge is shared by two faces, and the two induced edge orientations cancel.

For a solid E, \partial E is a closed surface. It is the right kind of object for integrating a 2-form. It is not, by itself, the right kind of boundary for a 1-form line integral, because there is no outer rim to walk around.
This explains a useful consequence. A closed surface can have nonzero flux: \int_{\partial E}\Phi may be positive or negative. The sphere with the radial field (x,y,z) is an example.

But if the 2-form on a closed surface happens to be the exterior derivative of a globally defined 1-form, \Phi=d\omega, then \int_{\partial E}\Phi = \int_{\partial E}d\omega. Using generalized Stokes on the closed surface \partial E, \int_{\partial E}d\omega = \int_{\partial(\partial E)}\omega = 0. So \boxed{\int_{\partial E}d\omega=0.}
Flux through a closed surface can be nonzero. Flux of a curl through a closed surface is zero. The difference is whether the 2-form is arbitrary or is already the derivative of a 1-form.

exercise.title: Why must a curl's flux cancel?
