statement.p: If the 2-form is already d\omega for a globally defined 1-form \omega, its total flux through any closed surface \partial E is zero. Conceptually, why does writing the form as d\omega force the cancellation, when an arbitrary 2-form need not cancel at all? What role does "a boundary has no boundary" play here?

hint.p: Apply generalized Stokes one extra time, to the closed surface itself, and ask what \partial(\partial E) can possibly be. There is nothing left for \omega to be integrated over.

subsection.p: At this point the four old theorems have become one sentence: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. The sentence is short, but it is not magic. The next section opens the mechanism. On rectangles and boxes, the theorem is just the one-variable Fundamental Theorem of Calculus used several times. On larger shapes, interior boundary pieces cancel in pairs. That cancellation is the engine behind the whole chapter.

section.title: Proof ideas
section.p: The generalized Stokes theorem now has four familiar faces: \text{FTC},\qquad \text{Green},\qquad \text{classical Stokes},\qquad \text{divergence theorem}. The proof idea is the same in all of them. First prove the theorem on a simple coordinate piece. Then cut a complicated object into many simple pieces. Interior boundary contributions cancel. The outside boundary remains.
We start with the cleanest two-dimensional calculation.

subsection.title: Proof on a rectangle
subsection.p: Let R=[a,b]\times[c,d] with the standard orientation dx\wedge dy. Then \partial R is oriented counterclockwise.
Take a C^1 1-form \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy. We will prove \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega directly.
The boundary has four sides.
On the bottom side y=c, x goes from a to b, and dy=0. The contribution is \int_a^b P(x,c)\,dx.
On the right side x=b, y goes from c to d, and dx=0. The contribution is \int_c^d Q(b,y)\,dy.
On the top side y=d, x goes from b back to a, and dy=0. The contribution is -\int_a^b P(x,d)\,dx.
On the left side x=a, y goes from d back to c, and dx=0. The contribution is -\int_c^d Q(a,y)\,dy.

Add them:
\int_{\partial R}\omega \amp= \int_a^b P(x,c)\,dx + \int_c^d Q(b,y)\,dy \amp\qquad - \int_a^b P(x,d)\,dx - \int_c^d Q(a,y)\,dy \amp= \int_c^d\bigl(Q(b,y)-Q(a,y)\bigr)\,dy - \int_a^b\bigl(P(x,d)-P(x,c)\bigr)\,dx.

This proof is Green's theorem on a rectangle. It is also Stokes' theorem on a flat coordinate patch. The tools were the one-dimensional Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Fubini's theorem for continuous functions, which identifies the two orders of integration.

subsection.title: Proof on a box
subsection.p: The three-dimensional box calculation is the same idea with one more pair of faces.
Let B=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f] with the standard orientation dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy. Then d\Phi=(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

The x-faces contribute
\int_{\text{\(x\)-faces}}\Phi \amp= \int_c^d\int_e^f \bigl(P(b,y,z)-P(a,y,z)\bigr)\,dz\,dy \amp= \int_c^d\int_e^f\int_a^b P_x(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.
The last equality is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in the x-direction.

Similarly, the y-faces contribute \int_B Q_y\,dx\,dy\,dz, and the z-faces contribute \int_B R_z\,dx\,dy\,dz. Adding the three pairs of opposite faces gives \boxed{\int_{\partial B}\Phi = \int_B (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = \int_B d\Phi.}
So the divergence theorem on a rectangular box is also just the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, used once in each coordinate direction.

subsection.title: Interior faces cancel
subsection.p: Now cut a larger rectangle into smaller rectangles. Apply the rectangle proof to each small rectangle: \int_{\partial R_{ij}}\omega=\int_{R_{ij}}d\omega. Then add the equations.
On the right side, the small integrals combine: \sum_{i,j}\int_{R_{ij}}d\omega=\int_R d\omega.

On the left side, every interior edge is counted twice. One neighboring rectangle walks that shared edge in one direction. The other neighboring rectangle walks it in the opposite direction. A 1-form integral changes sign when direction reverses, so the two contributions cancel.

statement.p: Every interior edge is shared by two neighboring rectangles. Without computing anything, explain why those two contributions cancel rather than add. What feature of the shared edge is different for the two rectangles, and why does that difference flip the sign of a 1-form integral?

hint.p: Ask yourself which direction each rectangle walks along that shared edge as it traces its own counterclockwise boundary. They are neighbors looking at the same wall from opposite sides.

subsection.p: Only the outer boundary remains: \sum_{i,j}\int_{\partial R_{ij}}\omega = \int_{\partial R}\omega.

The same cancellation happens in three dimensions. If a solid is cut into small boxes, then every interior face belongs to two neighboring boxes. One box gives the face one orientation; the other gives the opposite orientation. A 2-form integral changes sign when the surface orientation reverses, so the two face integrals cancel.
This is the geometric reason that only the outside boundary appears in Stokes' theorem.

subsection.title: Pullback to parameter domains
subsection.p: The rectangle and box proofs live in coordinate space. A curved surface or a curved solid is usually handled by parametrizing it.

For a surface, suppose \mathbf r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to S\subseteq\mathbb R^3 is a smooth oriented parametrization. A 1-form \omega in space pulls back to a 1-form on the parameter region: \mathbf r^*\omega. Surface integrals also pull back: \int_S d\omega=\int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega). Boundary integrals pull back as well: \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega.

The link between the two sides is the identity \boxed{\mathbf r^*(d\omega)=d(\mathbf r^*\omega).} For a C^2 regular patch this follows from the product and chain rules and equality of mixed partials, as calculated in the coordinate calculation for a parametrized surface.

Now apply Green's theorem on the parameter region D: \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega = \int_D d(\mathbf r^*\omega). Using the pullback identity, \int_D d(\mathbf r^*\omega) = \int_D \mathbf r^*(d\omega). Translating back to the surface gives \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.}
This is classical Stokes' theorem on a parametrized surface.

For a solid coordinate map T:C\subseteq\mathbb R^3\to E\subseteq\mathbb R^3, the same pattern gives T^*(d\Phi)=d(T^*\Phi). So Stokes on the coordinate box C becomes Stokes on the curved solid E, with the Jacobian and orientation signs carried automatically by the pullback.

subsection.title: Approximation by small pieces
subsection.p: A general region is not one rectangle. A general surface is not one parameter patch. A general solid is not one box.

But many of the objects in this book can be cut into finitely many simple pieces, or approximated by many small simple pieces: \text{rectangles in the plane}, \qquad \text{parameter patches on a surface}, \qquad \text{boxes in space}. On each piece, the theorem is a coordinate calculation. When the pieces are added, the interior boundaries cancel.

statement.p: On a single rectangle the theorem is just the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Yet adding many such local statements produces a fact about the one outer boundary. Conceptually, what does the cancellation of interior boundaries accomplish that lets a pile of tiny local equalities become a single global one?

hint.p: Track what happens to the two sides of the equation separately. The right sides simply add up to the whole region. Something special must happen on the left so that the interior bookkeeping vanishes and only the rim is left to speak.

subsection.p: For a curved boundary, there is a small extra step. A grid of rectangles does not fit the boundary perfectly. Some small pieces near the edge are cut off. As the grid becomes finer, the leftover boundary error shrinks. The C^1 condition on the form and the piecewise smooth condition on the boundary make that shrinking error controllable.

That is why the theorem allows corners but not wild boundaries. A polygon is fine. A box is fine. A smooth surface made from finitely many patches is fine. A boundary so jagged that it has no tangent direction in any ordinary sense is outside the rules of this course.

subsection.title: What is hidden in a fully rigorous proof
subsection.p: First, the object must be covered by pieces whose parameter maps are well behaved. For surfaces, this means smooth regular patches. For solids, this means pieces that can be handled by coordinate maps or by limits of boxes.

Second, overlaps must be counted with the right signs. If two pieces share an interior edge or face, their induced orientations must be opposite. This is exactly what the boundary orientation rules in were designed to guarantee.

Third, the integrals over small leftover pieces must go to zero as the pieces shrink. This is where compactness, piecewise smoothness, and C^1 coefficients enter the proof. They keep the quantities being integrated from behaving wildly while the mesh gets smaller.

Fourth, the form must be defined on an open set containing the whole object. A singularity inside the region cannot be ignored. The punctured-plane form \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy and the inverse-square flux form \frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz + \frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx + \frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy showed exactly what goes wrong. A missing point can be detected by a loop or a closed surface around it.
These details are not new ideas. They are the careful bookkeeping needed to make the cancellation proof honest.

subsection.title: Two twin facts: \partial^2=0 and d^2=0
subsection.p: They are twins.

statement.p: The algebraic fact d^2=0 and the geometric fact \partial(\partial M)=\emptyset look like they belong to different worlds, one about forms and one about shapes. Using only the idea that Stokes' theorem links d with \partial, explain why these two facts are forced to mirror each other rather than being a lucky coincidence.

hint.p: Imagine applying Stokes' theorem twice in a row to \omega. Each application can push a d across to a \partial. What must the two zeros on the two sides be saying about each other?

subsection.p: If Stokes' theorem is applied twice, it says \int_M d(d\omega) = \int_{\partial M}d\omega = \int_{\partial(\partial M)}\omega. The left side is zero because d^2\omega=0. The right side is zero because a boundary has no boundary.
This is more than a coincidence. The operator d is the algebraic mirror of the boundary operator \partial. Stokes' theorem is the bridge between them: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.

The theorem has now been stated, used, and partly explained. What remains is to strip away the old names and place the four disguises side by side. The next section is the translation table: intervals, plane regions, surfaces, and solids all saying the same sentence in their own dialect.

section.title: The grand translation table
section.p: opened the proof idea: prove the theorem on simple pieces, then let interior boundaries cancel. That proof idea explains why one formula can wear so many familiar faces: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.
Now we slow down and make the translation explicit.

subsection.title: A small dictionary before the table
subsection.p: The same symbols appear again and again.
A scalar function is a 0-form: f. Its exterior derivative is the 1-form df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz.
So the old vector calculus operations appear as:

table.title: Old vector calculus operations as exterior derivatives.

subsection.p: This dictionary is the key to the translation table.

subsection.title: Dimension 1: intervals, functions, and endpoints
subsection.p: Let M=[a,b], oriented from a to b. Its boundary is \partial M=\{b\}-\{a\}. The form on the boundary must have degree 0, so it is a function: \omega=f. Then d\omega=df=f'(x)\,dx.

Stokes' theorem becomes \int_{\partial[a,b]} f=\int_{[a,b]}df. The left side is \int_{\partial[a,b]} f=f(b)-f(a), and the right side is \int_{[a,b]}df=\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx. Therefore \boxed{f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx.}
This is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

table.title: Stokes symbols in dimension one.

subsection.p: The interval is the first place where the boundary carries signs. Without the sign \{b\}-\{a\}, the theorem would not know the difference between f(b)-f(a)\qquad\text{and}\qquad f(a)+f(b).

statement.p: The boundary \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\} attaches opposite signs to the two endpoints, even though both are just points. What is the minus sign actually keeping track of here, and why would the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus collapse if both endpoints came in with a plus?

hint.p: Think about orientation: the interval runs from a to b. The boundary should remember which end is the start and which is the finish.

subsection.title: Dimension 2: regions, 1-forms, and boundary curves
subsection.p: Let M=R be an oriented plane region with positive orientation dx\wedge dy. Its boundary \partial R is oriented so that the region stays on the left.
The form on the boundary must have degree 1. Write \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. Then \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}
Stokes' theorem becomes \int_{\partial R}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. In ordinary vector calculus notation, \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dA.}
This is Green's theorem in circulation form.

There is also a flux version. For a plane vector field \mathbf F=(A,B), outward flux across the positively oriented boundary is represented by the 1-form \phi=A\,dy-B\,dx. Then d\phi=(A_x+B_y)\,dx\wedge dy. So Stokes gives \boxed{\oint_{\partial R} A\,dy-B\,dx=\iint_R (A_x+B_y)\,dA.} In vector notation, \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_{\mathrm{out}}\,ds=\iint_R \nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dA.}
Thus Green's theorem has two common dialects:

table.title: Two dialects of Green's theorem.

subsection.p: The theorem is the same. The 1-form decides what the boundary is measuring.

subsection.title: Surfaces in space: 1-forms and curl
subsection.p: Now let M=S be an oriented surface in space. Its boundary \partial S, if it has one, is an oriented curve. The boundary orientation is determined by the chosen side of the surface.
The form on the boundary is again a 1-form: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. This is the work form of the vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R).
Stokes' theorem becomes \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. In vector notation, \boxed{\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS.}
This is classical Stokes' theorem.

table.title: Forms language and vector language for surfaces.

subsection.p: Green's theorem was the flat version of this story. Classical Stokes lets the inside surface bend.

subsection.title: Solids in space: 2-forms and divergence
subsection.p: Finally let M=E be an oriented solid region in space. Its boundary \partial E is an outward-oriented surface.

statement.p: For a curve we integrated a 1-form, but for the boundary of a solid we suddenly need a 2-form. Without computing anything, what feature of the boundary \partial E forces the form to have degree 2 rather than degree 1?

hint.p: Ask what kind of object \partial E is. The degree of a form should match the dimension of the thing you are integrating it over.

subsection.p: The form on the boundary must have degree 2. For a vector field \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), use its flux 2-form: \boxed{\Phi_{\mathbf F}=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy.} Then \boxed{d\Phi_{\mathbf F}=(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.} The coefficient is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F.

Stokes' theorem becomes \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf F}=\int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf F}. In vector notation, \boxed{\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{out}}\,dS=\iiint_E\nabla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV.}
This is the divergence theorem.

table.title: Forms language and vector language for solids.

subsection.p: Here the boundary is not a curve. It is a surface. That is why the boundary form has degree 2, not degree 1.

subsection.title: The same theorem in four familiar disguises
subsection.p: All four translations can be placed in one table.

table.title: The same theorem in four familiar disguises.

statement.p: FTC, Green, Stokes, and the divergence theorem each fill exactly one row of the table, yet all four collapse into the single line \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. In your own words, why does choosing the dimension of M and the degree of \omega determine which classical theorem you are looking at?

hint.p: Once M, \partial M, and \omega are fixed, everything else is forced. Try reading one row of the table and naming what changed from the row above it.

subsection.p: A useful way to read the theorem is:

p.md: \boxed{\text{boundary accumulation of a form}=\text{interior accumulation of its derivative}.}

subsection.p: In one dimension, the boundary is two signed endpoints. In two dimensions, the boundary is a signed curve. In three dimensions, the boundary of a solid is a signed surface. The word signed is doing quiet work in every case.

subsection.title: A translation checklist
subsection.p: When a problem mentions one of the classical theorems, translate it by asking four questions.

table.title: A translation checklist.

row.cell: What is the inside object M?
What is its oriented boundary \partial M?
What form \omega is being integrated on the boundary?

subsection.p: For example, if a problem asks for \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r and C bounds a surface S, the boundary form is \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. Then the interior form is d\omega_{\mathbf F}=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}. So the problem is a Stokes problem.

If a problem asks for outward flux through a closed surface, the boundary form is \Phi_{\mathbf F}. Then the interior form is d\Phi_{\mathbf F}=(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dV. So the problem is a divergence theorem problem.

This is not just a memory device. It is a way to avoid using the wrong theorem. A line integral of a 1-form belongs on a curve. A flux 2-form belongs on a surface. A volume 3-form belongs inside a solid. The degree tells us where the form can live.

The table makes the theorem look tidy. But tidy tables can hide danger. The formula works only when its grammar is respected: the orientation must be induced, the whole boundary must be present, the form must be defined where the theorem uses it, and the smoothness assumptions must be honest. The next section is a collection of failures. They are not exceptions to Stokes' theorem. They are examples of what happens when we try to speak the theorem's sentence with one word missing.

section.title: Warning examples
section.p: The grand table in compresses many theorems into one line: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. But the line is not a spell. It is a precise sentence. Each hypothesis tells us how to read the sentence correctly.
This section collects the most common ways the formula is misread.

subsection.title: Boundary orientation reversed
subsection.p: Start with the simplest two-dimensional example: R=[0,1]\times[0,1], oriented by dx\wedge dy. The induced boundary orientation is counterclockwise.
Take \omega=x\,dy. Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy. So the interior integral is \int_R d\omega=\int_R dx\wedge dy=1.

Now compute the boundary integral with the correct orientation. The bottom edge and top edge have dy=0, so they contribute 0. On the right edge, x=1,\qquad 0\le y\le1, so \int_{\text{right edge}}x\,dy=\int_0^1dy=1. On the left edge, x=0, so the contribution is 0. Therefore \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=1=\int_Rd\omega.}
But if we walk the same square clockwise, every 1-form integral changes sign: \int_{-\partial R}\omega=-1. The interior integral is still \int_R d\omega=1. So the false statement would be -1=1.
The theorem did not fail. We used the wrong boundary orientation.

statement.p: When we walked the square clockwise we landed on the false statement -1=1. Yet neither \int_R d\omega nor the form \omega changed. So which of the two sides of \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega was secretly altered, and which hypothesis of the theorem is the one we quietly violated?

hint.p: Ask yourself what the symbol \partial M is actually told to mean by the theorem. Only one side of the equation depends on the direction we walk.

subsection.p: The same warning appears for surfaces. If a disk is oriented upward, its boundary is counterclockwise when viewed from above. If we keep the upward surface but walk the boundary clockwise, Stokes' theorem changes sign on only one side. The two sides no longer match.

figure.caption: Reversing the boundary direction reverses the boundary integral.

subsection.title: Missing boundary components around holes
subsection.p: A hole is not empty bookkeeping. It creates an inner boundary.

Let A=\{(x,y):1\le x^2+y^2\le4\} be the annulus between the circles of radius 1 and 2. Use the standard orientation dx\wedge dy. The outer boundary is counterclockwise, and the inner boundary is clockwise.
Take the area-measuring form \omega=\frac12(-y\,dx+x\,dy). Then d\omega=dx\wedge dy. So \int_A d\omega=\operatorname{Area}(A)=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.

Now compute the boundary integral. On a counterclockwise circle of radius r, x=r\cos t,\qquad y=r\sin t,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-r\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=r\cos t\,dt. Substitute:
\omega \amp= \frac12\left(-r\sin t(-r\sin t\,dt)+r\cos t(r\cos t\,dt)\right) \amp= \frac12r^2\,dt.
So a counterclockwise circle of radius r contributes \pi r^2.

The outer circle contributes 4\pi. The inner circle has radius 1, but it is oriented clockwise, so it contributes -\pi. Therefore \boxed{\int_{\partial A}\omega=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.} This matches \int_A d\omega=3\pi.
If we forgot the inner boundary, we would get 4\pi, which is wrong.
subsection.md: \boxed{\text{The boundary of a region with holes has all its boundary components.}}
subsection.p: The same warning holds in three dimensions. A solid shell b\le x^2+y^2+z^2\le a^2 has two boundary spheres. The outer sphere is oriented outward from the shell, away from the origin. The inner sphere is also oriented outward from the shell, which points toward the origin. That sign is exactly what makes flux contributions cancel when the field has no source inside the shell.

subsection.title: Singularities inside the region
subsection.p: Some forms look harmless on the boundary but fail inside. Stokes' theorem needs the form to be defined on an open set containing the whole object M, not only on \partial M.
Consider the 1-form \alpha=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. It is defined on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. Where it is defined, d\alpha=0.

A careless argument would say: d\alpha=0,\qquad \text{so } \int_C\alpha=0. But that argument tries to use Stokes' theorem on the unit disk. The form \alpha is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the disk. The theorem is not available.

If we remove a small disk around the origin, the theorem works again. The region is an annulus: \varepsilon\le x^2+y^2\le1. On that annulus, d\alpha=0. The outer boundary contributes 2\pi. The inner boundary is clockwise, so it contributes -2\pi. The total boundary integral is 2\pi-2\pi=0, matching \int_{\text{annulus}}d\alpha=0.
The singularity did not disappear. We turned it into a boundary component.

exercise.title: If d\alpha=0, why isn't the loop integral zero?

statement.p: Everywhere it is defined, \alpha satisfies d\alpha=0, and yet \int_C\alpha=2\pi\neq 0. The careless argument tries to write \int_C\alpha=\int_D d\alpha=0 over the unit disk D. Exactly which requirement of the generalized Stokes theorem does the disk D fail to meet, and why does switching to the annulus rescue the computation?

hint.p: The theorem asks \omega to be defined on an open set containing all of M. Look hard at the single point sitting at the center of the disk.

subsection.md: \boxed{\text{A missing point inside can be detected by a loop around it.}}
subsection.p: There is a three-dimensional version of the same warning. Let r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} and consider the flux 2-form \Psi=\frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz+\frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx+\frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy. This is the flux form of \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{r^3}. The field is not defined at the origin. Away from the origin, d\Psi=0.

Yet the outward flux through a sphere of radius a is 4\pi. It would be wrong to apply the divergence theorem to the whole ball and conclude zero flux. The form is not defined at the origin. If we remove a smaller ball around the origin, the outer flux 4\pi and inner flux -4\pi cancel, just as they should.
A singularity inside a region behaves like a source the ordinary derivative does not see, because the ordinary derivative is not defined there.

subsection.title: Smoothness assumptions and piecewise smooth objects
subsection.p: The theorem also asks for the form to be smooth enough. In this book, the safe condition is: \omega\text{ has }C^1\text{ coefficients} on an open set containing M.
A jump can hide an internal boundary.

exercise.title: Where did the missing -2 come from?

statement.p: On each open half of the square H(y) is constant, so the careless reader sets d\omega=0 and predicts \int_{\partial R}\omega=0; the honest boundary calculation gives -2. Since the theorem balances \int_{\partial R}\omega against \int_R d\omega, which hypothesis broke along the line y=0, and what is the geometric object the jump is secretly standing in for?

hint.p: Constant on each piece is not the same as smooth across the seam. Think about what d\omega would have to record at y=0 for the two sides to balance.

subsection.p: Let R=[-1,1]\times[-1,1], and define H(y)=\begin{cases}0, & y<0,\\1, & y\ge 0.\end{cases} Consider the 1-form \omega=H(y)\,dx. This form is not continuous across the line y=0. It is certainly not C^1.
If we ignore the jump and look only on the two open halves of the square, then H is constant on each half, so a careless computation would say d\omega=0. That would suggest \int_{\partial R}\omega=0.

But compute the boundary integral directly. On the bottom edge, y=-1, so H(y)=0, and the contribution is 0. On the right and left edges, dx=0, so the contribution is 0. On the top edge, y=1, and the positive boundary orientation travels from x=1\quad\text{to}\quad x=-1. There H(y)=1, so the top contributes \int_1^{-1}dx=-2. Thus \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=-2.}

The jump along y=0 is hiding an internal edge. The C^1 theorem is not designed to ignore that edge. More advanced versions of Stokes' theorem can handle jumps, but then the jump contributes its own term.
Smoothness of the boundary is a separate issue.

A rectangle is allowed even though it has corners. Its boundary is made of finitely many smooth edges. A box is allowed even though it has edges and corners. Its boundary is made of finitely many smooth faces. That is what piecewise smooth means.
Corners do not create extra terms. Interior shared edges cancel.

For example, split the rectangle [0,2]\times[0,1] into two rectangles: R_1=[0,1]\times[0,1],\qquad R_2=[1,2]\times[0,1]. The shared edge is x=1,\qquad 0\le y\le1. As part of \partial R_1, that edge is traveled upward. As part of \partial R_2, the same edge is traveled downward. The two line integrals cancel for every 1-form: \int_{\text{shared edge from }R_1}\omega+\int_{\text{shared edge from }R_2}\omega=0. Only the outside boundary survives.
So the warning is not corners are bad. The warning is more precise:

subsection.title: The checklist
subsection.p: Before using \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega, check the grammar.
subsection.md: \begin{array}{c|l} \text{Check} \amp \text{Question} \\ \hline \text{Degree} \amp \omega\text{ has degree }\dim M-1\text{?}\\[1mm] \text{Boundary} \amp \text{Is every boundary component included?}\\[1mm] \text{Orientation} \amp \text{Does }\partial M\text{ have the induced orientation?}\\[1mm] \text{Domain} \amp \omega\text{ is defined on an open set containing }M\text{?}\\[1mm] \text{Smoothness} \amp \omega\text{ has }C^1\text{ coefficients where needed?}\\[1mm] \text{Geometry} \amp M\text{ and }\partial M\text{ are compact and piecewise smooth?} \end{array}
subsection.p: When one of these checks fails, the formula may still have a more advanced version. But the missing condition must be paid for. A reversed orientation pays with a minus sign. A missing hole pays with an extra boundary component. A singularity pays by acting like a hidden source. A jump pays by creating an internal edge or sheet.

This is why the generalized Stokes theorem is both simple and strict. It gives one sentence for the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem. But the sentence only works when every word is read correctly.

The chapter review will turn this into practice: translate the old vector formulas into forms, choose the right boundary, and decide which side of the theorem is easier to compute. After that, the same boundary idea begins to move in time. A conserved quantity changes inside a region only because it flows through the boundary. That is where Stokes' theorem becomes the language of conservation laws.

introduction.p: was a warning label. It showed that Stokes' theorem is simple, but not loose. The boundary must have the right orientation. Holes must be counted. Singularities cannot be ignored. The form must be smooth enough for d\omega to mean what we say it means.
Now we put the chapter in working order.

subsection.title: The one sentence, read slowly
subsection.p: The symbol M is the object with an inside. It may be an interval, a plane region, a surface, or a solid.
The symbol \partial M is its oriented boundary.
The form \omega lives on the boundary. The form d\omega lives inside.

The degree of \omega is always one less than the dimension of M:
\deg \omega=\dim M-1.
Then d\omega has degree
\deg(d\omega)=\dim M,
so it can be integrated over M.
That is why the dimensions match.

subsection.title: A final worked translation
subsection.p:
Let C be the unit circle in the plane z=0, oriented counterclockwise when viewed from above:
C:\quad x^2+y^2=1,\qquad z=0.
Take the 1-form
\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz.

First compute the boundary integral directly. Parametrize C by
x=\cos t,\qquad y=\sin t,\qquad z=0, \qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi.
Then
dx=-\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=\cos t\,dt, \qquad dz=0.
So
\begin{aligned} \omega \amp = -\sin t(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt)+0\\ \amp = (\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t)\,dt\\ \amp = dt. \end{aligned}
Therefore
\boxed{ \int_C\omega=2\pi. }

Now compute using Stokes' theorem. The exterior derivative is
\begin{aligned} d\omega \amp = d(-y\,dx)+d(x\,dy)+d(z\,dz)\\ \amp = -dy\wedge dx+dx\wedge dy+0\\ \amp = 2\,dx\wedge dy. \end{aligned}

Let D be the flat unit disk in the plane z=0, oriented upward. Its boundary is C. Then
\begin{aligned} \int_C\omega \amp = \int_D d\omega\\ \amp = \int_D 2\,dx\wedge dy\\ \amp = 2\operatorname{Area}(D)\\ \amp = 2\pi. \end{aligned}

But the flat disk was not special. Let S be the downward-opening paraboloid cap
z=1-x^2-y^2, \qquad x^2+y^2\le1,
oriented upward. Its boundary is the same circle C, with the same induced orientation. Stokes' theorem gives
\int_C\omega=\int_S d\omega.
Since
d\omega=2\,dx\wedge dy,
the surface integral measures twice the signed area of the shadow of S on the xy-plane. With upward orientation, that shadow is the unit disk with positive orientation. Hence
\boxed{ \int_S d\omega=2\pi. }

The flat disk and the curved cap give the same answer because the boundary is the same. Stokes' theorem says the integral of d\omega over a surface depends only on the boundary, as long as \omega is defined on the region swept between the surfaces.

subsection.title: The formulas to keep
subsection.p: The formulas below are not separate miracles. They are the same theorem in different degrees.

For a space 1-form,
\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz,
\boxed{ \begin{aligned} d\omega \amp = (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz\\ \amp \quad+ (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx\\ \amp \quad+ (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. \end{aligned} }
This is the flux 2-form of
\nabla\times(P,Q,R).

statement.p: What degree should \omega have if M is a surface?
What degree should \omega have if M is a solid?
Why is the boundary of an interval written \{b\}-\{a\} instead of just \{a,b\}?
For a positively oriented plane region, why is an inner boundary around a hole walked clockwise?
If a surface is oriented upward, how do you determine the positive direction of its boundary curve?
What does \partial(\partial M)=\emptyset mean for a solid box?
What does d^2=0 say in vector language for d(df)?
What does d^2=0 say in vector language for d(d(P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz))?
Why can a form with d\omega=0 still have a nonzero integral around a closed curve?
Why must Stokes' theorem require \omega to be defined on the inside region, not only on the boundary?

exercises.title: Skills: translating between vector calculus and forms

statement.p: Compute df for f(x,y,z)=x^2y+yz^3-\cos x.
Compute d\omega for the plane 1-form \omega=(x^2-y)\,dx+(xy+3y^2)\,dy.
Compute d\omega for the space 1-form \omega=yz\,dx+xz\,dy+xy\,dz. Identify the vector field whose flux form is d\omega.
Compute d\Phi for \Phi=x^2\,dy\wedge dz+y^2\,dz\wedge dx+z^2\,dx\wedge dy. Translate your answer into divergence language.
Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R). Write the work 1-form of \mathbf F. Then write d\omega_{\mathbf F} and identify the vector field it represents.
Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R). Write the flux 2-form of \mathbf F. Then write d\Phi_{\mathbf F} and identify its coefficient.
Let R be a positively oriented plane region. Translate \oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r into a 1-form integral.
Let E be a solid region. Translate \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{out}}\,dS into a 2-form integral.
Let I=[-2,5] with the usual orientation, and let f(x)=x^3-4x. Compute both sides of \int_{\partial I}f=\int_I df.
Let R=[0,3]\times[0,2] with positive orientation, and let \omega=(y^2+x)\,dx+x^2\,dy. Compute \int_{\partial R}\omega using Green's theorem.
Compute the same integral in Problem 2 directly by integrating along the four sides of the rectangle.
Let C be the positively oriented boundary of the triangle with vertices (0,0),\qquad (4,0),\qquad (0,3). Compute \int_C x\,dy. Explain why this integral gives the area of the triangle.
Let A=\{(x,y):1\le x^2+y^2\le9\} with the standard orientation. Compute \int_{\partial A}x\,dy. Be careful with the orientation of the inner boundary.
Let \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy. Use Green's theorem to compute \int_{\partial R}\omega when R is the ellipse \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}\le1.
Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=4,\qquad z\ge0, oriented upward. Its boundary is the circle x^2+y^2=4,\qquad z=0. Use Stokes' theorem to compute \int_{\partial S}(-y\,dx+x\,dy).
Let S be any smooth upward-oriented surface whose boundary is the circle x^2+y^2=1,\qquad z=0. Use Stokes' theorem to compute \int_S 3\,dx\wedge dy.
Let E be the box [0,1]\times[0,2]\times[0,3], and let \Phi=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy. Compute \int_{\partial E}\Phi using the divergence theorem.
Compute the same integral in Problem 9 by adding the six face integrals.
Let B_a be the ball of radius a centered at the origin. Use the divergence theorem to compute the outward flux of \mathbf F=(x,y,z) through \partial B_a.
Let \mathbf F=(y,z,x). Compute the outward flux of \nabla\times\mathbf F through any closed surface \partial E, assuming \mathbf F is defined on a region containing E.
Let \alpha=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. Compute \int_C\alpha where C is the unit circle oriented counterclockwise. Explain why this does not contradict Green's theorem.
Let \mathbf G=\frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}. Compute its outward flux through the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2. Explain why the divergence theorem cannot be applied to the whole ball.
Let \omega=x\,dy on the square R=[0,1]\times[0,1]. Compute \int_{\partial R}\omega with positive orientation, and then compute the integral with the clockwise orientation. What changed?
Let S be the flat disk x^2+y^2\le1,\qquad z=0, oriented downward. What is the induced orientation on \partial S? Compute \int_{\partial S}(-y\,dx+x\,dy).
Let E be the spherical shell 1\le x^2+y^2+z^2\le4. Describe the induced orientations on the two boundary spheres.

Let \Psi=\frac{x}{r^3}\,dy\wedge dz+\frac{y}{r^3}\,dz\wedge dx+\frac{z}{r^3}\,dx\wedge dy, \qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. Use the shell in Problem 17 to explain why \int_{\partial E}\Psi=0, even though each boundary sphere has nonzero flux.
Suppose \omega=d\eta on a region containing a compact oriented surface S with no boundary. Prove that \int_S\omega=0.
Suppose \Phi=d\omega on a region containing a solid E. Prove that \int_{\partial E}\Phi=0. Translate this into a vector calculus statement.

exercises.title: Capstone project: derive the four classical theorems from one statement

introduction.p: The goal of this project is to start with \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega and recover the four classical theorems.
Write one page for each theorem. Each page should include:

statement.p: the object M,
its oriented boundary \partial M,
the form \omega,
the exterior derivative d\omega,
the forms version of the theorem,
the classical vector-calculus version, if there is one,
one warning about orientation, holes, or singularities.

conclusion.p: The project is not about memorizing four formulas. It is about showing that the four formulas are the same sentence with different nouns.

exercises.title: Capstone project: one boundary, three surfaces

introduction.p: Let C be the unit circle x^2+y^2=1,\qquad z=0, oriented counterclockwise when viewed from above. Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy.
Compute \int_C\omega in four ways.

statement.p: Directly parametrize C.
Use the flat disk D:\quad x^2+y^2\le1,\qquad z=0, oriented upward.
Use the upper hemisphere S_1:\quad x^2+y^2+z^2=1,\qquad z\ge0, oriented outward.

Use the cone S_2:\quad z=1-\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\qquad x^2+y^2\le1, oriented upward. The apex is not a smooth surface point. Apply Stokes first to the truncated cone \varepsilon\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le1, and then let \varepsilon\to0.

hint.p: The inner boundary is clockwise as viewed from above. Its integral of -y\,dx+x\,dy is -2\pi\varepsilon^2, which tends to zero. Parametrize the cone by (r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,1-r) to check that the omitted tip contributes 2\pi\varepsilon^2 to the surface integral of 2\,dx\wedge dy, also tending to zero.

conclusion.p: In your write-up, explain why the three surface computations agree. Then reverse the orientation of C and describe what changes.

exercises.title: Capstone project: find the hidden mistake

introduction.p: Each statement below is wrong or incomplete. Find the missing condition or sign error.

statement.p: Since d\left(\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy\right)=0, the integral of this form around the unit circle must be 0.
The boundary of an annulus is only its outer circle.
If a disk is oriented upward, we may choose either clockwise or counterclockwise orientation on its boundary and Stokes' theorem will still hold.
Since the disk x^2+y^2\le1,\qquad z=0 has no volume, the divergence theorem says the flux of (0,0,1) through it is 0.
Since \nabla\cdot\left(\frac{(x,y,z)}{r^3}\right)=0 away from the origin, the outward flux through a sphere around the origin is 0.
A cube surface has edges, so as a surface it must have a boundary curve.
If \nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0, then every line integral of \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r around a closed curve is 0, even if the domain has holes.
If two surfaces have the same boundary, then \int_S \Phi must be the same for every 2-form \Phi.

subsection.title: Where the theorem leads next
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem compares what happens on a boundary with what happens inside: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. That sentence is already a conservation law in disguise.

Imagine a pollutant spread through a fixed tank E. Let \rho(x,y,z,t) be its density at time t. The amount inside the tank is \int_E \rho\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. If pollutant flows out through the boundary, the amount inside decreases. Let \Phi_{\mathbf J}=J_1\,dy\wedge dz+J_2\,dz\wedge dx+J_3\,dx\wedge dy be the outward flux 2-form of the flux vector field \mathbf J=(J_1,J_2,J_3). Then the boundary loss is \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J}. Stokes' theorem turns that boundary flux into an interior integral:
\int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J} = \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf J} = \int_E (\nabla\cdot\mathbf J)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

figure.caption: A conservation law compares change inside a region with flux through its boundary.

subsection.p: The next chapter follows that idea. Stokes' theorem was a theorem about space: boundary versus interior. Conservation laws add time. A quantity changes inside a region only because it is created, destroyed, or carried through the boundary. The same boundary principle that unified calculus now becomes the language of fluids, heat, waves, and fields.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

introduction.p: Using the boundary theorems of Chapter 18, we translate conservation of a stored quantity into a local equation for density, flux, and sources. Time-dependent fields use the same partial derivatives and chain rules as earlier chapters. Each physical model supplies its own flux or force law; the additional formulas needed for heat, waves, potentials, and Maxwell equations are introduced here.

section.title: Balance laws from flux
section.p: Recall from that the divergence theorem is Stokes' theorem for a solid: \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi. When \Phi is a flux form, the boundary integral measures what crosses the surface \partial E. A conservation law begins by asking what that crossing does to the amount stored inside E.

subsection.title: A fixed window in moving dye
subsection.p: Imagine a clear box sitting inside a tank of water. The box is not a physical wall. It is only a measuring window: E=[0,3]\times[0,1]\times[0,1]. Dye flows through the tank. Let \rho(x,y,z,t) be the dye density at time t, measured in grams per cubic meter.
The amount of dye inside the window is \boxed{A(t)=\iiint_E \rho(x,y,z,t)\,dV.}

Now suppose that, for 0\le t\lt 10, \rho(x,y,z,t)=10-t and that the dye flux field is \mathbf J(x,y,z,t)=(x,0,0). The vector \mathbf J measures dye transported per unit area per unit time. It is not just a velocity. It is the actual transported amount.

First compute the stored amount: \boxed{\begin{aligned} A(t) &= \int_0^3\int_0^1\int_0^1 (10-t)\,dz\,dy\,dx\\ &= 3(10-t). \end{aligned}} Therefore \boxed{A'(t)=-3.} The window is losing dye at rate 3.
Now compute the outward flux across the boundary. Since \mathbf J=(x,0,0), only the left and right faces can contribute.
On the right face x=3, the outward normal is \widehat{\mathbf n}=(1,0,0), so \mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=3. The face has area 1, so the outward flux through the right face is 3.

On the left face x=0, the outward normal is \widehat{\mathbf n}=(-1,0,0), but \mathbf J=(0,0,0), so the flux is 0. The other four faces also have zero flux because their normals are perpendicular to (x,0,0).
Thus \boxed{\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=3.}

The two calculations match the bookkeeping rule: \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV = -\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS.} Outward flux is positive, but it decreases what remains inside. That is why the minus sign is there.

statement.p: Suppose every reading of \mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} on the boundary is positive. Without computing anything, is the stored amount inside E going up or down at that instant, and why does the balance law need a minus sign in front of the flux to record that?

hint.p: Picture the arrows: positive normal flux means stuff is heading out through the surface. Ask yourself what leaving does to the count of what is still inside.

figure.caption: With no sources or sinks, for a fixed region E, the rate at which the stored quantity decreases is exactly equal to the net outward flux through the boundary \partial E. The negative sign accounts for the fact that a positive outward flux results in a loss of internal density.

subsection.title: Stored amount and flux density
subsection.p: The example contains the main objects.
The density \rho measures how much material is stored per unit volume.
The flux density \mathbf J measures how much material is transported through a unit area per unit time.

If the material has density \rho and moves with velocity \mathbf v, then the flux density is \boxed{\mathbf J=\rho\mathbf v.} A fast flow in a nearly empty region may carry little material. A slow flow in a dense region may carry a lot. The product \rho\mathbf v measures what is actually being transported.

statement.p: A flux density is a vector field \mathbf J whose normal component \mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} measures the amount crossing a unit area per unit time in the normal direction.

subsection.p: A vector tangent to the boundary may be large, but it contributes no flux across the boundary. It slides along the boundary instead of crossing it.

statement.p: A strong current runs parallel to one face of E, never pointing into or out of it. The flow is fast, yet it contributes nothing to the flux across that face. What feature of \mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} explains how something so vigorous can still cross no boundary?

hint.p: The dot product only listens to the part of \mathbf J that lines up with \widehat{\mathbf n}. What is that component when the flow and the normal are at right angles?

subsection.title: The flux form
subsection.p: The same flux can be written in the language of forms.

For a vector field \mathbf J=(J_1,J_2,J_3), the corresponding flux 2-form is \boxed{\Phi_{\mathbf J} = J_1\,dy\wedge dz + J_2\,dz\wedge dx + J_3\,dx\wedge dy.} Then \boxed{\int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J} = \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS.}

For the previous example, \mathbf J=(x,0,0), so \Phi_{\mathbf J}=x\,dy\wedge dz. On the right face x=3, this becomes 3\,dy\wedge dz. The face has y,z-area 1, so its contribution is 3. On the left face x=0, the form is zero. The form gives the same outward flux.
This is why flux forms were worth building. They remember which oriented area pieces a vector field crosses.

In the plane, the matching formula is simpler. If \mathbf J=(M,N), then the outward flux form on a positively oriented boundary is \boxed{\phi_{\mathbf J}=M\,dy-N\,dx.} Indeed, \int_{\partial R}\phi_{\mathbf J} = \int_{\partial R}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,ds. The small vector (dy,-dx) is the outward normal times arclength when \partial R is walked with the region on the left.

subsection.title: Sources and sinks
subsection.p: Let s(x,y,z,t) be the source rate per unit volume. Positive s means creation. Negative s means destruction.

For a fixed solid E, the total source inside E is \iiint_E s\,dV. The full balance law becomes \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV = -\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS + \iiint_E s\,dV.}
Equivalently, \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV + \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E s\,dV.}
The left side says: \text{accumulation inside}+\text{outflow through boundary}. The right side says: \text{creation inside}.

statement.p: Let E be a fixed solid region. A density \rho, flux density \mathbf J, and source rate s satisfy the integral balance law on E if \boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV + \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E s\,dV.} When s=0, the quantity is locally conserved by transport alone.

example.title: A source in still water

statement.p: Suppose the water is still, so \mathbf J=\mathbf 0. Let s(x,y,z,t)=2 inside a box E of volume 5. Then the balance law says \frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV = \iiint_E 2\,dV = 10. The amount inside increases at rate 10. Nothing crossed the boundary. The increase came from a source inside.

subsection.title: What the fixed-region assumption means
subsection.p: The region E in the balance law is fixed in space. It is a window, not a moving blob of material.
This matters.

Suppose a cloud of dye moves to the right with constant velocity. If we follow the dye cloud itself, the total dye in that moving blob may stay constant. But a fixed window on the table may first gain dye, then lose dye, as the cloud passes through.

statement.p: The dye in a moving cloud can stay constant while the dye in our fixed window rises and then falls as the cloud drifts by. What is the balance law actually keeping track of here—the contents of a fixed place in space, or the contents of a chosen lump of material—and why does that choice change the story?

hint.p: The boundary \partial E never moves in our setup. Think about whose perspective you are taking: someone standing still watching one window, or someone riding along with the dye.

subsection.p: So the balance law above is a statement for fixed control regions: \text{watch this place, and count what enters, leaves, or is created there.}

That is exactly the viewpoint needed for the divergence theorem. The boundary \partial E is fixed, so flux through it is well-defined. Moving regions require an extra transport correction. That correction is important in fluid mechanics, but it is not needed for the first form of conservation laws.

The balance law is still global. It speaks about a whole region E. But if the same balance holds for every small box we could draw inside space, then the law should have a pointwise version. The next step is to shrink the bookkeeping until only one local equation remains.

section.title: The continuity equation
section.p:
gave the integral balance law:
\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV + \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E s\,dV.
This equation counts a whole region. To turn it into a differential equation, we use the divergence theorem to move the boundary flux into the interior.

subsection.title: From a box balance to a local equation
subsection.p:
Return to the box E=[0,3]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] from . There we used
\rho(x,y,z,t)=10-t, \qquad \mathbf J(x,y,z,t)=(x,0,0).
There was no source: s=0.

The global balance A'(t)=-3 was not a coincidence. Inside every tiny box, the density decreases at rate 1, while the outward spreading of the flux contributes divergence 1. The two effects balance locally.

figure.caption: The local continuity equation with no sources or sinks. If more material leaves a tiny neighborhood than enters it (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} \gt 0), the local density must drop (\rho_t \lt 0) to balance the loss.

subsection.title: Deriving the local balance law
subsection.p:
Assume E is fixed and compact, and that \rho and \rho_t are continuous on a neighborhood of E times a closed time interval. Then the time derivative can pass inside the integral:
\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E \rho\,dV = \iiint_E \rho_t\,dV.
The justification is the same uniform difference-quotient estimate as in : by the one-variable Mean Value Theorem, the difference quotient converges uniformly to \rho_t on the compact region. The error in its integral is at most the uniform error times \operatorname{Volume}(E), which tends to zero. With \mathbf J continuously differentiable in space, the divergence theorem gives
\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV.
Substitute both into the integral balance law:
\iiint_E \rho_t\,dV + \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV = \iiint_E s\,dV.
Combine the integrals:
\boxed{ \iiint_E \left( \rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J-s \right) dV = 0. }

statement.p: The argument concludes that the integrand vanishes only because \iiint_E(\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J-s)\,dV=0 holds for every small region E, not just one. In your own words, why would knowing this for a single fixed region not be enough to pin down the integrand at a point?

hint.p: Picture the integrand being positive in one corner of E and negative in another. What can the regions you are allowed to choose do that a single fixed region cannot?

proof.p: The proof is the calculation above, with one final observation.
Let g=\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J-s. The integral balance law and the divergence theorem imply \iiint_E g\,dV=0 for every fixed solid region E.

If g(\mathbf p)\gt 0 at some point \mathbf p, then by continuity g is still positive in a small box around \mathbf p. The integral over that box would be positive, not zero. Similarly, g(\mathbf p)\lt 0 would give a small box with negative integral.
So g must be zero at every point: \rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J-s=0.

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: Two small warnings prevent a common mistake.
First, an integral over one region being zero does not force the integrand to be zero.

For example, \int_{-1}^{1} x\,dx=0, but x is certainly not the zero function. The positive and negative parts cancel. That is why the theorem needs the balance law to hold for every small region, not merely for one large symmetric region.

Continuity rules out this kind of hidden spike. In more advanced courses, weak or distributional versions of conservation laws handle discontinuities such as shocks. In this book, the smooth case is the right first model.

subsection.title: The continuity equation for moving material
subsection.p: For a conserved quantity with no source, s=0, the local law is \boxed{\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0.} If the material moves with velocity field \mathbf v, then \mathbf J=\rho\mathbf v. So the conservation law becomes \boxed{\rho_t+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0.}
This is called the continuity equation.

statement.p: Let \rho(x,y,z,t) be a density transported by a velocity field \mathbf v(x,y,z,t). If the quantity is conserved and has no sources or sinks, then \boxed{\rho_t+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0.} In coordinates, if \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3), then \boxed{\rho_t+(\rho v_1)_x+(\rho v_2)_y+(\rho v_3)_z=0.}

subsection.p: In the plane, the same equation is \boxed{\rho_t+(\rho v_1)_x+(\rho v_2)_y=0.}

subsection.title: A density profile moving down a pipe
subsection.p: In a long narrow pipe, suppose the velocity is constant: v=2. The continuity equation in one spatial dimension becomes \rho_t+(\rho v)_x=0, so \rho_t+(2\rho)_x=0. Since 2 is constant, \boxed{\rho_t+2\rho_x=0.}

Let f be any differentiable one-variable function, and define \rho(x,t)=f(x-2t). Then \rho_t=-2f'(x-2t), and \rho_x=f'(x-2t). Therefore
\rho_t+2\rho_x = -2f'(x-2t)+2f'(x-2t) = 0.
So every density profile of the form f(x-2t) solves the equation. The shape moves to the right at speed 2, without changing.

figure.caption: The solution \rho(x,t)=f(x-2t) moves to the right with speed 2.

subsection.p: A fixed sensor at one x-value may see the density rise and fall as the profile passes. But a tiny observer moving with speed 2 sees the same density value stay with it.

subsection.title: Expansion, compression, and the material derivative
subsection.p:
The compact equation ho_t+
abla\cdot(ho\mathbf v)=0 has another useful form. Expand the divergence using the product rule:

abla\cdot(ho\mathbf v) = \mathbf v\cdot
ablaho + ho\,
abla\cdot\mathbf v.
Thus  oxed{ho_t+\mathbf v\cdot
ablaho+ho\,
abla\cdot\mathbf v=0.}

statement.p:
The split ho_t+\mathbf v\cdot
ablaho+ho\,
abla\cdot\mathbf v=0 separates two kinds of density change. One is felt by an observer drifting along with the flow; the other comes from the flow squeezing or stretching space itself. Which term belongs to which observer, and what does it mean for \dfrac{Dho}{Dt} to be zero even while ho_t
eq 0?

hint.p: A fixed sensor and a particle riding the current can disagree. The material derivative reports the riding particle's view; ask what stays constant for that particle.

subsection.p: So the continuity equation can be written as \boxed{\frac{D\rho}{Dt}+\rho\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0.}

example.title: Expansion lowers a uniform density

statement.p: In the plane, take \mathbf v(x,y)=(x,y). This field pushes points away from the origin. Its divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=1+1=2.

Suppose the density is uniform in space: \rho(x,y,t)=a(t). Then \nabla\rho=\mathbf 0, and the continuity equation becomes a'(t)+2a(t)=0. Hence \boxed{a(t)=Ce^{-2t}.} The material is conserved, but the flow expands area, so the density decreases.

example.title: Compression raises a uniform density

statement.p: Now take \mathbf v(x,y)=(-x,-y). Then \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=-1-1=-2. For a spatially uniform density \rho(x,y,t)=a(t), the continuity equation gives a'(t)-2a(t)=0. Therefore \boxed{a(t)=Ce^{2t}.} The flow compresses material toward the origin, so density rises.

subsection.p: Divergence is not just a symbolic derivative. It measures local expansion or compression of the flow.

subsection.title: Incompressible flow and divergence-free fields
subsection.p: A flow is called incompressible when tiny moving blobs keep the same volume in space, or the same area in the plane.

statement.p: It is tempting to read \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0 as nothing is moving. Yet a rotating or shearing flow can be vigorously in motion and still be divergence-free. What, precisely, is the quantity that incompressibility holds fixed, and why does that leave so much freedom for the flow to swirl and stir?

hint.p: Watch a tiny blob carried by the flow. Divergence reports one specific thing about that blob. Its shape and orientation are not on that list.

subsection.p: If \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0, then the continuity equation becomes \boxed{\rho_t+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla\rho=0.} Equivalently, \boxed{\frac{D\rho}{Dt}=0.} The density is constant along the path of each moving particle.

example.title: A rotating incompressible flow

statement.p:
The swirling velocity field \mathbf v(x,y)=(-y,x) has divergence
\nabla\cdot\mathbf v = \frac{\partial(-y)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial x}{\partial y} = 0+0 = 0.
So the flow is incompressible.
A small blob rotates around the origin. Its shape may turn, but to first order its area does not grow or shrink.

example.title: A shear flow with zero divergence

statement.p:
Let \mathbf v(x,y)=(y,0). Then
\nabla\cdot\mathbf v = \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial 0}{\partial y} = 0.
This flow is also incompressible.
Horizontal speed depends on height. A small square is sheared into a slanted parallelogram. Its shape changes, but its area does not.

figure.caption: Zero divergence does not mean no motion. It means no local area or volume change.

subsection.p: Divergence-free motion can still rotate, shear, fold, and stir. It simply does not create local expansion or compression.

subsection.title: The forms version of the continuity equation
subsection.p: The forms language shows the structure without extra words.

In space, the stored density is the 3-form \rho\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. The flux density \mathbf J=(J_1,J_2,J_3) has flux 2-form
\Phi_{\mathbf J} = J_1\,dy\wedge dz + J_2\,dz\wedge dx + J_3\,dx\wedge dy.
Its exterior derivative is
d\Phi_{\mathbf J} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf J)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
The local balance law \rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=s is therefore the form equation
\boxed{ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \bigl(\rho\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz\bigr) + d\Phi_{\mathbf J} = s\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }

The continuity equation gives the shape of a conservation law, but it does not yet tell us what the flux \mathbf J should be. That choice comes from physics. Heat flows from hot to cold, so its flux is tied to the gradient of temperature. Waves carry tension and acceleration. Equilibrium removes time and leaves a condition with no sources. Different stories will now begin producing equations with the same skeleton: heat, wave, and Laplace equations.

section.title: Heat, wave, and equilibrium equations
section.p: gave us the shape of a conservation law: \rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=s. The density \rho tells what is stored. The flux \mathbf J tells what moves across boundaries. The source s tells what is created or destroyed inside.

That equation is not yet a physical law by itself. It is bookkeeping. To get a specific equation, we must say what the flux is. Heat, waves, and equilibrium all make different choices, but the same few operators keep appearing: \nabla,\qquad \nabla\cdot,\qquad \Delta.

subsection.title: Heat flow and the heat equation
subsection.p: Imagine a thin metal plate on a table. Let u(x,y,t) be its temperature at the point (x,y) and time t.
Heat flows from warmer places toward colder places. The gradient \nabla u points in the direction where temperature increases fastest. So heat should flow in the opposite direction.
This modeling rule is called Fourier's law: \boxed{\mathbf J=-k\nabla u.} Here k\gt 0 is the thermal conductivity. A larger k means heat moves more easily through the material.

Let c be the heat capacity per unit area of the thin plate. Then the stored thermal energy per unit area is proportional to temperature: ho=c u. If there is no internal heat source, the conservation law says (cu)_t+
abla\cdot\mathbf J=0. Substitute Fourier's law: c u_t+
abla\cdot(-k
abla u)=0. If c and k are constant, this becomes c u_t-k
abla\cdot(
abla u)=0. The expression 
abla\cdot(
abla u) is the Laplacian:  oxed{\Delta u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}} in the plane. Therefore c u_t-k\Delta u=0, or  oxed{u_t=\alpha\Delta u,} where \alpha= rac{k}{c} is called the thermal diffusivity.
This is the heat equation.

example.title: A warm bump on a rod

statement.p: Consider a thin rod with coordinate 0\le x\le1, whose ends are held at temperature 0. Let u(x,t)=e^{-\alpha\pi^2t}\sin(\pi x). Then u_t=-\alpha\pi^2e^{-\alpha\pi^2t}\sin(\pi x), while u_{xx}=-\pi^2e^{-\alpha\pi^2t}\sin(\pi x). Therefore u_t=\alpha u_{xx}. So this is a solution of the one-dimensional heat equation.
The factor e^{-\alpha\pi^2t} shrinks as time passes. The sine-shaped temperature profile fades away. Heat spreads until the rod settles to the boundary temperature.

subsection.p: The heat equation is not just a formula. It says that temperature changes because heat flows down its gradient. The Laplacian measures the net effect of that flow.

To make the neighboring-average interpretation precise, suppose u is C^2 and hold time fixed. The one-variable second-order Taylor formulas along the two coordinate lines give \frac{u(x+h,y)+u(x-h,y)+u(x,y+h)+u(x,y-h)}4-u(x,y) =\frac{h^2}4\Delta u(x,y)+o(h^2). Thus the sign of a nonzero Laplacian gives the sign of this nearby-average difference for sufficiently small h.

exercise.title: What is the Laplacian really telling us?

statement.p: The heat equation says u_t=\alpha\Delta u. In plain words, what does the sign of \Delta u at a point tell you about how that point compares to its immediate surroundings, and why does that comparison decide whether the point warms up or cools down?

hint.p: Think of \Delta u as comparing a point's temperature to the average of nearby points. Heat always moves from warmer to cooler. Which way must heat flow if a point sits below the local average?

subsection.p: A point where \Delta u\gt 0 is colder than its surroundings in an averaged second-order sense, so heat flows in and u_t\gt 0. A point where \Delta u\lt 0 is warmer than its surroundings, so heat flows out and u_t\lt 0.

subsection.title: Heat sources and nonconstant materials
subsection.p:
Allow the material coefficients c and k to vary with position but not with time. If heat is created inside the plate, the balance law is (cu)_t+
abla\cdot\mathbf J=s. Using \mathbf J=-k
abla u, we get  oxed{c u_t-
abla\cdot(k
abla u)=s.} If c and k are constant, then  oxed{u_t=\alpha\Delta u+ rac{s}{c}.}

example.title: A heater under a plate

statement.p: Suppose a small electric heater under a metal plate produces heat at rate s(x,y,t)=10e^{-x^2-y^2}. This source is strongest near the origin and weak far away. If the plate has constant c and k, its temperature satisfies u_t=\alpha\Delta u+\frac{10}{c}e^{-x^2-y^2}. The first term spreads heat. The second term creates heat.

subsection.p: The assumption \mathbf J=-k\nabla u is a physical assumption, not a theorem of calculus. Some materials conduct better in one direction than another. Then k is not just a number; it is a matrix, and the flux law becomes \mathbf J=-K\nabla u. The conservation law stays the same. The constitutive law, the rule connecting flux to the field, changes.

subsection.title: Vibrating strings and the wave equation
subsection.p: Heat spreads and fades. Waves travel.
The simplest wave model is a stretched string. Let u(x,t) be the vertical displacement of the string at position x and time t.

Take a short piece of string from x to x+\Delta x. Suppose the tension has constant magnitude T, and suppose the slopes are small. The vertical component of the tension at the right end is approximately T u_x(x+\Delta x,t). The vertical component at the left end pulls the other way and is approximately T u_x(x,t). So the net vertical force is approximately T\bigl(u_x(x+\Delta x,t)-u_x(x,t)\bigr). For small \Delta x, u_x(x+\Delta x,t)-u_x(x,t)\approx u_{xx}(x,t)\Delta x. Thus \text{net vertical force}\approx T u_{xx}(x,t)\Delta x.

If the string has mass density m per unit length, then the mass of this small piece is m\Delta x. Newton's law gives m\Delta x\,u_{tt}\approx T u_{xx}\Delta x. Cancel \Delta x: m u_{tt}=T u_{xx}. Therefore \boxed{u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},} where c^2=\frac{T}{m}.
This is the one-dimensional wave equation.

example.title: A traveling wave

statement.p: Let u(x,t)=f(x-ct), where f is twice differentiable. Then u_t=-c f'(x-ct), and u_{tt}=c^2 f''(x-ct). Also u_x=f'(x-ct), and u_{xx}=f''(x-ct). Therefore u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}.
The shape f travels to the right with speed c. Unlike heat, it does not have to fade just because it moves.

subsection.p: There is also a left-moving wave: u(x,t)=g(x+ct). Indeed, any sum \boxed{u(x,t)=f(x-ct)+g(x+ct)} solves the one-dimensional wave equation. This formula says that, in one dimension, waves split naturally into right-moving and left-moving pieces.

exercise.title: Why does a wave travel but heat fade?

statement.p: The heat equation has a single time derivative, u_t, while the wave equation has a second, u_{tt}. Both share the same spatial operator \Delta u. Why should changing only the order of the time derivative turn a profile that smooths and fades into one that travels and oscillates?

hint.p: A first-order time law sets the rate of change directly, like friction settling toward rest. A second-order time law sets the acceleration, the way Newton's law does. What does a system that stores momentum tend to do when pushed back toward equilibrium?

subsection.title: Vibrating membranes
subsection.p: A drumhead is a two-dimensional version of the string. Let u(x,y,t) be its vertical displacement. The membrane tension pulls in both the x- and y-directions. The net vertical force on a small rectangle is controlled by u_{xx}+u_{yy}. Thus the model becomes \boxed{u_{tt}=c^2(u_{xx}+u_{yy})=c^2\Delta u.}

example.title: A standing wave on a square membrane

statement.p: On the square 0\le x\le1,\qquad 0\le y\le1, consider u(x,y,t)=\cos(\omega t)\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). Then u_{tt}=-\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). Also u_{xx}=-\pi^2\cos(\omega t)\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y), and u_{yy}=-\pi^2\cos(\omega t)\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). So \Delta u=-2\pi^2\cos(\omega t)\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). The wave equation u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u holds exactly when -\omega^2=-2c^2\pi^2, or \boxed{\omega=c\pi\sqrt2.}
This is one normal mode of the square membrane. The shape \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y) stays the same while its amplitude oscillates in time.

subsection.title: Equilibrium and Laplace's equation
subsection.p: Equilibrium means no time change.
For heat, equilibrium means u_t=0. If there are no sources and the material is constant, the heat equation becomes 0=\alpha\Delta u, so \boxed{\Delta u=0.}
For a membrane at rest, equilibrium means u_{tt}=0. The wave equation becomes 0=c^2\Delta u, so again \boxed{\Delta u=0.}
This is Laplace's equation.

example.title: A saddle that is in equilibrium

statement.p: Let u(x,y)=x^2-y^2. Then u_{xx}=2,\qquad u_{yy}=-2. Therefore \Delta u=2-2=0. So u is harmonic.
Its graph is a saddle. Equilibrium does not mean flat. It means the upward curvature in one direction is balanced by the downward curvature in another direction.

example.title: A steady temperature on a rectangle

statement.p: Suppose a plate has no heat sources, and its temperature is no longer changing. Then inside the plate \Delta u=0. The boundary temperatures determine the solution. If the left edge is kept hot, the right edge cold, and the top and bottom insulated or prescribed, the interior temperature adjusts until there is no net accumulation of heat anywhere.
The equation \Delta u=0 does not by itself tell the whole story. Boundary conditions complete the physical problem.

subsection.p: That last sentence is essential. Partial differential equations almost never describe a physical situation alone. They need a region, boundary conditions, and often initial conditions.
For heat, one usually needs u(x,y,0) and boundary temperatures or boundary fluxes.
For waves, one needs both u(x,y,0) and u_t(x,y,0), because the equation is second order in time.
For equilibrium, there is no initial time, but the boundary data are crucial.

subsection.title: Why different physical systems share the same mathematics
subsection.p: The heat equation, wave equation, and Laplace equation come from different stories.

table.title: Three physical stories behind the same operator.

row.cell: thermal energy is conserved, and heat flows down the temperature gradient.
force equals mass times acceleration, and tension reacts to curvature.
net flow, net force, or net source disappears.

subsection.p: Yet the same operator appears: \Delta.

The reason is geometric. The Laplacian measures a kind of net second-order imbalance around a point. In one dimension, that imbalance is just u_{xx}. In two dimensions, there are two independent coordinate directions, so the imbalance is u_{xx}+u_{yy}. In three dimensions, it is u_{xx}+u_{yy}+u_{zz}.

exercise.title: Why the same operator for different physics?

statement.p: Heat conservation, Newton's law for a vibrating membrane, and the equilibrium condition are three completely different physical stories, yet each produces the same operator \Delta. What feature common to all three situations forces this shared mathematics, even though the underlying physics is not the same?

hint.p: Look at what \Delta u measures geometrically: a net second-order imbalance between a point and its neighbors. Ask what each story is ultimately responding to. Is it the point's value, or how that value compares with the surrounding ones?

subsection.p: A hot spot with \Delta u\lt 0 loses heat. A string segment with u_{xx}\lt 0 is pulled downward. A membrane with \Delta u=0 has its directional curvatures balanced.

The equations in this section used scalar fields: temperature, displacement, potential. But nature also has fields that are already vectorial. Electric fields push charges. Magnetic fields measure flux through surfaces. They do not merely diffuse or vibrate; they create each other's circulation and flux. The final capstone of the forms language is to write those laws in the notation the book has been building from the beginning.

section.title: Maxwell's equations as a forms gateway
section.p: This section is the main capstone of the book.
It is not an electromagnetism course. We will not derive every physical constant or solve realistic engineering problems. The goal is different: to see why the language of forms is not decoration.
Maxwell's equations are the place where the main ideas of the book meet:

li.p: fields attached to space,
circulation along curves,
flux through surfaces,
sources inside volumes,
the exterior derivative d,
the identity d^2=0,
and conservation laws.

section.p: Standard vector calculus treats these as four distinct formulas. The language of forms strips that away, unifying them into simple rules about boundaries and derivatives. The math doesn't obscure the physics; it reveals the underlying structure.

subsection.title: Electric and magnetic fields
subsection.p: In the smooth calculations below, assume the field coefficients have continuous second derivatives in space and time on the regions used. The integration surfaces and solids are fixed in time. Time derivatives act on the coefficients of a spatial form, leaving dx,dy,dz fixed. The integral-differentiation argument in then applies in fixed parameter domains.
Electric and magnetic fields do different kinds of measuring.

An electric field measures work per unit charge along a small displacement. That makes it naturally a 1-form: \boxed{\mathcal E=E_1\,dx+E_2\,dy+E_3\,dz.} If a unit positive charge moves by a tiny vector, \mathcal E measures the electric work along that tiny motion.

A magnetic field is naturally measured by flux through an oriented surface. So we write the magnetic field as a 2-form: \boxed{\mathcal B=B_1\,dy\wedge dz+B_2\,dz\wedge dx+B_3\,dx\wedge dy.} This form measures magnetic flux through small oriented area pieces.

In vacuum, the pairs are related by physical constants: \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf H. In materials, the relations can be more complicated. Those relations belong to physics. The forms structure of Maxwell's equations does not depend on their simplest vacuum form.
The roles are summarized below.

table.title: The field forms and what they measure.

subsection.p: This table is already half the story. The degree of each form tells us what kind of geometric object it belongs to.

subsection.title: The four equations in forms language
subsection.p: These are Maxwell's equations in three-dimensional space, written with spatial forms.
Here is the translation into vector notation:

table.title: Maxwell's equations in forms and vector notation.

subsection.p: The forms equations are not shorter only because of notation. They say which kind of integral each law wants.

table.title: The natural integral form of each equation.

subsection.p: These integral forms are where the equations become physical.

subsection.title: Gauss's law: charge is detected by electric flux
subsection.p: The equation d\mathcal D=\mathcal Q says that the exterior derivative of the electric flux form is the charge density 3-form.
The boundary surface detects what is stored inside.

example.title: A point charge, seen from outside

statement.p: A positive point charge at the origin creates electric flux through every sphere around it. In a fully realistic treatment, the charge density is concentrated at a point, so it is not an ordinary continuous function. The smooth version of Stokes' theorem in this book does not directly handle that singularity.

But the moral is exactly the same as the warning examples in : a closed surface can detect something inside. If a field is singular at a missing point, we cannot apply the ordinary smooth theorem across that point as though nothing were there.

subsection.p: For smooth charge density, there is no singularity. The law simply says that charge is the source of electric flux.

subsection.title: No magnetic monopoles: magnetic flux has no source
subsection.p: The magnetic equation d\mathcal B=0 says that magnetic flux has no volume source.
Magnetic field lines may pass through a closed surface, but as much flux enters as leaves. There is no isolated magnetic charge inside the region.

example.title: A uniform magnetic field through a box

statement.p: Let \mathbf B=(0,0,B_0), so \mathcal B=B_0\,dx\wedge dy. For a rectangular box, the top face has upward orientation and contributes positive flux B_0(\text{area of top}). The bottom face has downward orientation and contributes the negative of the same amount. The side faces contribute 0, because the field is tangent to them.
The total magnetic flux through the closed box is 0.

subsection.p: Again the sign is not decoration. Flux through a closed surface is an oriented sum. Entering and leaving must be counted with opposite signs.

subsection.title: Faraday's law: changing magnetic flux creates electric circulation
subsection.p: Faraday's law is \boxed{d\mathcal E+\frac{\partial\mathcal B}{\partial t}=0.} Let S be an oriented surface with boundary \partial S. Integrate over S: \int_S d\mathcal E+\int_S \frac{\partial\mathcal B}{\partial t}=0. By Stokes' theorem, \int_S d\mathcal E=\int_{\partial S}\mathcal E. So \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\mathcal E=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_S\mathcal B.} In words: \boxed{\text{electric circulation around a loop}=-\text{rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop.}}

This is one of the cleanest places to see why a 1-form and a 2-form belong in the same theorem. The electric field is integrated around a boundary curve. The magnetic field is integrated through a surface spanning that curve.

example.title: A changing magnetic field through a circular loop

statement.p: Let S be the disk x^2+y^2\le R^2,\qquad z=0, oriented upward. Its boundary circle is oriented counterclockwise as viewed from above.
Suppose the magnetic field is vertical and spatially uniform: \mathcal B=b(t)\,dx\wedge dy. Then \int_S\mathcal B=b(t)\pi R^2. Faraday's law gives \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\mathcal E=-b'(t)\pi R^2.}

If b'(t)\gt 0, then the upward magnetic flux is increasing, and the induced electric circulation is negative relative to the counterclockwise orientation. That means the electric circulation is clockwise when viewed from above.
The minus sign is the mathematical form of Lenz's law: the induced circulation opposes the change in magnetic flux.

subsection.p: We can even find one possible electric form in this symmetric example. Recall that d(-y\,dx+x\,dy)=2\,dx\wedge dy. If \mathcal E=-\frac{b'(t)}{2}(-y\,dx+x\,dy), then d\mathcal E=-b'(t)\,dx\wedge dy. Since \mathcal B_t=b'(t)\,dx\wedge dy, we get d\mathcal E+\mathcal B_t=0. So this \mathcal E satisfies Faraday's law.

subsection.title: Ampere--Maxwell law: current and changing electric flux create magnetic circulation
subsection.p: Integrate over an oriented surface S: \int_S d\mathcal H=\int_S\mathcal J+\frac{d}{dt}\int_S\mathcal D. By Stokes' theorem, \int_S d\mathcal H=\int_{\partial S}\mathcal H. Therefore \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\mathcal H=\int_S\mathcal J+\frac{d}{dt}\int_S\mathcal D.} In words: \boxed{\text{magnetic circulation around a loop}=\text{current through the loop}+\text{changing electric flux through the loop.}}

The second term, \frac{\partial\mathcal D}{\partial t}, is Maxwell's displacement-current term. It is not a decorative correction. It is the term that makes the equation compatible with conservation of charge.

subsection.title: One loop, two surfaces: why Maxwell's correction is necessary
subsection.p: This example is the heart of the capstone.

Picture a wire charging a parallel-plate capacitor. A current flows through the wire toward one plate. Between the plates there is no conduction current crossing the gap, but the electric field between the plates is changing.
Let C be a loop around the wire. The loop can be spanned by many different surfaces.
One surface, call it S_1, cuts through the wire. The current flux through S_1 is \int_{S_1}\mathcal J=I.
