Another surface, call it S_2, bulges out between the capacitor plates and crosses the gap instead of cutting the wire. No conduction current crosses this surface: \int_{S_2}\mathcal J=0.
If the law were only d\mathcal H=\mathcal J, then Stokes' theorem would give \int_C\mathcal H=\int_{S_1}\mathcal J=I using S_1, but \int_C\mathcal H=\int_{S_2}\mathcal J=0 using S_2.
That is impossible. The same boundary loop C cannot have two different magnetic circulations.

exercise.title: Why should the surface not matter?

statement.p: The contradiction came from getting two different answers for \int_C\mathcal H depending on whether we spanned the loop C with S_1 or S_2. Why should a quantity attached to the boundary loop be blind to the choice of spanning surface? What does this expectation reveal about the kind of object \mathcal J+\mathcal D_t has to be?

hint.p: Think about Stokes' theorem: \int_{\partial S}\mathcal H=\int_S d\mathcal H. If the left side depends only on the loop, what must be true of the right side as we slide the surface around? Closing a small gap between S_1 and S_2 turns two surfaces into the boundary of a solid region.

subsection.p: Maxwell's corrected law says d\mathcal H=\mathcal J+\mathcal D_t. Now the two surfaces agree.

For S_1, the conduction current contributes \int_{S_1}\mathcal J=I. For S_2, the changing electric flux contributes \frac{d}{dt}\int_{S_2}\mathcal D=I. So both surfaces give \boxed{\int_C\mathcal H=I.}

figure.caption: The same loop can bound different surfaces. Maxwell's displacement-current term makes the answer independent of the spanning surface.

subsection.p: This example shows the power of the forms viewpoint. A boundary integral should not depend on which spanning surface we use, unless something singular or omitted lies between the surfaces. The displacement-current term is exactly what restores that surface independence during charging.

subsection.title: Charge conservation from d^2=0
subsection.p: Now the continuity equation returns.

Start with Ampere--Maxwell: d\mathcal H-\mathcal D_t=\mathcal J. Apply d to both sides: d(d\mathcal H)-d(\mathcal D_t)=d\mathcal J. Since d^2=0, we have d(d\mathcal H)=0. Also, equality of the continuous mixed space-time partial derivatives gives commutation of time differentiation with the spatial exterior derivative: d(\mathcal D_t)=(d\mathcal D)_t. By Gauss's law, d\mathcal D=\mathcal Q. Therefore -\mathcal Q_t=d\mathcal J. So \boxed{\mathcal Q_t+d\mathcal J=0.}
This is charge conservation.

statement.p: We derived charge conservation after writing down Maxwell's equations, yet the text insists conservation was there all along. In what sense is conservation a consequence of the structure rather than an extra physical law we chose to add? What role does d^2=0 play in making it unavoidable?

hint.p: Notice that the only physics we used was Ampere--Maxwell and Gauss. The step d(d\mathcal H)=0 is pure geometry, true for any form. Ask yourself what would have to fail for charge not to be conserved.

subsection.p: In vector notation, \mathcal Q=\rho_{\mathrm e}\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, and d\mathcal J=(\nabla\cdot\mathbf J)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Thus \boxed{\rho_{\mathrm e,t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0.}
This is the continuity equation from , now forced by Maxwell's equations.
The logic is worth pausing over:
This is one of the deepest payoffs of the notation. Conservation is not pasted onto the equations afterward. It is built into their differential-form structure.

subsection.title: The homogeneous equations and potentials
subsection.p: Two of Maxwell's equations have no source terms: d\mathcal B=0, and d\mathcal E+\mathcal B_t=0. They are called the homogeneous equations.

The first says that \mathcal B is closed: d\mathcal B=0. On a small rectangular box, closed 2-forms are exact, as the construction below shows. Thus locally we can write \boxed{\mathcal B=d\mathcal A} for some 1-form \mathcal A, called the magnetic vector potential.

For completeness, write \mathcal B=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy on a box with fixed interior coordinates x_0,y_0; time is a parameter. Closedness is P_x+Q_y+R_z=0. Set
A_1=0,\qquad A_2(x,y,z)\amp=\int_{x_0}^x R(s,y,z)\,ds, A_3(x,y,z)\amp=-\int_{x_0}^x Q(s,y,z)\,ds+\int_{y_0}^y P(x_0,s,z)\,ds.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives -(A_3)_x=Q and (A_2)_x=R. Differentiating the other integrals as in gives (A_3)_y-(A_2)_z=P(x_0,y,z)-\int_{x_0}^x(Q_y+R_z)(s,y,z)\,ds=P(x,y,z). Consequently \mathcal A=A_1\,dx+A_2\,dy+A_3\,dz satisfies d\mathcal A=\mathcal B. This is a local construction; it makes no claim about one potential on a whole domain with holes.

Then Faraday's law becomes d\mathcal E+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(d\mathcal A)=0. Because d and \partial/\partial t commute, d(\mathcal E+\mathcal A_t)=0. A closed 1-form on this box is exact by . So we can write \mathcal E+\mathcal A_t=-d\varphi, or \boxed{\mathcal E=-d\varphi-\mathcal A_t.} The function \varphi is the electric scalar potential.
These formulas are not needed to use Maxwell's equations, but they show another place where the identity d^2=0 organizes the theory.

There is a warning from : closed does not always mean globally exact. Missing points, holes, and topology can matter. The equation d\mathcal B=0 is local. Writing \mathcal B=d\mathcal A globally may require assumptions about the region.

subsection.title: What changes in space-time
subsection.p: So far, time has been a parameter. At each time t, we wrote forms on ordinary space: \mathcal E,\quad \mathcal B,\quad \mathcal D,\quad \mathcal H.
But Maxwell's equations are really space-time equations. Time is not merely a label outside the geometry. It joins the coordinates: (t,x,y,z).
Let d_4 denote the exterior derivative in space-time. It differentiates with respect to t, x, y, and z.

This extension uses the same coordinate rule as in space. Add the coordinate covector dt, and set d_4f=f_t\,dt+f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz. On each term f\,d\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\xi_k, where every \xi_i is one of t,x,y,z, define d_4(f\,d\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\xi_k) =d_4f\wedge d\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\xi_k, and add the results. Swapping coordinate covectors changes sign, and a repeated coordinate factor gives zero. In d_4^2, every mixed partial appears twice with opposite wedge orders; continuous second partials therefore give d_4^2=0, by the same calculation as in .
Now apply d_4 again: d_4(d_4G)=d_4\mathscr J. Since d_4^2=0, we get \boxed{d_4\mathscr J=0.} That is charge conservation in space-time.
This is the gateway.

statement.p: Four separate vector equations collapsed into just d_4F=0 and d_4G=\mathscr J. Beyond looking tidier, what does this compression actually tell us? Why is it meaningful that the homogeneous pair becomes a single statement that F is closed, and what does that suggest about how \mathcal E and \mathcal B are related?

hint.p: A single equation d_4F=0 treats \mathcal E and \mathcal B as two faces of one space-time form. Ask what changing your point of view (mixing t with a space coordinate) would then do to that one object, and why a frame-independent statement is more honest than four frame-dependent ones.

subsection.p: Electric and magnetic fields are no longer two unrelated vector fields. They are pieces of space-time forms. The equations are no longer four separate vector identities. They are two exterior-derivative equations, with conservation following from d_4^2=0.

A later course explains how the geometry of space-time relates F and G. That relationship uses the metric of space-time, and the operation that appears there is the Hodge star. We do not need it here. The point for this book is simpler and more important: \boxed{\text{the language of forms is the natural language of Maxwell's equations.}}

subsection.title: The book's main arc, seen from the end
subsection.p: The book began with a displacement: (3,4). It was only an instruction to move.

Then we learned that vectors could measure length, area, and volume. The wedge product remembered orientation: dx\wedge dy,\qquad dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Functions became 0-forms. Work integrands became 1-forms. Flux integrands became 2-forms. Densities became 3-forms.

The exterior derivative connected them: 0	ext{-forms}\xrightarrow{d}1	ext{-forms}\xrightarrow{d}2	ext{-forms}\xrightarrow{d}3	ext{-forms}. In vector language, those arrows became 
abla,\qquad 
abla	imes,\qquad 
abla\cdot. The identity d^2=0 became the quiet reason behind 
abla	imes
abla f=\mathbf 0 and 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0.
Stokes' theorem then said: \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. Boundary measurements and interior derivatives were two views of the same thing.

Finally, conservation laws added time. The continuity equation said: \text{time change of stored amount}+\text{spatial derivative of flux}=\text{source}. Heat, waves, and equilibrium showed how physical assumptions choose fluxes and forces.
Maxwell's equations show the whole structure at once. Electric circulation, magnetic flux, charge density, current flux, Stokes' theorem, d, and d^2=0 all appear in one system.
So the final lesson is not a formula. It is a way of seeing.
That is the promise of multivariable calculus fulfilled: from tiny changes near one point to global laws over curves, surfaces, solids, and finally space-time.

section.title: Potential theory and harmonic functions
section.p: Maxwell's equations were the broad capstone: fields, flux, circulation, sources, boundaries, and the identity d^2=0 all appeared together. This section is a quieter coda. It returns to one scalar field u(x,y,z), but now we read it with the whole book behind us.

A scalar field can be a temperature, an electric potential, a height, or a pressure. When its gradient field has no source inside a region, the field satisfies \Delta u=0. Those functions are called harmonic. They are the steady states of heat flow, the potentials of source-free fields, and the energy-minimizing shapes among all functions with the same boundary values.

subsection.title: The Laplacian as divergence of the gradient
subsection.p: Start with steady heat in a thin metal plate. Let u(x,y) be the temperature. Fourier's law says heat flows down the temperature gradient: \mathbf J=-k\nabla u, where k>0 is constant.

If there are no heat sources inside the plate and the temperature is no longer changing, then the local balance law from becomes 
abla\cdot\mathbf J=0. Substitute the flux law: 
abla\cdot(-k
abla u)=0. Since k is constant, -k
abla\cdot(
abla u)=0. So  oxed{
abla\cdot(
abla u)=0.}
This expression is the Laplacian: \boxed{\Delta u=\nabla\cdot(\nabla u).}

statement.p: For a twice differentiable scalar field u, the Laplacian of u is \boxed{\Delta u=\nabla\cdot(\nabla u).} In \mathbb R^2, \Delta u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}. In \mathbb R^3, \Delta u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}+u_{zz}.

example.title: A source-free temperature pattern

statement.p: Let u(x,y)=e^x\cos y. Then u_{xx}=e^x\cos y, while u_{yy}=-e^x\cos y. Therefore \Delta u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0. This field can describe a steady temperature pattern with no internal heat sources, provided the boundary temperatures are chosen to match it.

subsection.p: So the Laplacian is the coefficient of the exterior derivative of the gradient flux form. It measures the source strength of the gradient field.

subsection.title: Harmonic functions
subsection.p: A function with zero Laplacian gets its own name.

example.title: A saddle in balance

statement.p: Let u(x,y)=x^2-y^2. Then u_{xx}=2,\qquad u_{yy}=-2. So \Delta u=2-2=0. The graph is a saddle. Harmonic does not mean flat. It means that the upward bending in one direction balances the downward bending in another.

The saddle u=x^2-y^2 is harmonic, yet it is far from flat. In plain words, what is being balanced when we say \Delta u=0, and why does that allow a surface to bend a lot while still counting as harmonic?

hint.p: Look at u_{xx} and u_{yy} separately. The Laplacian adds them, so it is the sum of the bendings that must vanish, not each one on its own.

theorem.title: Harmonic functions have zero gradient flux through small boundaries

proof.p: In space, Stokes' theorem gives \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\nabla u}=\int_E d\Phi_{\nabla u}=\int_E \Delta u\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. If \Delta u=0, every such boundary flux is 0.
Conversely, if the boundary flux is 0 for every small E, then \int_E \Delta u\,dV=0 for every small E. Since \Delta u is continuous, the same argument used in forces \Delta u=0 pointwise.
The plane proof is the same, with dA replacing dV.

subsection.p: The hypotheses matter. The function must be defined and smooth on the whole region where we apply the theorem.

example.title: A hidden source at a missing point

statement.p: On the punctured plane \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, define u(x,y)=\log r,\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Away from the origin, u is harmonic: \Delta u=0. But its gradient is \nabla u=\left(\frac{x}{r^2},\frac{y}{r^2}\right).

On the circle r=a, the outward unit normal is \widehat{\mathbf n}=\left(\frac{x}{a},\frac{y}{a}\right), and \nabla u\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=\frac{1}{a}. Since ds=a\,d\theta,
\int_{r=a}\nabla u\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,ds \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\frac1a(a\,d\theta) \amp= 2\pi.

This does not contradict the theorem. The disk r\le a contains the origin, where \log r is not defined. The missing point behaves like a hidden source. A theorem about smooth functions on a whole region cannot be applied across a hole in the domain.

subsection.p: This example is the same kind of warning we saw for closed but non-exact forms. A puncture in the region can carry information that no local derivative sees away from the puncture.

subsection.title: Mean value ideas
subsection.p: Harmonic functions have a surprising averaging property: the value at the center of a circle is the average value on the circle.

figure.caption: A harmonic function is balanced: its center value equals its circular average.

subsection.p: The example is not a coincidence.

statement.p: Let u be C^2 and harmonic on an open disk containing the closed disk (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2\le r^2. Then \boxed{u(a,b)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(a+r\cos\theta,b+r\sin\theta)\,d\theta.} That is, the value at the center equals the average value on every circle around it, as long as the whole closed disk lies inside the domain.

subsection.p: Again the hypotheses are real. The function must be harmonic on the whole disk.

example.title: Why harmonicity is needed

statement.p: Let u(x,y)=x^2+y^2. On the circle x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta, we have u=r^2. So the average value on that circle is r^2. But u(0,0)=0. The mean value property fails. The reason is visible in the Laplacian: \Delta u=2+2=4. This function has positive source strength everywhere.

subsection.p: The mean value property has a powerful consequence.

statement.p: Let R be a bounded connected open region in the plane, and let u be continuous on its closure and harmonic on R. If u reaches its maximum at a point of R, then u is constant on R.
The same statement holds for an interior minimum.

proof.title: Proof idea
proof.p: If u(a,b) is a maximum, every value on a small circle around (a,b) is at most u(a,b). But the average around that circle must equal u(a,b). The only way an average of numbers all no larger than u(a,b) can equal u(a,b) is if all those numbers equal u(a,b).

So u is constant on every sufficiently small circle around the point, hence on a disk. The set of points in R attaining this maximum is therefore open in R; it is also closed in R by continuity. It is nonempty, so connectedness forces it to be all of R.

subsection.p: A steady temperature with no internal heat sources cannot have a lonely hot spot inside. Its hottest and coldest values must come from the boundary, unless the whole plate is already at one temperature.

exercise.title: Why can the hot spot only live on the edge?

statement.p: Using the mean value property as your guide, explain intuitively why a harmonic temperature cannot reach its highest value at an interior point unless it is constant. What goes wrong at a would-be interior peak?

hint.p: At a peak, every nearby value is no larger than the center value. Now ask: how can the average over a surrounding circle still equal that center value?

subsection.title: Gradient fields and energy minimization
subsection.p: Harmonic functions also arise from an energy principle.

Imagine a flexible membrane stretched over a wire frame. The boundary wire fixes the height of the membrane along the edge. Among all surfaces with that boundary height, the physical membrane chooses the one with least stretching energy. In the small-slope model, that energy is \boxed{\mathcal E[u]=\frac12\iint_R |\nabla u|^2\,dA.} This is called the Dirichlet energy.
The energy is small when u changes gently, and large when u changes sharply.
A simple example shows the minimization idea.

example.title: The straight ramp minimizes energy

statement.p: Let R=[0,1]\times[0,1], and consider u(x,y)=x. Now perturb u by a smooth function \eta that vanishes on the boundary: u_\varepsilon=u+\varepsilon\eta=x+\varepsilon\eta. The boundary values do not change, because \eta=0 on \partial R.

Compute the energy:
\mathcal E[u_\varepsilon] \amp= \frac12\iint_R\left|(1,0)+\varepsilon\nabla\eta\right|^2\,dA \amp= \frac12\iint_R\left(1+2\varepsilon\eta_x+\varepsilon^2|\nabla\eta|^2\right)\,dA.
The middle term is \iint_R \eta_x\,dA. Integrate in x:
\iint_R \eta_x\,dA \amp= \int_0^1\int_0^1 \eta_x(x,y)\,dx\,dy \amp= \int_0^1\bigl[\eta(1,y)-\eta(0,y)\bigr]\,dy \amp= 0,
because \eta is zero on the boundary.

Therefore \boxed{\mathcal E[u_\varepsilon]=\mathcal E[u]+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\iint_R|\nabla\eta|^2\,dA.} The added term is always nonnegative. So the ramp u=x has the smallest energy among these boundary-preserving perturbations.

subsection.p: The example works because \Delta x=0. The same principle holds for every harmonic function.

statement.p: Let R be a bounded plane region with piecewise smooth boundary. Let u be C^2 on a neighborhood of its closure and harmonic in its interior, and let w be C^1 on that neighborhood with the same boundary values as u. Write w=u+\eta, where \eta=0\quad\text{on }\partial R. Then \boxed{\mathcal E[w]\ge \mathcal E[u].} More precisely, \boxed{\mathcal E[u+\eta]=\mathcal E[u]+\frac12\iint_R|\nabla\eta|^2\,dA.}

Expand:
\mathcal E[u+\eta] \amp=  rac12\iint_R|

abla\eta\,dA+ rac12\iint_R|
abla\eta|^2\,dA.
So \mathcal E[u+\eta]=\mathcal E[u]+\iint_R

abla\eta\,dA+ rac12\iint_R|
abla\eta|^2\,dA.

Apply the plane divergence theorem to \eta

abla\eta\cdot

abla\eta\,dA=\int_{\partial R}\eta\, rac{\partial u}{\partial n}\,ds-\iint_R\eta\,\Delta u\,dA. The boundary term is zero because \eta=0\quad	ext{on }\partial R. The interior term is zero because \Delta u=0. Thus \iint_R

subsection.p: The boundary condition is part of the theorem, not a technical afterthought.

exercise.title: Why fix the boundary before minimizing?

statement.p: The theorem says a harmonic u has the least Dirichlet energy among functions sharing its boundary values. Conceptually, why is that boundary restriction essential? What would minimize the energy mean if we were allowed to change the boundary too?

hint.p: Think about the flat function w=0. Its energy is as small as possible, but compare its edge values to those of u=x. Without a fixed frame, what stops the membrane from simply collapsing?

example.title: Why the same boundary values matter

statement.p: On the unit square, the function u(x,y)=x has positive energy: \mathcal E[u]=\frac12\iint_R 1\,dA=\frac12. The function w(x,y)=0 has energy \mathcal E[w]=0. So w has smaller energy.
But w does not have the same boundary values as u. Along the right edge, u(1,y)=1, while w(1,y)=0. The minimization theorem compares only functions attached to the same boundary data.

subsection.p: A harmonic function can now be seen in several equivalent ways:

The same equation has become a statement about sources, averages, and energy. That is a good place for the chapter to end. What remains is not another new theorem, but a set of projects that lets the whole chapter work as a modeling language.

introduction.p:
turned Stokes' theorem into a modeling tool. The theorem said that boundary measurements and interior derivatives are two forms of the same information:
\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.
Conservation laws added time. A density changes inside a region because flux crosses the boundary or because sources act inside.

subsection.p: The repeated pattern is:

subsection.title: Project 1: conservation of mass in a pipe network
subsection.p:
A small water system has three tanks connected by pipes. Let
M_1(t),\quad M_2(t),\quad M_3(t)
be the mass of water in the tanks.

Water flows from tank 1 to tank 2 at rate
q_{12}=0.4M_1,
from tank 2 to tank 3 at rate
q_{23}=0.3M_2,
and from tank 3 back to tank 1 at rate
q_{31}=0.2M_3.
An external pump adds water to tank 1 at rate 5, and water leaves tank 3 at rate 2.

li.p:
Write the balance law for each tank:
\frac{d}{dt}(\text{mass in tank}) = \text{inflow}-\text{outflow}+\text{source}.

Show that
M_1+M_2+M_3
changes at rate
3.
Explain why the internal pipe flows cancel in the total balance.
Change the external pump rate from 5 to 2. Show that the total mass is then conserved.
Interpret the cancellation of internal flows as a discrete version of the divergence theorem: what leaves one small region enters a neighboring one.

subsection.p:
This project is deliberately finite. It uses tanks instead of a continuum. The same logic becomes
\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=s
when the tanks shrink to tiny regions.

subsection.title: Project 2: heat diffusion on a plate
subsection.p:
A square metal plate occupies
0\le x\le1,\qquad 0\le y\le1.
Its boundary is held at temperature 0. The initial temperature is
u(x,y,0)=\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y).

li.p:
Verify that
u(x,y,t)=e^{-2\alpha\pi^2t}\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)
solves
u_t=\alpha(u_{xx}+u_{yy})
and satisfies the boundary condition.

Compute the total heat, up to a constant heat capacity factor:
H(t)=\int_0^1\int_0^1 u(x,y,t)\,dy\,dx.

Now compare with the higher-frequency initial temperature
u(x,y,0)=\sin(3\pi x)\sin(\pi y).
Find the exponential decay rate. Which pattern fades faster?
Give a physical explanation: why should a temperature pattern with sharper spatial oscillation smooth out faster?

subsection.p: This project connects the Laplacian with smoothing. The second derivatives detect sharp bending, and sharp bending drives faster heat flow.

subsection.title: Project 3: incompressible vector fields and stream functions
subsection.p:
In the plane, let
\psi(x,y)
have continuous second partial derivatives, and define
\boxed{ \mathbf v=(\psi_y,-\psi_x). }
This construction produces a divergence-free vector field.

li.p:
Verify directly that
\nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0.

Take
\psi(x,y)=\sin x\sin y.
Compute
\mathbf v=(\psi_y,-\psi_x).

Show that the velocity field is tangent to the level curves of \psi. That is, show
\mathbf v\cdot\nabla\psi=0.
Explain why a particle following this flow stays on one level curve of \psi.

Compute the scalar curl of \mathbf v:
\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf v = Q_x-P_y,
where
\mathbf v=(P,Q).
Show that
\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf v=-\Delta\psi.

subsection.p: The function \psi is called a stream function. Its level curves are stream lines of the incompressible flow. This is another place where a scalar field secretly organizes a vector field.

subsection.title: Project 4: Maxwell's equations in forms and vectors
subsection.p:
This project is a translation exercise. Let
\mathcal E=E_1\,dx+E_2\,dy+E_3\,dz
and
\mathcal B=B_1\,dy\wedge dz+B_2\,dz\wedge dx+B_3\,dx\wedge dy.

li.p:
Compute
d\mathcal E.
Write its three coefficients next to the components of
\nabla\times\mathbf E.

Compute
d\mathcal B.
Show that its coefficient is
\nabla\cdot\mathbf B.

Translate
d\mathcal E+\mathcal B_t=0
into vector notation.

Translate
d\mathcal B=0
into vector notation.

Explain why applying d to
d\mathcal E+\mathcal B_t=0
does not produce a new equation. Use
d^2=0.

subsection.p: The goal is not to memorize two languages. The goal is to see that the vector formulas and the forms formulas describe the same geometry.

subsection.title: Project 5: harmonic functions and boundary data
subsection.p:
Let
R=[0,1]\times[0,1].
A steady temperature u on R satisfies
\Delta u=0.

li.p:
Check that
u_1(x,y)=x
is harmonic.

Check that
u_2(x,y)=y
is harmonic.

Check that
u_3(x,y)=xy
is harmonic.
For each function, describe the boundary temperatures on the four sides of the square.

Choose constants a,b,c and form
u=a u_1+b u_2+c u_3.
Show that u is still harmonic.
Explain why linear combinations of harmonic functions are harmonic.
Use the maximum principle to explain why a harmonic function on R cannot have a strict interior maximum unless it is constant.

subsection.p: This project shows one of the reasons Laplace's equation is manageable: it is linear. Solutions can be added and scaled.

subsection.title: Final reflection: from local change to global balance
subsection.p:
A 1-form measures along curves. A 2-form measures through surfaces. A 3-form measures throughout solids. The exterior derivative moves from one degree to the next:
0\longrightarrow 1\longrightarrow 2\longrightarrow 3.
The generalized Stokes theorem says that an interior derivative is the same information as a boundary measurement:
\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.
added the last ingredient: time.

Once time enters, Stokes' theorem becomes a bookkeeping machine. What is stored inside a region changes because something crosses the boundary or because something is created inside:
\frac{d}{dt}\int_E \rho\,dV + \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J} = \int_E s\,dV.
Using Stokes' theorem, this becomes the local equation
\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=s.
That one sentence contains a large part of applied mathematics.

Heat chooses
\mathbf J=-k\nabla u.
Waves choose a force law tied to curvature. Equilibrium sets time change to zero. Maxwell's equations choose electric and magnetic forms whose derivatives encode charge, current, flux, and circulation.
The book's central promise was that multivariable calculus is more than a list of formulas. It is a way to move between local and global information:

That is why the same theorem appears under so many names: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, the divergence theorem, and finally the generalized Stokes theorem. They are not separate tricks. They are the same idea learning to speak in higher dimensions.

chapter.title: Capstone Projects and Extended Explorations

introduction.p: Chapter closed the main story. We began the book with points and vectors, and we ended with fields, flux, conservation laws, and the generalized Stokes theorem. The path was long, but the pattern became simple:

This last chapter is a workshop. The projects are meant to make the ideas visible, computable, and explainable. Some can be done by hand. Some are better with graphing software. Some are short reports. A good project should not only get an answer; it should tell a mathematical story.

Geometry was the first language of the book. Before derivatives, integrals, and forms, we needed points, vectors, curves, surfaces, and coordinates. These projects return to that beginning, but now with the whole course available.

The goal is not to make pretty pictures only. A picture should answer a question: Where does the surface bend? Where does a parametrization collapse? Which direction is normal? What does a linear approximation really approximate?

subsection.title: Project 1: build and classify quadric surfaces
subsection.p: A surface that looks mysterious in three dimensions often becomes clear when we set one variable equal to a constant and study the resulting trace.

A seed example: a shifted ellipsoid. Consider
\frac{(x-1)^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}+(z+2)^2=1.
The shifted terms tell us the center:
(1,0,-2).
The denominators tell us the semiaxis lengths:
3 \text{ in the }x\text{-direction},\qquad 2 \text{ in the }y\text{-direction},\qquad 1 \text{ in the }z\text{-direction}.
So the surface is an ellipsoid, stretched most in the x-direction and least in the z-direction.
A few slices confirm this.

If z=-2, then
\frac{(x-1)^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1,
an ellipse in the horizontal plane through the center.

If y=0, then
\frac{(x-1)^2}{9}+(z+2)^2=1,
an ellipse in the xz-plane.

If x=1, then
\frac{y^2}{4}+(z+2)^2=1,
an ellipse in the yz-plane.
The surface was not guessed from a memorized shape. It was read from its slices.

figure.caption: Two traces of the same ellipsoid, drawn in coordinates centered at (1,0,-2). The traces reveal the stretches.

subsection.p: Your task. Create a visual gallery of at least six quadric surfaces.

li.p: Which surfaces are connected? Which have two separate pieces?
Which equations contain a missing variable? What geometric effect does that missing variable have?
Which surfaces have horizontal traces that are circles? Which have horizontal traces that are ellipses? Which have hyperbolas?

What changes when
x^2+y^2-z^2=1
is replaced by
z^2-x^2-y^2=1?

What changes when an equation is shifted, as in
\frac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^2}{9}+\frac{z^2}{16}=1?

subsection.p: A good gallery should make a reader feel that a quadric equation is not a code to memorize. It is a set of instructions for building a shape.

subsection.title: Project 2: visualize tangent planes and linear approximations
subsection.p:
gave the tangent plane formula for a differentiable graph
z=f(x,y). At the point
(a,b,f(a,b)),
the tangent plane is
\boxed{ z=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b). }
This plane is the best first-order model of the surface near the point.
The word near matters. A tangent plane is not a replacement for the whole surface. It is a local microscope.

A seed example: a curved roof. Suppose a small roof has height
f(x,y)=5+\frac12x-\frac14y+\frac18x^2-\frac1{16}y^2+\frac18xy.
At
(a,b)=(2,1),
the height is
\begin{aligned} f(2,1) &= 5+1-\frac14+\frac12-\frac1{16}+\frac14\\ &= \frac{103}{16}. \end{aligned}
The partial derivatives are
f_x(x,y)=\frac12+\frac14x+\frac18y,
and
f_y(x,y)=-\frac14-\frac18y+\frac18x.
So
f_x(2,1)=\frac98, \qquad f_y(2,1)=-\frac18.
The tangent plane is
\boxed{ z=\frac{103}{16}+\frac98(x-2)-\frac18(y-1). }

Now compare the true height with the plane at a nearby point, say
(2.2,0.9).
The tangent plane predicts
L(2.2,0.9) = \frac{103}{16} + \frac98(0.2) - \frac18(-0.1).
The actual error is
f(2.2,0.9)-L(2.2,0.9).
If we move the point twice as close to (2,1), the error should become much smaller. That is what differentiability means: the linear model wins at small scales.

figure.caption: A tangent plane is seen in every slice as a tangent line.

subsection.p: Your task. Choose one smooth surface and one nonsmooth surface.
Part A. The smooth surface. Pick a point (a,b). Then:

li.p:
Compute
f(a,b),\qquad f_x(a,b),\qquad f_y(a,b).

Plot the surface
z=f(x,y)
and the tangent plane
z=L(x,y)
on the same axes.

Choose several nearby displacement vectors
\mathbf h=(h,k).
For each one, compute the error
E(\mathbf h)=f(a+h,b+k)-L(a+h,b+k).

Make a table containing
\|\mathbf h\|, \qquad |E(\mathbf h)|, \qquad \frac{|E(\mathbf h)|}{\|\mathbf h\|}, \qquad \frac{|E(\mathbf h)|}{\|\mathbf h\|^2}.

subsection.p:
The first ratio should get small as
\|\mathbf h\|\to0.
That is the signature of differentiability.

Part B. The nonsmooth surface. At the origin, draw or plot
z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}
or
z=|x|+|y|.
Then answer:

li.p: Does the surface look like it has one tangent plane at the origin?
What do the slices along the x-axis and y-axis look like?
Why is a tangent plane not the same thing as matching a few coordinate slices?
How does the picture explain the warning from : partial information in some directions does not guarantee a true linear approximation in all directions?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: the smooth surface and point you chose,
the tangent plane calculation,
one plot or hand sketch showing the surface and tangent plane together,
an error table,
one plot or hand sketch of the nonsmooth surface,
a paragraph explaining why the smooth surface has a local linear model and the nonsmooth surface does not.

subsection.p: The main lesson is visual: differentiability means that the graph becomes flatter and flatter under a microscope. A corner, cusp, or cone tip refuses to become one plane.

subsection.title: Project 3: plot gradient fields and contour maps together
subsection.p:
A contour map shows level sets:
f(x,y)=c.
A gradient field shows vectors:
\nabla f(x,y).
connected them:
\boxed{ \nabla f \text{ is perpendicular to the level curves of } f. }
This project asks you to draw both at once.

A seed example: temperature on a plate. Let
T(x,y)=20+4x-y-x^2-\frac12y^2.
Then
\nabla T(x,y)=(4-2x,\,-1-y).
At the point
(1,-1),
we get
\nabla T(1,-1)=(2,0).
So the temperature rises fastest toward the positive x-direction.

The level curve through (1,-1) has tangent directions (u,v) satisfying
\nabla T(1,-1)\cdot(u,v)=0.
Thus
(2,0)\cdot(u,v)=0,
so
u=0.
The tangent direction is vertical. The gradient is horizontal. They are perpendicular.

figure.caption: Contours and gradient arrows carry different information, but they fit together geometrically.

subsection.p:
Your task. Choose two scalar fields from the list below:
\begin{array}{c} f_1(x,y)=4-\dfrac{x^2}{4}-y^2,\\[3mm] f_2(x,y)=xy,\\[1mm] f_3(x,y)=6+2x-y-\dfrac14x^2-\dfrac12y^2,\\[3mm] f_4(x,y)=\sin x+\cos y,\\[1mm] f_5(x,y)=\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\quad\text{on }\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. \end{array}
For each chosen field:

li.p:
Compute
\nabla f.

Draw several level curves
f(x,y)=c.
Draw gradient arrows on the same picture.

Pick three points on three different level curves. At each point, show that the gradient is perpendicular to the level curve. You may do this by using
f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy=0
for tangent directions.

Find the critical points, if any:
\nabla f=\mathbf 0.
Where possible, use the Hessian from to classify the critical points.

subsection.p:
Extra exploration: following the arrows. A path
\mathbf r(t)
that follows the gradient field satisfies
\mathbf r'(t)=\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)).
Wherever the gradient is nonzero, such a path heads in the direction of greatest increase per unit distance.
For one of your chosen fields, sketch a few paths that follow the gradient arrows.
Then answer:

li.p: Do the paths cross level curves at right angles?
Do they move toward a maximum, away from a minimum, or through a saddle?
What happens near a critical point?

If your field is
f_5(x,y)=\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2},
what role does the missing origin play?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: two combined contour-gradient plots,
the gradient formulas,
at least three perpendicularity checks,
critical point calculations,
Hessian classifications where possible,
a paragraph comparing the two fields. Which one looks like a bowl, a hill, a saddle, a wave, or a singular field?

subsection.p: The goal is to make the gradient feel less like a formula and more like a geometric compass.

subsection.title: Project 4: compare parameter grids on a sphere, torus, and cone
subsection.p:
A parametrization is a coordinate system on a surface. It does more than draw the surface. It creates a grid, gives tangent directions, chooses an orientation, and supplies the area scale factor
\|\mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v\|.
Different parametrizations reveal different parts of the geometry. They also hide different parts.
The three surfaces. Use the following parametrizations.

1. Sphere of radius a.
\mathbf r_S(\theta,\phi) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, a\cos\phi),
where
0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi.

2. Torus. Let R>r>0. The torus with major radius R and minor radius r is
\mathbf r_T(\theta,\phi) = \bigl((R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta,\, (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta,\, r\sin\phi\bigr),
where
0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le\phi\le2\pi.

3. Upper cone.
\mathbf r_C(\theta,s) = (s\cos\theta,\, s\sin\theta,\, s),
where
0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le s\le a.

figure.caption: The same two-parameter idea produces very different surface grids. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)
sphere
torus
cone z=r

subsection.p: Your task. For each surface:

li.p: Draw the parameter domain.

Draw the two families of parameter curves:
\theta=\text{constant}, \qquad \phi=\text{constant}
or
\theta=\text{constant}, \qquad s=\text{constant}.
Compute the two tangent vectors.

Compute the magnitude of the cross product:
\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|.
Find where the parametrization repeats points.

Find where the parametrization collapses or becomes nonregular:
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\mathbf 0.
Describe how the parameter grid stretches or crowds on the surface.

subsection.p:
Useful checkpoints. For the sphere,
\boxed{ \|\mathbf r_{S,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{S,\phi}\| = a^2\sin\phi. }
The factor vanishes at the poles
\phi=0,\qquad \phi=\pi.
All longitude lines meet there.

For the cone,
\mathbf r_{C,\theta}=(-s\sin\theta,s\cos\theta,0),
and
\mathbf r_{C,s}=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,1).
Thus
\boxed{ \mathbf r_{C,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{C,s} = (s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,-s), }
so
\boxed{ \|\mathbf r_{C,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{C,s}\|=s\sqrt2. }
The factor vanishes at
s=0.
That is the cone tip.

conclusion.p: The geometry projects end with pictures, but the next question is already present in the pictures. Once a surface has shape, it is natural to ask where it is highest, where it is lowest, where it balances, and how to choose the best point under restrictions. That question pulls us back into optimization.

introduction.p:
Chapter taught us the local tests for best points: 
abla f=\mathbf 0 for free interior extrema, the Hessian for second-order shape, and 
abla f=\lambda
abla g for one smooth constraint.
These projects turn those tools into models. The hardest part is often not taking derivatives. It is deciding what the variables are, what must be optimized, and what constraints cannot be broken.

subsection.title: Project 1: constrained design problems
subsection.p: A design problem becomes a calculus problem only after we name the variables.
A tank has dimensions. A package has side lengths. A fence has segments. A shape has area, volume, cost, or strength. Optimization begins when those quantities become functions.

p.em: A seed example: a closed cylindrical tank.

subsection.p: A field station needs a closed cylindrical water tank with fixed volume V. Let r be the radius and h be the height.

Use the constraint to eliminate h: h=\frac{V}{\pi r^2}. Then
A(r) \amp = 2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\frac{V}{\pi r^2}\right) \amp = 2\pi r^2+\frac{2V}{r}.
Differentiate: A'(r)=4\pi r-\frac{2V}{r^2}. At a critical point, 4\pi r=\frac{2V}{r^2}, so 4\pi r^3=2V, and therefore \boxed{r^3=\frac{V}{2\pi}.} Now use the constraint: h=\frac{V}{\pi r^2}. Since V=2\pi r^3, we get \boxed{h=2r.} The height equals the diameter.
This result is not a coincidence. If the tank is too tall and narrow, the side wall is expensive. If it is too flat and wide, the top and bottom are expensive. The optimum balances those costs.
Your task. Choose one design problem from the list below, or create your own.

Option A. Open-top box. An open-top rectangular box has side lengths x,\qquad y,\qquad z. Its volume must be xyz=32. The material area is A(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz. Find the dimensions that minimize material.
Option B. Closed cylindrical tank. A closed cylinder has volume V. Minimize A(r,h)=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh subject to \pi r^2h=V.
Option C. Open cylindrical tank. An open cylindrical tank has no top. Its volume is V. Minimize A(r,h)=\pi r^2+2\pi rh subject to \pi r^2h=V. Compare your answer with the closed-tank answer.

Option D. Rectangular package with square cross-section. A shipping tube has square cross-section x\times x and length L. Its volume is fixed: x^2L=V. The material cost is C(x,L)=2x^2+4xL. Find the least-cost dimensions.
Required steps. For your chosen problem:

li.p: Draw a diagram and label the variables.
Write the quantity to be optimized.
Write the constraint.
Solve the problem in two ways if possible: \text{eliminate one variable} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \text{use Lagrange multipliers}.
Check that your critical point is a minimum, not a maximum or a saddle. You may use a one-variable second derivative test after eliminating a variable.
Interpret the answer in words. Why does the shape make physical or economic sense?

subsection.title: Project 2: least-squares fitting and the Hessian
subsection.p: A best-fit model usually does not pass through every data point. The errors remain. The least-squares idea chooses the model that makes the squared errors as small as possible.
Chapter studied a best-fit line. This project moves one step higher: fitting a plane.

Now check that this critical point is a minimum. The Hessian is
H_E= \begin{pmatrix} 12\amp6\amp8\\ 6\amp6\amp6\\ 8\amp6\amp10 \end{pmatrix}.
Its leading principal minors are 12\gt0,
\begin{vmatrix} 12\amp6\\ 6\amp6 \end{vmatrix} = 72-36=36\gt0,
and \det H_E=120\gt0. We can verify positive definiteness directly from the sum of squares, without a further matrix criterion. For h=(h_a,h_b,h_c), h^T H_E h=2\sum_{i=1}^5(h_a x_i+h_b y_i+h_c)^2. The first three data points force h_c=h_a=h_b=0 if this sum is zero. Thus it is positive for every nonzero h. Since E is quadratic, its expansion at the critical point has zero linear term and this positive quadratic term. The critical point is the unique absolute minimum.
Your task. Choose one of the following.
Option A. Fit a line. Use data points (0,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,2),\qquad (3,4),\qquad (4,5). Fit y=mx+b by minimizing E(m,b)=\sum (mx_i+b-y_i)^2.
Option B. Fit a plane. Use the calibration data from the seed example, or collect your own data with two inputs and one output. Fit z=ax+by+c.
Option C. Fit a quadratic curve. Use data points (-2,5),\qquad (-1,2),\qquad (0,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,6). Fit y=Ax^2+Bx+C. Minimize E(A,B,C)=\sum (Ax_i^2+Bx_i+C-y_i)^2.

li.p: Write the model.
Write the residuals.
Write the squared-error function.
Differentiate and set the partial derivatives equal to zero.
Solve the resulting linear system.
Compute the Hessian of the error function.
Explain why the Hessian shows that the critical point is a minimum.
Plot the data and the fitted model.

subsection.p:
The geometry of the residual. For a line fit, the predicted vector has the form \widehat{\mathbf y}=m\mathbf x+b\mathbf 1. At the best fit, the residual \mathbf r=\widehat{\mathbf y}-\mathbf y is perpendicular to the prediction directions:
\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf x=0, \qquad \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf 1=0.
For a plane fit, the same idea appears with three prediction directions: \mathbf x,\qquad \mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf 1. At the best-fit plane, the residual is perpendicular to all three.
This is why the equations are called normal equations. The remaining error is normal to the space of predictions.
What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: the data table,
the model,
the error function,
the normal equations,
the fitted coefficients,
the Hessian calculation,
a plot,
a paragraph explaining the perpendicular-residual interpretation.

subsection.p: The best-fit model is not magic. It is the nearest point in a space of possible predictions.

subsection.title: Project 3: entropy maximization as a Lagrange multiplier problem
subsection.p: Optimization is not only about boxes and tanks. It also appears in probability.

Suppose a system can fall into several states. A probability distribution is a list p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n with
p_i\ge0, \qquad p_1+\cdots+p_n=1.
The entropy of this distribution is \boxed{S(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\ln p_i.} Entropy measures spread. A distribution concentrated in one state has low entropy. A distribution spread evenly across many states has high entropy.
For this project, use the convention 0\ln0=0.

A seed example: no information except total probability. Suppose there are n possible states and no extra information. Maximize S=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\ln p_i subject to p_1+\cdots+p_n=1. Inside the region where all p_i\gt0, use a Lagrange multiplier: g(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=p_1+\cdots+p_n. The equation \nabla S=\lambda\nabla g gives -\ln p_i-1=\lambda for every i. Therefore all the p_i's are equal: p_1=p_2=\cdots=p_n. Since they add to 1, \boxed{p_i=\frac1n \qquad \text{for every }i.} The maximum-entropy distribution is uniform.

The Hessian of S in the positive region is diagonal:
H_S= \begin{pmatrix} -1/p_1\amp0\amp\cdots\amp0\\ 0\amp-1/p_2\amp\cdots\amp0\\ \vdots\amp\vdots\amp\ddots\amp\vdots\\ 0\amp0\amp\cdots\amp-1/p_n \end{pmatrix}.
For every nonzero vector h, h^TH_Sh=-\sum_i h_i^2/p_i\lt0. Along any line segment of positive probabilities starting at the uniform distribution, the first derivative is initially zero and the second derivative is negative. Entropy therefore decreases along that segment. Extending continuously to the boundary using 0\ln0=0 shows that no boundary distribution has larger entropy. This proves the claimed global maximum.
Your task. Choose one of the following entropy problems.

Option A. Four equally possible rooms. A robot is in one of four rooms, but you have no information about which room. Let p_1+p_2+p_3+p_4=1. Maximize S=-p_1\ln p_1-p_2\ln p_2-p_3\ln p_3-p_4\ln p_4. Show that \boxed{p_1=p_2=p_3=p_4=\frac14.}

Option B. A loaded three-state system. A system has three energy levels: E_1=0,\qquad E_2=1,\qquad E_3=2. The probabilities satisfy p_1+p_2+p_3=1. Suppose the average energy is fixed with 0\lt U\lt2: 0p_1+1p_2+2p_3=U. Maximize S=-p_1\ln p_1-p_2\ln p_2-p_3\ln p_3 subject to the two constraints.

Use two Lagrange multipliers: 
abla S=\lambda
abla(p_1+p_2+p_3)+\mu
abla(p_2+2p_3). Show that the solution has the form  oxed{p_i=C e^{- eta E_i}} for constants C and  eta.

This is the beginning of the Boltzmann distribution. Check that a positive solution exists for the prescribed U, and use the same strict-concavity argument to compare it with the boundary. At U=0 or U=2, only a distribution concentrated at the corresponding extreme energy is possible; it is not represented by finite \beta with all probabilities positive.

Option C. Three states with average energy 1/2. Continue Option B with U=\frac12. Write q=e^{-\beta}. Then (p_1,p_2,p_3)=C(1,q,q^2). The constraints become C(1+q+q^2)=1, and C(q+2q^2)=\frac12. Eliminate C to show that 3q^2+q-1=0. Thus \boxed{q=\frac{-1+\sqrt{13}}{6}.} Then compute C=\frac{1}{1+q+q^2} and find the three probabilities.
Required steps. For your chosen option:

li.p: Write the entropy function.
Write every constraint.
Set up the Lagrange multiplier equations.
Solve the equations.
Use the Hessian or a concavity argument to explain why the critical point gives a maximum.
Interpret the result. Why does the distribution spread out as much as the constraints allow?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: the probability variables,
the entropy function,
the constraints,
the Lagrange multiplier equations,
the solution,
a short explanation of why this is a maximum,
a paragraph explaining what the answer means in ordinary language.

subsection.p: This project shows a different face of Lagrange multipliers. The constraint is not a curve or a surface in physical space. It is a rule inside probability space.

subsection.title: Project 4: numerical gradient descent
subsection.p: The equation \nabla f=\mathbf 0 finds candidates for minima, but many functions are too large or too complicated to solve exactly. A computer often searches by taking small downhill steps.
The simplest version is gradient descent: \boxed{\mathbf x_{n+1}=\mathbf x_n-\alpha\nabla f(\mathbf x_n).} The number \alpha\gt0 is the step size.
The gradient points uphill. The negative gradient points downhill.

A seed example: a tilted quadratic bowl. Let f(x,y)=\frac12(x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2. The minimum is visibly at (2,-1). The gradient is \nabla f(x,y)=(x-2,\ 4(y+1)). Start at \mathbf x_0=(6,4) and take step size \alpha=0.2. Then \nabla f(6,4)=(4,20), so
\mathbf x_1 \amp = (6,4)-0.2(4,20) \amp = (5.2,0).
Now \nabla f(5.2,0)=(3.2,4), so
\mathbf x_2 \amp = (5.2,0)-0.2(3.2,4) \amp = (4.56,-0.8).
The points are moving toward (2,-1).

figure.caption: Gradient descent takes repeated steps in the negative-gradient direction.

subsection.p: Why step size matters. Even in one variable, the step size can break the method.
Let f(x)=x^2. Then f'(x)=2x. Gradient descent gives x_{n+1}=x_n-\alpha(2x_n)=(1-2\alpha)x_n. If 0\lt\alpha\lt1, then |1-2\alpha|\lt1 as long as \alpha\ne1, and the iterates move toward 0.
If \alpha=1, then x_{n+1}=-x_n. The sequence bounces back and forth forever.
If \alpha\gt1, then |1-2\alpha|\gt1, and the iterates grow in size. The method runs away from the minimum.
The direction was right, but the step was too large.
Your task. Choose one function from Group A and one from Group B.
For each function:

Try a smaller step size and a larger step size. Compare what happens.
Did the function value decrease at every step?

Did a large step size cause bouncing or divergence?

subsection.p: Gradient descent is simple enough to write in one line, but it is not magic. It listens only to local slope. If the landscape has a saddle, a flat valley, many wells, or a step size that is too large, the path can surprise us.

conclusion.p: Optimization chooses best points. Integration asks a different kind of question: not where a quantity is largest or smallest, but how much of it is spread across a region. The next group of projects returns to the adding machines of Chapters –: double integrals, triple integrals, and change of variables.

introduction.p: Optimization chose best points. Integration asks a different question:
introduction.md: \text{How much is spread over the whole region?}
introduction.p: That region may be a plate, a room, a pond, a solid object, or a distorted image. The same idea keeps returning. Cut the region into small pieces. Estimate the contribution from each piece. Add.
These projects turn that sentence into measurements.

subsection.p: A formula is not always available. Sometimes the density is known only from measurements.

subsection.title: Project 2: moments of inertia of real objects
subsection.p: Mass tells how much material an object has. Moment of inertia tells how that mass is spread around an axis.

A heavy object is harder to spin if more of its mass is far from the axis. That is why a figure skater spins faster when pulling in her arms. The mass has not changed, but the mass has moved closer to the rotation axis.

conclusion.p: The integration projects mostly add scalar quantities: density, brightness, mass, volume, and moment. Vector calculus adds direction. A force pushes along a path. A fluid crosses a surface. A boundary can reveal an area, and a flux balance can reveal a source. The next projects return to the book's boundary theme.

introduction.p: The previous projects added quantities over regions. Vector calculus asks what happens along boundaries and through surfaces. Work follows curves. Flux crosses surfaces. Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem say that boundary measurements can reveal interior information.
The projects below are meant to make that principle measurable.

subsection.title: Project 1: work around closed curves
subsection.p: A closed curve returns to where it started. A conservative field does no net work around such a curve. A rotating field may do positive or negative work, depending on the direction of travel.
The line integral detects the difference.

A seed example: a field that measures area. Let
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left(-\frac y2,\frac x2\right),
and let
\omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy
be its work 1-form.

Walk counterclockwise around the rectangle
R=[0,4]\times[0,3].
We compute the work around the four sides.

Bottom side. Here y=0 and dy=0. So
\omega=0.
The bottom contributes 0.

Right side. Here x=4, dx=0, and y goes from 0 to 3. Thus
\int_{\text{right}}\omega \amp = \int_0^3 \frac{4}{2}\,dy \amp = 6.

Top side. Here y=3, dy=0, and x goes from 4 back to 0. Thus
\int_{\text{top}}\omega \amp = \int_4^0 -\frac32\,dx \amp = 6.

Left side. Here x=0, dx=0, and y goes downward. Thus
\omega=0.
The left side contributes 0.

So
\boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\omega=12. }
The rectangle has area
4\cdot3=12.
This is not a coincidence. Compute the exterior derivative:
d\omega \amp = d\left(-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy\right) \amp = \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac x2 - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\frac y2\right) \right)dx\wedge dy \amp = \left(\frac12+\frac12\right)dx\wedge dy \amp = dx\wedge dy.

figure.caption: A rotational field can do positive work around a closed curve.

subsection.p: A closed curve can hide a surprise. Even if every local test looks harmless, a missing point inside the loop can change the answer.

subsection.title: Project 2: flux through complicated surfaces
subsection.p: Flux measures how much a vector field crosses a surface. A flat disk is friendly. A curved dome is less friendly. A surface made of several pieces can look intimidating.
The divergence theorem offers a shortcut, but only after the surface is closed.

A seed example: flux through a paraboloid dome. Let S be the dome
z=4-x^2-y^2, \qquad x^2+y^2\le4,
oriented upward. Together with the disk
D:\quad z=0,\qquad x^2+y^2\le4,
the dome bounds a solid E.

Let
\mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z).
We want the flux through the dome S.

The closed surface is
\partial E=S\cup D,
with outward orientation. On the dome, outward means upward and outward. On the bottom disk, outward means downward.

The divergence is
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F = 1+1+1 = 3.
By the divergence theorem,
\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E 3\,dV = 3\operatorname{Volume}(E).

Find the volume of E:
\operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2(4-r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp = 2\pi\left[ 2r^2-\frac14r^4 \right]_0^2 \amp = 2\pi(8-4) \amp = 8\pi.
So the total outward flux through the closed surface is
3(8\pi)=24\pi.

Now check the bottom disk. On D,
z=0, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,-1).
Thus
\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} = (x,y,0)\cdot(0,0,-1) = 0.
So the bottom disk contributes 0. Therefore the flux through the dome is
\boxed{ \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=24\pi. }

In forms language, the flux form is
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = x\,dy\wedge dz + y\,dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy,
and
d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.
The same computation says
\int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf F} = \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf F}.

subsection.p: A surface integral can be hard because the surface is curved. The divergence theorem moves the difficulty into the solid it bounds. Sometimes the inside is easier than the skin.

subsection.title: Project 3: Green's theorem and area from GPS boundary data
subsection.p: A region's area can be found without filling the region with a grid. It can be found by walking around the boundary.
Green's theorem explains why.

Let
\eta=\frac12(x\,dy-y\,dx).
Then
d\eta \amp = \frac12(dx\wedge dy-dy\wedge dx) \amp = dx\wedge dy.
So, for a positively oriented boundary,
\boxed{ \operatorname{Area}(R) = \oint_{\partial R}\frac12(x\,dy-y\,dx). }
This formula is the continuous version of the shoelace formula for polygons.

On a line segment from
(x_i,y_i)
to
(x_{i+1},y_{i+1}),
the integral of \eta is
\boxed{ \frac12(x_i y_{i+1}-y_i x_{i+1}). }
Therefore
\operatorname{Area} \amp = \frac12\sum_{i=0}^{3} (x_i y_{i+1}-y_i x_{i+1}) \amp = \frac12\Bigl[ (0\cdot1-0\cdot5) + (5\cdot4-1\cdot4) \amp \qquad + (4\cdot3-4\cdot1) + (1\cdot0-3\cdot0) \Bigr] \amp = \frac12(0+16+8+0) \amp = 12.
So the field has area
\boxed{ 12\text{ m}^2. }

If the points were listed clockwise, the same calculation would give
-12.
The negative sign would not mean negative physical area. It would mean the boundary orientation was reversed.

figure.caption: Green's theorem turns a boundary walk into an area calculation.

subsection.p: This project is a good example of the book's main theme. The area lies inside the region, but the calculation only walks around the edge.

subsection.title: Project 4: divergence theorem and numerical flux balance
subsection.p:
The divergence theorem says that outward flux through a closed surface equals total divergence inside:
\boxed{ \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E \nabla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV. }
In , this became a conservation law. If \mathbf J is a flux density, then outward flux is loss from the region unless sources replace it.
This project checks that balance numerically.

A seed example: flux through a unit cube. Let
E=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1],
and let
\mathbf J(x,y,z)=(x^2,y,z).
First compute the divergence:
\nabla\cdot\mathbf J = 2x+1+1 = 2x+2.
The volume integral is
\iiint_E(2x+2)\,dV \amp = \int_0^1\int_0^1\int_0^1(2x+2)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp = \int_0^1(2x+2)\,dx \amp = \left[x^2+2x\right]_0^1 \amp = 3.

Numerical flux balance. In a numerical calculation, the two sides may not match exactly. We can measure the error by the residual
\boxed{ \mathcal R = \left( \text{estimated outward boundary flux} \right) - \left( \text{estimated interior divergence} \right). }
For an exact calculation,
\mathcal R=0.
For a numerical calculation, a small residual means the discretization is respecting the balance law well. A large residual means that the grid, the data, or the orientation may be wrong.
Your task. Choose one version.
Option A. Exact cube check. Use a rectangular box and a polynomial field. Compute both sides exactly.
Option B. Numerical cube check. Use midpoint or trapezoid sums on the six faces and inside the box. Estimate both sides and compute the residual.

Option C. Incompressible flow. Choose a divergence-free field, such as
\mathbf J=(-y,x,0)
or
\mathbf J=(yz,xz,xy)
after checking its divergence. Estimate the outward flux through a closed surface and explain why it should be close to 0.

Option D. Flux balance with sources. Use a source function s(x,y,z). Compare the conservation law
\frac{d}{dt}\iiint_E\rho\,dV + \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E s\,dV.
Use simple functions so the terms can be computed by hand or by a small program.

conclusion.p:
Vector calculus has two dialects. One uses gradients, curls, divergences, dot products, and normal vectors. The other uses 1-forms, 2-forms, 3-forms, and the single operator d. The next group of projects asks you to translate between those dialects and to check, by examples, that the theorem underneath them is the same:
\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.

introduction.p: The vector calculus projects ended with two dialects. In one dialect, we used vector fields, dot products, curls, divergences, and normal vectors. In the other, we used forms: 1\text{-forms},\qquad 2\text{-forms},\qquad 3\text{-forms}, together with the exterior derivative d.

These projects ask you to practice that translation. A successful project should make the reader feel that Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem are not three unrelated miracles. They are one boundary principle seen in different dimensions.

subsection.title: Project 1: translate a classical vector calculus problem into forms
subsection.p: A classical vector calculus problem often begins with a vector field: \mathbf F=(P,Q) \qquad\text{or}\qquad \mathbf F=(P,Q,R). A forms solution begins by asking what kind of integral we are doing.
For flux through a surface, we use a 2-form: \boxed{\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.}
The same vector field may produce different forms, depending on what we are measuring.

A seed example: circulation around the unit circle. Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x). Classically, the work around a closed curve C is \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r. The corresponding 1-form is \boxed{\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy.}

Now use Green's theorem in forms language. Compute
d\omega \amp = d(-y\,dx+x\,dy) \amp = 2\,dx\wedge dy.
If D is the unit disk, then
\int_D d\omega \amp = \int_D 2\,dx\wedge dy \amp = 2\operatorname{Area}(D) \amp = 2\pi.
So \boxed{\int_{\partial D}\omega=\int_D d\omega.}

The classical statement is \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_D \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right) dA. The forms statement is \int_{\partial D}\omega=\int_D d\omega. They are the same calculation. The form notation simply keeps the integrand and the orientation together.

figure.caption: The boundary integral measures circulation. The exterior derivative measures circulation per unit area.

subsection.p:
Your task. Choose one classical vector calculus problem and translate it completely into forms. Use one of the following, or choose your own.
\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Classical problem} \amp \text{Classical theorem} \amp \text{Forms version} \\ \hline \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \text{Green's theorem} \amp \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega \\[1mm] \oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \text{Stokes' theorem} \amp \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega \\[1mm] \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp \text{Divergence theorem} \amp \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi \\[1mm] \int_C \nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \text{Fundamental theorem for line integrals} \amp \int_C df=\int_{\partial C}f \end{array}

li.p: State the classical problem.
Identify the correct form: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz or \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy.
Compute the exterior derivative: d\omega \qquad\text{or}\qquad d\Phi.
Compute the integral directly, if possible.
Compute the integral using \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega.
Write a translation table showing each classical object and its forms version.
Explain which notation made orientation easier to track.

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: the original classical problem,
the form version of the problem,
the calculation of d\omega or d\Phi,
both sides of the theorem,
a short translation table,
a paragraph explaining what the forms notation clarifies.

subsection.p: The best reports do not merely replace dots and crosses by wedges. They explain why the form is the natural integrand for the geometric object.

subsection.title: Project 2: closed but not exact forms on punctured domains
subsection.p: A 1-form \omega is called closed if d\omega=0. It is called exact if there is a function f such that \omega=df. Every exact form is closed, because d(df)=0. But the converse can fail when the domain has a hole.
This project is about that failure.
A seed example: the angular form. On the punctured plane \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, define \boxed{\omega= \frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}.} This form measures change in angle around the origin.

Let P=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. Then \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. Compute:
Q_x \amp = \frac{(x^2+y^2)-2x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} = \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2},
and
P_y \amp = \frac{-(x^2+y^2)+2y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} = \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.
Thus Q_x-P_y=0. So \boxed{d\omega=0.} The form is closed.

If \omega were exact on the punctured plane, say \omega=df, then every closed-curve integral would be zero: \oint_C df=f(\text{endpoint})-f(\text{starting point})=0. But we found \oint_C\omega=2\pi. So \omega is closed but not exact on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}.
The missing origin stores the obstruction.

figure.caption: A closed form can fail to be exact when the domain has a hole.

subsection.p: The second form is different from the angular form. In fact, \omega_2=d\left(\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right). So \omega_2 is exact on the punctured plane. Comparing \omega_1 and \omega_2 is a good way to see that closed and exact are not the same idea.

li.p: State the domain carefully. Do not include points where the formula is undefined.
Compute d\omega.
Decide whether the form is closed.
Integrate \omega around at least two closed curves: \text{one loop that surrounds the missing point} and \text{one loop that does not surround the missing point}.
Decide whether the form is exact on the whole domain.
If possible, find a potential function on a smaller domain, such as a plane with a ray removed.
Explain what the hole changes.
Why does d\omega=0 not automatically imply \omega=df?
What happens to the integral if a loop winds around the puncture twice?
Why does a loop that does not surround the puncture give a different kind of answer?
What is the role of the angle function \theta? Why can it be chosen locally but not globally around the puncture?
What does this example teach about the hypotheses in conservative-field theorems?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: the form and its domain,
the calculation of d\omega,
at least two closed-curve integrals,
a conclusion about closedness and exactness,
a drawing of the domain and the loops,
a paragraph explaining why the missing point matters.

subsection.p: The important lesson is not the formula itself. The important lesson is that local information can miss global topology. A form may have no local curl and still remember a hole.

subsection.title: Project 3: the generalized Stokes theorem on a cube
subsection.p: The generalized Stokes theorem says \boxed{\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.} For a solid cube, the form \omega must be a 2-form, because the boundary of a solid is a surface.
This project asks you to verify the theorem face by face.

A seed example: a flux form on the unit cube. Let B=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] with orientation dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Consider the 2-form \boxed{\Phi = x\,dy\wedge dz + y\,dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy.} This is the flux form of the vector field \mathbf F=(x,y,z).

Now compute the boundary integral. The boundary has six faces. Using the outward orientation, the induced face orientations are:
\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Face} \amp \text{Induced orientation} \\ \hline x=1 \amp dy\wedge dz\\ x=0 \amp -dy\wedge dz\\ y=1 \amp dz\wedge dx\\ y=0 \amp -dz\wedge dx\\ z=1 \amp dx\wedge dy\\ z=0 \amp -dx\wedge dy \end{array}
On the face x=1, \Phi=1\,dy\wedge dz+\text{terms involving }dx. Terms involving dx vanish on this face because x is constant there. Hence \int_{x=1}\Phi=1.
On the face x=0, the coefficient x is zero, so the contribution is 0. Similarly, \int_{y=1}\Phi=1, \qquad \int_{y=0}\Phi=0, and \int_{z=1}\Phi=1, \qquad \int_{z=0}\Phi=0.

li.p: State the region and its orientation.
State the form \omega.
Compute d\omega.
Compute the interior integral: \int_M d\omega.
List all boundary pieces.
State the induced orientation on each boundary piece.
Compute each boundary contribution.
Add the boundary contributions and compare with the interior integral.
Which boundary pieces contribute zero? Why?
Where does orientation enter the calculation?
What would change if the region were given the opposite orientation?
In the three-dimensional case, what vector field has the chosen 2-form as its flux form?
In the two-dimensional case, what vector field has the chosen 1-form as its work form?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: a drawing of the region,
the form and its exterior derivative,
the interior integral,
a table of boundary pieces and orientations,
the boundary integral,
a sentence explaining how this example fits \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega.

subsection.p: A cube is simple enough that no geometry is hidden. Every sign must be earned. That is why it is such a good testing ground for Stokes' theorem.

subsection.title: Project 4: orientation errors as sign errors
subsection.p: Many wrong answers in vector calculus are not calculus mistakes. They are orientation mistakes.
A curve is walked the wrong way. A normal vector points inward instead of outward. An inner boundary is treated like an outer boundary. A parametrization reverses the surface orientation.
Forms do not remove these errors, but they make them visible. A form integral changes sign when orientation reverses. If the sign is wrong, the geometry is usually wrong too.
The area is \pi(2^2)-\pi(1^2)=3\pi.

Now compute the boundary integral. On a counterclockwise circle of radius R, x=R\cos t,\qquad y=R\sin t. Then dx=-R\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=R\cos t\,dt, so
\eta \amp = \frac12 \left( R\cos t(R\cos t\,dt) - R\sin t(-R\sin t\,dt) \right) \amp = \frac12R^2\,dt.
Therefore \int_{\text{ccw circle radius }R}\eta = \pi R^2.

The outer boundary of the annulus is oriented counterclockwise, so it contributes 4\pi. The inner boundary is oriented clockwise, so it contributes -\pi. Thus \boxed{\int_{\partial A}\eta=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.}
If we accidentally orient the inner boundary counterclockwise, we get 4\pi+\pi=5\pi. That answer is not the area of the annulus. The sign error has added the hole instead of subtracting it.

figure.caption: An inner boundary is positively oriented clockwise, because the region must stay on the left.

li.p: State the region, curve, or surface.
State its correct orientation.
Compute the integral correctly.
Deliberately make one orientation error.
Compute the incorrect result.
Explain exactly where the sign changed.
State a practical rule for avoiding that error.

subsection.p: What to hand in. Your report should include:

li.p: a drawing showing the correct orientation,
the correct calculation,
the incorrect calculation,
a comparison of the two answers,
a short sign diagnosis explaining the mistake,
a final checklist for future problems.

conclusion.p: These forms projects are computational, but they also train a habit of attention: form integrals depend on oriented shapes. Scalar integrals with ds or dS do not change sign under orientation reversal. The last projects in the chapter ask for a different skill. After learning to compute, translate, and check signs, a mathematician has one more job: explain the story clearly enough that someone else can see why it matters.

introduction.p: A calculation can be correct and still leave the reader unmoved. A good mathematical essay does more. It chooses a question, follows it honestly, explains the necessary ideas, and ends with a sharper understanding than it began with.
These writing projects are not research papers in the graduate-school sense. They are mathematical explanations. The goal is to take one thread from the book and tell its story.
A good essay should contain:

subsection.title: Project 1: Hamilton, quaternions, and the birth of vector algebra
subsection.p: This writing project asks you to explain that split.

A seed calculation. A pure imaginary quaternion has the form A=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k. We identify it with the vector \mathbf a=(a_1,a_2,a_3). Similarly, B=b_1i+b_2j+b_3k corresponds to \mathbf b=(b_1,b_2,b_3). Using i^2=j^2=k^2=-1, and ij=k,\qquad jk=i,\qquad ki=j, with the reversed products changing sign, one finds \boxed{AB=-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf a\times\mathbf b.} More explicitly,
AB \amp = -(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3) \amp \qquad + (a_2b_3-a_3b_2)i \amp \qquad + (a_3b_1-a_1b_3)j \amp \qquad + (a_1b_2-a_2b_1)k.
The scalar part is -\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b. The vector part is \mathbf a\times\mathbf b.
So the dot product and cross product were not born as two unrelated formulas. They are two pieces of one multiplication.
Your task. Write an essay explaining how quaternions connect complex numbers, dot products, and cross products.
Your essay should answer:

li.p: Why does complex multiplication feel geometrically natural in the plane?
What changes when we try to multiply triples?
What are the rules for quaternion units i,j,k?
Why is quaternion multiplication noncommutative?
How do the dot product and cross product appear inside the product of two pure imaginary quaternions?
Why did vector algebra eventually separate the scalar part and vector part?
How does the wedge product give another way to think about oriented area?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Submit a 3- to 5-page essay with:

li.p: a title,
a clear thesis statement,
at least two worked examples,
one diagram,
a short comparison between quaternions and the vector operations used in this book,
a bibliography or source list if historical claims are included.

subsection.p: A strong essay will not only say that quaternions came before vector algebra. It will show, through a calculation, why dot and cross products are two shadows of a larger multiplication.

subsection.title: Project 2: why the cross product is both useful and suspicious
subsection.p: The cross product is one of the most useful tools in three-dimensional calculus: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v. It gives normal vectors, areas of parallelograms, torque, angular momentum, and the curl of a vector field.
But it is also suspicious.

Two vectors in the plane span an oriented parallelogram. Two vectors in space also span an oriented parallelogram. The cross product replaces that parallelogram by a perpendicular vector. This works beautifully in \mathbb R^3, because a plane has one perpendicular direction, up to sign.

The ordered pair of vectors spans an oriented parallelogram. A coordinate 2-form, such as dx\wedge dy, measures its signed projected area. These forms are alternating bilinear measurements on pairs of vectors, as defined in . The cross product encodes the three coordinate area measurements as a vector by using the Euclidean geometry and orientation of space.

A seed comparison. Let \mathbf u=(1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,2,0). The parallelogram has area 2. The cross product is \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(0,0,2). This vector has length 2 and points in the positive z-direction.

Evaluating the wedge of coordinate covectors gives (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=1\cdot2-0\cdot0=2. It says that this parallelogram has signed xy-area 2. The form dx\wedge dy is the measuring rule; the vectors are its inputs. The number 2 is its output.
Both descriptions contain the same area information in three dimensions. But they store it differently.
Your task. Write an essay explaining the double personality of the cross product.

li.p: What geometric quantity is \norm{\mathbf u\times\mathbf v} measuring?
Why does the direction of \mathbf u\times\mathbf v depend on orientation?
Why does swapping the vectors change the sign? \mathbf v\times\mathbf u=-(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v).
How do the coordinate area-measuring forms dx\wedge dy,\qquad dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx record the signed projected areas used by a normal vector?
Why is the cross product especially convenient for parametrized surfaces?
What does forms language clarify about flux?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Submit a 3- to 5-page essay with:

li.p: a clear thesis,
a diagram of an oriented parallelogram,
at least three worked examples,
one paragraph defending the cross product,
one paragraph criticizing or limiting the cross product,
a concluding paragraph explaining what the wedge product changes.

subsection.p: The best essays will not treat the cross product as wrong. It is not wrong. It is a brilliant shortcut. But every shortcut hides a path, and forms reveal the path.

subsection.title: Project 3: the many lives of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
subsection.p: Single-variable calculus has a central theorem: \boxed{\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a).} This theorem says that adding derivative information over an interval gives boundary information at the endpoints.
By the end of this book, the same sentence has grown into \boxed{\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega.}
This writing project asks you to tell that story.

p.md: \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Object }M \amp \text{Form }\omega \amp \text{Theorem} \\ \hline [a,b] \amp f \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial[a,b]}f=\int_{[a,b]}df\\[3mm] \text{plane region }R \amp P\,dx+Q\,dy \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_Rd\omega\\[3mm] \text{surface }S \amp P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_Sd\omega\\[3mm] \text{solid }E \amp P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_Ed\Phi \end{array}

subsection.p: In the first row, \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}, so \int_{\partial[a,b]}f=f(b)-f(a).
In the last row, d\Phi=(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, so the theorem becomes the divergence theorem.
The boundary changes dimension. The form changes degree. But the pattern does not change.

li.p: What does boundary mean for an interval, a region, a surface, and a solid?
Why do signs and orientations become unavoidable?
What changes when d acts on a 0-form, a 1-form, and a 2-form?
How do gradient, curl, and divergence fit into one operation?
Why is the statement \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega not just shorter, but more revealing?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Submit a 4- to 6-page essay with:

li.p: a central thesis,
a translation table,
at least three examples,
at least one diagram showing an object and its boundary,
a paragraph on orientation,
a conclusion explaining what the word fundamental means after this course.

subsection.p: A strong essay should make the reader feel that the Fundamental Theorem did not disappear after single-variable calculus. It kept changing clothes.

subsection.title: Project 4: how conservation laws unify physics and calculus
subsection.p: Chapter added time to Stokes' theorem. A conserved quantity can be stored inside a region, carried across the boundary, and created or destroyed by sources.

In forms language, the flux term becomes \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J}, where \Phi_{\mathbf J} = J_1\,dy\wedge dz + J_2\,dz\wedge dx + J_3\,dx\wedge dy. By Stokes' theorem, \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J} = \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf J}. Since d\Phi_{\mathbf J} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf J)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, the integral balance becomes, locally, \boxed{\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=s.} That equation is the skeleton of many physical theories.

A seed explanation: dye in water. Let \rho be dye density and let \mathbf J=\rho\mathbf v be dye flux density. If there are no sources, then s=0. The local conservation law becomes \boxed{\rho_t+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0.} This says: \text{Rate of change of stored dye} + \text{Net outward flow of dye} = 0.
If more dye flows out of a small region than flows in, the density inside must decrease. If more flows in than out, the density must increase.
The equation is not a mysterious new law. It is careful accounting.
Your task. Write an essay explaining how conservation laws connect calculus to physics.

Choose one theme:
 egin{array}{c|c} 	ext{Theme} \amp 	ext{Possible law} \ \hline 	ext{Fluid or dye flow} \amp ho_t+
abla\cdot(ho\mathbf v)=0\[1mm] 	ext{Heat flow} \amp u_t=\kappa\Delta u\[1mm] 	ext{Electric charge} \amp ho_t+
abla\cdot\mathbf J=0\[1mm] 	ext{Population movement} \amp ho_t+
abla\cdot(ho\mathbf v)=s\[1mm] 	ext{Chemical concentration} \amp ho_t+
abla\cdot\mathbf J=s \end{array}
Required structure. Your essay should include:

li.p: A physical story. What is moving, stored, created, or destroyed?
A density \rho. What does it measure?
A flux \mathbf J. What does it mean physically?
A source term s, or a clear statement that s=0.
The integral balance law over a fixed region E.
The local differential equation.
An explanation of how the divergence theorem or Stokes' theorem connects the two.

subsection.p:
A useful derivation to include. Assume the continuity and differentiability hypotheses in , so that differentiation under the integral and the passage from local integrals to pointwise equality are justified. Start with  rac{d}{dt}\iiint_E ho\,dV + \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E s\,dV.
