Use the divergence theorem: \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E
abla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV. Then \iiint_E ho_t\,dV + \iiint_E
abla\cdot\mathbf J\,dV = \iiint_E s\,dV. So \iiint_E \left( ho_t+
abla\cdot\mathbf J-s ight)dV=0. If this holds for every reasonable fixed region E, then the integrand must vanish:  oxed{ho_t+
abla\cdot\mathbf J=s.}

In forms notation, the same derivation is \frac{d}{dt}\int_E \rho\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf J} = \int_E s\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, then \int_E \left( \rho_t\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + d\Phi_{\mathbf J} - s\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz \right)=0.

li.p: What does outward flux mean in your physical setting?
Why does outward flux appear with a plus sign in the balance equation but causes stored amount to decrease when there are no sources?
What does a positive source term mean?
What does the local equation say in ordinary language?
Where does Stokes' theorem enter?
Why do very different systems share the same mathematical form?

subsection.p: What to hand in. Submit a 4- to 6-page essay with:

li.p: a physical introduction,
the integral balance law,
the local differential equation,
at least one worked example with simple functions,
a diagram of a region with flux arrows crossing its boundary,
a paragraph connecting the derivation to the generalized Stokes theorem.

p.em: A short rubric for the writing projects.

conclusion.p: This chapter began as a workshop, but it ends as a mirror for the whole book. Vectors gave us direction. Derivatives gave us local change. Integrals gave us accumulation. Forms gave us the right integrands for curves, surfaces, and solids. Stokes' theorem tied boundaries to interiors.

The story is not finished. It never is. But the next time a problem asks you to measure change, flow, circulation, flux, or balance, you have a question that reaches farther than any single formula: \boxed{\text{What is the object, what is its boundary, and what form belongs on it?}}

introduction.p: This appendix is a reference for the single-variable facts used throughout the book. It is meant to be scanned, not read like a chapter.

table.title: How single-variable ideas reappear in several variables.

row.cell: double, triple, line, and surface integrals

subsection.title: Limits
subsection.p: The value f(a) does not have to exist.

subsection.title: Common limit laws
subsection.p: If the limits exist, then \lim_{x\to a}(f+g)=\lim_{x\to a}f+\lim_{x\to a}g, \lim_{x\to a}(fg)=\left(\lim_{x\to a}f\right)\left(\lim_{x\to a}g\right), and, if \lim_{x\to a}g(x)\ne0, \lim_{x\to a}\frac{f}{g}=\frac{\lim_{x\to a}f}{\lim_{x\to a}g}.

subsection.title: Continuity
subsection.p: A function f is continuous at a if \boxed{\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).}
This requires three things: f(a)\text{ is defined}, \lim_{x\to a}f(x)\text{ exists}, and \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).

subsection.title: Common continuous functions
subsection.p: Polynomials are continuous everywhere.
Rational functions are continuous where their denominators are nonzero.
The functions \sin x,\qquad \cos x,\qquad e^x are continuous everywhere.
The function \ln x is continuous for x\gt0.
Compositions of continuous functions are continuous where they are defined.

statement.p: If f is continuous on [a,b], and N lies between f(a) and f(b), then there is some c\in[a,b] such that f(c)=N.
If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [a,b].

subsection.title: Warnings
subsection.p: A limit can exist even if f(a) is missing.
A function can be defined at a but still fail to be continuous there.
Continuity on an open interval does not guarantee an absolute maximum or minimum.
In several variables, checking only one path is not enough to prove a limit exists.

subsection.title: Derivative
subsection.p: \boxed{f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}} when the limit exists.
The derivative is:

table.title: Three meanings of the derivative.

subsection.title: Derivative rules
subsection.p: \boxed{\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))g'(x)} This is the chain rule.

subsection.title: Linear approximation
subsection.p: If f is differentiable at a, then near a, \boxed{f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a).}
The tangent line is \boxed{L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a).}

subsection.title: Differential notation
subsection.p: The coordinate covector dx acts on an increment by dx(h)=h. For a small input change h, the predicted output change is df_x(h)=f'(x)h.
Usually, \Delta f\ne df_x(h), but for small changes, \Delta f\approx df_x(h).

table.title: Concavity from the second derivative.

subsection.title: Critical points
subsection.p: A critical point occurs where f'(x)=0 or where f' does not exist.
For absolute extrema on [a,b], check: \text{critical points in }(a,b), \qquad a, \qquad b.

subsection.title: Warnings
subsection.p: Differentiability implies continuity: \boxed{f\text{ differentiable at }a \Longrightarrow f\text{ continuous at }a.}
The converse is false. For example, f(x)=|x| is continuous at 0, but not differentiable at 0.
The derivative may fail because of:

table.title: Ways differentiability can fail.

subsection.title: Definite integral
subsection.p: If f(x)\ge0, it is area under the graph.
If f is a rate, then \int_a^b f(x)\,dx is total change.

subsection.title: Basic properties
subsection.p: If f(x)\ge0 on [a,b], then \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\ge0.
If f(x)\le g(x) on [a,b], then \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\le \int_a^b g(x)\,dx.

subsection.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part I
subsection.p: If f is continuous and A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt, then \boxed{A'(x)=f(x).}
Accumulation differentiates back to the integrand.

subsection.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part II
subsection.p: If F'(x)=f(x), with f continuous on [a,b] and F continuous at the endpoints, then \boxed{\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).}
Equivalently, \boxed{\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).}
This is the net change theorem.

subsection.title: Boundary form
subsection.p: The oriented boundary of an interval is \boxed{\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}.}
So the Fundamental Theorem can be read as \boxed{\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]}F.}
This is the one-dimensional model for the generalized Stokes theorem ().

subsection.title: Average value
subsection.p: The average value of f on [a,b] is \boxed{f_{\operatorname{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.}

subsection.title: Warnings
subsection.p: Do not forget the constant C in an indefinite integral.
Do not put +C on a definite integral.
The definite integral \int_a^b f(x)\,dx depends on the orientation of the interval. Reversing the endpoints changes the sign.

subsection.title: Substitution
subsection.p: Substitution reverses the chain rule.

subsection.title: Warning
subsection.p: The substitution u=g(x) requires the matching factor g'(x)\,dx.
For example, \int 2x e^{x^2}\,dx is directly handled by u=x^2, but \int e^{x^2}\,dx is not.

subsection.title: Integration by parts
subsection.p: Integration by parts reverses the product rule.

subsection.title: Useful choices
subsection.p: For \int x e^x\,dx, take u=x,\qquad dv=e^x\,dx.
For \int x\cos x\,dx, take u=x,\qquad dv=\cos x\,dx.
For \int \ln x\,dx, take u=\ln x,\qquad dv=dx.

subsection.title: Warning
subsection.p: Integration by parts creates a boundary term: [uv]_a^b. Do not drop it.

subsection.title: Parametric curves
Velocity, speed, and acceleration
Arc length
subsection.p: For a curve \mathbf r(t), a\le t\le b, \boxed{L=\int_a^b |\mathbf r'(t)|\,dt.}

subsection.title: Slope of a parametric plane curve
subsection.p: If x'(t)\ne0, then \boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}.} If x'(t)=0\quad\text{and}\quad y'(t)\ne0, the tangent is vertical.

subsection.title: Common parametrizations
Polar coordinates
subsection.p: A polar curve r=f(\theta) can be parametrized by \boxed{\mathbf r(\theta)=\bigl(f(\theta)\cos\theta,\ f(\theta)\sin\theta\bigr).}

subsection.title: Polar area
subsection.p: If r=f(\theta) traces the region once for \alpha\le\theta\le\beta, then \boxed{A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta f(\theta)^2\,d\theta.}

subsection.title: Polar arc length
subsection.p: For r=f(\theta), \boxed{L=\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{r^2+\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta.}

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A parametrization remembers orientation and speed. The same geometric curve may give different work integrals if it is traced in the opposite direction or traced multiple times.

subsection.title: Sequences
subsection.p: A sequence is a list a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots.
It converges to L if \boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=L.}

subsection.title: Series
subsection.p: A series is an infinite sum: \boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n.}
Its partial sums are s_N=a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_N.
The series converges if \lim_{N\to\infty}s_N exists.

subsection.title: Geometric series
subsection.p: If |r|\ge1, the geometric series diverges unless a=0, in which case every term is zero.

subsection.title: Basic convergence facts
subsection.p: If \sum a_n converges, then \boxed{a_n\to0.}
The converse is false. The harmonic series \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n diverges, even though \frac1n\to0.

subsection.title: Power series
subsection.p: A power series centered at a has the form \boxed{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n(x-a)^n.}
A power series usually converges only on an interval.

subsection.title: Common Taylor series
Taylor polynomial
subsection.p: The degree n Taylor polynomial of f at a is \boxed{T_n(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2 + \cdots + \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n.}

subsection.title: Taylor's theorem with remainder
subsection.p: If f has n+1 derivatives near a, then \boxed{f(x)=T_n(x)+R_n(x).}

subsection.title: Warning
subsection.p: A Taylor polynomial is always a local approximation.
A Taylor series may fail to equal the original function, even when the function has derivatives of all orders.

subsection.title: Multivariable connection
subsection.p: The one-variable approximation f(a+h)\approx f(a)+f'(a)h becomes f(\mathbf p+\mathbf h) \approx f(\mathbf p)+Df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf h).

The one-variable quadratic approximation f(a+h)\approx f(a)+f'(a)h+\frac12 f''(a)h^2 becomes f(\mathbf p+\mathbf h) \approx f(\mathbf p) + Df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf h) + \frac12\mathbf h^T H_f(\mathbf p)\mathbf h.

subsection.title: The fundamental theorem as a boundary statement

appendix.title: Algebra, Trigonometry, and Complex Numbers Quick Reference

introduction.p: This appendix collects the algebra, trigonometry, and complex-number facts used in the book. It is meant to be scanned.

table.title: Where each algebraic and trigonometric tool appears in the book.

subsection.title: Quadratic formula
subsection.p: If ax^2+bx+c=0, \qquad a\ne0, then \boxed{x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}.}
The discriminant is \boxed{\Delta=b^2-4ac.}

table.title: Sign of the discriminant.

subsection.title: Completing the square
Circle form
subsection.p: Center: (h,k).
Radius: R.

subsection.title: Distance on the line
subsection.p: \boxed{|x-a|} is the distance from x to a.

p.md: \boxed{|x-a|\gt r \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\lt a-r \text{ or } x\gt a+r.}

subsection.title: Absolute value rules
subsection.p: \boxed{|a+b|\le |a|+|b|} This is the triangle inequality.

subsection.title: Inequality rules
subsection.p: Adding or subtracting the same number preserves the inequality: a\lt b \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+c\lt b+c.
Multiplying by a positive number preserves the inequality: a\lt b,\ c\gt0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad ac\lt bc.
Multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality: a\lt b,\ c\lt0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad ac\gt bc.

subsection.title: Quadratic inequalities
subsection.p: To solve ax^2+bx+c\gt0 or ax^2+bx+c\lt0, use this process:

li.p: Find the zeros.
Put the zeros on the number line.
Test one point in each interval.
Include endpoints only for \le or \ge.

subsection.title: Logarithm rules
subsection.p: For a\gt0, b\gt0, and r\in\mathbb R,

warning.p: Do not divide by a quantity unless it is known to be nonzero.
Do not take square roots of both sides of an inequality without tracking signs.
x^2\gt9 means x\lt-3 \quad\text{or}\quad x\gt3, not just x\gt3.
The identity \sqrt{x^2}=|x| is usually safer than writing \sqrt{x^2}=x.

subsection.title: Unit circle
subsection.p: On the unit circle, (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) is the point at angle \theta.

subsection.title: Radians
subsection.p: s=r\theta where s is arc length, r is radius, and \theta is measured in radians.

table.title: Cosine and sine at common angles.
Signs of cosine and sine in each quadrant.

subsection.title: Polar conversion
subsection.p: \tan\theta=\frac yx with quadrant care.

warning.p: Radians are the default in calculus.
\sin^2\theta means (\sin\theta)^2, not \sin(\theta^2).
The equation \tan\theta=\frac yx does not determine the quadrant by itself.

subsection.title: Complex numbers
subsection.p: Real part: \boxed{\operatorname{Re}(a+bi)=a.}
Imaginary part: \boxed{\operatorname{Im}(a+bi)=b.}
Plane point: \boxed{a+bi \longleftrightarrow (a,b).}

subsection.title: Multiplication
subsection.p: Multiplication by i: \boxed{i(a+bi)=-b+ai.}

subsection.title: Conjugate
subsection.p: Geometrically, conjugation reflects across the real axis: (a,b)\mapsto(a,-b).

subsection.title: Division
subsection.p: To divide by c+di, multiply top and bottom by c-di.

subsection.title: Polar form
subsection.p: The angle \theta satisfies \cos\theta=\frac ar, \qquad \sin\theta=\frac br.

subsection.title: Multiplication in polar form
subsection.p: If z=r(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha), and w=s(\cos\beta+i\sin\beta), then \boxed{zw = rs\bigl(\cos(\alpha+\beta)+i\sin(\alpha+\beta)\bigr).}
Complex multiplication: \boxed{\text{multiplies lengths and adds angles.}}

subsection.title: De Moivre's formula
subsection.p: For unit complex numbers: \boxed{(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^n = \cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta).}

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p: The number 0 has no polar angle.
Angles in polar form are not unique: \theta \quad\text{and}\quad \theta+2\pi k describe the same direction.
Complex multiplication is not componentwise multiplication: (a,b)(c,d)\ne(ac,bd).

subsection.title: Euler form
Polar form with Euler notation
Rotation
Euler formula and trig identities
subsection.p: The identity e^{i(\alpha+\beta)}=e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta} contains the angle addition formulas: \cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta, \sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta.

warning.title: Common warning
warning.p: The symbol e^{i\theta} does not mean growth away from the origin. It lies on the unit circle. It represents rotation.

subsection.title: nth roots of a complex number
subsection.p: Let w=Re^{i\Theta}, \qquad R>0. The solutions of z^n=w are \boxed{ z_k = R^{1/n}e^{i(\Theta+2\pi k)/n}, \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,n-1. }
There are n distinct roots.
They lie on the circle of radius R^{1/n}.
Their angles are spaced by \boxed{ \frac{2\pi}{n}. }

subsection.title: Roots of unity
subsection.p: The solutions of z^n=1 are \boxed{ z_k=e^{2\pi i k/n}, \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,n-1. }
These are the nth roots of unity.
They form a regular n-gon on the unit circle.

subsection.title: Primitive root
Sum of roots of unity
subsection.p: For n>1, \boxed{ 1+\omega+\omega^2+\cdots+\omega^{n-1}=0. } Reason: 1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^{n-1} = \frac{1-\omega^n}{1-\omega} = 0, because \omega^n=1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \omega\ne1.

subsection.title: Square roots
subsection.p: To solve z^2=Re^{i\Theta}, use \boxed{ z_0=\sqrt R e^{i\Theta/2}, \qquad z_1=\sqrt R e^{i(\Theta+2\pi)/2}. }
The two roots are opposites.

subsection.title: Examples
subsection.p: Fourth roots of unity: \boxed{ 1,\quad i,\quad -1,\quad -i. }
Cube roots of unity: \boxed{ 1,\quad -\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i,\quad -\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i. }
Solutions of z^3=8: write 8=8e^{i0}. Then z_k=2e^{2\pi i k/3}, \qquad k=0,1,2. So \boxed{ z=2,\quad -1+\sqrt3\,i,\quad -1-\sqrt3\,i. }
Solutions of z^3=-8: write -8=8e^{i\pi}. Then z_k=2e^{i(\pi+2\pi k)/3}, \qquad k=0,1,2. So \boxed{ z=1+\sqrt3\,i,\quad -2,\quad 1-\sqrt3\,i. }

subsection.title: Geometric meaning
subsection.p: The extra 2\pi k is why there are n roots.

introduction.p: Matrices are the bookkeeping language for linear maps. In this book they appear as linear transformations, Jacobian matrices, Hessian matrices, coordinate changes, and quadratic forms.
This appendix is a reference. It is meant to be scanned.

table.title: Where each matrix idea appears in the book.

row.cell: Where it appears in the book

subsection.title: Matrix notation
Addition
subsection.p: Matrices can be added only when they have the same size.

subsection.title: Matrix-vector multiplication
Matrix multiplication
Identity matrix
Zero matrix
Transpose
subsection.p: The transpose of A is A^T. Rows become columns.

subsection.title: Symmetric matrix
subsection.p: Symmetric matrices are especially important for Hessians and quadratic forms.

warning.p: The product AB may exist even when BA does not.
If both AB and BA exist, they may have different sizes.
Always check dimensions before multiplying.

subsection.title: Linear systems
subsection.p: A system of linear equations can be written as \boxed{A\mathbf x=\mathbf b.}
The augmented matrix is \boxed{[A\mid \mathbf b].}

subsection.title: Elementary row operations
subsection.p: The allowed row operations are:

li.p: Swap two rows.
Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar.
Add a multiple of one row to another row.

subsection.p: These operations do not change the solution set of the system.

subsection.title: Row echelon form
subsection.p: A matrix is in row echelon form if:

li.p: All zero rows are at the bottom.
Each leading entry is to the right of the leading entry above it.
All entries below a leading entry are zero.

subsection.title: Reduced row echelon form
subsection.p: A matrix is in reduced row echelon form if it is in row echelon form and:

li.p: Each leading entry is 1.
Each leading 1 is the only nonzero entry in its column.

subsection.title: Pivot
subsection.p: A pivot is a leading nonzero entry in a row.
A pivot column is a column containing a pivot.
Variables corresponding to pivot columns are pivot variables.
Variables corresponding to non-pivot columns are free variables.

subsection.title: Rank
subsection.p: The rank of a matrix is the number of pivots: \boxed{\operatorname{rank}(A)=\text{number of pivot columns in }A.}

subsection.title: Consistency test
subsection.p: For the system A\mathbf x=\mathbf b, row reduce [A\mid \mathbf b].
If a row has the form \boxed{0\quad 0\quad \cdots\quad 0\mid c} with c\ne0, then the system has no solution.
Otherwise, the system is consistent.

subsection.title: Number of solutions
subsection.p: For a consistent system:

subsection.title: Homogeneous systems
subsection.p: A homogeneous system has the form \boxed{A\mathbf x=\mathbf 0.}
It is always consistent because \mathbf x=\mathbf 0 is always a solution.
This is called the trivial solution.
A homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution exactly when there is at least one free variable.

subsection.title: Null space
subsection.p: The null space of A is \boxed{\operatorname{Null}(A)=\{\mathbf x:A\mathbf x=\mathbf 0\}.}
It is the set of vectors that A sends to zero.

subsection.title: Column space
subsection.p: The column space of A is \boxed{\operatorname{Col}(A)=\text{span of the columns of }A.}
The equation A\mathbf x=\mathbf b has a solution exactly when \boxed{\mathbf b\in\operatorname{Col}(A).}

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p: Row operations preserve the solution set of a linear system, but they do not usually preserve determinants.
Do not row reduce A alone if the system is A\mathbf x=\mathbf b. Row reduce the augmented matrix [A\mid \mathbf b].
Free variables are not errors. They describe infinitely many solutions.

introduction.p: The arbitrary-size determinant is defined by the permutation formula in . The formulas below specialize it to dimensions two and three and collect its consequences.

subsection.title: Only square matrices have determinants
2\times2 determinant
subsection.p: Geometric meaning:
The sign records orientation.

subsection.title: 3\times3 determinant
subsection.p: Geometric meaning:
The sign records orientation.

subsection.title: Determinant and orientation
Singular matrices
subsection.p: Equivalently, the linear map collapses some nonzero direction to zero.

subsection.title: Determinant properties
Effect of row operations
subsection.p: Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant.
Multiplying one row by c multiplies the determinant by c.
Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant.

subsection.title: Determinant and linear independence
Determinant and change of variables

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p:
The determinant is not linear in the whole matrix:
\det(A+B)\ne\det(A)+\det(B)
in general.
A determinant can be negative. Ordinary area and volume use |\det A|.
If row reduction uses row swaps or row scaling, track how the determinant changes.

subsection.title: Definition
subsection.p: The matrix A^{-1} is the inverse of A.

subsection.title: Meaning
subsection.p: The inverse matrix undoes the linear map A.

subsection.title: 2\times2 inverse formula
Invertibility test
subsection.p: For an n\times n matrix A, the following statements are equivalent:

p.md: \begin{array}{ll} 1. & A\text{ is invertible.}\\[1mm] 2. & \det A\ne0.\\[1mm] 3. & A\mathbf x=\mathbf 0\text{ has only the trivial solution.}\\[1mm] 4. & A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\text{ has a unique solution for every }\mathbf b.\\[1mm] 5. & \text{The columns of }A\text{ are linearly independent.}\\[1mm] 6. & \text{The columns of }A\text{ span }\mathbb R^n.\\[1mm] 7. & \operatorname{rref}(A)=I. \end{array}

subsection.title: Finding an inverse by row reduction
subsection.p:
If
[A\mid I] \longrightarrow [I\mid B],
then
\boxed{ B=A^{-1}. }
If the left side cannot be reduced to I, then A is not invertible.

subsection.title: Solving systems with inverses
Inverse rules

warning.p:
The inverse of a product reverses the order:
(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}.
Not every square matrix has an inverse.
Non-square matrices do not have two-sided inverses.
In practice, row reduction is usually better than explicitly computing A^{-1} to solve a system.

subsection.title: Definition
subsection.p: Let A be an n\times n matrix.
The scalar \lambda is the eigenvalue.

subsection.title: Meaning
subsection.p: An eigenvector is a direction that A does not turn.
The matrix A only stretches, shrinks, or reverses that direction.

subsection.title: Finding eigenvalues
subsection.p:
Start with
A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v.
Rewrite:
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf 0.
For a nonzero solution \mathbf v, the matrix A-\lambda I must be singular:
\boxed{ \det(A-\lambda I)=0. }
This equation is the characteristic equation.

subsection.title: Characteristic polynomial
2\times2 shortcut
Finding eigenvectors
subsection.p: The solution space is the eigenspace for \lambda.

subsection.title: Diagonal matrices
subsection.p:
If
D= \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1\amp0\amp\cdots\amp0\\ 0\amp\lambda_2\amp\cdots\amp0\\ \vdots\amp\vdots\amp\ddots\amp\vdots\\ 0\amp0\amp\cdots\amp\lambda_n \end{pmatrix},
then the standard basis vectors are eigenvectors:
\boxed{ D\mathbf e_i=\lambda_i\mathbf e_i. }

subsection.title: Diagonalization
subsection.p:
If A has n linearly independent eigenvectors
\mathbf v_1,\ldots,\mathbf v_n,
then put them into a matrix
\boxed{ P= \begin{pmatrix} |\amp|\amp\amp|\\ \mathbf v_1\amp\mathbf v_2\amp\cdots\amp\mathbf v_n\\ |\amp|\amp\amp| \end{pmatrix}. }

subsection.title: Powers
Symmetric matrices
subsection.p: Symmetric matrices are the clean case. Hessian matrices are symmetric when mixed partials agree.

warning.p: Eigenvectors must be nonzero.
Eigenvalues can be repeated.
A matrix may fail to have enough eigenvectors to diagonalize.
Eigenvalues are defined only for square matrices.
For real matrices, complex eigenvalues may occur unless the matrix is symmetric.

subsection.title: Definition
subsection.p: A quadratic form is a function built from degree-two terms.
In matrix form: \boxed{q(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^T A\mathbf x.}
Usually A is taken to be symmetric.

subsection.title: Two-variable form
subsection.p:
For
\mathbf x= \begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix},
and
A= \begin{pmatrix} a&b\\ b&c \end{pmatrix},
we get
\boxed{ \mathbf x^T A\mathbf x = ax^2+2bxy+cy^2. }

subsection.title: Symmetric part
subsection.p: So only the symmetric part of A matters for a quadratic form.

subsection.title: Positive definite
Negative definite
Indefinite
subsection.p: A quadratic form is indefinite if it takes both positive and negative values.

subsection.title: Semidefinite
subsection.p: Semidefinite forms can be zero on nonzero vectors.

subsection.title: 2\times2 test

table.title: Classification of a 2\times2 quadratic form by determinant.

subsection.title: Eigenvalue test
subsection.p: For a symmetric matrix A:

table.title: Classification of a quadratic form by the eigenvalues of A.

row.cell: all nonnegative, at least one zero
all nonpositive, at least one zero

subsection.title: Diagonalization of a quadratic form
subsection.p:
Let \mathbf y=Q^T\mathbf x. Then
\boxed{ \mathbf x^T A\mathbf x = \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y = \lambda_1 y_1^2+\cdots+\lambda_n y_n^2. }
The eigenvalues are the coefficients along the orthogonal principal directions. The second derivative of q in the corresponding unit direction is 2\lambda_i.

subsection.title: Connection to Hessians
subsection.p: When mixed partials agree, f_{xy}=f_{yx}, so H_f is symmetric.

Near a critical point \mathbf p, the quadratic approximation is
\boxed{ f(\mathbf p+\mathbf h) \approx f(\mathbf p) + \frac12\mathbf h^T H_f(\mathbf p)\mathbf h. }

subsection.title: Second derivative test in two variables
subsection.p: Suppose f is C^2 near (a,b) and \nabla f(a,b)=\mathbf 0.
Then:

table.title: Second derivative test for a critical point in two variables.

warning.p: A zero determinant in the Hessian test does not mean there is no maximum or minimum. It means the quadratic test does not decide.

The matrix for ax^2+bxy+cy^2 is
\begin{pmatrix} a & b/2\\ b/2 & c \end{pmatrix},
not
\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ b & c \end{pmatrix}.
The form \mathbf x^T A\mathbf x uses a symmetric matrix when reading geometry.

section.title: One-page formula summary
section.p: Determinant and inverse formulas concern square matrices. The final Hessian test assumes f is C^2 near the critical point being tested.

md.mrow: \boxed{ax^2+2bxy+cy^2 = \begin{pmatrix}x\amp y\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a\amp b\\ b\amp c \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}}
\boxed{A\text{ positive definite} \Longleftrightarrow \mathbf x^T A\mathbf x\gt 0 \text{ for every }\mathbf x\ne\mathbf 0}
\boxed{ \begin{array}{c|c} D\gt 0,\ f_{xx}\gt 0 \amp \text{local minimum}\\ D\gt 0,\ f_{xx}\lt 0 \amp \text{local maximum}\\ D\lt 0 \amp \text{saddle}\\ D=0 \amp \text{inconclusive} \end{array} }

introduction.p: Coordinate systems are different languages for the same geometry. Cartesian coordinates are best for boxes and planes. Polar and cylindrical coordinates are best for circular symmetry. Spherical coordinates are best for balls, shells, cones, and radial fields.

This appendix is a reference. It is meant to be scanned. Differential formulas assume continuous derivatives of the indicated order. Integration formulas use regular coordinate patches covering each interior point once, apart from boundary seams. Wedge identities that use two coordinate systems abbreviate pullbacks by the displayed maps. Scalar elements ds,dA,dV remain unsigned.

table.title: Which coordinate system to reach for.

subsection.title: Conversion formulas
subsection.p: Polar coordinates describe a point in the plane by radius and angle: \boxed{(r,\theta).}
Conversion to Cartesian: \boxed{x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.}
Conversion to polar: \boxed{r^2=x^2+y^2.}
\boxed{\tan\theta=\frac yx} with quadrant care.

subsection.title: Usual ranges
subsection.p: Usually, \boxed{r\ge0, \qquad 0\le\theta\lt2\pi.}
If signed radii are allowed, then \boxed{(-r,\theta)=(r,\theta+\pi).}

subsection.title: Unit vectors
subsection.p: The vector \widehat{\mathbf e}_r points outward.
The vector \widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta points in the direction of increasing \theta.

subsection.title: Unit-vector derivatives
subsection.p: The polar unit vectors depend on position.

subsection.title: Line element
subsection.p: So \boxed{ds=\sqrt{dr^2+r^2\,d\theta^2}.}
For a circle r=a: \boxed{ds=a\,|d\theta|.}

For a radial line \theta=\theta_0: \boxed{ds=|dr|.} Along an increasing-angle or increasing-radius parametrization, the absolute values may be omitted. In general, ds remains nonnegative when direction reverses.

subsection.title: Area element
subsection.p: Ordinary area: \boxed{dA=r\,dr\,d\theta.}
Oriented area: \boxed{dx\wedge dy = r\,dr\wedge d\theta.}

subsection.title: Common polar curves
subsection.p: Circle centered at origin: \boxed{r=a.}
Ray from the origin (for nonnegative r): \boxed{\theta=\theta_0.}
Vertical line: \boxed{x=a \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\cos\theta=a.}
Horizontal line: \boxed{y=b \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\sin\theta=b.}
Circle through the origin with center on the x-axis: \boxed{r=2a\cos\theta.}
Circle through the origin with center on the y-axis: \boxed{r=2b\sin\theta.}

subsection.title: Polar integration
subsection.p: Area of a region: \boxed{\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_{\widetilde R} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.}
Area enclosed by r=f(\theta), traced once: \boxed{A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta f(\theta)^2\,d\theta.}

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p: The formula \tan\theta=\frac yx does not determine the quadrant by itself.
The point at the origin has no unique angle.
The factor r in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta must not be dropped.
Formulas containing 1/r are singular at r=0.

subsection.title: Conversion formulas
subsection.p: Conversion to Cartesian: \boxed{x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta, \qquad z=z.}
Conversion from Cartesian: \boxed{r^2=x^2+y^2, \qquad \tan\theta=\frac yx, \qquad z=z.}

subsection.title: Volume element
subsection.p: Ordinary volume: \boxed{dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz.}
Oriented volume: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = r\,dr\wedge d\theta\wedge dz.}

subsection.title: Coordinate surfaces
subsection.p: Cylinder: \boxed{r=a.}
Vertical half-plane: \boxed{\theta=\theta_0.}
Horizontal plane: \boxed{z=c.}

subsection.title: Useful equations
subsection.p: Cylinder of radius a: \boxed{x^2+y^2=a^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r=a.}
Paraboloid: \boxed{z=x^2+y^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=r^2.}
Cone: \boxed{z^2=x^2+y^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z^2=r^2.}

warning.p: Cylindrical r is distance from the z-axis, not distance from the origin in space.
The factor r in dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz must not be dropped.
At r=0, the angle \theta is not unique.

subsection.title: Convention used in this book
subsection.p: Spherical coordinates are \boxed{(\rho,\phi,\theta).}
Here:

table.title: Meaning of the spherical coordinates.

row.cell: angle down from the positive z-axis
angle around the z-axis in the xy-plane

subsection.title: Conversion formulas
Unit vectors
subsection.p: The vector \widehat{\mathbf e}_\rho points outward from the origin.
The vector \widehat{\mathbf e}_\phi points in the direction of increasing \phi.
The vector \widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta points in the direction of increasing \theta.

subsection.title: Volume element
subsection.p: Ordinary volume: \boxed{dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta.}
Oriented volume: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = \rho^2\sin\phi\, d\rho\wedge d\phi\wedge d\theta.}

subsection.title: Coordinate surfaces
subsection.p: Sphere: \boxed{\rho=a.}
Cone: \boxed{\phi=\phi_0.}
Vertical half-plane: \boxed{\theta=\theta_0.}

subsection.title: Useful equations
subsection.p: Sphere of radius a: \boxed{x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \rho=a.}
Upper cone: \boxed{z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \phi=\frac{\pi}{4}.}
Plane z=c: \boxed{\rho\cos\phi=c.}
Cylinder x^2+y^2=a^2: \boxed{\rho\sin\phi=a.}

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p: Different books sometimes swap the names \theta and \phi. In this book, \phi is measured down from the positive z-axis.
At \rho=0, the angles are not unique.
At \phi=0 and \phi=\pi, the angle \theta is not unique.
The factor \rho^2\sin\phi must not be dropped.

section.title: Grad, curl, and divergence in common coordinates

subsection.title: Cartesian coordinates
subsection.p: That is, \boxed{\nabla\times\mathbf F=(R_y-Q_z)\mathbf i+(P_z-R_x)\mathbf j+(Q_x-P_y)\mathbf k.}
The Laplacian is \boxed{\Delta f=\nabla\cdot\nabla f=f_{xx}+f_{yy}+f_{zz}.}

subsection.title: Plane Cartesian formulas
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(P,Q), the scalar curl in the plane is \boxed{\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf F=Q_x-P_y.}
The associated exterior derivative is \boxed{d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}

subsection.title: Polar coordinates
subsection.p: Write \mathbf F=F_r\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_r+F_\theta\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta.
Gradient: \boxed{\nabla f=f_r\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_r+\frac1r f_\theta\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta.}
Divergence: \boxed{\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rF_r)+\frac1r\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}.}
Scalar curl: \boxed{\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf F=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rF_\theta)-\frac1r\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}.}
Laplacian: \boxed{\Delta f=f_{rr}+\frac1r f_r+\frac1{r^2}f_{\theta\theta}.}

subsection.title: Cylindrical coordinates
subsection.p: Write \mathbf F=F_r\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_r+F_\theta\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta+F_z\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_z.
Gradient: \boxed{\nabla f=f_r\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_r+\frac1r f_\theta\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta+f_z\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_z.}
Divergence: \boxed{\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rF_r)+\frac1r\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}+\frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z}.}
Laplacian: \boxed{\Delta f=f_{rr}+\frac1r f_r+\frac1{r^2}f_{\theta\theta}+f_{zz}.}

subsection.title: Spherical coordinates
subsection.p: Write \mathbf F=F_\rho\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\rho+F_\phi\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\phi+F_\theta\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta.
Gradient: \boxed{\nabla f=f_\rho\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\rho+\frac1\rho f_\phi\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\phi+\frac1{\rho\sin\phi}f_\theta\,\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta.}

Divergence: \boxed{\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac1{\rho^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}(\rho^2F_\rho)+\frac1{\rho\sin\phi}\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}(\sin\phi\,F_\phi)+\frac1{\rho\sin\phi}\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta}.}

Curl:
\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \nabla\times\mathbf F \amp= \frac1{\rho\sin\phi} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}(\sin\phi\,F_\theta) - \frac{\partial F_\phi}{\partial\theta} \right) \widehat{\mathbf e}_\rho\\[1mm] \amp\quad+ \frac1\rho \left( \frac1{\sin\phi}\frac{\partial F_\rho}{\partial\theta} - \frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}(\rho F_\theta) \right) \widehat{\mathbf e}_\phi\\[1mm] \amp\quad+ \frac1\rho \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}(\rho F_\phi) - \frac{\partial F_\rho}{\partial\phi} \right) \widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta. \end{aligned} }
Laplacian: \boxed{\Delta f=f_{\rho\rho}+\frac2\rho f_\rho+\frac1{\rho^2}f_{\phi\phi}+\frac{\cot\phi}{\rho^2}f_\phi+\frac1{\rho^2\sin^2\phi}f_{\theta\theta}.}

Equivalently, \boxed{\Delta f=\frac1{\rho^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\left(\rho^2 f_\rho\right)+\frac1{\rho^2\sin\phi}\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}\left(\sin\phi\,f_\phi\right)+\frac1{\rho^2\sin^2\phi}f_{\theta\theta}.}

warning.p: In polar, cylindrical, and spherical formulas, F_r,\ F_\theta,\ F_\rho,\ F_\phi,\ F_z are components in the local unit-vector basis, not Cartesian components.
For example, \mathbf F=F_r\widehat{\mathbf e}_r+F_\theta\widehat{\mathbf e}_\theta does not mean \mathbf F=(F_r,F_\theta) in Cartesian coordinates.
Polar and cylindrical formulas with 1/r require r\gt 0.
Spherical formulas with 1/\rho require \rho\gt 0.
Spherical formulas with 1/\sin\phi require \sin\phi\ne0.
Coordinate singularities do not always mean the field itself is singular. They may mean the coordinate system has broken down.

subsection.title: Scale factors
subsection.p: For orthogonal coordinates (u_1,u_2,u_3), the scale factors are \boxed{h_i=\left|\frac{\partial\mathbf r}{\partial u_i}\right|.}
The line element is \boxed{ds^2=h_1^2\,du_1^2+h_2^2\,du_2^2+h_3^2\,du_3^2.}
The volume element is \boxed{dV=h_1h_2h_3\,du_1\,du_2\,du_3.}

table.title: Scale factors and volume or area elements in common coordinate systems.

subsection.title: Parametric surface
subsection.p: For a surface \mathbf r(u,v), the vector area element is \boxed{d\mathbf S=(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv.}
The scalar surface area element is \boxed{dS=|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v|\,du\,dv.}
Flux through the oriented surface is \boxed{\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=\iint_D \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv.}

subsection.title: Graph surface
subsection.p: For a graph z=f(x,y), use \mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,f(x,y)).
Then \boxed{\mathbf r_x\times\mathbf r_y=(-f_x,-f_y,1).}
Upward-oriented vector area: \boxed{d\mathbf S=(-f_x,-f_y,1)\,dx\,dy.}
Surface area element: \boxed{dS=\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}\,dx\,dy.}

subsection.title: Polar area
subsection.p: For a polar curve r=f(\theta), area traced once: \boxed{A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta f(\theta)^2\,d\theta.}

subsection.title: Cylindrical surface elements
subsection.p: For the cylinder r=a, with parameters (\theta,z), \boxed{dS=a\,d\theta\,dz.}
For the plane z=c, with polar parameters (r,\theta), \boxed{dS=r\,dr\,d\theta.}
For the half-plane \theta=\theta_0, with parameters (r,z), \boxed{dS=dr\,dz.}

subsection.title: Spherical surface elements
subsection.p: For the sphere \rho=a, with parameters (\phi,\theta), \boxed{dS=a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta.}
For the cone \phi=\phi_0, with parameters (\rho,\theta), \boxed{dS=\rho\sin\phi_0\,d\rho\,d\theta.}
For the half-plane \theta=\theta_0, with parameters (\rho,\phi), \boxed{dS=\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi.}

subsection.title: Boundary orientation reminders
subsection.p: In the plane, positive boundary orientation means: \boxed{\text{walk so the region stays on your left.}}
For an upward-oriented surface, use the right-hand rule to orient the boundary.
For a solid, the positive boundary orientation is outward.

subsection.title: Forms version of common elements
subsection.p: Polar: \boxed{dx\wedge dy=r\,dr\wedge d\theta.}
Cylindrical: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=r\,dr\wedge d\theta\wedge dz.}
Spherical: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\wedge d\phi\wedge d\theta.}

warning.p: Swapping the parameters u and v reverses orientation: \boxed{\mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u=-(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v).}
Ordinary area and volume use positive scale factors.
Differential forms keep orientation signs.

introduction.p: Differential forms are integrands with orientation built in. A 1-form is built for curves. A 2-form is built for surfaces. A 3-form is built for solids.

This appendix is a reference. It is meant to be scanned. Coefficients and maps are assumed smooth enough for the displayed derivatives: C^1 for one exterior derivative and C^2 for identities using two derivatives. Parametrizations used for integration cover the interior once with compatible orientation. Wedge identities using two coordinate systems abbreviate pullbacks by the coordinate map.

table.title: Forms by degree, what they integrate over, and their typical meaning.

subsection.title: 0-forms
subsection.p: A 0-form is a function: \boxed{ f. }
Examples: f(x), \qquad f(x,y), \qquad f(x,y,z).
A 0-form is integrated over signed points: \boxed{ \int_{+P}f=f(P), \qquad \int_{-P}f=-f(P). }
For an oriented interval, \boxed{ \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}. }
So \boxed{ \int_{\partial[a,b]}f=f(b)-f(a). }

subsection.title: 1-forms
subsection.p: A 1-form in the plane has the form \boxed{ \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy. }
A 1-form in space has the form \boxed{ \omega=P(x,y,z)\,dx+Q(x,y,z)\,dy+R(x,y,z)\,dz. }
It is integrated over oriented curves.
If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), then the work 1-form is \boxed{ \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz. }
Line integral: \boxed{ \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_C \omega_{\mathbf F}. }

subsection.title: 2-forms in the plane
subsection.p: A 2-form in the plane has the form \boxed{ \alpha=f(x,y)\,dx\wedge dy. }
It is integrated over oriented plane regions.
\boxed{ \iint_R f\,dx\wedge dy } means signed accumulation of f over R.

subsection.title: 2-forms in space
subsection.p: A general 2-form in space can be written as \boxed{ \Phi = A\,dy\wedge dz + B\,dz\wedge dx + C\,dx\wedge dy. }
This ordering matches flux.
If \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), the flux 2-form is \boxed{ \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy. }
Flux integral: \boxed{ \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iint_S \Phi_{\mathbf F}. }

subsection.title: 3-forms
subsection.p: A 3-form in space has the form \boxed{ \Omega=f(x,y,z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. }
It is integrated over oriented solids.

subsection.title: Degree
subsection.p: The degree of a form is the number of differentials wedged together.

table.title: Degree of a form.

statement.p: A 1-form is not a vector field, though a vector field can produce a 1-form.
A 2-form is not a vector field, though a vector field can produce a flux 2-form.
Forms remember orientation. Reversing orientation changes the sign of the integral.

subsection.title: Basic antisymmetry
subsection.p: Swapping two 1-form factors changes the sign.

subsection.title: Repeated factors vanish
subsection.p: Any wedge product with a repeated differential is zero.

subsection.title: Positive volume order
subsection.p: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz} is the positive volume form in the usual orientation of \mathbb R^3.
Cyclic orders are positive: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=dy\wedge dz\wedge dx=dz\wedge dx\wedge dy.}
Reversed cyclic orders are negative: \boxed{dx\wedge dz\wedge dy=dy\wedge dx\wedge dz=dz\wedge dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}

subsection.title: Distributive rules
subsection.p: Functions can be moved through wedge products: \boxed{(f\alpha)\wedge\beta=f(\alpha\wedge\beta).}

subsection.title: Graded sign rule
subsection.p: If \alpha is a k-form and \beta is an \ell-form, then \boxed{\alpha\wedge\beta=(-1)^{k\ell}\beta\wedge\alpha.}
Examples: \boxed{\text{\(1\)-forms anticommute.}}

subsection.title: Two 1-forms in the plane
subsection.p: Let \alpha=a\,dx+b\,dy, \qquad \beta=c\,dx+d\,dy.
Then \boxed{\alpha\wedge\beta=(ad-bc)\,dx\wedge dy.}
This is the determinant: \boxed{ad-bc=\det\begin{pmatrix} a&c\\ b&d \end{pmatrix}.}

subsection.title: Two 1-forms in space
subsection.p: Let \alpha=a_1\,dx+a_2\,dy+a_3\,dz, and \beta=b_1\,dx+b_2\,dy+b_3\,dz.

Then
\boxed{\begin{aligned} \alpha\wedge\beta \amp= (a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\,dy\wedge dz\\ \amp\quad+ (a_3b_1-a_1b_3)\,dz\wedge dx\\ \amp\quad+ (a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\,dx\wedge dy. \end{aligned}}
The coefficients are the components of \boxed{\mathbf a\times\mathbf b.}

subsection.title: Three 1-forms in space
subsection.p: Let \alpha=a_1dx+a_2dy+a_3dz, \beta=b_1dx+b_2dy+b_3dz, \gamma=c_1dx+c_2dy+c_3dz.
Then \boxed{\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma=\det\begin{pmatrix} a_1&b_1&c_1\\ a_2&b_2&c_2\\ a_3&b_3&c_3 \end{pmatrix} dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p: The wedge product is not ordinary multiplication.
Order matters.
Repeated differentials vanish.
In \mathbb R^3, every 4-form is zero because there are only three coordinate directions.

subsection.title: Meaning
subsection.p: A pullback rewrites a form in new parameters.
If F:\text{parameter space}\to\text{physical space}, then \boxed{F^*\omega} is the form \omega written in the parameter variables.
Pullbacks are the form version of substitution.

subsection.title: Pullback along a curve
subsection.p: Therefore \boxed{\int_C \omega = \int_a^b \mathbf r^*\omega.}

subsection.title: Pullback over a parametrized surface
Flux form pullback
subsection.p: Let \Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy. Then \boxed{\mathbf r^*\Phi_{\mathbf F} = \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v) \,du\wedge dv.}
Thus \boxed{\iint_S \Phi_{\mathbf F} = \iint_D \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v) \,du\,dv.}

subsection.title: Pullback under a coordinate change
subsection.p: Let T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)). Then \boxed{T^*(dx\wedge dy) = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \,du\wedge dv.}

subsection.title: Polar pullback
Cylindrical pullback
Spherical pullback
subsection.p: For x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta, y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta, z=\rho\cos\phi, \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz = \rho^2\sin\phi\, d\rho\wedge d\phi\wedge d\theta.}

subsection.title: Common warnings
subsection.p: Pullbacks respect wedge products: \boxed{F^*(\alpha\wedge\beta)=F^*\alpha\wedge F^*\beta.}
Pullbacks respect exterior derivatives: \boxed{F^*(d\omega)=d(F^*\omega).}

warning.p: Ordinary change of variables uses absolute values for positive area and volume. Differential forms keep orientation signs.

subsection.title: Main idea
subsection.p: The exterior derivative raises degree by one: \boxed{d:\text{\(k\)-forms}\longrightarrow \text{\((k+1)\)-forms}.}

subsection.title: Derivative of a 0-form
subsection.p: In the plane: \boxed{df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy.}
In space: \boxed{df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz.}
This corresponds to the gradient.

subsection.title: Derivative of a plane 1-form
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy.
Then \boxed{d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.}
This is scalar curl times signed area.

subsection.title: Derivative of a space 1-form
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.
Then \boxed{\begin{aligned} d\omega &= (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz\\ &\quad+ (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx\\ &\quad+ (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. \end{aligned}}
This corresponds to curl.

subsection.title: Derivative of a space 2-form
subsection.p: Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy.
Then \boxed{d\Phi=(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.}
This corresponds to divergence.

subsection.title: Derivative of a 3-form in \mathbb R^3
subsection.p: If \Omega=f\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, then \boxed{d\Omega=0} in \mathbb R^3.
There are no nonzero 4-forms in three-dimensional space.

subsection.title: Product rule
subsection.p: If \alpha is a k-form, then \boxed{d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta.}
Special case for a function f: \boxed{d(f\alpha)=df\wedge\alpha+f\,d\alpha.}

subsection.title: Exterior derivative squared
subsection.p: Usually written: \boxed{d^2=0.}
Classical meanings: \boxed{\operatorname{curl}(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0.}

subsection.title: Closed and exact forms
subsection.p: A form \omega is closed if \boxed{d\omega=0.}
Exact forms are always closed: \boxed{\omega=d\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d\omega=d^2\eta=0.}
The converse is not always true. Holes in the domain can prevent a closed form from being exact.

warning.p: Partial derivative notation depends on the coordinate variables being used.
The exterior derivative does not depend on a metric.
The gradient, curl, and divergence interpretations use Euclidean structure to translate forms back into vectors.

section.title: Classical vector calculus translated into forms

subsection.title: Gradient
subsection.p: Classical: \nabla f=(f_x,f_y,f_z).
Forms: df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy+f_z\,dz.
Translation: df(\mathbf v)=\nabla f\cdot \mathbf v.

subsection.title: Work form
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), classical line integral: \int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.
Forms: \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.

subsection.title: Curl
subsection.p:
Classical:
\nabla\times\mathbf F = (R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).

Forms:
d\omega_{\mathbf F} = (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz + (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx + (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

Translation:
d\omega_{\mathbf F} = \Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}.

subsection.title: Flux form
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), classical flux: \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS.

Forms:
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Divergence
subsection.p: Classical: \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=P_x+Q_y+R_z.

Forms:
d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

Translation:
d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

subsection.title: Plane circulation
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(P,Q), work form: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy.
Scalar curl: \operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf F=Q_x-P_y.
Forms: d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Plane flux
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(M,N), the outward flux form on a positively oriented boundary is \phi_{\mathbf F}=M\,dy-N\,dx.

Then
\int_{\partial R}\phi_{\mathbf F} = \int_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,ds.

Its exterior derivative is
d\phi_{\mathbf F} = (M_x+N_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

So
d\phi_{\mathbf F} = (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Vector identities from d^2=0
subsection.p: From d(df)=0, we get \nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0.
From d(d\omega_{\mathbf F})=0, we get \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0.

table.title: Classical language and forms language.

warning.title: Common warnings
warning.p:
The same vector field \mathbf F can produce two different forms: \omega_{\mathbf F}=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz for work and circulation.
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy
for flux.
Do not confuse these.

subsection.title: The theorem
subsection.p: Here M is compact and oriented with piecewise smooth boundary, and \omega is a C^1 form of degree \dim M-1 on an open neighborhood of M. The boundary has the induced orientation. This is the generalized Stokes theorem.
It says:

subsection.title: Degree matching
subsection.p: If M is k-dimensional, then \omega is a (k-1)-form and d\omega is a k-form.

table.title: Degree matching between a region, its form, and the derivative.

subsection.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
subsection.p: Let M=[a,b], and let \omega=f. Then d\omega=df=f'(x)\,dx.

subsection.title: Green's theorem: circulation form
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy.
Then d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Green's theorem: flux form
subsection.p: Let \mathbf F=(M,N), and let \phi_{\mathbf F}=M\,dy-N\,dx.
Then d\phi_{\mathbf F}=(M_x+N_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Stokes' theorem in space
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.
Then d\omega=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}.

subsection.title: Divergence theorem
subsection.p:
Let
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy.

Then
d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

subsection.title: Orientation rules
Hypotheses checklist
subsection.p: Before using Stokes' theorem, check:

ol.li: The form is defined on the region and its boundary.
The needed partial derivatives exist and are continuous.
The boundary has the induced orientation.
Singularities are not inside the region unless handled separately.
The surface or region is piecewise smooth.

warning.p: If \omega=d\eta, then d\omega=0.
So exact implies closed.
But closed does not always imply exact.
A missing point or hole in the domain can prevent a potential from existing globally.

subsection.title: Boundary of a boundary
subsection.p: These are two sides of the same idea.

p.md: \boxed{dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=dy\wedge dz\wedge dx=dz\wedge dx\wedge dy}
\boxed{\mathbf r^*\Phi_{\mathbf F}=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v))\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\wedge dv}

introduction.p: This appendix records why the main theorems are true and which earlier facts they use. It is not a full proof chapter. It is a map of the logic. In particular, the subdivision discussions for general curved boundaries and coordinate changes are proof outlines; they do not supply all limiting estimates. The complete rectangle and box calculations are in . These sketches should not be read as full proofs of every stated general case.
Each entry gives:

table.title: What each entry records.

row.cell: the assumptions that make the theorem safe
the main mechanism behind the proof
why the hypotheses are not decoration

table.title: The main source of each theorem's proof.

row.cell: single-variable Mean Value Theorem along coordinate steps
two orders of measuring rectangle change

subsection.title: Statement
subsection.p: Let f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R. If the first partial derivatives of f exist in a neighborhood of \mathbf p and are continuous at \mathbf p, then f is differentiable at \mathbf p.
In two variables: \boxed{ f(a+h,b+k) = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)h + f_y(a,b)k + \text{error} } where \boxed{ \frac{\text{error}}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}\to0 \quad\text{as }(h,k)\to(0,0). }

subsection.title: Differential form
Hypotheses

md.mrow: 1. \amp \text{The partial derivatives exist near the point.}
2. \amp \text{The partial derivatives are continuous at the point.}

subsection.p: The theorem is a sufficient condition, not a necessary condition.
A function can be differentiable even if its partial derivatives are not continuous.

subsection.title: Proof idea in two variables
subsection.p: Move from (a,b) to (a+h,b+k) in two coordinate steps: (a,b)\to(a+h,b)\to(a+h,b+k).

Then
f(a+h,b+k)-f(a,b) \amp= \bigl[f(a+h,b+k)-f(a+h,b)\bigr] \amp\quad+ \bigl[f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)\bigr].
Apply the one-variable Mean Value Theorem to each coordinate slice: f(a+h,b)-f(a,b) \approx f_x(a,b)h, f(a+h,b+k)-f(a+h,b) \approx f_y(a,b)k.

Continuity of f_x and f_y makes the approximation uniform as (h,k)\to(0,0). More precisely, the Mean Value Theorem writes the two increments as h f_x(a+\theta h,b) and k f_y(a+h,b+\tau k) for some 0\lt\theta,\tau\lt1 (a zero increment contributes zero). Continuity at (a,b) makes each partial differ from its value there by less than \varepsilon when \sqrt{h^2+k^2} is small enough. Hence the error after subtracting the proposed linear part has magnitude at most \varepsilon(|h|+|k|)\le\sqrt2\varepsilon\sqrt{h^2+k^2}. Dividing by the increment length proves the required limit. In n variables, use n coordinate steps and \sum_i|h_i|\le\sqrt n\,|\mathbf h|.

subsection.title: What can fail
subsection.p: Partial derivatives can exist without differentiability.
At the origin, f_x(0,0)=0, \qquad f_y(0,0)=0.
If these partial derivatives gave a true differential, the linear approximation would be zero.
But along the path (x,y)=(t,t), we get f(t,t)=\frac{t^2}{\sqrt{2t^2}}=\frac{|t|}{\sqrt2}.
The distance to the origin is \sqrt{t^2+t^2}=\sqrt2\,|t|.
The ratio is \frac{|t|/\sqrt2}{\sqrt2\,|t|}=\frac12, which does not go to 0.
So f is not differentiable at the origin.

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: Coordinate slopes alone do not guarantee a true tangent plane. Continuous partial derivatives stitch the coordinate information into one linear approximation.

subsection.title: Statement
subsection.p: More generally, if the relevant higher partial derivatives are continuous, then the order of differentiation can be switched.

md.mrow: 1. \amp f_{xy}\text{ and }f_{yx}\text{ exist near the point.}
2. \amp f_{xy}\text{ and }f_{yx}\text{ are continuous near the point.}

subsection.title: Proof idea
subsection.p: Measure the net change of f around a small rectangle: [a,a+h]\times[b,b+k].
Form the corner difference \boxed{\Delta=f(a+h,b+k)-f(a+h,b)-f(a,b+k)+f(a,b).}
Compute \Delta in two ways.
First, take x-changes, then y-changes. This connects \Delta to f_{xy}.
Second, take y-changes, then x-changes. This connects \Delta to f_{yx}.
Both computations measure the same corner difference. After division by hk and letting h,k\to0, continuity forces f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b).

subsection.title: What can fail
subsection.p: If the mixed partials are not continuous, they can differ.
Also, f_y(x,0)=x, so f_{yx}(0,0)=1.
Thus \boxed{f_{xy}(0,0)\ne f_{yx}(0,0).}

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: The equality of mixed partials is not only about the symbols xy and yx. It is about enough smoothness to make the small-rectangle measurement independent of the order in which it is taken.

section.title: Fubini's theorem and change of variables

subsection.title: Fubini's theorem: statement
subsection.p:
If f is continuous on a rectangle R=[a,b]\times[c,d], then
\boxed{ \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_c^d\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy. }

subsection.title: Fubini: hypotheses
subsection.p: For the version used most often in this book:

md.mrow: 1. \amp \text{The region is a rectangle, box, or a region described by clean bounds.}
2. \amp \text{The function is continuous on the compact region.}

subsection.title: Fubini: proof idea
subsection.p: A double integral is a limit of sums over small rectangles: \sum f(x_i^*,y_j^*)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y.

Group the same sum by columns:
\sum_i \left( \sum_j f(x_i^*,y_j^*)\,\Delta y \right) \Delta x.
The inner sum becomes an integral in y. The outer sum becomes an integral in x.
Group by rows instead, and the order reverses.

subsection.title: Fubini: what can fail
subsection.p: For continuous functions on compact regions with piecewise smooth boundary, Fubini is safe.
For improper integrals, changing the order can change the value if the integral is not absolutely convergent.
The safe rule is:
Without absolute convergence, be careful.

subsection.title: Change of variables: statement
subsection.p:
For a C^1 coordinate map T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)), the change of variables formula is
\boxed{ \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_{\widetilde R} f(T(u,v)) \left| \det DT(u,v) \right| \,du\,dv. }
The ordinary area formula uses |\det DT|.

subsection.title: Change of variables: hypotheses
subsection.p: The standard version assumes:

md.mrow: 2. \amp T\text{ is one-to-one on the region, except possibly on boundary pieces.}
4. \amp \text{The regions are compact with piecewise smooth boundary; }T(\widetilde R)=R.

subsection.title: Change of variables: proof idea
subsection.p:
Near a point (u,v), the map T is almost linear:
T(u+\Delta u,v+\Delta v) \approx T(u,v)+DT \begin{pmatrix} \Delta u\\ \Delta v \end{pmatrix}.
A tiny rectangle in the uv-plane becomes almost a parallelogram in the xy-plane.
Add over many tiny rectangles and pass to the limit.

md.mrow: 2. \amp \text{Determinant as area or volume scale factor.}

subsection.title: Change of variables: what can fail
subsection.p: If the map is not one-to-one, the integral may count points more than once.
Example: polar coordinates with 0\le \theta\le4\pi trace a full disk twice.
If the Jacobian vanishes on a whole region, the map may collapse area.
If the orientation matters, do not replace \det DT by |\det DT|. The sign is part of the form.

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: Fubini explains how to add by slices. Change of variables explains how small pieces change size and orientation under a new coordinate language.

subsection.title: Statement in forms
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy.

Since d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy, this is
\boxed{ \int_{\partial R}P\,dx+Q\,dy = \iint_R (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. }

subsection.title: Classical statement
Hypotheses

md.mrow: 1. \amp R\text{ is a bounded plane region with piecewise smooth boundary.}
3. \amp P\text{ and }Q\text{ have continuous first partial derivatives on a region containing }R.

subsection.title: Proof idea
subsection.p: First prove the theorem for one small rectangle.
For R=[a,a+h]\times[b,b+k], the line integral around the rectangle compares opposite sides.
Horizontal sides produce the term -P_y\,hk.
Vertical sides produce the term Q_x\,hk.

Together:
\int_{\partial R}P\,dx+Q\,dy \approx (Q_x-P_y)hk.
Then subdivide a larger region into many small rectangles.
Interior edges are walked twice in opposite directions, so their contributions cancel.
Only the outer boundary remains.
Let the mesh size go to zero.

subsection.title: What can fail
subsection.p: Orientation matters.
If the boundary is walked clockwise instead of counterclockwise, the sign changes.
The field must be defined on the whole region.

Example:
\omega= \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx + \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy.
This form is defined on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}.
On that punctured plane, d\omega=0.
But around the unit circle, \int_{C}\omega=2\pi.
Green's theorem cannot be applied to the disk bounded by C, because \omega is not defined at the origin.

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: Green's theorem is a cancellation theorem. Local rotation inside a region adds up to circulation around the boundary, as long as the field is smooth on the whole region.

subsection.title: Statement in forms
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.
If S is an oriented surface with oriented boundary \partial S, then \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.}

subsection.title: Classical statement
Hypotheses

md.mrow: 1. \amp S\text{ is a compact oriented piecewise smooth surface.}
2. \amp \partial S\text{ has the boundary orientation induced by }S.
3. \amp P,Q,R\text{ have continuous first partial derivatives near }S.
4. \amp \omega\text{ is defined on a region containing }S.

subsection.p: Boundary orientation is given by the right-hand rule: \boxed{\text{thumb points along the chosen normal, fingers curl along }\partial S.}

subsection.title: Proof idea
subsection.p: For a single regular patch, use a C^2 parametrization that is one-to-one in the interior and traces the boundary once: \mathbf r(u,v).
Pull back the 1-form: \mathbf r^*\omega.
Now \mathbf r^*\omega is a 1-form in the uv-plane.
Apply Green's theorem in the parameter region: \int_{\partial D}\mathbf r^*\omega=\int_D d(\mathbf r^*\omega).
Use the pullback identity, established by the coordinate calculation in the surface case: \boxed{d(\mathbf r^*\omega)=\mathbf r^*(d\omega).}
This gives \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.

subsection.title: What can fail
subsection.p: Orientation matters.
If the surface normal is reversed, then the boundary orientation reverses and both sides change sign.
The field must be defined on the surface.
Singularities can break the theorem if they lie on the chosen surface.
If S has no boundary, then \partial S=\varnothing, so Stokes gives \boxed{\int_S d\omega=0.}

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: Stokes' theorem is Green's theorem on a curved surface. The pullback flattens the surface into a parameter region where Green's theorem can do the work.

subsection.title: Statement in forms
subsection.p:
Let
\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.

subsection.title: Proof idea
subsection.p: First prove the theorem for a small rectangular box.

Flux through the two x-faces gives approximately
P_x\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z.

Flux through the two y-faces gives approximately
Q_y\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z.

Flux through the two z-faces gives approximately
R_z\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z.

Together:
\text{outward flux} \approx (P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,\Delta V.
Now subdivide a solid into many small boxes.
Flux through interior faces cancels because each shared face is outward for one box and inward for the neighboring box.
Only the outer boundary remains.
Let the box sizes shrink.

subsection.title: What can fail
subsection.p: The field must be defined inside the solid, not only on the boundary.

Example:
\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \frac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}.
This field is not defined at the origin.

Away from the origin,
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0.

But on the unit sphere,
\mathbf F=\widehat{\mathbf n},
so
\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iint_S 1\,dS = 4\pi.
The divergence theorem cannot be applied to the unit ball because the field is singular at the origin.

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: The divergence theorem is a flux bookkeeping theorem. What leaves through the boundary is accounted for by sources and sinks inside, provided the field is smooth throughout the solid.

subsection.title: Statement
subsection.p:
For an oriented k-dimensional region M and a (k-1)-form \omega,
\boxed{ \int_{\partial M}\omega = \int_M d\omega. }
This single statement includes:

subsection.title: Degree matching
subsection.p: If \dim M=k, then \omega must be a (k-1)-form and d\omega is a k-form.

subsection.title: Hypotheses
subsection.p: The clean version assumes:

md.mrow: 1. \amp M\text{ is compact, oriented, and piecewise smooth.}
2. \amp \partial M\text{ has the induced boundary orientation.}
3. \amp \omega\text{ is }C^1\text{ on an open neighborhood of }M.

subsection.title: Proof idea
subsection.p: Break M into many small oriented pieces.
On each small piece, the theorem reduces to the coordinate version.
When the small pieces are added, every interior boundary appears twice with opposite orientations.
Those interior contributions cancel.
Only the boundary of the whole region remains.
This is the same cancellation pattern behind Green's theorem and the divergence theorem.

subsection.title: Boundary of a boundary
subsection.p: These two facts match.
If \partial(\partial M)=0, then for a C^2 form \omega of degree k-2, applying Stokes twice gives \int_{\partial(\partial M)}\omega=0.
On the derivative side, \int_M d(d\omega)=\int_M 0=0.

subsection.title: Closed and exact
subsection.p: Closed need not imply exact.
A hole in the domain can prevent exactness.

subsection.title: What can fail
subsection.p: If the form is not defined on all of M, Stokes' theorem may fail.
If the orientation of \partial M is wrong, the sign is wrong.
If M has corners, edges, or several patches, it must be handled as a piecewise smooth object with consistent orientations.
If singularities are inside the region, remove small neighborhoods around them and include the new boundary pieces.

subsection.title: Moral
subsection.p: Every version of Stokes' theorem says the same thing:
The shape of the region changes from interval to surface to solid, but the mechanism is always the same: orient, differentiate, integrate, and cancel interior boundaries.

table.title: What each result depends on.

section.title: One-page theorem summary
section.p: for continuous f on a suitable region.

introduction.p: Computers are useful in multivariable calculus for three jobs:

table.title: Three jobs a computer does in multivariable calculus.

row.cell: symbolic derivatives, Jacobians, line and surface integrals

introduction.p: This appendix gives compact lab recipes. It uses Python-style notation, with NumPy, Matplotlib, SciPy, and SymPy. The mathematics does not depend on the software.

table.title: Each mathematical task and the computational tool that fits it.

row.cell: iterated integral, midpoint rule, Monte Carlo

subsection.title: Standard imports

program.code: import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

subsection.p: For symbolic work:

program.code: import sympy as sp

subsection.p: For numerical integration and ODEs:

program.code: from scipy.integrate import dblquad, tplquad, solve_ivp

subsection.title: Grid for a function of two variables
subsection.p: For z=f(x,y), make arrays of x- and y-values:

program.code: x = np.linspace(a, b, 200) y = np.linspace(c, d, 200) X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y) Z = f(X, Y)

subsection.p: Here X, Y, and Z are arrays. The function f must accept arrays.

program.code:
fig = plt.figure() ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")
ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z)
ax.set_xlabel("x") ax.set_ylabel("y") ax.set_zlabel("z") plt.show()

subsection.title: Wireframe plot

program.code:
fig = plt.figure() ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")
ax.plot_wireframe(X, Y, Z)
plt.show()

subsection.p: A wireframe is often easier to read than a solid surface.

subsection.title: Contour plot
subsection.p: A contour plot shows level curves: f(x,y)=c.

program.code: plt.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=20) plt.xlabel("x") plt.ylabel("y") plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.p: Filled contour plot: contourf

program.code: plt.contourf(X, Y, Z, levels=30) plt.colorbar() plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.title: Implicit curves
subsection.p: To plot F(x,y)=0, plot the zero contour:

program.code: Z = F(X, Y) plt.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=[0]) plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.p: To plot F(x,y)=c, use:

program.code: plt.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=[c])

subsection.title: Common examples
subsection.p: Plane: z=ax+by+c.
Bowl: z=x^2+y^2.
Saddle: z=x^2-y^2.
Radial wave: z=\sin\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.

subsection.title: Plotting a parametrized surface
subsection.p: For \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)), use a parameter grid:

program.code:
u = np.linspace(u0, u1, 150) v = np.linspace(v0, v1, 150) U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v)
X = x(U, V) Y = y(U, V) Z = z(U, V)
fig = plt.figure() ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d") ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z) plt.show()

theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 150) z = np.linspace(z0, z1, 100) Theta, Z = np.meshgrid(theta, z)
X = R*np.cos(Theta) Y = R*np.sin(Theta)
ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z)

phi = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 150) theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 150) Phi, Theta = np.meshgrid(phi, theta)
X = R*np.sin(Phi)*np.cos(Theta) Y = R*np.sin(Phi)*np.sin(Theta) Z = R*np.cos(Phi)
ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z)

table.title: Plotting checklist

row.cell: Choose a domain large enough to show the important feature.
Use enough grid points to avoid jagged artifacts.
Check whether the plot hides singularities or holes.

warning.p: A computer plot is a sample, not a proof.
A surface may look smooth because the grid is too coarse.
A contour may disappear if the requested level is outside the range of plotted values.
A 3-D plot may distort scale unless the axes are adjusted.

subsection.title: Vector field in the plane
subsection.p: A vector field in the plane has the form \mathbf F(x,y)=(P(x,y),Q(x,y)).
On a grid:

program.code:
x = np.linspace(a, b, 25) y = np.linspace(c, d, 25) X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
P = Pfun(X, Y) Q = Qfun(X, Y)
plt.quiver(X, Y, P, Q) plt.axis("equal") plt.xlabel("x") plt.ylabel("y") plt.show()

subsection.title: Normalized arrows
subsection.p: Sometimes large arrows hide the pattern. Normalize arrows:

program.code:
speed = np.sqrt(P**2 + Q**2) P0 = P / (speed + 1e-12) Q0 = Q / (speed + 1e-12)
plt.quiver(X, Y, P0, Q0) plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.p: This shows direction but not magnitude.

subsection.title: Stream plot
subsection.p: Streamlines solve \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)).

program.code: plt.streamplot(X, Y, P, Q) plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.title: Common vector fields
subsection.p: Constant field: \mathbf F(x,y)=(1,0).
Radial source: \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,y).
Radial sink: \mathbf F(x,y)=(-x,-y).
Rotation: \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x).
Saddle field: \mathbf F(x,y)=(x,-y).
Inverse radial field: \mathbf F(x,y)=\frac{(x,y)}{x^2+y^2}.

subsection.title: Gradient field
subsection.p: For f=f(x,y), \nabla f=(f_x,f_y).
Numerically, use np.gradient if f is sampled on a grid:

program.code:
Z = f(X, Y)
dy = y[1] - y[0] dx = x[1] - x[0]
Z_y, Z_x = np.gradient(Z, dy, dx)
plt.quiver(X, Y, Z_x, Z_y) plt.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=20) plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.title: Vector field in space
subsection.p: A vector field in space has the form \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(P,Q,R).
A 3-D quiver plot:

program.code:
fig = plt.figure() ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")
ax.quiver(X, Y, Z, P, Q, R)
plt.show()

subsection.p: Use fewer grid points in 3-D. Too many arrows quickly become unreadable.

subsection.title: Field line through one point
subsection.p: For \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)), use an ODE solver:

program.code:
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
def ode(t, r): x, y = r return [Pfun(x, y), Qfun(x, y)]
sol = solve_ivp(ode, [t0, t1], [x0, y0], max_step=0.02)
plt.plot(sol.y[0], sol.y[1]) plt.axis("equal") plt.show()

subsection.title: Common warnings
subsection.p: Arrow length in a plot may be automatically rescaled.
A normalized quiver plot hides speed.
A stream plot may hide sources, sinks, or singularities.
A vector field with a hole in its domain should not be plotted as if the hole were ordinary.

subsection.title: Forward difference
subsection.p: For a one-variable function, f'(a)\approx \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.
This is simple but less accurate.

subsection.title: Central difference
subsection.p: This is usually better.

subsection.title: Partial derivatives
subsection.p: For f=f(x,y), f_x(a,b) \approx \frac{f(a+h,b)-f(a-h,b)}{2h}. f_y(a,b) \approx \frac{f(a,b+h)-f(a,b-h)}{2h}.

subsection.title: Jacobian matrix
subsection.p:
For F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, the Jacobian matrix is
J_F(\mathbf p) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} \amp \cdots \amp \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_n}\\[2mm] \vdots \amp \ddots \amp \vdots\\[2mm] \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_1} \amp \cdots \amp \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}_{\mathbf p}.

subsection.title: Numerical Hessian
subsection.p: For f=f(x,y), f_{xx}\approx \frac{f(x+h,y)-2f(x,y)+f(x-h,y)}{h^2}. f_{yy}\approx \frac{f(x,y+h)-2f(x,y)+f(x,y-h)}{h^2}. f_{xy}\approx \frac{f(x+h,y+h)-f(x+h,y-h)-f(x-h,y+h)+f(x-h,y-h)}{4h^2}.

subsection.title: Symbolic Jacobian
subsection.p: Using SymPy:

program.code:
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
F = sp.Matrix([ x**2 + y, sp.sin(x*y) ])
J = F.jacobian([x, y])
f = x**3 + x*y + y**2 H = sp.hessian(f, (x, y))

warning.p: If h is too large, the approximation error is large.
If h is too small, roundoff error can dominate.
Numerical derivatives can produce misleading numbers near:
A finite-difference approximation does not prove differentiability.

subsection.title: Midpoint rule in one variable
subsection.p: Here \Delta x=\frac{b-a}{N}, and x_i^* is the midpoint of the ith subinterval.

subsection.title: Midpoint rule over a rectangle
subsection.p: For R=[a,b]\times[c,d], \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA \approx \sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{N} f(x_i^*,y_j^*)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y.

program.code:
def midpoint_double(f, a, b, c, d, M=200, N=200): dx = (b - a) / M dy = (d - c) / N
x = a + (np.arange(M) + 0.5)*dx y = c + (np.arange(N) + 0.5)*dy
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y) values = np.broadcast_to(f(X, Y), X.shape) return np.sum(values)*dx*dy

subsection.title: Region under variable bounds
subsection.p: For a\le x\le b, \qquad g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x), \iint_R f\,dA = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.
Using dblquad:

program.code:
from scipy.integrate import dblquad
value, error = dblquad( lambda y, x: f(x, y), a, b, lambda x: g1(x), lambda x: g2(x) )

subsection.title: Polar numerical integration
subsection.p: If x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta, then dA=r\,dr\,d\theta.
So \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_{\widetilde R} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
Code pattern:

program.code: value, error = dblquad( lambda r, theta: f(r*np.cos(theta), r*np.sin(theta))*r, theta0, theta1, lambda theta: r0(theta), lambda theta: r1(theta) )

subsection.title: Triple integral over a box
subsection.p: For B=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f], \iiint_B F(x,y,z)\,dV \approx \sum F(x_i^*,y_j^*,z_k^*)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z.

subsection.title: Triple integral with variable bounds
subsection.p: For a\le x\le b, g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x), h_1(x,y)\le z\le h_2(x,y), \iiint_E F\,dV = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} \int_{h_1(x,y)}^{h_2(x,y)} F(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.
Using tplquad:

program.code:
from scipy.integrate import tplquad
value, error = tplquad( lambda z, y, x: F(x, y, z), a, b, lambda x: g1(x), lambda x: g2(x), lambda x, y: h1(x, y), lambda x, y: h2(x, y) )

subsection.p: Again, the innermost variable comes first.

subsection.title: Cylindrical numerical integration
subsection.p: Use the integrand F(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r.

subsection.title: Spherical numerical integration
subsection.p: Use the integrand F(\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\rho\cos\phi) \rho^2\sin\phi.

subsection.title: Monte Carlo estimate
subsection.p: For a region R inside a box B: \iint_R f\,dA \approx \operatorname{Area}(B) \cdot \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i,y_i)\mathbf 1_R(x_i,y_i).
Code pattern:
Monte Carlo is usually slow but useful in irregular regions or high dimensions.

subsection.title: Common warnings
subsection.p: Numerical integration returns an approximation and often an error estimate.
Singularities require special care.
Highly oscillatory functions require finer sampling.
Coordinate changes require Jacobian factors.
Improper integrals may appear finite on a finite sample but still diverge.

subsection.title: Symbolic setup

program.code: import sympy as sp

subsection.p: Define variables:

program.code: x, y, z, t, u, v = sp.symbols("x y z t u v")

subsection.title: Line integral of a 1-form
subsection.p: Let \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.
Let \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)), \qquad a\le t\le b.

Then
\int_C\omega = \int_a^b \left[ P(\mathbf r(t))x'(t) + Q(\mathbf r(t))y'(t) + R(\mathbf r(t))z'(t) \right]\,dt.

program.code:
x, y, z, t = sp.symbols("x y z t")
P = ... Q = ... R = ...
xt = ... yt = ... zt = ...
integrand = ( P.subs({x: xt, y: yt, z: zt})*sp.diff(xt, t) + Q.subs({x: xt, y: yt, z: zt})*sp.diff(yt, t) + R.subs({x: xt, y: yt, z: zt})*sp.diff(zt, t) )
value = sp.integrate(integrand, (t, a, b))

subsection.title: Line integral of a vector field
subsection.p: For \mathbf F=(P,Q,R), \int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r uses the same formula as the 1-form P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz.

subsection.title: Surface flux integral
subsection.p: Let \mathbf F=(P,Q,R).
Let \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)).

Then
\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iint_D \mathbf F(\mathbf r(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v) \,du\,dv.

subsection.title: SymPy surface flux pattern

program.code:
x, y, z, u, v = sp.symbols("x y z u v")
P = ... Q = ... R = ...
xu = ... yu = ... zu = ...
r = sp.Matrix([xu, yu, zu]) ru = r.diff(u) rv = r.diff(v)
normal = ru.cross(rv)
F = sp.Matrix([ P.subs({x: xu, y: yu, z: zu}), Q.subs({x: xu, y: yu, z: zu}), R.subs({x: xu, y: yu, z: zu}) ])
integrand = sp.simplify(F.dot(normal))
value = sp.integrate( integrand, (u, u0, u1), (v, v0, v1) )

subsection.p: The order of (u,v) bounds must match the expression.

subsection.title: Surface area
subsection.p: Symbolic pattern:

program.code: area_integrand = sp.sqrt(normal.dot(normal)) area = sp.integrate(area_integrand, (u, u0, u1), (v, v0, v1))

subsection.title: Curl
subsection.p:
For \mathbf F=(P,Q,R),
\nabla\times\mathbf F = (R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y).
SymPy pattern:

program.code: curlF = sp.Matrix([ sp.diff(R, y) - sp.diff(Q, z), sp.diff(P, z) - sp.diff(R, x), sp.diff(Q, x) - sp.diff(P, y) ])

subsection.title: Divergence
subsection.p: SymPy pattern:

program.code: divF = sp.diff(P, x) + sp.diff(Q, y) + sp.diff(R, z)

subsection.title: Gradient
subsection.p: SymPy pattern:

program.code: gradf = sp.Matrix([ sp.diff(f, x), sp.diff(f, y), sp.diff(f, z) ])

subsection.title: Jacobian
subsection.p:
For F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m),
J_F=\left(\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}\right).
SymPy pattern:

program.code: F = sp.Matrix([F1, F2, F3]) J = F.jacobian([x, y, z])

subsection.title: Green's theorem check
subsection.p:
For \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy,
d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.
Symbolic scalar curl:

program.code: scalar_curl = sp.diff(Q, x) - sp.diff(P, y)

subsection.title: Orientation warnings
subsection.p: For a curve, reversing the parametrization changes the sign of a 1-form integral.
For a surface, switching u and v changes \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v to -\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v.
Flux changes sign when orientation reverses.
Surface area does not.

subsection.title: Symbolic warnings
subsection.p: A symbolic answer may be correct but hard to read.
Use: \texttt{sp.simplify}
Always check assumptions, especially signs and parameter ranges.

subsection.title: Flow lines
subsection.p: A flow line of a vector field \mathbf F solves the differential equation \frac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)).
In the plane: x'=P(x,y), \qquad y'=Q(x,y).
In space: x'=P(x,y,z), \qquad y'=Q(x,y,z), \qquad z'=R(x,y,z).

subsection.title: Euler method
